Show that $X \rightarrow A^{-1} X A \equiv\left(A^{-1} X\right) A=A^{-1}(X A)$ is an automorphism in $\mathfrak{A}_{n}$. If $\mathfrak{A}$ has an involution $x \rightarrow \bar{x}$ and $\bar{A}^{t}= \pm A$ then $X \rightarrow A^{-1} \bar{X}^{t} A$ is an involution in $\mathfrak{A}_{n}$.
8. (Sasser). Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be an alternative algebra with 1 and an involution $x \rightarrow \bar{x}$ whose symmetric elements are in the nucleus. Prove that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}\right)$ is a special Jordan algebra.
6. Varieties of algebras. Free algebras. In this section we wish to make precise the notion of an algebra satisfying a set of identities. Associative, Lie, alternative and Jordan algebras are special cases and it is desirable, when possible, to treat these as special cases of a general theory of classes of algebras satisfying identities. We shall construct free algebras for such classes and formulate conditions on a given set of identities which insure that the algebras obtained by extending the base field remain in the given class and the same holds for the algebras obtained by adjoining an identity element.
We shall use the following terminology: a set $S$ with a binary composition (associative binary composition) $(a, b) \rightarrow a b$ will be called a monad (monoid). It is customary in these definitions to assume the existence of an identity element. However, this is inconvenient for us so we shall use monad (monoid) with 1 when the existence of an identity element is assumed. We wish to give a construction first of a free monad generated by a given set. While this can be done directly it is perhaps clearer to base the construction on monoids and we shall follow this method. Let $X$ be an arbitrary nonvacuous set and let $M(X)^{\prime}$ denote the set of words or monomials $x_{\alpha_{1}} x_{\alpha_{2}} \cdots x_{\alpha_{k}}, k \geqq 1$, formed of $x_{\alpha_{i}} \in X$. We define a product in $M(X)^{\prime}$ by juxtaposition: $\left(x_{\alpha_{1}} \cdots x_{\alpha_{k}}\right)\left(x_{\beta_{1}} \cdots x_{\beta_{1}}\right)=x_{\alpha_{1}} \cdots x_{\alpha_{k}} x_{\beta_{1}} \cdots x_{\beta_{1}}{ }^{3}$ This is clearly an associative composition so $M(X)^{\prime}$ with its multiplication is a monoid. The monoid $M(X)^{\prime}$ does not have an identity element. However, we can adjoin one by forming $M(X)=M(X)^{\prime} \cup\{1\}$ where $1 \notin M(X)^{\prime}$ and defining $1 m=m=m 1$, $m \in M(X)$. Then the associative law is valid also in $M(X)$, so this is a monoid with 1 . The monoid $M(X)^{\prime}(M(X))$ has the following universal property. If $S$ is any monoid (monoid with 1 ) then any mapping $x \rightarrow y$ of $X$ into $S$ has a unique extension to a homomorphism of $M(X)^{\prime}(M(X))$ into $S$ (sending 1 into 1). Accordingly, we call $M(X)^{\prime}(M(X))$ the free monoid (free monoid with 1$)$ generated by $X$. If $Y$ is a subset of $X$ then we define the $Y$-degree of $m=x_{\alpha_{1}} \cdots x_{\alpha_{k}}$ to be the number of $x_{\alpha_{j}} \in Y$ occuring in $m$. If $Y=\{x\}$ then we speak of the $x$-degree rather than the $\{x\}$-degree.
We remark next that if $S$ is any monoid and $p$ is a fixed element in $S$ then we can define three $p$-compositions in $S$ by the formulas

$$
\begin{equation*}
x_{p_{L}} y=p x y, \quad x_{p_{M}} y=x p y, \quad x_{p_{R}} y=x y p . \tag{42}
\end{equation*}
$$

[^2]The middle one of these is associative but not the other two and either of these can be used in the construction we now give of a free monad generated by a set. Let $X$ be a nonvacuous set and form the free monoid $M(X, p)^{\prime} \equiv M(X \cup\{p\})^{\prime}$ generated by $X$ and an element $p \notin X$. We introduce the right $p$-composition $p_{R}$ in $M(X, p)^{\prime}$ and let $N(X)^{\prime}$ be the smallest submonad of $M(X, p)^{\prime}$ relative to the composition $p_{R}$ containing $X$. One sees easily that $N(X)^{\prime}$ can be defined inductively by degree by the rules that $X \subseteq N(X)^{\prime}$ and if $a, b \in N(X)^{\prime}$ then $a b p \in N(X)^{\prime}$. It is clear from this that the $X$-degree of any $m \in N(X)^{\prime}$ exceeds its $p$-degree by one. The elements of $N(X)^{\prime}$ of degree $>1$ have the form $u v p$ where $u, v \in N(X)^{\prime}$. It follows by induction on degree that if $w \in N(X)^{\prime}$ then no proper right factor of $w$ is of $X$-degree exceeding its $p$-degree. We use this remark to prove the following

Lemma. If $w \in N(X)^{\prime}$ has degree $>1$ then the representation of $w$ as uvp, $u, v \in N(X)^{\prime}$, is unique.

Proof. Let $w=u v p, u, v \in N(X)$,' and let $v^{\prime}$ be the right factor of least degree of $u v$ with the property that its $X$-degree exceeds its $p$-degree. Since $v$ has this property, $v^{\prime}$ is a right factor of $v$. Hence, by the result noted, we have $v^{\prime}=v$. Hence $v$ is uniquely determined. Since the cancellation law holds in $M(X)^{\prime}$, $u$ is also determined by $w$.

We now adjoin an identity element 1 to $N(X)^{\prime}$ obtaining $N(X)=\{1\} \cup N(X)^{\prime}$. We define the degree (or $Y$-degree for $Y$ a subset of $X$ ) of $w \in N(X)^{\prime}$ to be the $X$-degree ( $Y$-degree) of $w$ as element of $M(X, p)^{\prime}$. Also we define the degree ( $Y$-degree) of 1 to be 0 . Let $S$ be any monad (monad with 1 ) and let $\alpha$ be a mapping of $X$ into $S$. We extend $\alpha$ to $N(X)^{\prime}(N(X))$ inductively on degree by requiring that if $w=u v p, u, v \in N(X)^{\prime}$ then $w^{\alpha}=u^{\alpha} v^{\alpha}$ (and $1^{\alpha}=1$ ). Since the writing of $w$ as $u v p$ is unique it is clear that $\alpha$ is single valued. Also $\alpha$ is a homomorphism of $N(X)^{\prime}(N(X))$ into $S$ (sending 1 into 1). Moreover, $\alpha$ is uniquely determined by these properties. We shall call $N(X)^{\prime}(N(X))$ the free monad (free monad with 1$)$ generated by $X$. From now on we revert to the usual notation $u v$ for the product $u_{p_{R}} v$ in $N(X)^{\prime}$.

If $\mathfrak{A}$ is an algebra (associative algebra) then $\mathfrak{A}$ is a monad (monoid) relative to its multiplication composition. We shall call this the multiplicative monad (multiplicative monoid) of $\mathfrak{A}$. Let $S$ be any monad and $\Phi$ a field. Then we can form the vector space $\Phi S$ over $\Phi$ with $S$ as basis and define a product in $\Phi S$ by

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left(\sum \alpha_{i} s_{i}\right)\left(\sum \beta_{j} t_{j}\right)=\sum \alpha_{i} \beta_{j}\left(s_{i} t_{j}\right) \tag{43}
\end{equation*}
$$

for $\alpha_{i}, \beta_{j} \in \Phi, s_{i}, t_{j} \in S$. Then $\Phi S$ is an algebra over $\Phi$ which is associative if $S$ is associative and has an identity element if $S$ has one. The mapping $s \rightarrow 1 s$ is a monomorphism of $S$ into the multiplicative monoid of $\Phi S$. We shall identify $S$ with its image $1 S, s$ with $1 s$. If $\eta$ is a homomorphism of $S$ into the multiplicative monad of an algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ then $\sum \alpha_{i} s_{i} \rightarrow \sum \alpha_{i} s_{i}{ }^{\eta}$ is an algebra homomorphism of
$\Phi S$ which extends $\eta$. This is unique. We now let $S$ be one of the free systems $M(X)^{\prime}, M(X), N(X)^{\prime}, N(X)$ and accordingly we denote the resulting algebras $\Phi M(X)^{\prime}$ etc. by $\Phi\{X\}^{\prime}, \Phi\{X\}, \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}, \Phi\{\{X\}\}$ and call these respectively the free associative algebra, free associative algebra with 1, free nonassociative algebra, free nonassociative algebra with 1 generated by the set $X$.

In view of the universal property of $N(X)^{\prime}$ and of $\Phi S$ for $S$ a monad it is clear that if $\eta$ is any mapping of $X$ into an algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ then there exists a unique extension of $\eta$ to a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$. Similar statements hold for the other free algebras we have defined.

If $\mathfrak{A}$ is an algebra and $f$ is an element of a free nonassociative algebra $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ then we say that $\mathfrak{A}$ satisfies the identity $f$ (strictly speaking $f=0$ ) or $f$ is an identity for $\mathfrak{A}$ if $f$ is mapped into 0 under every homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$. Clearly $f$ is contained in a subalgebra of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ generated by a finite subset $\left\{x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}\right\}$ of $X$ so $f$ is a linear combination of products of the $x_{i}$. Accordingly, we write $f=f\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)$. If $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}$ are arbitrary elements of $\mathfrak{A}$ then there exists a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ sending $x_{i} \rightarrow a_{i}$, $t=1, \cdots, n$. The image of $f$ under such a homomorphism is unique and we denote it as $f\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)$. Hence $\mathfrak{U}$ satisfies the identity $f$ if and only if $f\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)=0$ for all $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}$. If $I$ is a subset of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ then we shall call the class $\mathscr{V}(I)$ of algebras satisfying every identity $f \in I$ the variety defined by $I$. If $I=\{f\}$ where $f=\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{3}-x_{1}\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right)$ then $\mathscr{V}(I)$ is the variety of associative algebras. If $I=\{f, g\}$ where $f=x_{1}{ }^{2}, g=\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{3}+\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right) x_{1}+\left(x_{3} x_{1}\right) x_{2}$ then $\mathscr{V}(I)$ is the variety of Lie algebras. If $I=\{f, g\}, f=x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}-x_{1}\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right), g=x_{2} x_{1}{ }^{2}-\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right) x_{1}$ then $\mathscr{V}(I)$ is the variety of alternative algebras. If $I=\{f, g\}, f=x_{1} x_{2}-x_{2} x_{1}$, $g=\left(x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}\right) x_{1}-x_{1}{ }^{2}\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)$ then $\mathscr{V}(I)$ is the variety of Jordan algebras.

If $\mathfrak{A}$ is an algebra then the subset $\operatorname{Id}(\mathfrak{A})$ of identities $f \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ satisfied by $\mathfrak{A}$ is an ideal in $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$. It is clear that $\operatorname{Id}(\mathfrak{A})^{\eta} \subseteq \operatorname{Id}(\mathfrak{A})$ for every endomorphism $\eta$ of the free nonassociative algebra $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$. An ideal having this property is called a $T$-ideal in $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$. Clearly the subsets $I$ and $I^{\prime}$ of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ define the same variety $\mathscr{V}=\mathscr{V}(I)=\mathscr{V}\left(I^{\prime}\right)$ if the $T$-ideals generated by $I$ and $I^{\prime}$ are the same.

It is easily seen that in dealing with varieties of algebras $\mathscr{V}(I)$ there is no loss in generality in assuming that the set $X$ is countably infinite, say $X=\left\{x_{i}\right\}$, $i=1,2,3, \cdots$, and $I$ is a subset of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$. At any rate, we shall do this from now on. Now let $Y$ be any nonvacuous set and let $T(I, Y)$ be the set of images in $\Phi\{\{Y\}\}^{\prime}$ of the set $I$ under all homomorphisms of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\Phi\{\{Y\}\}^{\prime}$. It is clear that $T(I, Y)$ is mapped into itself by every endomorphism of $\Phi\{\{Y\}\}^{\prime}$. Hence the ideal $\mathfrak{T}(I, Y)$ in $\Phi\{\{Y\}\}^{\prime}$ generated by $T(I, Y)$ is a $T$-ideal in $\Phi\{\{Y\}\}^{\prime}$. Let $F I(Y)^{\prime}=\Phi\{\{Y\}\}^{\prime} \mid \mathfrak{T}(I, Y)$. Then $F I(Y)^{\prime} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$. For, let $\eta$ be a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $F I(Y)^{\prime}$. For each $x_{i} \in X$ let $b_{i}$ be an element of $\Phi\{\{Y\}\}^{\prime}$ such that $x_{i}{ }^{\eta}=b_{i}+\mathfrak{T}(I, Y)$ and let $\tau$ be the homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into
$\Phi\{\{Y\}\}^{\prime}$ such that $x_{i}{ }^{\tau}=b_{i}$. Then clearly $\eta=\tau v$ where $v$ is the canonical homomorphism $b \rightarrow b+\mathfrak{T}(I, Y)$ of $\Phi\{\{Y\}\}^{\prime}$ onto $F I(Y)^{\prime}$. If $f \in I$ then $f^{\tau} \in T(I, Y)$, so $f^{\eta}=f^{\tau \nu}=0$. Thus $f^{\eta}=0$ for every $f \in I$ and every homomorphism $\eta$ of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $F I(Y)^{\prime}$, which means that $F I(Y)^{\prime} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$. Next let $\mathfrak{A}$ be any algebra in $\mathscr{V}(I)$ and let $\alpha$ be a mapping of $Y$ into $\mathfrak{A}$. We claim that there exists a homomorphism $\bar{\alpha}$ of $F I(Y)^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $\alpha=v \bar{\alpha}$, that is, the following diagram is commutative:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-035.jpg?height=232&width=394&top_left_y=667&top_left_x=683)

Let $\alpha^{\prime}$ be the homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{Y\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ which extends $\alpha$. If $f \in I$ and $\tau$ is a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\Phi\{\{Y\}\}^{\prime}$ then $f^{\tau \alpha^{\prime}}=0$ since $\tau \alpha^{\prime}$ is a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$. This shows that every element $f^{\tau^{\prime}} \in T(I, Y)$ is mapped into 0 by $\alpha^{\prime}$. Hence $\mathfrak{T}(I, Y) \subseteq \operatorname{ker} \alpha^{\prime}$ and so we have a homomorphism $\bar{\alpha}$ of $F I(Y)^{\prime}=\Phi\{\{Y\}\}^{\prime} \mid \mathfrak{T}(I, Y)$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $\alpha^{\prime}=v \bar{\alpha}$. Then if $y \in Y, y^{\alpha}=y^{\alpha^{\prime}}=y^{v \bar{\alpha}}$ so (44) is commutative. We remark that $\bar{\alpha}$ is unique since the $y^{v}, y \in Y$, generate $F I(Y)^{\prime}$. In view of the properties we have shown we shall call $F I(Y)^{\prime}$ the free $I$-algebra determined by the set $Y$. If there exist nonzero algebras in $\mathscr{V}(I)$ then it is easy to construct, using direct sums, an algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathscr{V}(I)$ having cardinal number $\geqq|Y|$ the cardinal number of $Y$. Then there exists a 1-1 mapping $\alpha$ of $Y$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ and it follows from (44) that the restriction to $Y$ of the canonical homomorphism $v$ of $\Phi\{\{Y\}\}^{\prime}$ is 1-1. Then one can identify $Y$ with its image in $F I(Y)^{\prime}$. We shall do this and call $F I(Y)^{\prime}$ the free $I$-algebra generated by $Y$. This is the case in the examples of the classes of alternative, Lie, etc. algebras which we singled out above. In the cases we noted we call $F I(Y)^{\prime}$ the free alternative, Lie, etc. algebra generated by $Y$. We remark that if

$$
I \equiv\left\{\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{3}-x_{1}\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right)\right\}
$$

so that $\mathscr{V}(I)$ is the class of associative algebras then the homomorphism of $F I(Y)^{\prime}$ into $\Phi\{Y\}^{\prime}$ which is the identity on $Y$ is an isomorphism. Accordingly, we need not distinguish between these two algebras.
An element $f \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ (or any one of the other free algebras $\Phi\{\{X\}\}$ etc.) is homogeneous of degree $j$ in $x_{i} \in X$ if it is a linear combination of elements of $N(X)^{\prime}$ all of which are of $x_{i}$-degree $j$. It is clear that for fixed $x_{i}, \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ is a graded algebra relative to the subspaces $\mathfrak{H}\left(x_{i}, j\right)$ of elements which are homogeneous of degree $j$ in $x_{i}$. This means that $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ is a direct sum of the spaces $\mathfrak{H}\left(x_{i}, j\right), j=0,1,2, \cdots$ and $\mathfrak{H}\left(x_{i}, j\right) \mathfrak{H}\left(x_{i}, k\right) \subseteq \mathfrak{H}\left(x_{i}, j+k\right)$.

We shall now formulate some simple conditions on the sets $I$ defining varieties of algebras $\mathscr{V}(I)$. The first of these is the homogeneity condition:
H. Every $f \in I$ is homogeneous in every $x_{i} \in X$.

This condition is satisfied by the sets defining associative, Lie, alternative and Jordan algebras. Moreover, let $\mathfrak{T}$ be a $T$-ideal in $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ and let $f=f\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}\right) \in \mathfrak{T}$. Write $f=f_{0}{ }^{(i)}+f_{1}{ }^{(i)}+\cdots+f_{r}{ }^{(i)}$ where $f_{J}{ }^{(i)}$ is homogeneous of degree $j$ in $x_{i}$. Let $\alpha \in \Phi$ and consider the endomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ such that $x_{i} \rightarrow \alpha x_{i}, x_{k} \rightarrow x_{k}$ if $k \neq i$. This maps $f$ into $f_{0}{ }^{(i)}+\alpha f_{1}{ }^{(i)}+\cdots+\alpha^{r} f_{r}{ }^{(i)}$. It follows that if $\Phi$ contains $r+1$ distinct elements then every $f_{j}^{(i)} \in \mathfrak{T}$. Thus when $\Phi$ is infinite there is no loss in generality in assuming H .

We now introduce another element $y \notin X$ and form the free nonassociative algebra $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ where $Z=X \cup\{y\}$. For each $i=1,2, \cdots$ let $\lambda_{i}$ be the homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ such that $x_{i} \rightarrow x_{i}+y, x_{k} \rightarrow x_{k}, k \neq i$. If $f \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ has degree $m_{i}$ in $x_{i}$ then we can write

$$
\begin{equation*}
f\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{i-1}, x_{i}+y, x_{i+1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)=\sum_{j=0}^{m_{i}} f_{i j}\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}, y\right) \tag{45}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $f_{i j}=f_{i j}\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}, y\right)$ is homogeneous of degree $j$ in $y$. The $f_{i j}$ are uniquely determined and we have the mappings $D_{i j}: f \rightarrow f_{i j}, i=1,2, \cdots, j=0,1,2, \cdots$ of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$. The $D_{i j}$ are linear and it is clear from (45) that

$$
\begin{equation*}
(f g) D_{i j}=\sum_{k=0}^{j}\left(f D_{i k}\right)\left(g D_{i, j-k}\right) \tag{46}
\end{equation*}
$$

Also, if we apply the homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ sending $x_{i} \rightarrow x_{i}, y \rightarrow 0$ to (45) we obtain $f\left(x_{1}, \cdots x_{n}\right)=f_{i 0}=f D_{\imath 0}$. Hence $D_{i 0}=1$ and $\left\{D_{i 0}=1, D_{i 1}, D_{i 2}, \cdots\right\}$ is a higher derivation of infinite rank of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ (cf. Jacobson, Lectures in Abstract Algebra, vol. III, p. 191). In particular, $D_{i} \equiv D_{i 1}$ is a derivation of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$. This is characterized by the conditions

$$
\begin{equation*}
x_{k} D_{i}=\delta_{i k} y, \quad i, k=1,2, \cdots \tag{47}
\end{equation*}
$$

If $f$ is homogeneous of degree $m_{k}$ in $x_{k} \neq x_{i}$ then the same holds for $f D_{i j}$, and if $f$ is homogeneous of degree $m_{i}$ in $x_{i}$ and $j \leqq m_{i}$ then $f D_{i j}$ is homogeneous of degree $m_{i}-j$ in $x_{i}$. Also in this case $f D_{i m_{i}}=f\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{i-1}, y, x_{i+1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)$ and $f D_{i j}=0$ if $j>m_{i}$. These assertions follow from (46) for the elements $f \in N(X)^{\prime}$ if we use induction on the degree. Then they follow for all $f$ by linearity of the operators $D_{i j}$.

We now apply a 1-1 mapping of the set $Z$ onto $X$. The corresponding homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ maps the elements $f D_{i j}=f D_{i j}\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}, y\right)$ into elements $f D_{i j}\left(x_{i_{1}}, \cdots, x_{i_{n}}, x_{i_{n+1}}\right)$ of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$. The elements obtained in this
way from $f$ and by iterating the process will be called linearizations of $f$. For example, consider the element $g=\left(x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}\right) x_{1}-x_{1}{ }^{2}\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)$ which is one of the two elements defining the class of Jordan algebras. We have

$$
\begin{align*}
& g D_{11}=\left(\left(x_{1} y+y x_{1}\right) x_{2}\right) x_{1}+\left(x_{1}^{2} x_{2}\right) y-\left(x_{1} y+y x_{1}\right)\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)-x_{1}^{2}\left(x_{2} y\right), \\
& g D_{12}=\left(y^{2} x_{2}\right) x_{1}+\left(\left(x_{1} y+y x_{1}\right) x_{2}\right) y-\left(x_{1} y+y x_{1}\right)\left(x_{2} y\right)-y^{2}\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right) . \tag{48}
\end{align*}
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{align*}
& g_{1}=\left(\left(x_{1} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}\right) x_{2}\right) x_{1}+\left(x_{1}^{2} x_{2}\right) x_{3}-\left(x_{1} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}\right)\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)-x_{1}^{2}\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right) \\
& g_{2}=\left(x_{3}^{2} x_{2}\right) x_{1}+\left(\left(x_{1} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}\right) x_{2}\right) x_{3}-\left(x_{1} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}\right)\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right)-x_{3}^{2}\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right) \tag{49}
\end{align*}
$$

are linearizations of $g$. Also

$$
\begin{align*}
g_{1} D_{1}= & g_{1} D_{11}=\left(\left(y x_{3}+x_{3} y\right) x_{2}\right) x_{1}+\left(\left(x_{1} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}\right) x_{2}\right) y \\
& +\left(\left(x_{1} y+y x_{1}\right) x_{2}\right) x_{3}-\left(y x_{3}+x_{3} y\right)\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)-\left(x_{1} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}\right)\left(x_{2} y\right)  \tag{50}\\
& -\left(x_{1} y+y x_{1}\right)\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right)
\end{align*}
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{align*}
h= & \left(\left(x_{4} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{4}\right) x_{2}\right) x_{1}-\left(x_{4} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{4}\right)\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right) \\
& +\left(\left(x_{1} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}\right) x_{2}\right) x_{4}-\left(x_{1} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}\right)\left(x_{2} x_{4}\right)  \tag{51}\\
& +\left(\left(x_{1} x_{4}+x_{4} x_{1}\right) x_{2}\right) x_{3}-\left(x_{1} x_{4}+x_{4} x_{1}\right)\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right)
\end{align*}
$$

is a linearization of $g$. .
Let $f=f\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)$ be homogeneous of degree $m_{i}$ in $x_{i}, i=1,2, \cdots, n$. Then we call $\Sigma_{m_{i}>0}\left(m_{t}-1\right)$ the height of $f$. Thus the height is 0 if and only if $f$ is multilinear, that is, $f$ is homogeneous of degree $\leqq 1$ in all the $x$ 's. It is clear from the results noted before that the linearizations of $f$ are homogeneous and have heights $\leqq$ the height $h$ of $f$. Moreover, the height of a linearization of $f$ is $h$ only if this element has the form $f\left(x_{i_{1}}, x_{i_{2}}, \cdots, x_{i_{n}}\right)$ where the $i_{j}$ are distinct. Now suppose $\Phi$ contains $r$ distinct elements where $r \geqq m_{i}$, the degree of $f$ in $x_{i}$, $i=1,2, \cdots$ and let $\mathfrak{T}$ be a $T$-ideal in $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ containing $f$. Let $\eta$ be a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ mapping $Z$ in a 1-1 way onto $X$. Then $\mathfrak{T}$ contains

$$
f\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{i-1}, x_{i}+y, x_{i+1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)^{\eta}-f\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)^{\eta}-f D_{i m_{i}}^{\eta}=\sum_{j=1}^{m_{i}-1} f D_{i j}^{\eta}
$$

and $f D_{i j}{ }^{\eta}$ is homogeneous of degree $j$ in $y^{\eta}$. Since there exist $m_{i}-1$ distinct nonzero elements of $\Phi$ it follows that every linearization $f D_{i j}{ }^{\eta} \in \mathfrak{T}$. Also it is clear that $\Phi$ contains as many elements as the degree of these linearizations in any of the $x$ 's. Hence it is clear that $\mathfrak{T}$ contains every linearization of $f$. We shall now formulate the following condition on the sets $I$ of defining varieties $\mathscr{V}(I)$ :
L. If $f \in I$ then every linearization of $f$ is contained in the $T$-ideal $\mathfrak{T}$ generated by $I$.

The result we have just shown is that L is automatically satisfied if the elements of $I$ are homogeneous in every $x_{i}$ and $\Phi$ contains as many distinct elements as the degree of every $f \in I$ in every $x_{i}$. It is clear for the specification of the sets $I$ defining associative, Lie and alternative algebras that these satisfy the conditions H and L . If we recall that for Jordan algebras the characteristic of the base field $\Phi$ is $\neq 2$, so that $\Phi$ contains at least three distinct elements we see also that the set $I$ defining Jordan algebras also satisfies the conditions.

We shall now show that if the condition H and L hold for $I$ then $\mathscr{V}(I)$ is closed under extension of base field in a sense which will be defined below. For this we require the following

Lemma. Let $I^{\prime}$ be a subset of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ satisfying condition H and having the property that $I^{\prime}$ contains all linearizations of every $f \in I^{\prime}$. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be an algebra over $\Phi,\left(u_{i}\right)$ a basis for $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$. Then $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}\left(I^{\prime}\right)$ if and only if $f\left(u_{\imath_{1}}, u_{\imath_{2}}, \cdots, u_{\imath_{n}}\right) =0$ for all $f \in I^{\prime}$ and all $u_{i_{j}} \in\left(u_{t}\right)$.

Proof. We have to show that the conditions given imply that $f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)=0$ for all $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}, f \in I^{\prime}$. We shall prove this by induction on the height of $f$. For this it is convenient to adjoin 0 to $I^{\prime}$ and call this an element of height -1 . We now assume that $g\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{m}\right)=0$ for all $a_{j} \in \mathfrak{A}$ and $g \in I^{\prime}$ of height less than the height of $f$. We assume also that $f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{r-1}, u_{\imath_{r}}, \cdots, u_{\imath_{n}}\right)=0$ for all $a_{j} \in \mathfrak{A}$, $u_{\iota_{k}} \in\left(u_{\imath}\right)$. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be the subset of elements $b \in \mathfrak{A}$ such that

$$
f\left(a_{1} \cdots, a_{r-1}, b, u_{i_{r+1}}, \cdots, u_{i_{n}}\right)=0, \quad a_{j} \in \mathfrak{A}, \quad u_{i_{k}} \in\left(u_{\imath}\right) .
$$

Then $\mathfrak{B}$ contains the basis ( $u_{\imath}$ ). Also since $f$ is homogeneous in $x_{r}, \mathfrak{B}$ is closed under multiplication by elements of $\Phi$. Now let $a_{j} \in \mathfrak{A}, u_{t_{k}} \in\left(u_{\imath}\right), b \in \mathfrak{B}$, and consider

$$
\begin{aligned}
f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{r-1}, b+u_{t_{s}}, u_{t_{r+1}}, \cdots, u_{t_{n}}\right)= & f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{r-1}, b, u_{t_{r+1}}, \cdots, u_{t_{n}}\right) \\
& +f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{r-1}, u_{t_{r}}, u_{t_{r+1}}, \cdots, u_{t_{n}}\right) \\
& +\sum f_{r j}\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{r-1}, b, u_{i_{r+1}}, \cdots, u_{t_{n}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where the $f_{r j}$ are linearizations of $f$ and have lower height than $f$. Our induction assumptions imply that $f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{r-1}, b+u_{\iota_{r}}, u_{\iota_{r+1}}, \cdots, u_{\iota_{n}}\right)=0$. Hence $b+u_{\iota_{r}} \in \mathfrak{B}$. This now implies that $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{A}$. Thus $f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{r}, u_{\iota_{r+1}}, \cdots, u_{\iota_{n}}\right)=0$ and $f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right) =0$ by induction on $r$.

Let $\Gamma$ be an extension field of $\Phi$. Then the elements $f \in I$ can be regarded as elements of $\Gamma\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$. Hence these determine the class of algebras over $\Gamma$ which satisfy the identities of $I$. We denote this as $\mathscr{V}(I, \Gamma)$ and the class determined by $I$ and $\Phi$ as $\mathscr{V}(I, \Phi)(=\mathscr{V}(I))$. Then we have the

Theorem 5. Let I be a subset of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ satisfying the conditions $H$ and $L$ and let $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I, \Phi)$. Then the extension algebra $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}=\Gamma \otimes_{\Phi} \mathfrak{U} \in \mathscr{V}(I, \Gamma)$.

Proof. Let ( $u_{\imath}$ ) be a basis for $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$, hence, for $\mathfrak{A} / \Gamma$ and let $I^{\prime}$ be the set of linearizations of the elements of $I$. Then $I^{\prime} \supseteq I, I^{\prime}$ satisfies H and $I^{\prime}$ contains the linearizations of the elements of $I^{\prime}$, since, by definition, a linearization of a linearization of $f$ is a linearization of $f$. Also since $I$ satisfies L every $f \in I^{\prime}$ is in the $T$-ideal generated by $I$. Hence $f\left(u_{t_{1}}, u_{t_{2}}, \cdots, u_{t_{n}}\right)=0$ for all $u_{t_{k}} \in\left(u_{\imath}\right)$, since $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I, \Phi)$. Then the lemma implies that $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma} \in \mathscr{V}(I, \Gamma)$.
In particular, this theorem shows that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is associative, Lie, alternative or Jordan then the same is true of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$.
If $\mathfrak{A}$ is an algebra over $\Phi$ then we can adjoin an identity element 1 to $\mathfrak{A}$ by forming $\mathfrak{A}^{*}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \Phi 1$ and extending the multiplication in $\mathfrak{A}$ to one in $\mathfrak{A}{ }^{*}$ so that $1 a^{*}=a^{*}=a^{*} 1$ for $a^{*} \in \mathfrak{A}^{*}$. We shall now give a condition on a subset $I$ of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ that along with H and L will insure that if $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ then $\mathfrak{A}^{*} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$. This is
U. If $f=f\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)$ is a linearization of an element of $I$ then the elements obtained from $f$ by replacing any number of the $x$ 's by 1 , which are elements of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}$, are in $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ and in the $T$-ideal of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ generated by $I$.
If $f$ is multilinear its linearizations are equivalent to $f$ in the sense that they have the form $f\left(x_{i_{1}}, x_{i_{2}}, \cdots, x_{i_{n}}\right), i_{j}$ distinct. Hence if $I$ consists of multilinear elements, then $I$ satisfies U if the condition given in U holds for every $f \in I$. For example, if $I=\left\{\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right]\right\}$, the set defining associative algebras then $\left[1, x_{2}, x_{3}\right]=\left[x_{1}, 1, x_{3}\right]=\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, 1\right]=0$ since 1 is in the nucleus of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}$. Hence $I$ satisfies U . If $I=\left\{\left[x_{1}, x_{1}, x_{2}\right],\left[x_{2}, x_{1}, x_{1}\right]\right\}$, the set defining alternative algebras, then the linearizations are equivalent to the elements of $I$ or to one of the two elements: $\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right]+\left[x_{2}, x_{1}, x_{3}\right],\left[x_{3}, x_{1}, x_{2}\right]+\left[x_{3}, x_{2}, x_{1}\right]$. Substituting $x_{i}=1$ in any of these gives 0 . Hence $I$ satisfies condition U. Finally, let $I=\left\{\left[x_{1}, x_{2}\right],\left[x_{1}{ }^{2}, x_{2}, x_{1}\right]\right\}$, the set defining Jordan algebras. One sees easily (cf. (48)-(51)) that the linearizations of the elements of $I$ are equivalent to these or to one of the following two elements: $\left[x_{1}{ }^{2}, x_{3}, x_{2}\right]+\left[x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{1}, x_{3}, x_{1}\right]$, $\left[x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{1}, x_{3}, x_{4}\right]+\left[x_{1} x_{4}+x_{4} x_{1}, x_{3}, x_{2}\right]+\left[x_{2} x_{4}+x_{4} x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{1}\right]$. Substitution of an $x_{i}=1$ in these linearizations gives 0 or elements equivalent to $2\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{1}\right], 2\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right]+2\left[x_{3}, x_{2}, x_{1}\right]$. Substitution of $x_{i}=1$ in the latter gives 0 . Now $\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{1}\right]=\left[x_{1}, x_{2}\right] x_{1}+\left[x_{2} x_{1}, x_{1}\right]$ and $\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right]+\left[x_{3}, x_{2}, x_{1}\right] =\left[x_{1} x_{2}\right] x_{3}+\left[x_{3} x_{2}\right] x_{1}+\left[x_{2} x_{1}, x_{3}\right]+\left[x_{2} x_{3}, x_{1}\right]$ so $\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{1}\right]$ and $\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right] +\left[x_{3}, x_{2}, x_{1}\right]$ are in the $T$-ideal generated by $\left[x_{1}, x_{2}\right]$. Hence $I=\left\{\left[x_{1}, x_{2}\right]\right.$, $\left.\left[x_{1}{ }^{2}, x_{2}, x_{1}\right]\right\}$ satisfies U .

We now have
Theorem 6. Let I be a subset of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ satisfying the conditions $\mathrm{H}, \mathrm{L}, \mathrm{U}$, and let $\mathfrak{A}$ be an algebra in the class $\mathscr{V}(I)$. Then the algebra $\mathfrak{A}{ }^{*}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \Phi 1$ obtained by adjoining an identity element 1 to $\mathfrak{U}$ is in $\mathscr{V}(I)$.

Proof. Let $\left(u_{\imath}\right)$ be a basis for $\mathfrak{A}$, so $\left(u_{\imath}, 1\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{A}$ *. Let $I^{\prime}$ be the set of linearizations of the elements of $I$ so $I^{\prime} \supseteq I, I^{\prime}$ satisfies H and every linearization of an element of $I^{\prime}$ is contained in $I^{\prime}$. If $f=f\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right) \in I^{\prime}$ then $f$ evaluated at a subset of $\left(u_{l}, 1\right)$ amounts to the evaluation of a suitable polynomial $g$ obtained by putting some of the $x_{i}=1$ in $f$ at a subset of $\left(u_{i}\right)$. By U, $g$ is in the $T$-ideal generated by $I$. Since $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ the evaluation of $g$ at the subset of $\left(u_{\imath}\right)$ gives 0 . It follows from the Lemma that $\mathfrak{A}^{*} \in \mathscr{V}\left(I^{\prime}\right)$, so $\mathfrak{A}^{*} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$.

We have seen that the sets $I$ defining associative, alternative, or Jordan algebras satisfy conditions $\mathrm{H}, \mathrm{L}$ and U . Hence the adjunction of an identity element to an algebra of one of these classes gives an algebra in the same class. We remark also that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is a Lie algebra then $\mathfrak{A}^{*}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{A}$ is not.

Let $f=f\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}\right) \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ be homogeneous of degree $m_{i}$ in $x_{i}$ and consider the element $f D_{i}\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}, y\right)$ obtained by applying the derivation $D_{i}$ to $f\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)$. The usual argument via elements of $N(X)^{\prime}$ and linearity shows that $f D_{i}\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}, x_{i}\right)=m_{i} f\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)$. If the characteristic is 0 or is a prime exceeding $m_{i}$ then this shows that $f$ is contained in any $T$-ideal which contains a linearization $f D_{i}\left(x_{i_{1}}, \cdots, x_{i_{n}}, x_{i_{n+1}}\right)$ of $f$. We can use this to prove the following sufficient condition that a class of algebras $\mathscr{V}(I)$ be definable by multilinear elements, that is, $\mathscr{V}(I)=\mathscr{V}\left(I^{\prime}\right)$ where $I^{\prime}$ is a set of multilinear elements of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$.

Theorem 7. Let $I$ be a set of elements of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ and assume the characteristic of $\Phi$ is either 0 or exceeds the degree of homogeneity of every $f \in I$ in every $x_{i}$. Then the $T$-ideal $\mathfrak{T}(I)$ generated by $I$ is identical with the $T$-ideal $\mathfrak{T}\left(I^{\prime}\right)$ generated by a set of multilinear elements.

Proof. The result will follow if we can show that if $f \in I$ then there exists a multilinear element $g$ such that the $T$-ideal $\mathfrak{T}(f)$ generated by $f$ coincides with $\mathfrak{T}(g)$. If $f$ is multilinear there is nothing to prove so we assume $f=f\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)$ is homogeneous of degree $m_{i}>1$ in $x_{i}$. Then $f D_{i}\left(x_{i_{1}}, \cdots, x_{i_{n}}, x_{i_{n+1}}\right), i_{j} \neq i_{k}$ for $j \neq k$, is a linearization of $f$ of lower height than $f$. Since the hypothesis on $\Phi$ implies that there exist $m_{i}$ distinct elements in $\Phi$, all linearizations of $f$ are in $\mathfrak{T}(f)$. In particular, $f D_{i}\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{i_{n}}, x_{i_{n+1}}\right) \in \mathfrak{T}(f)$. On the other hand, we have seen above that $f$ is contained in the $T$-ideal generated by $f D_{i}\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{i_{n}}, x_{i_{n+1}}\right)$. If we use induction on the height we may suppose that the $T$-ideal generated by $f D_{i}\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{i_{n}}, x_{i_{n+1}}\right)$ coincides with $\mathfrak{T}(g)$ where $g$ is multilinear. Hence $\mathfrak{T}(f)=\mathfrak{T}(g)$.

## Exercises

1. Show that the number of elements of degree $m$ in the free monad generated by $n$ elements is given by the formula

$$
N(n, m)=\frac{(2 m-2)!}{m!(m-1)!} n^{m}
$$

2. Let $\mathscr{V}(I)$ be a variety of algebras defined by a set of identities $I \subseteq \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$.

Show that if $f \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ is an identity for every algebra in $\mathscr{V}(I)$ then $f$ is contained in the $T$-ideal generated by $I$.
3. Let $Y^{\prime}$ be a nonvacuous subset of $Y, I$ a subset of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ and $F I(Y)^{\prime}$ the free $I$-algebra determined by $Y$. Show that the subalgebra of $F I(Y)^{\prime}$ generated by the cosets of the elements of $Y^{\prime}$ is canonically isomorphic to the free $I$-algebra generated by $Y^{\prime}$.
4. Prove that an element $f \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ satisfies $f D_{i}=0$ if and only if $f$ is homogeneous of degree 0 in $x_{i}$. Use this to show that any nonzero $T$-ideal in $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ contains a nonzero multilinear element. (This implies that if $\mathfrak{A}$ satisfies an identity $f$ where $f \neq 0$ in $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ then $\mathfrak{A}$ satisfies a nonzero multilinear identity.)
5. (Glennie). Let $I$ be a set of multilinear elements in $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}, T(I)$ the set of elements $F=f\left(m_{1}, m_{2} \cdots, m_{n}\right)$ where $f \in I$ and $m_{j} \in N(X)^{\prime}, U(I)$ the set of elements of the form $m\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{k}, F\right)$ where $F \in T(I)$ and $m\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{k}, y\right)$ is an element of $N(Z)^{\prime}, Z=X \cup\{y\}$ which is homogeneous of degree 1 in $y$. Show that the subspace $\Phi U(I)$ of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ is the $T$-ideal $\mathfrak{T}(I)$ generated by $I$. Show that if $I$ is finite and $X$ is finite then the subset $U^{(r)}(I)$ of elements of $U(I)$ of degree $\leqq r$ is finite. Use this to prove that there is a finite procedure for deciding whether or not a given element $g \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ belongs to $\mathfrak{T}(I)$. (This shows that there is an algorithm for deciding whether or not a given $g \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ is an identity for the variety $\mathscr{V}(I), I$ a finite set of multilinear elements.)
6. Let $f\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n+1}\right) \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}, X=\left\{x_{i}\right\}, i=1,2, \cdots$, be homogeneous of degree $m$ in $x_{n+1}$. Write $x$ for ( $x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}$ ) and define

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^{(m)}\left(x, x_{n+1}, \cdots, x_{n+m}\right)= & f\left(x, x_{n+1}+\cdots+x_{n+m}\right) \\
& -\sum_{i} f\left(x, x_{n+1}+\cdots+\hat{x}_{n+i}+\cdots+x_{n+m}\right) \\
& +\sum_{i<j} f\left(x, x_{n+1}+\cdots+\hat{x}_{n+i}+\cdots+\hat{x}_{n+j}+x_{n+m}\right) \\
& -\cdots+(-1)^{m-1} \sum_{i} f\left(x, x_{n+i}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where ${ }^{\wedge}$ denotes the omission of the variable appearing below it. Prove that $f^{(m)}$ can be obtained by the following inductive process: $f^{(1)}=f\left(x, x_{n+1}\right), f^{(k+1)} =f^{(k)} D_{n+1}\left(x, x_{n+1}, \cdots, x_{n+k}, x_{n+k+1}\right)$ (that is, the result of putting $y=x_{n+k+1}$ in the derivative $f^{(k)} D_{n+1}\left(x, x_{n+1}, \cdots, x_{n+k}, y\right)$ ). Prove that

$$
f^{(m)}=f^{(m)}\left(x, x_{n+1}, \cdots, x_{n+m}\right)
$$

is homogeneous of degree 1 in every $x_{i+i}, 1 \leqq i \leqq m$ and that

$$
f^{(m)}\left(x, x_{n+1}, x_{n+1}, \cdots, x_{n+1}\right)=m!f .
$$

7. An ideal $\mathfrak{T}$ in $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ is called homogeneous in $x_{i}$ if the following condition holds: an element $f=\Sigma f_{j}, f_{j}$ homogeneous of degree $j$ in $x_{i}, \in \mathfrak{T}$ if and only if
every $f_{j} \in \mathfrak{T}$. Show that an ideal is homogeneous in $x_{i}$ if and only if it has a set of generators which are homogeneous in $x_{i}$. Show that if $I$ is a set satisfying H and L then the $T$-ideal generated by $I$ is homogeneous in every $x_{i}$.
8. The class of noncommutative Jordan algebra is defined by the set of five identities: $x_{1}\left(x_{1}^{2} x_{2}\right)-x_{1}^{2}\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right),\left(x_{2} x_{1}^{2}\right) x_{1}-\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right) x_{1}^{2},\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{1}-x_{1}\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)$, $\left(x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}\right) x_{1}-x_{1}{ }^{2}\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right),\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{1}{ }^{2}-x_{1}\left(x_{2} x_{1}{ }^{2}\right)$. Note that this set satisfies H, L, U if the characteristic is not two and that the class of noncommutative Jordan algebras can be defined by multilinear identities if the characteristic is not two or three. Show that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is a noncommutative Jordan algebra of characteristic not two then $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$is a Jordan algebra.
9. Prove that every alternative algebra is a noncommutative Jordan algebra.
10. The class of Malcev algebras is defined by the following identities: $x_{1}{ }^{2}$, $\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right)\left(x_{1} x_{3}\right)-\left(\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{3}\right) x_{1}-\left(\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right) x_{1}\right) x_{1}-\left(\left(x_{3} x_{1}\right) x_{1}\right) x_{2}$. Show that this class includes the class of Lie algebras. Show that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is alternative of characteristic not two then $\mathfrak{A}^{-}$is a Malcev algebra.
11. Basic Jordan identities. Jordan triple product. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra over a field $\Phi$ (of characteristic not two). We write the product in $\mathfrak{J}$ as $a . b$ and use this notation also for $\frac{1}{2}(a b+b a)$ in any algebra over $\Phi$. Also we shall use the abbreviation $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \cdots, a_{k}$ for $\left(\cdots\left(\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right), a_{3}\right), \cdots a_{k}\right)$ and $a^{\cdot k}$ for $a, a, \cdots, a$ with $k$ factors. The linear mapping $x \rightarrow x . a(=a . x)$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ will be denoted as $R_{a}$ and if $\mathfrak{A}$ is any algebra with product $a b$ then we write $a_{L}$ for $x \rightarrow a x, a_{R}$ for $x \rightarrow x a$ and $R_{a}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a_{L}+a_{R}\right)$. We have seen in §6 (eq. (51)) that

$$
\begin{aligned}
h= & \left(\left(x_{4} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{4}\right) x_{2}\right) x_{1}-\left(x_{4} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{4}\right)\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right) \\
& +\left(\left(x_{1} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}\right) x_{2}\right) x_{4}-\left(x_{1} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}\right)\left(x_{2} x_{4}\right) \\
& +\left(\left(x_{1} x_{4}+x_{4} x_{1}\right) x_{2}\right) x_{3}-\left(x_{1} x_{4}+x_{4} x_{1}\right)\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right) \\
= & {\left[x_{4} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{4}, x_{2}, x_{1}\right]+\left[x_{1} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{4}\right]+\left[x_{1} x_{4}+x_{4} x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right] }
\end{aligned}
$$

is a linearization of the defining identity $\left(x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}\right) x_{1}-x_{1}{ }^{2}\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)=\left[x_{1}{ }^{2}, x_{2}, x_{1}\right]$ for Jordan algebras. If we specialize $x_{2} \rightarrow a, x_{1} \rightarrow b, x_{3} \rightarrow c, x_{4} \rightarrow d$ in $h$ and use commutativity and the fact that the characteristic is not two we obtain the following identity for any Jordan algebra:

$$
\begin{align*}
& (a \cdot b) \cdot(c \cdot d)+(a \cdot d) \cdot(b \cdot c)+(a \cdot c) \cdot(b \cdot d) \\
& =a \cdot(c \cdot d) \cdot b+a \cdot(b \cdot c) \cdot d+a \cdot(b \cdot d) \cdot c \cdot \tag{1}
\end{align*}
$$

This is equivalent to

$$
\begin{equation*}
[c \cdot d, a, b]+[b \cdot c, a, d]+[b \cdot d, a, c]=0 \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

Also since $[a, b, c]=a . b . c-a .(b . c)=-c . b . a+c .(b . a)=-[c, b, a]$ we have also

$$
\begin{equation*}
[b, a, c . d]+[d, a, b . c]+[c, a, b . d]=0 \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

We now put

$$
\begin{align*}
(a b c d) & =(a \cdot b) \cdot(c \cdot d)+(a \cdot d) \cdot(b \cdot c)+(a \cdot c) \cdot(b \cdot d),  \tag{52}\\
(a ; b c d) & =a \cdot(b \cdot c) \cdot d+a \cdot(b \cdot d) \cdot c+a \cdot(c \cdot d) \cdot b .
\end{align*}
$$

Then $\left(\mathrm{B}_{1}\right)$ reads $(a b c d)=(a ; b c d)$. If we take into account the commutative law we see that ( $a b c d$ ) is symmetric in all of its arguments while ( $a ; b c d$ ) is symmetric in the last three. Hence ( $\mathbf{B}_{\mathbf{1}}$ ) and commutativity imply

$$
\begin{equation*}
(a ; b c d)=(b ; a c d)=(c ; a b d)=(d ; a b c) . \tag{53}
\end{equation*}
$$

The equality of the first and third of these is equivalent to

$$
\begin{align*}
& a \cdot(b \cdot c) \cdot d+a \cdot(b \cdot d) \cdot c+a \cdot(c \cdot d) \cdot b \\
& =a \cdot b \cdot c \cdot d+a \cdot d \cdot c \cdot b+a \cdot(b \cdot d \cdot c) \tag{2}
\end{align*}
$$

By ( $B_{1}$ ) and ( $B_{2}$ ) we have also

$$
\begin{align*}
& a \cdot b \cdot c \cdot d+a \cdot d \cdot c \cdot b+a \cdot(b \cdot d \cdot c) \\
& \quad=(a \cdot b) \cdot(c \cdot d)+(a \cdot c) \cdot(b \cdot d)+(a \cdot d) \cdot(b \cdot c) . \tag{3}
\end{align*}
$$

In operator form the defining relation $\left(a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b\right) \cdot a=a^{\cdot 2}(b \cdot a)$ and commutativity give

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[R_{a} R_{a \cdot 2}\right]=0 \tag{O}
\end{equation*}
$$

If we consider $a$ as a variable in $\left(\mathbf{B}_{1}\right),\left(\mathbf{B}_{2}\right)$ and $\left(\mathbf{B}_{3}\right)$ and $b, c, d$ etc. as defining multiplications then we see that these identities are equivalent to the following operator identities:

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[R_{b . c} R_{d}\right]+\left[R_{b . d} R_{c}\right]+\left[R_{c . d} R_{b}\right]=0 \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

( $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ )

$$
R_{b . d . c}=R_{b . c} R_{d}+R_{b . d} R_{c}+R_{c . d} R_{b}-R_{b} R_{c} R_{d}-R_{d} R_{c} R_{b},
$$

( $\mathrm{O}_{3}$ )

$$
R_{b . d . c}=R_{d} R_{b . c}+R_{c} R_{b . d}+R_{b} R_{c . d}-R_{b} R_{c} R_{d}-R_{d} R_{c} R_{b}
$$

If we interchange $b$ and $c$ in ( $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ ) and subtract from ( $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ ) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_{b . d . c}-R_{b .(d . c)} & =R_{c} R_{b} R_{d}+R_{d} R_{b} R_{c}-R_{b} R_{c} R_{d}-R_{d} R_{c} R_{b} . \\
& =\left[\left[R_{c} R_{b}\right] R_{d}\right] .
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $R_{a}$ is linear in $a, R_{b . d . c}-R_{b .(d . c)}=R_{(b . d) . c-b .(d . c)}=R_{[b, d, c]}$. Hence we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[\left[R_{c} R_{b}\right] R_{d}\right]=R_{[b, d, c]} \tag{54}
\end{equation*}
$$

This result shows that the set $R(\mathfrak{J})$ of multiplications $R_{a}$ in a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ is a subspace of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ closed under the iterated Lie multiplication $[[A B] C]$. Such a subspace of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ is called a Lie triple system of linear
transformations in the vector space $\mathfrak{J}$. The result (54) has another important interpretation which is more readily seen by writing (54) as

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[R_{d}\left[R_{b} R_{c}\right]\right]=R_{d\left[R_{b} R_{c}\right]} \tag{54'}
\end{equation*}
$$

Now we recall that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is an arbitrary algebra then a derivation $D$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ is a linear mapping $\mathfrak{A}$ satisfying $(x y) D=(x D) y+x(y D)$. This condition is equivalent to either one of the following operator conditions:

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[x_{L}, D\right]=(x D)_{L}, \quad\left[y_{R}, D\right]=(y D)_{R}, \quad x, y \in \mathfrak{A} \tag{55}
\end{equation*}
$$

We recall also that the set Der $\mathfrak{A}$ (more precisely $\operatorname{Der}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$ ) of derivations is a Lie algebra of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$, that is, a subalgebra of the Lie algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})^{-}$. Moreover, this is restricted in the sense that $D^{p} \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{A}$ for $D \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{A}$ if the characteristic is $p \neq 0$ (Jacobson, Lie Algebras, p. 7). Now it is clear from (54') and (55) that any mapping $\left[R_{b} R_{c}\right]$ in a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ is a derivation. More generally, the mappings $\sum_{i}\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right]$ are derivations. We shall call the derivations of this form inner derivations of $\mathfrak{J}$. It is easy to check that the inner derivations form an ideal in Der J (ex. 2 below) and it can be proved that this ideal, which we shall denote as Inder $\mathfrak{J}$, is closed under the $p$-power mapping if the characteristic is $p \neq 0$. (ex. 2 below and ex. 6 on p. 49).

We now put $b=a^{\cdot k}, k \geqq 1, c=d=a$ in $\mathrm{O}_{2}$. This gives

$$
R_{a^{\cdot k+2}}=2 R_{a^{\cdot k+1}} R_{a}+R_{a \cdot 2} R_{a \cdot k}-R_{a \cdot k} R_{a}^{2}-R_{a}^{2} R_{a \cdot k}
$$

We know that $R_{a}$ and $R_{a \cdot 2}$ commute, and the foregoing recursion formula implies that $R_{a \cdot k+2}, k \geqq 1$ is contained in the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ generated by $R_{a}$ and $R_{a \cdot 2 \cdot}$. Hence $\left[R_{a \cdot k} R_{a \cdot l}\right]=0, k, l \geqq 1$, which permits the simplification of the recursion formula to

$$
\begin{equation*}
R_{a^{\cdot k+2}}=2 R_{a} R_{a \cdot k+1}-\left(2 R_{a}^{2}-R_{a \cdot 2}\right) R_{a \cdot k}, \quad k \geqq 1 . \tag{56}
\end{equation*}
$$

This recursion formula can be solved explicitly to give

$$
\begin{equation*}
R_{a \cdot k}=\frac{1}{2}\left\{\left(R_{a}+\left(R_{a \cdot 2}-R_{a}^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{k}+\left(R_{a}-\left(R_{a \cdot 2}-R_{a}^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{k}\right\} \tag{57}
\end{equation*}
$$

which makes sense since the odd powers of $\left(R_{a \cdot 2}-R_{a}^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ cancel off. The formula can be established by induction on $k .^{4}$

[^3]A nonassociative algebra is called power associative if the subalgebras generated by single elements of the algebra are associative. This is equivalent to the identities $a^{k} a^{l}=a^{k+l}, k, l=1,2, \cdots$, if $a^{k}$ is defined by $a^{1}=a, a^{k}=a^{k-1} a$. Nearly all the interesting nonassociative algebras are power associative. In particular, we have

Theorem 8. Any Jordan algebra is power associative.
Proof. We shall prove $a^{\cdot k} \cdot a^{\cdot l}=a^{\cdot k+l}$ by induction on $l$. For $l=1$ this holds by definition of $a^{\cdot k}$. Now assume $a^{\cdot k} \cdot a^{\cdot r}=a^{\cdot k+r}$. Then $a^{\cdot k} \cdot a^{\cdot r+1}=a^{\cdot k} \cdot\left(a^{\cdot r} \cdot a\right) =a^{\cdot r} R_{a} R_{a^{\cdot} k}=a^{r} R_{a^{\cdot} k} R_{a}=\left(a^{\cdot r} \cdot a^{\cdot k}\right) \cdot a=a^{\cdot k+r} \cdot a=a^{\cdot k+r+1}$. Hence $a^{\cdot k} \cdot a^{\cdot l}=a^{\cdot k+l}$ for $k, l=1,2,3, \cdots$.
An important composition in a Jordan algebra is given by the Jordan triple product

$$
\begin{equation*}
\{a b c\} \equiv a . b . c+b . c . a-a . c . b . \tag{58}
\end{equation*}
$$

If the algebra is special and $a \cdot b=\frac{1}{2}(a b+b a)$ in terms of the associative product $a b$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\{a b c\}= & \frac{1}{4}(a b c+b a c+c a b+c b a+b c a+c b a+a b c+a c b \\
& \quad-a c b-c a b-b a c-b c a) \\
= & \frac{1}{2}(a b c+c b a) .
\end{aligned}
$$

In particular, $\{a b a\}=a b a$ in a special Jordan algebra. In any Jordan algebra we shall denote the linear mapping $x \rightarrow\{a x b\}$ by $U_{a, b}$ and we abbreviate $U_{a, a}=U_{a}$. We have

$$
\begin{align*}
U_{a, b} & =R_{a} R_{b}+R_{b} R_{a}-R_{a \cdot b},  \tag{59}\\
U_{a} & =2 R_{a}^{2}-R_{a \cdot 2} . \tag{60}
\end{align*}
$$

The recursion formula (56) can be written in terms of $U_{a}$ as

$$
\begin{equation*}
R_{a \cdot k+2}=2 R_{a} R_{a \cdot k+1}-U_{a} R_{a \cdot k} . \tag{57'}
\end{equation*}
$$

Clearly the $U_{a^{\cdot k}}$ are contained in the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ generated by $R_{a}$ and $R_{a \cdot 2}$. We note also that $U_{a}$ is a quadratic form in $a$ since for $\alpha \in \Phi, U_{\alpha a}=\alpha^{2} U_{a}$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{2}\left(U_{a+b}-U_{a}-U_{b}\right)=U_{a, b} \tag{61}
\end{equation*}
$$

is bilinear in $a$ and $b$. We also have the following immediate consequence of the definition of $\{a b c\}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
\{a b c\} & =\{c b a\} \\
\{1 a b\} & =\{a 1 b\}=\{a b 1\}=a \cdot b
\end{aligned}
$$

if $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element 1 , and

$$
\left\{a^{\cdot k} a^{\cdot l} b\right\}=a^{\cdot k+l} \cdot b
$$

## Exercises

1. Verify that the derivations of any algebra form a Lie algebra of linear transformations and that this is restricted if the characteristic is $p \neq 0$.
2. Verify that the set Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ of inner derivations of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ is an ideal in Der $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{A}^{+}, \mathfrak{A}$ associative, then $x\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right]=\frac{1}{4}[x[a b]]$ (where $[a b]=a b-b a$ ). Use this, ex. 6, p. 10 ắnd the $p$ power formulas in associative algebras of characteristic $p$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
{\left[a b^{p}\right] } & =[\cdots[a b] b] \cdots] \quad(p \text { times }), \\
(a+b)^{p} & =a^{p}+b^{p}+\sum_{1}^{p-1} s_{i}(a, b)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $s_{i}(a, b)$ are certain Lie elements in $a$ and $b$ (Jacobson's Lie Algebras pp. 186-187) to prove that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a special Jordan algebra then Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ is a restricted subalgebra of Der $\mathfrak{J}$. (The extension of this to arbitrary Jordan algebras will be considered in ex. 6, p. 49.)
3. Show that $R_{a \cdot p}=R_{a}^{p}$ in any Jordan algebra of characteristic $p \neq 0$.
4. Show that the following Jordan triple product identities hold in special Jordan algebras:

$$
\begin{align*}
\{a b a\}^{2} & =\left\{a\left\{b a^{2} b\right\} a\right\}  \tag{62}\\
\{\{a b a\} c\{a b a\}\} & =\{a\{b\{a c a\} b\} a\}  \tag{63}\\
\{\{\{a c a\} c b\} c a\} & =\{\{a c a\} c\{a c b\}\} \tag{64}
\end{align*}
$$

5. Prove the following identities for arbitrary Jordan algebras:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\{a b c\} . d=\{(a . d) b c\}-\{a(b . d) c\}+\{a b(c . d)\} \\
\{a b c\} . d=\{a(b . c) d\}-\{(a . c) b d\}+\{c(a . b) d\} \\
\{a(b . c) d\}=\{a b c\} . d-\{(a . d) b c\}+\{d c b\} . a
\end{gathered}
$$

8. Strongly associative subalgebras. Jordan triple product identities. In this section we shall derive some Jordan triple product identities which will be needed for the proof of an important general theorem on identities (Macdonald's theorem) which we shall give in §9. While these identities will be required only for the cases in which certain of the variables are powers of a single element, it appears to be of interest to generalize them to the situation in which these variables are in a strongly associative subalgebra which is defined as follows.

Definition 4. A subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}$ of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ is called a strongly associative subalgebra if $\left[R_{a} R_{a^{\prime}}\right]=0$ for all $a, a^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{A}$ where $R_{a}$ denotes the multiplication $(x \rightarrow x . a)$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ determined by $a$.

The condition is clearly equivalent to $\left[a, x, a^{\prime}\right]=0$ for $a, a^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{A}, x \in \mathfrak{I}$. Specializing $x$ to $\mathfrak{A}$ we see that $\mathfrak{A}$ is an associative subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is any subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ then we write $R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{A})$ for the set of multiplications $R_{a}$ in $\mathfrak{J}, a \in \mathfrak{A}$. If $S$ is a subset of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), \mathfrak{M}$ a vector space over $\Phi$ then we denote the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ generated by $S$ and the identity mapping 1 by $S^{*}$. In particular, $R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{A})^{*}$ is the subalgebra generated by 1 and the $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{A}$. Since an associative algebra is commutative if and only if it has a set of generators which commute, it is clear that $\mathfrak{A}$ is a strongly associative subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ if and only if $R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{A})^{*}$ is a commutative algebra of linear transformations.
Examples. (1) If $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $\left[R_{a \cdot k} R_{a \cdot 1}\right]=0$. Hence any subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ generated by a single element is a strongly associative subalgebra. Also if $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element then it is clear that the subalgebra $\Phi[a]$ generated by 1 and any $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ is a strongly associative subalgebra.
(2) If $\mathfrak{A}$ is a strongly associative subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ then we have seen that $\mathfrak{A}$ is an associative subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$. We shall now give an example of a subalgebra which is associative but not strongly associative. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ the Jordan algebra of the symmetric bilinear for $f$ on the vector space $\mathfrak{M} / \Phi$. If $x, y, z \in \mathfrak{M}$ then $y\left[R_{x} R_{z}\right]=x . y . z-x .(y . z)=f(x, y) z-f(y, z) x$. If $\mathfrak{N}$ is a subspace of $\mathfrak{M}$ then $\Phi 1+\mathfrak{N}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ and if $\mathfrak{N}$ is totally isotropic then $[x, y, z]=0$ for all $x, y, z \in \mathfrak{N}$ which implies that $\mathfrak{A}=\Phi 1+\mathfrak{N}$ is an associative subalgebra. Now suppose there exist vectors $x, z \in \mathfrak{N}, y \in \mathfrak{M}$ such that $f(x, y)=1, f(z, y)=0$. This will be the case, for example, if $\mathfrak{M}$ has a basis $\left(u_{1}, \cdots, u_{m}, v_{1}, \cdots, v_{m}\right)$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f\left(u_{i}, u_{j}\right)=0=f\left(v_{i}, v_{j}\right), \\
& f\left(u_{i}, v_{j}\right)=\delta_{i j}=f\left(v_{j}, u_{i}\right) .
\end{aligned}
$$

Then we can take $\mathfrak{N}=\Sigma \Phi u_{i}, x=u_{1}, z=u_{2}, y=v_{1}$. Assuming the indicated condition, we have $y\left[R_{x} R_{z}\right]=f(x, y) z-f(y, z) x=z$. Hence $\mathfrak{A}=\Phi 1+\mathfrak{N}$ is not a strongly associative subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$.
We shall now prove the following result on Jordan triple products.
Lemma 8. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a strongly associative subalgebra of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$. Then the following relations hold for $a, a^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{A}, b \in \mathfrak{J}$ :

$$
\begin{equation*}
U_{a . a^{\prime}, a}=U_{a} R_{a^{\prime}}, \tag{65}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
U_{a} U_{a^{\prime}}=U_{a \cdot a^{\prime}}, \tag{66}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
U_{b} R_{a}=2 R_{b} U_{a, b}-U_{a, b \cdot 2}, \tag{67}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
U_{a} U_{a^{\prime}, b}=2 R_{a} U_{a \cdot a^{\prime}, b}-U_{a \cdot 2 \cdot a^{\prime} \cdot b}, \tag{68}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\begin{align*}
& 2 U_{a \cdot a^{\prime}, b} R_{a}=U_{a^{\prime}, b} U_{a}+U_{a^{\cdot 2} \cdot a^{\prime}, b}  \tag{69}\\
& U_{a, b} R_{a \cdot a^{\prime}}=U_{a^{\cdot 2} \cdot a^{\prime}, b}+R_{b} R_{a^{\prime}} U_{a}-U_{a \cdot a^{\prime}, b} R_{a^{\cdot}} 5 \tag{70}
\end{align*}
$$

Proof. Since we can adjoin an identity to $\mathfrak{J}$ and obtain a Jordan algebra, we may assume without loss of generality that $\mathfrak{J}$ has a 1 and $\mathfrak{A}$ contains 1 . We now substitute $U_{x, y}=R_{x} R_{y}+R_{y} R_{x}-R_{x, y}, U_{x \cdot 2, y}=R_{x \cdot 2} R_{y}+R_{y} R_{x \cdot 2}-R_{x \cdot 2, y}$ in $R_{x \cdot 2} R_{y}+2 R_{x \cdot y} R_{x}=R_{y} R_{x \cdot 2}+2 R_{x} R_{x \cdot y}=2 R_{x} R_{y} R_{x}+R_{x \cdot, 2}$ which are obtained from $\left(\mathrm{B}_{1}\right)$, $\left(\mathrm{B}_{2}\right)$ and $\left(\mathrm{B}_{3}\right)$. This gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
U_{x \cdot 2, y}=2 U_{x, y} R_{x}-R_{y} U_{x}=2 R_{x} U_{x, y}-U_{x} R_{y} \tag{71}
\end{equation*}
$$

Linearizing the $x$ gives

$$
\begin{align*}
U_{x . z, y} & =U_{x, y} R_{z}+U_{z, y} R_{x}-R_{y} U_{x, z}  \tag{72}\\
& =R_{z} U_{x, y}+R_{x} U_{z, y}-U_{x, z} R_{y}
\end{align*}
$$

If we put $x=y=a, z=a^{\prime}$ in the first of these and use the commutativity of $R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{A})^{*}$ we obtain (65). If we linearize (65) with respect to $a$ in $\mathfrak{U}$ we obtain

$$
\begin{equation*}
U_{a . a^{\prime}, a^{\prime \prime}}+U_{a^{\prime \prime}, a^{\prime}, a}=2 U_{a, a^{\prime \prime}} R_{a^{\prime}} \tag{73}
\end{equation*}
$$

for $a, a^{\prime}, a^{\prime \prime} \in \mathfrak{A}$. We have

$$
\begin{align*}
U_{a} U_{a^{\prime}} & =2 U_{a} R_{a^{\prime}}^{2}-U_{a} R_{\left(a^{\prime}\right) \cdot 2} \\
& =2 U_{a \cdot a^{\prime}, a} R_{a^{\prime}}-U_{a \cdot\left(a^{\prime}\right) \cdot 2, a}  \tag{65}\\
& =U_{\left(a \cdot a^{\prime}\right) \cdot a^{\prime}, a}+U_{a \cdot a^{\prime}}-U_{a \cdot\left(a^{\prime}\right) \cdot 2, a}  \tag{73}\\
& =U_{a \cdot a^{\prime}}
\end{align*}
$$

which proves (66). If we put $x=z=b, y=a$ in the second part of (72) we obtain $U_{b \cdot \mathbf{2}, a}=R_{b} U_{a, b}+R_{b} U_{a, b}-U_{b} R_{a}$ which is equivalent to (67). We now replace $x$ by $x^{.2}$ in (72) to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
U_{x \cdot 2 \cdot z, y} & =U_{x \cdot 2, y} R_{z}+U_{z, y} R_{x \cdot 2}-R_{y} U_{x \cdot 2, z} \\
& =R_{z} U_{x \cdot 2, y}+R_{x \cdot 2} U_{z, y}-U_{x \cdot 2, z} R_{y}
\end{aligned}
$$

If we use (71) and the definition of $U_{x}$ in these relations we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
U_{x \cdot 2 \cdot z, y}= & 2 U_{x, y} R_{x} R_{z}-R_{y} U_{x} R_{z}+U_{z, y}\left(2 R_{x}^{2}-U_{x}\right) \\
& -2 R_{y} R_{x} U_{x, z}+R_{y} U_{x} R_{z} \\
= & 2 U_{x, y}\left[R_{x} R_{z}\right]+2 U_{x, y} R_{z} R_{x} \\
& +2 U_{z, y} R_{x}^{2}-U_{z, y} U_{x} \\
& +2 R_{y}\left[U_{x, z} R_{x}\right]-2 R_{y} U_{x, z} R_{x}
\end{aligned}
$$

[^4]Hence by (72),

$$
\begin{align*}
U_{x \cdot 2 . z, y}= & 2 U_{x, y}\left[R_{x} R_{z}\right]+2 U_{x . z, y} R_{x}-U_{z, y} U_{x} \\
& +2 R_{y}\left[U_{x, z} R_{x}\right] . \tag{74}
\end{align*}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{align*}
U_{x \cdot 2 . z, y}= & 2\left[R_{z} R_{x}\right] U_{x, y}+2 R_{x} U_{x . z, y}-U_{x} U_{z, y} \\
& +2\left[R_{x} U_{x, z}\right] R_{y .} \tag{75}
\end{align*}
$$

If we put $x=a, z=a^{\prime}, y=b$ in (75) and (74) we obtain (68) and (69) respectively. To obtain (70) we set $a^{\prime}=1$ in (69) and linearize with respect to $a$ in $\mathfrak{A}$. This gives

$$
U_{a, b} R_{a^{\prime}}+U_{a^{\prime}, b} R_{a}=R_{b} U_{a, a^{\prime}}+U_{a . a^{\prime}, b}
$$

Replace $a^{\prime}$ by $a \cdot a^{\prime}$ in this equation. Then we obtain

$$
\begin{align*}
U_{a, b} R_{a \cdot a^{\prime}} & =R_{b} U_{a, a \cdot a^{\prime}}+U_{a \cdot 2 \cdot a^{\prime}, b}-U_{a \cdot a^{\prime}, b} R_{a} \\
& =R_{b} R_{a^{\prime}} U_{a}+U_{a \cdot 2 \cdot a^{\prime}, b}-U_{a \cdot a^{\prime}, b} R_{a} \tag{65}
\end{align*}
$$

which is (70).

## Exercise

1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a subalgebra of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{A}^{+}, \mathfrak{A}$ associative. Show that $\mathfrak{J}$ is associative if and only if $[[a b] c]=0$ for all $a, b, c \in \mathfrak{J}$. Let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a vector space over $\Phi, E(\mathfrak{M})$ the exterior algebra over $\mathfrak{M}$. Show that $E(\mathfrak{M})^{+}$is an associative Jordan algebra.
2. Macdonald's theorem. Shirshov's theorem. In this section we shall prove the most important general theorem on identities in Jordan algebras, namely, that any three variable identity which is of degree at most one in one of these and which holds for all special Jordan algebras is valid for all Jordan algebras. More precisely, let $f\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right)$ be an element in the free nonassociative algebra generated by $x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}$ which is of degree $\leqq 1$ in $x_{3}$. Assume $f$ is an identity for all special Jordan algebras. Then $f$ is an identity for all Jordan algebras. For example, write $\left\{x_{1} x_{2} x_{1}\right\}=2\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right) x_{1}-x_{2} x_{1}{ }^{2}$ and let $f=\left\{x_{1} x_{2} x_{1}\right\}^{2}-\left\{x_{1}\left\{x_{2} x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}\right\} x_{1}\right\}, g =\left\{\left\{x_{1} x_{2} x_{1}\right\} x_{3}\left\{x_{1} x_{2} x_{1}\right\}\right\}-\left\{x_{1}\left\{x_{2}\left\{x_{1} x_{3} x_{1}\right\} x_{2}\right\} x_{1}\right\}$. Then it is easily seen that $f$ and $g$ are identities for special Jordan algebras (ex. 4, §7). The first of these is of degree 0 in $x_{3}$, the second of degree 1 . Hence, it will follow from the theorem that we shall prove that these are identities for all Jordan algebras.

It is convenient for the present considerations to deal with algebras having identity elements. Accordingly, we define the free Jordan algebra with $1 F J(Y)$ generated by a (nonvacuous) set $Y$ as $F J(Y)=\Phi\{\{Y\}\} / \mathfrak{T}(Y)$ where $\Phi\{\{Y\}\}$ is
the free nonassociative algebra with 1 generated by $Y$ and $\mathfrak{T}(Y)$ is the ideal in $\Phi\{\{Y\}\}$ generated by all the elements of the form $a b-b a,\left(a^{2} b\right) a-a^{2}(b a)$, $a, b \in \Phi\{\{Y\}\}$. One sees easily as in §7 that $F J(Y)$ is a Jordan algebra with 1 , that we can identify $Y$ with its image in $F J(Y)$ (under the canonical homomorphism $v$ ) and that if $\alpha$ is any mapping of $Y$ into a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 then $\alpha$ has a unique extension to a homomorphism of $F J(Y)$ into $\mathfrak{J}$ sending 1 into 1 . If $Y$ is finite and $|Y|=r$ we write $Y=\left\{y_{1}, y_{2}, \cdots, y_{r}\right\}$ and put $F J(Y)=F J^{(r)}$.

We recall the definition of the free special Jordan algebra with $1 F S J^{(r)}$. This is the subalgebra of $\Phi\left\{u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{r}\right\}^{+}$generated by 1 and the $u_{i}$ where $\Phi\left\{u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{r}\right\}$ is the free associative algebra with 1 generated by $r$ distinct elements $u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{r}$. We have the homomorphism $\sigma$ of $F J^{(r)}$ onto $F S J^{(r)}$ such that $1^{\sigma}=1, y_{i}{ }^{\sigma}=u_{i}, 1 \leqq i \leqq r$, whose kernel we denote as $\Re^{(r)}$. For $r=3$ we use the notations $x, y, z$ and $u, v, w$ for $y_{1}, y_{2}, y_{3}$ and $u_{1}, u_{2}, u_{3}$ respectively. The main esult we shall prove in this section is
Macdonald's Theorem. Let $F J^{(3)}$ be the free Jordan algebra with 1 generated by $x, y, z, F S J^{(3)}$ the free special Jordan algebra with 1 generated by $u, v, w, \sigma$ the homomorphism of $F J^{(3)}$ onto $F S J^{(3)}$ mapping $1 \rightarrow 1, x \rightarrow u, y \rightarrow v$, $z \rightarrow w, \mathfrak{A}^{(3)}$ the kernel of $\sigma$ and let 3 be the subspace of elements of $F J^{(3)}$ which are homogeneous of degree 1 in $z$. Then $\mathfrak{K}^{(3)} \cap 3=0$.

We shall see that this result will imply the results we stated above on identities. It will imply also an earlier result due to Shirshov that $\Re^{(2)}=0$, or, equvalently, the free Jordan algebra $F J^{(2)}$ is special. A precise definition of the set 3 in the theorem is that this is the image of the space of elements of $\Phi\{\{x, y, z\}\}$ homogeneous of degree one in $z$ under the canonical homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{x, y, z\}\}$ onto $F J^{(3)}=\Phi\{\{x, y, z\}\} / \mathfrak{T}$. It is immediate by induction on degree that any element of $\Phi\{\{x, y, z\}\}$ which is a product of $x$ 's, $y$ 's and one $z$ has the form $z P$ where $P$ is product of left and right multiplications by elements which are products of $x$ 's and $y$ 's. It follows that the elements of $\Phi\{\{x, y, z\}\}$ which are homogeneous of degree one in $z$ have the form $z L$ where $L$ is in the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}(\Phi\{\{x, y, z\}\}$, $\Phi\{\{x, y, z\}\})$ generated by the multiplications $b_{L}, b_{R}$ where $b$ is in the subalgebra $\Phi\{\{x, y\}\}$ generated by $x, y$. This implies that $3=z R_{F J^{(3)}}\left(F J^{(2)}\right)^{*}$ where $R_{F J^{(3)}}\left(F J^{(2)}\right)^{*}$ is the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}\left(F J^{(3)}, F J^{(3)}\right)$ generated by the $R_{c}, c \in F J^{(2)}$ the subalgebra of $F J^{(3)}$ generated by $1, x, y$.
We shall now formulate Macdonald's Theorem in an equivalent operator form. We observe first that if $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ are arbitrary algebras and $\sigma$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ onto $\mathfrak{B}$ then we have a homomorphism of the subalgebra $M(\mathfrak{A})$ of $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$ generated by 1 and the $a_{L}, a_{R}, a \in \mathfrak{A}$ onto $M(\mathfrak{B})$ mapping $1 \rightarrow 1, a_{L} \rightarrow\left(a^{\sigma}\right)_{L}$, $a_{R} \rightarrow\left(a^{\sigma}\right)_{R}$. To see this let $X$ and $Y$ be two disjoint sets which are bijective with $\mathfrak{A}$ under mappings $a \rightarrow x_{a} \in X, a \rightarrow y_{a} \in Y$ and let $Z=X \cup Y$. We have homomorphism $\tau$ and $\tau^{\prime}$ of the free associative algebra with $1 \Phi\{Z\}$ onto $M(\mathfrak{A})$ and $M(\mathfrak{B})$ such that $1^{\tau}=1, x_{a}{ }^{\tau}=a_{L}, y_{a}{ }^{\tau}=a_{R}, 1^{\tau^{\prime}}=1, x_{a}{ }^{\tau^{\prime}}=\left(a^{\sigma}\right)_{L}, y_{a}{ }^{\tau^{\prime}}=\left(a^{\sigma}\right)_{R}$. If $F \in \Phi\{Z\}$
and $u \in \mathfrak{A}$ then one sees easily via monomials that $\left(u F^{\tau}\right)^{\sigma}=u^{\sigma} F^{\tau^{\prime}}$. Since $\sigma$ is surjective this implies that if $F^{\tau}=0$ then $F^{\tau^{\prime}}=0$. It follows that we have a homomorphism of $M(\mathfrak{A})$ onto $M(\mathfrak{B})$ such that $F^{\tau} \rightarrow F^{\tau^{\prime}}$ and hence $1 \rightarrow 1, a_{L} \rightarrow\left(a^{\sigma}\right)_{L}$, $a_{R} \rightarrow\left(a^{\sigma}\right)_{R}$. In particular, the homomorphism $\sigma$ of $F J^{(3)}$ onto $F S J^{(3)}$ gives rise to a homomorphism of $M\left(F J^{(3)}\right)=R\left(F J^{(3)}\right)^{*}$ onto $R\left(F S J^{(3)}\right)^{*}$ sending $1 \rightarrow 1$, $R_{a} \rightarrow R_{a^{\sigma}}, a \in F S J^{(3)}$. By restriction we obtain the homomorphism $\Sigma$ of $R_{F J^{(3)}}\left(F J^{(2)}\right)^{*}$, the subalgebra generated by the $R_{b}, b \in F J^{(2)}$, (the subalgebra generated by $1, x, y$ ), onto $R_{F S J^{(3)}}\left(F S J^{(2)}\right)^{*}$. Now suppose $\Sigma$ is an isomorphism and let $a \in \mathcal{Z} \cap \mathfrak{A}^{(3)}$. Then $a=z L$ where $L \in R_{F J^{(3)}}\left(F J^{(2)}\right)^{*}$ and $w L^{\Sigma}=(z L)^{\sigma} =a^{\sigma}=0$. Since there exists an endomorphism of $F S J^{(3)}$ leaving $1, u$ and $v$ fixed and mapping $w$ into any element of $F S J^{(3)}, w L^{\Sigma}=0$ implies $b L^{\Sigma}=0$ for all $b \in F S J^{(3)}$. Thus $L^{\Sigma}=0$ and $L=0$ so $a=0$. Hence we have the conclusion of Macdonald's Theorem: $3 \cap \mathfrak{K}^{(3)}=0$. Conversely, assume this holds and let $L \in R_{F J^{(3)}}\left(F J^{(2)}\right)^{*}$ satisfy $L^{\Sigma}=0$. Then $w L^{\Sigma}=(z L)^{\sigma}=0$ and $z L \in Z \cap \Re^{(3)}$. Hence $z L=0$. Since we have an endomorphism of $F J^{(3)}$ fixing $1, x, y$ and sending $z$ into any $a \in F J^{(3)}$ we see that $L=0$. Hence we have shown that Macdonald's Theorem is equivalent to the operator result that $\Sigma$ is an isomorphism of $R_{F J^{(3)}}\left(F J^{(2)}\right)^{*}$ onto $R_{F S J^{(3)}}\left(F S J^{(2)}\right)^{*}$. We shall prove this statement by choosing generators for the two algebras of operators and establishing the same defining relations for these generators. Our choice of generators will be based on the following

Lemma 1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with $1, \mathfrak{B}$ a subalgebra containing 1, $X$ a set of generators for $\mathfrak{B}$ containing 1. Then the set of operators $U_{x, y}, x, y \in X$, is a set of generators for $R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ *.

Proof. We have $R_{x}=U_{x, 1}, R_{x, y}=R_{x} R_{y}+R_{y} R_{x}-U_{x, y}$. Hence it suffices to show that the elements $R_{x . y}, x, y \in X$, generate $R_{\mathfrak{y}}(\mathfrak{B})^{*}$. Since $X$ generates $\mathfrak{B}$ every element of $\mathfrak{B}$ is a linear combination of products of $x$ 's in $X$. Hence it is enough to show that if $m$ is such a product then $R_{m}$ is contained in the subalgebra $\mathfrak{X}$ of $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ generated by the $R_{x . y}, x, y \in X$. Since $\mathfrak{B}$ is commutative it is enough to show that $R_{m} \in \mathfrak{X}$ for $m=m_{1} \cdot m_{2} \cdot m_{3}$ where $m_{i}$ is a product of $x$ 's in $\mathfrak{X}$. Using induction on the number of factors we may assume that $R_{m_{i}}$ and $R_{m_{i}, m_{j}} \in \mathfrak{X}$. By $O_{2}$ we have $R_{m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}}=R_{m_{1}, m_{2}} R_{m_{3}}+R_{m_{1}, m_{3}} R_{m_{2}}+R_{m_{2}, m_{3}} R_{m_{1}} -R_{m_{1}} R_{m_{3}} R_{m_{2}}-R_{m_{2}} R_{m_{3}} R_{m_{1}}$ which is contained in $\mathfrak{X}$ by our induction assumption.
If we apply this lemma to $\mathfrak{J}=F J^{(3)}, \mathfrak{B}=F J^{(2)}$, which is generated by $X=\{1, x, y\}$, then we see that $R_{F J^{(3)}}\left(F J^{(2)}\right)^{*}$ is generated by the five elements 1 , $R_{x}, R_{y}, U_{x}, U_{y}, U_{x, y}$. However, it appears to be difficult to obtain a set of defining relations for these generators. On the other hand, we shall succeed in doing this for the infinite set of generators $1, R_{x^{\cdot i}}, R_{y^{\cdot i}}, U_{x^{\cdot i}}, U_{y^{\cdot i}}, U_{x^{\cdot i}, y^{\cdot j}}$ where $i, j \geqq 1$.
Accordingly, we introduce the free associative algebra with 1 :

$$
\mathfrak{F}=\Phi\left\{a_{i}, b_{i}, c_{i}, d_{i}, e_{i j}\right\}
$$

(freely) generated by distinct elements $a_{i}, b_{i}, c_{i}, d_{i}, e_{i j}, i, j=1,2,3 \cdots$. Let $\tau$ be the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{F}$ into $R_{F J}{ }^{(3)}\left(F J^{(2)}\right)^{*}$ such that

$$
\begin{align*}
& 1 \rightarrow 1, a_{i} \rightarrow R_{x \cdot i}, b_{i} \rightarrow R_{y^{\cdot i}}  \tag{76}\\
& c_{i} \rightarrow U_{x \cdot i}, d_{i} \rightarrow U_{y^{\cdot i}}, e_{i j} \rightarrow U_{x \cdot i, y^{\cdot j}}
\end{align*}
$$

$\tau^{\prime}$ the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{F}$ into $R_{F S J^{(3)}}\left(F S J^{(2)}\right)^{*}$ such that

$$
\begin{gather*}
1 \rightarrow 1, \quad a_{i} \rightarrow R_{u \cdot i}, \quad b_{i} \rightarrow R_{v^{\cdot i}}  \tag{77}\\
c_{i} \rightarrow U_{u \cdot i}, \quad d_{i} \rightarrow U_{v \cdot i}, \quad e_{i j} \rightarrow U_{u \cdot i, \cdot j}
\end{gather*}
$$

Then $\tau$ and $\tau^{\prime}$ are surjective and $\tau^{\prime}=\tau \Sigma$ where $\Sigma$ is the homomorphism we defined before of $R_{F J^{(3)}}\left(F J^{(2)}\right)^{*}$ onto $F_{F S J^{(3)}}\left(F S J^{(2)}\right)^{*}$. Let $\Re=\operatorname{ker} \tau, \Re^{\prime}=\operatorname{ker} \tau^{\prime}$. Then $\Re^{\prime} \supseteq \Re$ and $\Sigma$ is an isomorphism if and only if $\Re^{\prime}=\Re$. We shall prove this by showing that both of these coincide with a third ideal $\mathfrak{G}$ of $\mathfrak{F}$ defined by generators.

Lemma 2. The following elements are contained in $\Re$ :

$$
\begin{gather*}
{\left[a_{i}, a_{j}\right], \quad\left[a_{i}, c_{j}\right], \quad\left[b_{i}, b_{j}\right], \quad\left[b_{i}, d_{j}\right],}  \tag{i}\\
2 a_{i} a_{j}-a_{i+j}-a_{i-j} c_{j}, \quad 2 b_{i} b_{j}-b_{i+j}-b_{i-j} d_{j}, \quad i \geqq j \geqq 1 \tag{ii}
\end{gather*}
$$

where we take $a_{0}=b_{0}=1$ if $i=j$,

$$
\begin{gather*}
c_{i} c_{j}-c_{i+j}, \quad d_{i} d_{j}-d_{i+j},  \tag{iii}\\
c_{i} e_{j k}-2 a_{i} e_{i+j, k}+e_{2 i+j, k}, \quad d_{i} e_{j k}-2 b_{i} e_{j, i+k}-e_{j, k+2 i},  \tag{iv}\\
d_{i} a_{j}-2 b_{i} e_{j i}+e_{j, 2 i}, \quad c_{i} b_{j}-2 a_{i} e_{i j}+e_{i, 2 j},  \tag{v}\\
2 e_{i j} a_{k}-e_{i-k, j} c_{k}-e_{i+k, j}, \quad 2 e_{j i} b_{k}-e_{j, i-k} d_{k}-e_{j, i+k}, \quad i>k,  \tag{vi}\\
2 e_{i j} a_{i}-e_{2 i, j}-b_{j} c_{i}, \quad 2 e_{j i} b_{i}-e_{j, 2 i}-a_{j} d_{i},  \tag{vii}\\
e_{i j} a_{k}-e_{i+k, j}-b_{j} a_{k-i} c_{i}+e_{k j} a_{i},  \tag{viii}\\
e_{j i} b_{k}-e_{j, i+k}-a_{j} b_{k-i} c_{i}+e_{j k} b_{i}, \quad i<k .
\end{gather*}
$$

Proof. In view of the definition of $\Re$ and (76) the assertions are equivalent to the following identities for arbitrary Jordan algebras with 1 :

$$
\begin{align*}
{\left[R_{p^{\cdot i}} R_{p^{\cdot j}}\right] } & =0, \quad\left[R_{p^{\cdot i}}, U_{p^{\cdot j}}\right]=0,  \tag{i'}\\
2 R_{p^{\cdot i}} R_{p^{\cdot j}} & =R_{p^{\cdot i+j}}+R_{p^{\cdot i}-j} U_{p^{\cdot j}}, \quad i \geqq j,  \tag{ii'}\\
U_{p^{\cdot i}} U_{p^{\cdot j}} & =U_{p^{\cdot i+j}}  \tag{iii'}\\
U_{p^{\cdot i}} U_{p^{\cdot j}, q^{\cdot k}} & =2 R_{p^{\cdot i}} U_{p^{\cdot i+j}, q^{\cdot k}}-U_{p^{\cdot 2 i+j}, q^{\cdot k+}},  \tag{$\prime$}\\
U_{q^{\cdot i}} R_{p^{\cdot i}} & =2 R_{q^{\cdot i}} U_{p^{\cdot j}, q^{\cdot i}}-U_{p^{\cdot j}, q^{\cdot 2 i}}, \tag{$\prime$}
\end{align*}
$$

$$
\begin{align*}
& 2 U_{p^{\cdot i}, q^{\cdot j}} R_{p^{\cdot k}}=U_{p^{\cdot i-k}, q^{\cdot j}} U_{p^{\cdot k}}+U_{p^{\cdot i+k}, q^{\cdot j}}, \quad i>k,  \tag{vi'}\\
& 2 U_{p^{\cdot i}, q^{\cdot j}} R_{p^{\cdot i}}=U_{p^{\cdot 2 i}, q^{\cdot j}}+R_{q^{\cdot j}} U_{p^{\cdot i}},  \tag{vii'}\\
& U_{p^{\cdot i}, q^{\cdot j}} R_{p^{\cdot k}}=U_{p^{\cdot i+k}, q^{\cdot j}}+R_{q^{\cdot j}} R_{p^{\cdot k-i}} U_{p^{\cdot i}}-U_{p^{\cdot k}, q^{\cdot j}} R_{p^{\cdot i}}, \quad i<k . \tag{viii'}
\end{align*}
$$

Now (i') is clear and (ii') for $i=j$ follows from the definition of $U_{a}$. Also (ii') for $i>j$ is a special case of ( $\mathrm{vi}^{\prime}$ ) if we allow $j=0$ in ( $\mathrm{vi}^{\prime}$ ). Now ( $\mathrm{vi}^{\prime}$ ) with $j \geqq 0$ can be obtained by putting $a^{\prime}=p^{\cdot i-k}, a=p^{\cdot k}, b=q^{\cdot j}$ in (69). To obtain (iii') we put $a=p^{. i}, a^{\prime}=p^{. j}$ in (66). For (iv') we put $a=p^{. i}, a^{\prime}=p^{. j}, b=q^{. k}$ in (68) and for (v') we put $b=q^{. i}, a=p^{. j}$ in (67). For (vii') and (viii') we put $a=p^{. i}$, $b=q^{. j}, a^{\prime}=1$ and $a=p^{. i}, b=q^{. j}, a^{\prime}=p^{. k-i}$ respectively in (70).

Now let $\mathfrak{G}$ be the ideal in $\mathfrak{F}$ generated by the elements (i)-(viii) given in Lemma 2. Then we have $\Re^{\prime} \supseteq \Re \supseteq \mathfrak{G}$. We shall now show that there exists a set of elements $B=\{b\}$ in $\mathfrak{F}$ such that: (1) the cosets $\left\{b+\Re^{\prime} \mid b \in B\right\}$ are linearly independent in $\mathfrak{F} / \Re^{\prime}$ and (2) every coset $a+\mathfrak{G}, a \in \mathfrak{F}$, in $\mathfrak{F} / \mathfrak{G}$ is a linear combination of the cosets $b+\mathfrak{G}, b \in B$. The desired equality $\Re^{\prime}=\Re=\mathfrak{G}$ will follow from these two facts since, if $\mathfrak{B}$ is the subspace of $\mathfrak{F}$ spanned by $B$, then $\mathfrak{F}=\mathfrak{B}+\mathfrak{G}$ and $\mathfrak{B} \cap \Re^{\prime}=0$. Then since $\Re^{\prime} \supseteq \mathfrak{G}, \Re^{\prime}=\mathfrak{F} \cap \Re^{\prime}=\left(\mathfrak{B} \cap \Re^{\prime}\right)+\left(\mathfrak{G} \cap \Re^{\prime}\right)=\mathfrak{G}$. For the set $B$ we take the set of monomials of the form $P Q R$ where $P$ is a product of terms which are alternately $a_{t}$ and $b_{j}$ in the set of generators of $\mathfrak{F}=\Phi\left\{a_{i}, b_{i}, c_{i}, d_{i}, e_{i j}\right\}, Q$ is any product of $e$ 's and $R$ is a product of terms which are alternately $c$ 's and $d$ 's. We shall also include 1 in the set $B$. We introduce a bigrading in $\mathfrak{F}$ by defining an $x$-degree and $y$-degree of monomials in the generators by the following rules: 1 has $x$-degree and $y$-degree $0, a_{i}$ has $x$-degree $i$ and $y$-degree $0, b_{i}$ has $x$-degree 0 and $y$-degree $i, c_{i}$ has $x$-degree $2 i$ and $y$-degree $0, d_{i}$ has $x$-degree 0 and $y$-degree $2 i, e_{i j}$ has $x$-degree $i$ and $y$-degree $j$. Moreover, the $x$ - and $y$-degrees of any monomial are the sums of the corresponding degrees of the factors. Let $\mathfrak{F}_{r, s}$ be the subspace of linear combinations of monomials of $x$-degree $r$ and $y$-degree $s$. Then $\mathfrak{F}=\Sigma \oplus \mathfrak{F}_{r, s}$. Also let $B(r, s)=\mathfrak{F}_{r, s} \cap B$.

Lemma 3. Every monomial in the generators $a_{i}, b_{i}, \cdots$, of

$$
\mathfrak{F}=\Phi\left\{a_{i}, b_{i}, c_{i}, d_{i}, e_{i j}\right\}
$$

of $x$-degree $r$ and $y$-degree $s$ is congruent modulo $\mathfrak{G}$ to a linear combination of elements of $B(r, s)$.

Proof. We use induction on $r+s$. The result will follow if we can show that if $K^{\prime} \in B$ and $K=K^{\prime} a_{i}, K^{\prime} b_{i}, K^{\prime} c_{i}, K^{\prime} d_{i}, K^{\prime} e_{i j}$ has $x$-degree $r$ and $y$-degree $s$ then $K$ is congruent to a linear combination of elements of $B(r, s)$ modulo $\mathfrak{G}$. We consider the various cases in the following order:

Case I. $K=K^{\prime} c_{i}, K^{\prime} \in B(r-2 i, s)$. If $K^{\prime}$ ends in anything except a $c_{j}$ then $K^{\prime} c_{i} \in B(r, s)$. Hence we may assume $K^{\prime}=K^{\prime \prime} c_{j}, K^{\prime \prime} \in B(r-2 i-2 j, s)$. Then
$K=K^{\prime \prime} c_{j} c_{\imath} \equiv K^{\prime \prime} c_{i+j}(\bmod \mathfrak{G})$ by (iii). It is clear that $K^{\prime \prime} c_{\imath+j} \in B(r, s)$ so the result holds in this case.

Case II. $K=K^{\prime} d_{i}$ where $B^{\prime} \in B(r, s-2 i)$. This is exactly like Case I.
Case III. $K=K^{\prime} e_{j k}, K^{\prime} \in B(r-j, s-k)$. If $j+k=r+s$ then $K^{\prime}=1$ and the result is clear. We shall now treat this case by induction downward for $j+k$.
