Moreover, $\zeta_{s}$ is a homomorphism of algebras with involution of $(S(\mathfrak{J}), \pi)$ into $\left(S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right), \pi^{\prime}\right)$ where $\pi$ and $\pi^{\prime}$ are the main involutions in $S(\mathfrak{J})$ and $S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$.
(5) If $0 \rightarrow \mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow_{\eta} \mathfrak{J} \rightarrow_{\zeta} \mathfrak{J}^{\prime} \rightarrow 0$ is exact and $\left(S(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right)$, ( $S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right), \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}$ ) are special universal envelopes for $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ respectively, then $S(\mathfrak{J}) \rightarrow_{\zeta s} S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow 0$ is exact and $\operatorname{ker} \zeta_{s}$ is the ideal in $S(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime \sigma_{u}}$.
(6) If $\Gamma$ is an extension of the base field $\Phi$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\sigma_{u}$ is the linear extension to $\mathfrak{J}_{\Gamma}$ (into $S(\mathfrak{J})_{\Gamma}$ ) of $\sigma_{u}$ then ( $S(\mathfrak{J})_{\Gamma}, \sigma_{u}$ ) is a special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}_{\Gamma}$.
(7) If $D$ is a derivation in $\mathfrak{J}$ then there exists a unique derivation $D_{u}$ in $S(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $D \sigma_{u}=\sigma_{u} D_{u}$. Moreover, $D_{u}$ is a derivation for the algebra with involution ( $S(\mathfrak{J}), \pi$ ) in the sense that $D_{u} \pi=\pi D_{u}$.
(8) If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}=n$ then $\operatorname{dim} S(\mathfrak{J}) \leqq 2^{n}$.

Proofs. (1) If we apply the definition of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ with $\mathfrak{G}=S^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ we obtain a homomorphism $\imath$ of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $S^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $\sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}=\sigma_{u}$ l. By symmetry, we have a homomorphism $\imath^{\prime}$ of $S^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $S(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $\sigma_{u}=\sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime} \imath^{\prime}$. Then $\sigma_{u}=\sigma_{u} \imath^{\prime}{ }^{\prime}$. On the other hand, if $1_{S(\mathfrak{I})}$ is the identity mapping on $S(\mathfrak{I})$ then $\sigma_{u}=\sigma_{u} 1_{S(\mathfrak{I})}$. If we apply the definition of $\left(S(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right)$ taking $\mathfrak{G}=S(\mathfrak{J})$ we see that $1_{S(\mathfrak{\mathfrak { I }})}$ is the only homomorphism of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $S(\mathfrak{J})$ satisfying $\sigma_{u}=\sigma_{u} 1_{S(\mathfrak{J})}$. Hence $\mathfrak{u}^{\prime}=1_{S(\mathfrak{J})}$. By symmetry $\imath^{\prime} \imath=1_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathfrak{I})}$. Hence $\imath$ is an isomorphism of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $S^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$.
(2) Let $S^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ be the subalgebra of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by 1 and $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}}$. Then $\sigma_{u}$ can be considered as an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $S^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\left(S^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right)$ is a special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. The injection mapping $\imath^{\prime}$ of $S^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $S(\mathfrak{J})$ satisfies $\sigma_{u}=\sigma_{u} \imath^{\prime}$. Hence by (1) $\imath^{\prime}$ is an isomorphism of $S^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $S(\mathfrak{J})$. Thus $\mathfrak{t}^{\prime}$ is surjective and $S^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})=S(\mathfrak{J})$.
(3) Let $\mathfrak{A}^{\circ}$ be the opposite algebra of $\mathfrak{A}=S(\mathfrak{I})$. Then $u \rightarrow u$ is an anti-isomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}^{\circ}$. Hence $\sigma_{u}$ is an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{A}^{\circ}$ and there exists a homomorphism $\pi^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{A}^{\circ}$ such that $1^{\pi^{\prime}}=1$ and $a^{\sigma_{u} \pi^{\prime}}=a^{\sigma_{u}}$. If we compose $\pi^{\prime}$ with the anti-isomorphism $u \rightarrow u$ of $\mathfrak{U}^{\circ}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}$ we obtain an anti-homomorphism $\pi$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $1^{\pi}=1$ and $a^{\sigma_{u} \pi}=\grave{a}^{\sigma_{u}}$, $a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then $\pi^{2}$ is an endomorphism in $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $1^{\pi^{2}}=1, a^{\sigma_{u} \pi^{2}}=a^{\sigma_{u}}$. Since 1 and the $a^{\sigma_{u}}$ generate $\mathfrak{A}$ we have $\pi^{2}=1$ and $\pi$ is an involution in $\mathfrak{A}$.
(4) If $\zeta$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ then $\zeta \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}$ is an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$. Hence, by definition of $\left(S(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right)$, there exists a unique homomor-
phism $\zeta_{s}$ of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and (5) is commutative. If $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $a^{\sigma_{u} \pi \zeta_{s}}=a^{\sigma_{u} \zeta_{s}}=a^{\zeta \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}}=a^{\zeta \sigma^{\prime}{ }_{u} \pi^{\prime}}=a^{\sigma_{u} \zeta_{s} \pi^{\prime}}$. Since 1 and the $a^{\sigma_{u}}$ generate $S(\mathfrak{J})$ this implies that $\pi \zeta_{s}=\zeta_{s} \pi^{\prime}$ so $\zeta_{s}$ is a homomorphism of $(S(\mathfrak{J}), \pi)$ into $\left(S\left(\mathfrak{I}^{\prime}\right), \pi^{\prime}\right)$.
(5) The hypothesis implies that $\mathfrak{J}^{\zeta}=\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u} \zeta_{s}}=\mathfrak{J}^{\zeta \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}}=\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}}$. Now 1 and $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}}$ generate $S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ and $S(\mathfrak{J})$ contains 1 and $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}}$ so $S(\mathfrak{J})^{\zeta_{s}}$ contains the set of generators 1 and $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u} \zeta_{s}}=\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}}$. Since $S(\mathfrak{J})^{\zeta_{s}}$ is a subalgebra of $S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ it follows that $S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)=S(\mathfrak{J})^{\zeta_{s}}$. Hence $S(\mathfrak{J}) \rightarrow_{\zeta_{s}} S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow 0$ is exact. We have $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime} \eta \sigma_{u} \zeta_{s}=\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime} \eta \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}=0$ so $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime} \sigma_{u} \subseteq \operatorname{ker} \zeta_{s}$. Then the ideal $\Re$ in $S(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime} \sigma_{u}$ is contained in $\operatorname{ker} \zeta_{s}$. If $v$ denotes the canonical homomorphism $u \rightarrow u+\mathfrak{M}$ of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $S(\mathfrak{J}) / \mathfrak{M}$ then $\sigma_{u} v$ is an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ is mapped into 0 by $\sigma_{u} v$ we have the associative specialization $a+\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime \boldsymbol{\eta}} \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{u} \nu}$ of $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime \boldsymbol{\eta}}$ in $S(\mathfrak{J}) / \mathfrak{K}$. Now the exactness of $0 \rightarrow^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow_{\eta} \mathfrak{J} \rightarrow_{\zeta} \mathfrak{J}^{\prime} \rightarrow 0$ implies that $a^{\zeta} \rightarrow a+\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime \eta}$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ onto $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime}{ }^{\eta}$. (6) Let $\sigma$ be an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}_{\Gamma}$ in an associative algebra $\mathfrak{G} / \Gamma$ with 1. Considering $\mathfrak{J}$ as a $\Phi$-subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}_{\Gamma}$ ( $\mathfrak{J}$ identified with the set of elements $1 \otimes a, a \in \mathfrak{J}$ ) and $\mathfrak{G}$ an algebra over $\Phi$ then the restriction $\sigma \mid \mathfrak{J}$ of $\sigma$ to $\mathfrak{J}$ is an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{G} / \Phi$. Then $\sigma_{u}$ is an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}_{\Gamma}$ in $S(\mathfrak{J})_{\Gamma}$. This proves that $\left(S(\mathfrak{J})_{\Gamma}, \sigma_{u}\right)$ is a special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}_{\Gamma}$.
(7) Let $D$ be a derivation in $\mathfrak{J}$. Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be the two-dimensional commutative associative algebra over $\Phi$ with identity 1 and basis $(1, t)$ such that $t^{2}=0$ and form $\mathfrak{D} \otimes_{\Phi} S(\mathfrak{J})$. With the obvious identifications we can consider $\mathfrak{D}$ and $S(\mathfrak{J})$ as subalgebras of $\mathfrak{D} \otimes S(\mathfrak{J})$ and the elements of $\mathfrak{D} \otimes S(\mathfrak{J})$ can be written uniquely in the form $x_{1}+x_{2} t$ where $x_{i} \in S(\mathfrak{J})$. Hence we have a homomorphism of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{D} \otimes S(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $1^{\eta}=1$ and $a^{\sigma_{u} \eta}=a^{\sigma_{u}} +(a D)^{\sigma_{u}} t$. If $x \in S(\mathfrak{J})$ then we have $x^{\eta}=x+x^{\prime} t$ since $1^{\eta}=1, a^{\sigma_{u} \eta}=a^{\sigma_{u}}+(a D)^{\sigma_{u}} t$ and 1 and the $a^{\sigma_{u}}$ generate $S(\mathfrak{J})$. The facts that $t^{2}=0$ and $t x=x t, x \in S(\mathfrak{J})$,
imply that $x \rightarrow x^{\prime}$ is a derivation $D_{u}$ in $S(\mathfrak{J})$. We have $a^{\sigma_{u} \eta}=a^{\sigma_{\cdots}}+(a D)^{\sigma_{u}} t= a^{\sigma_{u}}+\left(a^{\sigma_{u}}\right) D_{u} t$. Hence $D \sigma_{u}=\sigma_{u} D_{u}$. As in (4), it is clear that $D_{u} \pi=\pi D_{u}$.
(8) Let $\left(u_{\imath}\right), \imath$ belonging to an ordered set, be a basis for $\mathfrak{J}$. Then we claim that every element of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ is a linear combination of 1 and the "standard" monomials $v_{t_{1}} v_{t_{2}} \cdots v_{t_{r}}, v_{t_{j}}=u_{t_{j}}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}, \mathrm{l}_{1}<\mathrm{l}_{2}<\cdots<\mathrm{l}_{r}$. Since $\mathfrak{A}=S(\mathfrak{J})$ is generated by 1 and $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma{ }^{\prime \prime}}$ every element of $\mathfrak{A}$ is a linear combination of 1 and monomials in the $v_{\imath}=u_{\imath}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}$. Hence it suffices to show that every monomial in the $v_{\imath}$ is a linear combination of standard monomials. We have the relations $v_{\imath} v_{\kappa}=-v_{\kappa} v_{\imath}+2\left(u_{\imath} . u_{\kappa}\right)^{\sigma_{n}}$, by (1), and $\left(u_{\imath} \cdot u_{\kappa}\right)^{\sigma_{u}}$ is a linear combination of the $v$ 's. This permits us to replace a product $v_{\imath} v_{\kappa}$ with $\mathrm{r}>\kappa$ in a monomial in the $v^{\prime}$ 's by $v_{\kappa} v_{\imath}$ at the expense of a linear combination of monomials of lower formal degree than that of the given one. Also since $v_{\imath}{ }^{2}=\left(u_{\imath}{ }^{2}\right)^{\sigma_{u}}$ we can apply the same procedure to a square $v_{\imath}{ }^{2}$ occurring in a monomial. A succession of such reductions can be used to express any monomial in the $v$ 's as a linear combination of standard monomials in the $v$ 's (see Jacobson, Lie Algebras, p. 157 for a more formal argument). Now let $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}=n$ and assume $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$. Then our result shows that every element of $\mathfrak{A}$ is a linear combination of 1 and the elements $v_{i_{1}} v_{i_{2}} \cdots v_{i_{r}}$, $i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{r}, v_{i_{j}}=u_{i_{j}}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}$. Hence $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A} \leqq 2^{n}$.

In connection with (8) we remark that one can give examples in which the bound $2^{n}$ is attained. On the other hand, in the interesting cases $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A}<2^{n}$.

We shall now give a construction of a special universal envelope for any Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$. For this purpose we form the tensor algebra $T(\mathfrak{J})=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{J}^{(2)} \oplus \mathfrak{J}^{(3)} \oplus \cdots$ where $\mathfrak{J}^{(i)}=\mathfrak{J} \otimes \mathfrak{J} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathfrak{J}, i$ factors. The associative algebra has the following universal mapping property: Let $\sigma$ be a linear mapping $\mathfrak{J}$ into an associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 . Then $\sigma$ has a unique extension to a homomorphism of $T(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ mapping 1 into 1 . Now let $\Re_{s}$ be the ideal in $T(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by all elements of the form $(a . b)-\frac{1}{2}(a \otimes b+b \otimes a), a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$. Put $S(\mathfrak{J})=T(\mathfrak{J}) / \Re_{s}$ and $a^{\sigma_{u}}=a+\Re_{s}, \quad a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then $(a . b)^{\sigma_{u}}-\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\sigma_{u}} b^{\sigma_{u}}+b^{\sigma_{u}} a^{\sigma_{u}}\right)=(a . b) -\frac{1}{2}(a \otimes b+b \otimes a)+\Re_{s}=\Re_{s}$ the 0 -element of $S(\mathfrak{J})$. Hence $\sigma_{u}$ is an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $S(\mathfrak{J})$. Next let $\sigma$ be any associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in an associative algebra $\mathfrak{5}$ with 1 and let $\eta^{\prime}$ denote the extension of $\sigma$ to a homomorphism of $T(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{5}$ mapping $1 \rightarrow 1$. Then $\left(a . b-\frac{1}{2}(a \otimes b+b \otimes a)\right)^{\eta^{\prime}} =(a . b)^{\sigma}-\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\sigma} b^{\sigma}+b^{\sigma} a^{\sigma}\right)=0$, if $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$. Hence the generators of $\Re_{s}$ and consequently $\Re_{s}$ is mapped into 0 by $\eta^{\prime}$. Hence we have the homomorphism $\eta$ of $S(\mathfrak{J})=T(\mathfrak{J}) / \Re$ into $\mathfrak{5}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $\left(a^{\sigma_{u}}\right)^{\eta}=\left(a+\Re_{s}\right)^{\eta}=a^{\eta^{\prime}}=a^{\sigma}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Thus ( $S(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}$ ) satisfies the definition of a special universal envelope. From now on we shall take the $\left(S(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right)$ we have just constructed as our standard one and refer to this as the special universal envelope of the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$.

The result (4) of Theorem 1 which we indicated in the diagram (5) gives a multiplicative property of the mapping $\zeta \rightarrow \zeta_{s}$. More precisely, suppose we have a homomorphism $\zeta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ and a homomorphism $\lambda$ of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime}$ and let $\left(S(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right),\left(S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right), \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}\right),\left(S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime}\right), \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime \prime}\right)$ be the special universal multiplication envelopes
of $\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime}$ respectively. Then we have the homomorphism $\zeta \lambda$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime}$ and $\zeta_{s} \lambda_{s}$ of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime}\right)$ in the diagram
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-078.jpg?height=240&width=409&top_left_y=427&top_left_x=660)

Since the two squares are commutative: $\zeta \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}=\sigma_{u} \zeta_{s}, \lambda \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime \prime}=\sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime} \lambda_{s}$ it follows that the rectangle is commutative, that is, $\zeta \lambda \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime \prime}=\sigma_{u} \zeta_{s} \lambda_{s}$. Since $(\zeta \lambda)_{s}$ is the unique homomorphism of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime}\right)$ such that $(\zeta \lambda) \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime \prime}=\sigma_{u}(\zeta \lambda)_{s}$ it follows that we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
(\zeta \lambda)_{s}=\zeta_{s} \lambda_{s} . \tag{7}
\end{equation*}
$$

We note also that if $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{J}$ and $\zeta=1_{\mathfrak{J}}$ in (5) then $S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)=S(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\zeta_{s}=1_{\boldsymbol{S}(\mathfrak{I})}$. This and (7) imply that the mappings $\mathfrak{J} \rightarrow S(\mathfrak{J}), \zeta \rightarrow \zeta_{s}$ define a functor $S$ from the category of Jordan algebras into the category of associative algebras with 1 where the morphisms in the latter are the homomorphisms mapping 1 into 1. We recall also that $\zeta_{s}$ is a homomorphism of algebras with involution of ( $S(\mathfrak{J}), \pi$ ) into ( $\left.S\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right), \pi^{\prime}\right), \pi$ and $\pi^{\prime}$ the main involutions in the algebras. Hence we can consider the second category to be that of associative algebras with 1 and involutions. We shall do this from now on and refer to the functor just defined as the special universal functor from the category of Jordan algebras to the category of associative algebras with 1 and involutions.

We recall the notion of a direct limit of algebras. We are given a partially ordered set $A=\{\alpha\}$ which is directed in the sense that for any given $\alpha, \beta \in A$ there exists a $\gamma$ in $A$ such that $\gamma \geqq \alpha, \gamma \geqq \beta$. Next we have a collection of algebras $\mathfrak{U}_{\alpha}$ indexed by the set $A$ and if $\alpha \leqq \beta$ we have a homomorphism $\phi_{\alpha \beta}$ of $\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$ into $\mathfrak{A}_{\beta}$ satisfying the following conditions: (1) $\phi_{\alpha \alpha}=1_{\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}}$, (2) if $\alpha \leqq \beta \leqq \gamma$ then $\phi_{\alpha \beta} \phi_{\beta \gamma}=\phi_{\alpha \gamma}$. Let $\mathfrak{S}$ be the disjoint union of the sets $\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$ and define a relation $\sim$ in $\mathfrak{S}$ by $a_{\alpha} \sim a_{\beta} \left(a_{\alpha} \in \mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}, \quad a_{\beta} \in \mathfrak{A}_{\beta}\right)$ if there exists a $\gamma \geqq \alpha, \beta$ such that $a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha \gamma}}=a_{\beta}{ }^{\phi_{\beta \gamma}}$. This is an equivalence. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ denote the set of equivalence classes $\left[a_{\alpha}\right]$.

We define addition, multiplication by elements of $\Phi$ and a product in $\mathfrak{A}$ by:

$$
\begin{align*}
{\left[a_{\alpha}\right]+\left[b_{\beta}\right] } & =\left[a_{\alpha}^{\phi_{\alpha \gamma}}+b_{\beta}^{\phi_{\beta \gamma}}\right] \quad \text { where } \gamma \geqq \alpha, \beta, \\
\rho\left[a_{\alpha}\right] & =\left[\rho a_{\alpha}\right], \quad \rho \in \Phi,  \tag{8}\\
{\left[a_{\alpha}\right]\left[b_{\beta}\right] } & =\left[a_{\alpha}^{\phi_{\alpha \gamma}} b_{\beta}^{\phi_{\beta \nu}}\right], \quad \gamma \geqq \alpha, \beta .
\end{align*}
$$

It is easy to check that these are well defined and give an algebra structure on $\mathfrak{A}$. We call $\mathfrak{A}$ the direct limit of the $\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$ and write $\mathfrak{A}=\lim _{\rightarrow} \mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$. If all the $\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$ are
in a variety $\mathscr{V}(I)$ of algebras defined by identities then the direct limit is in the variety $\mathscr{V}(I)$. We have the mapping $\phi_{\alpha}$ of $\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ defined by $a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha}}=\left[a_{\alpha}\right]$. This is a homomorphism. Moreover, if $\alpha \leqq \beta$ then $a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha \beta} \phi_{\beta}}=\left[a_{\alpha} \phi_{\alpha \beta}\right]=\left[a_{\alpha}\right] =a_{\alpha}^{\phi_{\alpha}}$. Hence the diagram
is commutative. Note also that every element of $\mathfrak{A}$ has the form $\left[a_{\alpha}\right]$ for some $a_{\alpha} \in \mathfrak{S} . \mathfrak{A}=\lim _{\rightarrow} \mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$ has the following universal mapping property. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be any algebra such that for each $\alpha$ there is a homomorphism $\psi_{\alpha}$ of $\mathfrak{U}_{\alpha}$ into $\mathfrak{B}$ such that if $\alpha \leqq \beta$ then $\phi_{\alpha \beta} \psi_{\beta}=\psi_{\alpha}$. Then there exists a unique homomorphism $\psi$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $\psi_{\alpha}=\phi_{\alpha} \psi$, that is, making the triangles $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$ and $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{A}_{\beta}$ in the following diagram commutative:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-079.jpg?height=317&width=587&top_left_y=1070&top_left_x=603)

To define $\psi$ let $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ and write $a=a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha}}$. Then we define $a^{\psi}=a_{\alpha}{ }^{\psi_{\alpha}}$. If $a_{\alpha}^{\phi_{\alpha}}=a_{\beta}{ }^{\phi_{\beta}}$ then we choose $\gamma \geqq \alpha, \beta$ so that $a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha \gamma}}=a_{\beta}{ }^{\phi_{\beta \gamma}}$. Then $a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha \gamma} \psi_{\gamma}}=a_{\beta}{ }^{\phi_{\beta \gamma} \psi^{\gamma}}$. Hence $a_{\alpha}{ }^{\psi_{\alpha}}=a_{\beta}{ }^{\psi_{\beta}}$ and so $\psi$ is single-valued. Also $\psi$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}$ and $a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha} \psi}=a^{\psi}=a_{\alpha}^{\cdot \psi_{\alpha}}$ so $\phi_{\alpha} \psi=\psi_{\alpha}$ as required. Since the $a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha}}$ generate $\mathfrak{A}$ it is clear that $\psi$ is unique.

We now assume that every $\mathfrak{U}_{\alpha}=\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$ is Jordan. Then $\mathfrak{J}=\lim _{\rightarrow} \mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$ is Jordan. Let $\left(S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right), \sigma_{\alpha u}\right)$ be the special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$. The homomorphism $\phi_{\alpha \beta}, \alpha \leqq \beta$, of $\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$ into $\mathfrak{J}_{\beta}$ gives a unique homomorphism $\Phi_{\alpha \beta}\left(=\phi_{\alpha \beta s}\right)$ of $S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)$ into $S\left(\Im_{\beta}\right)$ making the following diagram commutative:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-079.jpg?height=241&width=302&top_left_y=1842&top_left_x=705)

We have $\Phi_{\alpha \alpha}=1_{S\left(\mathfrak{I}_{\alpha}\right)}, \Phi_{\alpha \beta} \Phi_{\beta \gamma}=\Phi_{\alpha \gamma}$ if $\alpha \leqq \beta \leqq \gamma$. Hence we can define $\lim _{\rightarrow} S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)$.

Let $\Phi_{\alpha}$ be the homomorphism of $S\left(\Im_{\alpha}\right)$ into $\lim S\left(\Im_{\alpha}\right)$ such that $u_{\alpha}{ }^{\Phi}=\left[u_{\alpha}\right]$. This is a homomorphism and $\Phi_{\alpha \beta} \Phi_{\beta}=\Phi_{\alpha}$ if $\alpha \geqq \beta$. Set $\Sigma_{\alpha}=\sigma_{\alpha u} \Phi_{\alpha}$. This is an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$ in $\underset{\rightarrow}{\lim } S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)$. We have $\phi_{\alpha \beta} \Sigma_{\beta}=\phi_{\alpha \beta} \sigma_{\beta u} \Phi_{\beta}=\sigma_{\alpha u} \Phi_{\alpha \beta} \Phi_{\beta} =\sigma_{\alpha u} \Phi_{\alpha}=\Sigma_{\alpha}$ if $\alpha \leqq \beta$. Hence $\overrightarrow{\text { we }}$ have a unique associative specialization $\Sigma_{u}$ of $\mathfrak{J}=\lim _{\rightarrow} \mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$ in $\lim _{\rightarrow} S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)$ such that $\Sigma_{\alpha}=\phi_{\alpha} \Sigma_{u}$.

We shall now prove that the special universal functor commutes with direct limits in the following sense:

THEOREM 2. $\left(\lim _{\rightarrow} S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right), \Sigma_{u}\right)$ is a special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}=\lim _{\rightarrow} \mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$.
Proof. We have seen that $\Sigma_{u}$ is an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\lim _{\rightarrow} S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)$. Now let $\sigma$ be an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in an associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1. Then $\sigma_{\alpha}=\phi_{\alpha} \sigma$ is an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$. Hence we have a homomorphism $\eta_{\alpha}$ of $S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $\phi_{\alpha} \sigma=\sigma_{\alpha}=\sigma_{\alpha u} \eta_{\alpha}$. We claim that $\Phi_{\alpha \beta} \eta_{\beta}=\eta_{\alpha}$. Since 1 and $\mathcal{J}_{\alpha}{ }^{\sigma_{\alpha u}}$ generates $S\left(\Im_{\alpha}\right)$ it suffices to show that if $a_{\alpha} \in \mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$ then $a_{\alpha}{ }^{\sigma_{\alpha u} \Phi_{\alpha \beta} \eta_{\beta}}=a_{\alpha}{ }^{\sigma_{\alpha u} \eta_{\alpha}}$. By (11), $\sigma_{\alpha u} \Phi_{\alpha \beta}=\phi_{\alpha \beta} \sigma_{\beta u}$ so $\sigma_{\alpha u} \Phi_{\alpha \beta} \eta_{\beta}=\phi_{\alpha \beta} \sigma_{\beta u} \eta_{\beta} =\phi_{\alpha \beta} \phi_{\beta} \sigma=\phi_{\alpha} \sigma=\sigma_{\alpha u} \eta_{\alpha}$. It follows that $\Phi_{\alpha \beta} \eta_{\beta}=\eta_{\alpha}$ and so by the universal property of $\lim S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)$ we can define a homomorphism $\eta$ of $\lim S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $1 \rightarrow \overrightarrow{1}$ and $\eta_{\alpha}=\Phi_{\alpha} \eta$. Then if $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ we can write $\vec{a}=a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha}}, a_{\alpha} \in \mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$ for some $\alpha$, and $a^{\Sigma_{u} \eta}=a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha} \Sigma_{u} \eta}=a_{\alpha}{ }^{\Sigma_{\alpha} \eta}$ since $\Sigma_{\alpha}=\phi_{\alpha} \Sigma_{u}$. On the other hand, $a^{\sigma}=a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha} \sigma}=a_{\alpha}{ }^{\sigma_{\alpha u} \eta_{\alpha}}=a_{\alpha}{ }^{\sigma_{\alpha u} \Phi_{\alpha} \eta}=a_{\alpha}{ }^{\Sigma_{\alpha} \eta}$. Hence $\sigma=\Sigma_{u} \eta$. Since the subalgebras $S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)^{\Phi_{\alpha}}$ generate $\lim S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)$ and each $S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)$ is generated by 1 and $\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}{ }^{\sigma_{\alpha u}}$ it is clear that $\lim \overrightarrow{S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)}$ is generated by 1 and $\bigcup \mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}^{\sigma_{\alpha u} \Phi_{\alpha}}=\bigcup \mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}^{\Sigma_{\alpha}}$. Also $\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}^{\Sigma_{\alpha}}=\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha} \Sigma_{u}} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}^{\Sigma_{u}}$. Hence 1 and $\mathfrak{J}^{\Sigma_{u}}$ generate $\lim S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)$. It follows that the homomorphism $\eta$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $\Sigma_{u} \eta=\sigma$ is unique. This proves that $\left(\lim _{\rightarrow} S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right), \Sigma_{u}\right)$ is a special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}=\lim _{\rightarrow} \mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$.

An important special case of a direct limit is the following. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be an algebra and let $F$ be the set of finite subsets of $\mathfrak{A}$ ordered by inclusion. Then $F$ is directed. If $\alpha \in F$ we let $\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$ be the subalgebra generated by $\alpha$, so $\left\{\mathfrak{U}_{\alpha}\right\}$ is the set of finitely generated subalgebras of $\mathfrak{A}$. If $\alpha \leqq \beta$ then $\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha} \subseteq \mathfrak{A}_{\beta}$, and we let $\phi_{\alpha \beta}$ be the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$ in $\mathfrak{U}_{\beta}$. It is clear that our conditions are satisfied and it is easy to see (using the universal property of the direct limit) that $\mathfrak{A}$ can be identified with $\lim \mathfrak{U}_{\alpha}$. More generally, let $A=\{\alpha\}$, an ordered directed set, $\mathfrak{A}$ an algebra and suppose that we have a mapping $\alpha \rightarrow \mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$ of $A$ into the set of subalgebras of $\mathfrak{A}$ such that if $\alpha \leqq \beta$ then $\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha} \subseteq \mathfrak{A}_{\beta}$ and $\mathfrak{A}=\bigcup \mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$. If $\alpha \leqq \beta$ then we let $\phi_{\alpha \beta}$ be the injection of $\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{\beta}$. Then every $\phi_{\alpha \beta}$ is a monomorphism and $\mathfrak{A}$ can be identified with $\lim _{\rightarrow} \mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$. We shall say that $\mathfrak{A}$ is a union of a directed set of subalgebras $\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}$.

The notion of a special universal envelope permits us to replace the original definition of a special Jordan algebra by the following more definite condition.

Theorem 3. A Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ is special if and only if the associative specialization $\sigma_{u}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $S(\mathfrak{J})$ is 1-1.

Proof. The definition that $\mathfrak{J}$ is special is that there exists an associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ and a monomorphism $\sigma$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{G}^{+}$. Clearly we may assume that $\mathfrak{G}$ has a 1 , so that $\sigma$ is an associative specialization. Then $\sigma=\sigma_{u} \eta$ where $\eta$ is a homomorphism of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{G}$. Since $\sigma$ has zero kernel the same is true of $\sigma_{u}$. Hence $\sigma_{u}$ is 1-1. Conversely, if $\sigma_{u}$ is 1-1 then this is a monomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $S(\mathfrak{J})^{+}$and $\mathfrak{J}$ is special.

We can use this criterion and the commutativity of the special universal functor with direct limits to prove the following

Theorem 4. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra which is a union of a directed set of special subalgebras $\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is special. In particular a Jordan algebra is special if every finitely generated subalgebra is special.

Proof. We identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with $\lim _{\rightarrow} \mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$, so that the homomorphism $\phi_{\alpha}$ of $\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$ into $\mathfrak{J}$ is the injection mapping. We $\overrightarrow{\text { know }}$ that $S(\mathfrak{J})=\lim _{\rightarrow} S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)$ where the associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\lim S\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}\right)$ is the mapping $\Sigma_{u}$ defined above. Using the notations of the proof $\overrightarrow{\text { of }}$ Theorem 2, we have $\sigma_{\alpha u} \Phi_{\alpha}=\phi_{\alpha} \Sigma_{u}$. Let $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ satisfy $a^{\Sigma_{u}}=0$. Then $a=a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha}}$ for some $a_{\alpha}$ in $\mathfrak{J}_{\alpha}$ and $0=a^{\Sigma_{u}}=a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha} \Sigma_{u}}=a^{\sigma_{\alpha u} \Phi_{\alpha}}$. Then $a^{\sigma_{\alpha u} \phi_{\alpha \beta \mu}}=0$ for some $\beta \geqq \alpha$. Hence $a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha \beta} \sigma_{\beta u}}=0$. Since $\mathfrak{J}_{\beta}$ is special this gives $a_{\alpha}{ }^{\phi_{\alpha \beta}}=0$ and since $\phi_{\alpha \beta}$ is injective, $a_{\alpha}=0$. Hence $a=0$. Thus $\Sigma_{u}$ is $1-1$ and $\mathfrak{J}$ is special.
2. Special universal envelopes for Jordan algebras with $\mathbf{1}$ and for direct sums. Let $\sigma$ be an associative specialization of the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ in the associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 . If $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ and $n$ is a positive integer then $\left(a^{n}\right)^{\cdot \sigma}=\left(a^{\sigma}\right)^{\cdot n}=\left(a^{\sigma}\right)^{n}$. Also if $a, b, c \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $\{a b c\}^{\sigma}=\left\{a^{\sigma} b^{\sigma} c^{\sigma}\right\}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\sigma} b^{\sigma} c^{\sigma}+c^{\sigma} b^{\sigma} a^{\sigma}\right)$ in $\mathfrak{G}$ since $\{a b c\} a . b . c+b . c . a-a . c . b$. In particular, $\{a b a\}^{\sigma}=a^{\sigma} b^{\sigma} a^{\sigma}$. If $e^{2}=e$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ then $\left(e^{\sigma}\right)^{2}=e^{\sigma}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$. Now suppose $e \cdot a=0$ for the idempotent element $e$ of $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\{e a e\}=e . a . e+a . e . e-e . e . a=0$. Hence we have $e^{\sigma} a^{\sigma}+a^{\sigma} e^{\sigma}=0,\left(e^{\sigma}\right)^{2}=e^{\sigma}$ and $e^{\sigma} a^{\sigma} e^{\sigma}=0$. These imply that $e^{\sigma} a^{\sigma}=0=a^{\sigma} e^{\sigma}$. It follows that if $e_{1}, e_{2}, \cdots, e_{n}$ are orthogonal idempotent elements of $\mathfrak{J}\left(e_{i}^{\cdot 2}=e_{i}, e_{i} \cdot e_{j}=0\right.$ if $\left.i \neq j\right)$ then $e_{1}^{\sigma}, e_{2}^{\sigma}, \cdots, e_{n}^{\sigma}$, are orthogonal idempotents of $\mathfrak{G}$. Also one sees easily that $e . a=a$ implies $e^{\sigma} a^{\sigma}=a^{\sigma}=a^{\sigma} e^{\sigma}$ if $e$ is idempotent.

Now assume $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element 1 and let $\left(S(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right)$ be the special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $1^{\sigma_{u}} a^{\sigma_{u}}=a^{\sigma_{u}}=a^{\sigma_{u}} 1^{\sigma_{u}}$ in $S(\mathfrak{J})$ and since 1 and $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}}$ generate $S(\mathfrak{J})$ it is clear that $1^{\sigma_{u}}$ is a central idempotent (=idempotent in the center) of $S(\mathfrak{J})$. It follows that if we put $z=1-1^{\sigma_{u}}$ then $S(\mathfrak{J})=\Phi z \oplus S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ where $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is the subalgebra of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}}$ (without 1). $\Phi z$ and $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ are ideals and $z^{2}=z$. Moreover, $\Phi z \neq 0$ since we have an associative specialization $\sigma$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ in the one-dimensional algebra $\Phi=\Phi 1$ such that $a^{\sigma}=0, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. If $\eta$ is the homomorphism of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\Phi$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a^{\sigma}=a^{\sigma_{u}{ }^{\eta}}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, then $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u} \eta}=0$ and $S(\mathfrak{J})^{\eta}=\Phi$. Hence $(\Phi z)^{\eta}=\Phi$ and $\Phi z \neq 0$. The associative specialization $\sigma_{u}$ can be regarded as an associative specialization
of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. When this is done $\sigma_{u}$ is unital in the sense that $1^{\sigma_{u}}$ is the identity element of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. Now let $\sigma$ be any unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$ and let $\eta$ be the homomorphism of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a^{\sigma}=a^{\sigma_{u} \eta}$. Since $a^{\sigma_{u}} \in S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ and if $\eta$ is the restriction of $\eta$ to $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ then $a^{\sigma}=a^{\sigma_{u} \eta}$ where $\sigma_{u}$ is regarded as a mapping into $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\eta$ as a mapping of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. Moreover, $\eta$ is uniquely determined by this property. Thus we see that ( $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}$ ) is a unital spectal universal envelope in the sense of the definition obtained from Definition 1 by prefixing "unital" before "associative specialization" everywhere in the definition. We shall call $\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right)$ the unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. The properties (1)-(7) of ( $S(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}$ ) given in Theorem 1 carry over for unital special universal envelopes. In particular, we have the main involution $\pi$ in $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $a^{\sigma_{u} \pi}=a^{\sigma_{u}}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. This is the restriction to $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ of the main involution in $S(\mathfrak{J})$. The analogue of property (4) of Theorem 1 is that if $\zeta$ is a homomorphism of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 into a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ with 1 such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ then there exists a unique homomorphism $\zeta_{s}$ of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ such that $a^{\sigma_{u} \zeta_{s}}=a^{\zeta \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}}$ where ( $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right), \sigma^{\prime}{ }_{u}$ ) is the unital special universal envelope of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Also this respects the main involutions. The argument used to establish (8) shows that if $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}=n$ then $\operatorname{dim} S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \leqq 2^{n-1}$. Since $S(\mathfrak{J})=S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus \Phi z$ we see that $\operatorname{dim} S(\mathfrak{J}) \leqq 2^{n-1}+1$ if $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element.

Again assume $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element 1 and let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus_{\mathfrak{J}}$ where the $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ are ideals. Then $1=1_{1}+1_{2}$ where $1_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Then $1_{i}{ }^{\cdot 2}=1_{i}$ and $1_{i} \cdot 1_{j}=0$ if $i \neq j$. Hence if $\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right)$ is the unital special universal envelope of $\mathfrak{J}$, then the elements $f_{i}=1_{i}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}, i=1,2$, are orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{A} \equiv S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $f_{1}+f_{2}=1$. Also $f_{i}$ acts as identity for $\mathfrak{J}_{i}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}$ and hence is the identity for the subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ generated by $\mathfrak{J}_{i}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}$. Also $f_{i} a_{j}=0=a_{j} f_{i}$ if $a_{j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{j}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}$ and $i \neq j$. Hence $f_{i} a_{j}=0 =a_{j} f_{i}$ if $a_{j} \in \mathfrak{A}_{j}$. We have $\mathfrak{A}_{1} \mathfrak{A}_{2}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} f_{1} \mathfrak{A}_{2}=0$ and $\mathfrak{A}_{2} \mathfrak{A}_{1}=0$. Hence $\mathfrak{A}_{1}+\mathfrak{A}_{2}$ is the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{A}$ generated by $\mathfrak{A}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{A}_{2}$. Since $\mathfrak{A}$ is generated by $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}}=\mathfrak{J}_{1}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}+\mathfrak{J}_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}$ we have $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{1}+\mathfrak{A}_{2}$. Since $f_{1}$ is the identity for $\mathfrak{A}_{1}$ and annihilates $\mathfrak{U}_{2}$ we have $\mathfrak{U}_{1} \cap \mathfrak{U}_{2}=0$. Hence the $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ are ideals in $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{2}$. Let $\sigma_{i}$ denote the restriction of $\sigma_{u}$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Then $\sigma_{i}$ maps $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ into $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ so we may consider this as a mapping of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ into $\mathfrak{U}_{i}$. Clearly, this is a unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$. If $\left(S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right), \sigma_{i u}\right)$ is the unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ then we have the homomorphism of $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1_{i}$ and $a_{i}^{\sigma_{\text {iu }}} \rightarrow a_{i}^{\sigma_{i}}$, $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i}$, and consequently the homomorphism of $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right) \oplus S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, a_{1}^{\sigma_{1 u}}+a_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{2 u}} \rightarrow a_{1}{ }^{\sigma_{1}}+a_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{2}}$. On the other hand, $a_{1}+a_{2} \rightarrow a_{1}{ }^{\sigma_{1 u}}+a_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{2 u}}$ is a unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence we have the homomorphism of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right) \oplus S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1,\left(a_{1}+a_{2}\right)^{\sigma_{u}}=a_{1}^{\sigma_{1}}+a_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{2}} \rightarrow a_{1}{ }^{\sigma_{1 u}}+ +a_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{2 u}}$. Hence both homomorphisms are isomorphisms. It follows that we have an isomorphism of $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right)$ onto $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ mapping $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a_{i}{ }^{\sigma_{i u}} \rightarrow a_{i}{ }^{\sigma_{i}}$. Hence $\left(\mathfrak{A}_{i}, \sigma_{i}\right)$ is a unital special envelope for $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$. It is clear that our result implies the following

Theorem 5. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with $1, \mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2}$ where $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ is
an ideal in $\mathfrak{J},\left(S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right), \sigma_{i u}\right)$ the unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Then $\left(S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{I}_{1}\right) \oplus S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right), \sigma_{1 u}+\sigma_{2 u}\right)$ where $\left(a_{1}+a_{2}\right)^{\sigma_{1 u}+\sigma_{2 u}}=a_{1}^{\sigma_{1 u}}+a_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{2 u}}, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i}$, is a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$.
3. Examples. In the first three examples we shall consider the Jordan algebras $\mathfrak{J}$ will be associative with 1 . Hence these are associative commutative algebras with 1 . Considering $\mathfrak{J}$ as Jordan algebra we write the product as $a . b$ and considering $\mathfrak{J}$ as associative algebra we write $a b$ for $a . b$. We have $a . b=a b= =\frac{1}{2}(a b+b a)$. Hence the identity mapping is a unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{J}$.
(1) $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi[a]$ the Jordan algebra with 1 generated by 1 and a single element $a$. Let $\sigma$ be a unital associative specialization in $\mathfrak{G}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\left(a^{k}\right)^{\sigma}=\left(a^{\cdot k}\right)^{\sigma}=\left(a^{\sigma}\right)^{\cdot k} =\left(a^{\sigma}\right)^{k}$. Hence $\sigma$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ as associative algebra with 1 into $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 . It follows that $\mathfrak{J}$ and the identity mapping is a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. This implies that $\operatorname{dim} S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}=n<2^{\sigma-1}+1$, the bound given above.
(2) $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi[a, b]$, the Jordan algebra with 1 generated by an invertible element $a$ and its inverse $b$. If $\sigma$ is a unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi[a, b]$ in $\mathfrak{G}$ then $a^{\sigma} . b^{\sigma}=1$ and $\left(a^{\sigma}\right)^{\cdot 2} . b^{\sigma}=a^{\sigma}$. Hence, as we saw in §1.11, $a^{\sigma} b^{\sigma}=b^{\sigma} a^{\sigma}=1$. It follows that $\sigma$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ as associative algebra. Consequently, $\mathfrak{J}$ and the identity mapping is a unital special universal envelope of the Jordan algebra J.
(3) Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{B}$ the Jordan algebra of the symmetric bilinear form $f=0$ on $\mathfrak{V}$ and let $E(\mathfrak{V})$ be the exterior algebra based on $\mathfrak{V}$. $\mathfrak{J}$ is an associative Jordan algebra and the injection mapping $\alpha 1+x \rightarrow \alpha 1+x, x \in \mathfrak{B}$, of $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1+\mathfrak{V}$ in $E(\mathfrak{B})$ is a unital associative specialization. This can be verified directly using the relations $x^{2}=0, x y=-y x, x, y \in \mathfrak{B}$, in $E(\mathfrak{B})$. It is known that if $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B} =n-1<\infty$, so that $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}=n$, then $\operatorname{dim} E(\mathfrak{B})=2^{n-1}$. Since $\operatorname{dim} S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \leqq 2^{n-1}$ it is clear that the homomorphism of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $E(\mathfrak{B})$ such that $a^{\sigma_{u}} \rightarrow a, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, is an isomorphism. Hence $E(\mathfrak{B})$ and the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{J}$ is a unital special universal envelope of $\mathfrak{J}$ if $\mathfrak{V}$ is finite dimensional. The same result follows also for infinite dimensional $\mathfrak{B}$ by using Theorem 2 for unital special universal envelopes. These results are also special cases of the determination of unital special universal envelopes for Jordan algebras of symmetric bilinear forms which we shall consider in our next example. We observe that if $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}>1$ then $E(\mathfrak{B}) \neq \mathfrak{J}$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}$ and the identity mapping is not a unital special universal envelope for the associative algebra $\mathfrak{J}$. We remark also that if $\mathfrak{B}$ is a trivial Jordan algebra, that is, $\mathfrak{B}$ is a vector space with product $x . y=0$, then $E(\mathfrak{B})$ is the special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence this gives an example in which the bound given in Theorem 1 (8) is reached.
(4) A generalization of (3) is obtained by taking $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$, the Jordan algebra of an arbitrary symmetric bilinear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{V}$. We recall the definition
of the Clifford algebra $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ and $f$. This is $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)=T(\mathfrak{B}) / \Re$ where $T(\mathfrak{B})$ is the tensor algebra based on $\mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{K}$ is the ideal in $T(\mathfrak{B})$ generated by the elements $x \otimes x-f(x) 1, f(x)=f(x, x)$. It is well known, and easily seen, that $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is characterized by the following universal mapping property: If $\sigma$ is a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{V}$ into an associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 such that $\left(x^{\sigma}\right)^{2}=f(x) 1$ then there exists a unique homomorphism $\eta$ of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $1^{\eta}=1$ and $(x+\mathfrak{K})^{\eta}=x^{\sigma}$ (cf. Chevalley, Algebraic Theory of Spinors, p. 39). Now let $\sigma_{u}$ denote the mapping $(\alpha 1+x) \rightarrow(\alpha 1+x)^{\sigma_{u}} \equiv \alpha 1+x+\mathfrak{K}, x \in \mathfrak{V}$, of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Clearly this is linear and $1^{\sigma_{u}}$ is the identity element of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Also, if $x, y \in \mathfrak{B}$ then $x^{\sigma_{u}} \cdot y^{\sigma_{u}}=\frac{1}{2}(x+\mathfrak{K}) \cdot(y+\mathfrak{K})=\frac{1}{2}(x \otimes y+y \otimes x)+\mathfrak{K}= \frac{1}{2}[(x+y) \otimes(x+y)-x \otimes x-y \otimes y]+\mathfrak{K}=\frac{1}{2}[f(x+y)-f(x)-f(y)] 1+\mathfrak{K}= =f(x, y) 1+\mathfrak{K}=f(x, y) 1^{\sigma_{u}}=(x . y)^{\sigma_{u}}$. It follows directly that $\sigma_{u}$ is a unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Moreover, if $\sigma$ is any unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in an associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ then we have $1^{\sigma}=1$ and $\left(x^{\sigma}\right)^{2} =\left(x^{\cdot 2}\right)^{\sigma}=f(x) 1, x \in \mathfrak{B}$. Hence, by the universal property of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$, we have a unique homomorphism $\eta$ of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $(x+\mathfrak{K})^{\eta}=x^{\sigma}$. Then $(\alpha 1+x)^{\sigma_{u} \eta}=(\alpha 1+x+\mathfrak{K})^{\eta}=\alpha 1+x^{\sigma}=(\alpha 1+x)^{\sigma}$, which shows that $\left(C(\mathfrak{B}, f), \sigma_{u}\right)$ is a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. We remark also that the main involution in $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ as usually defined (characterized by $1 \rightarrow 1$, $\left.x^{\sigma_{u}} \rightarrow x^{\sigma_{u}}\right)$ is the same as the main involution which we defined in $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$.
(5) Let $\mathfrak{J}=F J^{(r)}$ the free Jordan algebra with 1 and $r$ (free) generators $x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{r}, \Phi\left\{u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{r}\right\}$ the free associative algebra with 1 and $r$ generators $u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{r}$. It follows directly from the definition and the universal property of $\Phi\left\{u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{r}\right\}$ that $\Phi\left\{u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{r}\right\}$ and the homomorphism $\sigma_{u}$ of $F J^{(r)}$ into $\Phi\left\{u_{1}, \cdots, u_{r}\right\}^{+}$such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $x_{i} \rightarrow u_{i}, 1 \leqq i \leqq r$, is a unital special universal envelope of $F J^{(r)}$. The main involution in $\Phi\left\{u_{1}, \cdots, u_{r}\right\}$ satisfies $u_{i}{ }^{\pi}=u_{i}$. Hence this coincides with the reversal operator in $\Phi\left\{u_{1}, \cdots, u_{r}\right\}$.

## Exercises

1. Prove the existence of a unital special universal envelope for any Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 by using Theorem 1 (5) (for the unital case) and the existence of such an envelope for free Jordan algebras with 1.
2. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be an associative Jordan algebra ( $S(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}$ ) the special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that for every $a, b \in \mathfrak{J},\left[a^{\sigma_{u}}, b^{\sigma_{u}}\right]$ is in the center of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\left[a^{\sigma_{u}}, b^{\sigma_{u}}\right]^{2}=0$.
3. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be an associative Jordan algebra, ( $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}$ ) the unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ contains a nil ideal $\mathfrak{N}$ such that the mapping $a \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{u}}+\mathfrak{N}$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ as associative algebra onto $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) / \mathfrak{N}$.
4. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi[x, y]^{+}$where $\Phi[x, y]$ is the usual commutative associative polynomial algebra in the indeterminates $x, y$, and let $\mathfrak{A}=\Phi\{u, v, w\} / \mathfrak{R}$ where $\Phi\{u, v, w\}$ is the free associative algebra with 1 generated by $u, v, w$ and $\mathfrak{K}$ is the ideal generated by $[u, v]-w,[u, w],[v, w], w^{2}$. Show that $w+\mathfrak{K} \neq 0$ so $\mathfrak{A}$
is not commutative. Show that the linear mapping $\sigma_{u}$ of $\Phi[x, y]$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $1 \rightarrow \overline{1}, x^{k} y^{l} \rightarrow \bar{u}^{\cdot k} \cdot \bar{v}^{\cdot l}$ where $\bar{a}=a+\mathfrak{K}$ is a unital associative specialization and ( $\mathfrak{A}, \sigma_{u}$ ) is universal.
5. Show that the unital special universal envelope of a purely inseparable field of characteristic $p \neq 0$ with basis $x^{i} y^{j}, 0 \leqq i, j<p, x^{p}=\xi \in \Phi, y^{p}=\eta \in \Phi$ is not commutative.
6. Associative algebras with involutions and Jordan algebras. Let $\mathscr{A}_{1}$ denote the category of associative algebras with involution ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) such that $\mathfrak{A}$ has identity element. The morphisms of $\mathscr{A}_{1}$ are the homomorphisms of algebras with involution mapping 1 into 1 . Let $\mathscr{J}_{1}$ be the category of Jordan algebras with 1 in which the morphisms are homomorphisms mapping 1 into 1 . If $(\mathfrak{A}, J) \in \mathscr{A}_{\mathscr{I}_{1}}$ then $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \in \mathscr{J}_{1}$ and if $\eta$ is a morphism in $\mathscr{A}_{1}$ of $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ into $(\mathfrak{B}, K)$ then the restriction $\eta^{\prime}$ of $\eta$ to $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is a morphism in $\mathscr{J}_{1}$ of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ into $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{B}, K)$. In this way we obtain a functor $H$ of $\mathscr{A} \mathscr{I}_{1}$ into $\mathscr{J}_{1}$ (cf. §I.4). On the other hand, we have the special universal functor $S_{1}$ of $\mathscr{J}_{1}$ into $\mathscr{A}_{1}$ which maps a $\mathfrak{J} \in \mathscr{J}_{1}$ into $\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$ where $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is the unital special universal envelope of $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\pi$ is its main involution. Moreover, if $\zeta$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J} \in \mathscr{J}_{1}$ into $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} \in \mathscr{J}_{1}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ then $S_{1}$ maps $\zeta$ into the homomorphism $\zeta_{s}$ of ( $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi$ ) into $\left(S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right), \pi^{\prime}\right)$ where $\pi^{\prime}$ is the main involution in $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$.

If $\mathfrak{J} \in \mathscr{J}_{1}$ then $\sigma_{u}$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})^{+}$and since $a^{\sigma_{u} \pi}=a^{\sigma_{u}}$ it is clear that $\sigma_{u}$ can be considered also as a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right) \in \mathscr{J}_{1}$. Also $1^{\sigma_{u}}=1$ so $\sigma_{u}$ is a morphism in the category $\mathscr{J}_{1}$ of Jordan algebras with 1 . We have noted that $\mathfrak{J}$ is special if and only if the mapping $\sigma_{u}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $S(\mathfrak{J})$ is injective. Since $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is the subalgebra of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}}$ it is clear that $\mathfrak{J}$ is special if and only if $\sigma_{u}$ considered as a mapping into $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is injective. We shall now call a Jordan algebra with 1 reflexive if $\sigma_{u}$ is surjective on $\mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$. Thus if $\mathfrak{J}$ is special and reflexive then $\mathfrak{J}$ is isomorphic to a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is an associative algebra with involution and $\mathfrak{A}$ has an identity element.

If $(\mathfrak{A}, J) \in \mathscr{A} \mathscr{I}_{1}$ then the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ is a unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ in $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence we have a unique homomorphism $\imath_{u}$ of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J))$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $a^{\sigma_{u} l_{u}}=a, a \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. We have $a^{\sigma_{u} \pi l_{u}}=a^{\sigma_{u} l_{u}}=a$ and $a^{\sigma_{u} u_{u} J}=a$. Since the $a^{\sigma_{u}}$ generate $S_{1}(\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J))$ this implies that $\imath_{u}$ is a homomorphism of algebras with involution mapping 1 into 1 . Thus $\imath_{u}$ is a morphism in the category $\mathscr{A} \mathscr{I}_{1}$. Since $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)^{\sigma_{u}}$ generates $S_{1}(\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)), \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)^{\sigma_{u} l_{u}}$ generates $S_{1}(\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J))^{\iota_{u}}$. Hence $\imath_{u}$ is surjective if and only if $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ generates $\mathfrak{A}$. We shall say that the associative algebra with involution ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) is perfect if $\mathbf{t}_{\boldsymbol{u}}$ is an isomorphism of $\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)), \pi\right)$ onto $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. This is the case if and only if $\mathfrak{A}$ and the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ is a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. More explicitly, ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) is perfect if and only if any unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ has a unique extension to a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$.

We now proceed to give some elementary properties of reflexivity and perfection. We prove first

Theorem 6. Any Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 which is generated by 1 and at most three elements is reflexive.

Proof. We have seen that for the free Jordan algebra $F J^{(r)}$ with 1 and generators $x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{r}$, the free associative algebra $\Phi\left\{u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{r}\right\}$ and the unital associative specialization $\sigma_{u}$ such that $x_{i} \rightarrow u_{i}$ is universal. Also the main involution in $\Phi\left\{u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{r}\right\}$ is the reversal operator. The image of $F J^{(r)}$ under $\sigma_{u}$ is the free special Jordan algebra $F S J^{(r)}$ and we know by Cohn's Theorem (p. 8) that this coincides with the space of reversible elements if and only if $r \leqq 3$. This means that $F J^{(r)}$ is reflexive if and only if $r \leqq 3$. The proof of the theorem will now follow by showing that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is reflexive then any homomorphic image of $\mathfrak{J}$ is reflexive. Let $\zeta$ be a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Then we have the homomorphism $\zeta_{s}$ of $\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$ onto $\left(S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right), \pi^{\prime}\right)$ such that $a^{\sigma_{u} \zeta_{s}}=a^{\zeta \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}}$ where $\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right)$ and $\left(S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right), \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}\right)$ are the unital special universal envelopes, $\pi$ and $\pi^{\prime}$ the main involutions. Let $a^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right), \pi^{\prime}\right)$. Then $a^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\prime}+a^{\prime \pi^{\prime}}\right)$ and $a^{\prime}=a^{\zeta s}$ for some $a \in S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. Then $a^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\prime}+a^{\prime \pi^{\prime}}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\zeta_{s}}+a^{\zeta_{s} \pi^{\prime}}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\zeta_{s}}+a^{\pi \zeta_{s}}\right)=b^{\zeta_{s}}$ where $b=\frac{1}{2}\left(a+a^{\pi}\right) \in \mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is reflexive then $b \in \mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{s}}$. Hence $b=c^{\sigma_{u}} c \in \mathfrak{J}$, and $a^{\prime}=b^{\zeta_{s}}=c^{\sigma_{u} \zeta_{s}}=c^{\zeta \sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}} \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime \sigma_{u}}$. Thus $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is reflexive.

The theorem of Shirshov-Cohn (p. 48) states that any Jordan algebra with 1 and two generators (and 1 ) is special. Theorem 6 states that such an algebra is reflexive. Together the two results have the following consequence, which is a strengthening of Shirshov-Cohn:

Corollary 1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with 1 which is generated by 1 and two elements. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is isomorphic to an algebra $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $\mathfrak{A}$ is an associative algebra with 1.

For three generators we obtain in the same way the following
Corollary 2. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is a special Jordan algebra with 1 generated by 1 and three elements then $\mathfrak{J}$ is isomorphic to an algebra $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $\mathfrak{A}$ is an associative algebra with 1.

It is immediate from the definition that if ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) is a perfect associative algebra with involution then the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is reflexive. On the other hand, suppose $\mathfrak{J}$ is a Jordan algebra with 1 which is reflexive. Let $\sigma$ be a unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$ into the associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 . Then $\sigma_{u} \sigma$ is a unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence there exists a homomorphism $\eta$ of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{5}$ such that $a^{\sigma_{u} \sigma}=a^{\sigma_{u} \eta}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. If $h \in \mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$ then the reflexivity of $\mathfrak{J}$ implies that $h=a^{\sigma_{u}}$ for some $a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Hence we have $h^{\sigma}=h^{\eta}$ so $\sigma$ can be extended to the homomorphism $\eta$ of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{G}$. Also since $\mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)=\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}}$
generates $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ it is clear that $\eta$ is unique. Hence we see that if $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 is reflexive then $\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$ is perfect. We also have the following

Theorem 7. For any Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 the associative algebra with involution $\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$ is isomorphic to an ideal direct summand of $\left(S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right), \pi\right)\right)$.

Proof. Put $\mathfrak{A}=S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right), \mathfrak{B}=S_{1}(\mathfrak{K})$ and let $\sigma_{u}$ and $\tau_{u}$ be the given unital associative specializations of $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{K}$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ respectively. Considering $\sigma_{u}$ as a homomorphism of the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ into the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{K}$ we obtain a homomorphism $\Sigma$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}$ such that
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-087.jpg?height=222&width=263&top_left_y=835&top_left_x=755)
is commutative. Then if $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ we have $a^{\sigma_{u} \tau_{u}}=a^{\sigma_{u} \Sigma}$. Let $\mathfrak{1}_{u}$ be the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}=S_{1}(\mathfrak{K})$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $k^{\tau_{u} l_{u}}=k, k \in \mathfrak{K}$. Now if $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $a^{\sigma_{u}} \in \mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right) \pi\right)$. Hence $a^{\sigma_{u}}=a^{\sigma_{u} \tau_{u} \iota_{u}}=a^{\sigma_{u} \Sigma_{\iota_{u}}}$. Since $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}}$ generates $\mathfrak{A}$ this implies that $\Sigma_{\mathbf{l}_{u}}=1_{\mathfrak{A}}$ for the homomorphisms $\Sigma, \mathbf{l}_{u}$ of associative algebras with involution. Now put $\eta=\mathrm{l}_{u} \Sigma$. Then $\eta$ is a homomorphism of the algebra with involution ( $\mathfrak{B}, \pi$ ) into itself and $\eta^{2}=\mathbf{l}_{u} \Sigma \mathbf{l}_{u} \Sigma=\mathbf{l}_{u} \mathbf{1}_{\mathfrak{A}} \Sigma=\mathbf{l}_{u} \Sigma=\eta$. Hence we have the direct decomposition $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{B} \eta \oplus \mathfrak{B}(1-\eta)$ where $\mathfrak{B} \eta$ and $\mathfrak{B}(1-\eta)$ are ideals of $(\mathfrak{B}, \pi)$. It is immediate that $\Sigma$ is an isomorphism of ( $\mathfrak{A}, \pi$ ) onto ( $\mathfrak{B} \eta, \pi$ ). This proves the result.

An important feature of the properties: $\mathfrak{J}$ is special or reflexive and $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is perfect is that these hold for an algebra obtained by a base field extension if and only if they hold for the given algebra. If ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) is an algebra with involution and $\Gamma$ is an extension of the base field $\Phi$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ then the linear extension $J$ of $J$ to $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ is an involution in $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$. Hence ( $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}, J$ ) is an algebra with involution over $\Gamma$. If we identify $\mathfrak{A}$ with the $\Phi$ subalgebra $1 \otimes \mathfrak{A}$ of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}=\Gamma \otimes \mathfrak{A}$ then $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}, J\right)$ is the $\Gamma$-subspace spanned by $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)(=1 \otimes \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J))$. Since $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and $\Gamma=\Gamma \otimes 1$ are linearly disjoint over $\Phi$ it is clear that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}, J\right)=\Gamma \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ can be identified with $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)_{\Gamma}$. We shall call a property $P$ of algebras (algebras with involution) linear if the validity of $P$ for an algebra $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ (algebra with involution $(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi, J)$ ) is equivalent to the validity of $P$ for $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}\left(\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}, J\right)\right)$ for any extension field $\Gamma / \Phi$. The result we indicated can now be stated in the following way.

Theorem 8. The property that a Jordan algebra is special or that a Jordan algebra with 1 is reflexive is linear. The property that an associative algebra with involution and 1 is perfect is linear.

Proof. Suppose $\mathfrak{J}$ (with 1) is special (reflexive). Then the associative specialization $\sigma_{u}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $S(\mathfrak{J})$ ( $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ ) is injective (surjective on $\mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$ ). Since $\left(S(\mathfrak{J})_{\Gamma}, \sigma_{u}\right)\left(\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})_{\Gamma}, \sigma_{u}\right)\right)$ is a special universal envelope (unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}_{\Gamma}$ and $\left.\mathfrak{H}\left(S(\mathfrak{J})_{\Gamma}, \pi\right)=\mathfrak{H}(S(\mathfrak{J}), \pi)_{\Gamma}\right), \sigma_{u}$ is injective (surjective on $\mathfrak{H}\left(S(\mathfrak{J})_{\Gamma}, \pi\right)$ ). Hence $\mathfrak{J}_{\Gamma}$ is special (reflexive). Conversely, if $\mathfrak{J}_{\Gamma}$ is special (reflexive) then a reversal of the argument shows that $\mathfrak{J}$ is special (reflexive). Next let ( $\mathfrak{A}, J)$ be an associative algebra with involution and 1 which is perfect. Then $\mathfrak{A}$ and the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ is a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. Hence $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ and the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}, J\right)$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ is a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}, J\right)$ and so $\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}, J\right)$ is perfect. Conversely, suppose $\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}, J\right)$ is perfect and let $\sigma$ be a unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ in $\mathfrak{G} / \Phi$. The linear extension $\sigma$ of $\sigma$ to $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)_{\Gamma}$ into $\mathfrak{G}_{\Gamma}$ is a unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)_{\Gamma}$. Since we can identify $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)_{\Gamma}$ with $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}, J\right)$ we may consider $\sigma$ as a unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}, J\right)$. Then $\sigma$ can be extended to a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ to $\mathfrak{G}_{\Gamma}$. This implies that the given mapping $\sigma$ of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ can be extended to a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{G}$. Since $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}, J\right)$ generates $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}, \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ generates $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence $\sigma$ is unique and consequently ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) is perfect.

Remarks. There are a number of places in the foregoing discussion where we could have referred to well-known facts in categories and functors. In particular, properties (1), (2) and (4) of Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 are well-known properties of universal functors. Also the two functors $H$ and $S$ which we have been considering in this section are adjoint functors: We have a natural equivalence of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr{J}_{1}}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J))$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr{A} \mathscr{I}_{1}}\left(\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right),(\mathfrak{A}, J)\right)$. Theorem 7 can be derived from this fact.

## Exercises

1. Note that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is a commutative associative algebra then the identity mapping is an involution in $\mathfrak{A}$. Use this to give an example of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ which is not reflexive.
2. Show that $\left(S_{1}\left(F J^{(r)}\right), \pi\right)$ is not perfect if $r \geqq 4$.
3. Bimodules for algebras in a variety $\mathscr{V}(I)$.

Let $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ be an algebra, $\mathfrak{M} / \Phi$ a vector space and suppose we have a pair of bilinear mappings $(a, u) \rightarrow a u,(a, u) \rightarrow u a, a \in \mathfrak{A}, u \in \mathfrak{M}$, of $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$. Thus we have

$$
\begin{align*}
\left(a_{1}+a_{2}\right) u & =a_{1} u+a_{2} u, \quad a\left(u_{1}+u_{2}\right)=a u_{1}+a u_{2}  \tag{12}\\
\alpha(a u) & =(\alpha a) u=a(\alpha u), \alpha(u a)=(\alpha u) a=u(\alpha a)
\end{align*}
$$

for $a, a_{1}, a_{2} \in \mathfrak{A}, u, u_{1}, u_{2} \in \mathfrak{M}$ and $\alpha \in \Phi$. Now let $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ the vector space direct sum of $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{M}$ and define a product composition in $\mathfrak{E}$ by

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left(a_{1}+u_{1}\right)\left(a_{2}+u_{2}\right)=a_{1} a_{2}+a_{1} u_{2}+u_{1} a_{2} \tag{13}
\end{equation*}
$$

It is clear that this product is bilinear, so $\mathfrak{E}$ is an algebra. Moreover, $\mathfrak{A}$ is a subalgebra and $\mathfrak{M}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\mathfrak{M}^{2}=0$. We shall call $\mathfrak{E}$ the split null extension of $\mathfrak{A}$ determined by the given bilinear mappings of $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{M}$. Now let $I$ be a subset of the free nonassociative algebra $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ where $X=\left\{x_{i}\right\}$, $i=1,2,3, \cdots$ (cf. p. 25) and let $\mathscr{V}(I)$ be the variety of algebras satisfying the identities in $I$. Let $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ and let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a vector space, $(a, u) \rightarrow a u,(a, u) \rightarrow u a$ two bilinear mappings of $\mathfrak{A} \times \mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$, as before. Then $\mathfrak{M}$ and the two bilinear compositions constitute an I-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ if the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ is in the variety $\mathscr{V}(I) .^{1}$ In particular, if $I$ is the set defining associative, Lie, alternative or Jordan algebras then we say that $\mathfrak{M}$ is an associative, Lie, alternative or Jordan bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$.

As in §1.6, we define $f D_{i}\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}, y\right)$ for $f=f\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)$ as the part of $f\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{i-1}, x_{i}+y, x_{i+1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)$ which is homogeneous of degree one in $y$. Thus we have

$$
\begin{align*}
f\left(x_{1},\right. & \left.\cdots, x_{i-1}, x_{i}+y, x_{i+1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right) \\
& \equiv f\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)+f D_{i}\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}, y\right)\left(\bmod (y)^{2}\right) \tag{14}
\end{align*}
$$

where ( $y$ ) is the ideal in $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}, Z=X \cup\{y\}$, generated by $y$. We now introduce another infinite set $Y=\left\{y_{i}\right\}$ disjoint with $X$ and put $W=X \cup Y$. Then it follows easily from (14) that

$$
\begin{align*}
f\left(x_{1}+y_{1}, x_{2}+y_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}+y_{n}\right) \equiv & f\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right) \\
& +\sum f D_{i}\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}, y_{i}\right)\left(\bmod \mathfrak{Y}^{2}\right) \tag{15}
\end{align*}
$$

where $\mathfrak{Y}$ is the ideal in $\Phi\{\{W\}\}^{\prime}$ generated by the set $Y$.
We can now establish the following criterion for an $I$-bimodule.
Theorem 9. Let $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ and let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a vector space over $\Phi,(a, u) \rightarrow a u$ and $(a, u) \rightarrow$ ua bilinear compositions of $\mathfrak{A} \times \mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$. Then $\mathfrak{M}$ with these compositions is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ if and only if we have the relations $f D_{i}\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}, u\right)=0$ in $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ for all $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}, u \in \mathfrak{M}$ and $f \in I$.

Proof. $\mathfrak{M}$ with the given bilinear compositions is an $I$-bimodule if and only if the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{M} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$. If this is the case then $f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{i-1}, a_{i}+u, a_{i+1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)=0$ for $a_{k} \in \mathfrak{A}, u \in \mathfrak{M}, f \in I$. By (14) and the fact that $\mathfrak{M}$ is an ideal such that $\mathfrak{M}^{2}=0$, we have $f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{i-1}, a_{i}+u, a_{i+1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right) =f D_{i}\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}, u\right)$. Hence $f D_{i}\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}, u\right)=0$. Conversely, suppose the indicated conditions hold. Then, by (15), we obtain

$$
f\left(a_{1}+u_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}+u_{n}\right)=\sum_{i} f D_{i}\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}, u_{i}\right)=0
$$

[^7]This shows that $f\left(b_{1}, \cdots, b_{n}\right)=0$ for all $b_{i} \in \mathbb{E}, f \in I$. Hence $\mathbb{E} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ and $\mathbb{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$.

We now suppose that the conditions H and L of §1.6 are satisfied by the set $I$. We recall that this is the case for the sets defining associative, Lie, alternative and Jordan algebras. Now let $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$, take $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{A}$ as vector space and let $a u$, $u a, a \in \mathfrak{A}, u \in \mathfrak{M}$ be the products as defined in the algebra $\mathfrak{A}$. Then if $f \in I$ condition L implies that $f D_{i}\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{u}, u\right)=0$ for all $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}, u \in \mathfrak{M}$. Hence $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{A}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$. We shall call this the regular bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$.

Examples. (1) $\mathscr{V}(I)$, the variety of associative algebras. Here $I=\{f\}$ where $f=\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{3}-x_{1}\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right)$. We have

$$
\begin{align*}
& f D_{1}=\left(y x_{2}\right) x_{3}-y\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right), \\
& f D_{2}=\left(x_{1} y\right) x_{3}-x_{1}\left(y x_{3}\right),  \tag{16}\\
& f D_{3}=\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) y-x_{1}\left(x_{2} y\right) .
\end{align*}
$$

Hence $\mathfrak{M}$ is an associative bimodule for the associative algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ if and only if $(u a) b=u(a b),(a u) b=a(u b),(a b) u=a(b u)$ for $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}, u \in \mathfrak{M}$. This is the usual definition of a bimodule (or two-sided module) for an associative algebra.
(2) $\mathscr{V}(I)$ the variety of Lie algebras. Here $I=\{f, g\}$ where $f=x_{1}{ }^{2}$, $g=\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{3}+\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right) x_{1}+\left(x_{3} x_{1}\right) x_{2}$. Then

$$
\begin{align*}
& f D_{1}=x_{1} y+y x_{1} \\
& g D_{1}=\left(y x_{2}\right) x_{3}+\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right) y+\left(x_{3} y\right) x_{2} \\
& g D_{2}=\left(x_{1} y\right) x_{3}+\left(y x_{3}\right) x_{1}+\left(x_{3} x_{1}\right) y  \tag{17}\\
& g D_{3}=\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) y+\left(x_{2} y\right) x_{1}+\left(y x_{1}\right) x_{2}
\end{align*}
$$

The corresponding conditions for a Lie bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$ for the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ are $a u=-u a,(u a) b+(a b) u+(b u) a=0,(a u) b+(u b) a+(b a) u=0$, $(a b) u+(b u) a+(u a) b=0$. These are equivalent to: $a u=-u a, u(a b)=(u a) b -(u b) a$.
(3) $\mathscr{V}(I)$, the variety of alternative algebras. Here $I=\{f, g\}$ where $f=x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}-x_{1}\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right), g=x_{2} x_{1}{ }^{2}-\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right) x_{1}$. Then

$$
\begin{align*}
& f D_{1}=\left(x_{1} y+y x_{1}\right) x_{2}-x_{1}\left(y x_{2}\right)-y\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) \\
& f D_{2}=x_{1}^{2} y-x_{1}\left(x_{1} y\right)  \tag{18}\\
& g D_{1}=x_{2}\left(x_{1} y+y x_{1}\right)-\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right) y-\left(x_{2} y\right) x_{1} \\
& g D_{2}=y x_{1}^{2}-\left(y x_{1}\right) x_{1}
\end{align*}
$$

Hence the alternative bimodule conditions are: $(a u+u a) b=a(u b)+u(a b)$, $a^{2} u=a(a u), b(a u+u a)=(b a) u+(b u) a, u a^{2}=(u a) a, a, b \in \mathfrak{A}, u \in \mathfrak{M}$.
(4) $\mathscr{V}(I)$, the variety of Jordan algebras. Here $I=\{f, g\}$ where $f=x_{1} x_{2}-x_{2} x_{1} g=\left(x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}\right) x_{1}-x_{1}{ }^{2}\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)$. Then

$$
\begin{align*}
f D_{1} & =y x_{2}-x_{2} y, \quad f D_{2}=x_{1} y-y x_{1} \\
g D_{1} & =\left(\left(x_{1} y+y x_{1}\right) x_{2}\right) x_{1}+\left(x_{1}^{2} x_{2}\right) y-\left(x_{1} y+y x_{1}\right)\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)-x_{1}^{2}\left(x_{2} y\right)  \tag{19}\\
g D_{2} & =\left(x_{1}^{2} y\right) x_{1}-x_{1}^{2}\left(y x_{1}\right)
\end{align*}
$$

The corresponding bimodule conditions are $a u=u a, \quad((a u+u a) b) a+\left(a^{2} b\right) u =(a u+u a)(b a)+a^{2}(b u),\left(a^{2} u\right) a=a^{2}(u a)$. These are equivalent to

$$
\begin{align*}
a u & =u a \\
\left(u a^{2}\right) a & =(u a) a^{2}  \tag{20}\\
2((u a) b) a+u\left(a^{2} b\right) & =2(u a)(a b)+(u b) a^{2}
\end{align*}
$$

6. Birepresentations for an algebra in a variety $\mathscr{V}(I)$. If $(a, u) \rightarrow a u$ is a bilinear mapping of $\mathfrak{A} \times \mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$, then the mapping $u \rightarrow a u, u \in \mathfrak{M}$ is an element $a^{\lambda}$ of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. Moreover, the mapping $a \rightarrow a^{\lambda}$ is a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. Conversely, if we are given a linear mapping $\lambda: a \rightarrow a^{\lambda}$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ then the mapping $(a, u) \rightarrow u a^{\lambda}$ is a bilinear mapping of $\mathfrak{A} \times \mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$. Thus if we are given a pair of bilinear mappings $(a, u) \rightarrow a u$ and $(a, u) \rightarrow u a$ of $\mathfrak{A} \times \mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ then we have a pair of linear mappings $\lambda$ and $\rho$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ and conversely. We shall now seek to formulate the $I$-bimodule conditions given in Theorem 9 as conditions on the mappings $\lambda$ and $\rho$ determined by the given bilinear compositions.

For this purpose we consider again the free nonassociative algebra $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ where $Z=X \cup\{y\}, X=\left\{x_{i}\right\}, i=1,2,3, \cdots, y \notin X$. The subalgebra of $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ generated by $X$ can be identified with $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$. Let $\mathfrak{V}$ be the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}, \Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}\right)$ generated by 1 and the multiplications $a_{L}, a_{R}$ in $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ by the elements $a \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$. As in §1.6, let $N(X)^{\prime}$ be the (free) monad generated by the $x$ 's, so that $N(X)^{\prime}$ is a basis for $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$. Then clearly $\mathfrak{B}$ is generated by 1 and the multiplications $m_{L}, m_{R}, m \in N(X)^{\prime}$. We now introduce a set $P$ which is a disjoint union of two copies of $N(X)^{\prime}$. Thus we assume we have two injective mappings $m \rightarrow l(m), m \rightarrow r(m)$ of $N(X)^{\prime}$ into $P$ such that $P=l\left(N(X)^{\prime}\right) \cup r\left(N(X)^{\prime}\right)$ and $l\left(N(X)^{\prime}\right) \cap r\left(N(X)^{\prime}\right)=\varnothing$. Let $\Phi\{P\}$ be the free associative algebra with 1 generated by 1 and the set $P$. Then we have a homomorphism $v$ of $\Phi\{P\}$ onto $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, l(m) \rightarrow m_{L}, r(m) \rightarrow m_{R}, m \in N(X)^{\prime}$. More generally, let $\eta$ be a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into an algebra $\mathfrak{A}$. Then we have the homomorphism $\eta^{\prime}$ of $\Phi\{P\}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, l(m) \rightarrow\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{L}, r(m) \rightarrow\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{R}$. We have now the following

Lemma 1. There exists a homomorphism $\eta^{\prime \prime}$ of $\mathfrak{B}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}, \Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}\right)$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
m_{L}^{\eta^{\prime \prime}}=\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{L}, \quad m_{R}^{\eta^{\prime \prime}}=\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{R}, \quad m \in N(X)^{\prime} . \tag{21}
\end{equation*}
$$

Proof. Let $u$ be any element of $\mathfrak{A}$ and let $(\eta, u)$ denote the homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ which coincides with $\eta$ on $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ and sends $y$ into $u$. We claim that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left(y Q^{\nu}\right)^{(\eta, u)}=u Q^{\eta^{\prime}} \tag{22}
\end{equation*}
$$

for every $Q \in \Phi\{P\}$. Since $1, l(m), r(m), m \in N(X)^{\prime}$ generate $\Phi\{P\}$ this will follow if we can show that if (22) holds for a $Q \in \Phi\{P\}$ then it holds for $Q l(m)$ and for $\operatorname{Qr}(m), m \in N(X)^{\prime}$. Now if (22) holds then $y(Q l(m))^{\nu}=y Q^{\nu} l(m)^{\nu}=y Q^{\nu} m_{L} =m\left(y Q^{\nu}\right)$ and $\left(y(Q l(m))^{\nu}\right)^{(\eta, u)}=\left(m\left(y Q^{\nu}\right)\right)^{(\eta, u)}=m^{\eta}\left(y Q^{\nu}\right)^{(\eta, u)}=m^{\eta}\left(u Q^{\eta^{\prime}}\right) =\left(u Q^{\eta^{\prime}}\right)\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{L}=\left(u Q^{\eta^{\prime}}\right) l(m)^{\eta^{\prime}}=u(Q l(m))^{\eta^{\prime}}$. Similarly, $\left(y(Q r(m))^{\nu}\right)^{(\eta, u)}=u(Q r(m))^{\eta^{\prime}}$. Hence (22) holds for all $Q$. Now suppose $Q^{\nu}=0$. Then (22) implies that $u Q^{\eta^{\prime}}=0$ for all $u$. Hence $Q^{\eta^{\prime}}=0$. Thus the kernel of the homomorphism $v$ of $\Phi\{P\}$ into $\mathfrak{B}$ is contained in the kernel of the homomorphism $\eta^{\prime}$ of $\Phi\{P\}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$. Hence we have a homomorphism $\eta^{\prime \prime}$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$ such that
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-092.jpg?height=206&width=335&top_left_y=1031&top_left_x=710)
is commutative. Then $1^{\eta^{\prime \prime}}=1^{\nu \eta^{\prime \prime}}=1^{\eta^{\prime}}=1, m_{L}{ }^{\eta^{\prime \prime}}=l(m)^{\nu \eta^{\prime \prime}}=l(m)^{\eta^{\prime}}=\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{L}$ and $m_{R}{ }^{\eta^{\prime \prime}}=\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{R}$, as required in (21).

Lemma 2. v is an isomorphism of $\Phi\{P\}$ onto $\mathfrak{B}$.
Proof. We take a $1-1$ representation $\sigma$ of $\Phi\{P\}$ by linear transformations in a vector space $\mathfrak{N} / \Phi$. For example, we can take $\mathfrak{N}=\Phi\{P\}$ and let $Q^{\sigma}$ be the multiplication $A \rightarrow A Q$ in $\mathfrak{N}$. We now define bilinear compositions of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime} \times \Re$ into $\mathfrak{N}$ such that for any $m \in N(X)^{\prime}, n \in \mathfrak{N}$ we have $(m, n) \rightarrow n l(m)^{\sigma}$ and $(m, n) \rightarrow n r(m)^{\sigma}$. This can be done since $N(X)^{\prime}$ is a basis for $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$. The bilinear compositions determine the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime} \oplus \mathfrak{N}$.
