Let $\eta$ be the injection of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ in $\mathfrak{E}$ and let $\eta^{\prime \prime}$ be the corresponding homomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{E}, \mathfrak{E})$ given in Lemma 1. By definition of the multiplication in $\mathfrak{E}$, we have $n\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{L}=n l(m)^{\sigma}, n\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{R}=n r(m)^{\sigma}$ if $n \in \mathfrak{N}, m \in N(X)^{\prime}$. Hence $m_{L}{ }^{\eta^{\prime \prime}}=\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{L}$ and $m_{R}{ }^{\eta^{\prime \prime}}=\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{R}$ map $\mathfrak{N}$ into itself and consequently the elements of $\mathfrak{B}^{\eta^{\prime \prime}}$ map $\mathfrak{N}$ into itself. Let $v^{\eta^{\prime \prime \prime}}$ denote the restriction to $\mathfrak{N}$ of $v^{\eta^{\prime \prime}}$. Then $\eta^{\prime \prime \prime}$ : $v \rightarrow v^{\eta^{\prime \prime \prime}}$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{V}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{N})$ such that $m_{L}{ }^{\eta^{\prime \prime \prime}}=l(m)^{\sigma}$, $m_{R}{ }^{\eta^{\prime \prime \prime}}=r(m)^{\sigma}$. Since $\sigma$ is a monomorphism we have the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\Phi\{P\}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, m_{L} \rightarrow l(m), m_{R} \rightarrow r(m)$. Clearly this is the inverse of the homomorphism $v$ of $\Phi\{P\}$ onto $\mathfrak{B}$. Hence $v$ is an isomorphism.

It is clear from the definition of $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ that any element $q$ of this algebra
which is homogeneous of degree one in $y$ has the form $y Q^{\nu}$ where $Q \in \Phi\{P\}$. It is an easy consequence of Lemma 2 that $Q$ is uniquely determined. We can now translate the conditions of Theorem 9 for a bimodule for a class of algebras defined by a set of identities into conditions on the associated mappings $\lambda, \rho$, as follows.

Theorem 10. Let $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ a variety of algebras defined by a set of identities $I \subseteq \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$. Let $\Phi\{P\}$ be the free associative algebra with 1 generated by 1 and the set $P$ which is a disjoint union of two copies $l\left(N(X)^{\prime}\right)$ and $r\left(N(X)^{\prime}\right)$ of $N(X)^{\prime}$, v the homomorphism of $\Phi\{P\}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}, \Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}\right)$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, l(m) \rightarrow m_{L}, r(m) \rightarrow m_{R}$ the multiplications in $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ determined by the element $m \in N(X)^{\prime}$. For each $f \in I$ and $i=1,2,3, \cdots$ write $f D_{i}\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}, y\right) =y F_{i}{ }^{\nu}, F_{i} \in \Phi\{P\}$. Let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a vector space over $\Phi,(a, u) \rightarrow a u,(a, u) \rightarrow u a$ bilinear compositions of $\mathfrak{A} \times \mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ and let $a^{\lambda}, a^{\rho}$ for $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ be the linear mappings $u \rightarrow a u$ and $u \rightarrow u a$ respectively in $\mathfrak{M}$. If $\eta$ is a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ let $\tau=\tau(\eta)$ be the homomorphism of $\Phi\{P\}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, l(m)^{\tau}=m^{\eta \lambda}, r(m)^{\tau}=m^{\eta \rho}$. Then $\mathfrak{M}$ with the given bilinear compositions is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ if and only if $F_{i}{ }^{\tau}=0$ for every $f \in I, i=1,2, \cdots$ and every homomorphism $\eta$.

Proof. Let $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ be the split null extension defined by the given bilinear mappings. If $\eta$ is a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ then we have the homomorphism $\eta^{\prime}$ of $\Phi\{P\}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{E}, \mathfrak{E})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, l(m)^{\eta^{\prime}}=\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{L}$, $r(m)^{\eta^{\prime}}=\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{R}$ where $m \in N(X)^{\prime}$ and $L$ and $R$ denote left and right multiplications in $\mathfrak{E}$. Since $a^{\lambda}$ and $a^{\rho}$ are the restrictions to $\mathfrak{M}$ of $a_{L}$ and $a_{R}$, respectively, we have for $u \in \mathfrak{M}, u l(m)^{\tau}=u m^{\eta \lambda}=u\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{L}=u l(m)^{\eta^{\prime}}$ and $u r(m)^{\tau}=u r(m)^{\eta^{\prime}}$. Consequently, $u F^{\tau}=u F^{\eta^{\prime}}$ for all $F \in \Phi\{P\}$. Now let $f \in I$ and let $f D_{i}=y F_{i}{ }^{\nu}$ where $F_{i} \in \Phi\{P\}$. Consider the homomorphism $(\eta, u)$ of $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ which extends $\eta$ and maps $y$ into $u$. Then, by (22), $\left(y F_{i}{ }^{\nu}\right)^{(\eta, u)}=u F_{i}{ }^{\eta^{\prime}}=u F_{i}{ }^{\tau}$. Hence $\left(f D_{i}\right)^{(\eta, u)}=u F_{i}{ }^{\tau}$. By Theorem 9, $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule if and only if $\left(f D_{i}\right)^{(\eta, u)}=0$ for all $f \in I$, all $i=1,2, \cdots$, all homomorphisms $\eta$ and all $u \in \mathfrak{M}$. Clearly this is equivalent to $F_{i}{ }^{\tau}=0$ for all $f \in I, i=1,2, \cdots$ and all homomorphisms $\tau=\tau(\eta)$.

If $f \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ then we shall call the elements $F_{i} \in \Phi\{P\}$ such that $f D_{i}\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}, y\right)=y F_{i}{ }^{\nu}$ the derived elements of $f$ in $\Phi\{P\}$. We can now give the following

Definition 2. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be an algebra in a variety $\mathscr{V}(I)$ defined by a set of identities $I$ (in $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ ) and let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a vector space. Then a pair of linear mappings ( $\lambda, \rho$ ) of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ is called an I-birepresentation for $\mathfrak{A}$ if the following conditions hold: Given any homomorphism $\eta$ of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$, let $\tau$ be the homomorphism of $\Phi\{P\}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$, $l(m)^{\tau}=m^{\eta \lambda}, r(m)^{\tau}=m^{\eta \rho}, m \in N(X)^{\prime}$. Then $F_{i}{ }^{\tau}=0$ for every derived element $F_{i}$ of every $f \in I$.

It is clear from Theorem 10 that the notions of $I$-bimodule and $I$-birepresentation of an algebra $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ are equivalent in the following sense. If $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ then $(\lambda, \rho)$ where $a^{\lambda}: u \rightarrow a u$ and $a^{\rho}: u \rightarrow u a, a \in \mathfrak{A}, u \in \mathfrak{M}$, is an $I$-birepresentation for $\mathfrak{A}$. Conversely, if ( $\lambda, \rho$ ) is an $I$-birepresentation of $\mathfrak{A}$ such that the domains of $a^{\lambda}$ and $a^{\rho}$ are $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ then $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule if we define $a u=u a^{\lambda}$ and $u a=u a^{\rho}$.

We now consider the explicit form of the birepresentation conditions for the important classes we have singled out.
(1) Associative algebras. If we refer to (16) we obtain that the nonzero derived elements of $f=\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{3}-x_{1}\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right)$ are

$$
\begin{align*}
& F_{1}=r\left(x_{2}\right) r\left(x_{3}\right)-r\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right) \\
& F_{2}=l\left(x_{1}\right) r\left(x_{3}\right)-r\left(x_{3}\right) l\left(x_{1}\right)  \tag{23}\\
& F_{3}=l\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right)-l\left(x_{2}\right) l\left(x_{1}\right)
\end{align*}
$$

Let $\eta$ be a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into an associative algebra $\mathfrak{A},(\lambda, \rho)$ a pair of linear mappings of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ and let $\tau$ be the homomorphism of $\Phi\{P\}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, l(m)^{\tau}=m^{\eta \lambda}, r(m)^{\tau}=m^{\eta \rho}$. Then if $x_{1}{ }^{\eta}=a, x_{2}{ }^{\eta}=b, x_{3}{ }^{\eta}=c$ we have $r\left(x_{2}\right)^{\tau}=x_{2}{ }^{\eta \rho}=b^{\rho}, r\left(x_{3}\right)^{\tau}=c^{\rho}, r\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right)^{\tau} =\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right)^{\eta \rho}=(b c)^{\rho}, l\left(x_{1}\right)^{\tau}=a^{\lambda}, l\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right)^{\tau}=(a b)^{\lambda}, l\left(x_{2}\right)^{\tau}=b^{\lambda}$. With a slight change in notations this leads to the following conditions for an associative birepresentation of $\mathfrak{A}$ :

$$
\begin{equation*}
(a b)^{\rho}=a^{\rho} b^{\rho}, \quad a^{\rho} b^{\lambda}=b^{\lambda} a^{\rho}, \quad(a b)^{\lambda}=b^{\lambda} a^{\lambda}, \tag{24}
\end{equation*}
$$

for all $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$.
(2) Lie algebras. Using (17) we see that the nonzero derived elements of $f=x_{1}{ }^{2}$ and $g=\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{3}+\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right) x_{1}+\left(x_{3} x_{1}\right) x_{2}$ are

$$
\begin{align*}
& F_{1}=l\left(x_{1}\right)+r\left(x_{1}\right), \\
& G_{1}=r\left(x_{2}\right) r\left(x_{3}\right)+l\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right)+l\left(x_{3}\right) r\left(x_{2}\right),  \tag{25}\\
& G_{2}=l\left(x_{1}\right) r\left(x_{3}\right)+r\left(x_{3}\right) r\left(x_{1}\right)+l\left(x_{3} x_{1}\right), \\
& G_{3}=l\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right)+l\left(x_{2}\right) r\left(x_{1}\right)+r\left(x_{1}\right) r\left(x_{2}\right) .
\end{align*}
$$

These lead to the following conditions for a birepresentation ( $\lambda, \rho$ ) of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ :

$$
\begin{align*}
\lambda & =-\rho  \tag{26}\\
(a b)^{\rho} & =a^{\rho} b^{\rho}-b^{\rho} a^{\rho}
\end{align*}
$$

$a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$.
(3) Alternative algebras. By(18)the derived elements $\neq 0$ of $f=x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}-x_{1}\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right)$, $g=x_{2} x_{1}{ }^{2}-\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right) x_{1}$ are

$$
\begin{align*}
& F_{1}=\left(l\left(x_{1}\right)+r\left(x_{1}\right)\right) r\left(x_{2}\right)-r\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right)-r\left(x_{2}\right) l\left(x_{1}\right), \\
& F_{2}=l\left(x_{1}^{2}\right)-l\left(x_{1}\right)^{2},  \tag{27}\\
& G_{1}=\left(l\left(x_{1}\right)+r\left(x_{1}\right)\right) l\left(x_{2}\right)-l\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)-l\left(x_{2}\right) r\left(x_{1}\right), \\
& G_{2}=r\left(x_{1}^{2}\right)-r\left(x_{1}\right)^{2} .
\end{align*}
$$

These give the alternative birepresentation conditions

$$
\begin{align*}
a^{\lambda+\rho} b^{\rho} & =(a b)^{\rho}+b^{\rho} a^{\lambda} \\
\left(a^{2}\right)^{\lambda} & =\left(a^{\lambda}\right)^{2}  \tag{28}\\
a^{\lambda+\rho} b^{\lambda} & =(b a)^{\lambda}+b^{\lambda} a^{\rho} \\
\left(a^{2}\right)^{\rho} & =\left(a^{\rho}\right)^{2}
\end{align*}
$$

(4) Jordan algebras. By (19) the nonzero derived elements of the defining identities $f=x_{1} x_{2}-x_{2} x_{1}, g=\left(x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}\right) x_{1}-x_{1}{ }^{2}\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)$ are

$$
\begin{align*}
F_{1}= & r\left(x_{2}\right)-l\left(x_{2}\right) \\
F_{2}= & l\left(x_{1}\right)-r\left(x_{1}\right) \\
G_{1}= & \left(l\left(x_{1}\right)+r\left(x_{1}\right)\right) r\left(x_{2}\right) r\left(x_{1}\right)+l\left(x_{1}^{2} x_{2}\right)  \tag{29}\\
& -\left(l\left(x_{1}\right)+r\left(x_{1}\right)\right) r\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)-l\left(x_{2}\right) l\left(x_{1}^{2}\right) \\
G_{2}= & l\left(x_{1}^{2}\right) r\left(x_{1}\right)-r\left(x_{1}\right) l\left(x_{1}^{2}\right)
\end{align*}
$$

These give the following Jordan birepresentation conditions:

$$
\begin{align*}
\lambda & =\rho \\
\left(a^{2}\right)^{\rho} a^{\rho} & =a^{\rho}\left(a^{2}\right)^{\rho}  \tag{30}\\
2 a^{\rho} b^{\rho} a^{\rho}+\left(a^{2} b\right)^{\rho} & =2 a^{\rho}(b a)^{\rho}+b^{\rho}\left(a^{2}\right)^{\rho}
\end{align*}
$$

## Exercise

1. Derive the bimodule and birepresentation conditions for noncommutative Jordan algebras (ex. 8, p. 33) and Malcev algebras (ex. 10, p. 33).
2. Multiplication specializations and universal envelopes. It is convenient to generalize the notion of an $I$-birepresentation for an algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ in a variety $\mathscr{V}(I)$ by replacing $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ by any associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 . Using the notations of the last section, we define an I-multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ in the associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 to be a pair of linear mappings $(\lambda, \rho)$ of $\mathfrak{A}$
into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that if $\eta$ is any homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\tau$ is the homomorphism of $\Phi\{P\}$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, l(m)^{\tau}=m^{\eta \lambda}, r(m)^{\tau}=m^{\eta \rho}, m \in N(X)^{\prime}$, then $F_{i}{ }^{\tau}=0$ for all derived polynomials $F_{i} \in \Phi\{P\}$ of every $f \in I$. Thus an $I$-birepresentation is an $I$-multiplication specialization in $\mathfrak{G}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. It is clear that if $(\lambda, \rho)$ is an $I$-multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$ and $\mu$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{G}$ into another associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}^{\prime}$ with 1 such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ then $(\lambda \mu, \rho \mu)$ is an $I$-multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{G}^{\prime}$. In particular, this holds if $\mu$ is a unital representation of $\mathfrak{G}$, that is, a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{G}$ into an algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$. It is clear also that if $\mu$ is a $1-1$ unital representation of $\mathfrak{G}$ then a pair of linear mappings $(\lambda, \rho)$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ is an $I$-multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$ if and only if $(\lambda \mu, \rho \mu)$ is an $I$-birepresentation of $\mathfrak{A}$.

Now let $\zeta$ be a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ into $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ and let $(\lambda, \rho)$ be an $I$-multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$. We claim that $(\zeta \lambda, \zeta \rho)$ is an $I$-multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$. By the remark just made and the fact that any associative algebra with 1 has a 1-1 unital representation, it is sufficient to consider the case in which $\mathfrak{G}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$, that is, $(\lambda, \rho)$ is an $I$-birepresentation of $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$. In view of Theorem 10, this will follow if we can show that if $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$, then $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ relative to the compositions

$$
\begin{equation*}
a u=a^{\zeta} u, \quad u a=u a^{\zeta}, \quad a \in \mathfrak{A}, \quad u \in \mathfrak{M} . \tag{31}
\end{equation*}
$$

Clearly these compositions are bilinear so we have to show that the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ determined by them is in $\mathscr{V}(I)$. Let $\eta$ be the homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $x_{i} \rightarrow a_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}, y \rightarrow u \in \mathfrak{M}$. Then it follows from (31) by induction on the degree that if $m\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}, y\right)$ is an element of $N(Z)^{\prime}$ of first degree in $y$ then $m\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}, y\right)^{n}=m\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}, u\right)=m\left(a_{1}{ }^{\zeta}, \cdots, a_{n}{ }^{\zeta}, u\right)$, which is an element of $\mathfrak{M}$. Hence if $g\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}, y\right)$ is an element of $\Phi\{\{Z\}\}^{\prime}$ homogeneous of degree 1 in $y$ then

$$
\begin{equation*}
g\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}, u\right)=g\left(a_{1}^{\zeta}, \cdots, a_{n}^{\zeta}, u\right) . \tag{$\prime$}
\end{equation*}
$$

Now let $f\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right) \in I$. Then $f D_{i}\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}, u\right)=f D_{i}\left(a_{1}^{\zeta}, \cdots, a_{n}^{\zeta}, u\right)=0$ since $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ '. Hence, by Theorem 9, $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$.

We suppose next that $(\lambda, \rho)$ is an $I$-multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$ and $\mathfrak{R}$ is an ideal of $\mathfrak{A}$ contained in $\operatorname{ker} \lambda \cap \operatorname{ker} \rho$. If $\overline{\mathfrak{A}}=\mathfrak{A} / \mathfrak{R}$ and $\bar{a}=a+\mathfrak{R}$, $a \in \mathfrak{A}$, then the linear mappings $\bar{\lambda}, \bar{\rho}$ of $\overline{\mathfrak{A}}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $\bar{a}^{\bar{\lambda}}=a^{\lambda}, \bar{a}^{\bar{\rho}}=a^{\rho}$ constitute an $I$-multiplication specialization of $\overline{\mathfrak{A}}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$. Again, it is enough to consider the case in which $\mathfrak{G}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. Then the assertion is equivalent to the following: If $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{K}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $\mathfrak{M} \mathfrak{M}=0=\mathfrak{M} \mathfrak{K}$ then $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\overline{\mathfrak{A}}=\mathfrak{A} / \mathfrak{K}$ relative to the compositions $\bar{a} u=a u, u \bar{a}=u a, a \in \mathfrak{A}, \bar{a}=a+\mathfrak{K}$. It is clear that $(\bar{a}, u) \rightarrow a u$, $(\bar{a}, u) \rightarrow u a$ are bilinear. Also we have the homomorphism $a+u \rightarrow \bar{a}+u$ of the
split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ onto the split null extension $\overline{\mathfrak{E}}=\overline{\mathfrak{A}} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$. Since $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{E} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$. Hence $\overline{\mathfrak{E}} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ and $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\overline{\mathfrak{A}}$.

We are now ready to consider the universal objects defined by the notion of an $I$-multiplication specialization. These are defined as follows.

Definition 3. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be an algebra in a variety $\mathscr{V}(I)$ defined by a set of identities $I$. Then an associative algebra $\mathfrak{U}$ with identity element 1 together with an I-multiplication specialization ( $\lambda_{u}, \rho_{u}$ ) of $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{U}$ is called a universal I-multiplication envelope of $\mathfrak{A}$ if for any I-multiplication specialization $(\lambda, \rho)$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ in an associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 there exists a unique homomorphism $\mu$ of $\mathfrak{U}$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $\lambda_{u} \mu=\lambda, \rho_{u} \mu=\rho$, that is, the following diagrams are commutative:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-097.jpg?height=218&width=210&top_left_y=890&top_left_x=523)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-097.jpg?height=206&width=212&top_left_y=898&top_left_x=1064)

We can now state the following basic result.
Theorem 11. There exists a universal I-multiplication envelope for any algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ in a variety $\mathscr{V}(I)$. Universal multiplication envelopes have the following properties:
(1) If $\left(\mathfrak{U}, \lambda_{u}, \rho_{u}\right)$ and $\left(\mathfrak{U}^{\prime}, \lambda_{u}^{\prime}, \rho_{u}^{\prime}\right)$ are universal I-multiplication envelopes for $\mathfrak{U}$ then there exists a unique isomorphism $\mathfrak{\imath}$ of $\mathfrak{U}$ onto $\mathfrak{U}^{\prime}$ such that $\lambda_{u}^{\prime}=\lambda_{u} \mathfrak{\imath}$, $\rho_{u}^{\prime}=\rho_{u} \mathrm{l}$.
(2) $\mathfrak{U}$ is generated by $\mathfrak{U}^{\lambda_{u}} \cup \mathfrak{U}^{\rho_{u}} \cup\{1\}$.
(3) If $\zeta$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ into another algebra $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$ in $\mathscr{V}(I)$ and ( $\mathfrak{U}^{\prime}, \lambda_{u}^{\prime}, \rho_{u}^{\prime}$ ) is an $I$-multiplication envelope for $\mathfrak{U}^{\prime}$ then there exists a unique homomorphism $\zeta_{u}$ of $\mathfrak{U}$ into $\mathfrak{U}^{\prime}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and the following diagrams are commutative:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-097.jpg?height=238&width=253&top_left_y=1710&top_left_x=554)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-097.jpg?height=238&width=245&top_left_y=1710&top_left_x=957)
(4) If $0 \rightarrow \mathfrak{A}^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow_{\xi} \mathfrak{A} \rightarrow_{\zeta} \mathfrak{A}^{\prime} \rightarrow 0$ is exact and $\mathfrak{U}, \mathfrak{U}^{\prime}$ and $\zeta_{u}$ are as in (3) then $\mathfrak{U} \rightarrow_{\xi_{u}} \mathfrak{U}^{\prime} \rightarrow 0$ is exact and $\operatorname{ker} \zeta_{u}$ is the ideal in $\mathfrak{U}$ generated by $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime \prime \xi \lambda_{u}} \cup \mathfrak{U}^{\prime \prime \xi \rho_{u}}$.
(5) Suppose the set of identities $I$ satisfies conditions $H$ and $L$ of §1.6. Let $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ and let $\Gamma$ be an extension of the base field $\Phi$. Then ( $\mathfrak{U}_{\Gamma}, \lambda_{u}, \rho_{u}$ ) where
$\mathfrak{U}_{\Gamma}=\Gamma \otimes_{\Phi} \mathfrak{U}$ and $\lambda_{u}, \rho_{u}$ are the $\Gamma$-linear extensions of $\lambda_{u}, \rho_{u}$ to $\mathfrak{U}_{\Gamma}$ is a universal I-multiplication envelope for $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$.
(6) Suppose the set of identities $I$ satisfies conditions $H, L$ and $U$ of §1.6. Then the mappings $\lambda_{u}, \rho_{u}$ of $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ into a universal I-multiplication envelope $\mathfrak{U}$ are 1-1.

Proof. To construct $\left(\mathfrak{U}, \lambda_{u}, \rho_{u}\right)$ for a given $\mathfrak{U}$ in $\mathscr{V}(I)$ we form $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ where $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ is a vector space isomorphic to $\mathfrak{A}$ under an isomorphism $a \rightarrow a_{i}, i=1,2$. Let $T(\mathfrak{B})$ be the tensor algebra $\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{B} \oplus(\mathfrak{B} \otimes \mathfrak{B}) \oplus \cdots$ based on the vector space $\mathfrak{B}$. Let $\eta$ be a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ and let $\eta_{i}$ be the resultant of $\eta$ and the mapping $a \rightarrow a_{i}$ regarded as a mapping of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2}$. Then there exists a unique homomorphism $\psi=\psi(\eta)$ of $\Phi\{P\}$ into $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $l(m)^{\psi}=m^{\eta_{1}}, r(m)^{\psi}=m^{\eta_{2}}, m \in N(X)^{\prime}$. Let $\Re$ be the ideal in $T(\mathfrak{B})$ generated by all $F_{i}{ }^{\psi}$ where the $F_{i}$ are the derived elements ( $\in \Phi\{P\}$ ) of the $f \in I$ and the $\psi$ 's are all the homomorphisms obtained by varying $\eta$. Set $\mathfrak{U}=T(\mathfrak{B}) / \Re$ and let $\lambda_{u}$ and $\rho_{u}$ be the linear mappings of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{U}$ such that $a^{\lambda_{u}}=a_{1}+\Re$, $a^{\rho .,}=a_{2}+\Re$. We proceed to show that $\left(\mathfrak{U}, \lambda_{u}, \rho_{u}\right)$ is a universal $I$-multiplication envelope for $\mathfrak{A}$. Let $\eta$ be a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ and let $\tau=\tau(\eta)$ be the homomorphism of $\Phi\{P\}$ into $\mathfrak{U}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, l(m)^{\tau}=m^{\eta \lambda_{u}}=m^{\eta_{1}}+\Re$. $r(m)^{\tau}=m^{\eta \rho_{u}}=m^{\eta_{2}}+\Re, m \in N(X)^{\prime}$. Since $l(m)^{\psi}=m^{\eta_{1}}, r(m)^{\psi}=m^{\eta_{2}}$ we have $l(m)^{\tau}=l(m)^{\psi}+\Re, r(m)^{\tau}=r(m)^{\psi}+\Re$. Since $\psi$ and $\tau$ are homomorphisms of $\Phi\{P\}$ into $T(\mathfrak{B})$ and $\mathfrak{U}=T(\mathfrak{B}) / \Re$ respectively and 1 and the $l(m)$ and $r(m)$ generate $\Phi\{P\}$, we have $F^{\tau}=F^{\psi}+\Re$ for any $F \in \Phi\{P\}$. In particular, if $F_{i}$ is a derived element of $f \in I$ then $F_{i}{ }^{\tau}=F_{i}{ }^{\psi}+\Re=0$, since $F_{i}{ }^{\psi} \in \Re$. Thus ( $\lambda_{u}, \rho_{u}$ ) is an $I$-multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{U}$. Next let ( $\lambda, \rho$ ) be any $I$-multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{A}$ in an associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 . We have a homomorphism $\mu^{\prime}$ of $T(\mathfrak{B})$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, a_{1}{ }^{\mu^{\prime}}=a^{\lambda}, a_{2}^{\mu^{\prime}}=a^{\rho}$, $a \in \mathfrak{A}$. Let $\eta$ be a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}, \tau$ the corresponding homomorphism of $\Phi\{P\}$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, l(m)^{\tau}=m^{\eta \dot{\lambda}}, r(m)^{\tau}=m^{\eta \rho}$. Then $F_{i}{ }^{\tau}=0$ for all $i$ and $f \in I$. We have $l(m)^{\psi \mu^{\prime}}=m^{\eta \mu^{\prime}}=\left(m^{\eta}\right)_{1}{ }^{\mu^{\prime}}=m^{\eta \lambda}$ and $r(m)^{\psi \mu^{\prime}} =m^{\eta \rho}$. Hence $l(m)^{\psi \mu^{\prime}}=l(m)^{\tau}, r(m)^{\psi \mu^{\prime}}=r(m)^{\tau}$ so $\tau=\psi \mu^{\prime}$. Then $F_{i}{ }^{\tau}=0$ for the derived elements $F_{i}$ gives $F_{i}^{\psi \mu^{\prime}}=0$. Thus the ideal $\Re$ generated by the $F_{i}{ }^{4}$ is mapped into 0 by $\mu^{\prime}$ and hence we have the homomorphism $\mu$ of $\mathfrak{U}=T(\mathfrak{B}) / \Re$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a^{\lambda_{u} \mu}=\left(a_{1}+\Re\right)^{\mu}=a_{1}{ }^{\mu^{\prime}}=a^{\lambda}, a^{\rho_{u} \mu}=a^{\rho}$. Thus $\lambda_{u} \mu=\lambda, \rho_{u} \mu=\rho$. Since the elements $1, a_{1}, a_{2}$ for $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ generate $T(\mathfrak{B})$ the elements $1, a^{\lambda_{u}}, a^{\rho_{u}}$ generate $\mathfrak{U}$. Consequently, the homomorphism $\mu$ is unique and we have proved that $\left(\mathfrak{X}, \lambda_{u}, \rho_{u}\right)$ is a universal $I$-multuplication envelope for $\mathfrak{A}$.

The properties (1)-(3) are strictly functorial and the proofs are the same as those of (1), (2) and (4) of Theorem 1. The proof of (4) is exactly like that of (5) of Theorem 1 since we have the necessary properties relating $I$-multiplication specializations and homomorphisms which we noted above. We now consider (5). Suppose the set $I$ satisfies $H$ and $L$ of §1.6. Then we have seen that if $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$
and $\Gamma$ is an extension of the base field $\Phi$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ then $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma} \in \mathscr{V}(I, \Gamma)$ (Corollary 1 to Theorem 1.4). Let ( $\lambda, \rho$ ) be an $I$-multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$ and let $\lambda, \rho$ be the $\Gamma$-linear extensions of these mappings to $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ into $\mathfrak{G}_{\Gamma}$. We claim that $(\lambda, \rho)$ is an $I$-multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ into $\mathfrak{G}_{\Gamma}$. In view of the remarks made on $I$-multiplication specializations and birepresentations and the fact that $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Gamma}\left(\mathfrak{M}_{\Gamma}, \mathfrak{M}_{\Gamma}\right)$ can be identified with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})_{\Gamma}$ if $\mathfrak{M}$ is a vector space over $\Phi$, our claim will follow if we can show that if $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ then $\mathfrak{M}_{\Gamma}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ relative to the extensions of the bilinear mappings of $\mathfrak{A} \times \mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$. Hence let $\mathfrak{M}$ be an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$. Then the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{M} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$. Then $\mathfrak{E}_{\Gamma}=\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma} \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{\Gamma} \in \mathscr{V}(I, \Gamma)$ which implies that $\mathfrak{M}_{\Gamma}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$. The proof of Theorem 1 (6) can now be carried over to show that $\left(\mathfrak{U}_{\Gamma}, \lambda, \rho\right)$ is a universal $I$-multiplication envelope of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$. We now consider (6). If $I$ satisfies H and L then $\mathfrak{A}$ itself is an $I$-bimodule, the regular $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence we have the regular birepresentation ( $L, R$ ) where $L$ and $R$ are $a \rightarrow a_{L} a \rightarrow a_{R}$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$. If $\mathfrak{A}$ has an identity element then $L$ and $R$ are 1-1. Hence, $\lambda_{u}$ and $\rho_{u}$ are 1-1. If $\mathfrak{A}$ does not have an identity element then by $\mathrm{H}, \mathrm{L}, \mathrm{U}$, we can adjoin one to obtain $\mathfrak{A}^{*}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{A}$ which is in the class $\mathscr{V}(I)$ (Corollary 2 to Theorem 1.4). Then $a \rightarrow a_{L}, a \rightarrow a_{R}$ acting in $\mathfrak{A}^{*}$ are birepresentations of $\mathfrak{A}$. Since these linear mappings of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{A}^{*}, \mathfrak{A}^{*}\right)$ are 1-1 it follows again that $\lambda_{u}$ and $\rho_{u}$ are 1-1.

Property (3) of the foregoing theorem permits us to define a functor from the category $\mathscr{V}(I)$ of algebras satisfying a set of identities $I$ to the category of associative algebras with 1 . If $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ then we let $U(\mathfrak{A})$ be the associative algebra $\mathfrak{U}$ with 1 given in the construction above for a universal $I$-multiplication envelope. Then if $\zeta$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ into $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ we have the homomorphism $\zeta_{u}$ of $U(\mathfrak{A})$ into $U\left(\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}\right)$ sending 1 into 1 . The mappings we have indicated define a functor which we shall call the universal multiplication functor from $\mathscr{V}(I)$ to the category of associative algebras with 1 .

Let $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I),\left(\mathfrak{U}, \lambda_{u}, \rho_{u}\right)$ a universal $I$-multiplication envelope for $\mathfrak{A}$ and let $\mathfrak{M}$ be an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$. Then we have the homomorphism $\mu$ of $\mathfrak{U}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that $a^{\lambda_{u} \mu}$ is the mapping $u \rightarrow a u$ and $a^{\rho_{u} \mu}$ the mapping $u \rightarrow u a$ in $\mathfrak{M}$. The homomorphism $\mu$ of $\mathfrak{U}$ permits us to endow $\mathfrak{M}$ with a right $\mathfrak{U}$-module structure in which $u b=u b^{\mu}, u \in \mathfrak{M}, b \in \mathfrak{U}$. This is a unital right module for $\mathfrak{U}$ since $1^{\mu}=1$. Also we have $u a^{\lambda_{u}}=a u$ and $u a^{\rho_{u}}=u a$. Since 1 and the $a^{\lambda_{u}}$ and $a^{\rho_{u}}$ generate $\mathfrak{U}$ these equations determine the module structure on $\mathfrak{M}$. Conversely, assume $\mathfrak{M}$ is a unital right module for $\mathfrak{U}$. Then we have the homomorphism $\mu$ of $\mathfrak{U}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that $b^{\mu}$ is $u \rightarrow u b, b \in \mathfrak{U}$. Then $\left(\lambda_{u} \mu, \rho_{u} \mu\right)$ is an $I$-birepresentation of $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. Consequently, $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ in which $a u=u a^{\lambda_{u} \mu}=u a^{\lambda_{u}}$ and $u a=u a^{\rho_{u} \mu}=u a^{\rho_{u}}$. Thus we see that we have an equivalence between the notions of an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ and of a unital right module for the associative algebra $\mathfrak{U}$.

Now assume that $I$ satisfies conditions H and L . Let $\mathfrak{B} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ and let $\mathfrak{A}$ be
a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{B}$. Then $a \rightarrow a_{L}, a \rightarrow a_{R}, a \in \mathfrak{A}, a_{L}$ and $a_{R}$ acting in $\mathfrak{B}$, constitute a birepresentation of $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence we have a homomorphism $\mu$ of $U(\mathfrak{A})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, a^{\lambda_{u}} \rightarrow a_{L}, a^{\rho_{u}} \rightarrow a_{R}$. We note also that we can construct an algebra $\mathfrak{B} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ containing $\mathfrak{A}$ as a subalgebra so that the homomorphism $\mu$ is a monomorphism of $U(\mathfrak{A})$. For this purpose we take a $1-1$ unital representation of $U(\mathfrak{A})$ in an algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. Accordingly, we may consider $\mathfrak{M}$ as a right $U(\mathfrak{A})$-module and as before as an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$. Then $\mathfrak{A}$ is a subalgebra of the split null extension $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ and one sees easily that the homomorphism $\mu$ of $U(\mathfrak{A})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, a^{\lambda_{u}} \rightarrow a_{L}$ (acting in $\mathfrak{B}$ ), $a^{\rho_{u}} \rightarrow a_{R}$ is 1-1.

## Exercise

1. Show that the universal multiplication functor on a class $\mathscr{V}(I)$ commutes with direct limits in the sense that the analogue of Theorem 2 holds for multiplication specializations.
2. Extension of algebras and factor sets. If $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{M} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ then we define an I-extension of $\mathfrak{A}$ by $\mathfrak{M}$ as a short exact sequence

$$
\begin{equation*}
0 \longrightarrow \mathfrak{M} \underset{\alpha}{\longrightarrow} \mathfrak{E} \underset{\beta}{\longrightarrow} \mathfrak{U} \longrightarrow 0 \tag{32}
\end{equation*}
$$

such that $\mathfrak{E} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$. Two $I$-extensions are called equivalent if they can be imbedded in a commutative diagram
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-100.jpg?height=202&width=562&top_left_y=1363&top_left_x=632)

It follows from this that $\gamma$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{E}$ onto $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime}$. The extension (32) is called inessential (or split) if there exists a homomorphism $\delta: \mathfrak{A} \rightarrow \mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta \beta=1_{\mathfrak{A}}$ the identity mapping on $\mathfrak{A}$. If this is the case we have the vector space decomposition $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{A}^{\delta} \oplus \mathfrak{M}^{\alpha}$ and $\mathfrak{U}^{\delta}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{E}$ isomorphic to $\mathfrak{U}$. If $\mathfrak{M}$ is a trivial algebra in the sense that $\mathfrak{M}^{2}=0$ (necessarily contained in $\mathscr{V}(I)$ ) then the extension of $\mathfrak{A}$ by $\mathfrak{M}$ will be called a null extension. We shall now analyze these extensions assuming that the set of identities $I$ satisfies conditions H and L of §1.6.

We note first that (32) implies that $\alpha$ is injective. Hence we may identify $\mathfrak{M}$ and $\mathfrak{M}^{\alpha}$ and so take $\alpha$ to be the injection of $\mathfrak{M}$ in $\mathfrak{E}$. Since $\mathfrak{M}$ has a complementary vector subspace in $\mathfrak{E}$ there exists a linear mapping $\delta$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta \beta=1_{\mathfrak{A}}$. Then we have the vector space decomposition $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{M} \oplus \mathfrak{U}^{\delta}$. If $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$ then
$\left(a^{\delta} b^{\delta}-(a b)^{\delta}\right)^{\beta}=a b-a b=0$. Since (32) is exact this implies that $a^{\delta} b^{\delta}-(a b)^{\delta} \in \mathfrak{M}$. Hence we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
a^{\delta} b^{\delta}=(a b)^{\delta}+h(a, b) \tag{34}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $h(a, b) \in \mathfrak{M}$. It is clear that $(a, b) \rightarrow h(a, b)$ is a bilinear mapping of $\mathfrak{A} \times \mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$.

We shall show next that $\mathfrak{M}$ is an I-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ relative to the bilinear products

$$
\begin{equation*}
a u=a^{\delta} u, \quad u a=u a^{\delta}, \quad a \in \mathfrak{A}, \quad u \in \mathfrak{M} \tag{35}
\end{equation*}
$$

where the right-hand sides are the products in $\mathfrak{E}$. Since $I$ satisfies H and L , we can consider $\mathfrak{E}$ as $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{E}$ relative to the algebra products. Since $\mathfrak{M}$ is an ideal $\mathfrak{M}$ is a sub-bimodule of $\mathfrak{E}$ and since $\mathfrak{M}^{2}=0, \mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\overline{\mathfrak{E}}=\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$ relative to $\bar{e} u=e u, u \bar{e}=u e, e \in \mathfrak{E}, \bar{e}=e+\mathfrak{M}$. Since (32) is exact $\bar{e} \rightarrow e^{\beta}$ is an isomorphism of $\overline{\mathfrak{E}}=\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ relative to $e^{\beta} u=e u, u e^{\beta}=u e$. If we take $e=a^{\delta}$ in this we obtain $a u=a^{\delta \beta} u =e^{\beta} u=e u=a^{\delta} u$ and $u a=u a^{\delta}$. Hence $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ relative to (35).

We shall now derive the conditions on $h(a, b)$ which are imposed by the identities in the set $I$. Let $\eta$ be a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$. Then we define a mapping $(\eta, h)$ of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into the $\mathfrak{A}$-bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$ as follows: $(\eta, h)$ is $\Phi$-linear, $x_{i}^{(\eta, h)}=0,\left(x_{i} x_{j}\right)^{(\eta, h)}=h\left(x_{i}{ }^{\eta}, x_{j}{ }^{\eta}\right)$, and if $M$ is a monomial of degree $\geqq 3$ and $M=M_{1} M_{2}$ is the (unique) factorization of $M$ as a product of two monomials then

$$
\begin{equation*}
M^{(\eta, h)}=M_{1}^{\eta} M_{2}^{(\eta, h)}+M_{1}^{(\eta, h)} M_{2}^{\eta}+h\left(M_{1}^{\eta}, M_{2}^{\eta}\right) \tag{36}
\end{equation*}
$$

Let $\eta$ be the homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $x_{i} \rightarrow a_{i}$ and let $\eta^{\prime}$ be the homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $x_{i} \rightarrow a_{i}^{\delta}$. Then we claim that

$$
\begin{equation*}
f\left(a_{1}^{\delta}, \cdots, a_{n}^{\delta}\right)=f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)^{\delta}+f^{(\eta, h)} \tag{37}
\end{equation*}
$$

for all $f=f\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right) \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$. This is clear if $f$ is of degree 1 since in this case $f^{(\eta, h)}=0$. Also, it holds if $f$ is a monomial of degree two, since $f^{(\eta, h)}=h\left(x_{i}{ }^{\eta}, x_{j}{ }^{\eta}\right)=h\left(a_{i}, a_{j}\right)$ and (34) holds. Now assume (37) holds for the monomials $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ and let $M=M_{1} M_{2}$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
M\left(a_{1}^{\delta}, \cdots, a_{n}^{\delta}\right)= & M_{1}\left(a_{1}^{\delta}, \cdots, a_{n}^{\delta}\right) M_{2}\left(a_{1}^{\delta}, \cdots, a_{n}^{\delta}\right) \\
= & \left(M_{1}\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)^{\delta}+M_{1}^{(\eta, h)}\right)\left(M_{2}\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)^{\delta}+M_{2}^{(\eta, h)}\right) \\
= & M\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)^{\delta}+h\left(M_{1}\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right), M_{2}\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)\right) \\
& +M_{1}\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right) M_{2}^{(\eta, h)}+M_{1}^{(\eta, h)} M_{2}\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

by (34), (35) and $\mathfrak{M}^{2}=0$. Hence, by (36),

$$
M\left(a_{1}^{\delta}, \cdots, a_{n}^{\delta}\right)=M\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)^{\delta}+M^{(\eta, h)}
$$

which implies (37) for all $f \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$.
Now suppose $f \in I$. Then since $\mathfrak{E}$ and $\mathfrak{U} \in \mathscr{V}(I), f\left(a_{1}{ }^{\delta}, \cdots, a_{n}{ }^{\delta}\right)=0$ and $f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)=0$. Hence (37) implies that

$$
\begin{equation*}
f^{(\eta, h)}=0 \tag{38}
\end{equation*}
$$

for every homomorphism $\eta$ of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$. This leads us to formulate the following

Definition 4. Let $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ and let $\mathfrak{M}$ be an I-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$. Then a bilinear mapping h of $\mathfrak{A} \times \mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ is called an I-factor set for $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{M}$ if (38) holds for all $f \in I$ and all homomorphisms $\eta$ of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$.

Our result is that we if have an extension (32) of $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ by $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $\mathfrak{M}^{2}=0$ and $\alpha$ is the injection mapping then if $\delta$ is a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta \beta=1_{\mathfrak{A}}$, then $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ via (35) and $h$ defined by $h(a, b)=a^{\delta} b^{\delta}-(a b)^{\delta}$ is an $I$-factor set for $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{M}$. Conversely, suppose $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$, $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ and $h$ is an $I$-factor set of $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{M}$. Let $\mathfrak{E}$ be a vector space containing $\mathfrak{M}$ such that we have a linear isomorphism $\delta$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{M} \oplus \mathfrak{U}^{\delta}$. Then we define an algebra structure on $\mathfrak{E}$ by defining

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left(a^{\delta}+u\right)\left(b^{\delta}+v\right)=(a b)^{\delta}+h(a, b)+a v+u b \tag{39}
\end{equation*}
$$

$a, b \in \mathfrak{A}, u, v \in \mathfrak{M}$. Clearly $\mathfrak{M}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\mathfrak{M}^{2}=0$. Hence, by (15),

$$
\begin{aligned}
f\left(a_{1}^{\delta}+u_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}^{\delta}+u_{n}\right)= & f\left(a_{1}^{\delta}, \cdots, a_{n}^{\delta}\right) \\
& +\sum_{i=1}^{n} f D_{i}\left(a_{1}^{\delta}, \cdots, a_{n}^{\delta}, u_{i}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

for $f \in \Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}, u_{i} \in \mathfrak{M}$. Also (37) holds as before for $\eta$ the homomorphism such that $x_{i}^{\eta}=a_{i}$. Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
f\left(a_{1}^{\delta}+u_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}^{\delta}+u_{n}\right)= & f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)^{\delta}+f^{(\eta, h)} \\
& +\sum f D_{i}\left(a_{1}^{\delta}, \cdots, a_{n}^{\delta}, u_{i}\right) .
\end{aligned}
$$

If $f \in I, f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}\right)=0$ and $\sum f D_{i}\left(a_{1}{ }^{\delta}, \cdots, a_{n}{ }^{\delta}, u_{i}\right)=0$ since (38) gives $a^{\delta} u=a u$, $u a^{\boldsymbol{\delta}}=u a$ and $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $I$-bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$. Also $f^{(\boldsymbol{\eta}, \boldsymbol{h})}=0$ by hypothesis. Hence $f\left(a_{1}^{\delta}+u_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}^{\delta}+u_{n}\right)=0$ and $\mathfrak{E} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$.

We now replace $\delta$ by another linear mapping $\delta^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta^{\prime} \beta=1_{\mathfrak{A}}$. Such a $\delta^{\prime}$ has the form $\delta+\mu$ where $\mu$ is a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$. Then $a^{\delta^{\prime}} u=a^{\delta} u, u a^{\delta^{\prime}}=u a^{\delta}$ so the bimodule structure on $\mathfrak{M}$ is unchanged. The bilinear mapping $h$ is replaced by $h^{\prime}$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}
h^{\prime}(a, b) & =a^{\delta^{\prime}} b^{\delta^{\prime}}-(a b)^{\delta^{\prime}}=\left(a^{\delta}+a^{\mu}\right)\left(b^{\delta}+b^{\mu}\right)-(a b)^{\delta}-(a b)^{\mu} \\
& =h(a, b)-(a b)^{\mu}+a b^{\mu}+a^{\mu} b
\end{aligned}
$$

Accordingly, we call the $I$-factor sets $h$ and $h^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{M}$ equivalent if there exists a linear mapping $\mu$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
h^{\prime}(a, b)=h(a, b)-(a b)^{\mu}+a b^{\mu}+a^{u} b \tag{40}
\end{equation*}
$$

$a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$. This is an equivalence relation in the set of factor sets of $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{A}$. The set of equivalence classes thus determined is denoted as $H^{2}(I, \mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{M})$. It is now easy to complete the proof of the following

Theorem 12. If $\mathfrak{A} \in \mathscr{V}(I)$ and $\mathfrak{M}$ is an I-bimodule then we have a bijection of $H^{2}(I, \mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{M})$ with the set of equivalence classes of null I-extensions of $\mathfrak{A}$ by $\mathfrak{M}$ such that the associated bimodule structure on $\mathfrak{M}(b y(35))$ is the given one. In this correspondence the equivalence class of 0 in $H^{2}(I, \mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{M})$ corresponds to the isomorphism class of inessential extensions.

We leave the rest of the details to the reader (cf. Cartan-Eilenberg's Homological Algebra, p. 295). We now list the factor set conditions in the cases which we have singled out throughout the discussion.
(1) Associative algebras. Let $\eta$ be a homomorphism of $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ such that $x_{1}{ }^{\eta}=a, x_{2}{ }^{\eta}=b, x_{3}{ }^{\eta}=c, h$ a bilinear mapping of ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A}$ ) into $\mathfrak{M}$. Then $\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right)^{(\eta, h)}=h(a, b), x_{3}{ }^{(\eta, h)}=0,\left(\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{3}\right)^{(\eta, h)}=h(a, b) c+h(a b, c), x_{1}{ }^{(\eta, h)}=0$, $\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right)^{(\eta, h)}=h(b, c),\left(x_{1}\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right)\right)^{(\eta, h)}=a h(b, c)+h(a, b c)$. Hence the factor set condition $f^{(\eta, h)}=0$ for $f=\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{3}-x_{1}\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right)$ is

$$
\begin{equation*}
h(a, b) c+h(a b, c)=a h(b, c)+h(a, b c) \tag{41}
\end{equation*}
$$

(2) Lie algebras. Let $\eta$ be as in (1). Then $x_{1}{ }^{2(\eta, h)}=h(a, a),\left(\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{3}\right)^{(\eta, h)} =h(a, b) c+h(a b, c)$. Hence the factor set conditions $f^{(\eta, h)}=0$ for $f=x_{1}{ }^{2}$ and $g^{(\eta, h)}=0$ for $g=\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right) x_{3}+\left(x_{2} x_{3}\right) x_{1}+\left(x_{3} x_{1}\right) x_{2}$ are

$$
\begin{gather*}
h(a, a)=0 \\
h(a, b) c+h(a b, c)+h(b, c) a+h(b c, a)+h(c, a) b+h(c a, b)=0 \tag{42}
\end{gather*}
$$

(3) Alternative algebras. Let $\eta$ be as before. Then $\left(x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}\right)^{(\eta, h)}=h(a, a) b +h\left(a^{2}, b\right),\left(x_{1}\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right)\right)^{(\eta, h)}=a h(a, b)+h(a, a b),\left(x_{2} x_{1}{ }^{2}\right)^{(\eta, h)}=b h(a, a)+h\left(b, a^{2}\right)$, $\left(\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right) x_{1}\right)^{(\eta, h)}=h(b, a) a+h(b a, a)$. Hence the factor set conditions given by $f=x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}-x_{1}\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right)$ and $g=x_{2} x_{1}{ }^{2}-\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right) x_{1}$ are

$$
\begin{align*}
& h(a, a) b+h\left(a^{2}, b\right)=a h(a, b)+h(a, a b)  \tag{43}\\
& b h(a, a)+h\left(b, a^{2}\right)=h(b, a) a+h(b a, a)
\end{align*}
$$

(4) Jordan algebras. Let $\eta$ be as before. Then $\left(x_{1} x_{2}\right)^{(\eta, h)}=h(a, b)$,
$\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)^{(\eta, h)}=h(b, a),\left(\left(x_{1}^{2} x_{2}\right) x_{1}\right)^{(\eta, h)}=(h(a, a) b) a+h\left(a^{2}, b\right) a+h\left(a^{2} b, a\right)$, $\left(x_{1}{ }^{2}\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)\right)^{(\eta, h)}=a^{2} h(b, a)+h(a, a)(b a)+h\left(a^{2}, b a\right)$. Hence the conditions given by $f=x_{1} x_{2}-x_{2} x_{1}$ and $g=\left(x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}\right) x_{1}-x_{1}{ }^{2}\left(x_{2} x_{1}\right)$ are

$$
\begin{align*}
h(a, b) & =h(b, a)  \tag{44}\\
(h(a, a) b) a+h\left(a^{2}, b\right) a+h\left(a^{2} b, a\right) & =a^{2} h(b, a)+h(a, a)(b a)+h\left(a^{2}, b a\right)
\end{align*}
$$

9. Jordan bimodules and universal multiplication envelopes. We shall now specialize the theory of bimodules and multiplication specializations to the Jordan case. As before, we denote the Jordan product as $a . b, a^{\cdot 2}$, etc. Correspondingly, we denote the products in a bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ as $a \cdot u$ and $u \cdot a, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, $u \in \mathfrak{M}$. The conditions on these given in (20) are $a \cdot u=u \cdot a$ and

$$
\begin{align*}
(u \cdot a) \cdot a^{2} & =\left(u \cdot a^{2}\right) \cdot a, \\
2((u \cdot a) \cdot b) \cdot a+u \cdot\left(a^{2} \cdot b\right) & =2(u \cdot a) \cdot(a \cdot b)+(u \cdot b) \cdot a^{2} . \tag{45}
\end{align*}
$$

Since $a . u=u . a$ we shall generally drop the composition $a . u$. Similarly, if $(\lambda, \rho)$ is a multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in an associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 then $\lambda=\rho$. Hence we may drop $\lambda$. The conditions on $\rho$ given by (30) are

$$
\begin{align*}
{\left[a^{\rho}, a^{.2 \rho}\right] } & =0 \\
2 a^{\rho} b^{\rho} a^{\rho}+\left(a^{.2} \cdot b\right)^{\rho} & =2 a^{\rho}(a \cdot b)^{\rho}+b^{\rho}\left(a^{.2}\right)^{\rho} \tag{46}
\end{align*}
$$

From now on we shall understand by a multiplication specialization of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$ a linear mapping $\rho$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that (46) holds. Clearly this is equivalent to the earlier definition. We make a corresponding alteration in the definition of a universal multiplication envelope $\left(U(\mathfrak{J}), \rho_{u}\right)$.

We can now give a simpler construction of a universal envelope than the one provided in the proof of Theorem 11. For this we begin with the tensor algebra $T(\mathfrak{J})$ and we let $\Re$ be the ideal in this algebra generated by the elements $a \otimes a^{.2}-a^{.2} \otimes a, \quad 2 a \otimes b \otimes a+a^{.2} . b-2 a \otimes a . b-b \otimes a^{.2}, \quad a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$. Let $U(\mathfrak{J})=T(\mathfrak{J}) / \Re, a^{\rho_{u}}=a+\Re, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then one sees, as in the proof of Theorem 11, that $\left(U(\mathfrak{J}), \rho_{u}\right)$ is a universal multiplication envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. We shall take this to be our standard construction and we shall call ( $U(\mathfrak{J}), \rho_{u}$ ) the universal multiplication envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. Also we write the associative product in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ as $x y$. Since the identities defining Jordan algebras satisfy conditions $\mathrm{H}, \mathrm{L}$ and U , the mapping $\rho_{u}$ is $1-1$. Accordingly, we may identify $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ with its image $a^{\rho_{u}}$ in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{J}$ with the corresponding subset of $U(\mathfrak{J})$. We shall usually do this. Then the defining property of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ is that if $\rho$ is a multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$ then $\rho$ can be extended in a unique way to a homomorphism of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ sending 1 into 1 . Similarly, any bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ can be regarded as a unital right module for $U(\mathfrak{J})$ and conversely.

For the subset $\mathfrak{J}$ of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ we have the Jordan product $a . b \in \mathfrak{J}$ and the associative product $a b \in U(\mathfrak{J})$. In this connection one should note that $a . b$ is not the same as $\frac{1}{2}(a b+b a)$ as defined in $\mathfrak{J}$. Instead one has the following basic relations connecting these compositions which are obtained from (46):

$$
\begin{align*}
{\left[a, a^{\cdot 2}\right] } & =0  \tag{$\prime$}\\
2 a b a+a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b & =2 a(a \cdot b)+b\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)
\end{align*}
$$

These relations have the following consequences:

$$
\begin{align*}
{[a, b . c]+[b, c . a]+[c, a . b] } & =0 \\
a b c+c b a+(a . c) \cdot b & =a(b . c)+b(a . c)+c(a . b)  \tag{47}\\
{[[c a] b] } & =[a, b, c]
\end{align*}
$$

These correspond to the identities $\left[R_{a} R_{b . c}\right]+\left[R_{b} R_{c . a}\right]+\left[R_{c} R_{a . b}\right]=0, R_{a} R_{b} R_{c} +R_{c} R_{b} R_{a}+R_{a . c . b}=R_{a} R_{b . c}+R_{b} R_{c . a}+R_{c} R_{a . b},\left[\left[R_{c} R_{a}\right] R_{b}\right]=R_{[a, b, c]}$ and can be derived from ( $46^{\prime}$ ) by linearization and subtraction. However, it is easier to obtain these relations and others by noting that it is sufficient to prove

$$
\begin{align*}
{\left[a^{\rho},(b \cdot c)^{\rho}\right]+\left[b^{\rho},(c \cdot a)^{\rho}\right]+\left[c^{\rho},(a \cdot b)^{\rho}\right] } & =0 \\
a^{\rho} b^{\rho} c^{\rho}+c^{\rho} b^{\rho} a^{\rho}+((a \cdot c) \cdot b)^{\rho} & =a^{\rho}(b \cdot c)^{\rho}+b^{\rho}(a \cdot c)^{\rho}+c^{\rho}(a \cdot b)^{\rho}  \tag{$\prime$}\\
{\left[\left[c^{\rho} a^{\rho}\right] b^{\rho}\right] } & =[a, b, c]^{\rho}
\end{align*}
$$

for any birepresentation $\rho$. This follows from the remarks preceding the proof of Theorem 11. If we form the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ where $\mathfrak{M}$ is the bimodule determined by $\rho$ then $a^{\rho}$ is the restriction to $\mathfrak{M}$ of $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Since we have the basic identities: $\left[R_{a}, R_{b . c}\right]+\left[R_{b} R_{a . c}\right]+\left[R_{c} R_{a . b}\right]=0, R_{a} R_{b} R_{c}+R_{c} R_{b} R_{a} +R_{(a . c) . b}=R_{a} R_{b . c}+R_{b} R_{a . c}+R_{c} R_{a . b},\left[\left[R_{c} R_{a}\right] R_{b}\right]=R_{[a, b, c]}$ in E, it is clear that (47') and hence (47) hold. In a similar fashion we see that $\left[a^{\cdot k}, a^{\cdot l}\right]=0$ and we have the recursion formula

$$
\begin{equation*}
a^{\cdot k+2}=2 a a^{\cdot k+1}+\left(a^{\cdot 2}-2 a^{2}\right) a^{\cdot k}, \quad k \geqq 1 \tag{48}
\end{equation*}
$$

In general, any operator identity for Jordan algebras yields a corresponding relation in the universal multiplication envelopes. As another example we note that if we set $u(a)=2 a^{2}-a^{2}$ then we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
u(a) u(b) u(a)=u\left(b U_{a}\right), \quad a, b \in \mathfrak{J} \tag{49}
\end{equation*}
$$

in $U(\mathfrak{J})$. This comes from the identity $U_{a} U_{b} U_{a}=U_{b U_{a}}$ in any Jordan algebra. Similarly, we have $u\left(a^{\cdot k}\right)=u(a)^{k}, k=1,2, \cdots$.

In addition to the properties (i)-(vi) of Theorem 11, all of which are valid in the Jordan case, we have the following

Theorem 13. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{U}=U(\mathfrak{J})$ the universal multiplication envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$ (identified with a subset of $\mathfrak{U}$ ). Then: (i) $\mathfrak{U}$ has a unique involution $\pi$ such that $a^{\pi}=a, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. (ii) Any derivation $D$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ has a unique extension to a derivation $D$ in $\mathfrak{U}$. Moreover, $D \pi=\pi D$. (iii) If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi=n<\infty$ then $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{U} \leqq\binom{ 2 n+1}{n}$.

Proof. (i) Let $\mathfrak{U}^{0}$ be the opposite algebra of $\mathfrak{U}$. Then the relations (46') give the following relations in $\mathfrak{U}^{0}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
{\left[a, a^{\cdot 2}\right] } & =0 \\
2 a b a+a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b & =2(a . b) a+a^{\cdot 2} b
\end{aligned}
$$

Also, by (47), $2(a . b) a+a^{\cdot 2} b=2 a(a . b)+b a^{\cdot 2}$. Hence we have $2 a b a+a^{\cdot 2} . b =2 a(a . b)+b a^{.2}$ in $\mathfrak{U}^{0}$. Thus the mapping $a \rightarrow a, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, in $\mathfrak{U}^{0}$ is a multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{U}^{0}$. Hence we have a homomorphism $\pi$ of $\mathfrak{U}$ into $\mathfrak{U}^{0}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a \rightarrow a, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. By definition of $\mathfrak{U}^{0}$, we have an antiisomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}^{0}$ onto $\mathfrak{U}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, a \rightarrow a$. Hence we have an antihomomorphism $\pi$ of $\mathfrak{U}$ into $\mathfrak{U}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, a \rightarrow a, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. It follows that $\pi^{2}=1$ and it is clear that $\pi$ is characterized by the property $a^{\pi}=a, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, since 1 and $\mathfrak{J}$ generate $\mathfrak{U}$.
(ii) As in the proof of Theorem 1 (7), let $\mathfrak{D}$ be the commutative associative algebra over $\Phi$ with basis $(1, t)$ such that $t^{2}=0$ and consider $U(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes \mathfrak{D}$. With the usual identifications, the elements of this algebra are uniquely representable in the form $x+y t, x, y \in U(\mathfrak{J})$, and $y t=t y$. Let $D$ be a derivation in $\mathfrak{J}$ and define $a^{\rho}$ for $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ as $a^{\rho}=a+(a D) t$. Then $\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)^{\rho}=a^{\cdot 2}+\left(a^{\cdot 2} D\right) t=a^{\cdot 2}+2(a . a D) t$ and $\left[a^{\rho},\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)^{\rho}\right]=\left(\left[a D, a^{\cdot 2}\right]+2[a, a \cdot a D]\right) t=0$, by (47). Also $2 a^{\rho} b^{\rho} a^{\rho}+\left(a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b\right)^{\rho} -2 a^{\rho}(a . b)^{\rho}-b^{\rho}\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)^{\rho}=\left(2(a D) b a+2 a(b D) a+2 a b(a D)+\left(a^{\cdot 2} . b\right) D-2 a D(a . b)\right. \left.-2 a(a . b) D-(b D) a^{.2}-b\left(a^{.2} D\right)\right) t=(2(a D) b a+2 a(b D) a+2 a b(a D) -2 a D(a . b)+a^{\cdot 2} . b D+2 a . a D . b-2 a(a D . b)-2 a(a . b D)-(b D) a^{\cdot 2} -2 b(a . a D) t=\left(2 a(b D) a+a^{\cdot 2} . b D-2 a(a . b D)-(b D) a^{\cdot 2}\right) t$ (by $\left.(47)\right)=0$, by $\left.\left(46^{\prime}\right)\right)$. Thus $a \rightarrow a^{\rho}$ is a multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $U(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes \mathfrak{D}$ so this can be extended to a homomorphism of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ into $U(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes \mathfrak{D}$ sending $1 \rightarrow 1$. Since 1 and $\mathfrak{J}$ generate $U(\mathfrak{J})$ it is clear that this homomorphism has the form $x \rightarrow x+x^{\prime} t$. Then $x \rightarrow x^{\prime}$ is a derivation $D$ in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ which extends $D$. Since $1 D \pi=0=1 \pi D$ and $a D \pi=a D=a \pi D, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, it is clear that $D \pi=\pi D$.
(iii) We shall show first that if $\left(u_{\imath}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{J}$ then every element of $\mathfrak{U}$ is a linear combination of the monomials

$$
\begin{equation*}
u_{t_{1}}{ }^{2} u_{t_{2}}{ }^{2} \cdots u_{t_{r}}{ }^{2} u_{t_{r+1}} u_{t_{r+2}} \cdots u_{t_{s}} \tag{50}
\end{equation*}
$$

where the $i_{j}$ are distinct and satisfy

$$
\begin{align*}
& \mathfrak{l}_{1}<\mathfrak{l}_{2}<\cdots<\mathfrak{l}_{r}, \\
& \mathfrak{l}_{r+1}<\mathfrak{l}_{r+3}<\mathfrak{l}_{r+5}<\cdots,  \tag{51}\\
& \mathfrak{l}_{r+2}<\mathfrak{l}_{r+4}<\mathfrak{l}_{r+6}<\cdots
\end{align*}
$$

By (46') and (47) we have the relations $2 a b a=2 a(a \cdot b)+b a^{\cdot 2}-a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b$, $a b c=-c b a+a(b . c)+b(a . c)+c(a . b)-(a . c) . b, a b^{2}=-b^{2} a+a b^{\cdot 2} +2 b(a . b)-(a . b) . b$ for $a, b, c \in \mathfrak{J}$. Now consider a monomial in the $u_{\imath}$. The middle relation just noted permits us to move a $c=u_{\imath}$ in such a monomial two places to the left at the expense of a linear combination of monomials in the $u$ 's of lower formal degree. If a monomial contains a $u_{i}$ in three places then by moving two of these to the left we can replace the monomial by one of the same formal degree containing a factor $u_{\imath} u_{\kappa} u_{\imath}$ plus a linear combination of monomials in the $u_{i}$ of lower formal degree. Then the first relation noted above shows that our monomial is a linear combination of monomials in the $u_{\imath}$ of lower formal degree. Hence we may assume the monomial contains a $u_{\imath}$ in at most two positions and if it contains $u_{\imath}$ in two places then these are consecutive. Then the last relation shows that the factor $u_{\imath}{ }^{2}$ can be permuted with any $u_{\kappa}$ preceding it at the expense of a linear combination of monomials of lower formal degree. We may therefore suppose that the factors $u_{\imath}{ }^{2}$ occur at the beginning and that the subscripts for these are in increasing order. Then the remaining $u_{\imath}$ in the monomial can be arranged by our process of moving two places to the left so that the conditions (51) are achieved. Since 1 and the $u_{t}$ generate $\mathfrak{U}$ it follows that every element of $\mathfrak{U}$ is a linear combination of 1 and the standard monomials in the $u_{\imath}$. Now suppose the basis is finite: $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$. Then it is clear from (51) that the number of distinct standard monomials together with 1 does not exceed

$$
\begin{equation*}
N=\sum_{s-0}^{n}\binom{n}{s} \sum_{r=0}^{s}\binom{s}{r}\binom{s-r}{\left[\frac{1}{2}(s-r)\right]} \tag{52}
\end{equation*}
$$

where [ $i$ ] denotes the largest integer in $i$. Since

$$
\binom{s}{r}\binom{s-r}{\left[\frac{1}{2}(s-r)\right]}=\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{s!}{r!\left(\frac{s-r}{2}\right)!\left(\frac{s-r}{2}\right)!} \text { if } s-r \text { is even }, \\
\frac{s!}{r!\left(\left[\frac{s-r}{2}\right]+1\right)!\left[\frac{s-r}{2}\right]!} \text { if } s-r \text { is odd. }
\end{array}\right.
$$

$f(s) \equiv \Sigma_{r=0}^{s}\binom{s}{r} \cdot\binom{s-r}{\left[\frac{1}{2}(s-r)\right]}$ is the sum of the coefficients of the terms in $(x+y+z)^{s}$ for which the exponents of $y$ and $z$ are equal and those for which the exponent of $y$ exceeds that of $z$ by 1 . This is the same as the sum of the constant term and the coefficient of $x$ in $(1+x+1 / x)^{s}$. Hence $N$ is the sum of the constant term and the coefficient of $x$ in

$$
\sum_{s=0}^{n}\binom{n}{s}\left(1+x+\frac{1}{x}\right)^{s}=\left(2+x+\frac{1}{x}\right)^{n} .
$$

This is the same as the sum of the coefficients of $x^{n}$ and $x^{n+1}$ in $\left(x^{2}+2 x+1\right)^{n} =(x+1)^{2 n}$. Hence

$$
N=\binom{2 n}{n}+\binom{2 n}{n+1}=\binom{2 n+1}{n}
$$

and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{U} \leqq N=\binom{2 n+1}{n}$.
Remark. It can be shown that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is trivial, that is, $a . b=0$ for all $a, b$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ then the bound given for $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{U}$ is attained.

## Exercises

1. Show that if the characteristic is $\neq 3$ then a linear mapping $\rho$ of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ in an associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 is a multiplication specialization if and only if
(i) $\left[a^{\rho}, a^{.2 \rho}\right]=0$,
(ii) $\left[\left[c^{\rho} a^{\rho}\right] b^{\rho}\right]=[a, b, c]^{\rho}$,
(iii) $\left(a^{\rho}\right)^{3}=\frac{3}{2} a^{\rho}\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)^{\rho}-\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\cdot 3}\right)^{\rho}$.
2. Prove that the universal multiplication envelope for a finite-dimensional alternative algebra is finite dimensional.
3. Associative specializations and multiplicative specializations. In this section we consider a basic relation between associative specializations and multiplication specializations and its consequences. Let $\sigma_{1}$ and $\sigma_{2}$ be associative specializations of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ in an associative algebra with 1 . Then we say that $\sigma_{1}$ and $\sigma_{2}$ commute if

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[a^{\sigma_{1}}, b^{\sigma_{2}}\right]=0 \tag{53}
\end{equation*}
$$

for all $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$. We now have
THEOREM 14. If $\sigma_{1}$ and $\sigma_{2}$ are associative specializations of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$ which commute then the average $\rho=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}\right)$ is a multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{i} \mathfrak{n} \mathfrak{G}$.

Proof. One can verify this by a direct calculation. However, it is more instructive to establish the result in the following way. We note first since $\mathfrak{G}$ has a 1-1 unital representation it is enough to prove the result for the case $\mathfrak{G}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), \mathfrak{M}$ a vector space over $\Phi$. Let $\left(S(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right)$ be the special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $\sigma_{1}$ is an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ we have the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}=S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a^{\sigma . .} \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{1}}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$.

Consequently, we can consider $\mathfrak{M}$ as a unital right $\mathfrak{A}$-module in which $u a^{\sigma_{u}}=u a^{\sigma_{1}}$. We have the associative specialization $\sigma_{2}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$, hence the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a^{\sigma_{u}} \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{2}}$. If we precede this with the main involution in $\mathfrak{A}$ we obtain an anti-homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, a^{\sigma_{u}} \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{2}}$. Consequently, $\mathfrak{M}$ is a unital left module for $\mathfrak{A}$ in which $a^{\sigma_{u}} u=u a^{\sigma_{2}}$. We have $\left(a^{\sigma_{u}} u\right) b^{\sigma_{u}}=a^{\sigma_{u}}\left(u b^{\sigma_{u}}\right)$, $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$, since $\sigma_{1}$ and $\sigma_{2}$ commute. Since $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}}$ and 1 generate $\mathfrak{A}$ this implies $(c u) d=c(u d), c, d \in \mathfrak{A}$. Thus $\mathfrak{M}$ is an associative bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence this gives rise to the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ which is an associative algebra. Consider the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{C}^{+}$. This contains $\mathfrak{M}$ as ideal and $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$as a subalgebra. Also $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{U}^{+}$, hence of $\mathfrak{C}^{+}$. We have the birepresentation $a^{\sigma_{u}} \rightarrow \bar{R}_{a \sigma_{u}}$ on $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}}$ where $\bar{R}$ denotes the restriction of $R$ to $\mathfrak{M}$. Since $a \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{u}}$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ as Jordan algebra, $a \rightarrow \bar{R}_{a \sigma_{u}}$ is a birepresentation of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. Now $u \bar{R}_{a \sigma_{u}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(u a^{\sigma_{u}}+a^{\sigma_{u}} u\right)=\frac{1}{2} u\left(a^{\sigma_{1}}+a^{\sigma_{2}}\right)$. Hence $a \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\sigma_{1}}+a^{\sigma_{2}}\right)$ is a birepresentation of $\mathfrak{J}$.

If we take $\sigma_{2}=0$ in Theorem 14 we obtain the
Corollary. If $\sigma$ is an associative specialization of a Jordan algebra then $\frac{1}{2} \sigma$ is a multiplication specialization.

The type of bimodule which we constructed in the foregoing proof is called special. More generally, we shall say that a bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ is special if there exists a monomorphism of $\mathfrak{M}$ into a bimodule $\mathfrak{N}$ such that if $v \in \mathfrak{N}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, then $v . a=\frac{1}{2} v\left(a^{\sigma_{1}}+a^{\sigma_{2}}\right)$ where $\sigma_{1}$ and $\sigma_{2}$ are commuting associative specializations of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{N})$.

We now consider the tensor product $S(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes S(\mathfrak{J})$ and put

$$
\begin{equation*}
a^{\prime \prime}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1+1 \otimes a^{\sigma_{u}}\right), \quad a \in \mathfrak{J} \tag{54}
\end{equation*}
$$

Clearly $a \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1$ and $a \rightarrow 1 \otimes a^{\sigma_{u}}$ are associative specializations of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $S(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes S(\mathfrak{J})$. Since $\left[a^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1,1 \otimes b^{\sigma_{u}}\right]=0$ these commute. Hence $\rho^{\prime \prime}: a \rightarrow a^{\prime \prime}$, which is their average, is a multiplication specialization. Let $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ be the subalgebra of $S(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes S(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by 1 and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime}=\left\{a^{\prime \prime} \mid a \in \mathfrak{J}\right\}$. We shall call $\left(S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}), \rho^{\prime \prime}\right)$ the squared special universal envelope of the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$. Let $\rho=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}\right)$ where $\sigma_{1}$ and $\sigma_{2}$ are commuting associative specializations of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{G}$. It follows from the basic property of the tensor product of algebras and the fact that we have a homomorphism of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ mapping $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a^{\sigma_{u}} \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{i}}$ that we have a homomorphism of $S(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes b^{\sigma_{u}} \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{1}} b^{\sigma_{2}}$. The restriction of this to $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ maps $a^{\prime \prime}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1+1 \otimes a^{\sigma_{u}}\right)$ into $\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\sigma_{1}}+a^{\sigma_{2}}\right)=a^{\rho}$. Since 1 and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \prime}$ generate $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ it is clear that this homomorphism is unique. This establishes the universal property of ( $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}), \rho^{\prime \prime}$ ) in the class of averages of commuting associative specializations. Also it is clear that if $\mathfrak{M}$ is a special bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\rho$ is the corresponding birepresentation then we have a homomorphism of $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and
$a^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow a^{\rho}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. If $\sigma$ is an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in the associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 and $b_{L}$ and $b_{R}$ denote the left and right multiplications by $b \in \mathfrak{G}$ and $\mathfrak{G}$ then $a \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{1}} \equiv\left(a^{\sigma}\right)_{R}$ and $a \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{2}} \equiv\left(a^{\sigma}\right)_{L}$ are commuting associative specializations of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$. Hence their average is a multiplication specialization and this coincides with the mapping $a \rightarrow R_{a^{\sigma}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a_{R}^{\sigma}+a_{L}^{\sigma}\right)$ where $R_{b}$ is the multiplication in $\mathfrak{G}^{+}$. It follows that we have a homomorphism of $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{G})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow R_{a^{\sigma}}$. More generally, let $\sigma$ be a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ in any special Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{K}$. Then the result just proved implies that we have a homomorphism of $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\Re, \Re)$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, a^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow R_{a^{\sigma}}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. If $\mathfrak{J}$ itself is special we have the indicated homomorphism of $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$.

The universal property of $\left(U(\mathfrak{J}), \rho_{u}\right)$ implies that we have an exact sequence

$$
\begin{equation*}
U(\mathfrak{J}) \underset{\xi}{\rightarrow} S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}) \rightarrow 0 \tag{55}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $1^{\xi}=1$ and $a^{\xi}=a^{\prime \prime}, a \in \mathfrak{J}(\subseteq U(\mathfrak{J}))$. Of particular interest is the situation in which $\xi$ is an isomorphism. In this case the study of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ is reduced to that of $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ which is determined by $S(\mathfrak{J})$ and the specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $S(\mathfrak{J})$. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is a subset of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ it is clear that if $\xi$ is an isomorphism then the mapping $a \rightarrow a^{\prime \prime}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, is injective. Since $a^{\prime \prime}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1+1 \otimes a^{\sigma_{u}}\right)$ this implies that $\sigma_{u}$ is injective and hence that $\mathfrak{J}$ is special. Accordingly, we shall say that $\mathfrak{J}$ is strongly special if $\xi$ is an isomorphism. We shall see later ( $\xi 7.4$ and ex. 3, p. 110) that there exist Jordan algebras which are special but not strongly special. On the positive side we note that if every bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ is special then $\mathfrak{J}$ is strongly special. For, let $U(\mathfrak{J})$ be considered as right $U(\mathfrak{J})$-module in the usual way, so that $u \rightarrow u_{R}$ is the corresponding representation. Then $U(\mathfrak{J})$ is a bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ with corresponding birepresentation $a \rightarrow a_{R}$. Hence the hypothesis implies that this bimodule is special and consequently we have a homomorphism of $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(U(\mathfrak{J}), U(\mathfrak{J}))$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, a^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow a_{R}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Since the homomorphism $u \rightarrow u_{R}$ is a monomorphism we have a homomorphism of $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $U(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, a^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow a, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Clearly, this is the inverse of the mapping $\xi$ so $\xi$ is an isomorphism.

The tensor product $S(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes S(\mathfrak{J})$ has an automorphism $\varepsilon$ of period two such that $u \otimes v \rightarrow v \otimes u$. We shall call $\varepsilon$ the exchange automorphism in $S(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes S(\mathfrak{J})$. The subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}$ of $\varepsilon$-fixed points is the set of elements of the form $\Sigma\left(u_{i} \otimes v_{i}+v_{i} \otimes u_{i}\right)$. If $\operatorname{dim} S(\mathfrak{J})=m$ then $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=m(m+1) / 2$. The generators 1 and $a^{\prime \prime}=a^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1+1 \otimes a^{\sigma_{u}}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, of $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ are evidently contained in $\mathfrak{B}$. Accordingly, we have the exact sequence

$$
\begin{equation*}
0 \rightarrow S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}) \underset{i}{\rightarrow} \mathfrak{V} \tag{56}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $i$ is the injection. Again the desirable situation is that in which $i$ is an isomorphism, that is, $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ coincides with the subalgebra of fixed elements under the exchange automorphism.
11. Universal multiplication envelopes for Jordan algebras with identity elements. Let $e$ be an idempotent element in $\mathfrak{J}$ and put $a=b=e$ in the second equation in (46'). This gives $2 e^{3}+e=3 e^{2}$ in $U(\mathfrak{J})$. Hence we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
e(e-1)(2 e-1)=0 . \tag{57}
\end{equation*}
$$

Put $E_{0}=(e-1)(2 e-1), E_{1}=e(2 e-1), E_{\frac{1}{2}}=-4 e(e-1)$. Then

$$
\begin{equation*}
E_{0}+E_{1}+E_{\frac{1}{2}}=1 \tag{58}
\end{equation*}
$$

and, by (57), $E_{i} E_{j}=0$ if $i \neq j$. This and (58) imply that the $E_{i}$ are idempotent elements of $\mathfrak{U}=U(\mathfrak{J})$. Hence these are orthogonal idempotents. Next let $a$ be an element of $\mathfrak{U}$ such that $a . e=a$. Then if we put $b=c=e$ in the first equation in (47) then we obtain $[a, e]=0$ and hence $\left[a, E_{i}\right]=0$. We also obtain the same commutativities if $a . e=0$.

We now suppose that $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity. In order to distinguish this from the identity element of $\mathfrak{U}$ we denote this as $c$. Then $c^{\cdot 2}=c$ so the foregoing considerations are applicable. They show that if $C_{0}=(c-1)(2 c-1), C_{1}=c(2 c-1)$, $C_{\frac{1}{2}}=-4 c(c-1)$ then these are central idempotents of $\mathfrak{U}$ which are orthogonal and have sum 1 . Consequently, we have the decomposition

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{U}=\mathfrak{U}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{1}, \quad \mathfrak{U}_{i}=\mathfrak{U} C_{i} \tag{59}
\end{equation*}
$$

and $\mathfrak{U} C_{i}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{U}$. If $x \in \mathfrak{U}$ we put $x_{i}=x C_{i}$. Since $c C_{0}=c(c-1)(2 c-1)=0$, $(c-1) C_{1}=0$ and $\left(c-\frac{1}{2}\right) C_{\frac{1}{2}}=0$, we have $c_{0}=0, c_{1}=C_{1}$ and $c_{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{2} C_{\frac{1}{2}}$. Since $x \rightarrow x_{i}$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}$ it is clear that $a \rightarrow a_{i}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, is a multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$. If $i=0$ we obtain a multiplication specialization into $\mathfrak{U}_{0}$ mapping the identity element $c$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into 0 . If $i=\frac{1}{2}$ the multiplication specialization maps $c$ into $\frac{1}{2} C_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $C_{\frac{1}{2}}$ is the identity of $\mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}}$. Finally for $i=1$ we obtain a unital multiplication specialization in the sense that $c$ is mapped into the identity element of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$.
Let $\rho$ be a multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 such that $c^{\rho}=0$. Then if we take $b=c$ in the second equation of (47') we obtain $a^{\rho}=0$. The same equation with $c^{\rho}=\frac{1}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
(a \cdot b)^{\rho}=a^{\rho} b^{\rho}+b^{\rho} a^{\rho} \tag{60}
\end{equation*}
$$

In particular, we have $a_{0}=0, a \in \mathfrak{J}$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
(a \cdot b)_{\frac{1}{2}}=a_{\frac{1}{2}} b_{\frac{1}{2}}+b_{\frac{1}{2}} a_{\frac{1}{2}} . \tag{61}
\end{equation*}
$$

Now let $\rho$ be any unital multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ and consider the homomorphism $\mu$ of $\mathfrak{U}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1=c^{\rho}$ and $a \rightarrow a^{\rho}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Since $C_{0}=(c-1)(2 c-1)$ and $C_{\frac{1}{2}}=-4 c(c-1)$ we have $C_{0}{ }^{\mu}=0=C_{\frac{1}{2}}{ }^{\mu}$. Hence $C_{1}{ }^{\mu}=1^{\mu}=1$ and the restriction $\mu_{1}$ of $\mu$ to $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ is a homomorphism sending the identity $C_{1}$ of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ into 1 . Also $\mathfrak{U}_{0}{ }^{\mu}=0, \mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}}{ }^{\mu}=0$, so $a_{1}{ }^{\mu_{1}}=a^{\mu}=a^{\rho}$. Since
$\mathfrak{J}_{1}=\left\{a_{1} \mid a \in \mathfrak{J}\right\}$ generates $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ it is clear that $\mu_{1}$ is uniquely determined by $a_{1}{ }^{\mu_{1}}=a^{\rho}$. We shall now call $\mathfrak{U}_{1}=U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ and the unital multiplication specialization $a \rightarrow a_{1}$ the universal unital multiplication envelope of $\mathfrak{J}$ since, as we have just shown, if $\rho$ is any unital multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ then there exists a unique homomorphism $\mu_{1}$ of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ such that $a_{1}{ }^{\mu_{1}}=a^{\rho}$.

We shall show next that $\mathfrak{U}_{0}+\mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ is canonically isomorphic to $S(\mathfrak{J})$ where $\left(S(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right)$ is the special universal envelope of $\mathfrak{J}$. First we recall that $\frac{1}{2} \sigma_{u}$ is a multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence we have the homomorphism $\mu$ of $\mathfrak{U}$ into $S(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a \rightarrow \frac{1}{2} a^{\sigma_{u}}$. Then $C_{1}{ }^{\mu}=(c(2 c-1))^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2} c^{\sigma_{u}}\left(c^{\sigma_{u}}-1\right)=0$ since $c^{\sigma_{u}}$ is an idempotent element. Hence $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\mu}=0$ and we have the homomorphism $\mu^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}}+\mathfrak{U}_{0}$ into $S(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $C_{\frac{1}{2}}+C_{0} \rightarrow 1, a_{\frac{1}{2}}+a_{0} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2} a^{\sigma_{u}}$. On the other hand, we have $a_{0}=0$ and $(a . b)_{\frac{1}{2}}=a_{\frac{1}{2}} b_{\frac{1}{2}}+b_{\frac{1}{2}} a_{\frac{1}{2}}, a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$. Hence $a \rightarrow 2\left(a_{\frac{1}{2}}+a_{0}\right)$ is an associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}}+\mathfrak{U}_{0}$. Consequently, we have the homomorphism $\eta$ of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}}+\mathfrak{U}_{0}$ such that $1 \rightarrow C_{\frac{1}{2}}+C_{0}$, $a^{\sigma_{u}} \rightarrow 2\left(a_{\frac{1}{2}}+a_{0}\right)$. It follows that $\eta$ and $\mu^{\prime}$ are inverses, so $\eta$ is an isomorphism of $S(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $\mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}}+\mathfrak{U}_{0}$.

We summarize our results in the following
Theorem 15. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with identity element $c$ and let $\mathfrak{U}=U(\mathfrak{J})$ be the universal multiplication envelope of $\mathfrak{J}$ where we consider $\mathfrak{J}$ as imbedded in $\mathfrak{U}$. Put $C_{0}=(c-1)(2 c-1), C_{1}=c(2 c-1), C_{\frac{1}{2}}=-4 c(c-1)$. Then the $C_{i}$ are central idempotents in $\mathfrak{U}$ which are orthogonal and have sum 1 and $\mathfrak{U}=\mathfrak{U}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ where $\mathfrak{U}_{i}=\mathfrak{U} C_{i}$ is an ideal. Moreover, if $x_{i}$ denotes the component of $x \in \mathfrak{U}$ in $\mathfrak{U}_{i}$ then $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ and $a \rightarrow a_{1}$ is a universal unital multiplication envelope, and $\mathfrak{U}_{0}+\mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $a \rightarrow 2\left(a_{0}+a_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ is a special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$.

It is clear also, by referring to §2, that $\mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and the mapping $a \rightarrow 2 a_{\frac{1}{2}}$ is a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. The argument used to establish the dimensionality inequality in Theorem 13 shows that $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{U}_{1} \leqq\binom{ 2 n-1}{n}$ if $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}=n<\infty$.
