We have also seen that $\operatorname{dim} S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}} \leqq 2^{n-1}$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{U}_{0}=1$. Hence we have the following improved inequality for the dimensionality of the universal multiplication envelope of a Jordan algebra with identity element:

$$
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{U} \leqq\binom{ 2 n-1}{n}+2^{n-1}+1 \tag{62}
\end{equation*}
$$

Let $\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right)$ be the unital special universal envelope of $\mathfrak{J}$ and set $a_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1+1 \otimes a^{\sigma_{u}}\right)$ an element of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. Let $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ be the subalgebra genrated by the $a_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then $a \rightarrow a_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ is a unital multiplication specialization in $S_{1}$ "(I). Hence we have the exact sequence

$$
\mathfrak{U}_{1} \underset{\xi_{1}}{S_{1}^{\prime \prime}}(\mathfrak{J}) \rightarrow 0
$$

where $\xi_{1}$ is the homomorphism such that $a_{1} \rightarrow a_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$. If we use the decompositions $\mathfrak{U}=\mathfrak{U}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{0}$ and $S(\mathfrak{J})=S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus \Phi z$ we see easily that $\xi_{1}$ is an isomorphism
if and only if the homomorphism $\xi$ of (55) is an isomorphism. In other words, an algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with identity element is strongly special if and only if $\xi_{1}$ is an isomorphism. If $\rho=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}\right)$ where the $\sigma_{i}$ are commuting unital associative specializations then we have a homomorphism of $S_{1}^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $a_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow a^{\rho}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. We shall call ( $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}), \rho^{\prime \prime}$ ) where $\rho^{\prime \prime}$ is the mapping $a \rightarrow a_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ the unital squared special universal envelope of $\mathfrak{J}$. We have called a bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ special if it is isomorphic to a sub-bimodule of a bimodule $\mathfrak{N}$ in which $v . a=\frac{1}{2} v\left(a^{\sigma_{1}}+a^{\sigma_{2}}\right)$ where the $\sigma_{i}$ are commuting associative specializations in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{N})$. We call $\mathfrak{M}$ unital special if the $\sigma_{i}$ are unital. We have seen that if every bimodule of a Jordan algebra is special then $\mathfrak{J}$ is strongly special (p. 101). The same argument shows that a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with identity element is strongly special if every unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ is unital special.

Let $e$ and $f$ be orthogonal idempotent elements of $\mathfrak{J}$. As before, we set $u(a)=2 a^{2}-a^{.2}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, which corresponds to the operator $U_{a}$. We have noted that $u\left(a U_{b}\right)=u(b) u(a) u(b)$ and $u\left(a^{\cdot k}\right)=u(a)^{k}$. Also we have $u(a+b)-u(a) -u(b)=2 u(a, b) \quad$ where $\quad u(a, b)=a b+b a-a . b=u(b, a) . \quad$ Now $e^{.2}=e$, $f^{.2}=f$ imply that $u(e)$ and $u(f)$ are idempotent elements of $\mathfrak{U}=U(\mathfrak{J})$. Also $e . f=0$ implies that $e$ and $f$ commute and since $u(e)=2 e^{2}-e$ and $u(f)=2 f^{2}-f$, it is clear that $u(e)$ and $u(f)$ commute. Since $\{e f e\}=f U_{e}=0$ we have $u(e) u(f) u(e)=0$. Hence, by the commutativity of $u(e)$ and $u(f)$ we have $u(e) u(f)=0=u(f) u(e)$. Now $g=e+f$ is an idempotent and $g . e=e=\{g e g\}$, $g . f=f=\{g f g\}$. Hence $u(g)$ is an idempotent which commutes with $u(e)$ and $u(f)$ and $u(g) u(e) u(g)=u(e), u(g) u(f) u(g)=u(f)$ which give $u(g) u(e)=u(e) =u(e) u(g), u(g) u(f)=u(f)=u(f) u(g)$. Now $u(g)=u(e)+u(f)+2 u(e, f)$ and $u(e, f)=e f+f e-e . f=2 e f$. Hence $u(e)=u(g) u(e)=u(e)+4 e f u(e)$. Hence $4 e f u(e)=0$. Similarly, $u(e)(4 e f)=0,4 e f u(f)=0=u(f)(4 e f)$. Then $u(g)^{2}=u(g)$ gives $(4 e f)^{2}=4 e f$ so the three elements $u(e), u(f), 4 e f$ are orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{U}$.

Suppose again that $\mathfrak{J}$ has identity element $c$ and consider $\mathfrak{U}_{1}=\mathfrak{U} C_{1}$. To avoid confusion with other indices we avoid using our earlier notation $x_{1}$ for the component $x C_{1}=C_{1} x$ in $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ of $x \in \mathfrak{U}$. Here, as above, $C_{1}=2 c^{2}-c$ is the identity of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$. Let $e_{1}, e_{2}, \cdots, e_{n}$ be orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $\sum e_{i}=c$. Since the elements $u\left(e_{i}\right), 4 e_{i} e_{j}, i<j$, are orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{U}$ it is clear that the $n(n+1) / 2$ elements $E_{i i}=u\left(e_{i}\right) C_{1}, E_{i j}=4 e_{i} e_{j} C_{1}=2 u\left(e_{i}, e_{j}\right) C_{1}, i \neq j$, are orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$. We note also that since $u(a, b)=a b+b a-a b$ is linear in $a$ and $b$ and $u(a+b)=u(a)+u(b)+2 u(a, b)$ we can prove by induction on $n$ that $u\left(\sum a_{i}\right)=\sum u\left(a_{i}\right)+2 \sum_{i<j} u\left(a_{i}, a_{j}\right)$. In particular, if $\sum e_{i}=c$ then $u(c)=\sum u\left(e_{i}\right)+2 \sum_{i<j} u\left(e_{i}, e_{j}\right)$. Also, since $c C_{1}=C_{1}, u(c) C_{1}=2\left(c C_{1}\right)^{2} -c C_{1}=C_{1}$ the identity of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$. Hence

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{1}=\sum_{i \leqq j} E_{i j} \tag{64}
\end{equation*}
$$

and the $E_{i j}$ are orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$.

We now suppose that $\mathfrak{J}$ with identity element $c$ is a direct sum of two ideals $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{2}$. Write $c=1_{1}+1_{2}, 1_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Then $1_{i}$ is the identity of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ and $1_{i} \cdot a_{j}=0$ if $a_{j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{j}$ and $i \neq j$. Hence $\left[1_{i}, a_{i}\right]=0$ and $\left[1_{i}, a_{j}\right]=0$ which implies that $1_{i}$ is in the center of $\mathfrak{U}$. It follows that the elements $u\left(1_{i}\right), i=1,2$, and $2 u\left(1_{1}, 1_{2}\right)$ are central idempotents of $\mathfrak{U}$ and $C_{11}=u\left(1_{1}\right) C_{1}, C_{22}=u\left(1_{2}\right) C_{1}, C_{12}= 2 u\left(1_{1}, 1_{2}\right) C_{1}=C_{21}$ are central idempotents of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$. Hence $\mathfrak{U}_{1}=\mathfrak{U}_{11} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{22} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{12}$ where $\mathfrak{U}_{i j}=\mathfrak{U}_{1} C_{i j}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$. We shall now prove

Theorem 16. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with identity element $c$ and suppose $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2}$ where the $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ are ideals. Let $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ be the unital universal multiplication envelope ${ }^{2}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ is a direct sum of three ideals isomorphic respectively to the unital universal multiplication envelopes of the $\mathfrak{J}_{i}, i=1,2$, and $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right) \otimes S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ where $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right)$ is the unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$.

Proof. We have $\mathfrak{U}_{1}=\mathfrak{U}_{11} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{22} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{12}$ as above. Let $a_{i j}=a C_{1} C_{i j}$ be the component in $\mathfrak{U}_{i j}$ of $a C_{1}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then $a \rightarrow a_{i j}$ is a unital multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$. We have $\left(1_{1}\right)_{11}=1_{1} C_{11}=1_{1}\left(2\left(1_{1}\right)^{2}-1_{1}\right) C_{1}=\left(2\left(1_{1}\right)^{2}-1_{1}\right) C_{1}=C_{11}$ since $1_{1}$ is an idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}$ so $2\left(1_{1}\right)^{3}-3\left(1_{1}\right)^{2}+1_{1}=0$ in $\mathfrak{U}$. It follows that the restriction of $a \rightarrow a_{11}$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ is a unital multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$. Hence we have the homomorphism of the unital universal envelope $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right)$ of $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ into $\mathfrak{U}_{11}$ such that $\left(a_{1}\right)_{1} \rightarrow\left(a_{1}\right)_{11}=a_{1} C_{1} C_{11}$ where $a_{1} \in \mathfrak{J}_{1}$ and $a_{1} \rightarrow\left(a_{1}\right)_{1}$ is the multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ in $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right)$. We note next that we have the unital multiplication specialization $a=a_{1}+a_{2} \rightarrow\left(a_{1}\right)_{1}$, hence the homomorphism $\eta$ of the unital universal envelope $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right)$ such that $a C_{1} \rightarrow\left(a_{1}\right)_{1}$. Clearly, $\left(1_{2} C_{1}\right)^{\eta}=0$ since the component of $1_{2}$ in $\mathfrak{I}_{1}$ is 0 . Hence $C_{22}{ }^{\eta}=\left(2\left(1_{2} C_{1}\right)^{2}-\left(1_{2} C_{1}\right)\right)^{\eta}=0$ and $C_{12}{ }^{\eta}=4\left(\left(1_{2} C_{1}\right)\left(1_{1} C_{1}\right)\right)^{\eta}=0$. Then $\mathfrak{U}_{22}{ }^{\eta}=0=\mathfrak{U}_{12}{ }^{\eta}$ and we have the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}_{11}$ into $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right)$ such that $\left(a_{1}\right)_{11} \rightarrow\left(a_{1}\right)_{1}$. It follows that $\left(a_{1}\right)_{1} \rightarrow\left(a_{1}\right)_{11}$ is an isomorphism of $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right)$ onto $\mathfrak{U}_{11}$. Similarly, $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ and $\mathfrak{U}_{22}$ are isomorphic. We now note that $\left(1_{1}\right)_{12}=1_{1} C_{1} C_{12}=1_{1} C_{1}\left(4\left(1_{1} 1_{2}\right) C_{1}\right)=4\left(1_{1} C_{1}\right)^{2}\left(1_{2} C_{1}\right)=4\left(1_{1} C_{1}\right)^{2}\left(C_{1}-1_{1} C_{1}\right) =4\left(1_{1} C_{1}\right)^{2}-4\left(1_{1} C_{1}\right)^{3}=4\left(1_{1} C_{1}\right)^{2}-6\left(1_{1} C_{1}\right)^{2}+2\left(1_{1} C_{1}\right)=-2\left(1_{1} C_{1}\right)^{2}+2\left(1_{1} C_{1}\right) =2\left(1_{1} C_{1}\right)\left(C_{1}-\left(1_{1} C_{1}\right)\right)=2\left(1_{1} C_{1}\right)\left(1_{2} C_{1}\right)=\frac{1}{2} C_{12}$. Similarly, $\left(1_{2}\right)_{12}=\frac{1}{2} C_{12}$. As we have seen before (p. 103), this implies that $a_{i} \rightarrow 2\left(a_{i}\right)_{12}$ is a unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ in $\mathfrak{U}_{12}$ so we have the homomorphism of $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{U}_{12}$ such that $a_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} \rightarrow 2\left(a_{i}\right)_{12}, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Since $\left[a_{1} \cdot 1_{1}, a_{2}\right]+\left[1_{1} \cdot a_{2}, a_{1}\right]+\left[a_{1} \cdot a_{2}, 1_{1}\right]=0$ in $\mathfrak{U}_{1},\left[a_{1}, a_{2}\right]=0$ and $\left[\left(a_{1}\right)_{12},\left(a_{2}\right)_{12}\right]=0$ in $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$. It follows that we have the homomorphism of $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right) \otimes S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{U}_{12}$ such that $a_{1}{ }^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes a_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{u}} \rightarrow 4\left(a_{1}\right)_{12}\left(a_{2}\right)_{12}$. We note next that we have the associative specializations $a_{1}+a_{2} \rightarrow a_{1}{ }^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1$, $a_{1}+a_{2} \rightarrow 1 \otimes a_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}$ which give rise to the unital multiplication specialization $a_{1}+a_{2} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\left(a_{1}{ }^{\sigma_{n}} \otimes 1+1 \otimes a_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}\right)$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right) \otimes S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$. From this we obtain

[^8]the homomorphism $\lambda$ of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ into $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right) \otimes S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ such that $\left(a_{1}+a_{2}\right) C_{1} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\left(a_{1}{ }^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1+1 \otimes a_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}\right)$. Now $C_{11}{ }^{\lambda}=\left(21_{1}{ }^{2}-1_{1}\right)^{\lambda} C_{1}{ }^{\lambda}=2\left(\frac{1}{4}\left(1_{1} \otimes 1\right)\right)-\frac{1}{2}\left(1_{1} \otimes 1\right)=0$ and similarly $C_{22}{ }^{\lambda}=0$. Hence we have the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}_{12}$ into $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right) \otimes S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ such that $a C_{1} C_{12} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\left(a_{1}{ }^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1+1 \otimes a_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}\right)$ for $a=a_{1}+a_{2}, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Then $\left(a_{1}\right)_{12} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\left(a_{1}{ }^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1\right)$ and $\left(a_{2}\right)_{12} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\left(1 \otimes a_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{u_{1}}}\right)$ so $\left(a_{1}\right)_{12}\left(a_{2}\right)_{12} \rightarrow \frac{1}{4}\left(a_{1}{ }^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes a_{2}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}\right)$ in this homomorphism. It follows that this is the inverse of the homomorphism we had before of $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{I}_{1}\right) \otimes S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{U}_{12}$. Hence these are isomorphic and the proof is complete.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with identity element $1, c$ an invertible element in $\mathfrak{J}, U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $a \rightarrow a_{1}$ a unital universal multiplication envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ and the mapping

$$
a \rightarrow a_{1}^{(c)}=\left[c_{1}, a_{1}\right]+(c \cdot a)_{1}
$$

constitute a unital universal multiplication envelope for the isotope $(\mathfrak{J}, c)$.
2. Let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a bimodule for a Jordan algebra with identity element and define $\mathfrak{M}_{i}$ for $i=0,1, \frac{1}{2}$ by $\mathfrak{M}_{i}=\left\{x_{i} \mid x_{i} . c=i x_{i}\right\}$. Prove that the $\mathfrak{M}_{i}$ are sub-bimodules, that $x_{0} \cdot a=0$ for every $x_{0} \in \mathfrak{M}_{0}, a \in \mathfrak{J}, x_{\frac{1}{2}} u(a)=0$ for every $x_{\frac{1}{2}} \in \mathfrak{M}_{\frac{1}{2}}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$.
3. Define unital multiplication specializations and unital universal envelopes for associative algebras with 1 in the obvious way. Show that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is an associative algebra with 1, $\mathfrak{A}^{0}$ the opposite algebra then $\mathfrak{A}^{e} \equiv \mathfrak{A}^{0} \otimes \mathfrak{A}$ and the mappings $a \rightarrow a^{\lambda}=a \otimes 1, a \rightarrow a^{\rho}=1 \otimes a$ constitute a unital universal multiplication envelope for $\mathfrak{A}$.
12. Some basic criteria. In this section we shall derive some useful conditions that a Jordan bimodule be special and that the homomorphisms $\xi, i$ of (55) and (56) be isomorphisms. We prove first

Theorem 17. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a special Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{M}$ a bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\mathfrak{M}$ is special if and only if the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ is a special Jordan algebra.

Proof. Suppose first that $\mathfrak{M}$ is special. Then we have an isomorphism $\mu$ of $\mathfrak{M}$ into a bimodule $\mathfrak{N}$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $v . a=\frac{1}{2}\left(v a^{\sigma_{1}}+v a^{\sigma_{2}}\right)$ where $\sigma_{1}$ and $\sigma_{2}$ are commuting associative specializations of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{N})$. We showed in the proof of Theorem 14 that $\mathfrak{N}$ is a unital associative bimodule for $S(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $v a^{\sigma_{u}}=v a^{\sigma_{1}}, a^{\sigma_{u}} v=v a^{\sigma_{2}}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Consider the mapping $a+u \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{u}}+u^{\mu}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, $u \in \mathfrak{M}$ of $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{F}=S(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus \mathfrak{N}$. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is special, $\sigma_{u}$ is 1-1. Hence $a+u \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{u}}+u^{\mu}$ is 1-1. A direct verification shows that this mapping is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{E}$ into $\mathfrak{F}^{+}$. Hence it is an isomorphism and $\mathfrak{E}$ is special. Conversely, assume $\mathfrak{E}$ is special. Then we have an isomorphism $\sigma$ of $\mathfrak{E}$ into $\mathfrak{G}^{+}$where $\mathfrak{G}$ is associative. If $L$ and $R$ denote the left and right multiplications in $\mathfrak{G}$ then we
have the associative specializations $a \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{1}}=\left(a^{\sigma}\right)_{L}, a \rightarrow a^{\sigma_{2}}=\left(a^{\sigma}\right)_{R}$ of $\mathfrak{I}$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{G})$. These commute and their average is $a \rightarrow R_{a} \sigma$ where $R_{c}=\frac{1}{2}\left(c_{L}+c_{R}\right)$ is the (right) multiplication in the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{G}^{+}$. Hence $\mathfrak{G}$ is a bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ so that $v . a \equiv v R_{a^{\sigma}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(v a^{\sigma_{1}}+v a^{\sigma_{2}}\right), v \in \mathfrak{G}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Now consider the restriction of $\sigma$ to $\mathfrak{M}$. If $u \in \mathfrak{M}, a \in \mathfrak{I}$, we have $(u . a)^{\sigma}=\frac{1}{2}\left(u^{\sigma} a^{\sigma}+a^{\sigma} u^{\sigma}\right) =\frac{1}{2}\left(u^{\sigma} a^{\sigma_{1}}+u^{\sigma} a^{\sigma_{2}}\right)=u^{\sigma} \cdot a$. Hence the restriction of $\sigma$ to $\mathfrak{M}$ is an isomorphism of this $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule into $\mathfrak{G}$ as $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule and so $\mathfrak{M}$ is special.
Theorem 17 is valid also for Jordan algebras with 1 and unital bimodules. In this case the statement is that a unital bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ is special if and only if the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ is a special Jordan algebra. The proof is the same as that of Theorem 17. We shall see in Chapter III (Corollary to the Coordinatization Theorem, p. 137) that there exist important Jordan algebras $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 such that every Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{K}$ with 1 containing $\mathfrak{J}$ as a subalgebra with the same identity element is special. For these we have the following

Corollary. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with 1 such that every Jordan algebra $\Re$ with 1 having $\mathfrak{J}$ as subalgebra with the same identity element is special. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is strongly special.

Proof. If $\mathfrak{M}$ is a unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ then the hypothesis implies that the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ is special. Hence $\mathfrak{M}$ is unital special by Theorem 17. Now we have seen that if every unital bimodule for an algebra is unital special then $\mathfrak{J}$ is strongly special. Thus the conclusion holds.

We shall derive next a condition that the fact that the canonical homomorphism $\xi$ of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ is an isomorphism carries over to a homomorphic image $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$. Thus suppose we have the exact sequence

$$
\begin{equation*}
\underset{\zeta}{\mathfrak{J}} \underset{\mathfrak{J}}{\overline{\mathfrak{J}}} \rightarrow 0 . \tag{65}
\end{equation*}
$$

Then we have the exact sequences

$$
\begin{equation*}
U(\mathfrak{J}) \underset{\zeta_{u}}{\rightarrow} U(\overline{\mathfrak{J}}) \rightarrow 0, \quad S(\mathfrak{J}) \underset{\zeta_{s}}{\rightarrow} S(\overline{\mathfrak{J}}) \rightarrow 0 . \tag{66}
\end{equation*}
$$

The homomorphism $\zeta_{s}$ gives rise to the homomorphism $\zeta_{s} \otimes \zeta_{s}$ of $S(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes S(\mathfrak{J})$ into $S(\overline{\mathfrak{J}}) \otimes S(\overline{\mathfrak{J}})$ and, by restriction, we obtain the homomorphism $\zeta^{\prime \prime}$ of $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$. Then

$$
\begin{equation*}
S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}) \underset{\zeta^{\prime \prime}}{\rightarrow} S^{\prime \prime}(\overline{\mathfrak{J}}) \rightarrow 0 \tag{67}
\end{equation*}
$$

is exact. Also we have the homomorphism $\xi$ of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ and a similar homomorphism $\bar{\xi}$ of $U(\overline{\mathfrak{J}})$ onto $S^{\prime \prime}(\overline{\mathfrak{J}})$. It follows directly from the definitions that
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-117.jpg?height=226&width=300&top_left_y=312&top_left_x=738)
is commutative. It is well known that the kernel $\operatorname{ker}\left(\zeta_{s} \otimes \zeta_{s}\right)=S(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes \operatorname{ker} \zeta_{s} +\operatorname{ker} \zeta_{s} \otimes S(\mathfrak{J})$. Hence

$$
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{ker} \zeta^{\prime \prime}=S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}) \cap\left(S(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes \operatorname{ker} \zeta_{s}+\operatorname{ker} \zeta_{s} \otimes S(\mathfrak{J})\right) \tag{69}
\end{equation*}
$$

Let $b \in \operatorname{ker} \zeta$. Since $\mathfrak{J} \subseteq U(\mathfrak{J})$ and the given multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ and of $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$ in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ are the injection mappings, we have $b^{\zeta_{u}}=0$. Hence, by (68), $b^{\prime \prime} \zeta^{\prime \prime}=b^{\xi \zeta^{\prime \prime}}=0$. Thus $b^{\prime \prime} \in \operatorname{ker} \zeta^{\prime \prime}$ and so the ideal $\mathfrak{R}^{\prime \prime}$ in $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by $(\operatorname{ker} \zeta)^{\prime \prime}=\left\{b^{\prime \prime} \mid b \in \operatorname{ker} \zeta\right\}$ satisfies

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{R}^{\prime \prime} \subseteq \operatorname{ker} \zeta^{\prime \prime} \tag{70}
\end{equation*}
$$

We can now prove
Theorem 18. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra, $\zeta$ a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$. Suppose the canonical homomorphism of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ is an isomorphism. Then the same thing is true of the canonical homomorphism $\bar{\xi}$ of $U(\overline{\mathfrak{J}})$ onto $S^{\prime \prime}(\overline{\mathfrak{J}})$ if and only if the ideal $\mathfrak{K}^{\prime \prime}$ in $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by $(\operatorname{ker} \zeta)^{\prime \prime}$ coincides with $\operatorname{ker} \zeta^{\prime \prime}$ where $\zeta^{\prime \prime}$ is the homomorphism of $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $S^{\prime \prime}(\overline{\mathfrak{J}})$ induced by $\zeta$.

Proof. Assume first that $\mathfrak{K}^{\prime \prime}=\operatorname{ker} \zeta^{\prime \prime}$ and let $\bar{v} \in \operatorname{ker} \bar{\xi}$. Let $v$ be an element of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $\bar{v}=v^{\zeta_{u}}$. Then $v^{\zeta_{u} \bar{\xi}}=0$ and the commutativity of (68) gives $v^{\xi \zeta^{\prime \prime}}=0$ so $v^{\xi} \in \operatorname{ker} \zeta^{\prime \prime}$. Hence $v^{\xi} \in \mathfrak{K}^{\prime \prime}$. Since $\xi$ is an isomorphism of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ it follows that $v$ is in the ideal in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by ker $\zeta$. By Theorem 11(4), we know that $\operatorname{ker} \zeta_{u}$ is the ideal in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by $\operatorname{ker} \zeta$. Hence $v \in \operatorname{ker} \zeta_{u}$ so $\bar{v}=v^{\zeta_{u}}=0$. This shows that $\bar{\xi}$ is an isomorphism. In the same way we see that if $\mathfrak{K}^{\prime \prime} \neq \operatorname{ker} \zeta^{\prime \prime}$ then $\mathfrak{K}^{\prime \prime} \subset \operatorname{ker} \zeta^{\prime \prime}$, by (70). Hence we can choose a $v^{\prime \prime} \in \operatorname{ker} \zeta^{\prime \prime}$, $\notin \mathfrak{R}^{\prime \prime}$. Then $v^{\prime \prime}=v^{\xi}$ for a $v \in U(\mathfrak{J})$. Since $v^{\xi} \notin \mathfrak{R}^{\prime \prime}$ and $\xi$ is an isomorphism, $v$ is not contained in the ideal in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by $\operatorname{ker} \zeta$. Hence $v \notin \operatorname{ker} \zeta_{u}$. Thus $v^{\zeta u} \neq 0$ while $v^{\zeta u \xi}=v^{\xi \zeta^{\prime \prime}}=v^{\prime \prime \zeta^{\prime \prime}}=0$. Hence $\bar{\xi}$ is not an isomorphism.

We remark that in view of (69) and (70) the condition $\mathfrak{K}^{\prime \prime}=\operatorname{ker} \zeta^{\prime \prime}$ of the theorem is equivalent to

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{K}^{\prime \prime} \supseteq S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}) \cap\left(S(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes \operatorname{ker} \zeta_{s}+\operatorname{ker} \zeta_{s} \otimes S(\mathfrak{J})\right) \tag{71}
\end{equation*}
$$

We remark also that Theorem 18 and its proof carry over word for word to the unital envelopes $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a Jordan algebra with identity element.

We obtain next two useful sufficient conditions for a Jordan algebra with 1 that $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ coincides with the subalgebra $\mathfrak{V}_{1}$ of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ of fixed points under the exchange automorphism.

Theorem 19. (1) Let J be a Jordan algebra with 1 which is reflexive and assume that $\mathfrak{S}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)=\left[\mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right), \mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)\right]$ where $\mathfrak{S}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$ and $\mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$ are the sets of skew and symmetric elements of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ relative to $\pi$. Then $S^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ coincides with the subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ of fixed elements under the exchange automorphism. (2) The same conclusion holds if $\mathfrak{J}$ has a 1 and is generated by 1 and two generators $x_{1}, x_{2} .^{3}$

Proof. (1) Since $x \otimes y+y \otimes x=(x \otimes 1+1 \otimes x)(y \otimes 1+1 \otimes y)-(x y \otimes 1 +1 \otimes x y)$ it is clear that $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ is generated by the elements $x \otimes 1+1 \otimes x, x \in S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. Hence it is enough to show that the elements $x \otimes 1+1 \otimes x, x \in S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$, are contained in $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is reflexive any $x \in \mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$ has the form $a^{\sigma_{u}}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then $x \otimes 1+1 \otimes x=a^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1+1 \otimes a^{\sigma_{u}}=a_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime} \in S_{1}^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$. Also since $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})= \mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)+\mathfrak{S}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$ it is enough to show that every $x \otimes 1+1 \otimes x$ with $x \in \mathfrak{S}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$ is contained in $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$. Now our second hypothesis is that if $x \in \mathfrak{S}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$ then $x$ is a sum of elements $[y z], y, z \in \mathfrak{H}\left(S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \pi\right)$. Since $[y \otimes 1+1 \otimes y, \quad z \otimes 1+1 \otimes z]=[y z] \otimes 1+1 \otimes[y z] \in S_{1}^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ the result is clear. (2) More generally, let $\mathfrak{J}$ be generated by $1, x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{r}$. Then we shall show that $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ is generated by $1=1 \otimes 1$ and the elements
(i) $\quad x_{i}^{\sigma_{u}^{\prime}} \otimes 1+1 \otimes x_{i}^{\sigma_{u}}$,
(ii) $x_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} \cdot x_{j}^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1+1 \otimes x_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} \cdot x_{j}^{\sigma_{u}}, \quad i \leqq j$,
(iii) $x_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} x_{j}^{\sigma_{u}} x_{k}^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1+1 \otimes x_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} x_{j}^{\sigma_{u}} x_{k}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}, \quad i<j<k$.

Since (i) and (ii) are contained in $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ and (iii) is nonexistent if $r=2$ this will imply that $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{B}_{1}$. Now $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is generated by $\mathfrak{J}^{\sigma_{u}}$ and $\mathfrak{J}$ is generated by 1 and the $x_{i}$. Since $\sigma_{u}$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})^{+}$it follows that $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is generated by 1 and the elements $x_{i}^{\sigma_{u}}$. Also we have seen in the proof of (1) that $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ is generated by the elements $x \otimes 1+1 \otimes x, x \in S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. Hence it suffices to show that if $p$ is a product (in the associative algebra $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ ) of $m$ elements $x_{i}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}$ then $p \otimes 1+1 \otimes p$ is in the subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}_{1}{ }^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ generated by the elements (i), (ii) and (iii). For $m=1$ this is clear. Also the result is clear for $m=2$ since $a b=a . b+\frac{1}{2}[a b]$ and $[a b] \otimes 1+1 \otimes[a b]=[a \otimes 1+1 \otimes a, b \otimes 1+1 \otimes b]$. Also this commutator relation for $a=x_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} x_{j}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}, b=x_{k}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}$ and the relation

$$
\begin{aligned}
(a b c+c b a) \otimes 1+1 \otimes(a b c+c b a)= & (a b \otimes 1+1 \otimes a b)(c \otimes 1+1 \otimes c) \\
& -(a \otimes c+c \otimes a)(b \otimes 1+1 \otimes b) \\
& +(c b \otimes 1+1 \otimes c b)(a \otimes 1+1 \otimes a)
\end{aligned}
$$

for $a=x_{i}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}, b=x_{j}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}, c=x_{k}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}$ imply that if $i^{\prime}, j^{\prime}, k^{\prime}$ is a permutation of $i, j, k$ then

[^9]$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} x_{j}^{\sigma_{u}} x_{k}^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1+1 \otimes x_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} x_{j}^{\sigma_{u}} x_{k}^{\sigma_{u}} \\
& \quad \equiv \pm x_{i^{\prime}}^{\sigma_{u}} x_{j^{\prime}}^{\sigma_{u}} x_{k^{\prime}}{ }^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1 \pm 1 \otimes x_{i^{\prime}}{ }^{\sigma_{u}} x_{j^{\prime}}{ }^{\sigma_{u}} x_{k^{\prime}}{ }^{\sigma_{u}}\left(\bmod \mathfrak{B}_{1}{ }^{\prime}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where the sign is + or - according as the permutation is even or odd. If two of the indices are equal this implies that $p \otimes 1+1 \otimes p \in \mathfrak{B}_{1}^{\prime}$ for $p=x_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} x_{j}^{\sigma_{u}} x_{k}^{\sigma_{u}}$. The same result holds for distinct indices since the elements (iii) are contained in $\mathfrak{B}_{1}{ }^{\prime}$. This proves the case $m=3$. For $m>3$ we obtain the result by induction using the relation

$$
\begin{aligned}
2(a b c d \otimes 1+1 \otimes a b c d)= & (a b \otimes 1+1 \otimes a b)(c d \otimes 1+1 \otimes c d) \\
& -(a \otimes c+c \otimes a)(b \otimes d+d \otimes b) \\
& +(a d \otimes 1+1 \otimes a d)(c b \otimes 1+1 \otimes c b) \\
& +[b \otimes 1+1 \otimes b, a d c \otimes 1+1 \otimes a d c] \\
& +(a b \otimes 1+1 \otimes a b)(c d \otimes 1+1 \otimes c d) \\
& -(a \otimes c d+c d \otimes a)(b \otimes 1+1 \otimes b) \\
& +(c d b \otimes 1+1 \otimes c d b)(a \otimes 1+1 \otimes a) \\
& -(c d \otimes 1+1 \otimes c d)(b a \otimes 1+1 \otimes b a) \\
& +(b a \otimes c+c \otimes b a)(d \otimes 1+1 \otimes d) \\
& -(b a d \otimes 1+1 \otimes b a d)(c \otimes 1+1 \otimes c) .
\end{aligned}
$$

## Exercises

1. (McCrimmon). Let $\mathfrak{H}$ and $\mathfrak{S}$ be the sets of symmetric and skew elements under the reversal operator in the free associative algebra with $1, \Phi\{x, y\}$. Show that $\mathfrak{S} \neq[\mathfrak{H}, \mathfrak{H}]$.
2. (Cohn). Let $F S J^{(2)}$ be the free special Jordan algebra with 1 and two generators $x, y$ and let $\mathfrak{J}=F S J^{(2)} / \Re$ where $\Re$ is the ideal generated by $x^{\cdot 2}-y^{\cdot 2}$ Also let $F S J^{(3)}$ be the free special Jordan algebra with 1 and generators $x, y, z, \mathcal{L}$ the ideal in $F S J^{(3)}$ generated by $x^{\cdot 2}-y^{\cdot 2}$ and all the symmetric elements of $\Phi\{x, y, z\}$ which are homogeneous of degree two in $z$. Show that $\mathfrak{E}=F S J^{(3)} / \mathfrak{L}$ is not special. Show that $\mathfrak{E}$ is a split null extension of $\mathfrak{J}$ by a bimodule which is not special.
3. (Cohn). Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with two generators which is strongly special (def. on p. 101). Show that any bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ is special. Use this to show that the $\mathfrak{J}$ given in exercise 2 is special but not strongly special.
4. Examples and applications. In this section we shall consider the universal multiplication envelopes for the Jordan algebras considered in §3. All of these have iden-
tity elements. Hence in view of the decomposition $\mathfrak{U}=\mathfrak{U}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and the fact that we have already determined the algebras $\mathfrak{U}_{\frac{1}{2}} \cong S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ it suffices to determine $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$.
(1) $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi[a]$ the Jordan algebra with 1 generated by 1 and the single element $a$. Suppose first that $a=x$ is transcendental. We have seen that $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi[x]$ and the identity mapping form a unital special universal envelope for J. The main involution $\pi$ is the identity mapping. We recall that $\Phi[x] \otimes \Phi[x]$ is isomorphic to $\Phi[x, y], x, y$ algebraically independent, under the isomorphism such that $x \otimes 1 \rightarrow x, 1 \otimes x \rightarrow y$. Hence we may consider $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}=S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ as the subalgebra of $\Phi[x, y]$ generated by the elements $\frac{1}{2}(f(x)+f(y)), f(x)$ a polynomial in $x$. The automorphism in $\Phi[x, y]$ corresponding to the exchange automorphism is the one which exchanges $x$ and $y$. Hence the set of fixed points is the subalgebra of symmetric polynomials. Since the main involution in $\Phi[x]$ is the identity mapping the set of skew elements $\mathfrak{S}=0$. Hence the condition $\mathfrak{S}=[\mathfrak{H}, \mathfrak{H}]$ of Theorem 19 (1) is fulfilled and consequently $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ " coincides with the subalgebra of symmetric polynomials. Next consider $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ the unital universal multiplication envelope. As in the considerations preceding (48), it is clear that $1, x_{1},\left(x^{\cdot 2}\right)_{1}$ ( $a_{1}$ the image of $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ ) commute and generate $\mathfrak{U}_{1}: \mathfrak{U}_{1}=\Phi\left[x_{1},\left(x^{2}\right)_{1}\right]$. The canonical homomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ onto $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ maps $x_{1} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}(x+y),\left(x^{\prime 2}\right)_{1} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)$. It is well known that the symmetric polynomials $x+y, x^{2}+y^{2}$ are algebraically independent. Hence the same is true of $x_{1}$ and $\left(x^{\cdot 2}\right)_{1}$, and the canonical homomorphism is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ onto $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$.
Next assume $a$ is algebraic and let $\mu(x) \in \Phi[x]$ be its minimum polynomial. We have the homomorphism $f(x) \rightarrow \overline{f(x)}=f(a)$ of $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi[x]$ into $\overline{\mathfrak{J}} \equiv \Phi[a]$ whose kernel is the principal ideal $(\mu(x))$. Let $\overline{\mathfrak{U}}_{1}=U_{1}(\overline{\mathfrak{J}}), \overline{\mathfrak{U}}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime} \equiv S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\overline{\mathfrak{J}})$. We know that $\Phi[a]$ and the identity mapping constitute a unital special universal envelope for $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\Phi[a]$. Also, as in the case of $\Phi[x]$, it is clear that $\overline{\mathfrak{U}}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ coincides with the subalgebra of $\Phi[a] \otimes \Phi[a]$ of fixed points under the exchange automorphism. Since $\operatorname{dim} \Phi[a]=n$, the degree of $\mu(x)$, it is clear that $\operatorname{dim} \overline{\mathfrak{U}}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}= n(n+1) / 2$. We now consider the kernel $\Re$ of the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}=\Phi\left[x+y, x^{2}+y^{2}\right]$ onto $\overline{\mathfrak{U}}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ corresponding to the homomorphism $f(x) \rightarrow \overline{f(x)}$. We note that $\Re=(\mu(x), \mu(y)) \cap \Phi\left[x+y, x^{2}+y^{2}\right] \quad$ where $(\mu(x), \mu(y))$ is the ideal in $\Phi[x, y]$ generated by $\mu(x)$ and $\mu(y)$. This is clear from (69) and the fact that $(\mu(x), \mu(y))$ is the ideal in $\Phi[x, y]$ corresponding to $(\mu(x)) \otimes \Phi[x]+\Phi[x] \otimes(\mu(x))$ in the isomorphism of $\Phi[x, y]$ with $\Phi[x] \otimes \Phi[x]$. It is clear that the symmetric polynomials

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mu_{0}=\mu(x)+\mu(y), \quad \mu_{1}=x \mu(x)+y \mu(y) \in \Re . \tag{72}
\end{equation*}
$$

We claim that these generate $\Re$. Thus let $g(x, y) \in \Re$. Then $g(x, y)=p(x, y) \mu(x)+q(x, y) \mu(y)$ where $p(x, y), q(x, y) \in \Phi[x, y]$. Then $g(x, y)=g(y, x)=\frac{1}{2}[g(x, y)+g(y, x)]$ gives $g(x, y)=r(x, y) \mu(x)+r(y, x) \mu(y)$ where $r(x, y)=\frac{1}{2}[p(x, y)+q(y, x)]$. Thus $g(x, y)$ is a linear combination of polynomials $x^{k} y^{l} \mu(x)+y^{k} x^{l} \mu(y), k, l=0,1,2, \cdots$. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
(x+y)\left[x^{k} \mu(x)+y^{k} \mu(y)\right]= & x^{k+1} \mu(x)+y^{k+1} \mu(y) \\
& +x y\left[x^{k-1} \mu(x)+y^{k-1} \mu(y)\right],
\end{aligned}
$$

which implies, by induction on $k$, that $x^{k} \mu(x)+y^{k} \mu(y)$ is in the ideal $\mathfrak{K}^{\prime}$ in $\Phi\left[x+y, x^{2}+y^{2}\right]$ generated by $\mu_{0}$ and $\mu_{1}$. Also

$$
y^{k} \mu(x)+x^{k} \mu(y)=\left(x^{k}+y^{k}\right) \mu_{0}-\left[x^{k} \mu(x)+y^{k} \mu(y)\right] \in \mathfrak{K}^{\prime} .
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{k} y^{l} \mu(x)+y^{k} x^{l} \mu(y) & =x^{l} y^{l}\left[x^{k-l} \mu(x)+y^{k-l} \mu(y)\right] \quad \text { if } \quad k \geqq l \\
& =x^{k} y^{k}\left[y^{l-k} \mu(x)+x^{l-k} \mu(y)\right] \quad \text { if } \quad k<l
\end{aligned}
$$

is in $\mathfrak{K}^{\prime}$. Hence $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{K}^{\prime}$ the ideal in $\Phi\left[x+y, x^{2}+y^{2}\right]$ generated by $\mu_{0}$ and $\mu_{1}$.
Now $\mu(x)$ and $x \mu(x)$ are in the kernel of the homomorphism of $\Phi[x]$ onto $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$. The image of these elements in $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}=S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\Phi[x])$ are $\mu(x)^{\prime \prime}=\frac{1}{2}[\mu(x)+\mu(y)] =\mu_{0},(x \mu(x))^{\prime \prime}=\frac{1}{2}[x \mu(x)+y \mu(y)]=\mu_{1}$. Since these elements generate $\mathfrak{K}$ we see that $\mathfrak{R} \subseteq \mathfrak{R}^{\prime \prime}$ the ideal generated by the elements $f(x)^{\prime \prime}, f(x) \in(\mu(x))$. Since the canonical homomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ onto $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ is an isomorphism it now follows from Theorem 18 that the same result holds for $\overline{\mathfrak{U}}_{1}$ and $\overline{\mathfrak{U}}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$. It follows that $\operatorname{dim} U_{1}(\Phi[a])=\operatorname{dim} \overline{\mathfrak{U}}_{1}^{\prime \prime}=n(n+1) / 2$.

We shall now apply the isomorphism of $U_{1}(\Phi[a])$ with $\overline{\mathfrak{U}}_{1}$ " to determine the minimum polynomials of the elements $a_{1}$ and $u(a)_{1}, u(a)=2 a^{2}-a^{\cdot 2}$, in $\mathrm{S}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\Phi[a])$. In view of this isomorphism these are the same as the minimum polynomials of the elements $\frac{1}{2}(a \otimes 1+1 \otimes a)$ and $2\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)(a \otimes 1+1 \otimes a)^{2}- \frac{1}{2}\left(a^{2} \otimes 1+1 \otimes a^{2}\right)=a \otimes a$ in $\Phi[a] \otimes \Phi[a]$. We require first the following

Lemma. Let $\Phi\left[z_{i}\right], i=1,2$, be an associative (and commutative) algebra generated by 1 and a nilpotent element $z_{i}$ of index $n_{i}\left(z_{i}^{n_{i}}=0, z_{i}^{n_{i}-1} \neq 0\right)$. Then the element $z_{1} \otimes 1+1 \otimes z_{2}$ in $\Phi\left[z_{1}\right] \otimes \Phi\left[z_{2}\right]$ is nilpotent of index $N=N\left(n_{1}, n_{2}\right)$ where $N\left(n_{1}, n_{2}\right)$ is either $n_{1}+n_{2}-1$ or the smallest positive integer $N<n_{1}+n_{2}-1$ such that all the binomial coefficients $\binom{N}{i}=0$ for $i<n_{1}$ and $N-i<n_{2}$, provided such integers $N$ exist. Also if $\rho_{1}, \rho_{2} \in \Phi$ then $z_{1} \otimes z_{2}+\rho_{1}\left(1 \otimes z_{2}\right)+\rho_{2}\left(z_{1} \otimes 1\right)$ is nilpotent of index $M=M\left(n_{1}, n_{2}, \rho_{1}, \rho_{2}\right)$ where $M\left(n_{1}, n_{2}, 0,0\right)=\min \left(n_{1}, n_{2}\right), \quad M\left(n_{1}, n_{2}, 0, \rho_{2}\right)=n_{1} \quad$ if $\quad \rho_{2} \neq 0$, $M\left(n_{1}, n_{2}, \rho_{1}, 0\right)=n_{2}$ if $\rho_{1} \neq 0$ and $M\left(n_{1}, n_{2}, \rho_{1}, \rho_{2}\right)$ for $\rho_{1} \neq 0, \rho_{2} \neq 0$ is either $n_{1}+n_{2}-1$ or is the smallest positive integer $M<n_{1}+n_{2}-1$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
Q\left(k, l, \rho_{1}, \rho_{2}\right)=\sum_{\substack{k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}=M \\ k_{1}+k_{3}=k \\ k_{1}+k_{2}=l}} \frac{M!}{k_{1}!k_{2}!k_{3}!} \rho_{1}^{k_{2}} \rho_{2}^{k_{3}} \tag{73}
\end{equation*}
$$

is 0 for all $k<n_{1}$ and $l<n_{2}$, provided such integers exist.

Proof. We recall that the elements $z_{1}{ }^{i} \otimes z_{2}{ }^{j}, 0 \leqq i<n_{1}, 0 \leqq j<n_{2}$ form a basis for $\Phi\left[z_{1}\right] \otimes \Phi\left[z_{2}\right]$. We have $\left(z_{1} \otimes 1+1 \otimes z_{2}\right)^{N}=\Sigma\binom{N}{i} z_{1}{ }^{i} \otimes z_{2}{ }^{N-i}=0$ if $N=n_{1}+n_{2}-1$, since in this case either $z_{1}{ }^{i}=0$ or $z_{2}{ }^{N-i}=0$. If $N<n_{1}+n_{2}-1$ then $\Sigma\binom{N}{i}{z_{1}}^{i} \otimes z_{2}{ }^{N-i}=0$ if and only if $\binom{N}{i}=0$ for all $i<n_{1}$, and $N-i<n_{2}$, by the linear independence of the elements $z_{1}^{i} \otimes z_{2}^{j}, 0 \leqq i<n_{1}, 0 \leqq j<n_{2}$. This proves the first statement. To establish the second we note first that $\left(z_{1} \otimes z_{2}\right)^{M} =z_{1}{ }^{M} \otimes z_{2}{ }^{M}=0$ if and only if $M \geqq \min \left(n_{1}, n_{2}\right)$. Hence $M\left(n_{1}, n_{2}, 0,0\right)=\min \left(n_{1}, n_{2}\right)$. Next let $\rho_{1}=0, \rho_{2} \neq 0$. Then $z_{1} \otimes z_{2}+\rho_{1}\left(1 \otimes z_{2}\right)+\rho_{2}\left(z_{1} \otimes 1\right)=z_{1} \otimes\left(z_{2}+\rho_{2} 1\right)$. Since $\rho_{2} \neq 0$ and $z_{2}$ is nilpotent $z_{2}+\rho_{2} 1$ is invertible in $\Phi\left[z_{2}\right]$. Hence $\left(z_{1} \otimes\left(z_{2}+\rho_{2} 1\right)\right)^{M}=z_{1}{ }^{M} \otimes\left(z_{2}+\rho_{2} 1\right)^{M}=0$ if and only if $z_{1}{ }^{M}=0$. Hence the minimum $M$ for this is $M=n_{1}$. This proves the second statement for $\rho_{1}=0, \rho_{2} \neq 0$. By symmetry, we have the case $\rho_{1} \neq 0, \rho_{2}=0$. Now assumes $\rho_{1} \neq 0, \rho_{2} \neq 0$ and consider

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(z_{1} \otimes z_{2}+\rho_{1}\left(1 \otimes z_{2}\right)+\rho_{2}\left(z_{1} \otimes 1\right)\right)^{M} \\
& \quad=\sum_{k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}=M} \frac{M!}{k_{1}!k_{2}!k_{3}!} \rho_{1}^{k_{2}} \rho_{2}^{k_{3}}\left(z_{1}^{k_{1}+k_{3}} \otimes z_{2}^{k_{1}+k_{2}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

This is 0 if $M \geqq n_{1}+n_{2}-1$ since in this case $2 k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}=M+k_{1} \geqq n_{1}+n_{2}-1$ and so either $k_{1}+k_{3} \geqq n_{1}$ or $k_{1}+k_{2} \geqq n_{2}$. On the other hand, if $M<n_{1}+n_{2}-1$ then the foregoing formula and the linear independence of the $z_{1}{ }^{i} \otimes z_{2}{ }^{j}, 0<i<n_{1} 0 \leqq j<n_{2}$, imply that $\left(z_{1} \otimes z_{2}+\rho_{1}\left(1 \otimes z_{2}\right)+\rho_{2}\left(z_{1} \otimes 1\right)\right)^{M}=0$ if and only if $Q\left(k, l, \rho_{1}, \rho_{2}\right)=0$ for all $k<n_{1}, l<n_{2}$. This completes the proof.

Theorem 20. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi[a]$, where $a$ is algebraic with minimum polynomial $\mu(x)$ which factors as

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mu(x)=\prod_{1}^{r}\left(x-\rho_{i}\right)^{n_{i}}, \quad \rho_{i} \neq \rho_{j} \quad \text { if } \quad i \neq j \tag{74}
\end{equation*}
$$

in a splitting field $\mathrm{P} / \Phi$. Then the polynomials

$$
\begin{align*}
& v(x)=\text { L.C.M. }\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\left(\rho_{i}+\rho_{j}\right)\right)^{N\left(n_{i}, n_{j}\right)}  \tag{75}\\
& \pi(x)=\text { L.C.M. }\left(x-\rho_{i} \rho_{j}\right)^{M\left(n_{i}, n_{j}, \rho_{i}, \rho_{j}\right)} \tag{76}
\end{align*}
$$

where $N\left(n_{i}, n_{j}\right)$ and $M\left(n_{i}, n_{j}, \rho_{i}, \rho_{j}\right)$ are as defined in the lemma, have coefficients in $\Phi$ and these are respectively the minimum polynomials of $a_{1}$ and $u(a)_{1}$ in $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) .^{4}$

Proof. We have seen that the minimum polynomials of $a_{1}$ and $u(a)_{1}$ coincide with the minimum polynomials respectively of $\frac{1}{2}(a \otimes 1+1 \otimes a)$ and $a \otimes a$ in $\Phi[a] \otimes \Phi[a]$. Since these are unchanged on extension of the base field we may

[^10]consider these elements in $\mathrm{P}[a] \otimes \mathrm{P}[a]$ where $\mathrm{P}[a]=\mathrm{P} \otimes \Phi[a]$ and $\mathrm{P} / \Phi$ is a splitting field in which we have the factorization (74). Then, by elementary algebra, $\mathrm{P}[a]=\mathrm{P}\left[z_{1}\right] \oplus \mathrm{P}\left[z_{2}\right] \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathrm{P}\left[z_{r}\right]$ where $\mathrm{P}\left[z_{i}\right]$ is an ideal with identity element $1_{i}$ which is generated by $1_{i}$ and a nilpotent $z_{i}$ of index $n_{i}$. Moreover, we have $a=a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{r}$ where $a_{i}=\rho_{i} 1_{i}+z_{i}$. Then $\mathrm{P}[a] \otimes \mathrm{P}[a] =\Sigma \oplus \mathrm{P}\left[z_{i}\right] \otimes \mathrm{P}\left[z_{j}\right]$ and the minimum polynomials of $\frac{1}{2}(a \otimes 1+1 \otimes a)$ and $a \otimes a$ are respectively the least common multiples of those of the components of these elements in the ideals $\mathrm{P}\left[z_{i}\right] \otimes \mathrm{P}\left[z_{j}\right]$. These components are $\frac{1}{2}\left(\rho_{i}+\rho_{j}\right)\left(1_{i} \otimes 1_{j}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left(z_{i} \otimes 1_{j}+1_{i} \otimes z_{j}\right)$ and $\rho_{i} \rho_{j}\left(1_{i} \otimes 1_{j}\right)+\rho_{i}\left(1_{i} \otimes z_{j}\right)+ \rho_{j}\left(z_{i} \otimes 1_{j}\right)+\left(z_{i} \otimes z_{j}\right)$. Since the minimum polynomial of an element of the form $\rho 1+z$ where $z$ is nilpotent is $(x-\rho)^{k}$ where $k$ is the index of nilpotency of $z$, it is clear from the lemma that the minimum polynomials of $\frac{1}{2}\left(\rho_{i}+\rho_{j}\right)\left(1_{i} \otimes 1_{j}\right) +\frac{1}{2}\left(z_{i} \otimes 1_{j}+1_{i} \otimes z_{j}\right)$ and $\rho_{i} \rho_{j}\left(1_{i} \otimes 1_{j}\right)+\rho_{i}\left(1_{i} \otimes z_{j}\right)+\rho_{j}\left(z_{i} \otimes 1_{j}\right)+\left(z_{i} \otimes z_{j}\right)$ are respectively $\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\left(\rho_{i}+\rho_{j}\right)\right)^{N\left(n_{i}, n_{j}\right)}$ and $\left(x-\rho_{i} \rho_{j}\right)^{M\left(n_{i}, n_{j}, \rho_{i}, \rho_{j}\right)}$. Hence the minimum polynomials of $\frac{1}{2}(a \otimes 1+1 \otimes a)$ and $a \otimes a$ are $\nu(x)$ and $\pi(x)$ and these have coefficients in $\Phi$.
(2) $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi\left[a, a^{-^{1}}\right]$ where $\mathfrak{J}$ is a Jordan algebra with 1 generated by 1 and an invertible element $a$ and its inverse $a^{-1}$. If $a$ is algebraic we know that $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi[a]$ so the preceding considerations apply. Hence we assume $a=x$ is transcendental. We have seen in §3 that J and the identity mapping form a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi\left[x, x^{-1}\right]$. The main involution is the identity mapping so the only skew element is 0 . We can identify $\Phi\left[x, x^{-1}\right] \otimes \Phi\left[x, x^{-1}\right]$ in the obvious way with $\Phi\left[x, x^{-1}, y, y^{-1}\right]$ the subalgebra generated by $x, y, x^{-1}, y^{-1}$ in the field of rational expressions in the algebraically independent elements $x, y$. By Theorem 19 (1), we may identify $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}=S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{I})$ with the subalgebra of $\Phi\left[x, y, x^{-1}, y^{-1}\right]$ of elements which are symmetric in $x$ and $y$. We have $\left(x^{\cdot k}\right)^{\prime \prime}=\frac{1}{2}\left(x^{k}+y^{k}\right), k=0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \cdots$ and these elements generate $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ since the $x^{\cdot k}$ form a basis for $\Phi\left[x, x^{-1}\right]$.

We now consider the unital universal multiplication envelope $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ of $\Phi\left[x, x^{-1}\right]$. We recall that if $a$ and $b$ are inverses in a Jordan algebra with 1 then $R_{a}, R_{b}, U_{a}$ and $U_{b}$ commute and we have the relations $U_{b}=U_{a}^{-1}, R_{b}=R_{a} U_{b} =R_{a} U_{a}{ }^{-1}$ (§1.11). We knowalso that $R_{a}, U_{a}, U_{a}{ }^{-1}$ generate the algebra of linear transformations generated by all $R_{a \cdot k}, k=0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \cdots$. As we have seen (§9), these results carry over to $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$. They imply that $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ is a commutative algebra generated by $x_{1}, u\left(x_{1}\right)$ and $u\left(x_{1}\right)^{-1}$. The images of these elements under the canonical homomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ onto $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ are respectively $\frac{1}{2}(x+y), x y$ and $(x y)^{-1}$. Since $x+y$ and $x y$ are algebraically independent it follows that the canonical homomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ onto $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ is an isomorphism and that $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}=\Phi\left[x+y, x y,(x y)^{-1}\right]$.

The commutativity of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ and of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ for any $\Phi\left[a, a^{-1}\right]$ imply the commutativity of the universal multiplication envelope $\mathfrak{U}$ of any Jordan algebra generated by an invertible element and its inverse.
(3) $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{B}$ the Jordan algebra of a symmetric bilinear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{B}$. We saw in §3 that the Clifford algebra $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. We shall now give a similar construction for the unital universal multiplication envelope $\mathfrak{U}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. For this we give the following

Definition 5. Let $\mathfrak{B} / \Phi$ be a vector space, $f$ a symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak{B}$. Let $T(\mathfrak{B})$ be the tensor algebra based on $\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{L}$ the ideal in $T(\mathfrak{B})$ generated by the elements $x \otimes y \otimes x-f(x, y) x, x, y \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)=T(\mathfrak{B}) / \mathfrak{L}$ is called the meson algebra of $f .{ }^{5}$

Let $\rho$ be a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{B} / \Phi$ into an associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 such that $x^{\rho} y^{\rho} x^{\rho}=f(x, y) x^{\rho}, x, y \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then there is a unique extension of $\rho$ to a homomorphism $\rho$ of $T(\mathfrak{B})$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $1^{\rho}=1$. In this homomorphism $(x \otimes y \otimes x-f(x, y) x)^{\rho}=x^{\rho} y^{\rho} x^{\rho}-f(x, y) x^{\rho}=0$. Hence we have an induced homomorphism of $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $\overline{\alpha 1+x} \equiv \alpha 1+x+\mathfrak{L} \rightarrow \alpha 1+x^{\rho}$, $\alpha \in \Phi, x \in \mathfrak{B}$. We note next that if $a=\alpha 1+x$ and $b=\beta 1+y, \alpha, \beta \in \Phi, x, y \in \mathfrak{V}$, then $a^{\cdot 2}=\left(\alpha^{2}+f(x, x)\right) 1+2 \alpha x, a . b=(\alpha \beta+f(x, y)) 1+\alpha y+\beta x, a^{\cdot 2} . b= \left(\alpha^{2} \beta+\beta f(x, x)+2 \alpha f(x, y)\right) 1+\alpha^{2} y+f(x, x) y+2 \alpha \beta x$. Also $\bar{x} \bar{y} \bar{x}=f(x, y) \bar{x}$ implies that

$$
\tilde{a} \bar{b} \bar{a}=\alpha^{2} \beta 1+2 \alpha \beta \bar{x}+\beta \bar{x}^{2}+\alpha(\bar{x} \bar{y}+\bar{y} \bar{x})+f(x, y) \bar{x}
$$

A direct verification now shows that

$$
2 \bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{a}+\overline{a^{\cdot 2} \cdot} \bar{b}=2 \bar{a} \overline{(a \cdot b)}+\tilde{b}\left(\overline{a^{\cdot 2}}\right)
$$

Since $\left[\bar{a}, \overline{a^{\cdot 2}}\right]=[\alpha 1+\bar{x},(\alpha+f(x, x)) 1+2 \alpha \bar{x}]=0$, it is clear that $a \rightarrow \bar{a}$ is a unital multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Now if $\rho$ is any unital multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ then $2 x^{\rho} y^{\rho} x^{\rho}+\left(x^{.2} \cdot y\right)^{\rho}=2 x^{\rho}(x . y)^{\rho}+y^{\rho}\left(x^{.2}\right)^{\rho}$ gives $x^{\rho} y^{\rho} x^{\rho}=f(x, y) x^{\rho}$ for $x, y \in \mathfrak{B}$. Hence the result noted before shows that we have a unique homomorphism of $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $\overline{\alpha 1+x} \rightarrow(\alpha 1+x)^{\rho}$. Hence $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ and the mapping $a \rightarrow \bar{a}$ constitute a unital universal multiplication envelope for $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{B}$.

If we take $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ and $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ for our choices of unital special universal envelope and unital universal multiplication envelope, then $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}=S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ becomes the subalgebra of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \otimes C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ generated by 1 and the elements $(x+\mathfrak{K}) \otimes 1+1 \otimes(x+\mathfrak{K}), x \in \mathfrak{B}$. The canonical homomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ onto $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ becomes the homomorphism of the meson algebra $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \otimes C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ mapping $x+\mathfrak{L} \rightarrow\left\{\frac{1}{2}(x+\mathfrak{K}) \otimes 1+1 \otimes(x+\mathfrak{K})\right\}$. We shall see later (§7.2)-after we give a self-contained development of the theory of Clifford algebras - that this homomorphism is an isomorphism.
(4) $\mathfrak{J}=F J^{(2)}$ the free Jordan algebra with 1 and two generators $x, y$. Let $\Phi\{u, v\}$ be free associative with 1 and generators $u, v$. Then we saw in §3 that

[^11]$\Phi\{u, v\}$ and the homomorphism $\sigma_{1 u}$ of $F J^{(2)}$ into $\Phi\{u, v\}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, x \rightarrow u$, $y \rightarrow v$ is a unital special universal envelope for $F J^{(2)}$. The main involution in $\Phi\{u, v\}$ is the reversal operator.

Let $F J^{(3)}$ be the free Jordan algebra with 1 and three generators $x, y, z$, E the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(F J^{(3)}, F J^{(3)}\right)$ generated by the $R_{b}, b \in F J^{(2)}\left(\subseteq F J^{(3)}\right.$, cf. §1.9). We claim that $(\mathfrak{E}, R)$ where $R$ is the mapping $b \rightarrow R_{b}, b \in F J^{(2)}$, $R_{b}$ acting in $F J^{(3)}$, is a unital universal multiplication envelope for $F J^{(2)}$. It is enough to show that if $\rho$ is a unital multiplication specialization of $F J^{(2)}$ in an associative algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ then there exists a unique homomorphism of $\mathfrak{E}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that $R_{b} \rightarrow b^{\rho}$. Also it is enough to prove existence of the homomorphism since uniqueness will then follow from the fact that the $\boldsymbol{R}_{\boldsymbol{b}}$ generate $\mathfrak{E}$. Now if we form the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ by the bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$, then it follows from Lemma 1 of §6 that we have a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{E}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{E}^{\prime}, \mathfrak{E}^{\prime}\right)$ such that $R_{b} \rightarrow R_{b}{ }^{\prime}$ where $R_{b}{ }^{\prime}$ is the multiplication in $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime}$ determined by $b \in F J^{(2)}$. By restriction we obtain the required homomorphism such that $R_{b} \rightarrow b^{\rho}$.

Let $F S J^{(3)}$ be the free special Jordan algebra with generators $u, v, w, \mathfrak{E}_{s}$ the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(F S J^{(3)}, F S J^{(3)}\right)$ generated by the elements $R_{c}, c$ in $F S J^{(2)}$ (generated by $u, v)$. By the operator form of Macdonald's Theorem we have the isomorphism of $\mathfrak{E}$ onto $\mathfrak{E}_{s}$ such that $R_{b} \rightarrow R_{b^{\sigma_{1 u}}}$. Since $F S J^{(3)}$ is special we have the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}=S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}\left(F J^{(2)}\right)$ onto $\mathfrak{E}_{s}$ such that $b_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow R_{b^{\sigma_{1 u}}}$. Hence we have the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ onto $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $b_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow R_{b}$. It follows that the canonical homomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ onto $\mathfrak{U}_{1}$ " is an isomorphism. Also by Theorem 19 (2), $\mathfrak{U}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ coincides with the subalgebra of $S\left(F J^{(2)}\right) \otimes S\left(F J^{(2)}\right)= \Phi\{u, v\} \otimes \Phi\{u, v\}$ of fixed elements under the exchange automorphism.

## Exercises

1. Show that the polynomial $v(x)$ of Theorem 20 is L.C.M. $\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\left(\rho_{i}+\rho_{j}\right)\right)^{n_{i}+n_{j}-1}$ if the field is of characteristic 0 . Show that if $\mu(x)$ has distinct roots then the same is true of $v(x)$ and $\pi(x)$ (any characteristic). Show that if $a$ is nilpotent of index $n$ then $a_{1}{ }^{2 n-1}=0$ and $u(a)_{1}{ }^{n}=0$. Show also that if $a$ is unipotent $(=1+a$ nilpotent) then $a_{1}$ and $u(a)_{1}$ are unipotent.
2. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi[a]$ with $\mu(x)$ as minimum polynomial as in Theorem 20. Determine the minimum polynomial of $\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)_{1}-\left(a_{1}\right)^{2}$ in $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. Show that if $a$ is unipotent then $\left(a^{.2}\right)_{1}-\left(a_{1}\right)^{2}$ is nilpotent.
3. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with basis $\left(e_{1}, e_{2}, \cdots, e_{n}\right)$ where the $e_{i}$ are nonzero orthogonal idempotents such that $\Sigma e_{i}=1$ the identity element of $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that $\operatorname{dim} U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=n(n+1) / 2$ and determine $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$.

## Chapter III

## PEIRCE DECOMPOSITIONS AND JORDAN MATRIX ALGEBRAS

In this chapter we shall develop some of the main tools for the structure theory of Jordan algebras. These concern the Peirce decomposition of a Jordan algebra relative to a finite set of orthogonal idempotent elements and the study of Jordan matrix algebras. If $e$ is an idempotent element in a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ then the multiplication $R_{e}$ determined by $e$ satisfies the equation $R_{e}\left(2 R_{e}-1\right)\left(R_{e}-1\right)=0$. Hence we can decompose $\mathfrak{J}$ as $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ where $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ is the space of the characteristic root $i$ of $R_{e}$. This decomposition is analogous to the two-sided Peirce decomposition of an associative algebra relative to an idempotent in the algebra. More generally, if $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element $1=\sum_{1}^{n} e_{i}$ where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents $\left(e_{i}^{{ }^{2}}=e_{i}, e_{i} \cdot e_{j}=0\right.$ if $\left.i \neq j\right)$ then we have the Peirce decomposition $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{i \leqq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ where

$$
\mathfrak{J}_{i i}=\left\{x_{i \imath} \mid x_{i i} \cdot e_{i}=x_{i \imath}\right\} \text { and } \mathfrak{J}_{i j}=\left\{x_{i j} \left\lvert\, x_{i j} \cdot e_{i}=\frac{1}{2} x_{i j}=x_{i j} \cdot e_{j}\right.\right\}
$$

if $i \neq j$. This is analogous to the two-sided Peirce decomposition of an associative algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ as $\mathfrak{A}=\sum \mathfrak{A}_{i j}, \mathfrak{A}_{i j}=e_{i} \mathfrak{A} e_{j}$, relative to the finite set of orthogonal idempotents $e_{i}$ with $\Sigma e_{i}=1$. There are a number of important multiplicative properties of the Peirce spaces $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. These are sorted out in Lemma 2 and 3 of §1.

If $\mathfrak{D}$ is an algebra with 1 and an involution $j(d \rightarrow \bar{d})$ then the algebra $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ of $n \times n$ matrices with entries in $\mathfrak{D}$ has the involution $X \rightarrow \bar{X}^{t}$ which is called the standard involution (associated with $j$ ) (cf §1.5). More generally, if $a$ is a diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}\right\}$ whose diagonal entries $a_{i}$ are $j$-symmetric elements of the nucleus of $\mathfrak{D}$ which have inverses in this nucleus, then we can define the involution $J_{a}: X \rightarrow a^{-1} \bar{X}^{t} a$ in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$. We call involutions of this type canonical involutions in the matrix algebra $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$. The set $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ of matrices $A \in \mathfrak{D}_{n}$ such that $A^{J_{a}}=A$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{D}_{n}^{+}$which is the vector space $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ considered as an algebra relative to the multiplication $A \cdot B=\frac{1}{2}(A B+B A)$. The algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ which are Jordan will be called Jordan matrix algebras. These play a role analogous to that of the matrix algebras $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ in the associative theory.

One of the main results of this chapter is a characterization of Jordan matrix algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ of order $n \geqq 3$ in terms of existence of certain types of idempotents. The result giving this is called the Coordinatization Theorem for Jordan algebras, since it is somewhat reminiscent of the introduction of coordinates in
projective geometry. This result will play an important role in the structure theory which will be developed in Chapters IV and V.

We shall establish in this chapter also some basic results on representation theory of Jordan matrix algebras. We shall show that if $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative and $n \geqq 3$ then the associative algebra $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ with canonical involution $J_{a}$ is perfect in the sense of §2.4. We shall show also that the study of unital bimodules for a Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n} . J_{a}\right)$ with $n \geqq 3$ can be reduced to that of certain types of bimodules with involution for the coefficient algebra $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. The Coordinatization Theorem and the determination of the ideals and certain subalgebras of the algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ will be needed to carry out this reduction.

1. Peirce decompositions. Let $e$ be an idempotent element of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$. Then we have seen in §2.11 that $e$ satisfies $e(e-1)(2 e-1)=0$ in the universal multiplication envelope $U(\mathfrak{J})$ and that the elements

$$
\begin{equation*}
E_{0}=(e-1)(2 e-1), \quad E_{1}=e(2 e-1), \quad E_{\frac{1}{2}}=-4 e(e-1) \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

are orthogonal idempotents in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $E_{0}+E_{1}+E_{\frac{1}{2}}=1$. It is clear also from the equation satisfied by $e$ that

$$
\begin{equation*}
E_{0} e=0, \quad E_{1}(e-1)=0, \quad E_{\frac{1}{2}}\left(e-\frac{1}{2} 1\right)=0 . \tag{2}
\end{equation*}
$$

If we use the canonical homomorphism of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ (sending $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a \rightarrow R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$ ) then we see that the elements

$$
\begin{equation*}
P_{0}=\left(R_{e}-1\right)\left(2 R_{e}-1\right), \quad P_{1}=R_{e}\left(2 R_{e}-1\right), \quad P_{\frac{1}{2}}=-4 R_{e}\left(R_{e}-1\right) \tag{3}
\end{equation*}
$$

are orthogonal idempotents in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ such that $P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{\frac{1}{2}}=1$ and $P_{0} R_{e}=0, P_{1}\left(R_{e}-1\right)=0, P_{\frac{1}{2}}\left(R_{e}-\frac{1}{2} 1\right)=0$. Since the $P_{i}$ are orthogonal projections in $\mathfrak{J}$ with sum 1 we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e) \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{1}(e) \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e), \quad \mathfrak{J}_{i}(e)=\mathfrak{J}_{i} . \tag{4}
\end{equation*}
$$

We shall call the decomposition (4) of $\mathfrak{J}$ (as a direct sum of the subspaces $\mathfrak{J}_{i}(e)$ ) the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the idempotent e. If $x_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i}=\mathfrak{J}_{i}(e)$, so that $x_{i}=x P_{i}, x \in \mathfrak{J}$, then $x_{i} . e=x_{i} R_{e}=x P_{i} R_{e}=x P_{i}\left(R_{e}-i 1+i 1\right)= x P_{i}\left(R_{e}-i 1\right)+i x P_{i}=i x P_{i}=i x_{i}$. It follows from the decomposition (4) that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{J}_{i}(e)=\left\{x_{i} \mid x_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}, \quad x_{i} \cdot e=i x_{i}\right\} . \tag{5}
\end{equation*}
$$

We note also that $P_{1}=2 R_{e}^{2}-R_{e}=U_{e}$ so

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)=\mathfrak{J} U_{e} . \tag{6}
\end{equation*}
$$

We shall now derive the main properties of the Peirce components $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$. The proofs will be based on the basic identities

$$
\begin{align*}
& (a \cdot b) \cdot(c \cdot d)+(a \cdot d) \cdot(b \cdot c)+(a \cdot c) \cdot(b \cdot d) \\
& =a \cdot(c \cdot d) \cdot b+a \cdot(b \cdot c) \cdot d+a \cdot(b \cdot d) \cdot c, \tag{1}
\end{align*}
$$

$$
a \cdot(b \cdot c) \cdot d+a \cdot(b \cdot d) \cdot c+a \cdot(c \cdot d) \cdot b
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
=a \cdot b \cdot c \cdot d+a \cdot d \cdot c \cdot b+a \cdot(b \cdot d \cdot c), \tag{2}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
a . b . c . d+a . d . c . b+a .(b . d . c)
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
=(a \cdot b) \cdot(c \cdot d)+(a \cdot c) \cdot(b \cdot d)+(a \cdot d) \cdot(b \cdot c) \tag{3}
\end{equation*}
$$

(see §1.7).
Lemma 1. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ be the Peirce decomposition of the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the idempotent e. Then: (i) $\mathfrak{J}_{0}{ }^{.2} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{0}, \mathfrak{J}_{1}{ }^{.2} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{1}, \mathfrak{J}_{0} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{1}=0$, (ii) $\mathfrak{I}_{\frac{1}{2}}{ }^{\cdot 2} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{0}+\mathfrak{J}_{1}, \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot\left(\mathfrak{J}_{0}+\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right) \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$, (iii) $x_{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot\left(a_{i} \cdot b_{i}\right)=x_{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot a_{i} \cdot b_{i}+x_{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot b_{i} \cdot a_{i}$ if $x_{\frac{1}{2}} \in \mathfrak{I}_{\frac{1}{2}}, a_{i}, b_{i} \in \mathfrak{I}_{i}, i=0$, 1. Also $\left[R_{a_{0}}, R_{a_{1}}\right]=0$ if $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i}$.

Proof. Let $a \in \mathfrak{J}_{i}, c \in \mathfrak{J}_{j}$ so $a . e=i a, c . e=j c, i, j=0,1, \frac{1}{2}$. Put $b=d=e$ in $\left(\mathrm{B}_{3}\right)$ to obtain 2a.e.c.e + a. $(c . e)=2 a . e .(c . e)+a . c . e$. This gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
(1-2 i)(a . c) R_{e}=j(1-2 i) a . c . \tag{7}
\end{equation*}
$$

If $i=j=0$ we obtain $(a . c) R_{e}=0$ and if $i=j=1$ we have $(a . c) R_{e}=a . c$. Hence the first two relations in (i) hold. Also $i=0, j=1$ and $i=1, j=0$ in (7) give $(a . c) R_{e}=a . c$ and $(a . c) R_{e}=0$. Hence $a . c=0$ and the last relation in (i) holds. Similarly, $i=0,1$ and $j=\frac{1}{2}$ in (7) give the second relation in (ii). Next, put $c=d=e$ in $\left(\mathrm{B}_{3}\right)$ to obtain a.b.e.e + a.e.e. $b+ a .(b . e . e)=a . b . e+2 a . e .(b . e)$. Then if $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ we obtain $a . b\left(R_{e}{ }^{2}-R_{e}\right)=0$. Writing $a . b=c_{0}+c_{1}+c_{\frac{1}{2}}$ where $c_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i}$ we obtain $0=(a . b)\left(\boldsymbol{R}_{e}{ }^{2}-\boldsymbol{R}_{e}\right) =c_{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}\right)$. Hence $c_{\frac{1}{2}}=0$ and $a . b \in \mathfrak{J}_{0}+\mathfrak{J}_{1}$. Hence the first assertion in (ii) holds. Next take $a=x_{\frac{1}{2}} \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}, b=e, c, d \in \mathfrak{J}_{1}$ in ( $\mathrm{B}_{3}$ ). This gives $x_{\frac{1}{2}}$. (c.d) $=x_{\frac{1}{2}} . c . d+x_{\frac{1}{2}} . d . c$. Similarly, the same relation with $c, d \in \mathfrak{J}_{0}$ gives $x_{\frac{1}{2}} .(c . d)$, $=x_{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot c \cdot d+x_{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot d . c$. This proves the first assertion in (iii). Now let $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i}, i=0,1$ and consider the basic operator identity $\left[R_{a} R_{b . c}\right]+\left[R_{b} R_{a . c}\right]+\left[R_{c} R_{a . b}\right]=0$ for $a=e, b=a_{0}, c=a_{1}$. This gives $\left[R_{a_{0}} R_{a_{1}}\right]=0$ and completes the proof.

We suppose next that $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element 1 and

$$
\begin{equation*}
1=e_{1}+e_{2}+\cdots+e_{n} \tag{8}
\end{equation*}
$$

where

$$
\begin{equation*}
e_{i}^{\cdot 2}=e_{i}, \quad e_{i} \cdot e_{j}=0, \quad i \neq j . \tag{9}
\end{equation*}
$$

Then, as in §2.11, the $n(n+1) / 2$ elements $E_{i i}=u\left(e_{i}\right) C_{1}, E_{i j}=E_{j i}=4 e_{i} e_{j} C_{1} =2 u\left(e_{i}, e_{j}\right) C_{1}, i \neq j$, of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$, where $C_{1}$ is the identity element of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$, are orthogonal idempotent elements and $\Sigma_{i \leqq j} E_{i j}=C_{1}$. The corresponding elements in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ are $P_{i i}=U_{e_{i}}, P_{i j}=4 R_{e_{i}} R_{e_{j}}=2 U_{e_{i}, e_{j}}$ which satisfy

$$
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{i \leqq j} P_{i j}=1, \quad P_{i j}^{2}=P_{i j}, \quad P_{i j} P_{k l}=0 \tag{10}
\end{equation*}
$$

if $\{i, j\} \neq\{k, l\}$. Hence we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{J}=\sum_{i \leqq j} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{i j}, \quad \mathfrak{J}_{i j}=\mathfrak{J} P_{i j} \tag{11}
\end{equation*}
$$

We shall call (11) the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the idempotents $e_{i}$ (orthogonal and with sum 1).

If $e$ is any idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}$ then $e_{1}=e, e_{2}=1-e$ are orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{J}$ with sum 1. Then $P_{11}=U_{e_{1}}=P_{1}$ determined by $e$ as in (3). Hence $\mathfrak{J}_{11}=\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$. Similarly, we have $P_{22}=U_{e_{2}}=2 R_{1-e}{ }^{2}-R_{1-e}=2\left(1-R_{e}\right)^{2}-1+R_{e}= \left(R_{e}-1\right)\left(2 R_{e}-1\right)=P_{0}$ and $P_{12}=2 U_{e_{1}, e_{2}}=4 R_{e_{1}} R_{e_{2}}=4 R_{e}\left(1-R_{e}\right)=P_{\frac{1}{2}}$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}_{22}=\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{12}=\mathfrak{J}_{21}=\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$. By symmetry we have also $\mathfrak{J}_{12}=\mathfrak{J}_{21} =\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\left(e_{2}\right)$.

Again let $1=e_{1}+e_{2}+\cdots+e_{n}$ where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents. Put $e_{i}^{\prime}=1-e_{i}=\Sigma_{j \neq i} e_{j}$. Then

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathfrak{J}_{1}\left(e_{i}\right) & =\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{i}}=\mathfrak{J}_{i i} \\
\mathfrak{J}_{0}\left(e_{i}\right) & =\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{i}^{\prime}}=\sum_{J \neq i} \mathfrak{J} U_{e_{j}}+\sum_{\substack{k \neq l \\
k, l \neq i}} \mathfrak{J}\left(2 U_{e_{k}, e_{l}}\right)  \tag{12}\\
& =\sum_{j, k \neq i} \mathfrak{J}_{j k} \\
\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\left(e_{i}\right) & =\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{i}, e_{i}^{\prime}}=\sum_{j \neq i} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}
\end{align*}
$$

It is clear from these formulas that

$$
\begin{align*}
& \mathfrak{J}_{i i}=\mathfrak{J}_{1}\left(e_{i}\right)=\left\{x_{i i} \mid x_{i i} \cdot e_{i}=x_{i i}\right\} \\
& \mathfrak{J}_{i j}=\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\left(e_{i}\right) \cap \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\left(e_{j}\right)=\left\{x_{i j} \left\lvert\, x_{i j} \cdot e_{i}=\frac{1}{2} x_{i j}=x_{i j} \cdot e_{j}\right.\right\} \text { if } i \neq j \tag{13}
\end{align*}
$$

Let $m \leqq n$ and set $e=\sum_{j=1}^{m} e_{j}$. Then $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)=\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ with $e$ as identity element. Also $e . e_{j}=e_{j}$ if $1 \leqq j \leqq m$ so $e_{j} \in \mathfrak{I}_{1}(e)$ and $e=\Sigma_{1}^{m} e_{j}$ is a decomposition of the identity $e$ of $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ as a sum of orthogonal idempotents in this subalgebra. We have $U_{e}=U_{\Sigma e_{j}}=\Sigma_{j=1}^{m} U_{e_{j}}+\Sigma_{j<k=1}^{m} 2 U_{e_{j}, e_{k}}$ and the operators $U_{e_{j}}, 2 U_{e_{j}, e_{k}}$ are orthogonal idempotents with sum $U_{e}$. Hence $U_{e} U_{e_{j}}=U_{e_{j}}$ and $U_{e}\left(2 U_{e_{j}, e_{k}}\right)=2 U_{e_{j}, e_{k}}$. Hence the Peirce component $\mathfrak{J} U_{e} U_{e_{j}} =\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{j}}$ and $\mathfrak{J} U_{e} U_{e_{j}, e_{k}}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{j}, e_{k}}$. Thus $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)=\sum_{j \leqq k=1}^{m} \mathfrak{J}_{j k}$ is the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ relative to the orthogonal idempotents $e_{1}, e_{2}, \cdots, e_{m}$.

We can now prove
Lemma 2. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with $1=\Sigma_{1}^{n} e_{i}$ where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents and let $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}, i=1, \cdots, n\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i j}=\mathfrak{J}_{j i}\right)$ be the Peirce components of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the $e_{i}$. Then:
(i) $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}{ }^{2} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{i i}, \mathfrak{J}_{i j} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{i i} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{i j}, \mathfrak{J}_{i j}{ }^{2} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{i i}+\mathfrak{J}_{j j}, \mathfrak{J}_{i i} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{j j}=0$ if $i \neq j$, (ii) $\mathfrak{J}_{i j} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{j k} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{i k}, \mathfrak{J}_{i j} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{k k}=0, \mathfrak{J}_{i j} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{k l}=0$ if $i, j, k, l$ are $\neq$.

Proof. Let $i \neq j$ and put $e=e_{i}+e_{j}, \mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{J} U_{c}$. Then $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{J}_{i i}+\mathfrak{J}_{j j}+\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ is the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{B}$ relative to $e_{i}, e_{j}$. We have $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}=\mathfrak{B}_{1}\left(e_{i}\right), \mathfrak{J}_{j j}=\mathfrak{B}_{0}\left(e_{i}\right) =\mathfrak{J}_{i j}=\mathfrak{B}_{\frac{1}{2}}\left(e_{i}\right)$. Hence (i) follows from (i) and (ii) of Lemma 1. Next let $i, j, k$ be $\neq$ and put $f=e_{i}+e_{j}+e_{k}, \mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{J} U_{f}$. Then $\mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{J}_{i i}+\mathfrak{J}_{j j}+\mathfrak{J}_{k k}+\mathfrak{J}_{i j}+\mathfrak{J}_{i k} +\mathfrak{J}_{j k}$ is the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{C}$ relative to $e_{i}, e_{j}, e_{k}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{p q}=\mathfrak{C}_{p q}\right)$. Also let $e=e_{i}+e_{j}$. Then $e$ is an idempotent contained in $\mathfrak{C}$ and $\mathfrak{C}_{1}(e)=\mathfrak{J}_{i i}+\mathfrak{J}_{i j}+\mathfrak{J}_{j j}$, $\mathfrak{C}_{0}(e)=\mathfrak{J}_{k k}$ and $\mathfrak{C}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)=\mathfrak{J}_{i k}+\mathfrak{J}_{j k}$. Since $\mathfrak{C}_{0}(e) \cdot \mathfrak{C}_{1}(e)=0$ we have $\mathfrak{J}_{i j} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{k k}=0$. Since $\mathfrak{C}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e) \cdot \mathfrak{C}_{1}(e) \subseteq \mathfrak{C}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$ we have $\mathfrak{J}_{i j} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{j k} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{i k}+\mathfrak{J}_{j k}$ and since $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}=\mathfrak{J}_{j i}$, $\mathfrak{J}_{j k}=\mathfrak{J}_{k j}$ we have also $\mathfrak{J}_{i j} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{j k}=\mathfrak{J}_{k j} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{j i} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{k i}+\mathfrak{J}_{j i}$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}_{i j} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{j k} \subseteq\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i k}+\mathfrak{J}_{j k}\right) \cap\left(\mathfrak{J}_{k i}+\mathfrak{J}_{j i}\right)=\mathfrak{J}_{i k}$. It remains to prove the last statement in (ii). For this we take $g=e_{i}+e_{j}+e_{k}+e_{l}$ and $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{J} U_{g}$. Then $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{J}_{i i}+\mathfrak{J}_{j j}+\mathfrak{J}_{k k}+\mathfrak{J}_{l l}+\mathfrak{J}_{i j}+\mathfrak{J}_{i k} +\mathfrak{J}_{i l}+\mathfrak{J}_{j k}+\mathfrak{J}_{j l}+\mathfrak{J}_{k l}$. Also $e=e_{i}+e_{j}$ is an idempotent contained in $\mathfrak{D}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{i j} \subseteq \mathfrak{D}_{1}(e)$ while $\mathfrak{J}_{k l} \subseteq \mathfrak{D}_{0}(e)$. Hence $\mathfrak{D}_{0}(e) \cdot \mathfrak{D}_{1}(e)=0$ gives $\mathfrak{J}_{i j} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{k l}=0$.

We shall list next some important formulas for products of elements in the Peirce components.

Lemma 3. Let $\mathfrak{J}, 1$ and the $e_{i}$ be as in Lemma 2, let $x_{i i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i i}, x_{i j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ etc. and assume $i, j, k, l$ are $\neq$. Then

$$
\begin{equation*}
x_{i j}^{\cdot 2} \cdot e_{i} \cdot x_{i j}=x_{i j}^{\cdot 2} \cdot e_{j} \cdot x_{i j} \tag{PD1}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
2 x_{i j} \cdot y_{i j} \cdot e_{i} \cdot x_{i j}+x_{i j}^{2} \cdot e_{i} \cdot y_{i j}=2 x_{i j} \cdot y_{i j} \cdot e_{j} \cdot x_{i j}+x_{i j}^{2} \cdot e_{j} \cdot y_{i j} \tag{$\prime$}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[x_{i i}, y_{i j}, z_{j j}\right]=0 \tag{PD2}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
x_{i i} \cdot y_{i i} \cdot z_{i j}=x_{i i} \cdot z_{i j} \cdot y_{i i}+y_{i i} \cdot z_{i j} \cdot x_{i i} \tag{PD3}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[x_{i j}, y_{i j}, z_{j j}\right]=\left(e_{j}-e_{i}\right) \cdot\left(x_{i j} \cdot z_{j j} \cdot y_{i j}\right) \tag{PD4}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
x_{i j} \cdot y_{i j} \cdot z_{j j}=x_{i j} \cdot z_{j j} \cdot y_{i j} \cdot e_{j}+y_{i j} \cdot z_{j j} \cdot x_{i j} \cdot e_{j}, \tag{PD5}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[x_{i j}, y_{j j}, z_{i j}\right] \cdot e_{i}=0 \tag{PD6}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[x_{\imath i}, y_{i j}, z_{j k}\right]=0 \tag{PD7}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[x_{i j}, y_{j j}, z_{j k}\right]=0 \tag{PD8}
\end{equation*}
$$

(PD9)

$$
\left[x_{i j}, y_{j k}, z_{k k}\right]=0
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
x_{i j} \cdot y_{i j} \cdot z_{j k}=x_{i j} \cdot z_{j k} \cdot y_{i j}+y_{i j} \cdot z_{j k} \cdot x_{i j} \tag{PD10}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[x_{i j}, y_{j k}, z_{k i}\right]=\left(e_{k}-e_{j}\right) \cdot\left(x_{i j} \cdot z_{k i} \cdot y_{j k}\right) \tag{PD11}
\end{equation*}
$$

(PD12)

$$
\left[x_{i j}, y_{j k}, z_{k i}\right] \cdot e_{i}=0
$$

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[x_{i j}, y_{j k}, z_{k l}\right]=0 \tag{PD13}
\end{equation*}
$$

Remark. The first six of these formulas involve just two (distinct) indices and so refer to two idempotents. Formulas (PD7)-(PD12) refer to three idempotents and (PD13) refers to four idempotents.

Proof. To obtain (PD1) we begin with the basic Jordan identity $x_{i j}{ }^{.2} \cdot e_{i} \cdot x_{i j}=x_{i j}{ }^{.2} \cdot\left(e_{i} \cdot x_{i j}\right)=\frac{1}{2} x_{i j}{ }^{.2} \cdot x_{i j}$. Also we have $x_{i j}{ }^{.2}=x_{i i}+x_{j j}$ where $x_{i i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i i}$ and $x_{j j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{j j}$. Then $x_{i j}{ }^{{ }^{2}} \cdot e_{i}=x_{i i}, x_{i j}{ }^{{ }^{2}} \cdot e_{j}=x_{j j}$ and the foregoing relation becomes $x_{i i} \cdot x_{i j}=\frac{1}{2} x_{i i} \cdot x_{i i}+\frac{1}{2} x_{j j} \cdot x_{i j}$. Hence $x_{i i} \cdot x_{i j}=x_{j j} \cdot x_{i j}$ and so $x_{i j} \cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{i} \cdot x_{i j} =x_{i j}{ }^{.2} \cdot e_{j} \cdot x_{i j}$ which is (PD1). (PD1') is obtained by linearization of (PD1). Precisely, let $f\left(x_{1}, x_{2}\right)=\left(x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}\right) x_{1}$ in the free nonassociative algebra $\Phi\{\{X\}\}^{\prime}$ (§1.6). Then $f D_{1}=\left(\left(x_{1} y+y x_{1}\right) x_{2}\right) x_{1}+\left(x_{1}{ }^{2} x_{2}\right) y$ is a linearization of $f$ and, by (PD1), $f\left(x_{i j}, e_{i}-e_{j}\right)=0$ for all $x_{i j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. Since the degree of $f$ in $x_{1}$ is three and $\Phi$ contains three distinct elements it follows as on p. 23 that $f D_{1}\left(x_{i j}, e_{i}-e_{j}, y_{i j}\right)=0$ for all $x_{i j}, y_{i j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. This is equivalent to (PD1'). (PD2) and (PD3) are obtained by applying Lemma 1 (iii) to the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{J}_{i i}+\mathfrak{J}_{j j}+\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ with identity $e_{i}+e_{j}$, idempotent $e_{i}$ and $\mathfrak{B}_{1}\left(e_{i}\right)=\mathfrak{J}_{i i}, \mathfrak{B}_{0}\left(e_{i}\right)=\mathfrak{J}_{j j}, \mathfrak{B}_{\frac{1}{2}}\left(e_{i}\right)=\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. The same considerations can be applied to obtain some of the other formulas. However, we shall derive (PD4)-(PD13) directly using the basic identities ( $\mathbf{B}_{1}$ )-( $\mathbf{B}_{3}$ ) and Lemma 2. We indicate the steps required. For (PD4) we put $a=z_{j j}, b=x_{i j}$, $c=y_{i j}, d=e_{j}$ in ( $\mathrm{B}_{3}$ ). For (PD5) multiply (PD4) by $e_{j}$. For (PD6) multiply (PD4) by $e_{i}$ and interchange $y$ and $z$. For (PD7) put $a=x_{i i}, b=y_{i j}, c=z_{j k}, d=e_{i}$ in ( $\mathrm{B}_{3}$ ). For (PD8) take $a=y_{j j}, b=x_{i j}, c=z_{j k}, d=e_{i}$ in ( $\mathrm{B}_{3}$ ). For (PD9) take $a=x_{i j}, b=y_{j k}, c=z_{k k}, d=e_{k}$ in ( $\mathrm{B}_{3}$ ). For (PD10) put $a=x_{i j}, b=y_{i j}, c=z_{j k}$, $d=e_{i}$ in ( $\mathrm{B}_{2}$ ). For (PD11) put $a=x_{i j}, b=z_{k i}, c=y_{j k}, d=e_{k}$ in ( $\mathrm{B}_{3}$ ). To obtain (PD12) multiply (PD11) by $e_{i}$. For (PD13) take $a=x_{i j}, b=y_{j k}, c=z_{k l}, d=e_{i}$ in ( $\mathbf{B}_{\mathbf{3}}$ ).

Let $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ be nonzero orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{J}$ (with 1 ) and put $v=e_{1} +e_{2}$. Then $e_{1}$ and $e_{2} \in \mathfrak{J} U_{v}$ which is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ with identity element $v$, and $\mathfrak{J} U_{v}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}} \oplus \mathfrak{J} U_{e_{2}} \oplus \mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{2}}$ is the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J} U_{v}$ with respect to $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$.
