We shall now call $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ connected orthogonal idempotents if there exists an element $u_{12}$ in $\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{2}}$ which is invertible in $\mathfrak{J} U_{v}$. We shall call the orthogonal idempotents $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ strongly connected if there exists an element $u_{12} \in \mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{2}}$ such that $u_{12}{ }^{.2}=e_{1}+e_{2}$. Evidently this implies connectedness of $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$. Clearly the relations of connectedness and strong connectedness are symmetric. We shall now prove transitivity of these relations in the following

Lemma 4. Let $e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}$ be nonzero orthogonal idempotent elements such that $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ are connected (strongly connected) and $e_{2}$ and $e_{3}$ are connected (strongly connected). Then $e_{1}$ and $e_{3}$ are connected (strongly connected).

Proof. We prove first the statement on connectedness. By hypothesis there exists an element $u_{12} \in \mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{2}}$ which is invertible in $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}}+\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{2}}+\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{2}}$. We prove first that the inverse $u_{21}$ of $u_{12}$ in $\mathfrak{B}$ is contained in $\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{2}}$. We put $\mathfrak{B}_{11}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}}, \mathfrak{B}_{22}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{2}}, \mathfrak{B}_{12}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{2}}$, so $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{B}_{11} \oplus \mathfrak{B}_{22} \oplus \mathfrak{B}_{12}$ is the Peirce decomposition of the algebra $\mathfrak{B}$ with identity element $v$ relative to the orthogonal idempotents $e_{1}, e_{2}$. Now it follows directly from Lemma 2 and
(PD5) that if $x_{12} \in \mathfrak{B}_{12}$ then $\mathfrak{B}_{12} U_{x_{12}} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}_{12}, \mathfrak{B}_{11} U_{x_{12}} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}_{22}$ and $\mathfrak{B}_{22} U_{x_{12}} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}_{11}$. Hence, if $x_{12}$ is invertible in $\mathfrak{B}$ then $\mathfrak{B}_{12} U_{x_{12}}=\mathfrak{B}_{12}$ and $\mathfrak{B}_{12} U_{x_{12}}{ }^{-1}=\mathfrak{B}_{12}$. In particular, $u_{21}=u_{12} U_{u_{12}}{ }^{-1} \in \mathfrak{B}_{12}$. Similarly, the connectedness of $e_{2}$ and $e_{3}$ implies that we have elements $u_{23}, u_{32}$ in $\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{2}, e_{3}}$ which are inverses in $\mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{2}}+\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{3}}+\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{2}, e_{3}}$. Now put $u_{13}=2 u_{12} . u_{23}, u_{31} =2 u_{32} . u_{21}$. Then $u_{13}$ and $u_{31} \in \mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{3}}$ by Lemma 2 applied to $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{J} U_{w}$, $w=e_{1}+e_{2}+e_{3}$. We shall show that $u_{13}$ and $u_{31}$ are inverses in $\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}}+\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{3}} +\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{3}}$ which will prove the connectedness of $e_{1}$ and $e_{3}$. We recall that the universal multiplication envelope of a Jordan algebra with 1 generated by an invertible element and its inverse is commutative (p. 102). It follows that if $a$ and $b$ are inverses in a subalgebra of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ then $R_{a}$ and $R_{b}$ commute in $\mathfrak{J}$. Applying this to $u_{23}$ and $u_{32}$ we obtain $u_{23} \cdot u_{31}=2 u_{23} \cdot\left(u_{32} \cdot u_{21}\right)=u_{23} \cdot\left(u_{32} \cdot u_{21}\right) +u_{32} \cdot\left(u_{23} \cdot u_{21}\right)=\left(u_{23} \cdot u_{32}\right) \cdot u_{21}$ (PD10) $=\left(e_{2}+e_{3}\right) \cdot u_{21}=\frac{1}{2} u_{21}$. Then

$$
\begin{align*}
\left(u_{13} \cdot u_{31}\right) \cdot e_{1} & =2\left(\left(u_{12} \cdot u_{23}\right) \cdot u_{31}\right) \cdot e_{1}=2\left(u_{12} \cdot\left(u_{23} \cdot u_{31}\right)\right) \cdot e_{1}  \tag{PD12}\\
& =\left(u_{12} \cdot u_{21}\right) \cdot e_{1}=e_{1} .
\end{align*}
$$

By symmetry, $\left(u_{13} \cdot u_{31}\right) \cdot e_{3}=e_{3}$. Hence $u_{13} \cdot u_{31}=e_{1}+e_{3}$. Next we have $u_{21} \cdot u_{13}=\frac{1}{2} u_{23}$ by the same argument used to prove $u_{23} \cdot u_{31}=\frac{1}{2} u_{21}$. Then $\left(u_{13} \cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{1}\right) \cdot u_{31}=2\left(u_{13} \cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{1}\right) \cdot\left(u_{32} \cdot u_{21}\right)=2\left(\left(u_{13} \cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{1}\right) \cdot u_{21}\right) \cdot u_{32}$ (PD9) $=2\left(u_{13} \cdot u_{21} \cdot u_{21}\right) \cdot u_{32}=4\left(u_{13} \cdot\left(u_{13} \cdot u_{21}\right)\right) \cdot u_{32}$ (PD10) $=2\left(u_{13} \cdot u_{23}\right) \cdot u_{32} =\left(u_{13} \cdot u_{23}\right) \cdot u_{32}+\left(u_{13} \cdot u_{32}\right) \cdot u_{23}=u_{13} \cdot\left(u_{23} \cdot u_{32}\right)=u_{13} \cdot\left(e_{2}+e_{3}\right)=\frac{1}{2} u_{13}$ where in the last part we have used the commutativity of $R_{u_{3,3}}$ and $R_{u_{32}}$ and (PD10). Similarly, we obtain $\left(u_{13}{ }^{\cdot 2} \cdot e_{3}\right) \cdot u_{31}=\frac{1}{2} u_{13}$. Hence $u_{13}{ }^{\cdot 2} \cdot u_{31}=u_{13}$. Since we had $u_{13} . u_{31}=e_{1}+e_{3}$ it follows that $u_{13}$ and $u_{31}$ are inverses in $\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}}+\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{3}}+\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{3}}$ as required. Now assume $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ and $e_{2} i_{i} e_{3}$, are strongly connected. Then we have elements $u_{12} \in \mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{2}}$ and $u_{23} \in \mathfrak{J} U_{e_{2}, e_{3}}$ such that $u_{12}{ }^{\cdot 2}=e_{1}+e_{2}, u_{23}{ }^{\cdot 2} =e_{2}+e_{3}$. Hence in the foregoing discussion we can take $u_{21}=u_{12}, u_{32}=u_{23}$. Then the argument shows that the inverse of $u_{13}=2 u_{12} \cdot u_{23}$ in $\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}}+\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{3}} +\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{3}}$ is $u_{31}=2 u_{32} . u_{21}$. Hence $u_{13}{ }^{\cdot 2}=e_{1}+e_{3}$ and $e_{1}$ and $e_{3}$ are strongly connected.

We shall need the following result on connected idempotents later.
Lemma 5. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with $1=\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_{i}$ where the $e_{i}$ are nonzero connected orthogonal idempotents and let $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{i \leqslant j} \mathfrak{S}_{i j}$ be the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the $e_{i}$. Let $u_{1 j}, u_{j 1}, j>1$, be elements of $\mathfrak{I}_{1 j}$ which are inverses in $\mathfrak{I}_{11}+\mathfrak{I}_{j j}+\mathfrak{I}_{1 j}$ and put

$$
\begin{align*}
f_{1} & =e_{1}=g_{1}, \quad f_{j}=u_{j 1} \cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{j}, \quad g_{j}=u_{1 j}^{\cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{j}, \quad j>1} \\
f & =\sum_{1}^{n} f_{i}, \quad g=\sum_{1}^{n} g_{i} . \tag{14}
\end{align*}
$$

Then $f$ and $g$ are inverses and the elements $f_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents in the
isotope $(\mathfrak{J}, g)$ and $\Sigma f_{i}=f$ the identity of $(\mathfrak{J}, g)$. Moreover, $u_{j 1}$ is in the Peirce space $(\mathfrak{J}, g)_{1 j}$ relative to the $f_{i}$ and $u_{j 1 \cdot g} u_{j 1}=f_{1}+f_{j}$.

Remark. In a less precise form the hypothesis is that the $e_{i}$ are connected idempotents with sum 1 in $\mathfrak{J}$ and the conclusion is that the $f_{i}$ are strongly connected idempotents with sum the identity element in the isotope $(\mathfrak{J}, g)$ of $\mathfrak{J}$.

Proof. Clearly $u_{1 j}{ }^{2}$ and $u_{j 1}{ }^{2}$ are inverses in $\mathfrak{J}_{11}+\mathfrak{J}_{j j}+\mathfrak{J}_{1 j}$. Since these elements are contained in $\mathfrak{J}_{11}+\mathfrak{J}_{j j}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{11} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{j j}=0$ it follows that $f_{j}=u_{j 1} \cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{j}$ and $g_{j}=u_{1 j}{ }^{2} \cdot e_{j}$ are inverses in $\mathfrak{J}_{j j}, j>1$. This implies that $f=\Sigma f_{i}$ and $g=\Sigma g_{i}$ are inverses in $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence we can form the isotope $(\mathfrak{J}, g)$ whose identity element is $f$. We have

$$
\begin{align*}
& \left\{f_{i} g f_{i}\right\}=\left\{f_{i}\left(\Sigma g_{k}\right) f_{i}\right\}=\left\{f_{i} g_{i} f_{i}\right\}=f_{i} \\
& \left\{f_{i} g f_{j}\right\}=\left\{f_{i} g_{i} f_{j}\right\}+\left\{f_{i} g_{j} f_{j}\right\}=0, \quad i \neq j \tag{15}
\end{align*}
$$

Hence the $f_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents in $(\mathfrak{J}, g)$ and their sum is the identity element $f$. We have for $j>1$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\{u_{j 1} g f_{1}\right\}= & \left\{u_{j 1} e_{1} e_{1}\right\}+\left\{u_{j 1} g_{j} e_{1}\right\} \\
= & u_{j 1} \cdot e_{1} \cdot e_{1}+e_{1} \cdot e_{1} \cdot u_{j 1}-u_{j 1} \cdot e_{1} \cdot e_{1} \\
& +u_{j 1} \cdot g_{j} \cdot e_{1}+g_{j} \cdot e_{1} \cdot u_{j 1}-u_{j 1} \cdot e_{1} \cdot g_{j} \\
= & \frac{1}{2} u_{j 1} \quad(\text { Lemma } 2) \\
\left\{u_{j 1} g f_{j}\right\}= & \left\{u_{1} e_{1} f_{j}\right\}+\left\{u_{j 1} g_{j} f_{j}\right\} \\
= & u_{j 1} \cdot e_{1} \cdot f_{j}+e_{1} \cdot f_{j} \cdot u_{j 1}-u_{j 1} \cdot f_{j} \cdot e_{1} \\
& +u_{j 1} \cdot g_{j} \cdot f_{j}+g_{j} \cdot f_{j} \cdot u_{j 1}-u_{j 1} \cdot f_{j} \cdot g_{j} \\
= & e_{j} \cdot u_{j 1} \quad\left(\text { Lemma } 2 \text { and commutativity of } R_{f_{j}} \text { and } R_{g_{j}}\right) \\
= & \frac{1}{2} u_{j 1} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $u_{j 1} \in(\mathfrak{J}, g)_{1 j}$. Also

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\{u_{j 1} g u_{j 1}\right\} & =\left\{u_{j 1} e_{1} u_{j 1}\right\}+\left\{u_{j 1} g_{j} u_{j 1}\right\} \\
& =2 e_{1} \cdot u_{j 1} \cdot u_{j 1}-e_{1} \cdot u_{j 1} \cdot 2+2 g_{j} \cdot u_{j 1} \cdot u_{j 1}-g_{j} \cdot u_{j 1}{ }^{2} \\
& =u_{j 1} \cdot 2-e_{1} \cdot u_{j 1} \cdot 2+2 u_{1 j} \cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{j} \cdot u_{j 1} \cdot u_{j 1}-u_{1 j} \cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{j} \cdot u_{j 1} \cdot 2 \\
& =e_{j} \cdot u_{j 1} \cdot 2+2 e_{j} \cdot u_{j 1} \cdot u_{1 j}{ }^{2} \cdot u_{j 1}-u_{1 j} \cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{j} \cdot\left(u_{j 1} \cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{j}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

(commutativity of $R_{u_{j 1}}$ and $R_{u_{1 j} \cdot 2}$, Lemma 2)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =f_{j}+e_{1}+e_{j}-e_{j} \\
& =f_{1}+f_{j} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $u_{j 1 \cdot g} u_{j 1}=f_{1}+f_{j}$ and the proof is complete.

## Exercises

1. Show that the set of restrictions of the $R_{x_{i i}}, x_{i i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i i}$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}, i \neq j$, form a subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\Im_{i j}, \Im_{i j}\right)^{+}$.
2. Verify that $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}{ }^{.2} \cdot e_{\imath}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}$.
3. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with 1 containing nonzero connected idempotents $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$. Let $u_{12} \in \mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{2}}$ be an invertible element in $\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}}+\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{2}}+\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{2}}$. Verify that $\left\{e_{1} u_{12} e_{1}\right\}=0$ and use this to show that there exists an isotope of $\mathfrak{J}$ in which $e_{1}$ is nilpotent.
4. Jordan matrix algebras. Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be an arbitrary algebra of characteristic not two with identity element 1 and involution $j: d \rightarrow \bar{d}$ and let $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ be the algebra of $n \times n$ matrices with entries in $\mathfrak{D}$. We have called the involution $X \rightarrow \bar{X}^{t}$ the standard involution in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ (§1.5). More generally, we shall consider involutions $J_{a}: X \rightarrow a^{-1} \bar{X}^{t} a$ where

$$
\begin{equation*}
a=\operatorname{diag}\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}\right\} \tag{16}
\end{equation*}
$$

and the $a_{i}$ satisfy: $\bar{a}_{i}=a_{i}, a_{i} \in N(\mathfrak{D})$, the nucleus of $\mathfrak{D}$, and $a_{i}{ }^{-1}$ exists in the associative algebra $N(\mathfrak{D})$. We shall call such involutions canonical and we let $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ denote the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{D}_{n}^{+}$of elements symmetric relative to $J_{a}$. We remark that in the present notation the standard involution is $J_{1}$, where 1 is the identity matrix. Moreover, we shall usually write $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)$ for $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$.

We shall now introduce a notation for certain elements of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ which will be used throughout this book. Let $e_{i j}, i, j=1, \cdots, n$, be the usual matrix units in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$, and if $x \in \mathfrak{D}$ then we identify $x$ with the diagonal matrix in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ all of whose diagonal entries are $x$. Then $x e_{i j}$ is the matrix with $x$ in the $(i, j)$-position and 0 's elsewhere. Now let $x \in \mathfrak{D}$ and let $i, j=1,2, \cdots, n$. Then we put

$$
\begin{equation*}
x[i j]=x e_{i j}+\left(x e_{i j}\right)^{J}=x e_{i j}+\left(a_{j}^{-1} \bar{x} a_{i}\right) e_{j i} . \tag{17}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since the characteristic is not two $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ coincides with the set of elements $X+X^{J_{a}}$. It follows that every element of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is a sum of elements $x[i j]$, $x \in \mathfrak{D}, i, j=1, \cdots, n$. We now put $\mathfrak{H}_{i j}=\{x[i j] \mid x \in \mathfrak{D}\}$. Then $\mathfrak{H}_{i j}=\mathfrak{H}_{j i}$ and $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)=\sum_{i \leqq j=1}^{n} \oplus \mathfrak{H}_{i j}$. We leave it to the reader to verify the following multiplication rules in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, \boldsymbol{J}_{a}\right)$ :

$$
\begin{align*}
2 x[i j] \cdot y[j k] & =x y[i k], \quad i, j, k \neq,  \tag{18}\\
2 x[i i] \cdot y[i j] & =\left(x y+\left(a_{i}^{-1} \bar{x} a_{i}\right) y\right)[i j], \quad i \neq j,  \tag{19}\\
2 x[i j] \cdot y[j i] & =x y[i i]+y x[j j], \quad i \neq j,  \tag{20}\\
2 x[i i] \cdot y[i i] & =\left(x+a_{i}^{-1} \bar{x} a_{i}\right) \cdot\left(y+a_{i}^{-1} \bar{y} a_{i}\right)[i i] . \tag{21}
\end{align*}
$$

Also we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
x[i j]=\left(a_{j}^{-1} \bar{x} a_{i}\right)[j i] \tag{22}
\end{equation*}
$$

and

$$
\begin{equation*}
x[i j] \cdot y[k l]=0, \quad \text { if } \quad\{i, j\} \cap\{k, l\}=\varnothing \tag{23}
\end{equation*}
$$

Clearly these formulas give every product $x[i j] . y[k l]$ for all possible pairs $(i, j)$, $(k, l)$. If the involution is standard, that is, $a=1$, then the foregoing formulas simplify to the following

$$
\begin{align*}
2 x[i j] \cdot y[j k] & =x y[i k], \quad i, j, k \neq  \tag{$\prime$}\\
2 x[i i] \cdot y[i j] & =(x+\bar{x}) y[i j], \quad i \neq j  \tag{$\prime$}\\
2 x[i j] \cdot y[j i] & =x y[i i]+y x[j j], \quad i \neq j  \tag{$\prime$}\\
2 x[i i] \cdot y[i i] & =(x+\bar{x}) \cdot(y+\bar{y})[i i]  \tag{$\prime$}\\
x[i j] & =\bar{x}[j i]  \tag{$\prime$}\\
x[i j] \cdot y[k l] & =0 \text { if } \quad\{i, j\} \cap\{k, l\}=\varnothing \tag{$\prime$}
\end{align*}
$$

We now assume that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is Jordan. Let $e_{i}=\frac{1}{2}[i i]$. Then, by (21) and (23), the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$. Moreover, $e_{i}=e_{i i}$ so $\sum e_{i}=1$. By (21) and (19), $e_{i} \cdot x[i i]=x[i i]$ and $e_{i} \cdot x[i j]=\frac{1}{2} x[i j]$. By (23), $e_{i} \cdot x[j k]=0$ if $i \neq j$ and $i \neq k$. It follows that the $\mathfrak{H}_{i j}$ are the Peirce spaces of $\mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ relative to the idempotents $\boldsymbol{e}_{\boldsymbol{i}}$. We shall now show that the fact that $\mathfrak{H}$ is a Jordan algebra implies that $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative if $n \geqq 4$ and $\mathfrak{D}$ is alternative with its symmetric elements in the nucleus if $n=3$. Assume first that $n \geqq 4$. Let $x, y, z$ be arbitrary in $\mathfrak{D}, i, j, k, l$ unequal indices. Then $4(x[i j] . y[j k]) . z[k l]=(x y) z[i l]$ and $4 x[i j] .(y[j k] . z[k l])=x(y z)[i l]$, by (18). On the other hand, since $x[i j] \in \mathfrak{H}_{i j}, y[j k] \in \mathfrak{H}_{j k}, z[k l] \in \mathfrak{H}_{k l}$ and these are the Peirce spaces of $\mathfrak{H}$ relative to the $e_{i}$, (PD13) implies that $(x[i j] \cdot y[j k]) \cdot z[k l]=x[i j] \cdot(y[j k] \cdot z[k l])$. Hence $(x y) z=x(y z)$ and $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative. Next assume $n=3$. We have shown in §1.12 that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is Jordan if and only if $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)$ is Jordan. Hence we may assume that the involution in $\mathfrak{D}_{3}$ is standard. Let $x, y, z$ be arbitrary in $\mathfrak{D}, i, j, k$ distinct indices. Then $2(x[i j] \cdot y[j k]) \cdot z[k k]=2 x[i j] \cdot(y[j k] \cdot z[k k])$ by (PD9). Using (18') and (19') this gives $(x y)(z+\bar{z})=x(y(z+\bar{z}))$, so $[x, y, z+\bar{z}]=0$. By (PD10) we have $4 x[i j] \cdot y[i j] \cdot z[j k]=4 x[i j] \cdot z[j k] \cdot y[i j]+4 y[i j] \cdot z[j k] \cdot x[i j]$. Using $\left(22^{\prime}\right)$, (20'), (19') and (18') this gives $((\bar{y} x+\bar{x} y) z)[j k]=(\bar{y}(x z)+\bar{x}(y z))[j k]$. Hence $[\bar{y}, x, z]+[\bar{x}, y, z]=0$. If we take $x=y$ this gives $[\bar{x}, x, z]=0$. Applying the involution to $[x, y, z+\bar{z}]=0$ gives $[z+\bar{z}, \bar{y}, \bar{x}]=0$ which is the same as $[z+\bar{z}, y, x]=0$. Then $[x+\bar{x}, x, z]=0$ and since $[\bar{x}, x, z]=0$ we have $[x, x, z] =0$. Applying the involution gives $[z, x, x]=0$. Hence $\mathfrak{D}$ is alternative. Then $[x, y, z+\bar{z}]=0$ implies also $[x, z+\bar{z}, y]=0$. Since we had $[z+\bar{z}, x, y]=0$ it is clear that $z+\bar{z}$ is in the nucleus. This implies that the symmetric elements are in the nucleus. Hence we have shown that necessary conditions that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ with $n \geqq 3$ is Jordan are that $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative if $n \geqq 4$ and $\mathfrak{D}$ is alternative with
self-adjoint elements in the nucleus if $\boldsymbol{n} \boldsymbol{=} \mathbf{3}$. In the Corollary to Theorem $\mathbf{1} . \mathbf{1 4}$ we proved that these conditions are also sufficient. Hence we have
Theorem 1. Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be an algebra over a field of characteristic not two with an identity element and an involution $j$, and let $J_{a}$ be a canonical involution in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$. Then $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ for $n \geqq 3$ is Jordan if and only if either $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative or $n=3$ and $\mathfrak{D}$ is alternative with symmetric elements in the nucleus.

We shall call the algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ which are Jordan, Jordan matrix algebras. Also we shall call the integer $n$ the order of the algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ (whether Jordan or not). The conditions for $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ to be Jordan if $n \geqq 3$ are given in the foregoing theorem. Necessary and sufficient conditions for the Jordan property for the case $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{2}, J_{a}\right)$ can also be given. Since these will not be required in the sequel we shall be content just to state these in an exercise (ex. 4 below). (For $n=1$ there seems to be nothing more to state than the Jordan condition $a^{2} \cdot b \cdot a =a^{\cdot 2} \cdot(b . a)$ for $a=d+\bar{d}, b=e+\bar{e}, d, e$ in $\mathfrak{D}$.)
We shall indicate next two important special cases of Jordan matrix algebras. First, let $\mathfrak{D}$ be an arbitrary associative algebra with 1 and let $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus \mathfrak{D}^{\circ}$ where $\mathfrak{D}^{\circ}$ is the opposite algebra of $\mathfrak{D}$. Thus $\mathfrak{E}$ is the set of pairs $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right), a_{1}, a_{2}$ in $\mathfrak{D}$ with the multiplication $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right)\left(b_{1}, b_{2}\right)=\left(a_{1} b_{1}, b_{2} a_{2}\right)$ (cf. §1.4). We have the involution $j:\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right) \rightarrow\left(a_{2}, a_{1}\right)$ in $\mathscr{E}_{\text {which }}$ gives rise to the standard involution $J_{1}$ in $\mathscr{E}_{n}$ and to the Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}\right)=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$. Next we consider $\mathfrak{F}=\mathfrak{D}_{n} \oplus \mathfrak{D}_{n}{ }^{\circ}$ where $\mathfrak{D}_{n}{ }^{\circ}$ is the opposite algebra of $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$. As we saw in §1.4, if $J$ is the involution $\left(A_{1}, A_{2}\right) \rightarrow\left(A_{2}, A_{1}\right)$ in $\mathfrak{F}$ then $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{F}, J)$ is the set of elements $(A, A)$ and the mapping $A \rightarrow(A, A)$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{D}_{n}{ }^{+}$onto $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{F}, J)$. Let ( $A_{1}, A_{2}$ ) be an element of $\mathfrak{F}$ and write $A_{1}=\left(a_{1 i j}\right), A_{2}=\left(a_{2 i j}\right)$ where $a_{k i j}$ is the ( $i, j$ )-entry of $A_{k}$. Let $\left(A_{1}, A_{2}\right)^{n}$ be the element of $\mathscr{E}_{n}$ whose $(i, j)$-entry is the element $\left(a_{1 i j}, a_{2 j i}\right)$ of $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus \mathfrak{D}^{\circ}$. Then one verifies directly that $\eta$ is an isomorphism of ( $\left.\mathfrak{F}, J\right)$ onto $\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$. Hence $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}\right) \cong \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{F}, J) \cong \mathfrak{D}_{n}{ }^{+}$. Thus we see that the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{D}_{n}{ }^{+}$, where $\mathfrak{D}$ is an arbitrary associative algebra with 1 , is isomorphic to the Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus \mathfrak{D}^{\circ}$ and $j$ is the usual involution exchanging the two factors.

We consider next the matrix algebra $\Phi_{2 n}$ and the involution $J_{S}: X \rightarrow S^{-1} X^{t} S$ in $\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\mathbf{2} \boldsymbol{n}}$ where

$$
\begin{equation*}
S=\operatorname{diag}\{Q, Q, \cdots, Q\} \tag{24}
\end{equation*}
$$

and

$$
Q=\left(\begin{array}{rr}
0 & 1  \tag{25}\\
-1 & 0
\end{array}\right) .
$$

A matrix which is symmetric relative to $J_{S}\left(S^{-1} A^{t} S=A\right)$ will be called symplectic symmetric. We shall show that the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}\right)$ consisting of these matrices is isomorphic to a Jordan matrix algebra.

Let $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi_{2}$ and let

$$
i_{1}=\left(\begin{array}{rr}
1 & 0  \tag{26}\\
0 & -1
\end{array}\right), \quad i_{2}=Q=\left(\begin{array}{rr}
0 & 1 \\
-1 & 0
\end{array}\right) .
$$

Then one checks that $\left(1, i_{1}, i_{2}, i_{1} i_{2}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{D}$ and we have the basic multiplication formulas: $i_{1}{ }^{2}=1, i_{2}{ }^{2}=-1, i_{1} i_{2}=-i_{2} i_{1}$. Hence $\mathfrak{D}$ is a quaternion algebra and in $\mathfrak{D}$ we have the standard involution $j: \alpha_{0}+\alpha_{1} i_{1}+\alpha_{2} i_{2}+\alpha_{3} i_{1} i_{2} \rightarrow \alpha_{0} -\alpha_{1} i-\alpha_{2} j-\alpha_{3} i_{1} i_{2}, \quad \alpha_{j} \in \Phi$. Since

$$
\begin{align*}
& Q^{-1} i_{1}{ }^{t} Q=\left(\begin{array}{rr}
0 & -1 \\
1 & 0
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{rr}
1 & 0 \\
0 & -1
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{rr}
0 & 1 \\
-1 & 0
\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}{ll}
-1 & 0 \\
0 & 1
\end{array}\right)=-i_{1},  \tag{27}\\
& Q^{-1} i_{2}{ }^{t} Q=\left(\begin{array}{rr}
0 & -1 \\
1 & 0
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{rr}
0 & -1 \\
1 & 0
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{rr}
0 & 1 \\
-1 & 0
\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}{rr}
0 & -1 \\
1 & 0
\end{array}\right)=-i_{2},
\end{align*}
$$

it is clear that $j$ is the involution $a \rightarrow Q^{-1} a^{t} Q$ in $\mathfrak{D}$.
We now consider $\mathfrak{D}_{n}=\left(\Phi_{2}\right)_{n}$ and let $J_{1}$ be the standard involution in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ corresponding to the involution $j$ in $\mathfrak{D}$. If $A \in \mathfrak{D}_{n}$ then $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix whose entries are $2 \times 2$ matrices with entries in $\Phi$. Hence $A$ determines a $2 n \times 2 n$ matrix $A^{\eta}$ in $\Phi_{2 n}$. It is well known and clear from block multiplication of matrices that $A \rightarrow A^{\eta}$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ onto $\Phi_{2 n}$. It is immediate also that $\eta$ is an isomorphism of ( $\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}$ ) onto ( $\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}$ ). Hence the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}\right)$ of symplectic symmetric matrices is isomorphic to a Jordan matrix algebra. We remark also that it is well known and easily seen that $\left(\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}\right)$ is isomorphic to $\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{V}), J\right)$ where $\mathfrak{B}$ is a $2 n$-dimensional vector space over $\Phi$ and $J$ is the involution $A \rightarrow A^{*}, A^{*}$ the adjoint (or transpose) of $A$ relative to a nondegenerate skew bilinear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{M}$.

Let $J_{a}$ be the canonical involution in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ defined by the involution $j$ in $\mathfrak{D}$ and the diagonal matrix $a=\operatorname{diag}\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}\right\}$ where $a_{i}=\bar{a}_{i}$ is in the nucleus of $\mathfrak{D}$ and $a_{i}{ }^{-1}$ exists in the nucleus. Then one checks directly that the mapping $k: d \rightarrow a_{1}{ }^{-1} \bar{d} a_{1}$ is an involution in $\mathfrak{D}$ and $J_{a}$ coincides with the canonical involution $J_{b}$ defined by the involution $k$ in $\mathfrak{D}$ and the diagonal matrix

$$
b=\operatorname{diag}\left\{1, a_{1}^{-1} a_{2}, \cdots, a_{1}^{-1} a_{n}\right\} .
$$

Hence there is no loss in generality in assuming that $a_{1}=1$ and we shall do this from now on.

If ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ) is an algebra with involution then, as in the associative case considered in §1.4, we define an ideal of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ to be an ideal of $\mathfrak{D}$ which is invariant under $j$. Similarly, a subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{D}$ invariant under $j$. If $\mathfrak{E}$ is an ideal (subalgebra) of $\mathfrak{D}$ then the set $\mathfrak{E}_{n}$ of $n \times n$ matrices with entries in $\mathfrak{E}$ is an ideal (subalgebra) of $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ and hence $\mathfrak{H} \cap \mathfrak{E}_{n}$ is an ideal (subalgebra) of $\mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$. We shall now prove

Theorem 2. Let $\mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ be a Jordan matrix algebra of order $n \geqq 3$ defined by the canonical involution $J_{a}$ in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ such that $a_{1}=1$. Then the mapping $\mathfrak{E} \rightarrow \mathfrak{H} \cap \mathfrak{E}_{n}$ is a lattice isomorphism of the lattice of subalgebras $\mathfrak{E}$ of ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ) containing the elements $a_{i}$ and $a_{i}{ }^{-1}$ onto the lattice of subalgebras of $\mathfrak{H}$ containing the elements $1[i j], i, j=1, \cdots, n$. Also the mapping $\mathfrak{E} \rightarrow \mathfrak{H} \cap \mathfrak{E}_{n}$ is a lattice isomorphism of the lattice of ideals $\mathfrak{E}$ of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ onto the lattice of ideals of $\mathfrak{H}$. In this $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{H} \cap \mathfrak{E}_{n}$ satisfies $\mathfrak{K}^{2}=0$ if and only if $\mathfrak{E}^{2}=0$.

Proof. In order to treat the case of ideals and subalgebras simultaneously we assume that $\mathfrak{K}$ is a subspace of $\mathfrak{H}$ which is mapped into itself by Jordan multiplication by the elements $1[i j], i, j=1, \cdots, n$. Let $\mathfrak{E}$ denote the subset of elements of $\mathfrak{D}$ which are entries of the matrices $\in \mathfrak{K}$. Let $k=\Sigma d_{i j} e_{i j}, d_{i j} \in \mathfrak{D}$, be in $\mathfrak{K}$. Then $k U_{e_{i i}}=d_{i i} e_{i i} \in \mathfrak{K}$ since $U_{e_{i i}}=2 R_{e_{i i}}{ }^{2}-R_{e_{i i}}$ and $e_{i i}=\frac{1}{2}[i i]$. Also $k U_{e_{i i}} \in \mathfrak{H}$ so $d_{i i} e_{i i}=a_{i}{ }^{-1} d_{i i} a_{i} e_{i i}$ and $d_{i i} e_{i i}=\frac{1}{2} d_{i i}[i i]$. By (19) and the hypothesis on $\Re, d_{i i}[i j]=d_{i i}[i i] .1[i j] \in \Re$ for any $j \neq i$. Also we have that $2 k U_{e_{i i}, e_{j j}}=d_{i j} e_{i j} +d_{j i} e_{j i} \in \mathfrak{K}$ for any $i \neq j$ since $U_{e_{i l}, e_{j j}}=R_{e_{i i}} R_{e_{j j}}+R_{e_{j j}} R_{e_{i i}}$. Since $d_{i j} e_{i j}+d_{j i} e_{j i} \in \mathfrak{H}$ it is clear that $d_{i j} e_{i j}+d_{j i} e_{j i}=d_{i j}[i j]$. We have therefore shown that $\mathfrak{E}$ is the set of elements $d \in \mathfrak{D}$ such that $d[i j] \in \Re$ for some pair $(i, j)$ with $i \neq j$. If $d[i j] \in \Re$ and $k \neq i, j$ then $d[i k]=2 d[i j] .1[j k] \in \Re$ and $d[k j]=2(1[k i] . d[i j]) \in \Re$. It follows that $d[k l] \in \Re$ for every ( $k, l$ ) with $k \neq l$. Also

$$
d[k k]=2 d[k l] .1[l k] \cdot \frac{1}{2}[k k] \in \mathfrak{N} .
$$

It is now clear that $\mathfrak{E}$ is a subspace of $\mathfrak{D}$ and if $d \in \mathfrak{E}$ then $d[i j] \in \Re$ for every $i, j$. Clearly $\mathfrak{R} \subseteq \mathfrak{E}_{n} \cap \mathfrak{H}$ holds by the definition of the set $\mathfrak{E}$. On the other hand, if $k=\Sigma d_{i j} e_{i j} \in \mathfrak{E}_{n} \cap \mathfrak{H}$ then every $d_{i j} \in \mathfrak{E}$ and hence $d_{i j}[i j] \in \mathfrak{R}$. Also since $k=\sum d_{i j} e_{i j} \in \mathfrak{H}, k=\sum_{i<j} d_{i j}[i j]+\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i} d_{i i}[i i]$ and this is contained in $\mathfrak{R}$. Hence $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{E}_{n} \cap \mathfrak{H}$. Now let $\mathfrak{K}$ be a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{H}$ containing the elements $1[i j], i, j =1, \cdots, n$. Then our results apply to $\mathfrak{K}$ so $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{E}_{n} \cap \mathfrak{H}$ where $\mathfrak{E}$ is the set of entries in $\mathfrak{D}$ of the matrices belonging to $\Re$ and $\mathfrak{E}$ is a subspace. Moreover, if $d \in \mathfrak{E}$ then $d[i j] \in \mathfrak{K}$ for all $i, j$. It is now clear from (18) that $\mathfrak{E}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{D}$. Also, since $a_{1}=1$ and $u_{j 1}=e_{j 1}+a_{1}^{-1} a_{j} e_{1 j}=e_{j 1}+a_{j} e_{1 j} \in \Re, a_{j} \in \mathfrak{E}$. Similarly, since $u_{1 j} \in \mathfrak{K}, a_{j}{ }^{-1} \in \mathfrak{E}$. Finally, if $d \in \mathfrak{E}$ then $d[12]=a_{2}{ }^{-1} d a_{1}[21] \in \mathfrak{K}$. Hence $a_{2}{ }^{-1} d a_{1} \in \mathfrak{E}$ and $d \in \mathfrak{E}$. Thus $\mathfrak{E}$ is a subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ containing the elements $a_{i}$ and $a_{i}{ }^{-1}$. The first statement of the theorem is now clear. A similar argument yields the second statement of the theorem. The last statement is clear from the multiplication formula (18).
Let $(\mathfrak{E}, k)$ be a second algebra with involution $k$ and identity element 1 and let $K_{b}$ be the canonical involution in $\mathfrak{E}_{n}$ defined by $k$ and $b=\operatorname{diag}\left\{b_{1}=1, b_{2}, \cdots, b_{n}\right\}$. If $e \in \mathfrak{E}$ we put $e\{i j\}=e e_{i j}+b_{j}{ }^{-1} e^{*} b_{i} e_{j i}, e^{*}=e^{k}$. Suppose $\eta$ is a homomorphism of ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ) into ( $\mathfrak{E}, k$ ) such that $a_{i}{ }^{\eta}=b_{i}, i=1,2, \cdots, n$. Then it is immediate that the mapping $\left(d_{i j}\right) \rightarrow\left(d_{i j}{ }^{\eta}\right)$ is a homomorphism of ( $\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}$ ) into ( $\mathfrak{E}_{n}, K_{b}$ ). Hence the restriction $\sigma$ of this mapping to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$
into $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{\boldsymbol{n}}, J_{\boldsymbol{b}}\right)$. Also it is clear that $1[i j]^{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}=1\{i j\}$ for $i, j=1,2, \cdots, n$. Now suppose $n \geqq 3$ and assume $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ and $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}, K_{b}\right)$ are Jordan. Let $\sigma$ be a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}, K_{b}\right)$ such that $1[i j]^{\sigma}=1\{i j\}, i, j=1, \cdots, n$. We have $e_{i i}{ }^{\sigma}=e_{i i}$ so the Peirce space $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)_{i j}$ relative to the $e_{i i}$ in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is mapped into the Peirce space $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}, K_{b}\right)_{i j}$. It follows that for every pair $(i, j)$ we have a mapping $\eta_{i j}$ of $\mathfrak{D}$ into $E$ such that $d[i j]^{\sigma}=d^{\eta_{i i}}\{i j\}$. Clearly $\eta_{i j}$ is linear and $1^{\eta_{i j}}=1$. By (18) and the corresponding formula in $\mathfrak{E}_{n}$ we have for $a, b \in \mathfrak{D}$ and $i, j, k$ distinct indices that $(a b)^{\eta i k}\{i k\}=a b[i k]^{\sigma}=2(a[i j] \cdot b[j k])^{\sigma}=2 a[i j]^{\sigma} \cdot b[j k]^{\sigma} =2 a^{\eta_{i j}}\{i j\} . b^{\eta_{j k}}\{j k\}=a^{\eta_{i j}} b^{\eta_{j k}}\{i k\}$. Hence $(a b)^{\eta_{i k}}=a^{\eta_{i j}} b^{\eta_{j k}}$. If we put $b=1$ in this we obtain $a^{\eta_{i k}}=a^{\eta_{i j}}$ and if we put $a=1$ we obtain $b^{\eta_{i k}}=b^{\eta_{j k}}$. It follows that $\eta_{i j}=\eta_{k l}$ for any $(i, j),(k, l)$ such that $i \neq j, k \neq l$. If we call this linear mapping $\eta$, then the relation $(a b)^{\eta_{i k}}=a^{\eta_{i j}} b^{\eta_{j k}}$ gives $(a b)^{\eta}=a^{\eta} b^{\eta}$, so $\eta$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{D}$ into $E$ such that $1^{\eta}=1$. If $i \neq 1$ we have for $d \in \mathfrak{D}: d[i 1]^{\sigma}=d^{\eta}\{i 1\} =b_{1}{ }^{-1}\left(d^{\eta}\right)^{*} b_{i}\{1 i\}=\left(d^{\eta}\right)^{*} b_{i}\{1 i\}$ and $d[i 1]^{\sigma}=a_{1}{ }^{-1} d a_{i}[1 i]^{\sigma}=d a_{i}[1 i]^{\sigma}=\left(d a_{i}\right)^{\eta}\{1 i\}$. Hence $\left(d^{\eta}\right)^{*} b_{i}=\left(d a_{i}\right)^{\eta}=d^{\eta} a_{i}{ }^{\eta}$. If we take $d=1$ in this we obtain $b_{i}=a_{i}{ }^{\eta}$. Then $\left(d^{\eta}\right)^{*}=\bar{d}^{\eta}$ so $\eta$ is a homomorphism of ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ) into ( $\mathfrak{E}, k$ ) sending $a_{i}$ into $b_{i}$ for $i=1,2, \cdots, n$. Then $\left(d_{i j}\right) \rightarrow\left(d_{i j}{ }^{7}\right)$ is a homomorphism of ( $\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}$ ) into ( $\mathfrak{E}_{n}, K_{b}$ ) so its restriction $\tau$ to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is a homomorphism into $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}, K_{b}\right)$. If $i \neq j$ and $d \in \mathfrak{D}$ then $d[i j]^{\sigma}=d^{\eta}\{i j\}=d^{\eta} e_{i j}+b_{j}{ }^{-1}\left(d^{\eta}\right)^{*} b_{i} e_{j i}$ and $d[i j]^{\tau}=\left(d e_{i j}+a_{j}{ }^{-1} d a_{i} e_{j i}\right)^{\tau} =d^{\eta} e_{i j}+\left(a_{j}{ }^{-1} d a_{i}\right)^{\eta} e_{j i}=d^{\eta} e_{i j}+b_{j}{ }^{-1} d^{\eta} b_{i} e_{j i}=d^{\eta} e_{i j}+b_{j}{ }^{-1}\left(d^{\eta}\right)^{*} b_{i} e_{j i}$. Thus $d[i j]^{\sigma}=d[i j]^{\tau}$. Now it is easily seen from (20) and (21) that the elements $d[i j]$, $d \in \mathfrak{D}, i \neq j$ generate $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$. Hence $\sigma=\tau$ and we have proved the following homomorphism theorem for Jordan matrix algebras.

Theorem 3. Let $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ and $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}, K_{b}\right)$ be Jordan matrix algebras of order $n \geqq 3$ determined by canonical involutions $J_{a}$ and $K_{b}$ respectively where the first of these is defined by an involution $j$ in $\mathfrak{D}$ and a diagonal matrix a such that $a_{1}=1$ and the second is defined by an involution $k$ in $\mathbb{E}$ and a diagonal matrix $b$ with $b_{1}=1$. Suppose $\eta$ is a homomorphism of ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ) into ( $\mathfrak{E}, k$ ) such that $a_{i}{ }^{\eta}=b_{i}, i=1, \cdots, n$. Then the restriction $\sigma$ to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ of the mapping $\left(d_{i j}\right) \rightarrow\left(d_{i j}{ }^{7}\right)$ of $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}, K_{b}\right)$ such that $1[i j]^{\sigma}=1\{i j\}$ where $d[i j]$ in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is defined by (17) and $e\{i j\}$ is defined in a similar fashion in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}, K_{b}\right)$. Conversely, assume $\sigma$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}, K_{b}\right)$ such that $1[i j]^{\sigma}=1\{i j\}, i, j=1, \cdots, n$. Then there exists a homomorphism $\eta$ of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ into $(\mathfrak{E}, k)$ such that $a_{i}^{\eta}=b_{i}, i=1, \cdots, n$, and such that $\sigma$ is the restriction to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ of the mapping $\left(d_{i j}\right) \rightarrow\left(d_{i j}{ }^{\eta}\right)$ of $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$.

If $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is an algebra with involution we let $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ denote the set of skew elements of $\mathfrak{D}$. This is a subspace closed under the composition $[a b] \equiv a b-b a$. Also, if $a \in \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ and $b \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ then $[a b] \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$, and if $a, b \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ then $[a b] \in \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. In other words, if $[\mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{B}]$ denotes the subspace spanned by all $[a b], a$ in the subspace $\mathfrak{A}$ and $b$ in the subspace $\mathfrak{B}$ then $[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)] \subseteq \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ and $[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j, j)] \subseteq \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ and $[\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)] \subseteq \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. In certain
considerations it is important to know that $[\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)]=\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. We shall now establish the following useful sufficient condition for this to hold for a matrix algebra with canonical involution.

Theorem 4. Let $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ be an algebra with involution and identity element, $J_{a}$ a canonical involution in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ determined by a diagonal matrix a with $a_{1}=1$. Assume $n \geqq 3$. Then $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)=\left[\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right), \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right]$ if

$$
\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)=[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)]+[\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)] .
$$

Proof. If $d \in \mathfrak{D}$ and $e_{i j}$ is the usual matrix unit then $d e_{i j}{ }^{J_{a}}=a_{j}{ }^{-1} \tilde{d} a_{i} e_{j i}$. Hence every element of $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is a sum of elements of the form $d e_{i j}-a_{j}{ }^{-1} \bar{d} a_{i} e_{j i}$. If $d[i j] \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is defined as usual then $[d[i j], 1[j k]]=d e_{i k}-a_{k}{ }^{-1} d a_{i} e_{k i}$ if $i, j, k$ are distinct. Hence every element $d e_{i k}-a_{k}{ }^{-1} d a_{i} e_{k i}$ with $i \neq k$ is contained in $\left[\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right), \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right]$. If $i \neq j$ then $[d[i j], 1[j i]]=\left(d-a_{i}^{-1} \bar{d} a_{i}\right) e_{i i} -\left(d-a_{j}{ }^{-1} d a_{j}\right) e_{j j}$. This and the result just noted imply that $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right) =\left[\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right), \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right]+\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j) e_{11}$ where $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j) e_{11}=\left\{q e_{11} \mid q \in \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)\right\}$. If $p_{1}, p_{2} \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ then $\left[p_{1} p_{2}\right] e_{11}=\left[p_{1} e_{11}, p_{2} e_{11}\right] \in\left[\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right), \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right]$ and if $q_{1}, q_{2} \in \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ then we can write $q_{1}=d_{1}-\bar{d}_{1}, q_{2}=d_{2}-\bar{d}_{2}, d_{i} \in \mathfrak{D}$, and we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[q_{1} q_{2}\right] e_{11}=\left[\left[d_{1}[1 j], 1[j 1]\right],\left[d_{2}[1 k], 1[k 1]\right]\right] \tag{28}
\end{equation*}
$$

for $1, j, k$ distinct. Put $\left[d_{2}[1 k], 1[k 1]\right]=L$ so that $L \in \mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$. Since $1[j 1]$ is in the nucleus of $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ the Jacobi identity: $\left[\left[d_{1}[1 j], 1[j 1]\right], L\right]=\left[\left[d_{1}[1 j], L\right], 1[j 1]\right] +\left[d_{1}[1 j],[1[j 1], L]\right]$ is valid. Since $\left[d_{1}[1 j], L\right]$ and $[1[j 1], L] \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ it is now clear that $\left[q_{1} q_{2}\right] e_{11} \in\left[\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right), \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right]$ and hence $[\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)] e_{11} +[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)] e_{11} \subseteq\left[\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right), \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right]$. Since $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)=[\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)] +[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)]$ we now have that $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)=\left[\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right), \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right]+\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j) e_{11} =\left[\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right), \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right]$.

## Exercises

1. Show that Theorems 2 and 3 are valid without the hypothesis that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ and $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{E}_{n}, J_{b}\right)$ are Jordan.
2. Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be an arbitrary algebra with $1, \mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus \mathfrak{D}^{\circ}, j$ the involution $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right) \rightarrow\left(a_{2}, a_{1}\right)$. Show that any ideal in $(\mathscr{E}, j)$ has the form $\Re \oplus \Re^{j}$ where $\Re$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{D}$, and that $\mathfrak{K} \rightarrow \mathfrak{K} \oplus \mathfrak{K}^{j}$ is a bijection of the set of ideals of $\mathfrak{D}$ and the set of ideals of ( $\mathfrak{E}, j$ ). Show that if $n \geqq 3$ then $\boldsymbol{\Omega} \rightarrow \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{n}$ is a bijection of the set of ideals of $\mathfrak{D}$ and the set of ideals of $\mathfrak{D}_{n}{ }^{+}$.
3. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be an $n$-dimensional vector space, $f$ a symmetric bilinear form such that

$$
f\left(u_{i}, u_{n-j+1}\right)=\delta_{i j}
$$

$i, j=1, \cdots, n$ for a basis $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ of $\mathfrak{B} / \Phi$. Note that $f$ is nondegenerate and has maximal Witt index. Let $\mathfrak{H}^{(n)}$ be the Jordan algebra of self-adjoint linear
transformations relative to $f$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the linear transformations in $\mathfrak{V}$ defined by

$$
\begin{array}{lc}
u_{1} E=0, \quad u_{i+1} E=i(i-n) u_{i}, & 1 \leqq i \leqq n-1 \\
u_{i} F=u_{i+1}, & 1 \leqq i \leqq n-1,
\end{array}
$$

Verify that $E, F \in \mathfrak{H}^{(n)}$ and that if $[A, B, C]=A . B . C-A .(B . C)$ then

$$
2[E, E, F]=E, \quad 2[F, F, E]=F, \quad E^{n}=0=F^{n}
$$

and that $E$ and $F$ generate $\mathfrak{H}^{(n)}$.
4. (Sasser). Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be an algebra of characteristic $\neq 2$ with identity element 1 and involution $j$ and let $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{2}\right)$ be the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{D}_{2}{ }^{+}$of symmetric elements under the standard involution. Prove that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{2}\right)$ is Jordan if and only if the following relations hold in $\mathfrak{D}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& {[h, a, k]=0} \\
& {[h, h, a]=0} \\
& \overline{[a, \bar{a}, h]}=-[a, \bar{a}, h] \\
& \overline{[a, h, b]}=-[a, h, b] \\
& {[a, \bar{a}, a]=0}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $a, b \in \mathfrak{D}, h, k \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ and $\bar{a}=a^{j}$.
5. (Sasser). Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be an algebra with 1 of characteristic $\neq 2$. Show that $\mathfrak{D}_{n}{ }^{+}, n \geqq 2$, is Jordan if and only if $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative.
3. Coordinatization theorems. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ be a Jordan matrix algebra determined by the canonical involution $J_{a}$ in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ where $a=\operatorname{diag}\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}\right\}$, as in §2. Also, as in §2, we write $x[i j]=x e_{i j}+\left(x e_{i j}\right)^{J_{a}}, e_{i}=\frac{1}{2}[i i]=e_{i i}$. Then the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\Sigma_{1}^{n} e_{i}=1$. Moreover, if $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}=\{x[i j] \mid x \in \mathfrak{D}\}$ then $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{i \leqq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ is the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the $e_{i}$. Now put $u_{1 j}=1[1 j], u_{j 1}=1[j 1], j=2,3, \cdots, n$. Then it follows from (20) and (19) that

$$
\begin{equation*}
u_{1 j} \cdot u_{j 1}=e_{1}+e_{j}, \quad u_{1 j}^{{ }^{2}} \cdot u_{j 1}=u_{1 j} \tag{29}
\end{equation*}
$$

Hence $u_{1 j}$ and $u_{j 1}$ are inverses in the subalgebra $\mathfrak{J}_{11}+\mathfrak{J}_{j j}+\mathfrak{J}_{1 j}$ whose identity is $e_{1}+e_{j}$ and, consequently, $e_{1}$ and $e_{j}$ are connected idempotents (cf. §1). If $a=1$, so the involution in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ is standard, then $u_{j 1}=u_{1 j}$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
u_{1 j}^{\cdot 2}=e_{1}+e_{j} . \tag{30}
\end{equation*}
$$

Hence $e_{1}$ and $e_{j}$ are strongly connected orthogonal idempotents. In this section we shall show that the situations we have just indicated characterize Jordan matrix algebras and Jordan matrix algebras defined by standard involutions respectively. We consider the latter case first and we shall prove the following

Theorem 5 (Strong Coordinatization Theorem). Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with 1 which is a sum of $n \geqq 3$ strongly connected nonzero idempotent elements. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is isomorphic to a Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)$ defined by a standard involution. More precisely, assume $1=\sum_{1}^{n} e_{i}$ where the $e_{i}$ are nonzero orthogonal idempotent elements and $n \geqq 3$. Assume also that there exist elements $u_{1 j}$, $j=2, \cdots, n$, such that

$$
\begin{align*}
e_{1} \cdot u_{1 j} & =\frac{1}{2} u_{1 j}=e_{j} \cdot u_{1 j}  \tag{31}\\
u_{1 j}^{\cdot 2} & =e_{1}+e_{j} . \tag{32}
\end{align*}
$$

Then there exists a Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)$ given by a standard involution in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ and an isomorphism $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)$ such that $e_{i}{ }^{\eta}=\frac{1}{2}[i i], u_{1 j}{ }^{\eta}=1[1 j]$.
The proof will be based on a number of lemmas.
Lemma 1. Let $u_{i j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i j}, i \neq j$, satisfy $u_{i j}{ }^{.2}=e_{i}+e_{j}$. Set $p_{i j}=1-e_{i}-e_{j} +u_{i j}=\Sigma_{k \neq i, j} e_{k}+u_{i j}, U_{(i j)}=U_{p_{i j}}, R_{i j}=R_{u_{i j}}$. Then $U_{(i j)}$ is an automorphism of period two in $\mathfrak{J}$ with the following properties:
(1) $U_{(i j)}$ interchanges the idempotents $e_{i}$ and $e_{j}$ and the spaces $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{j j}$, and maps $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ onto itself,
(2) $U_{(i j)}$ is the identity mapping on every $\mathfrak{J}_{k l}, k, l \neq i, j$,
(3) $U_{(i j)}$ interchanges $\mathfrak{J}_{i k}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{j k}$ if $k \neq i, j$ and coincides with $2 R_{i j}$ on these two spaces.
Proof. We have $p_{i j}{ }^{2}=\left(\Sigma_{k \neq i, j} e_{k}+u_{i j}\right)^{\cdot 2}=\Sigma_{k \neq i, j} e_{k}+u_{i j}{ }^{\cdot 2}=\Sigma_{k \neq i, j} e_{k}+e_{i} +e_{j}=1$. Hence $U_{(i j)}=U_{p_{i j}}$ is an automorphism of period two in $\mathfrak{J}$ (§1.12, p. 60). We have $e_{i} U_{(i j)}=2 e_{i} \cdot p_{i j} \cdot p_{i j}-e_{i}=u_{i j} \cdot p_{i j}-e_{i}=u_{i j} \cdot u_{i j}-e_{i}=e_{i}+e_{j}-e_{i} =e_{j}$. Since $U_{(i j)}{ }^{2}=1$ we have $e_{j} U_{(i j)}=e_{i}$. Since $\mathfrak{I}_{i i}=\mathfrak{I}_{1}\left(e_{i}\right), \mathfrak{J}_{j j}=\mathfrak{J}_{1}\left(e_{j}\right)$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}=\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\left(e_{i}\right) \cap \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\left(e_{j}\right)$ and $U_{(i j)}$ is an automorphism, it is clear that $U_{(i j)}$ interchanges $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{j j}$ and maps $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ onto itself. Let $x \in \mathfrak{J}_{k l}, k, l \neq i, j$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
x U_{(i j)} & =2 x_{\bullet} \cdot p_{i j} \cdot p_{i j}-x=2 x \cdot\left(\sum_{k \neq i, j} e_{k}+u_{i j}\right) \cdot\left(\sum_{k \neq i, j} e_{k}+u_{i j}\right)-x \\
& =2 x-x=x
\end{aligned}
$$

Next let $x \in \mathfrak{J}_{i k}, k \neq i, j$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
x U_{(i j)} & =2 x \cdot\left(\sum_{l \neq i, j} e_{l}+u_{i j}\right) \cdot\left(\sum_{l \neq i, j} e_{l}+u_{i j}\right)-x \\
& =\left(x+2 x \cdot u_{i j}\right) \cdot\left(\sum_{l \neq i, j} e_{l}+u_{i j}\right)-x \\
& =\frac{1}{2} x+x \cdot u_{i j}+x \cdot u_{i j}+2 x \cdot u_{i j} \cdot u_{i j}-x \\
& =\frac{1}{2} x+2 x \cdot u_{i j}+x \cdot u_{i j}{ }^{2}-x \quad(\mathrm{PD} 10) \\
& =\frac{1}{2} x+2 x \cdot u_{i j}+\frac{1}{2} x-x \\
& =x\left(2 R_{i j}\right) .
\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, it follows that $U_{(i j)}=2 R_{i j}$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{j k}$. Since $\mathfrak{J}_{i k} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{i j} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{j k}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{j k} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{i j} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{i k}$ and $U_{(i j)}$ is an automorphism it is clear that $\mathfrak{J}_{j k}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{i k}$ are interchanged by $U_{(i j)}$.

We apply this lemma to the $u_{1 j}$ which are given in the statement of the theorem. This gives $n-1$ automorphisms $U_{(1 j)}$ of period two in $\mathfrak{J}$. Set $u_{j 1}=u_{1 j}, j>1$ and $u_{i j}=u_{i 1} U_{(1 j)}$ if $1, i, j \neq$. Then, by Lemma $1(3), u_{i j}=2 u_{i 1} R_{1 j}=2 u_{i 1} \cdot u_{1 j}$. Hence $u_{i j}=u_{j i}$ for all $i, j(i \neq j)$. Since $U_{(1 j)}$ is an automorphism such that $\left(e_{1}+e_{i}\right) U_{1 j}=e_{i}+e_{j}$ and $u_{i 1}{ }^{.2}=e_{1}+e_{i}$ we have $u_{i j}{ }^{.2}=e_{i}+e_{j}$. Hence Lemma 1 is applicable to all the $u_{i j}$ and the corresponding mappings $U_{(i j)}$ and $R_{i j}$. Also we have $p_{i j}=p_{i 1} U_{(1 j)}$, so $U_{(i j)}=U_{p_{i j}}=U_{p_{i 1} U_{(1 j)}}=U_{(1 j)} U_{(1 i)} U_{(1 j)}=U_{(1 i)} U_{(1 j)} U_{(1 i)}$ because of the symmetry in $i$ and $j$.

Lemma 2. Let $\Sigma$ denote the group of automorphisms in $\mathfrak{J}$ generated by the $U_{(1 j)}, j=2, \cdots, n$. Then we have a unique isomorphism $\pi \rightarrow U_{\pi}$ of the symmetric group $S_{n}$ onto $\Sigma$ such that $(1 j) \rightarrow U_{(1 j)}$. We have $e_{i} U_{\pi}=e_{i \pi}$ for any $i=1,2, \cdots, n$ and any $\pi \in S_{n}$. Moreover, if $\pi$ and $\pi^{\prime} \in S_{n}$ and $i \pi=i \pi^{\prime}, j \pi=j \pi^{\prime}(i=j$ allowed) then $U_{\pi}$ and $U_{\pi^{\prime}}$ have the same effect on the Peirce space $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$.

Proof. Let $\mathfrak{F}$ be the free group with $n-1$ generators $x_{2}, x_{3}, \cdots, x_{n}, \theta$ the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{F}$ onto $S_{n}$ such that $x_{j} \rightarrow(1 j)$. It is known that the kernel $\Omega$ of $\theta$ is the invariant subgroup of $\mathfrak{F}$ generated by the elements

$$
x_{j}^{2},\left(x_{j} x_{k}\right)^{3},\left(x_{j} x_{k} x_{j} x_{l}\right)^{2}, \quad j, k, l \neq
$$

(Burnside's Theory of Groups of Finite Order, second edition, Dover reprint, p. 464). Now we have $U_{(1 j)}{ }^{2}=1 .\left(U_{(1 j)} U_{(1 k)}\right)^{3}=\left(U_{(1 j)} U_{(1 k)} U_{(1 j)}\right)\left(U_{(1 k)} U_{(1 j)} U_{(1 k)}\right) =U_{(j k)} U_{(j k)}=1$ and $\left(U_{(1 j)} U_{(1 k)} U_{(1 j)} U_{(11)}\right)^{2}$

$$
=\left(U_{(1 j)} U_{(1 k)} U_{(1 j)}\right) U_{(11)}\left(U_{(1 j)} U_{(1 k)} U_{(1 j)}\right) U_{(1 l)}=U_{(j k)} U_{(1 l)} U_{(j k)} U_{(1 l)} .
$$

We have $U_{(j k)}=U_{p_{j k}}, U_{1 i}=U_{p_{1 i}}$ and $U_{(j k)} U_{(1 i)} U_{(j k)}=U_{p_{j k}} U_{p_{1 i}} U_{p_{j k}}=U_{p_{1 i} U_{j k}} =U_{p_{11}}$ by Lemma 1 (2). Hence $U_{(j k)} U_{(11)} U_{(j k)} U_{(11)}=U_{(11)}{ }^{2}=1$. Hence $\Omega$ is mapped into 1 in the homomorphism of F onto $\Sigma$ such that $x_{j} \rightarrow U_{(1 j)}$. Consequently, we have a homomorphism of $S_{n}$ onto $\Sigma$ such that $(1 j) \rightarrow U_{(1 j)}$. If $U_{\pi}$ denotes the image of $\pi \in S_{n}$ in this homomorphism then $U_{\pi}$ is a product of $U_{(1 j)}$. Hence, by Lemma $1, U_{\pi}$ maps $\left\{e_{i}\right\}$ into itself. Moreover, since $U_{(1 j)}$ interchanges $e_{1}$ and $e_{j}$ and leaves the other $e_{i}$ fixed we have $e_{i} U_{(1 j)}=e_{i(1 j)}, i=1,2, \cdots, n$. Consequently, $e_{i} U_{\pi}=e_{i \pi}$ for any $i$ and $\pi \in S_{n}$. It is clear from this that $\pi \rightarrow U_{\pi}$ is 1-1. Also uniqueness is clear since the transpositions ( $1 j$ ) generate $S_{n}$. If $1, i, j \neq$ and $\pi=(i j)$ then $U_{\pi}=U_{(1 i)} U_{(1 j)} U_{(1 i)}=U_{(i j)}$ as defined before. Now let $\pi$ and $\pi^{\prime}$ satisfy $i \pi=i \pi^{\prime}, j \pi=j \pi^{\prime}$. Then $\pi^{\prime \prime}=\pi^{\prime} \pi^{-1}$ fixes $i$ and $j$. Hence this is a product of transpositions $(k l), k, l \neq i, j$. Hence, by Lemma $1, U_{\pi^{\prime \prime}}$, which is a product of $U_{(k l)}$, is the identity on $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. Hence $\pi$ and $\pi^{\prime}$ have the same effect on $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$.

We now let $\mathfrak{D}$ be the Peirce space $\mathfrak{J}_{12}$ and we define an algebra structure on $\mathfrak{D}$ by the multiplication

$$
\begin{equation*}
x y=2 x U_{(23)} \cdot y U_{(13)} \tag{33}
\end{equation*}
$$

Lemma 3. $\mathfrak{D}$ is an algebra with identity element $u_{12}$ and the mapping $d \rightarrow \bar{d}=d U_{(12)}$ is an involution in $\mathfrak{D}$.

Proof. It is clear that $x y$ is bilinear and $x y \in \mathfrak{D}$ since $x U_{(23)} \in \mathfrak{I}_{13}$ and $y U_{(13)} \in \Im_{23}$. Hence $\mathfrak{D}$ is an algebra. Put $y=u_{12}$ in (33). This gives $x u_{12} =2 x U_{(23)} \cdot u_{12} U_{(13)}=2 x U_{(23)} \cdot u_{23}=x U_{(23)}{ }^{2}=x$ since $x U_{(23)} \in \mathfrak{J}_{13}$ and $U_{(23)}$ coincides with $2 R_{u_{23}}$ on this space. Hence $u_{12}$ is a right identity element for $\mathfrak{D}$. We have $U_{(23)} U_{(12)}=U_{(12)} U_{(13)}$ and $U_{(13)} U_{(12)}=U_{(12)} U_{(23)}$ since (23)(12) $=(12)$ (13) and $(13)(12)=(12)(23)$ in $S_{n}$. Hence $\overline{x y}=2\left(x U_{(23)} \cdot y U_{(13)}\right) U_{(12)} =2 x U_{(23)} U_{(12)} \cdot y U_{(13)} U_{(12)}=2 x U_{(12)} U_{(13)} \cdot y U_{(12)} U_{(23)}=2 \bar{y} U_{(23)} \cdot \bar{x} U_{(13)} =\bar{y} \bar{x}$. Hence $x \rightarrow \bar{x}$ is an involution. It follows that $\mathfrak{D}$ has the left identity $\bar{u}_{12}$. This must coincide with $u_{12}$.

For each ordered pair of indices $i, j$ we shall now define mappings $x \rightarrow x_{i j}$ of $\mathfrak{D}$ into the Peirce space $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}=\mathfrak{J}_{j i}$. If $i \neq j$ we let $\pi$ be a permutation such that $1 \pi=i, 2 \pi=j$ and if $i=j$ then we let $\pi$ be a permutation such that $1 \pi=i$. Then we define

$$
\begin{equation*}
x_{i j}=x U_{\pi}, \quad i \neq j, \quad x_{i i}=2 x R_{12} R_{e_{1}} U_{\pi} \tag{34}
\end{equation*}
$$

It is clear that $x \rightarrow x_{i j}(i=j$ allowed $)$ is linear. If $i \neq j$ we have $x_{j i}=x U_{(12)} U_{\pi}=\bar{x}_{i j}$. Hence

$$
\begin{equation*}
x_{j i}=\bar{x}_{i j} \tag{35}
\end{equation*}
$$

holds for $i \neq j$. To establish this for $i=j$ we note that since $u_{12}{ }^{.2}=e_{1}+e_{2}$ and this is the identity on $\mathfrak{J}_{11}+\mathfrak{J}_{12}+\mathfrak{J}_{22}$, we see by Theorem 20 of §2.13 (or directly) that $\boldsymbol{R}_{\mathbf{1 2}}{ }^{\mathbf{3}}=\boldsymbol{R}_{\mathbf{1 2}}$ on $\mathfrak{I}_{\mathbf{1 1}}+\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbf{1 2}}+\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbf{2 2}}$. Hence $\boldsymbol{U}_{\mathbf{( 1 2 )}} \boldsymbol{R}_{\mathbf{1 2}}=\left(\mathbf{2} \boldsymbol{R}_{\mathbf{1 2}}{ }^{\mathbf{2}}-\mathbf{1}\right) \boldsymbol{R}_{\mathbf{1 2}}=\boldsymbol{R}_{\mathbf{1 2}}$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{11}+\mathfrak{J}_{12}+\mathfrak{J}_{22}$. Hence if $x \in \mathfrak{J}_{12}$ then $\bar{x}_{i i}=2 x U_{(12)} R_{12} R_{e_{1}} U_{\pi}=2 x R_{12} R_{e_{1}} U_{\pi}=x_{i i}$.

We note next that if $i \neq j$ then $x_{i j} U_{\pi^{\prime}}=x U_{\pi} U_{\pi^{\prime}}=x U_{\pi \pi^{\prime}}=x_{i \pi^{\prime}, j \pi^{\prime}}$. Also $x_{i i} U_{\pi^{\prime}}=2 x R_{12} R_{e_{1}} U_{\pi} U_{\pi^{\prime}}=2 x R_{12} R_{e_{1}} U_{\pi \pi^{\prime}}=x_{i \pi^{\prime}, i \pi^{\prime}}$. Hence for all $i, j$ we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
x_{i j} U_{\pi^{\prime}}=x_{i \pi^{\prime}, j \pi^{\prime}} \tag{36}
\end{equation*}
$$

If we now denote the identity element $u_{12}$ of $\mathfrak{D}$ as 1 , then we have $1_{i i}=2 u_{12}{ }^{.2} \cdot e_{1} U_{\pi} =2 e_{1} U_{\pi}=2 e_{i}$ and if $j>2$, then $1_{1 j}=u_{12} U_{(2 j)}=2 u_{12} \cdot u_{2 j}=4 u_{12} \cdot\left(u_{12} \cdot u_{1 j}\right) =u_{1 j} U_{(12)}{ }^{2}=u_{1 j}$. Since $1_{12}=u_{12}$ is clear, we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{1}_{i i}=2 e_{i}, \quad \mathbf{1}_{1 j}=u_{1 j}, \quad j \geqq 2 . \tag{37}
\end{equation*}
$$

If $1 \pi=i, 2 \pi=j$ then $U_{\pi}$ is an automorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ which permutes the Peirce spaces $\mathfrak{J}_{k l}, k \neq l$. Since it maps $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{J}_{12}$ into $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ it is clear that the mapping $x \rightarrow x_{i j}, i \neq j$, is a bijective linear mapping of $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{J}_{12}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. We shall now prove the following formulas for $x, y$ in $\mathfrak{D}$ :

$$
\begin{align*}
2 x_{i j} \cdot y_{j k} & =(x y)_{i k},  \tag{38}\\
2 x_{i i} \cdot y_{i j} & =((x+\bar{x}) y)_{i j},  \tag{39}\\
2 x_{i j} \cdot y_{j i} \cdot e_{i} & =(x y)_{i i},  \tag{40}\\
2 x_{i i}^{2} & =(x+\bar{x})_{i i}^{2}, \tag{41}
\end{align*}
$$

if $i, j, k$ are unequal. We note first that the definition (33) gives $(x y)_{12}=2 x_{13} \cdot y_{32}$. Now let $\pi$ be a permutation such that $1 \pi=i, 2 \pi=k, 3 \pi=j$. Then we have $(x y)_{12} U_{\pi}=2 x_{13} U_{\pi} \cdot y_{32} U_{\pi}$. Hence $(x y)_{i k}=2 x_{i j} \cdot y_{j k}$, which proves (38). The argument just used shows also that it is enough to prove (39)-(41) for $i=1, j=2$. If $x \in \mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{J}_{12}$ then $2 x_{13} \cdot 1_{31} \cdot e_{1}=2 x U_{(23)} \cdot u_{13} \cdot e_{1}=4 x \cdot u_{23} \cdot u_{13} \cdot e_{1} =4 x \cdot\left(u_{23} \cdot u_{13}\right) \cdot e_{1}(\mathrm{PD} 12)=2 x \cdot 1_{13} U_{(23)} \cdot e_{1}=2 x \cdot 1_{12} \cdot e_{1}=x_{11}$. Hence

$$
\begin{equation*}
2 x_{13} \cdot 1_{31} \cdot e_{1}=x_{11} . \tag{42}
\end{equation*}
$$

We now have $2 x_{11}, y_{12}=4 x_{13}, 1_{31}, e_{1}, y_{12}=4 x_{13}, 1_{31}, y_{12}=4 x_{13},\left(1_{31}, y_{12}\right) +41_{31} \cdot\left(x_{13} \cdot y_{12}\right)($ PD10 $)=2 x_{13} \cdot y_{32}+2\left(1_{31} \cdot(\bar{x} y)_{32}\right)((38),(35))=(x y)_{12} +(\bar{x} y)_{12}=((x+\bar{x}) y)_{12}$. This implies (39). Next we have $x_{11}, y_{11} =4 x_{12} \cdot 1_{21} \cdot e_{1} \cdot\left(y_{13} \cdot 1_{31} \cdot e_{1}\right)=4 x_{12} \cdot 1_{21} \cdot\left(y_{13} \cdot 1_{31}\right)=-4 x_{12} \cdot 1_{31} \cdot\left(1_{21} \cdot y_{13}\right) -4 x_{12} \cdot y_{13} \cdot\left(1_{21} \cdot 1_{31}\right)+4 x_{12} \cdot 1_{21} \cdot y_{13} \cdot 1_{31}+4 x_{12} \cdot 1_{31} \cdot y_{13} \cdot 1_{21} +4 x_{12} \cdot\left(1_{31} \cdot 1_{21} \cdot y_{13}\right)=-x_{32} \cdot y_{23}-(\bar{x} y)_{23} \cdot 1_{32}+2 x_{11} \cdot y_{13} \cdot 1_{31} +(y x)_{12} \cdot 1_{21}+x_{12} \cdot y_{12}$. By (39), this gives

$$
\begin{align*}
x_{11} \cdot y_{11}=-x_{32} \cdot y_{23}-(\bar{x} y)_{23} \cdot 1_{32} & +((x+\bar{x}) y)_{13} \cdot 1_{31} \\
& +(y x)_{12} \cdot 1_{21}+x_{12} \cdot y_{12} . \tag{43}
\end{align*}
$$

If we multiply this by $e_{3}$ we obtain

$$
x_{32} \cdot y_{23} \cdot e_{3}=-(\bar{x} y)_{23} \cdot 1_{32} \cdot e_{3}+((x+\bar{x}) y)_{13} \cdot 1_{31} \cdot e_{3} .
$$

Applying $2 U_{(13)}$ to both sides we obtain, by (42) and (35), $2 x_{12} \cdot y_{21} \cdot e_{1} =-(\bar{y} x)_{11}+(\bar{y}(x+\bar{x}))_{11}=(\bar{y} \bar{x})_{11}=(x y)_{11}$. Hence (40) is valid. Next we multiply (43) by $2 e_{1}$ and set $y=x$. This gives $2 x_{11}{ }^{.2}=((x+\bar{x}) x)_{11}+\left(x^{2}\right)_{11}+2 x_{12} \cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{1} =\left((x+\bar{x}) x+x^{2}+x \bar{x}\right)_{11}=\left((x+\bar{x}) x+\bar{x}^{2}+x \bar{x}\right)_{11}=(x+\bar{x})^{2}{ }_{11}$. This implies(41).
We can now give the
Proof of Theorem 5. Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be the algebra $\mathfrak{J}_{12}$ with the product (33), and consider the algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)$. We use the notation $x[i j]=x e_{i j}+\bar{x} e_{j i}, x \in \mathfrak{D}$, and the formulas (18')-(23') of §2. If $i \neq j$ then we have seen that $x \rightarrow x_{i j}$ is a $1-1$ linear mapping of $\mathfrak{D}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. Also $x_{i j}=\bar{x}_{j i}$. It follows that $x_{i j} \rightarrow x[i j]$ is a $1-1$ linear mapping $\eta_{i j}$ of $\mathfrak{I}_{i j}$ onto the subspace of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)$ of elements $x[i j], x \in \mathfrak{D}$, and $\eta_{i j}=\eta_{j i}$. Now let $y \in \mathfrak{J}_{11}$. Then $y U_{(12)} \in \mathfrak{J}_{22}$ so $y U_{(12)} \cdot e_{1}=0$. This gives $2 y \cdot u_{12} \cdot u_{12} \cdot e_{1}=y \cdot u_{12}{ }^{\cdot 2} \cdot e_{1}=y$. Since $x=y \cdot u_{12} \in \mathfrak{I}_{12}$ this shows that any $y \in \mathfrak{J}_{11}$ has the form $x_{11}=2 x . u_{12} . e_{1}$. Also since $x_{11}=\bar{x}_{11}$ we may write $y=x_{11}$
where $\bar{x}=x$. If we put $a=u_{12}, b=e_{1}$ in $2 R_{a} \dot{R}_{b} R_{a}+R_{b, \cdot 2}=2 R_{a} R_{a, b}+R_{b} R_{a \cdot 2}$ we obtain $2 R_{12} R_{e_{1}} R_{12}+R_{e_{1}}=R_{12}{ }^{2}+R_{e_{1}}\left(R_{e_{1}}+R_{e_{2}}\right)$. Since $e_{1}+e_{2}$ is the identity on $\mathfrak{J}_{11}+\mathfrak{J}_{12}+\mathfrak{J}_{22}$ this gives $2 x R_{12} R_{e_{1}} R_{12}=x R_{12}{ }^{2}$ if $x \in \mathfrak{J}_{12}$. Hence if $x \in \mathfrak{I}_{12}$ and $x_{11}=2 x R_{12} R_{e_{1}}=0$ then $x R_{12}{ }^{2}=0$. Then $\bar{x}=x U_{(12)}=2 x . u_{12} . u_{12} -x=-x$. Hence $x \rightarrow x_{11}$ is $1-1$ on the subspace of symmetric elements of $\mathfrak{D}$. Our results imply that the restriction $\eta_{i i}$ of the mapping $x \rightarrow x_{i i}$ to the space of symmetric elements of $\mathfrak{D}$ is $1-1$ and surjective on $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}$. Hence the mapping $\eta_{i i}: x_{i i} \rightarrow x[i i]$ is a 1-1 linear mapping of $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}$ onto the subspace of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)$ of elements $x[i i]$. It follows that if we let $\eta$ be the linear mapping of $\mathfrak{J}$ which coincides with $\eta_{i j}$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}, i, j=1,2, \cdots$, then $\eta$ is a bijection of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)$. A comparison of (35), (38)-(41) with (18')-(23') and properties of the Peirce decomposition show that $\eta$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)$. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is Jordan, clearly $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)$ is a Jordan matrix algebra. Also, by (37), $e_{i}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)_{i i} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}[i i]$ and $u_{i j}=1_{1 j} \rightarrow 1[1 j]$. Hence the theorem is proved.
We shall now extend the foregoing result to the following
Coordinatization Theorem. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with 1 which is a sum of $n \geqq 3$ connected nonzero orthogonal idempotent elements. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is isomorphic to a Jordan matrix algebra. More precisely, assume $1=\Sigma_{1}^{n} e_{i}$, $n \geqq 3$, where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents $\neq 0$ and let $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{i \leq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ be the Peirce decomposition relative to the $e_{i}$. Assume that for $j=2,3, \cdots, n$ there exists an element $u_{1 j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{1 j}$ which is invertible in $\mathfrak{J}_{11}+\mathfrak{J}_{j j}+\mathfrak{J}_{1 j}$. Then there exists a Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ and an isomorphism $\zeta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ such that $e_{i}{ }^{\zeta}=\frac{1}{2}[i i], u_{1 j}{ }^{\zeta}=1[1 j]$ (cf. (17)).

Proof. We shall obtain a reduction of the result to the preceding one via isotopy. ${ }^{\mathbf{1}}$ Let $u_{j 1}$ be the inverse of $u_{1 j}$ relative to $e_{1}+e_{j}$. As in Lemma 5 of §1, we introduce the elements $f_{1}=e_{1}=g_{1}, f_{j}=u_{j 1} \cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{j}, g_{j}=u_{1 j} \cdot{ }^{2} \cdot e_{j}, \quad j \geqq 2$, $f=\Sigma_{1}^{n} f_{i}, g=\Sigma_{1}^{n} g_{i}$ (cf. (14)). Then, by Lemma 1.5, $f$ and $g$ are inverses in $\mathfrak{J}$ and the $f_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotent elements of the isotope $(\mathfrak{J}, g)$ such that $\Sigma f_{i}=f$ is the identity of $(\mathfrak{J}, g)$. Moreover, $u_{j 1}$ is in the Peirce space $(\mathfrak{J}, g)_{1 j}$ relative to the $f_{i}$ and $u_{j 1 \cdot g} u_{j 1}=f_{1}+f_{j}$. Thus the $f_{i}$ and $u_{j 1}$ satisfy the conditions for the $e_{i}$ and $u_{1 j}$ given in Theorem 5. Consequently, we have an isomorphism $\eta$ of $(\mathfrak{J}, g)$ onto a Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)$ such that $f_{i}{ }^{\eta}=e_{i i}, u_{j 1}{ }^{\eta}=e_{1 j}+e_{j 1}$. Then $\eta$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$, which is the $f^{\cdot 2}$-isotope of $(\mathfrak{J}, g)$, onto $\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right),\left(f^{\cdot 2}\right)^{2}\right)$. We have $f^{\cdot 2}=\Sigma f_{i}^{\cdot 2}$ and $\left\{f_{i}{ }^{\cdot 2} g f_{i}\right\}=\left\{f_{i}{ }^{\cdot 2} g_{i} f_{i}\right\}=f_{i}{ }^{\cdot 2}$ since $f_{i}, g_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i i}$ and these are inverses in $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}$. Hence $f_{i}{ }^{2}$ is in the Peirce space $(\mathfrak{J}, g)_{i i}$ relative to the $f_{i}$. It follows that $\left(f_{i}^{\cdot 2}\right)^{\eta}=a_{i} e_{i i}$ where $a_{i}$ is a symmetric element of $\mathfrak{D}$. Also $f_{1}^{\cdot 2}=e_{1}$ so $\left(f_{1}^{\cdot 2}\right)^{\eta}=e_{11}$. Hence $\left(f^{\cdot 2}\right)^{\eta}=a=\operatorname{diag}\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}\right\}, a_{1}=1$, and $\eta$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto the isotope $\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right), a\right)$ of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)$. We recall also that the

[^12]mapping $X \rightarrow X a$ is an isomorphism of the isotope $\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)\right.$, a) onto the Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ where $J_{a}$ is the canonical involution $X \rightarrow a^{-1} \bar{X}^{t} a$ (§1.12, p. 60). Hence we have the isomorphism $\zeta: x \rightarrow x^{\eta} a$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$. It remains to verify that $e_{i}^{\zeta}=\frac{1}{2}[i i]$ and $u_{1 j}^{\zeta}=1[1 j]$. We have $u_{j 1}{ }^{\eta}=e_{1 j}+e_{j 1}$ so $u_{j 1}{ }^{\zeta}=\left(e_{1 j}+e_{j 1}\right) a=e_{j 1}+a_{j} e_{1 j}\left(\right.$ since $\left.a_{1}=1\right)$. Also we have $f_{i}{ }^{\eta}=e_{i i},\left(f_{i}{ }^{-2}\right)^{\eta}=a_{i} e_{i i}$. We now note that

$$
\begin{align*}
\left\{e_{i} g f_{i}\right\} & =\left\{e_{i} g_{i} f_{i}\right\}=e_{i}, \\
\left\{f_{i}^{.2} g f_{i}\right\} & =\left\{f_{i}^{.2} g_{i} f_{i}\right\}=f_{i}^{.2},  \tag{44}\\
\left\{e_{i} g f_{i}^{.2}\right\} & =\left\{e_{i} g_{i} f_{i}^{.2}\right\}=f_{i}, \\
\left\{\left\{e_{i} g e_{i}\right\} g f_{i}^{.2}\right\} & =\left\{g_{i} g_{i} f_{i}^{.2}\right\}=e_{i} .
\end{align*}
$$

These relations follow from the fact that $f_{i}$ and $g_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i i}$ are inverses in this subalgebra with identity $e_{i}$. On the other hand, (44) show that $f_{i}^{\cdot 2}$ and $e_{i} \in(\mathfrak{J}, g)_{i i}$ where $(\mathfrak{J}, g)_{i j}$ are the Peirce spaces of $(\mathfrak{J}, g)$ relative to the $f_{i}$, and $f_{i}{ }^{2}$ and $e_{i}$ are inverses in $(\mathfrak{J}, g)_{i i}$. Since $f_{i}{ }^{\boldsymbol{\eta}}=e_{i i}$ and $\left(f_{i}{ }^{\boldsymbol{-} \mathbf{2}}\right)^{\boldsymbol{\eta}}=a_{i} e_{i i}$ it follows that $e_{i}{ }^{\boldsymbol{\eta}}=a_{i}{ }^{\boldsymbol{-} \mathbf{1}} e_{i i}$ and $e_{i}^{\zeta}=e_{i}^{7} a=e_{i i}$. Also since $u_{1 j}$ is the inverse of $u_{j 1}$ relative to $e_{1}+e_{j}$ and $u_{j 1}^{\zeta}=e_{j 1}+a_{j} e_{1 j}$ it follows that $u_{1 j}^{\zeta}=e_{1 j}+a_{j}{ }^{-1} e_{j 1}=1[1 j]$. This completes the proof.

The Jordan matrix algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ with $n \geqq 4$ are necessarily special since in this case $\mathfrak{D}$ must be associative. It follows from the Coordinatization Theorem that any Jordan algebra with $1=\sum_{1}^{n} e_{i}, n \geqq 4, e_{i}$ nonzero connected orthogonal idempotents is special. Moreover, these conditions carry over to any Jordan algebra having the given Jordan algebra as subalgebra with the same identity. Hence we have the following

Corollary. Let J be a Jordan algebra with $1=\Sigma_{1}^{n} e_{i} n \geqq 4, e_{i}$ nonzero connected orthogonal idempotents. Then every Jordan algebra containing I as subalgebra with the same identity element is special.
4. Perfection of certain classes of associative algebras with involutions. We recall that an associative algebra with involution ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{J}$ ) is called perfect if $\mathfrak{A}$ and the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{J})$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ constitute a unital special universal envelope for the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}$ (§2.4). This means that given any homomorphism $\sigma$ of $\mathscr{H}$ into $\mathscr{G}^{+}$where $\mathscr{G}$ is an associative algebra with 1 such that $1^{\sigma}=1$, then $\sigma$ has a unique extension to a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{G}$. In this section we shall prove perfection for associative algebras with involution of the form ( $\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}$ ) where $J_{a}$ is a canonical involution and $n \geqq 3$. We shall establish also perfection for $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{2}, J_{a}\right)$ provided that the set $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, \mathfrak{j})$ of symmetric elements of $\mathfrak{D}$ generates $\mathfrak{D}$. The result for $n \geqq 3$ is due to Jacobson and Rickart in [2]. We shall derive this and also the result for $n=2$ as corollaries of a more general theorem which has been proved recently by Martindale in [1].

In this theorem one considers an arbitrary associative algebra with involution ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) such that $\mathfrak{A}$ has an identity element $1=\sum_{1}^{n} e_{i}$ where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotent elements in $\mathfrak{A}\left(e_{i}{ }^{2}=e_{i}, e_{i} e_{j}=0\right.$ if $\left.i \neq j\right)$ such that $e_{i} \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and $\mathfrak{U} e_{i} \mathfrak{U}=\mathfrak{A}, i=1,2, \cdots, n$. The last condition is that the (two-sided) ideal in $\mathfrak{U}$ generated by every $e_{i}$ is $\mathfrak{U}$ itself. In particular, this holds if $\mathfrak{U}$ is a simple algebra. Martindale's theorem asserts that under the given hypotheses, ( $\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is perfect if either $n \geqq 3$ or $n=2$ and the set $\mathfrak{H} \cap e_{i} \mathfrak{U} e_{i}$ of symmetric elements of $e_{i} \mathfrak{U} e_{i}$ generates the associative algebra $e_{i} \mathfrak{U} e_{i}$ for $i=1,2, \cdots, n$.

Now let $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ be an associative algebra with involution and identity element 1 and let $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ the $n \times n$ matrix algebra over $\mathfrak{D}$ and $J_{a}$ a canonical involution defined by $a=\operatorname{diag}\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}\right\}$ where $a_{i}=\bar{a}_{i}$ is invertible in $\mathfrak{D}$. Using the usual $x[i j]$ notation of (17) we put $e_{i}=\frac{1}{2}[i i]$ so that $e_{i}=e_{i i}$ where $e_{i j}, i, j=1,2, \cdots, n$ are the matrix units. Then the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{A}$ contained in $\mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ and $\sum_{1}^{n} e_{i}=1$. If $d \in \mathfrak{D}$ we have $d e_{j k}=d e_{j i} e_{i} e_{i k} \in \mathfrak{D}_{n} e_{i} \mathfrak{D}_{n}$. Hence the $e_{i}$ satisfy the first set of conditions of Martindale's theorem. Clearly $e_{i} \mathfrak{A} e_{i}$ is the set of matrices $d e_{i i}, d \in \mathfrak{D}$ and such a matrix is in $\mathfrak{H}$ if and only if $a_{i}{ }^{-1} d a_{i} =d$ or $a_{i} d=d a_{i} \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. In particular, $a_{i} e_{i i}$ and $a_{i}{ }^{-1} e_{i i} \in \mathfrak{H} \cap e_{i} \mathfrak{A} e_{i}$. It follows that $\mathfrak{H} \cap e_{i} \mathfrak{U} e_{i}$ generates $e_{i} \mathfrak{U} e_{i}$ if and only if $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ generates $\mathfrak{D}$. Hence Martindale's theorem will imply that ( $\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}$ ) is perfect if $n \geqq 3$, and ( $\mathfrak{D}_{2}, J_{a}$ ) is perfect if $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, \boldsymbol{j})$ generates $\mathfrak{D}$.
Now let ( $\mathfrak{U}, J)$ be an associative algebra with involution satisfying the hypotheses of Martindale's theorem relative to the orthogonal idempotents $e_{i}$. We have the associative two-sided Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{A}$ as $\mathfrak{U}=\Sigma_{i, j=1}^{n} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{i j}$ where $\mathfrak{U}_{i j}=e_{i} \mathfrak{U} e_{j}$. The condition $\mathfrak{A} e_{j} \mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}$ for $j=1,2, \cdots, n$ evidently implies that $\mathfrak{U}_{i j} \mathfrak{U}_{j k}=\mathfrak{U}_{i k}$. Also we have $\mathfrak{U}_{i j} \mathfrak{U}_{k l}=0$ if $j \neq k$ since $e_{j} e_{k}=0$. Since $e_{i}{ }^{J}=e_{i}$ it is clear that if $a_{i j} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i j}$ then $a_{i j}{ }^{j} \in \mathfrak{A}_{j i}$. It is evident also that the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents in the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$. Since $2 x U_{e_{i}, e_{j}}=e_{i} x e_{j}+e_{j} x e_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i j}+\mathfrak{U}_{j i}$ it is clear that the Peirce space $\mathfrak{A}_{i j}{ }^{+} \equiv \mathfrak{A} U_{e_{i, e_{j}}}=\mathfrak{A}_{i j}+\mathfrak{A}_{j i}$. Since $e_{i} \in \mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{H}$ relative to the $\boldsymbol{e}_{\boldsymbol{i}}$ is $\mathfrak{H}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{i} \leqq \boldsymbol{j}} \oplus \mathfrak{H}_{\boldsymbol{i} \boldsymbol{j}}$ where $\mathfrak{H}_{i j}=\mathfrak{H} \cap \mathfrak{A}_{i j}{ }^{+}=\mathfrak{H} \cap\left(\mathfrak{A}_{i j}+\mathfrak{A}_{j i}\right)$.
Let $\sigma$ be a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{H}$ into $\mathfrak{G}^{+}$where $\mathfrak{G}$ is an associative algebra with 1 . We assume also that $1^{\sigma}=1$. Put $g_{i}=e_{i}^{\sigma}, i=1,2, \cdots, n$. Then the $g_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{G}$ (cf. §2.2, p. 72) and $\Sigma_{1}^{n} g_{i}=1$. Hence we have the two-sided Peirce decomposition $\mathfrak{G}=\Sigma \oplus \mathfrak{G}_{i j}, \mathfrak{G}_{i j}=g_{i} \mathfrak{G}_{j}$, of the associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ and the Peirce decomposition of the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{G}^{+}$as $\mathfrak{G}^{+} =\Sigma \oplus \mathfrak{G}_{i j}{ }^{+}$where $\mathfrak{G}_{i j}{ }^{+}=\mathfrak{G}_{i j}+\mathfrak{G}_{j i}$. Since $e_{i}^{\sigma}=g_{i}$ it isclear that $\mathfrak{H}_{i j}{ }^{\sigma} \subseteq \mathfrak{G}_{i j}{ }^{+}=\mathfrak{G}_{i j} +\mathfrak{G}_{j i}$. Now let $i \neq j$ and let $x_{i j} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i j}$. Then $x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{j} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i j}{ }^{+} \cap \mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}_{i j}$ so $\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right)^{\sigma}=y_{i j}+y_{j i}$ where $y_{i j}$ and $y_{j i}$ are uniquely determined elements of $\mathfrak{G}_{i j}$ and $\mathfrak{G}_{j i}$ respectively. We use this to define a mapping $\eta_{i j}$ of $\mathfrak{U}_{i j}$ into $\mathfrak{G}_{i j}$ for $i \neq j$ by

$$
\begin{equation*}
x_{j}^{\eta_{i j}}=y_{i j} . \tag{45}
\end{equation*}
$$

It is clear that $\eta_{i j}$ is linear. Since $x_{i j}{ }^{J^{2}}=x_{i j}$ and $x_{i j}{ }^{J} \in \mathfrak{A}_{j i}$ we have $\left(x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right)^{\eta_{j i}}=y_{j i}$. Hence

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\sigma}=x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}}+\left(x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{j i}}, \quad i \neq j \tag{46}
\end{equation*}
$$

We now prove the following
Lemma. If $x_{i j} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i j}, x_{j i} \in \mathfrak{A}_{j i}$ etc. and $i, j, k$ are distinct then

$$
\begin{align*}
\left(x_{i j} x_{j i}+x_{j i}{ }^{J} x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right)^{\sigma} & =x_{i j}{ }^{\eta_{i j}} x_{j i}{ }^{\eta_{j i}}+\left(x_{j i}{ }^{J}\right)^{\eta_{i j}}\left(x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right)^{\eta_{j i}} .  \tag{47}\\
\left(x_{i j} x_{j k}\right)^{\eta_{i k}} & =x_{i j}{ }^{\eta_{i j}} x_{j k}{ }^{\eta_{j k}} . \tag{48}
\end{align*}
$$

If $h_{i i} \in \mathfrak{H}_{i i}$ and $h_{j j} \in \mathfrak{H}_{j j}$ then

$$
\begin{align*}
& \left(h_{i i} x_{i j}\right)^{\eta_{i j}}=h_{i i}^{\sigma} x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}}, \\
& \left(x_{i j} h_{j j}\right)^{\eta_{i j}}=x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}} h_{j j}^{\sigma} . \tag{49}
\end{align*}
$$

Proof. For the proof of (47) we consider

$$
\begin{array}{r}
\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right)\left(x_{j i}+x_{j i}{ }^{J}\right)+\left(x_{j i}+x_{j i}{ }^{J}\right)\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right) \\
=\left(x_{i j} x_{j i}+x_{j i}{ }^{J} x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right)+\left(x_{j i} x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{J} x_{j i}{ }^{J}\right) .
\end{array}
$$

Applying $\sigma$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\left(x_{i j} x_{j i}+x_{j i}^{J} x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\sigma}+\left(x_{j i} x_{i j}+x_{i j}^{J} x_{j i}^{J}\right)^{\sigma} \\
&=\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\sigma}\left(x_{j i}+x_{j i}^{J}\right)^{\sigma}+\left(x_{j i}+x_{j i}^{J}\right)^{\sigma}\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\sigma} \\
&=\left(x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}}+\left(x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{j i}}\right)\left(x_{j i}^{\eta_{j i}}+\left(x_{j i}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{i j}}\right) \\
&+\left(x_{j i}^{\eta_{j i}}+\left(x_{j i}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{i j}}\right)\left(x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}}+\left(x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{j i}}\right) \\
&=\left(x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}} x_{j i}^{\eta_{j i}}+\left(x_{j i}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{i j}}\left(x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{j i}}\right) \\
&+\left(x_{j i}^{\eta_{j i}} x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}}+\left(x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{j i}}\left(x_{j i}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{i j}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Comparison of the parts in $\mathfrak{G}_{i i}$ yields (47). Next assume $i, j, k$ unequal, $x_{i j} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i j}, x_{j k} \in \mathfrak{A}_{j k}$. Then $x_{i j} x_{j k} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i k}$ and $x_{i j} x_{j k}+x_{j k}{ }^{J} x_{i j}{ }^{J}=\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right)\left(x_{j k}+x_{j k}{ }^{J}\right) +\left(x_{j k}+x_{j k}{ }^{J}\right)\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right)$. Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(x_{i j} x_{j k}+x_{j k}^{J} x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\sigma}= & \left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\sigma}\left(x_{j k}+x_{j k}^{J}\right)^{\sigma} \\
& +\left(x_{j k}+x_{j k}^{J}\right)^{\sigma}\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\sigma} \\
= & \left(x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}}+\left(x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{j i}}\right)\left(x_{j k}^{\eta_{j k}}+\left(x_{j k}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{k j}}\right) \\
& +\left(x_{j k}^{\eta_{j k}}+\left(x_{j k}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{k j}}\right)\left(x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}}+\left(x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{j i}}\right) \\
= & x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}} x_{j k}^{\eta_{j k}}+\left(x_{j k}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{k j}}\left(x_{i j}^{J}\right)^{\eta_{j i}}
\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the $\eta$ 's this gives (48). For (49) we consider $h_{i i}\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right) +\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right) h_{i i}=h_{i i} x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{J} h_{i i}$ and apply $\sigma$. This gives

$$
\left(h_{i i} x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{J} h_{i i}\right)^{\sigma}=h_{i i}{ }^{\sigma}\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right)^{\sigma}+\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right)^{\sigma} h_{i i}{ }^{\sigma} .
$$

The definition of $\eta_{i j}$ then gives the first equation in (49). The second is obtained in the same way.

We are now ready to prove
Theorem 6. (Martindale). Let ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) be an associative algebra with involution and identity element $1=\Sigma_{1}^{n} e_{i}$ where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents such that (1) $e_{i} \in \mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and (2) $\mathfrak{A} e_{i} \mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}, i=1,2, \cdots, n$. Then ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) is perfect if either $n \geqq 3$ or $n=2$ and $\mathfrak{H} \cap e_{i} \mathfrak{A} e_{i}$ generates $e_{i} \mathfrak{A} e_{i}$ for $i=1,2$.

Proof. Suppose first that $n \geqq 3$.
