Assume we have elements $x_{i j}{ }^{(p)} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i j}$, $x_{j i}{ }^{(p)} \in \mathfrak{A}_{j i}, \quad i \neq j, \quad p=1,2, \cdots, m$ such that $\Sigma_{p} x_{i j}{ }^{(p)} x_{j i}{ }^{(p)}=0$. We claim that $\Sigma_{p} x_{i j}{ }^{(p) \eta_{i j}} x_{j i}{ }^{(p) \eta_{j i}}=0$. Let $k \neq i, j$ and let $a_{i k} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i k}$. Then, by (48),

$$
\begin{align*}
\sum_{p} x_{i j}^{(p) \eta_{i j}} x_{j i}^{(p) \eta_{j i}} a_{i k}{ }^{\eta_{i k}} & =\sum_{p} x_{i j}^{(p) \eta_{i j}}\left(x_{j i}^{(p)} a_{i k}\right)^{\eta_{j k}}  \tag{50}\\
& =\sum\left(x_{i j}^{(p)} x_{j i}^{(p)} a_{i k}\right)^{\eta_{i k}}=0 .
\end{align*}
$$

Now $\mathfrak{A}_{i k} \mathfrak{A}_{k i}=\mathfrak{A}_{i i}$ implies that $\frac{1}{2} e_{i}=\Sigma_{q} a_{i k}{ }^{(q)} a_{k i}{ }^{(q)}$ for suitable $a_{i k}{ }^{(q)} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i k}, a_{k i}{ }^{(q)} \in \mathfrak{A}_{k 1}$. Then

$$
\begin{equation*}
e_{i}=\frac{1}{2} e_{i}+\frac{1}{2} e_{i}^{J}=\sum_{q}\left(a_{i k}^{(q)} a_{k i}^{(q)}+a_{k i}^{(q) J} a_{i k}^{(q) J}\right) . \tag{51}
\end{equation*}
$$

Hence, by (47),

$$
\begin{equation*}
g_{i}=e_{i}^{\sigma}=\sum_{q}\left(a_{i k}^{(q) \eta_{i k}} a_{k i}^{(q) \eta_{k i}}+a_{k i}^{(q) J \eta_{i k}} a_{i k}^{\left.(q) J \eta_{k i}\right)}\right) \tag{52}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since $a_{i k}{ }^{(q)}, a_{k i}{ }^{(q) J} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i k}$ it follows from (50) and (52) that $\left(\Sigma_{p} x_{i j}{ }^{(p) \eta_{i j}} x_{j i}{ }^{(p) \eta_{j i}}\right) g_{i .}=0$. Since the term in the parenthesis is in $\mathfrak{G}_{i i}$ and $g_{i}$ is the identity in $\mathfrak{G}_{i i}$ we have $\sum x_{i j}{ }^{(p) \eta_{i j}} x_{j i}{ }^{(p) \eta_{j i}}=0$. The result just established implies that there exists a unique linear mapping $\eta_{i i}$ of $\mathfrak{A}_{i i}=\mathfrak{A}_{i j} \mathfrak{A}_{j i}$ into $\mathfrak{G}_{i i}$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left(x_{i j} x_{j i}\right)^{\eta_{i i}}=x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}} x_{j i}^{\eta_{j i}} . \tag{53}
\end{equation*}
$$

The mapping $\eta_{i i}$ has been defined by means of the index $j \neq i$. Let $\eta_{i i}{ }^{\prime}$ be the mapping similarly determined by $k \neq i, j$. We can write $x_{j i}=\sum_{q} x_{j k}{ }^{(q)} x_{k i}{ }^{(q)}$, $x_{j k}{ }^{(q)} \in \mathfrak{A}_{j k}, x_{k i}{ }^{(q)} \in \mathfrak{A}_{k i}$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(x_{i j} x_{j i}\right)^{\eta_{i i}} & =\left(\sum_{q}\left(x_{i j} x_{j k}^{(q)}\right) x_{k i}^{(q)}\right)^{\eta_{i i}} \\
& =\sum_{q}\left(x_{i j} x_{j k}^{(q)}\right)^{\eta_{i k}}\left(x_{k i}^{(q)}\right)^{\eta_{k i}} \\
& =\sum_{q} x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}} x_{j k}^{(q) \eta_{j k}} x_{k i}^{(q) \eta_{k i}} \\
& =\sum_{q} x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}}\left(x_{j k}^{(q)} x_{k i}^{(q)}\right)^{\eta_{j i}} \\
& =x_{i j}^{\eta_{i j}} x_{j i}^{\eta_{j i}} \\
& =\left(x_{i j} x_{j i}\right)^{\eta_{i i}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $\eta_{i i}$ is independent of $j \neq i$. Now let $\eta$ be the linear mapping of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ which coincides with $\eta_{i j}$ on $\mathfrak{U}_{i j}, i, j=1,2, \cdots, n$. We claim that $\eta$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{U}$ into $\mathfrak{G}$. Taking into account the products which are automatically 0 since $\mathfrak{U}_{i j}$ and $\mathfrak{G}_{i j}$ are Peirce spaces of $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{G}$ respectively it is enough to verify the homomorphism property for the following products: $x_{i j} x_{j k}, x_{i j} x_{j i}, x_{i i} x_{i j}, x_{i j} x_{j j}$, $x_{i i} y_{i i}$ where $i, j, k$ are distinct, $x_{i j} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i j}$ etc. The first two are clear by (48) and (53). To settle the third it is enough to consider the case in which $x_{i i}=x_{i k} x_{k i}, x_{i k} \in \mathfrak{U}_{i k}$, $x_{k i} \in \mathfrak{A}_{k i} \quad\left(\right.$ since $\left.\quad \mathfrak{U}_{i i}=\mathfrak{U}_{i k} \mathfrak{U}_{k i}\right) \quad$. Then $\quad\left(x_{i i} x_{i j}\right)^{\eta}=\left(x_{i k} x_{k i} x_{i j}\right)^{\eta}=x_{i k}{ }^{\eta}\left(x_{k i} x_{i j}\right)^{\eta} =x_{i k}{ }^{\eta} x_{k i}{ }^{\eta} x_{i j}{ }^{\eta}=\left(x_{i k} x_{k i}\right)^{\eta} x_{i j}{ }^{\eta}=x_{i i}{ }^{\eta} x_{i j}{ }^{\eta}$. The next case follows in a similar manner. For the last case we again assume $x_{i i}=x_{i k} x_{k i}$. Then $\left(x_{i i} y_{i i}\right)^{\eta}=\left(x_{i k} x_{k i} y_{i i}\right)^{\eta} =x_{i k}{ }^{\eta}\left(x_{k i} y_{i i}\right)^{\eta}=x_{i k}{ }^{\eta} x_{k i}{ }^{\eta} y_{i i}{ }^{\eta}=\left(x_{i k} x_{k i}\right)^{\eta} y_{i i}{ }^{\eta}=x_{i i}{ }^{\eta} y_{i i}{ }^{\eta}$. We show next that $\eta$ is an extension of $\sigma$. Since every element of $\mathfrak{H}$ has the form $a+a^{J}, a \in \mathfrak{A}$, and since $\mathfrak{A}_{i i}=\mathfrak{A}_{i j} \mathfrak{A}_{j i}$ it is clear that every element of $\mathfrak{H}$ is a sum of elements of the form $x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{J}$ and $x_{i j} x_{j i}+x_{j i}{ }^{J} x_{i j}{ }^{J}$ where $i \neq j, x_{i j} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i j}$ and $x_{j i} \in \mathfrak{A}_{j i}$. It is now clear from (46) and (47) that $\eta$ coincides with $\sigma$ on $\mathfrak{H}$. Now $\mathfrak{H}$ generates $\mathfrak{A}$ since $\left(x_{i j}+x_{i j}{ }^{j}\right) e_{j}=x_{i j}, i \neq j$ and the $\mathfrak{A}_{i j}, i \neq j$ generate $\mathfrak{U}$. It follows that $\eta$ is the only extension of $\sigma$ to a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$. This completes the proof for the case $n \geqq 3$.
Now assume $n=2$. In this case the supplementary hypothesis implies that every element of $\mathfrak{U}_{i i}, i=1,2$, is a sum of products of elements $h_{i i} \in \mathfrak{H} \cap \mathfrak{U}_{i i}$. Suppose we have a relation of the form $\Sigma_{p} m_{p}=0$ where each $m_{p}$ is a product $h_{1} h_{2} \cdots h_{q}$ where $h_{\boldsymbol{j}} \in \mathfrak{H} \cap \mathfrak{U}_{\boldsymbol{i} \boldsymbol{i}}$. Then we claim that we have the relation $\Sigma \boldsymbol{m}_{\boldsymbol{p}}{ }^{\prime}=\mathbf{0}$ where $m_{p}{ }^{\prime}=h_{1}{ }^{\sigma} h_{2}{ }^{\sigma} \ldots h_{q}{ }^{\sigma}$. To see this we let $x_{i k} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i k}, k \neq i$. Then, by iterating (49), we obtain $m_{p}{ }^{\prime} x_{i k}{ }^{\eta_{i k}}=\left(m_{p} x_{i k}\right)^{\eta_{i k}}$ and this implies that $\Sigma_{p} m_{p}{ }^{\prime} x_{i k}{ }^{\eta_{i k}}=0$. It then follows from (52) that $\left(\Sigma_{p} m_{p}{ }^{\prime}\right) g_{i}=0$. Since $\Sigma_{p} m_{p}{ }^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{G}_{i i}$ and $g_{i}$ is the identity for $\mathfrak{G}_{i i}$ this gives $\Sigma_{p} m_{p}{ }^{\prime}=0$. Our result implies that we have a homomorphism $\eta_{i i}$ of the associative algebra $\mathfrak{U}_{i i}$ into $\mathfrak{G}_{i i}$ which coincides with $\sigma$ on $\mathfrak{U}_{i i} \cap \mathfrak{H}$. Now let $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ be the linear mapping of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $\boldsymbol{\eta}=\boldsymbol{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{i} \boldsymbol{j}}$ on $\mathfrak{A}_{\boldsymbol{i} \boldsymbol{j}}, \boldsymbol{i}, \boldsymbol{j}=\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{2}$. Then the definition of $\eta$ implies that $\left(x_{i i} y_{i i}\right)^{\eta}=x_{i i}{ }^{\eta} y_{i i}{ }^{\eta}$ if $x_{i i}, y_{i i} \in \mathfrak{U}_{i i}$. Also, by (49) and the definition of $\eta$, we have $\left(h_{i i} x_{i j}\right)^{\eta}=h_{i i}{ }^{\eta} x_{i j}{ }^{\eta}$ and $\left(x_{i j} h_{j j}\right)^{\eta}=x_{i j}{ }^{\eta} h_{j j}{ }^{\eta}$ if $x_{i j} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i j}$, $\boldsymbol{h}_{\boldsymbol{i} \boldsymbol{i}} \in \mathfrak{A}_{\boldsymbol{i} \boldsymbol{i}} \cap \mathfrak{H}, \boldsymbol{h}_{\boldsymbol{j} \boldsymbol{j}} \in \mathfrak{A}_{\boldsymbol{j} \boldsymbol{j}} \cap \mathfrak{H}$. Since $\mathfrak{U}_{\boldsymbol{i} \boldsymbol{i}} \cap \mathfrak{H}$ generates $\mathfrak{U}_{\boldsymbol{i} \boldsymbol{i}}$ it follows that $\left(x_{i i} x_{i j}\right)^{\eta}=x_{i i}{ }^{\eta} x_{i j}{ }^{\eta}$ and $\left(x_{i j} x_{j j}\right)^{\eta}=x_{i j}{ }^{\eta} x_{j j}{ }^{\eta}$ if $x_{i j} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i j}, x_{i i} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i i}, x_{j j} \in \mathfrak{A}_{j j}$. Hence to prove $\eta$ is an algebra homomorphism it remains to show that $\left(x_{i k} x_{k i}\right)^{\eta}=x_{i k}{ }^{\eta} x_{k i}{ }^{\eta}$ if $x_{i k} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i k}, x_{k i} \in \mathfrak{A}_{k i}$ and $i \neq k$. Let $a_{i k} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i k}, a_{k i} \in \mathfrak{U}_{k i}$. Then by the results already established we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(x_{i k} x_{k i}\right)^{\eta} a_{i k}{ }^{\eta} a_{k i}{ }^{\eta} & =\left(x_{i k} x_{k i} a_{i k}\right)^{\eta} a_{k i}{ }^{\eta} \\
& =x_{i k}{ }^{\eta}\left(x_{k i} a_{i k}\right)^{\eta} a_{k i}{ }^{\eta}=x_{i k}{ }^{\eta}\left(x_{k i} a_{i k} a_{k i}\right)^{\eta} .
\end{aligned}
$$

By (52), this implies that $\left(x_{i k} x_{k i}\right)^{\eta} g_{i}=x_{i k}{ }^{\eta}\left(x_{k i} e_{i}\right)^{\eta}$. Since $x_{k i} \in \mathfrak{A}_{k i}$ and $\left(x_{i k} x_{k i}\right)^{\eta} \in \mathfrak{G}_{i i}$ we have $x_{k i} e_{i}=x_{k i}$ and $\left(x_{i k} x_{k i}\right)^{\eta} g_{i}=\left(x_{i k} x_{k i}\right)^{\eta}$. This shows that $\left(x_{i k} x_{k i}\right)^{\eta}=x_{i k}{ }^{\eta} x_{k i}{ }^{\eta}$ and completes the proof of the homomorphism property of $\eta$. It is clear that
$\eta$ is an extension of $\sigma$. Also, as before, $\mathfrak{A}$ is generated by $\mathfrak{H}$. Hence $\eta$ is unique and the proof is complete for $n=2$.
At the beginning of our discussion we showed that Theorem 6 has the following consequence.

Corollary 1. Let $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ be an associative algebra with involution and identity element, $J_{a}$ a canonical involution in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$. Then $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is perfect if either $n \geqq 3$ or $n=2$ and $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ generates $\mathfrak{D}$.

We remark that the supplementary condition or some alternative of it really is necessary to insure the validity of the result for the case $n=2$. An example which shows this is $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{2}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a quaternion algebra with standard involution. It is easily seen that in this case $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{2}\right)$ is isomorphic to the Jordan algebra of a symmetric bilinear form $f$ in a five dimensional space $\mathfrak{M}$. It follows that the unital special universal envelope of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{2}\right)$ is isomorphic to the Clifford algebra $C(\mathfrak{M}, f)(\S 2.3)$. Since $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{M}, f)=2^{5}=32$ (§7.1) and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}_{2}=16$ it is clear that $\mathfrak{D}_{2}$ is not a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{2}\right)$ (see also exercise 2 below). Hence ( $\mathfrak{D}_{2}, J_{1}$ ) is not perfect.
Theorem 6 can also be applied to Jordan algebras of the form $\mathfrak{A}^{+}, \mathfrak{A}$ associative, using the usual trick of replacing $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$by $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{B}, J)$ where $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{A}^{\circ}$ and $J$ is the involution $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right) \rightarrow\left(a_{2}, a_{1}\right)$. One obtains in this way the following result.

Corollary 2. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be an associative algebra with $1=\sum_{1}^{n} e_{i}$ where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotent elements in $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $\mathfrak{A} e_{i} \mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}, i=1,2, \cdots, n$. Let $\mathfrak{A}^{\circ}$ be the opposite algebra and $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{U} \oplus \mathfrak{U}^{\circ}$. Assume $n \geqq 3$. Then $\mathfrak{B}$ and the mapping $a \rightarrow(a, a)$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}$ is a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$.

Proof. We have the isomorphism of $a \rightarrow(a, a)$ of $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$into $\mathfrak{B}^{+}$whose image is $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{B}, J)$ the set of symmetric elements of $\mathfrak{B}$ under the involution $J$. If we set $f_{i}=\left(e_{i}, e_{i}\right)$ then the $f_{i} \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{B}, J)$ and these are orthogonal idempotents with sum 1. Moreover, since $\mathfrak{A} e_{i} \mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}$ we have $\mathfrak{B} f_{i} \mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{B}$. Hence the conditions of Theorem 6 are fulfilled and so $\mathfrak{B}$ and the mapping $a \rightarrow(a, a)$ constitute a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$.

Martindale's theorem and its corollaries can also be used to give important results on derivations. The theorem itself has the following consequence.

Corollary 3. Let ( $\mathfrak{A}, J)$ be as in Theorem 6. Then any derivation $D$ of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ has a unique extension to a derivation of the associative algebra $\mathfrak{A}$. Moreover, $J D=D J$.

Proof. This is an immediate consequence of property (7) of Theorem 2.1 and the fact proved in Theorem 6 that $\mathfrak{A}$ and the injection constitute a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. Also the main involution in $\mathfrak{A}$ coincides with $J$. Hence $D J=J D$ holds for the extension $D$ of $D$ to $\mathfrak{A}$.

It is natural to define a derivation $D$ of an algebra with involution $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ to be a derivation of $\mathfrak{A}$ which commutes with $J$. Then Corollary 3 states that under the hypothesis of the theorem, every derivation of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ has a unique extension to a derivation of ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ). The converse is general: If $D$ is a derivation of ( $\mathfrak{A}, J)$ then the restriction of $D$ to $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is a derivation. This is immediate from the definitions.

Another consequence for derivations of Theorem 6 is the following
Corollary 4. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be an associative algebra satisfying the conditions of Corollary 2. Then any derivation $D$ of $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$is a derivation of $\mathfrak{A}$.

Proof. Let $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{A}^{\circ}, J$ the involution $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right) \rightarrow\left(a_{2}, a_{1}\right)$ as before. The derivation $D$ in $\mathfrak{U}^{+}$gives the derivation $(a, a) \rightarrow(a D, a D)$ in $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{B}, J)$. By Corollary 3, we have a derivation $D^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $(a, a) D^{\prime}=(a D, a D)$. The ideal $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{B}$ consisting of the elements $(a, 0)$ is mapped into itself by $D^{\prime}$ since $\mathfrak{U}^{2}=\mathfrak{A}$, so $\mathfrak{A} D^{\prime}=\mathfrak{A}^{2} D^{\prime} \subseteq \mathfrak{A}\left(\mathfrak{A} D^{\prime}\right)+\left(\mathfrak{A} D^{\prime}\right) \mathfrak{A} \subseteq \mathfrak{A}$. Similarly, the ideal $\mathfrak{A}^{\circ}$ of elements $(0, a)$ is mapped into itself by $D^{\prime}$. Hence we can write $(a, 0) D^{\prime}=\left(a D_{1}, 0\right),(0, a) D^{\prime} =\left(0, a D_{2}\right)$ where the $D_{i}$ are linear mappings of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$. Since $(a, 0)+(0, a) =(a, a)$ we have $(a D, a D)=(a, a) D^{\prime}=(a, 0) D^{\prime}+(0, a) D^{\prime}=\left(a D_{1}, 0\right)+\left(0, a D_{2}\right) =\left(a D_{1}, a D_{2}\right)$. Hence $D_{1}=D_{2}=D$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}
((a b) D,(b a) D) & =(a b, b a) D^{\prime}=((a, a)(b, b)) D^{\prime} \\
& =\left((a, a) D^{\prime}\right)(b, b)+(a, a)\left((b, b) D^{\prime}\right) \\
& =(a D, a D)(b, b)+(a, a)(b D, b D) \\
& =((a D) b+a(b D), b(a D)+(b D) a)
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $(a b) D=a(b D)+(a D) b$ and $D$ is a derivation in $\mathfrak{A}$.

## Exercises

1. (Jacobson and Rickart). Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be an arbitrary associative algebra with 1 . Show that Corollary 2 holds for $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{D}_{2}$.
2. Let $\mathfrak{Q}$ be a quaternion algebra with standard involution and basis $(1, i, j, k)$ such that $i^{2}=\alpha 1, j^{2}=\beta 1, i j=-j i=k, \alpha, \beta$ in $\Phi$. Let $\sigma$ be the linear mapping of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{Q}_{2}\right)$ such that $e_{i i}{ }^{\sigma}=e_{i i}, 1[12]^{\sigma}=1[12], i[12]^{\sigma}=j[12], j[12]^{\sigma}=i[12], k[12]^{\sigma} =k[12]$. Show that $\sigma$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{Q}_{2}\right)$ which can not be extended to a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{Q}_{2}$.
3. Unital bimodules for Jordan matrix algebras. In this section we shall establish a basic equivalence between the theory of unital bimodules for a Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ with $n \geqq 3$ and certain types of bimodules with involution for the coefficient algebra $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. These are defined as follows.

Definition 1. Let ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ) be an algebra with involution and identity element 1 .

A unital bimodule with involution for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a pair $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$ such that $\mathfrak{N}$ is a unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{D}$ and $j: v \rightarrow \bar{v}$ is a linear transformation in $\mathfrak{N}$ such that $j^{2}=1$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
\overline{d v}=\bar{v} \bar{d}, \quad \overline{v d}=\bar{d} \bar{v}, \quad d \in \mathfrak{D}, \quad v \in \mathfrak{N} . \tag{54}
\end{equation*}
$$

If $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative (alternative) then ( $\mathfrak{N}, j$ ) is called associative (alternative) if $\mathfrak{N}$ is an associative (alternative) bimodule for $\mathfrak{D}$. In the alternative case $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$ is Jordan admissible if

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left(d_{1} d_{2}\right) v=d_{1}\left(d_{2} v\right), \quad\left(d_{1} v\right) d_{2}=d_{1}\left(v d_{2}\right), \quad v\left(d_{1} d_{2}\right)=\left(v d_{1}\right) d_{2} \tag{55}
\end{equation*}
$$

holds whenever $\bar{v}=v, \bar{d}_{1}=d_{1}$ or $\bar{d}_{2}=d_{2}\left(d_{i} \in \mathfrak{D}, v \in \mathfrak{N}\right)$.
Let $\mathfrak{F}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus \mathfrak{N}$ the split null extension of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ by the unital bimodule with involution ( $\mathfrak{N}, j$ ). Then we let $j$ be the linear mapping in $\mathfrak{F}$ which extends the given linear mappings $j$ on $\mathfrak{D}$ and $\mathfrak{N}$. Then $(\mathfrak{F}, j)$ is an algebra with involution and identity element 1 , the identity of $\mathfrak{D}$. If $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative (alternative) then $\mathfrak{F}$ is associative (alternative) if and only if $\mathfrak{N}$ is associative (alternative). In the alternative case if the symmetric elements of $\mathfrak{D}$ are in the nucleus then the symmetric elements of $\mathfrak{F}$ are in the nucleus if and only if $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$ is Jordan admissible. These conclusions are immediate from the definitions.

If $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$ is a bimodule with involution for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ a sub-bimodule $\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}$ of $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$ is a sub-bimodule of $\mathfrak{N}$ such that $\mathfrak{N}^{\prime} j=\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}$. If ( $\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}, j$ ) is a second bimodule with involution for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ then a homomorphism $\eta$ of $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$ into $\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}, j\right)$ is a homomorphism of the bimodule $\mathfrak{N}$ into the bimodule $\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}$ such that $\bar{v}^{\eta}=\overline{v \eta}$ for all $v \in \mathfrak{N}$.

Now let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ be a Jordan matrix algebra defined by the algebra with 1 and involution ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ) and the canonical involution $J_{a}$ such that $a_{1}=1$ for the diagonal matrix $a$. We assume first that $n \geqq 4$. Then $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative. Let $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$ be a unital associative bimodule with involution for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$, F the split null extension $\mathfrak{D} \oplus \mathfrak{N}$. Then ( $\mathfrak{F}, j$ ) is an associative algebra with involution and identity element 1 , the identity of $\mathfrak{D}$. We can form the Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{E} \equiv \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ which contains $\mathfrak{J}$ as a subalgebra. Also $\mathfrak{E}$ contains the ideal $\mathfrak{M} \equiv \mathfrak{N}_{n} \cap \mathfrak{E}$ which is just the set of matrices of $\mathfrak{E}$ whose entries are in the ideal ( $\mathfrak{N}, j$ ) of ( $\mathfrak{F}, j$ ). Then $\mathfrak{M}$ is a unital Jordan bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the multiplication defined in $\mathfrak{E}$. We shall call $\mathfrak{M}$ the $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule associated with the given bimodule with involution $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$ of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. Since $\mathfrak{F}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus \mathfrak{N}$ we have $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$. Also $\mathfrak{N}^{2}=0$ in $\mathfrak{F}$ implies $\mathfrak{M}^{2}=0$ in $\mathfrak{E}$ so $\mathfrak{E}$ is the split null extension of $\mathfrak{J}$ by its bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$.

Let $\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}, j\right)$ be a second unital associative bimodule with involution for $(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{F}^{\prime}$ the corresponding split null extension, $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}{ }^{\prime}, J_{a}\right), \mathfrak{M}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{E}^{\prime} \cap \mathfrak{N}_{n}{ }^{\prime}$. Then $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}^{\prime}$ is the split null extension of $\mathfrak{J}$ by the Jordan bimodule $\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}$. Let $\eta$ be a homomorphism of ( $\mathfrak{N}, j$ ) into ( $\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}, j$ ) and let $\eta$ also denote the linear extension of this mapping to a mapping of $\mathfrak{F}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus \mathfrak{N}$ into $\mathfrak{F}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus \mathfrak{N}^{\prime}$ which is the identity on $\mathfrak{D}$. Then $\eta$ is a homomorphism of the algebra with involution $(\mathfrak{F}, j)$
into ( $\mathfrak{F}^{\prime}, j$ ) which leaves the entries of the diagonal matrix $a$ fixed. Hence, by Theorem 3, the mapping $\left(f_{i j}\right) \rightarrow\left(f_{i j}{ }^{\eta}\right)$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}{ }^{\prime}, J_{a}\right)$. Evidently this leaves the elements of $\mathfrak{J}$ fixed. Hence the restriction $\sigma$ to $\mathfrak{M}$ of the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{E}$ is a $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule homomorphism of $\mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}$. Thus every homomorphism $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ of $(\boldsymbol{N}, \boldsymbol{j})$ into $\left(\boldsymbol{N}^{\prime}, \boldsymbol{j}\right)$ gives rise to a homomorphism $\sigma$ of the associated bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$ into the associated $\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}$. It is clear that the mappings $(\mathfrak{N}, j) \rightarrow \mathfrak{M}, \eta \rightarrow \sigma$ define a functor from the category of unital associative bimodules with involution for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ into the category of unital Jordan bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$.
We shall now study the properties of this functor. We show first that if $(\mathfrak{N}, j) \rightarrow \mathfrak{M}$ and $\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}, j\right) \rightarrow \mathfrak{M}^{\prime}$, that is, $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$ and $\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}, j\right)$ are unital associative bimodules with involutions for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ and $\mathfrak{M}$ and $\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}$ are the associated unital Jordan bimodule for $\mathfrak{I}$ then any homomorphism of $\mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}$ is obtained by applying the functor to a homomorphism of $(\Re, j)$ into $\left(\Re^{\prime}, j\right)$. Thus let $\sigma$ be a homomorphism of the $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$ into the $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule $\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}$. Then we obtain the algebra homomorphism of $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}^{\prime}$ which is the identity on $\mathfrak{J}$ and is $\sigma$ on $\mathfrak{M}$. This maps $1[i j], i, j=1, \cdots, n$, into itself. Hence, by Theorem 3, we have a homomorphism $\eta$ of ( $\mathfrak{F}, j$ ) into ( $\mathfrak{F}^{\prime}, j$ ) such that the given algebra homomorphism has the form $\left(f_{i j}\right) \rightarrow\left(f_{i j}{ }^{\eta}\right)$. Clearly $\eta$ is the identity on $\mathfrak{D}$ so the restriction $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ of $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ to $\mathfrak{N}$ is a homomorphism of ( $\mathfrak{N}, \boldsymbol{j}$ ) into ( $\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}, \boldsymbol{j}$ ). It is clear that the given homomorphism $\sigma$ of $\mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$ is obtained by applying the functor we defined to the homomorphism $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ of $(\Re, \boldsymbol{j})$ into $\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}, \boldsymbol{j}\right)$. An immediate consequence of this is that ( $\mathfrak{N}, j$ ) and ( $\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}, j$ ) are isomorphic if and only if $\mathfrak{M}$ and $\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}$ are isomorphic.

We consider next the sub-bimodules of ( $\mathfrak{N}, j$ ) and its associated $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$. Since $(\mathfrak{F}, \boldsymbol{j})$ and $\mathfrak{E}$ are the split null extensions of $(\mathfrak{D}, \boldsymbol{j})$ and $\mathfrak{J}$ by $(\mathfrak{N}, \boldsymbol{j})$ and $\mathfrak{M}$ respectively, it is clear that the sub-bimodules of $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$ and $\mathfrak{M}$ are just the ideals of $(\mathfrak{F}, j)$ contained in $\mathfrak{N}$ and of $\mathfrak{E}$ contained in $\mathfrak{M}$. Hence, by Theorem 2, the functorial mapping we defined gives a lattice isomorphism of the lattice of subbimodules of $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$ relative to $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ onto the lattice of sub-bimodules of $\mathfrak{M}$ relative to J.

To complete our reduction of the theory of unital bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$, $n \geqq 4$, to that of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ we shall now show that every unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ is isomorphic to a bimodule associated with a unital associative bimodule for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. Let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ and form $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ the split null extension of $\mathfrak{J}$ by $\mathfrak{M}$. Then $\mathfrak{E}$ contains the elements $e_{i}=\frac{1}{2}[i i]$ and $u_{1 j}=1[1 j]$, $j=2, \cdots, n$, which are contained in J. Hence, by the Coordinatization Theorem, there exists a Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}{ }^{\prime}, J_{a^{\prime}}\right)$ and an isomorphism $\zeta$ of $\mathfrak{E}$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}{ }^{\prime}, J_{a^{\prime}}\right)$ such that $e_{i}{ }^{\zeta}=\frac{1}{2}\{i i\}, u_{1 j}{ }^{\zeta}=1\{1 j\}$. Here we let $j^{\prime}$ be the involution in $\mathfrak{F}^{\prime}, J_{a^{\prime}}$ a canonical involution corresponding to $j^{\prime}$ and a diagonal matrix $a^{\prime}$ with first entry $a_{1}{ }^{\prime}=1$. Also $\mathscr{F}^{\prime}$ is associative, and if $f^{\prime} \in \mathscr{F}^{\prime}$ then $f^{\prime}\{i j\}=f^{\prime} e_{i j}+\left(f^{\prime} e_{i j}\right)^{J a^{\prime}}$. Since $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{I} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$, we have $\mathfrak{C}^{\zeta}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}{ }^{\prime}, J_{a^{\prime}}\right)=\mathfrak{I}^{\zeta} \oplus \mathfrak{M}^{\zeta}$. Moreover, $\mathfrak{M}^{\zeta}$ is an
ideal in $\mathfrak{C}^{\zeta}$ such that $\left(\mathfrak{M}^{\zeta}\right)^{-2}=0$ and $\mathfrak{I}^{\zeta}$ is a subalgebra containing all the elements $1\{i j\}=1[i j]^{\zeta}$. Hence, by Theorem 2, $\mathfrak{M}^{\zeta}=\mathfrak{N}_{n} \cap \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}{ }^{\prime}, J_{a^{\prime}}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{N}$ is an ideal in $\left(\mathfrak{F}^{\prime}, j^{\prime}\right)$ such that $\mathfrak{N}^{2}=0$. Also, $\mathfrak{J}^{\zeta}=\mathfrak{D}_{n}^{\prime} \cap \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}^{\prime}, J_{a^{\prime}}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ is a subalgebra of ( $\mathfrak{F}^{\prime}, j^{\prime}$ ) containing the $a_{i}{ }^{\prime}$, and since $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}{ }^{\prime}, J_{a^{\prime}}\right)=\mathfrak{J}^{\zeta} \oplus \mathfrak{M}^{\zeta}, \mathfrak{F}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{D}^{\prime} \oplus \mathfrak{N}$. We note next that the isomorphism $\zeta$ restricted to $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{\boldsymbol{a}}\right)$ maps 1 [ij] into $1\{i j\}$. Hence, by Theorem 3 applied to the restriction of $\zeta$ to $\mathfrak{J}$ and its inverse, there exists an isomorphism $\eta$ of ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ) into ( $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}, j^{\prime}$ ) such that $a_{i}{ }^{\boldsymbol{\eta}}=a_{i}{ }^{\prime}$ and $\left(d_{i j}\right)^{\zeta}=\left(d_{i j}{ }^{7}\right)$ for $\left(d_{i j}\right) \in \mathfrak{J}$. We now replace $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ by $\mathfrak{D}$ and consider $\mathfrak{N}$ as bimodule for $\mathfrak{D}$ by defining $d v=d^{n} v, v d=v d^{n}, v \in \Re, d \in \mathfrak{D}$. If we call the restriction of $j^{\prime}$ to $\mathfrak{R}, j$, we see that ( $\Re, j$ ) is a unital associative bimodule with involution for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ and if $\mathfrak{F}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus \Re$ is the corresponding split null extension then we have the isomorphism $\lambda: d+v \rightarrow d^{\eta}+v$ of (F,j) onto ( $\mathscr{F}^{\prime}, j^{\prime}$ ) sending $a_{i} \rightarrow a_{i}{ }^{\prime}$. We now have the isomorphism $\left(f_{i j}\right) \rightarrow\left(f_{i j}{ }^{\lambda}\right)$ of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Im_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Im_{n}{ }^{\prime}, J_{a^{\prime}}\right)$ which coincides with $\zeta$ on $\mathfrak{J}$ and is the identity on $\mathfrak{N}_{n} \cap \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}, J_{a}\right)=\mathfrak{N}_{n} \cap \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n^{\prime}}{ }^{\prime}, J_{a^{\prime}}\right)=\mathfrak{M}^{5}$. It follows that $\mathfrak{M}^{5}$ is the Jordan bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ associated with the unital associative bimodule with involution ( $\Re, j$ ). Moreover, the bimodule composition $a . x$ for $a \in \mathfrak{J}, x \in \mathfrak{M}^{\zeta}$, coincides with the product $a^{\zeta} . x$ as defined in the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}{ }^{\prime}, J_{a^{\prime}}\right)$. Hence $u \rightarrow u^{\zeta}$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{M}$ as $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule onto the bimodule associated with ( $\mathfrak{R}, j$ ).
The case $\boldsymbol{n}=\mathbf{3}$ can be treated in a similar fashion. Here ( $\boldsymbol{D}, \boldsymbol{j}$ ) is alternative with involution and identity element 1 and the symmetric elements of $\mathfrak{D}$ are in the nucleus. Let ( $\Re, j$ ) be a unital Jordan admissible (alternative) bimodule with involution for ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ), ( $\mathfrak{F}, j$ ) the corresponding split null extension. Then ( $\mathfrak{F}, j$ ) is alternative with involution and 1 and symmetric elements in the nucleus. Hence $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is Jordan and contains $\mathfrak{J}$ as subalgebra. The ideal $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{N}_{n} \cap \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is a Jordan bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ which we shall call the associated bimodule to $(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{j})$. All the results we proved for the case $n \geqq 4$ carry over. Hence in this case we have a reduction of the study of the unital bimodules for $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{a}\right)$ to unital Jordan admissible bimodules ( $\mathfrak{N}, \boldsymbol{j}$ ) for ( $\mathfrak{D}, \boldsymbol{j}$ ).
6. Some remarks on the universal envelopes of Jordan matrix algebras. We consider first the universal envelopes for Jordan matrix algebras of the form $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative and $n \geqq 3$. Since these algebras have identities it is sufficient to consider the universal envelopes $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right)$ and $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right)$. By Corollary 1 to Theorem 6, $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{n}\right)\right)=\mathfrak{D}_{n}$. We consider next $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{n}\right)\right)$ and here we assume that $n \geqq 4$. By the Corollary to the Coordinatization Theorem (p. 138) every Jordan algebra with 1 containing $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ as subalgebra with the same identity is special. This and Theorem 2.17 imply that every unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right), n \geqq 4$, is special. Then we can conclude (Corollary to Theorem 2.17) that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is strongly special. Hence the canonical homomorphism of $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right)$ onto the unital squared special envelope $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right)$ is an isomorphism. Thus we may replace the former algebra by the latter. We consider next
the question of the coincidence of $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right)$ with the subalgebra $\mathfrak{V}_{1}$ of $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right) \otimes S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right)$ of fixed elements of the exchange automorphism. Here we assume $n \geqq 3$ and $\mathfrak{D}$ associative. The theorems which are available to use for deriving sufficient conditions for $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right)=\mathfrak{V}_{1}$ are Theorems 2.19 and Theorem 4. By Theorem 2.19 (1) and Theorem 4 we obtain the sufficient condition that $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)=[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)]+[\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)]$. If we recall that $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right) =\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ and that $S_{1}^{\prime \prime}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right)=U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right)$ if $n \geqq 4$ we obtain the following

Theorem 7. Let $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ be an associative algebra with involution and identity element, $J_{a}$ a canonical involution in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ defined by the diagonal matrix a. Assume $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, J)=[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)]+[\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)]$. Then $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right)$ is the subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ of $\mathfrak{D}_{n} \otimes \mathfrak{D}_{n}$ of fixed elements of the exchange automorphism if $n \geqq 3$ and $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\right) \cong \mathfrak{B}_{1}$ if $n \geqq 4$.

We consider next the application of Theorem 2.19 (2). For this purpose one needs to know that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is generated by 1 and two elements. A simple sufficient condition for this, which we shall use in Chapter VII is the following

Theorem 8. Let $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ be a Jordan matrix algebra defined by a standard involution $J_{1}$. Assume $n \geqq 3$ and the base field infinite. Then $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ is generated by 1 and two elements if the algebra with involution $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is generated by 1 and $(n-1)(n-2) / 2$ elements.

Proof. The hypothesis is that there exist $(n-1)(n-2) / 2$ elements which we label as $u_{i j}, i<j=2,3, \cdots, n$ such that the smallest subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ containing these and 1 is $\mathfrak{D}$. Let $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}$ be distinct elements of $\Phi$ and put $a=\Sigma \alpha_{i} e_{i i} =\Sigma\left(\alpha_{i} / 2\right)[i i], \quad b=\sum_{j=2}^{n} 1[1 j]+\sum_{i<j=2}^{n} u_{i j}[i j]$. Then $\Phi[a]$ contains the idempotents $e_{i i}$ and the algebra $\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$ generated by $1, a$ and $b$ contains the elements $1[1 j]=2 b U_{e_{11}, e_{j j}}$ and $u_{i j}[i j]=2 b U_{e_{i i}, e_{j j}}$. Hence by Theorem 2, $\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$ has the form $\mathfrak{D}_{n}{ }^{\prime} \cap \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ is a subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ containing 1 (and the $a_{i}$ ). Evidently $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ contains the $u_{i j}$ since these appear as entries of the matrix $b$ contained in $\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$. Hence $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{D}$ and $\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{H}$.

This result, Theorem 2.19 (2) and the considerations preceding Theorem 7 imply the following

Theorem 9. Let $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ be an associative algebra with involution and identity element over an infinite field which is generated by 1 and $(n-1)(n-2) / 2$ elements, $n \geqq 3$. Then $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)\right)$ is the subalgebra $\mathfrak{V}_{1}$ of $\mathfrak{D}_{n} \otimes \mathfrak{D}_{n}$ of fixed elements of the exchange automorphism and $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)\right) \cong \mathfrak{B}_{1}$ if $n \geqq 4$.
7. Lifting of idempotents and Jordan matrix algebras. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with $1, \mathfrak{N}$ an ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$ which is nil in the sense that every element $z \in \mathfrak{N}$ is nilpotent $\left(z^{\cdot n}=0\right.$ for some $\left.n\right)$. Let $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{N}$ and let $\bar{e}=e+\mathfrak{N}$ be a nonzero idempotent element of $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$. Then for the representative $e$ of the coset $\bar{e}$ we have $e^{\cdot 2}-e=z \in \mathfrak{N}$, which s hows that $e$ is an algebraic element of $\mathfrak{J}$. Moreover, since
$0 \neq \bar{e}=\bar{e} \cdot{ }^{2}=\bar{e}^{3}=\cdots$ it is clear that $e$ is not nilpotent. We shall now show that we can choose an element $f \in \bar{e}$, that is, $f \equiv e(\bmod \mathfrak{N})$ such that $f^{\cdot 2}=f(\neq 0)$. For this we require the following well-known and useful

Lemma 1. Let $\Phi[a]$ be an associative algebra with 1 generated by 1 and a single algebraic element a which is not nilpotent. Then there exists a polynomial $g(x) \in \Phi[x], x$ an indeterminate, with 0 constant term such that $f=g(a)$ is a nonzero idempotent element. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is an associative algebra generated by a single algebraic element which is not nilpotent then $\mathfrak{A}$ contains a nonzero idempotent element.

Proof. It is clear that the second statement follows from the first by adjoining an identity element to $\mathfrak{A}$ to obtain $\Phi[a]$ with 1 . To prove the first statement let $f(x)$ be a nonzero polynomial of least degree such that $f(0)=0$ and $f(a)=0$. Write $f(x)=x^{k} h(x)$ where $h(0) \neq 0$ and $k \geqq 1$. Since $a$ is not nilpotent it is clear that the degree, $\operatorname{deg} h(x)>0$. Then there exist polynomials $p(x) \neq 0, q(x) \neq 0$ with $\operatorname{deg} p(x)<\operatorname{deg} h(x)$ such that $p(x) x^{k}+q(x) h(x)=1$. Then if $g(x)=p(x) x^{k}$ we have $g(0)=0, g(x) \neq 0$ and $\operatorname{deg} g(x)<\operatorname{deg} f(x)$. Hence $e=g(a) \neq 0$. Also $g(x)+q(x) h(x)=1$ and $f(x)=x^{k} h(x)$ give $g(x)^{2} \equiv g(x)(\bmod f(x))$. Hence $e^{2}=g(a)^{2}=g(a)=e$ as required.

We remark that the second statement of the lemma implies that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is a power associative algebra containing an algebraic element which is not nilpotent then $\mathfrak{A}$ contains an idempotent $e \neq 0$. We can now prove the following

Lemma 2. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with $1, \mathfrak{N}$ a nil ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$. Let $\bar{e}=e+\mathfrak{N}$ be a nonzero idempotent in $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{N}$. Then there exists an idempotent $f$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $\bar{f}=\bar{e}$.

Proof. We have seen that $e$ is algebraic and not nilpotent. Hence, by Lemma 1 applied to the subalgebra generated by 1 and $e$, there exists a polynomial $g(x)=\beta_{1} x+\beta_{2} x^{2}+\cdots+\beta_{r} x^{r}, \beta_{i}$ in $\Phi$, such that $f=g(e)=\beta_{1} e+\beta_{2} e^{\cdot 2}+\cdots+\beta_{r} e^{\cdot r}$ is a nonzero idempotent. Since $\bar{e}=\bar{e}^{\cdot 2}=\cdots=\bar{e}^{\cdot r}$ we have $\bar{f}=\beta \bar{e}$ where $\beta =\Sigma \beta_{i} \in \Phi$. Since $f^{.2}=f, \bar{f}^{.2}=\bar{f}$ so $\beta^{2} \bar{e}^{.2}=\beta \bar{e}$. Hence $\beta^{2}=\beta$ and either $\beta =0$ or $\beta=1$. If $\beta=0$ then $\bar{f}=0$ and $f$ is nilpotent contrary to $f^{.2}=f \neq 0$. Thus $\beta=1$ and $\bar{f}=\bar{e}$.

We now extend Lemma 2 to the following
Lemma 3. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{N}$ be as in Lemma 1. Let $\bar{e}_{i}=e_{i}+\mathfrak{N}, i=1,2, \cdots, n$, be nonzero orthogonal idempotents in $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{N}$. Then there exist orthogonal idempotents $f_{i}$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $\bar{f}_{i}=\bar{e}_{i}, i=1,2, \cdots, n$. Moreover, if $\sum \bar{e}_{i}=\overline{1}$ then $\sum f_{i}=1$.

Proof. The case $n=1$ of the first statement is covered by Lemma 1. Now assume that for $1 \leqq r<n$ we have orthogonal idempotents $f_{j}$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ such that
$\bar{f}_{j}=\bar{e}_{j}, j=1, \cdots, r$. Let $u_{1}=\Sigma_{1}^{r} f_{j}, u_{2}=1-u_{1}$ so $u_{1}$ and $u_{2}$ are orthogonal idempotents such that $u_{1}+u_{2}=1$. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{11} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{12} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{22}$ be the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to $u_{1}$ and $u_{2}$. Since $u_{1} \cdot f_{j}=f_{j}$ we have that $f_{j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{11}$, $j=1, \cdots, r$. Now put $e=e_{r+1} U_{u_{2}}$, so $e \in \mathfrak{J}_{22}$. Also $e=e_{r+1} U_{u_{2}}= 2 e_{r+1} \cdot\left(1-\Sigma_{1}^{r} f_{j}\right) \cdot\left(1-\Sigma_{1}^{r} f_{j}\right)-e_{r+1} \cdot\left(1-\Sigma_{1}^{r} f_{j}\right) \equiv e_{r+1}(\bmod \mathfrak{N})$ since $\bar{f}_{j}=\bar{e}_{j}$ and $\bar{e}_{j} \cdot \bar{e}_{r+1}=0$. Hence $\bar{e}^{\cdot \cdot 2}=\bar{e}$ and $\bar{e} \neq 0$. Now $\mathfrak{N}_{22}=\mathfrak{N} \cap \mathfrak{I}_{22}$ is a nil ideal in the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}_{22}$ with identity $u_{2}$ and $e^{2} \equiv e\left(\bmod \mathfrak{N}_{22}\right)$ and $e \not \equiv \mathbf{0}\left(\bmod \mathfrak{N}_{22}\right)$. Hence, by the case of a single idempotent, there exists an idempotent $f_{r+1}$ in $\mathfrak{J}_{22}$ such that $f_{r+1} \equiv e\left(\bmod \mathfrak{N}_{22}\right)$. Then $f_{r+1} \equiv e_{r+1}(\bmod \mathfrak{N})$ and we have completed the inductive step of the proof. This proves the first statement. Now suppose $\sum_{1}^{n} \bar{e}_{i}=\overline{1}$. Then $\sum_{1}^{n} \bar{f}_{i}=\overline{1}$ and if $u=\Sigma_{1}^{n} f_{i}$ then $u^{\cdot 2}=u$ and $\bar{u}=\overline{1}$. Hence $u=1+z$ where $z \in \mathfrak{N}$ and $u^{\cdot 2}=u$ gives $z+z^{\cdot 2}=0$. Then $z=-z^{\cdot 2}=z^{\cdot 3}=-z^{\cdot 4}=\cdots=0$ and $u=1$.

We shall show next that the relations of connectedness and strong connectedness for orthogonal idempotents can be lifted from $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{N}$ to $\mathfrak{J}$. For this we require the following

Lemma 4. Let J be a Jordan algebra with 1 and nil ideal N. Then: (1) If $u \in \mathfrak{J}$ and $\bar{u}=u+\mathfrak{N}$ is invertible in $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{N}$ then $u$ is invertible in $\mathfrak{J}$. (2) If $u \equiv 1(\bmod \mathfrak{N})$, so $u=1-4 z$ where $z \in \mathfrak{N}$ and $z^{n+1}=0$ then there exists an element $w$ of the form $\Sigma_{1}^{n} \beta_{i} z^{i}$ such that $(1-2 w)^{\cdot 2}=u=1-4 z$. (3) If $u^{\cdot 2} \equiv 1(\bmod \mathfrak{N})$ then there exists an element $v$ which is a linear combination of odd powers of $u$ such that $v \equiv u(\bmod \mathfrak{N})$ and $v^{2}=1$.

Proof. (1) Since $\bar{u}$ is invertible, $\overline{\mathfrak{J}} U_{\bar{u}}$ contains the identity $\overline{1}=1+\mathfrak{N}$ of $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$. Hence there exists a $v \in \mathfrak{J}$ such that $\{u v u\}=v U_{u}=1-z$ where $z \in \mathfrak{N}$. Clearly $1-z$ is invertible with inverse $1+z+z^{.2}+\cdots+z^{. n}$ if $z^{. n+1}=0$. Thus $\{u v u\}$ is invertible in $\mathfrak{J}$ and hence $u$ and $v$ are invertible (Theorem 1.13).
(2) The condition $(1-2 w)^{\cdot 2}=1-4 z$ is equivalent to $w-w^{\cdot 2}=z$ so if $w=\sum \beta_{i} z^{i}$ then the condition will hold if $\beta_{1}=1$ and $\beta_{i}=\sum_{k=1}^{i-1} \beta_{k} \beta_{i-k}$, $i=2, \cdots, n$. Evidently these have a solution in $\Phi$ (even in integers in the prime field). Hence (2) holds.
(3) We have $u^{\cdot 2}=1-4 z$ where $z \in \Re$. Hence, by (2) there exists an element $1-2 w, w=\sum \beta_{i} z^{i}$, such that $(1-2 w)^{\cdot 2}=1-4 z$. Clearly, $1-2 w$ is invertible with inverse $1+2 w+(2 w)^{\cdot 2}+\cdots$ and $v=u(1-2 w)^{\cdot-1}=u(\bmod \mathfrak{N})$. Also, since all the elements with which we are dealing are polynomials in $u$, we have $v^{\cdot 2}=u^{\cdot 2}(1-2 w)^{\cdot-2}=1$. Since $z, w \in \Phi\left[u^{\cdot 2}\right]$ it is clear that $v$ has the required form.

We can now prove
Lemma 5. Let J be a Jordan algebra with $1, \mathfrak{N}$ a nil ideal in $\mathfrak{J}, e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ nonzero orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ are connected (strongly connected) in $\mathfrak{J}$ if and only if $\bar{e}_{1}=e_{1}+\mathfrak{N}$ and $\bar{e}_{2}=e_{2}+\mathfrak{N}$ are connected (strongly connected) in $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{N}$.

Proof. If $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ are connected (strongly connected) then it is clear that $\bar{e}_{1}$ and $\bar{e}_{2}$ are connected (strongly connected). Conversely, assume $\bar{e}_{1}$ and $\bar{e}_{2}$ are connected in $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$. Then there exists an element $\bar{u}_{12} \in \overline{\mathfrak{J}} U_{\bar{e}_{1}, \bar{e}_{2}}$ which is invertible in the Jordan algebra $\overline{\mathfrak{J}} U_{\bar{v}}$ whose identity is $\bar{v}=\bar{e}_{1}+\bar{e}_{2}$. We have $\bar{u}_{12}=u_{12}+\mathfrak{N}$ and if we put $v_{12}=2 u_{12} U_{e_{1}, e_{2}}$ then $\bar{v}_{12}=\bar{u}_{12}$ since $2 U_{\bar{e}_{1}, \bar{e}_{2}}$ acts as identity on $\overline{\mathfrak{J}} U_{\bar{e}_{1}, \bar{e}_{2}}$. Now $\mathfrak{J} U_{v}, v=e_{1}+e_{2}$, is a Jordan algebra with identity $v$ and $\overline{\mathfrak{J}} U_{\bar{v}}$ is a homomorphic image of $\mathfrak{J} U_{v}$ with nil kernel. Since $\bar{v}_{12}=\bar{u}_{12}$ is invertible in $\overline{\mathfrak{J}} U_{\bar{v}}$ it follows that $v_{12}$ is invertible in $\mathfrak{J} U_{v}$. Since $v_{12} \in \mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}, e_{2}}$ this shows that $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ are connected in $\mathfrak{J}$. If $\bar{e}_{1}$ and $\bar{e}_{2}$ are strongly connected then we may assume that the element $\bar{u}_{12}$ in the foregoing argument satisfies $\bar{u}_{12}{ }^{.2}=\bar{e}_{1}+\bar{e}_{2}$. Then Lemma 4 (3) is applicable to show that we can choose $v_{12}$ in $\mathfrak{J}_{12}$ so that $v_{12}{ }^{.2}=e_{1}+e_{2}$. Then $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ are strongly connected.

We can now prove
Theorem 10. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with 1 containing a nil ideal $\mathfrak{N}$ such that $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{N} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{n}, J_{\bar{a}}\right)\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{n}\right)\right)$ a Jordan matrix algebra (determined by a standard involution) of order $n \geqq 3$. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is isomorphic to a Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)\right)$ where the ideal in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)\right)$ corresponding to $\mathfrak{N}$ has the form $\mathfrak{M}_{n} \cap \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)\left(\mathfrak{M}_{n} \cap \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}\right)\right)$ where $\mathfrak{M}$ is an ideal in $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ and $\overline{\mathfrak{D}} \cong \mathfrak{D} / \mathfrak{M}$ as algebras with involution.

Proof. Since the proof for the case $\mathfrak{H}\left(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{n}\right)$ is very similar to that of the case of a general Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{n}, J_{\bar{a}}\right)$ we shall give the proof only for the case $\mathfrak{H}\left(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{n}, J_{\bar{a}}\right)$. Let $\tau$ be an isomorphism of $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{n}, J_{\bar{a}}\right)$ and let $\bar{e}_{i}, i=1, \cdots, n$, be elements of $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$ such that $\bar{e}_{i}{ }^{\tau}=\frac{1}{2}[i i]$ (in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{n}, J_{\bar{a}}\right)$ ). By Lemma 3, we may assume that the elements $e_{i}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $\bar{e}_{i}=e_{i}+\mathfrak{N}$ are orthogonal idempotents such that $\sum e_{i}=1$. By the proof of Lemma 4 we can choose an element $u_{1 j}, j=2, \cdots, n$ in the Peirce space $\mathfrak{J}_{1 j}$ such that $\bar{u}_{1 j}{ }^{\tau}=1[1 j]$ and $u_{1 j}$ is invertible in $\mathfrak{J}_{11}+\mathfrak{J}_{j j}+\mathfrak{J}_{1 j}$ with inverse $u_{j 1}$. Also $\bar{u}_{j 1}{ }^{\tau}=1[j 1]$ since $1[j 1]$ is the inverse of $1[1 j]$ in the Peirce space $\mathfrak{H}\left(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{n}, J_{\bar{a}}\right)_{11}+\mathfrak{H}\left(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{n}, J_{\bar{a}}\right)_{j j}+\mathfrak{H}\left(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{n}, J_{\bar{a}}\right)_{1 j}$. By the Coordinatization Theorem, there exists a Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ and an isomorphism $\zeta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ such that $e_{i}{ }^{\zeta}=\frac{1}{2}[i i], \underline{u}_{1 j}=1[1 j]$ (in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ ). Let $v$ denote the canonical homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{N}$. Then $\sigma=\zeta^{-1} \nu \tau$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{n}, J_{\bar{a}}\right)$ such that $\frac{1}{2}[i i]^{\sigma}=\frac{1}{2}[i i], 1[1 j]^{\sigma}=1[1 j]$. It follows that $1[j 1]^{\zeta}=1[j 1]$ and, in general, $1[i j]^{\sigma}=1[i j]$. Hence, by Theorem 3, there exists a homomorphism $\eta$ of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ onto $(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}, j)$ such that $\sigma$ is the restriction to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ of the mapping $\left(d_{i j}\right) \rightarrow\left(d_{i j}{ }^{\eta}\right)$ of $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ onto $\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{n}$. If $\mathfrak{M}$ is the kernel of $\eta$ then $\mathfrak{M}$ is an ideal in ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ) and ( $\overline{\mathfrak{D}}, j$ ) $\cong(\mathfrak{D}, j) / \mathfrak{M}$. Moreover, the kernel of $\sigma$ is $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{M}_{n}, J_{a}\right)=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right) \cap \mathfrak{M}_{n}$. Hence $\mathfrak{N}^{\zeta}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{M}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ and the proof is complete.

## Chapter IV

## JORDAN ALGEBRAS WITH MINIMUM CONDITIONS ON QUADRATIC IDEALS

It is well known that one of the most satisfactory segments of the theory of associative rings is the theory of right (left) Artinian rings. These are defined as the rings which satisfy the minimum, or equivalently, the descending chain condition for right (left) ideals. If such a ring is semisimple in the sense that it has no nonzero nilpotent ideals then one has the classical Wedderburn-Artin structure theorems: I. Any semisimple right (left) Artinian ring has an identity element and is a direct sum of a finite number of minimal right (left) Artinian rings and conversely; II. A right (left) Artinian ring is simple if and only if it is isomorphic to a matrix ring $\Delta_{n}$ where $\Delta$ is a division ring. If one recalls the relation between linear transformations and matrices, it is clear that an alternative formulation of the second structure theorem is that an associative ring is right (left) Artinian and simple if and only if it is isomorphic to a ring $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ where $\mathfrak{M}$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over a division ring.

We recall also that the class of semisimple (left or right) Artinian rings has the following important module characterization: These are just the associative rings with 1 having the property that all unital left or right modules are completely reducible. Moreover, the isomorphism classes of irreducible right (left) modules are in 1-1 correspondence with the simple components of the ring, that is, with the uniquely determined simple ideals $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ in the decomposition of the ring $\mathfrak{A}$ as $\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{s}$. In particular, if $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple Artinian then all irreducible right (left) $\mathfrak{A}$-modules are isomorphic. This result leads easily to the uniqueness of $n$ and of the isomorphism class of the division ring $\Delta$ in the second WedderburnArtin theorem: $\mathfrak{A} \cong \Delta_{n}$.

The Wedderburn-Artin structure theorems are due to Wedderburn for the case of finite-dimensional algebras. The extension to rings satisfying the minimum and maximum conditions for right (left) ideals was given by Artin and the removal of the superfluous maximum condition in this connection is due to C . Hopkins. A structure theory of finite-dimensional Jordan algebras analogous to Wedderburn's associative theory was developed by Albert in three papers ([7], [9] and [17]). Until quite recently there was no analogue in the Jordan theory of Artin's associative structure theory, though it has been clear for some time that an essential step for developing such a theory was the formulation of a suitable
analogue or substitute for the associative concept of a one-sided ideal. Recently a notion of this sort, called quadratic ideals, was introduced by Topping ([1]) for Jordan algebras of operators in Hilbert space. This was appropriated to the general case by the author, and served as the basic concept for the development of an analogue for Jordan algebras of Artin's associative structure theory (in [38]). The hypotheses for this consist of existence of 1 , the validity of certain minimum conditions on quadratic ideals, and an assumption of "nondegeneracy", which is a substitute for the hypothesis of nonexistence of nilpotent ideals $\neq 0$. The author's structure theory for simple algebras contained two gaps: (1) determination of the structure of simple algebras of "capacity" two, and (2) determination of Jordan division algebras. The first of these was filled in a completely satisfactory manner by Osborn in [6]. The second remains an outstanding problem.

The theory which we shall present in this chapter deals, as usual in this book, with algebras over a field of characteristic not two. The final step in the development of an Artinian-like structure theory for Jordan rings was taken quite recently by McCrimmon ([6] and [14]). Since no assumptions are made on the additive group, his theory encompasses also a "good" structure theory for Jordan algebras of characteristic two. This follows the lines indicated at the beginning of this book (p. 4). Since we have decided at the outset to simplify the discussion by sticking to the characteristic not two theory, we shall indicate McCrimmon's results only in a sketchy fashion in the section on "Further Results and Open Questions" at the end of this volume.

1. Quadratic ideals. We now introduce the main concept on which our structure theory will be based. This is defined as follows:

Definition 1. A subspace $\mathfrak{B}$ of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ is called a quadratic ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$ if $\mathfrak{J} U_{b} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$ for every $b \in \mathfrak{B}$.

Since $U_{b_{1}+b_{2}}=U_{b_{1}}+U_{b_{2}}+2 U_{b_{1}, b_{2}}$ and $U_{b}=U_{b, b}$ it is clear that a subspace $\mathfrak{B}$ is a quadratic ideal if and only if $\left\{b_{1} a b_{2}\right\}=a U_{b_{1}, b_{2}} \in \mathfrak{B}$ for $a \in \mathfrak{J}, b_{1}, b_{2} \in \mathfrak{B}$. This condition is equivalent to: $\mathfrak{B}$ is a subalgebra of the $a$-homotope $(\mathfrak{J}, a)$ for every $a \in \mathfrak{J}$. If $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element 1 then this implies that any quadratic ideal is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$. In any case, if $\mathfrak{B}$ is a quadratic ideal then $\left\{b_{1} b_{2} b_{3}\right\} \in \mathfrak{B}$ for all $b_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$. Since $b_{1} \cdot b_{2} \cdot b_{3}=\frac{1}{2}\left\{b_{1} b_{2} b_{3}\right\}+\frac{1}{2}\left\{b_{2} b_{1} b_{3}\right\}$ we have also that $b_{1} . b_{2} . b_{3} \in \mathfrak{B}$ if $b_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$.

Clearly any ideal of $\mathfrak{J}$ is a quadratic ideal. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is an associative algebra then in the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$we have $x U_{b}=b x b$ in terms of the associative product. It is clear from this that any left or right ideal of $\mathfrak{A}$ is a quadratic ideal of $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$. If $\mathfrak{B}$ is a quadratic ideal in the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ and $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $\mathfrak{B} U_{a}$ is a quadratic ideal. For, if $c \in \mathfrak{B} U_{a}$ then $c=b U_{a}, b \in \mathfrak{B}$, and $\mathfrak{J} U_{c}=\mathfrak{J} U_{b U_{n}}=\mathfrak{J} U_{a} U_{b} U_{a} \subseteq \mathfrak{B} U_{a}$.

In particular, $\mathfrak{J} U_{a}$ is a quadratic ideal for any $a \in \mathfrak{J}$. We shall call this the principal quadratic ideal determined by $a$. An element $b$ will be called an absolute zero divisor (in $\mathfrak{J}$ ) if $U_{b}=0$, or equivalently, the principal quadratic ideal $\mathfrak{J} U_{b}=0$. In this case $\Phi b$ is a quadratic ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$. If $b$ is an absolute zero divisor then $b U_{a}$ is an absolute zero divisor for any $a$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ since $U_{b U_{a}}=U_{a} U_{b} U_{a}=0$.

If $e$ is an idempotent element in $\mathfrak{J}$ then the principal quadratic ideal $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ determined by $e$ coincides with the Peirce space $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)=\{x \mid x . e=x\}$. Then the quadratic ideal $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ having $e$ as identity element. Moreover, if $\mathfrak{B}$ is a quadratic ideal of the subalgebra $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ then $\mathfrak{B}$ is a quadratic ideal of $\mathfrak{J}$ since, if $b \in \mathfrak{B}$, then $b=b U_{e}$ and $\mathfrak{J} U_{b}=\mathfrak{J} U_{b U_{e}}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e} U_{b} U_{e} \subseteq \mathfrak{B} U_{e}=\mathfrak{B}$. Similarly, one sees that if $b \in \mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ is an absolute zero divisor in $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ then $b$ is an absolute zero divisor in J.
Again, let $e$ be idempotent and let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e) \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e) \oplus \mathfrak{I}_{1}(e)$ be the corresponding Peirce decomposition. By Lemma 1 of §1, we have $\mathfrak{J}_{0} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{1}=0$ and $x . b^{\cdot 2}=2 x . b . b$ if $x \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $b \in \mathfrak{J}_{0}$. It follows that $\mathfrak{J}_{1} U_{b}=0$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}} U_{b}=0$. Hence $\mathfrak{J} U_{b}=\mathfrak{J}_{0} U_{b}$ if $b \in \mathfrak{J}_{0}$. This implies that any quadratic ideal of the subalgebra $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ is a quadratic ideal of $\mathfrak{J}$. In particular, $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ is a quadratic ideal of $\mathfrak{J}$. It is clear also that if $b$ is an absolute zero divisor in $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ then it is an absolute zero divisor in J.

It is clear that the intersection of any set of quadratic ideals is a quadratic ideal. On the other hand, if $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ are quadratic ideals then $\mathfrak{B}_{1}+\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ need not be a quadratic ideal (see exercise 2 below). If $\{\mathfrak{B}\}$ is a collection of quadratic ideals which is totally ordered by inclusion then it is clear that $\cup \mathfrak{B}$ is a quadratic ideal. Of particular importance in our theory will be the minimal quadratic ideals. A quadratic ideal $\mathfrak{B}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ is called minimal if $\mathfrak{B} \neq 0$ and there exists no quadratic ideal $\mathfrak{C}$ such that $\mathfrak{B} \supset \mathfrak{C} \supset 0$. The possibilities for these is given in the following theorem.

Theorem 1. If $\mathfrak{B}$ is a minimal quadratic ideal in a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ then one has one of the following possibilities: I. $\mathfrak{B}=\Phi b$ where $b$ is an absolute zero divisor. II. $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{J} U_{b}$ for every nonzero $b \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2}=0$. III. $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ for an idempotent $e$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ is a division subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$.

Proof. Suppose $\mathfrak{B}$ contains an element $b \neq 0$ such that $U_{b}=0$. Then $\Phi b$ is a nonzero quadratic ideal contained in $\mathfrak{B}$ so $\mathfrak{B}=\Phi b$ and we have case I. Now assume that for every $b \in \mathfrak{B}$ we have $\mathfrak{J} U_{b} \neq 0$. Then $\mathfrak{J} U_{b}$ is a nonzero quadratic ideal contained in $\mathfrak{B}$ so $\mathfrak{J} U_{b}=\mathfrak{B}$ for every $b \neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{B}$. Also $\mathfrak{B} U_{b}$ is a quadratic ideal contained in $\mathfrak{B}$ so either $\mathfrak{B} U_{b}=0$ or $\mathfrak{B} U_{b}=\mathfrak{B}$. Suppose there exists a $b \neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $\mathfrak{B} U_{b}=0$ and let $b^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{B}$. Since $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{J} U_{b}, b^{\prime}=a U_{b}$ for $a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then $\mathfrak{B} U_{b^{\prime}}=\mathfrak{B} U_{a U b}=\mathfrak{B} U_{b} U_{a} U_{b}=0$. Thus $\mathfrak{B} U_{b}=0$ for all $b \in \mathfrak{B}$ and hence $b^{\cdot 3}=0$ for every $b \in \mathfrak{B}$. We prove next that $b^{\cdot 2} \in \mathfrak{B}$ for all $b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Now in any special Jordan algebra we have the identity

$$
\begin{equation*}
\{x y x\}^{\cdot 2}=\left\{x\left\{y x^{\cdot 2} y\right\} x\right\} \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

since $\{x y x\}=x y x$ in $\mathfrak{A}^{+}, \mathfrak{A}$ associative (see ex. 4 p. 40). Since this is a two variable identity it follows from Shirshov's Theorem that it holds for all Jordan algebras. Now let $b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then there exists an $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ such that $b=\{b a b\}$, so $b^{\cdot 2}=\left\{b\left\{a b^{\cdot 2} a\right\} b\right\} \in \mathfrak{J} U_{b} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$. Now suppose $b^{\cdot 2} \neq 0$. Since $b^{\cdot 2} \neq 0$ there exists a $c \in \mathfrak{J}$ such that $b=\left\{b^{\cdot 2} c b^{\cdot 2}\right\}$. Then $b^{\cdot 2}=\left\{b^{\cdot 2}\left\{c b^{\cdot 4} c\right\} b^{\cdot 2}\right\}=0$ since $b^{\cdot 3}=0$. This contradiction shows that $b^{\cdot 2}=0$ for all $b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is a commutative algebra of characteristic $\neq 2$ this implies that $\mathfrak{B}^{2}=0$. It remains to consider the remaining alternative for $\mathfrak{B}: \mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{B} U_{b}$ for every $b \neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{B}$. Take $b \neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{B}$. Then there exists a $c \in \mathfrak{B}$ such that $b=c U_{b}$. This implies that $U_{b}=U_{b} U_{c} U_{b}$ so $E=U_{b} U_{c}$ and $F=U_{c} U_{b}$ are idempotent linear transformations in $\mathfrak{J}$ which map $\mathfrak{B}$ into itself and have surjective restrictions to $\mathfrak{B}$. Hence these restrictions are the identity mapping $1_{\mathfrak{B}}$ on $\mathfrak{B}$, so $\bar{U}_{b} \bar{U}_{c}=1_{\mathfrak{B}}=\bar{U}_{c} \bar{U}_{b}$ where $\bar{U}$ denotes the restriction of $U$ to $\mathfrak{B}$. Consider $f=\left\{c b^{\cdot 2} c\right\} \in \mathfrak{B}$. We have $\bar{U}_{f} =\bar{U}_{c} \bar{U}_{b^{\cdot 2}} \bar{U}_{c}=1_{\mathfrak{B}}$ and $e=f^{\cdot 2}=\left\{c b^{\cdot 2} c\right\}^{\cdot 2}=\left\{c\left\{b^{\cdot 2} c^{\cdot 2} b^{\cdot 2}\right\} c\right\} \in \mathfrak{B}$, by (1). Hence $e^{.2}=f^{.4}=f^{.2} \bar{U}_{f}=f^{.2}=e$ so $e$ is an idempotent contained in $\mathfrak{B}$. Also $e \neq 0$ since $\bar{U}_{e}=\bar{U}_{f^{\cdot 2}}=\bar{U}_{f}{ }^{2}=1_{\mathfrak{B}}$. Then $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e}=\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ the Peirce 1 -space of $e$. Hence $\mathfrak{B}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$. If $d \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $d \neq 0$ then $\mathfrak{B} U_{d}=\mathfrak{B}$ contains $e$. This implies that $d$ is invertible in $\mathfrak{B}$ and so $\mathfrak{B}$ is a division algebra. Hence we have case III.

Corollary. A Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ is a division algebra if and only if $\mathfrak{J} U_{b}=\mathfrak{J}$ for every $b \neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{J}$.

Proof. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is a division algebra and $b \neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ then $b$ is invertible and $U_{b}$ is bijective. Hence $\mathfrak{J} U_{b}=\mathfrak{J}$. Conversely, the condition $\mathfrak{J} U_{b}=\mathfrak{J}, b \neq 0$, implies that $\mathfrak{J}$ is a minimal quadratic ideal of type III. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is a division algebra.

All three types of minimal quadratic ideals indicated in the theorem exist. To obtain one of type I let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra in which $a_{1} \cdot a_{2} \cdot a_{3}=0, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$. (For example, we can take $\mathfrak{J}$ to be a trivial algebra: $a . b=0$ for all $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$.) Then $U_{b}=0$ for all $b$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ and so $\Phi b$ for $b \neq 0$ is a minimal quadratic ideal of type I. Next let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi_{n}{ }^{+}$with the usual matrix units $e_{i j}$ as basis. Then $\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{12}} =e_{12} \mathfrak{J} e_{12}=\Phi e_{12}$ so $\Phi e_{12}$ is a minimal quadratic ideal. Since $e_{12}{ }^{\cdot 2}=0$ it is clear that this is of type II. For type III we take $\mathfrak{B}=\Phi e_{11}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{11}}$ in $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi_{n}{ }^{+}$. More generally, in any Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$, any quadratic ideal of the form $\mathfrak{J}_{e}=\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ where $e$ is a nonzero idempotent such that $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ is a division algebra is minimal.

We shall call a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ nondegenerate if $\mathfrak{J}$ contains no absolute zero divisors $\neq 0$. Thus $\mathfrak{J}$ is nondegenerate if and only if $U_{a}=0$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ implies $a=0$. We shall obtain next a sufficient condition that a nondegenerate Jordan algebra with 1 contain an idempotent $e \neq 0,1$. For this purpose we need to recall Lemma 1 of §3.7: If $\Phi[a]$ is an associative algebra generated by 1 and $a$ which is algebraic
and not nilpotent then there exists a polynomial $g(x)$ with 0 constant term such that $e=g(a)$ is an idempotent $\neq 0$. We remark that if $f(x)$ is a polynomial $\neq 0$ of least degree with 0 constant term such that $f(a)=0$ then we may assume $\operatorname{deg} g(x)<\operatorname{deg} f(x)$. This is clear from the division algorithm. We shall require also

Lemma 1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with 1 and elements $a, b$ such that $a^{\cdot 2}=0=b^{\cdot 2}, 2 a . b=1$. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ contains an idempotent $e \neq 0,1$.

Proof. One sees directly that $1, a, b$ are linearly independent. Choose $\alpha, \beta$ in $\Phi$ such that $\alpha \beta=1$ and put $f=1+\alpha a+\beta b$. Then $f^{\cdot 2}=2 f$. Hence $e=\frac{1}{2} f$ is an idempotent $\neq 0,1$.

We can now prove
Theorem 2. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a nondegenerate Jordan algebra with 1 and assume $\mathfrak{J}$ contains minimal quadratic ideals. Then either $\mathfrak{J}$ is a division algebra or $\mathfrak{J}$ contains an idempotent $\neq 0,1$.

Proof. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a minimal quadratic ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\mathfrak{B}$ is not of type I , since $\mathfrak{J}$ is nondegenerate. If $\mathfrak{B}$ is of type III either $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{B}$ is a division algebra or we have an idempotent $e \neq 0,1$. Hence we may assume $\mathfrak{B}$ is of type II. Also we have $\mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2}=0$. Now choose $b \neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{B}$ and $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ so that $b=\{b a b\}$. Let $c=a . b$. We have the identity

$$
\begin{equation*}
(a: b)^{\cdot 2}=\frac{1}{2} a \cdot\{b a b\}+\frac{1}{4}\left\{b a^{\cdot 2} b\right\}+\frac{1}{4}\left\{a b^{\cdot 2} a\right\} \tag{2}
\end{equation*}
$$

in any Jordan algebra. This can be verified directly for special Jordan algebras and concluded for arbitrary Jordan algebras from the fact that the identity involves only two variables. In the present situation (2) gives $c^{\cdot 2}=\frac{1}{2} c+\frac{1}{4}\left\{b a^{\cdot 2} b\right\}$. Since $\left\{b a^{\cdot^{2}} b\right\} \in \mathfrak{B}$ we have $\left(2 c^{\cdot^{2}}-c\right)^{\cdot 2}=0$. It follows from Lemma 1 of §3.7 quoted above that either $c^{\cdot 2}=0$ or there exists an idempotent $e \neq 0$ of the form $\alpha c+\beta c^{\cdot 2}+\gamma c^{\cdot 3}, \alpha, \beta, \gamma \in \Phi$. In the first case we have $-2 c=\left\{b a^{\cdot 2} b\right\}$ so $c \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then $b=a U_{b}=2(a . b) . b-a . b^{\cdot 2}=2 c . b=0$ since $\mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2}=0$. Hence we have the second case: $e=\alpha c+\beta c^{.2}+\gamma c^{.3}$ is a nonzero idempotent. Suppose $e=1$. Then $c$ is a root of a cubic equation with nonzero constant term. Since $\left(2 c^{.^{2}}-c\right)^{.2} =0$ This implies that $(2 c-1)^{.2}=4 c^{.2}-4 c+1=0$. Then $\left\{b a^{.2} b\right\}=4 c^{.2}-2 c =2 a . b-1$. Since $b^{\cdot 2}=0, x U_{b}=2(x . b) . b$ so the foregoing equation gives $2\left(a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b\right) \cdot b=2 a \cdot b \cdot-1$ or $2 a^{\prime} \cdot b=1$ for $a^{\prime}=a-a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b$. Then $2\left(a^{\prime} \cdot b\right) \cdot b=b$ so $a^{\prime} U_{b}=b$ and replacing $a$ by $a^{\prime}$ permits us to assume that $2 a . b=1$. Then $c=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\left\{b a^{\cdot 2} b\right\}=0$. Hence $\{a b a\}^{\cdot 2}=0$ by (1). Also the symmetry of the left-hand side of (2) in $a$ and $b$ implies that $\{a b a\} . b=a .\{b a b\}$. Hence $2\{a b a\} . b =2 a \cdot\{b a b\}=2 a \cdot b=1$ and $\{a b a\} U_{b}=2(\{a b a\} \cdot b) \cdot b=b$. Hence replacing $a$ by $\{a b a\}$ we have $a^{.2}=0=b^{.2}$ and $2 a \cdot b=1$. Then we obtain an idempotent $\neq 0,1$ by Lemma 1 .

## Exercises

1. Show that if $\mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal and $\mathbb{C}$ is a quadratic ideal then $\mathfrak{B}+\mathbb{C}$ is a quadratic ideal. Show that if $v$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ is a quadratic ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$ then $\mathfrak{B}^{v}$ is a quadratic ideal in $\mathfrak{J}^{v}$. Show also that if $\mathfrak{B}^{\prime}$ is a quadratic ideal in $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ then the inverse image of $\mathfrak{B}^{\prime}$ is a quadratic ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that if $\mathfrak{B}$ is a quadratic ideal in a Jordan algebra with 1 such that $\mathfrak{B} \neq \mathfrak{J}$ then $\mathfrak{B} U_{a}$ is a quadratic ideal $\neq \mathfrak{J}$ for any $a \in \mathfrak{J}$.
2. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi\{x, y\}^{+}$where $\Phi\{x, y\}$ is the free associative algebra with 1 generated by $x$ and $y$. Show that $\mathfrak{J} U_{x}+\mathfrak{J} U_{y}$ is not a quadratic ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$.
3. A quadratic ideal $\mathfrak{B}$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ is called maximal if $\mathfrak{J} \supset \mathfrak{B}$ and there is no quadratic ideal $\mathfrak{C}$ such that $\mathfrak{J} \supset \mathfrak{C} \supset \mathfrak{B}$. Show that every proper quadratic ideal in a Jordan algebra with 1 can be imbedded in a maximal quadratic ideal.
4. (Topping). Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with 1 and let $\Re$ denote the intersection of all maximal quadratic ideals of $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that if $z \in \Re$ then $1-z$ is invertible.
5. Show that if $z$ is an algebraic element contained in the quadratic ideal $\Re$ of exercise 4 then $z$ is nilpotent.
6. Determine the quadratic ideals of $\Phi[x]^{+}, x$ an indeterminate and show that this Jordan algebra has no minimal quadratic ideals.
7. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra $\neq 0$ such that $\mathfrak{J}$ and 0 are the only quadratic ideals in $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that either $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi b$ with $b^{\cdot 2}=0$ or $\mathfrak{J}$ is a division algebra.
8. Axioms and first structure theorem. We shall say that a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ satisfies the minimum conditions (for quadratic ideals) if (1) the minimum condition holds for quadratic ideals $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ determined by idempotent elements and (2) every quadratic ideal $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ where $e^{.2}=e \neq 0$ contains a minimal quadratic ideal. Condition (1) is that if $C$ is any collection of quadratic ideals of the form $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}, e^{.^{2}}=e$, ordered by inclusion, then $C$ contains minimal elements. This is equivalent to: there exist no infinite properly descending sequences $\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{1}} \supset \mathfrak{J} U_{e_{2}} \supset \mathfrak{J} U_{e_{3}} \supset \cdots$ where $e_{i}{ }^{\cdot 2}=e_{i}$. We shall now investigate the structure of Jordan algebras satisfying the following axioms:
(i) $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element 1 .
(ii) $\mathfrak{J}$ is nondegenerate.
(iii) $\mathfrak{J}$ satisfies the minimum conditions.

We note first that if $\mathfrak{J}$ satisfies these axioms and $e$ is a nonzero idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}$ then the Peirce quadratic ideal $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)=\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ also satisfies the axioms. It is clear that (i) holds in $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ and we have seen that if $b \in \mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ is an absolute zero divisor in $\mathfrak{J} U_{\boldsymbol{e}}$ then $b$ is an absolute zero divisor in $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence (ii) holds in $\mathfrak{J} U_{\boldsymbol{e}}$. Now let $f^{.2}=f \in \mathfrak{J} U_{e}$. Then $f=f U_{e}$, so $U_{f}=U_{e} U_{f} U_{e}$ and $\mathfrak{J} U_{e} U_{f}=\mathfrak{J} U_{f}$. It is clear from this equation and the fact that any quadratic ideal of $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ is a quadratic ideal of $\mathfrak{J}$ that if $\mathfrak{J}$ satisfies the minimum conditions then so does $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$.

An idempotent $e$ in a Jordan algebra will be called primitive if $e \neq 0$ and $e$ can not be written as $e=e_{1}+e_{2}$ where the $e_{i}$ are nonzero orthogonal idempotent elements. If $e=e_{1}+e_{2}$ where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents then $e . e_{i}=e_{i}$ so $e_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$. On the other hand, if $e_{1}$ is an idempotent element contained in $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ then $e_{2}=e-e_{1}$ is an idempotent orthogonal to $e_{1}$ and $e=e_{1}+e_{2}$. It follows that a nonzero idempotent $e$ is primitive if and only if the subalgebra $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ contains no idempotent $\neq 0, e$. Clearly the identity element is the only nonzero idempotent in a Jordan division algebra. Hence $e$ is primitive if $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ is a division algebra. We shall call an idempotent $e$ completely primitive if $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ is a division algebra. We now give the following

Definition 2. A Jordan algebra with 1 is said to have a (finite) capacity if $1=\Sigma_{1}^{n} e_{i}$ where the $e_{i}$ are completely primitive orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{J}$. The minimum $n$ for which this holds will be called the capacity of $\mathfrak{J}$.

It is clear that $\mathfrak{J}$ has capacity 1 if and only if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a division algebra and $\mathfrak{J}$ has capacity two if and only if $1=e_{1}+e_{2}$ where the $e_{i}$ are completely primitive orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{J}$. We now prove

Theorem 3. Any Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ satisfying axioms (i)-(iii) has a finite capacity.

Proof. Let $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}, e^{.2}=e \neq 0$, be a minimal element in the collection of quadratic ideals of the form $\mathfrak{J} U_{f}, f^{.2}=f \neq 0$. We claim that $e$ is completely primitive. Otherwise, since the axioms hold for $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$, we can apply Theorem 2 to conclude that $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ contains an idempotent $f \neq 0, e$. Then $\mathfrak{J} U_{f} \subset \mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ contrary to the minimality of $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$. Thus $\mathfrak{J}$ contains completely primitive idempotents. Now let $e_{1}, e_{2}, \cdots, e_{r}$ be orthogonal completely primitive idempotents. Put $f_{i}=1-\Sigma_{1}^{i} e_{j}$. Then $f_{i}$ is an idempotent and
$f_{i} \cdot f_{i+1}=\left(1-\sum_{1}^{i} e_{j}\right)\left(1-\sum_{1}^{i+1} e_{k}\right)=1-\sum_{1}^{i} e_{j}-\sum_{1}^{i+1} e_{k}+\sum_{1}^{i} e_{j}=f_{i+1} \neq f_{i}$.
Hence $\mathfrak{J} U_{f_{1}} \supset \mathfrak{J} U_{f_{2}} \supset \cdots \supset \mathfrak{J} U_{f_{r}}$, If $f_{r}=0$ then $1=\Sigma_{1}^{r} e_{j}$ and the theorem is proved. If $f_{r} \neq 0$ then $\mathfrak{J} U_{f_{r}} \neq 0$ satisfies the axioms so this contains a completely primitive idempotent $e_{r+1}$. Then $f_{i} \cdot e_{r+1}=f_{i-1} \cdot e_{r+1}=e_{r+1}$ for $i \leqq r$ gives $e_{i} \cdot e_{r+1}=0$. Hence $e_{1}, e_{2}, \cdots, e_{r+1}$ is a set of orthogonal completely primitive idempotents and $\mathfrak{J} U_{f_{1}} \supset \mathfrak{J} U_{f_{2}} \supset \cdots \supset \mathfrak{J} U_{f_{r+1}}$ for $f_{r+1}=1-\Sigma_{1}^{r+1} e_{j}$. By (iii), this process must terminate with an $f_{n}=0$, which proves the theorem.

Our analysis of the algebras satisfying the axioms will rest on some results on algebras of capacity two which we shall now derive. Suppose first that $\mathfrak{J}$ is a Jordan algebra with $1=e_{1}+e_{2}$ where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents and let $\mathfrak{J} =\mathfrak{J}_{11} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{12} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{22}$ be the corresponding Peirce decomposition. Let $a_{11}, b_{11} \in \mathfrak{I}_{11}, x_{12} \in \mathfrak{I}_{12}$, etc. Then, by (PD3) (p. 121), $a_{11} \cdot b_{11} \cdot x_{12}=a_{11} \cdot x_{12} \cdot b_{11}$
$+b_{11} \cdot x_{12} \cdot a_{11}$. Since $\mathfrak{I}_{12} \cdot \mathfrak{I}_{11} \subseteq \mathfrak{I}_{12}$ the multiplication $R_{a_{11}}$ maps $\mathfrak{I}_{12}$ into itself and, denoting the restriction of $R_{a_{11}}$ to $\mathfrak{I}_{12}$ by $\bar{R}_{a_{11}}$, the relation (PD3) can be written as

$$
\begin{equation*}
\bar{R}_{a_{11}, b_{11}}=\bar{R}_{a_{11}} \bar{R}_{b_{11}}+\bar{R}_{b_{11}} \bar{R}_{a_{11}} . \tag{3}
\end{equation*}
$$

Now put $V_{a_{11}}=2 \bar{R}_{a_{11}}$. Then we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
V_{a_{11}, b_{11}}=V_{a_{11}} . V_{b_{11}} \equiv \frac{1}{2}\left(V_{a_{11}} V_{b_{11}}+V_{b_{11}} V_{a_{11}}\right) . \tag{4}
\end{equation*}
$$

Thus the mapping

$$
\begin{equation*}
a_{11} \rightarrow V_{a_{11}} \equiv 2 \bar{R}_{a_{11}} \tag{5}
\end{equation*}
$$

is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}_{11}$ into the special Jordan algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{12}, \mathfrak{J}_{12}\right)^{+}$. Similarly, we have the homomorphism $a_{22} \rightarrow V_{a_{22}}=2 \bar{R}_{a_{22}}$, the restriction to $\mathfrak{I}_{12}$ of $2 R_{a_{22}}, a_{22} \in \mathfrak{J}_{22}$, into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{12}, \mathfrak{J}_{12}\right)^{+}$. By (PD4), we have $\left[a_{11}, x_{12}, a_{22}\right]=0$ and this implies that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[V_{a_{11}}, V_{a_{22}}\right]=0 \tag{6}
\end{equation*}
$$

if $a_{11} \in \mathfrak{I}_{11}, a_{22} \in \mathfrak{J}_{22}$. Now suppose that $\mathfrak{J}$ has capacity two, the $e_{i}$ are completely primitive and $\mathfrak{J}_{12} \neq 0$. Then $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}$ is a division algebra and hence is simple. Consequently, the homomorphism $a_{i i} \rightarrow V_{a_{i i}}$ of $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}$ is a monomorphism. It follows that $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}$ is special and the image $V\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i i}\right)$ is a division subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{12}, \mathfrak{J}_{12}\right)^{+}$. We recall that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is an associative algebra with 1 then $a$ and $b$ are inverses in $\mathfrak{A}$ if and only if they are inverses in $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$(§1.11).
