In both cases, $\Delta$ is a division algebra and $\Delta_{n}$ can be replaced by $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), \mathfrak{M}$ an $n$-dimensional vector space over $\Delta$. The form of the involutions in the algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ is well known (see, for example, the author's Lectures in Abstract Algebra. II, p. 270). The result is the following: Either $\Delta=\Gamma$ a field (extension field of $\Phi$ ), $\mathfrak{M}$ is even dimensional over $\Gamma$, and $J$ is the adjoint (or transpose) mapping in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Gamma}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ relative to a nondegenerate skew symmetric (alternate) bilinear form $f$ in $\mathfrak{M} / \Gamma$; or $\Delta$ has an involution $j$, and $J$ is the adjoint mapping on $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ relative to a nondegenerate hermitian form in $\mathfrak{M} / \Delta$ associated with $j(d \rightarrow \bar{d})$. In the first case, $f$ is bilinear and $f(x, x)=0, x \in \mathfrak{M} / \Gamma$. In the second case, $f\left(x_{1}+x_{2}, y\right)=f\left(x_{1}, y\right)+f\left(x_{2}, y\right)$, $f\left(x, y_{1}+y_{2}\right)=f\left(x, y_{1}\right)+f\left(x, y_{2}\right), f(d x, y)=d f(x, y), \quad f(x, d y)=f(x, y) \bar{d}, \quad d \in \Delta$. In both cases, $f(x, y) \in \Delta(=\Gamma$ in the first case) and nondegeneracy is defined as usual. If $f$ is skew there exists a basis ( $u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{2 n}$ ) (where $2 n=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M}$ ) for $\mathfrak{M} / \Gamma$ such that the matrix $\left(f\left(u_{i}, u_{j}\right)\right)$ of $f$ relative to this basis has the form

$$
S=\operatorname{diag}\{Q, Q, \cdots, Q\}, \quad Q=\left(\begin{array}{rl}
0 & 1  \tag{42}\\
-1 & 0
\end{array}\right) .
$$

If $l \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Gamma}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ has the matrix $L$ relative to the basis ( $u_{i}$ ) then the adjoint $l^{*}$ relative to $f\left(f(x l, y)=f\left(x, y l^{*}\right)\right)$ has the matrix $S^{-1} L^{t} S$ relative to this basis. It follows that if $J$ is the adjoint mapping $l \rightarrow l^{*}$ then $\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Gamma}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), J\right)$ is isomorphic to ( $\Gamma_{2 n}, J_{S}$ ) where $S$ is the involution $L \rightarrow S^{-1} L^{t} S$ in $\Gamma_{2 n}$. We have seen also that ( $\Gamma_{2 n}, J_{s}$ ) is isomorphic to ( $\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}$ ) where $\mathfrak{D}=\Gamma_{2}$ the split quaternion algebra over $\Gamma$, involution standard and $J_{1}$ is the standard involution in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ (p. 128).

If $f$ is a nondegenerate hermitian form on $\mathfrak{M} / \Delta$ where $(\Delta, j)$ is a division algebra with involution, then there exists a basis $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ for $\mathfrak{M} / \Delta$ such that the matrix of $f$ relative to this basis is

$$
\begin{equation*}
a=\operatorname{diag}\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}\right\}, \quad \bar{a}_{i}=a_{i} . \tag{43}
\end{equation*}
$$

Then the adjoint $l^{*}$ of $l \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ relative to $f$ has the matrix $a^{-1} \bar{L}^{t} a$ relative to $\left(u_{i}\right)$, where $L$ is the matrix of $l$. Hence if $J$ is the involution $l \rightarrow l^{*}$ then $\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), J\right)$ is isomorphic to $\left(\Delta_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ where $J_{a}$ is the canonical involution defined by $a$.

It is well known that any left ideal in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})(\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M}=n<\infty)$ is a principal left ideal $\mathrm{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}) e$ generated by an idempotent element $e$ (Jacobson, Lectures. II, ex. 4, p. 232). This implies another well-known fact, namely $\mathrm{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ is regular in the sense of von Neumann, which means that for any $a \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ there exists an $x$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that $a x a=a$. To see this we consider the left ideal $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}) a=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}) e$. Then $a=b e$, $b \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$, so $a=a e$. Also $e=x a, x \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. Hence $a=a e=a x a$. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is any associative algebra then $a x a=x U_{a}$ in $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$. This leads us to call an arbitrary Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ regular if $a \in \mathfrak{J} U_{a}$ for any $a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Thus if $\mathfrak{A}$ is associative then $\mathfrak{A}$ is regular if and only if the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$is regular, and this is the case for $\mathfrak{A}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. It is clear that a regular Jordan algebra is nondegenerate, that is it contains no absolute zero divisors $\neq 0$.

We are now ready to prove our second main structure theorem on Jordan algebras with minimum conditions on quadratic ideals.

Second Structure Theorem. The following conditions on a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ are equivalent:( $\alpha) \mathfrak{J}$ is a simple algebra satisfying the axioms (i)-(iii) (of §2); $(\beta) \mathfrak{J}$ is either a division algebra, a Jordan algebra of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form in a vector space $\mathfrak{M}$ over an extension field $\Gamma$ with $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M} / \Gamma>1$, a Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ where $n \geqq 2$ and $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is either $\Delta \oplus \Delta^{\circ}$ where $\Delta$ is an associative division algebra, $j$ the exchange involution, an associative division algebra with involution, a split quaternion algebra over an extension field, standard involution, an algebra of octonions over an extension field, standard involution (only if $n=3$ ); $(\gamma) \mathfrak{J}$ is either a division algebra, a Jordan algebra of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form in a vector space $\mathfrak{M} / \Gamma, \Gamma$ an extension field, $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M} / \Gamma>1$, a Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{D}$ is an octonion algebra over an extension field with standard involution and $J_{\gamma}$ is a canonical involution, or an algebra $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is simple Artinian with involution.

Proof. $(\alpha) \Rightarrow(\beta)$. Let $1=\sum_{1}^{n} e_{i}$ where the $e_{i}$ are completely primitive idempotents and let $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{i \leqq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ be the the corresponding Peirce decomposition (Theorem 3). If $n=1, \mathfrak{J}$ is a division algebra and if $n=2,(\beta)$ follows from Theorem 9. Hence assume $n \geqq 3$. Let $i \neq j$ and assume $\mathfrak{J}_{i j} \neq 0$. By Theorem 4 and the fact that $\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{i}, e_{j}}=\mathfrak{J}_{i i}+\mathfrak{J}_{i j}+\mathfrak{J}_{j j}$ satisfies the axioms (i)-(iii), we see that $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}{ }^{2} \neq 0$ so $e_{i}$ and $e_{j}$ are connected (Lemma 1 of §2). Thus either $e_{i}$ and $e_{j}$ are connected or $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}=0$. Let $e_{2}, e_{3}, \cdots, e_{m}$ be the complete set of $e_{i}$ connected with $e_{1}$ and put $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}=\Sigma_{k, t=1}^{m} \mathfrak{J}_{k i}$. Since connectedness is a transitive relation (Lemma 4 of §3.1)
every $\mathfrak{J}_{k i}$ with $k \leqq m$ and $i>m$ is 0 . This implies that $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is an ideal. Hence $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{J}$ so all the $e_{i}$ are connected. Then, by the Coordinatization Theorem (§3.3), $\mathfrak{J} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$. Also the proof of the Coordinatization Theorem (p. 137) shows that we may assume $a_{1}=1$ for the diagonal matrix $a=\operatorname{diag}\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}\right\}$. For the sake of simplicity we identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$. Then $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}=\{d[i j] \mid d \in \mathfrak{D}\}$ where $d[i j]=d e_{i j}+a_{j}^{-1} d a_{i} e_{j i}$ ((17) on p . 125) where $e_{i j}$ are the usual matrix units. Since $a_{1}=1, \mathfrak{J}_{11} \cong \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is the coordinate algebra with involution. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is simple $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is simple (Theorem 3.2). We know also that $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative if $n \geqq 4$ and is alternative with $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j) \subseteq N(\mathfrak{D})$ if $n=3$. Since $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j) \cong \mathfrak{J}_{11}$ which is a Jordan division algebra and $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j) \subseteq N(\mathfrak{D})$, it follows that every nonzero element of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ has an inverse in $N(\mathfrak{D})$. Thus $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 8 and, moreover, $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative if $n \geqq 4$. Hence, the statements made about $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ in $(\beta)$ are clear from Theorem 8.
$(\beta) \Rightarrow(\gamma)$. The assertion here is that associative algebras with involution $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ specified in $(\beta)$ are simple Artinian. If $\mathfrak{D}=\Delta \oplus \Delta^{\circ}, j$ the exchange involution, then $\mathfrak{D}_{n}=\Delta_{n} \oplus\left(\Delta^{\circ}\right)_{n}$ and the two components are simple by the Wedderburn-Artin theorem. Also it is immediate that $J_{a}$ exchanges the two simple components. Hence $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ is simple. Since $\Delta_{n} \oplus\left(\Delta^{\circ}\right)_{n}$ is Artinian the result holds in this case. In the remaining cases, $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ is simple Artinian.
$(\gamma) \Rightarrow(\alpha)$. It is clear that any Jordan division algebra is simple and satisfies the axioms. Next let $\mathfrak{J}$ be the Jordan algebra $\Gamma 1 \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{M} / \Gamma$ where $\Gamma / \Phi$ is a field and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M} / \Gamma>1$. The simplicity of $\mathfrak{J}$ (as algebra over $\Phi$ ) is immediate (cf. ex. 4, p. 14). It is immediate also that $\mathfrak{J}$ is a division algebra if and only if $f(x, x)$ is not a square for every $x \neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{M}$ (ex. 6, p. 14). Now assume this condition does not hold. Then we have $u \in \mathfrak{M}$ such that $f(u, u)=1$. Put $e_{1}=\frac{1}{2}(1+u), e_{2}=\frac{1}{2}(1-u)$. Then the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents and $e_{1}+e_{2}=1$. The conditions that $a=\alpha 1+x, \alpha \in \Gamma, x \in \mathfrak{M}$, is in $\mathfrak{J}_{11}=\mathfrak{J}_{1}\left(e_{1}\right)$ are $\frac{1}{2} \alpha+\frac{1}{2} f(x, u)=\alpha, \frac{1}{2} x+\frac{1}{2} \alpha u=x$. These give $x=\alpha u, a=2 \alpha e_{1}$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}_{11}=\Gamma e_{1}$ and similarly $\mathfrak{J}_{22}=\Gamma e_{2}$ so the $e_{i}$ are completely primitive and so $\mathfrak{J}$ is simple of capacity two. Hence $\mathfrak{J}$ is nondegenerate (Theorem 4). Since $\mathfrak{J}$ contains 1 it remains to show that $\mathfrak{J}$ satisfies the minimum conditions. The computation just used for $e_{1}$ shows that if $e$ is any idempotent $\neq 0,1$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ then $\mathfrak{J} U_{e} \cong \Gamma e$ is a division algebra. Hence $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ is a minimal quadratic ideal and the conditions in axiom (iii) are clear.
We consider next the exceptional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{O}$ is an algebra of octonions over an extension field $\Gamma / \Phi, j$ is the standard involution in $\mathfrak{O}$ and $J_{\gamma}$ is the canonical involution in $\mathfrak{O}_{3}$ defined by $\gamma=\operatorname{diag}\left\{\gamma_{1}, \gamma_{2}, \gamma_{3}\right\}$, $\gamma_{i} \neq 0$ in $\Gamma$. Clearly, $\mathfrak{O}$ and $\mathfrak{J}$ can be considered as algebras over $\Gamma$. We now note that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is any Jordan algebra over a field $\Gamma$ and $\mathfrak{J} / \Gamma$ satisfies axioms (i)-(iii) then $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ satisfies these axioms for any subfield $\Phi$ of $\Gamma$. This is obvious for (i) and (ii). It is clear also that the sets $\mathfrak{J} U_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, are the principal quadratic ideals of $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ as well as of $\mathfrak{J} / \Gamma$. Hence if the minimum condition holds for the principal
quadratic ideals of $\mathfrak{J} / \Gamma$ of the form $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}, e^{\cdot 2}=e$, then this condition holds also in $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$. Next assume $\mathfrak{J}$ is nondegenerate. Then Theorem 1 implies that a subspace $\mathfrak{B} / \Phi(\mathfrak{B} / \Gamma)$ of $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi(\mathfrak{J} / \Gamma)$ is a minimal quadratic ideal if and only if $\mathfrak{J} U_{b}=\mathfrak{B}$ for every $b \neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{B}$. This implies that $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ and $\mathfrak{J} / \Gamma$ have the same minimal quadratic ideals, so the validity of (iii) for $\mathfrak{J} / \Gamma$ implies (iii) for $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$. We observe next that since quadratic ideals are subspaces, it is clear that any finite-dimensional algebra satisfies axiom (iii). In particular, $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$, which is 27 dimensional over $\Gamma$, satisfies (iii) as algebra over $\Gamma$ and hence as algebra over $\Phi$. It is clear also that this $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element so (i) holds. It remains to prove nondegeneracy. We use the usual notation: $x[i j]=x e_{i j}+\gamma_{j}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{i} \bar{x} e_{j i}$. Let $z=\zeta_{1} e_{1}+\zeta_{2} e_{2}+\zeta_{3} e_{3} +u[12]+v[23]+w[31], \quad \zeta_{i} \in \Gamma, \quad u, v, w \in \mathfrak{O}$ be an absolute zero divisor in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$. Then $z U_{e_{i}}=\zeta_{i} e_{i}$ is an absolute zero divisor in $\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{i}}=\Gamma e_{i}$, so $\zeta_{i}=0$. Now $z U_{1[12]}=u[12] U_{1[12]}$ since $v[23] U_{1[12]}=0=w[31] U_{1[12]}$, by (PD10). Also $u[12] U_{1[12]}=1[12] u[12] 1[12]=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{1} u p[12]$. Hence $u$ [12] and consequently $u$ [12] and $u$ [21] are absolute zero divisors. By (2), $(x . u[12])^{2}=0$ for every $x \in \mathfrak{J}$ (since $u[12]^{.2}=1 U_{u[12]}=0$ and $U_{u[12]}=0$ ). In particular, $u[12] . d[21] =\frac{1}{2}(u \bar{d}+d \bar{u}) e_{11}+\frac{1}{2}(\bar{u} d+d \bar{u}) e_{22}$ is nilpotent. Hence $u \bar{d}+d \bar{u}=0, d \in \mathfrak{D}$. This implies $u=0$ by the nondegeneracy of $Q(a, b)$. Similarly, $v=0$ and $w=0$. Hence $z=0$ is the only absolute zero divisor in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, I_{y}\right)$ so this is a nondegenerate algebra. Since $(\mathfrak{O}, j) / \Phi$ is simple by Theorem 8, $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ is simple by Theorem 3.2. Hence $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ is a simple algebra satisfying the axioms.

Now assume ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) is a simple Artinian algebra with involution. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is not simple then $\mathfrak{A} \cong \Delta_{n} \oplus \Delta_{n}{ }^{\circ}$ where $\Delta$ is an associative division algebra. Then $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \cong \Delta_{n}{ }^{+} \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})^{+}$where $\mathfrak{M}$ is an $n$-dimensional vector space over $\Delta$. Clearly, axiom (i) holds and we have seen that $\mathfrak{J}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})^{+}$is regular. Hence the nondegeneracy condition (ii) holds for $\mathfrak{J}$. Now let $e$ be an idempotent in $\mathfrak{J} =\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})^{+}$. Then $e$ is a projection on $\mathfrak{M} e$, that is, $e$ maps $\mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{M} e$ and is the identity on $\mathfrak{M} e$. If $f$ is a second idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J} U_{f} \subseteq \mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ then $f=e f e$ and $e f=f=f e$. Hence $\mathfrak{M} f \subseteq \mathfrak{M} e$. Moreover, if $\mathfrak{M} f=\mathfrak{M} e$, then for any $x \in \mathfrak{M}, x e=y f, y \in \mathfrak{M}$. Then $x e f=y f^{2}=y f=x e$. Hence $e f=e$ and since $e f=f$ we have $e=f$. Thus $\mathfrak{J} U_{e} \supset \mathfrak{J} U_{f}$ implies $\mathfrak{M} e \supset \mathfrak{M} f$. This and the finiteness of dimensionality of $\mathfrak{M} / \Delta$ imply the minimum condition for quadratic ideal of the form $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}, e^{2^{2}}=e$. We note next that if $e$ is an idempotent then $e \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}) e \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M} e, \mathfrak{M} e)$. This is well known and is immediate from the decomposition $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M} e \oplus \mathfrak{M}(1-e)$. If $\mathfrak{M} e$ is one dimensional then $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M} e, \mathfrak{M} e) \cong \Delta$. Then $\mathfrak{J} U_{e} \cong \Delta^{+}$which is a Jordan division algebra and $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ is a minimal quadratic ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$. Now let $e$ be any nonzero idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}$ and let $\mathfrak{N}$ be a one-dimensional subspace of $\mathfrak{M} e$. Let $\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}$ be a complementary subspace of $\mathfrak{N}$ in $\mathfrak{M}$ containing $\mathfrak{M}(1-e)$ and let $f$ be the projection on $\mathfrak{N}$ determined by the decomposition $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{N} \oplus \mathfrak{N}^{\prime}$. Then $\mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak{M} f \subseteq \mathfrak{M} e$ so $f e=f$. Since $\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{M}(1-f) \supseteq \mathfrak{M}(1-e)$ we have $(1-e)(1-f)=1-e$ which implies ef $=f$. Hence efe $=f$ and $\mathfrak{J} U_{f} \subseteq \mathfrak{J} U_{e}$. Since $f$ is a projection on the one-dimensional $\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{J} U_{f}$ is a division algebra so
$\mathfrak{J} U_{f}$ is minimal. Hence we have shown that any quadratic ideal of the form $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}, e^{\cdot 2}=e$, contains a minimal quadratic ideal. This completes the verification of the axioms (i)-(iii) for $\mathfrak{J}$. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M}=1, \mathfrak{J}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ is a division algebra. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M}=2$ one sees easily that the capacity is two and the simplicity follows from Theorem 4. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M} \geqq 3$ we use the isomorphism $\mathfrak{J} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ and the simplicity of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ to conclude simplicity of $\mathfrak{J}$.

The remaining simple Artinian algebras with involution have the form $\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), J\right)$ where $\mathfrak{M}$ and $\Delta$ are as before and $J$ is the adjoint mapping relative to a nondegenerate hermitian or skew symmetric bilinear form $f$. The simplicity follows as in the case just considered and, of course, (i) holds. To prove (ii) we prove $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), J\right)$ is regular. Thus let $a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then, by the regularity of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$, there exists an $x \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that axa $=a$. Since $a^{J}=a$, we can replace $x$ by $y=\frac{1}{2}\left(x+x^{J}\right)$ in this equation. This shows that $\mathfrak{J}$ is regular. We note next that the mapping $e \rightarrow \mathfrak{M} e$ is bijective of the set $\mathfrak{P}$ of idempotents of $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), J\right)$ with the set of nonisotropic subspaces of $\mathfrak{M}$. For, if $e \in \mathfrak{P}$ then $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M} e \oplus \mathfrak{M}(1-e)$ and $\mathfrak{M}(1-e)=(\mathfrak{M} e)^{\perp}$ which implies that $\mathfrak{M} e$ is not isotropic. Conversely, if $\mathfrak{N}$ is not isotropic then $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{N} \oplus \mathfrak{N}^{\perp}$ and the projection $e$ determined by this decomposition is selfadjoint since $f(x e, y)=f(x, y e)$ holds if $x$ and $y$ are either in $\mathfrak{N}$ or in $\mathfrak{N}^{\perp}$. It is clear also that $e \rightarrow \mathfrak{M} e, \mathfrak{N} \rightarrow e$ are inverses. If $e$ and $f \in \mathfrak{P}$ and $\mathfrak{M} e \supseteq \mathfrak{M} f$ then $f e=f$ and $e f =(f e)^{J}=f^{J}=f$. Hence $f=e f e$ and $\mathfrak{J} U_{e} \supseteq \mathfrak{J} U_{f}$. The converse follows by retracing the steps. It is now clear that we have the minimum condition for quadratic ideals $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}, e \in \mathfrak{P}$. The nonzero minimal elements of the set of these quadratic ideals correspond to the minimal nonisotropic subspaces $\neq 0$ of $\mathfrak{M}$. If the form $f$ is hermitian these are one dimensional and if $f$ is skew then any nonzero minimal nonisotropic subspace is two dimensional and has a basis ( $u, v$ ) such that $f(u, u)=0=f(v, v), f(u, v)=1=-f(v, u)$. We claim that in either case, if $e$ is the corresponding projection then $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ is a division algebra so $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ is a minimal quadratic ideal. We note first that $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}) U_{e} \cap \mathfrak{J}$. If $f$ is hermitian $\mathfrak{M} e$ is one dimensional and, as we saw above, $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}) U_{e}$ is a division algebra. Then if $a \neq 0$ is in $\mathfrak{J} U_{\boldsymbol{e}}$ there exists a $b \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}) U_{\boldsymbol{e}}$ such that $a \cdot b=e, a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b=a$. Applying $J$ gives $a \cdot b^{J}=e, a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b^{J}=a$. Hence $b=b^{J} \in \mathfrak{J}$ by the uniqueness of the inverse. Thus $b \in \mathfrak{J} U_{e}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}) U_{e} \cap \mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ is a division algebra. Next assume $f$ skew, so $\Delta=\Gamma$ is a field and $\mathfrak{M} e$ has a basis $(u, v)$ such that $f(u, u)=0=f(v, v), f(u, v)=1=-f(v, u)$. If $a \in \mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ then $a=e a e$ and $\mathfrak{N} a \subseteq \mathfrak{N}$ for $\mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak{M} e$. Also since $\mathfrak{N}^{\perp}=\mathfrak{M}(1-e)$ it is clear that $\Re^{\perp} a=0$. We have $u a=\alpha u+\beta v, v a=\gamma a+\delta v$ where $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta \in \Gamma$. Since $a$ is selfadjoint relative to $f, f(u a, u)=f(u, u a)=-f(u a, u)=0$, so $f(u a, u)=0$. Similarly, $f(v a, v)=0$ and $f(u a, v)=f(u, v a)$. These relations imply that $\beta=0 =\gamma, \alpha=\delta$. Then $a-\alpha e$ annihilates $\mathfrak{N}$ as well as $\mathfrak{N}^{\perp}$. Hence $a=\alpha e$ and $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}=\Gamma e$, which is a division algebra. Since any nonisotropic subspace $\neq 0$ contains a minimal one, it is now clear that in both cases any quadratic ideal of the form
$\mathfrak{J} U_{e}, e^{e^{2}}=e$, contains a minimal quadratic ideal. This completes the verification of the axioms in this case and of the implication $(\gamma) \Rightarrow(\alpha)$.

The two structure theorems reduce the determination of the algebras satisfying the axioms to the determination of the Jordan division algebras. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is a Jordan algebra of a symmetric bilinear form $f$ such that $f(x, x) \neq 1$ for all $x \in \mathfrak{M}$ then $\mathfrak{J}$ is a division algebra. Also the Jordan algebras $\Delta^{+}$where $\Delta$ is an associative division algebra and the algebras $\mathfrak{H}(\Delta, j)$ where $(\Delta, j)$ is an associative division algebra with involution are Jordan division algebras. Finally, Albert has constructed some examples of exceptional Jordan division algebras. These are all "forms" of the exceptional algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ in the sense that they become this algebra on extension of the center (which is a field) to its algebraic closure. We shall see in the next chapter that every finite-dimensional Jordan division algebra is of one of the types just indicated. However, it seems likely that other types of examples of Jordan division algebras of infinite dimensionalities over their centers exist. (See the notes on Chapter I in "Further results and Open Question".)

## Exercises

1. Assuming that the Jordan algebra of a quadratic form is special (to be proved in §7.1) show that any exceptional simple Jordan algebra satisfying the axioms is either a division algebra or is isomorphic to an algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$, $\mathfrak{O}$ an algebra of octonions.
2. Use the Second Structure Theorem to prove that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a simple Jordan algebra satisfying the axioms and $\mathfrak{J}$ is of capacity $n$, then for any decomposition of $1=\sum_{1}^{m} f_{j}$, where the $f_{j}$ are orthogonal completely primitive idempotents one has $m=n$.
3. Special universal envelopes. Isomorphisms and derivations of special simple Jordan algebras satisfying the axioms. We shall now consider the problem of classifying the simple algebras which we determined in the last section. We pass over the cases of division algebras and the exceptional algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$. The problem for finite-dimensional special division algebras will be considered in the next chapter and the classification problem for the algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ will be considered in Chapter IX. There remain the Jordan algebras of symmetric bilinear forms and the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is simple Artinian with involution and the capacity $n \geqq 2$. The problem of classification of Jordan algebras of symmetric bilinear forms can be reduced immediately to that of equivalence of forms (ex. 5, p. 14). We have nothing to add to the well-known results on these so we shall pass to the final case of interest: the Jordan algebras $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ of capacity $\geqq 2$ where ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) is simple Artinian with involution.

We consider the algebras ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) first in their matrix form: $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$, where $n \geqq 2,(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is either an associative division algebra with involution or a direct
sum of an associative division algebra and its opposite with exchange involution, and $J_{a}$ is a canonical involution in $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$. If $n=2$ the definition of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ in the proof of Osborn's theorem (p. 176) shows that we may assume $\mathfrak{D}$ is generated by $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j) \left(=S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{11}\right)^{\nu}\right)$. We shall therefore suppose this is the case if $n=2$. Then the hypotheses of Corollary 1 to Martindale's Theorem (p. 141) are fulfilled and so the associative algebra with involution ( $\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}$ ) is perfect. This means that $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ and the injection mapping constitute a unital special universal envelope ( $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right), \sigma_{u}\right)$ for the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$. Thus any homomorphism of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{G}^{+}$where $\mathfrak{G}$ is an associative algebra with 1 has a unique extension to a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ into $\mathfrak{G}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$. It follows from Theorem 2.1 (4) (the functorial character of $S_{1}$ ) that any isomorphism between two of the Jordan algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$ has a unique extension to an isomorphism of the corresponding algebras with involution $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$. In this way the classification problem is reduced to that of the simple algebras with involution $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{a}\right)$. Since it is clear that one of these algebras with involution in which $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ is not simple cannot be isomorphic with any in which $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ is simple, we can separate the two cases: $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ not simple, $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ simple. In the first case $\mathfrak{D}_{n}=\Delta_{n} \oplus \Delta_{n}{ }^{J_{a}}$ where $\Delta_{n}$ is a simple ideal. The isomorphisms between two algebras with involution of this type correspond to the isomorphisms and antiisomorphisms of the simple component $\Delta_{n}$.

We now switch to the geometric point of view in which $\Delta_{n}$ is replaced by $\mathrm{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), \mathfrak{M}$ an $n$-dimensional vector space over the division algebra $\Delta$. Let $\mathfrak{N}$ be an $m$-dimensional vector space over the division algebra E. Then it is well known that $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{E}}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{M})$ are isomorphic if and only if $n=m$ and $\Delta \cong \mathrm{E}$. Moreover, if $\sigma$ is an isomorphism of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ onto $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{E}}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{N})$ then there exists a semilinear isomorphism of $\mathfrak{M} / \Delta$ onto $\mathfrak{N} / \mathbf{E}$ with associated isomorphism $s$ of $\Delta / \Phi$ onto $\mathrm{E} / \Phi$ such that $a^{\sigma}=S^{-1} a S, a \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ (Jacobson, Lectures. II, pp. 235-237). Next let $\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{E}}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathrm{E})$ the right vector space over E of linear functions on $\mathfrak{N}$ (to E ). Then $\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}$ can be regarded as a left vector space over $\mathrm{E}^{\circ}$ by putting $\varepsilon y^{\prime}=y^{\prime} \varepsilon$ where the $\varepsilon$ on the right is in E and that on the left is in $\mathrm{E}^{\circ}$. If $b \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{E}}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{N})$ then $b$ has a transpose linear transformation $b^{\prime}$ in the right vector space $\mathfrak{N}^{\prime} / \mathrm{E}$. This can be regarded as a linear transformation in $\mathfrak{N}^{\prime} / \mathbf{E}^{\circ}$. Then $b \rightarrow b^{\prime}$ is an antiisomorphism of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{E}}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{N})$ onto $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{E}^{\circ}}\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}, \mathfrak{N}^{\prime}\right)$. Hence if $a \rightarrow a^{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}$ is an antiisomorphism of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ onto $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{E}}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{N})$ then $a \rightarrow\left(a^{\sigma}\right)^{\prime}$ is an isomorphism of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ onto $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{E}^{\circ}}\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}, \mathfrak{N}^{\prime}\right)$. The form of this has been indicated and this gives the form of $\sigma$.

We consider next the isomorphisms of the algebras with involution $\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), J\right)$ where $J$ is the adjoint relative to a hermitian or skew symmetric form $f$. Thus we have $f(x a, y)=f\left(x, y a^{J}\right), x, y \in \mathfrak{M}, a \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. We note first that $f$ is determined by $J$ up to a right multiplier in $\Delta$. Let $g$ be a second nondegenerate hermitian or skew form such that $g(x a, y)=g\left(x, y a^{\boldsymbol{J}}\right), x, y \in \mathfrak{M}$, $a \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. Consider the linear mappings $x \rightarrow g(x, u) v$ and $x \rightarrow \varepsilon g(x, v) u$ where $\varepsilon=1$ or -1 according as $g$ is hermitian or skew. Since

$$
\begin{aligned}
g(g(x, u) v, y) & =g(x, u) g(v, y), \\
g(x, \varepsilon g(y, v) u) & =g(x, u) g(v, y),
\end{aligned}
$$

these are adjoints relative to $g$, hence, relative to $f$, so we have $f(g(x, u) v, y) =f(x, \varepsilon g(y, v) u)$. This gives $g(x, u) f(v, y)=f(x, u) \varepsilon \overline{g(y, v)}$ for all $x, y, u, v \in \mathfrak{M}$. Now we can choose $v, y$ so that $f(v, y)=1$ and obtain $g(x, u)=f(x, u) \gamma, x, u \in \mathfrak{M}$.

Let $\mathfrak{N} / \mathrm{E}$ be a second finite-dimensional vector space over a division algebra with involution, $g$ a nondegenerate hermitian or skew hermitian form on $\mathfrak{N}$, $K: b \rightarrow b^{\prime}$ the adjoint mapping determined by $g$. Let $\sigma$ be an isomorphism of the algebra with involution $\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), J\right)$ onto $\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{E}}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), K\right)$. Since $\sigma$ is an isomorphism of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ onto $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{E}}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{N})$ there exists a semilinear isomorphism of $\mathfrak{M}$ onto $\mathfrak{N}$ such that $a^{\sigma}=S^{-1} a S, a \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. Let $x, y \in \mathfrak{M}$ and let $s$ be the isomorphism of $\Delta$ onto E associated with $S$. Then one checks directly that the mapping $f^{\prime}$ defined by $f^{\prime}(x, y)=g(x S, y S)^{S^{-1}}$ is a nondegenerate hermitian or skew form on $\mathfrak{M} / \Delta$. Since $S a^{\sigma}=a S$ and $J \sigma=\sigma K$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
g(x a S, y S) & =g\left(x S a^{\sigma}, y S\right)=g\left(x S, y S a^{\sigma K}\right) \\
& =g\left(x S, y S a^{J \sigma}\right)=g\left(x S, y a^{J} S\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $g(x a S, y S)^{S^{-1}}=g\left(x S, y a^{J} S\right)^{S^{-1}}$ and so $f^{\prime}(x a, y)=f^{\prime}\left(x, y a^{J}\right)$. This implies that there exists a $\lambda \neq 0$ in $\Delta$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
f^{\prime}(x, y)^{S}=g(x S, y S)=f(x, y)^{S} \lambda^{S} . \tag{44}
\end{equation*}
$$

A form $f$ on $\mathfrak{M} / \Delta$ and a form $g$ on $\mathfrak{N} / \mathrm{E}$ will be called equivalent if there exists a semilinear isomorphism $S$ of $\mathfrak{M} / \Delta$ onto $\mathfrak{N} / E$ and a nonzero $\lambda \in \Delta$ such that (44) holds for all $x, y \in \mathfrak{M}$. Here $s$ is the isomorphism of $\Delta$ onto E associated with $S$. One sees easily that this is an equivalence relation. Our result is that any isomorphism of $\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), J\right)$ onto $\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{E}}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{M}), K\right)$ has the form $A \rightarrow S^{-1} A S$ where $S$ is an equivalence of $f$ with $g$.

We now consider the derivations of our Jordan algebras and again consider first the case of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})^{+}$. For simplicity we now assume $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M} / \Delta \geqq 3$. Then we know by Corollary 4 to Martindale's Theorem that any derivation of $\mathrm{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})^{+}$ is a derivation of $\mathrm{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$, so we consider the latter. If $d$ is a derivation in the division algebra $\Delta / \Phi$ then we define a $d$-semiderivation (or $d$-differential transformation) $D$ of $\mathfrak{M}$ to be an additive mapping in $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $(\rho x) D=\rho(x D) +\rho^{d} x, \rho \in \Delta, x \in \mathfrak{M}$. If $a \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ and $D$ is a semiderivation then a direct verification shows that $[a, D]=a D-D a \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. It is clear that the mapping $a \rightarrow[a, D]$ of $\mathrm{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ into itself is $\Phi$-linear. Also $[a b, D] =[a, D] b+a[b, D]$ for $a, b \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. Hence $a \rightarrow[a, D]$ is a derivation in $\mathrm{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. It is known that, conversely, every derivation in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ has the form $a \rightarrow[a, D], D$ a $d$-semiderivation of $\mathfrak{M} / \Delta$ (Jacobson's Structure of

Rings, p. 87). Our results now show that the derivations of $\mathrm{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})^{+}$with $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M} / \Delta \geqq 3$ have the form $a \rightarrow[a, D], D$ a semiderivation in $\mathfrak{M} / \Delta$.

Next let $\Delta$ have an involution and let $f$ be a nondegenerate hermitian or skew form associated with this involution. The nondegeneracy of $f$ implies that if $g: x \rightarrow g(x)$ is a linear function on $\mathfrak{M}$ then there exists a unique vector $y_{g}$ in $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $f\left(x, y_{g}\right)=g(x)$ for all $x \in \mathfrak{M}$. Let $D$ be a $d$-semiderivation in $\mathfrak{M} / \Delta$ and consider $g_{y}(x) \equiv f(x D, y)-f(x, y)^{d}$. If $\rho \in \Delta$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_{y}(\rho x) & =f((\rho x) D, y)-f(\rho x, y)^{d} \\
& =f\left(\rho(x D)+\rho^{d} x, y\right)-(\rho f(x, y))^{d} \\
& =\rho f(x D, y)+\rho^{d} f(x, y)-\rho^{d} f(x, y)-\rho f(x, y)^{d} \\
& =\rho g_{y}(x)
\end{aligned}
$$

Also it is clear that $g_{y}\left(x_{1}+x_{2}\right)=g_{y}\left(x_{1}\right)+g_{y}\left(x_{2}\right)$, so $g_{y}$ is a linear function on $\mathfrak{M} / \Delta$. Hence there exists a unique vector $z$ in $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $g_{y}(x)=f(x, z), x \in \mathfrak{M}$. We now have the mapping $y \rightarrow z$ in $\mathfrak{M}$, which we denote as $D^{J}$ and call the adjoint of $D$ relative to $f$. By definition, we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
f(x D, y)-f\left(x, y D^{J}\right)=f(y, x)^{d} \tag{45}
\end{equation*}
$$

If we apply $j$ to (45) we obtain

$$
\begin{equation*}
f\left(y D^{J}, x\right)-f(y, x D)=f(y, x)^{d} \tag{46}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\bar{d}$ is the derivation $-j d j$ in $\Delta$. This gives

$$
f\left((\rho y) D^{J}-\rho^{a} y-\rho\left(y D^{J}\right), x\right)=0
$$

for $x, y \in \mathfrak{M}, \rho \in \Delta$. Since $f$ is nondegenerate we obtain $(\rho y) D^{J}=\rho^{\bar{d}} y+\rho\left(y D^{J}\right)$. Since $D^{J}$ is clearly additive this shows that $D^{J}$ is a $\bar{d}$-semiderivation of $\mathfrak{M}$. Then (46) shows that $D$ is the adjoint of $D^{J}: D^{J^{2}}=D$. If $d=0$ then $D \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ and $D^{J}$ is the adjoint of $D$ relative to $f$ in the usual sense. If $a \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ and $D$ is a $d$-semiderivation in $\mathfrak{M}$, then $[a, D] \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}
f & (x[a, D], y)-f\left(x, y\left[D^{J}, a^{J}\right]\right) \\
= & f(x a D-x D a, y)-f\left(x, y D^{J} a^{J}-y a^{J} D^{J}\right) \\
= & f\left(x a, y D^{J}\right)+f(x a, y)^{d}-f\left(x D, y a^{J}\right) \\
& \quad-f\left(x, y D^{J} a^{J}\right)+f\left(x, y a^{J} D^{J}\right) \\
= & f\left(x, y D^{J} a^{J}\right)+f\left(x, y a^{J}\right)^{d}-f\left(x, y a^{J} D^{J}\right) \\
& \quad-f\left(x, y a^{J}\right)^{d}-f\left(x, y D^{J} a^{J}\right)+f\left(x, y a^{J} D^{J}\right) \\
= & 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $[a, D]^{J}=\left[D^{J}, a^{J}\right]$.
Now let $\delta$ be a derivation in the algebra with involution $\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), J\right)$ in the sense that $\delta$ is a derivation in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ which commutes with $J$. Then there exists a $d$-semiderivation $D$ in $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $a^{\delta}=[a, D], a \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$. Hence $a^{\delta J}=a^{J \delta}=\left[a^{J}, D\right]$ and $a^{\delta J}=[a, D]^{J}=\left[D^{J}, a^{J}\right]=-\left[a^{J}, D^{J}\right]$. Thus $D+D^{J}$ commutes with every linear transformation $a^{J}$ and consequently $D+D^{J}=\lambda_{L}$ where $\lambda_{L}$ is the multiplication $x \rightarrow \lambda x, \lambda \in \Delta$, in $\mathfrak{M}$. If $\mu \in \Delta$ then $\rho \rightarrow[\mu, \rho]$ is a derivation in $\Delta$ and $(\rho x) \mu_{L}=\mu(\rho x)=\rho \mu x+[\mu, \rho] x=\rho\left(x \mu_{L}\right)+[\mu, \rho] x$. Hence $\mu_{L}$ is a semiderivation in $\mathfrak{M}$ corresponding to the derivation ad $\mu: \rho \rightarrow[\mu, \rho]$ in $\Delta$. Since $f(\mu x, y)-f(x, \bar{\mu} y)=[\mu, f(x, y)]$ we see that $\mu_{L}{ }^{J}=\bar{\mu}_{L}$. It is clear also that if $a \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ then $\left[a, \mu_{L}\right]=0$. Now we have $D+D^{J}=\lambda_{L}$ which implies that $\lambda_{L}{ }^{J}=\lambda_{L}$ and $\bar{\lambda}=\lambda$. Put $E=D+\mu_{L}$ where $\mu=-\frac{1}{2} \lambda$. Then $E$ is an $e$-semiderivation for $e=d-\operatorname{ad} \mu$ and $E^{J}+E=D+\mu_{L}+D^{J}+\mu_{L}=D+D^{J}-\lambda_{L}=0$. Also $a \delta =[a, D]=[a, E]$. Hence we have shown that every derivation of $\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), J\right)$ has the form $a \rightarrow[a, E]$ where $E$ is a semiderivation of $\mathfrak{M}$ which is skew relative to $J: E^{J}=-E$. Conversely, if $E$ is any skew semiderivation then $a \rightarrow[a, E]$ is a derivation of $\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}), J\right)$.

In conclusion, our results reduce the problem of classifying the simple Jordan algebras we determined and of studying their derivations to well-defined problems on associative algebras. In particular, the isomorphism problem is reduced to one of classifying division algebras and classifying hermitian forms. For finite dimensional algebras over special fields, a fair amount of information on these problems is known.
7. Alternative set of axioms. In the next chapter we shall develop a structure theory for finite-dimensional Jordan algebras without the assumption that the algebras have identity elements. In order to be able to apply the results of this chapter it is necessary to modify our axioms (i)-(iii) by omitting the axiom (i) on existence of an identity element. We shall now show that we obtain the same class of algebras if we replace (i) by the following axiom on the quadratic ideals of the form $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ :
(iv) The minimum condition holds for quadratic ideals of form $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$, $e^{\cdot 2}=e$ and if $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e) \neq 0$ then $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ contains a minimal quadratic ideal.

Thus (iv) is a strengthening of the minimum conditions given in (iii) which, consists of adding the hypotheses made in (iii) on the quadratic ideals $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)=\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ to the quadratic ideals $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$. If $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element then $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)=\mathfrak{J}_{1}(1-e)$ so (iii) and (iv) are equivalent for Jordan algebras with 1. We shall now show that (ii), (iii) and (iv) imply (i) so the axioms (ii), (iii) and (iv) also characterize the class of Jordan algebras which we have studied in this chapter. The proof of this fact will be based on the standard trick of adjoining an identity element to an algebra.

Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra and let $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{J}$ be the algebra obtained by adjoining the identity element 1 to $\mathfrak{J}$. Then we know that $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is Jordan (p. 31).

If $b^{\prime}=\beta 1+b, \beta \in \boldsymbol{\Phi}, b \in \mathfrak{J}$, then $b^{\cdot 2}=\beta 1+\left(2 \beta b+b^{\cdot 2}\right)$ so $\left(b^{\prime}\right)^{\cdot 2}=0$ implies $\beta=0$ and $b^{\prime}=b \in \mathfrak{J}$. It follows that $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ has no absolute zero divisors $\neq 0$ if $\mathfrak{J}$ has none. Next assume $\left(b^{\prime}\right)^{.2}=b^{\prime}$. Then $\beta=0$ or $\beta=1$. In the first case, $b^{\prime}=b \in \mathfrak{J}$ and in the second, $b^{\cdot 2}=-b$ so $f=-b$ is an idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}$ and $b^{\prime}=1-f$. If $e^{\cdot 2}=e \in \mathfrak{J}$, then $\mathfrak{J}_{1}{ }^{\prime}(e)=\mathfrak{J}_{1}{ }^{\prime} U_{e}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} U_{e}$ since $1 U_{e}=e$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}_{1}{ }^{\prime}(e)=\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$. If $e^{\prime}=1-f, f^{\cdot 2}=f \in \mathfrak{J}$, then $\mathfrak{J}_{1}{ }^{\prime}\left(e^{\prime}\right)=\mathfrak{J}_{0}(f)+\Phi e^{\prime}$. Clearly the minimum condition holds for quadratic ideals of this form if and only if it holds for quadratic ideals of $\mathfrak{J}$ of the form $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(f), f^{\cdot 2}=f$.

Assume $\mathfrak{J}$ has no absolute zero divisors, so $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ has none. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a minimal quadratic ideal of $\mathfrak{J}$. By Theorem $1, \mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{J} U_{b}$ where $b \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} U_{b}=\mathfrak{J} U_{b}+\Phi b^{\cdot 2}=\mathfrak{B}$ so $\mathfrak{B}$ is a quadratic ideal of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$, which is clearly minimal. If $e^{\prime}=1-f, f^{\cdot 2}=f \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $\mathfrak{J}_{1}^{\prime}\left(e^{\prime}\right)=\mathfrak{J}_{0}(f)+\Phi e^{\prime}$. Hence if $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(f)$ contains a minimal quadratic ideal of $\mathfrak{J}$ then $\mathfrak{J}_{1}{ }^{\prime}\left(e^{\prime}\right)$ contains a minimal quadratic ideal of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. If $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(f)=0$ then $\mathfrak{J}_{1}{ }^{\prime}\left(e^{\prime}\right)=\Phi e^{\prime}$ is a minimal quadratic ideal of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$.

We can now prove
Theorem 10. If $\mathfrak{J}$ satisfies (ii), (iii) and (iv), then $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element, so the structure theorems hold for $\mathfrak{J}$.

Proof. The foregoing results show that $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{J}$ satisfies (i), (ii), (iii). Hence, by the proof of the First Structure Theorem. every ideal in $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ has a complementary ideal. In particular, $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{B}$ where $\mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element.

Axioms (iii) and (iv) are evidently satisfied if $\mathfrak{J}$ is finite dimensional over $\Phi$.

## Chapter V

## STRUCTURE THEORY FOR FINITE-DIMENSIONAL JORDAN ALGEBRAS

The structure theory of Jordan algebras was initiated by Jordan, von Neumann and Wigner in [1] in which they gave a complete determination of the finitedimensional Jordan algebras over the reals which are formally real in the sense that a relation $\sum a_{i}{ }^{2}=0$ holds in such an algebra only if every $a_{i}=0$. They showed that these algebras are direct sums of simple ones and they determined all the simple ones. The structure theory of finite-dimensional Jordan algebras over arbitrary fields has been developed b Albert in three papers [7], [9], [17]. In these he gave a definition of solvability and the radical and showed that a semisimple algebra, defined as one with 0 radical, is a direct sum of simple ideals. Moreover, he determined the finite-dimensional simple Jordan algebras over an algebraically closed field (with a small exception which was settled by the author in [19]). The extension of the determination and classification of special simple finite-dimensional Jordan algebras to the case of a nonalgebraically closed field is due to Kalisch [1] and F. D. Jacobson and N. Jacobson [1]. The problem of classifying exceptional simple Jordan algebras over arbitrary base fields has been studied by Albert and Jacobson [1], by Albert [25], [32] and by Springer [4] (see Chapter IX).

In this chapter we shall give Albert's theory of the radical of a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra and we shall show that his definition of semisimplicity is equivalent to nondegeneracy ( $=$ nonexistence of absolute zero divisors $\neq 0$ ) which we introduced in the last chapter. As a consequence, we shall obtain Albert's theorem that a finite-dimensional semisimple Jordan algebra is a direct sum of simple ones as a corollary to the First Structure Theorem of Chapter IV. We can also deduce from the Second Structure Theorem Albert's determination of the finite-dimensional simple Jordan algebras over an algebraically closed field and, more generally, the determination of the finite-dimensional simple Jordan algebras over an arbitrary field which are not division algebras. However, to get at the division algebras we shall require a base field extension argument which is applicable also to arbitrary finite-dimensional simple Jordan algebras. Moreover, this method can be made independent of the Second Structure Theorem by substituting for it a determination of another important class of Jordan algebras - the reduced simple Jordan algebras.

We shall follow the procedure just indicated in this chapter. We shall first reduce the study of the finite-dimensional simple Jordan algebras to those which are central in the sense that their centers coincide with the base field. We shall show that a finite-dimensional central simple Jordan algebra over $\Phi$ is one of the following types: I. a Jordan algebra of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form, II. a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is a finite-dimensional central simple associative algebra with involution, III. a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$, for $\Omega$ the algebraic closure of $\Phi$, is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{O}$ is the (uniquely determined) octonion algebra over $\Omega$. The classification of the algebras in $I$ is equivalent to that of symmetric bilinear forms. The classification of the algebras of type II is equivalent to the classification of the associative algebras with involution. The algebras in III are the only finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebras. We shall postpone the study of these to Chapter IX.

1. Ideals and associator ideals. A subspace $\mathfrak{B}$ of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ will be called an associator ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$ if any associator $\left[a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\right] \in \mathfrak{B}$ whenever any one of the $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$. Clearly any ideal is an associator ideal. If $\sigma$ is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ then, of course, the kernel of $\sigma$ is an ideal. On the other hand, if $\rho$ is a multiplication specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in an associative algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ with 1 then we know that $[a, b, c]^{\rho}=\left[\left[c^{\rho}, a^{\rho}\right], b^{\rho}\right]$ (ex. 1, p. 99). This evidently implies that the kernel of any multiplication specialization is an associator ideal. The kernel of a multiplication specialization need not be an ideal. For example, let $\mathfrak{T}$ be the subalgebra of $\Phi_{2}{ }^{+}$of triangular matrices $\alpha e_{11}+\beta e_{22}+\gamma e_{12}, \alpha, \beta, \gamma \in \Phi$, and let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi e_{11}+\Phi e_{22}, \mathfrak{M}=\Phi e_{12}$. Then $\left(\alpha e_{11}+\beta e_{22}\right) \cdot e_{12}=\frac{1}{2}(\alpha+\beta) e_{12}$ so $\mathfrak{M}$ relative to the multiplication defined in $\mathfrak{T}$ is a bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$. The formula just indicated shows that the kernel of the associated birepresentation is $\Phi\left(e_{11}-e_{22}\right)$. This is not an ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$.

If $a, b, c \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $[a, b, c]=a \cdot b \cdot c-c \cdot b \cdot a=-[c, b, a]$. Also $[a, b, c] +[b, c, a]+[c, a, b]=a . b . c-c . b . a+b . c . a-a . c . b+c . a . b-b . a . c=0$. This implies that a subspace $\mathfrak{B}$ is an associator ideal if and only if $\left[b, a_{1}, a_{2}\right] \in \mathfrak{B}$ for all $b \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$. If $\mathfrak{B}$ is an associator ideal then the subspace $\mathfrak{B}+\mathfrak{B} . \mathfrak{J}$ is an ideal since if $b \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $a_{1}, a_{2} \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $b \cdot a_{1} \cdot a_{2}=a_{1} \cdot a_{2} \cdot b+\left[b, a_{1}, a_{2}\right] \in \mathfrak{B} . \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{B}$. In particular, if $\mathfrak{B}$ is the kernel of a multiplication specialization then $\mathfrak{B}+\mathfrak{J} \cdot \mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal.

If $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ are ideals (associator ideals) then $\mathfrak{B}_{1} \cap \mathfrak{B}_{2}$ and $\mathfrak{B}_{1}+\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ are ideals (associator ideals). The product $\mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2}$ of two ideals need not be an ideal. We consider now some multiplicative properties of ideals in the following

Lemma 1. (1) If $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ are ideals then $\mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2}$ is an associator ideal; hence $\mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2}+\mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2} \cdot \mathfrak{J}$ is an ideal. (2) If $\mathfrak{B}_{1}, \mathfrak{B}_{2}, \mathfrak{B}_{3}$ are ideals then $\mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{3}+\mathfrak{B}_{2} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{3} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{1}+\mathfrak{B}_{3} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2}$ is an ideal. (3) If $\mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal then $\mathfrak{B}^{3}=\mathfrak{B} \cdot \mathfrak{B}^{2}$ is an ideal.

Proof. (1) Let $b_{1} \in \mathfrak{B}_{1}, b_{2} \in \mathfrak{B}_{2}, a_{1}, a_{2} \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
{\left[b_{1} \cdot b_{2}, a_{1}, a_{2}\right] } & =b_{1} \cdot b_{2} \cdot a_{1} \cdot a_{2}-b_{1} \cdot b_{2} \cdot\left(a_{1} \cdot a_{2}\right) \\
& =b_{1} \cdot a_{2} \cdot\left(b_{2} \cdot a_{1}\right)+b_{1} \cdot a_{1} \cdot\left(b_{2} \cdot a_{2}\right) \\
& -b_{1} \cdot a_{2} \cdot a_{1} \cdot b_{2}-b_{1} \cdot\left(b_{2} \cdot a_{2} \cdot a_{1}\right) \quad\left(\text { by } \mathrm{B}_{3}, \text { p } \cdot 34\right) \in \mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2} \cdot
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $\mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2}$ is an associator ideal and $\mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2}+\mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2} \cdot \mathfrak{J}$ is an ideal. (2) Let $b_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}_{i}, i=1,2,3$, and let $a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
b_{1} \cdot b_{2} \cdot b_{3} \cdot a= & -b_{1} \cdot a \cdot b_{3} \cdot b_{2}-b_{1}\left(b_{2} \cdot a \cdot b_{3}\right) \\
& +b_{1} \cdot b_{2} \cdot\left(a \cdot b_{3}\right)+b_{1} \cdot a \cdot\left(b_{2} \cdot b_{3}\right) \\
& +b_{1} \cdot b_{3} \cdot\left(a \cdot b_{2}\right) \\
\in \mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{3} & +\mathfrak{B}_{2} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{3} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{1}+\mathfrak{B}_{3} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2} \cdot
\end{aligned}
$$

This implies that $\mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{3}+\mathfrak{B}_{2} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{3} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{1}+\mathfrak{B}_{3} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2}$ is an ideal and proves (2). Evidently (3) is a special case of this.

Lemma 2. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be an ideal, $\mathfrak{S}$ an $m(<\infty)$ dimensional subspace of $\mathfrak{J}$. Define $\mathfrak{B}_{0}=\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B}_{k}=\mathfrak{B}_{k-1} \cdot \mathfrak{B} . \mathfrak{S}$. Then $\mathfrak{B}_{m+1} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}^{2}$.

Proof. Let $b, b_{1}, b_{2}, \cdots, b_{k} \in \mathfrak{B}, a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{k} \in \mathfrak{J}, k>1$, and consider the product $b . b_{1}, a_{1}, b_{2}, a_{2} \cdots b_{k}, a_{k}=b R_{b_{1}} R_{a_{1}} \cdots R_{b_{k}} R_{a_{k}}$. We claim that if two of the $a_{i}$ are equal then this product is contained in $\mathfrak{B}^{2}$. We assume first that $a_{k}=a_{i}=a$ for $i<k$. If $i=k-1$ then the product has the form $d R_{a} R_{b_{k}} R_{a}$ where $d \in \mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2}$. We have $2 d R_{a} R_{b_{k}} R_{a}=d\left(-R_{a \cdot \mathbf{2} \cdot b_{k}}+2 R_{a \cdot b_{k}} R_{a}+R_{a \cdot \mathbf{2}} R_{b_{k}}\right)$. Since $\mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal it is clear that $d R_{a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b_{k}}$ and $d R_{a_{\cdot 2}} R_{b_{k}} \in \mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2}$. Also $d R_{a \cdot b_{k}} \in \mathfrak{B}^{3}$ and this is an ideal. Hence $d R_{a . b_{k}} R_{a} \in \mathfrak{B}^{3} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}^{.2}$. Thus $d R_{a} R_{b_{k}} R_{a} \in \mathfrak{B}^{.2}$. Now let $i=k-r, r>1$. Then our product has the form $d R_{a} R_{b^{\prime}} R_{a^{\prime}} R_{b^{\prime \prime}} \cdots R_{a}$ where $d \in \mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2}, b^{\prime}, b^{\prime \prime} \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then $d R_{a} R_{b^{\prime}} R_{a^{\prime}}=d\left(-R_{a^{\prime}} R_{b^{\prime}} R_{a}-R_{a \cdot a^{\prime} \cdot b^{\prime}}+R_{a \cdot b^{\prime}} R_{a^{\prime}}+R_{a^{\prime}, b^{\prime}} R_{a}\right. \left.+R_{a . a^{\prime}} R_{b}\right)$ and since $d R_{a . a^{\prime} . b^{\prime}}, d R_{a . b^{\prime}} R_{a^{\prime}}, d R_{a^{\prime} . b^{\prime}} R_{a}$ and $d R_{a . a^{\prime}} R_{b} \in \mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2}$ our product is congruent modulo the ideal $\mathfrak{B}^{3}$ to $-d R_{a^{\prime}} R_{b^{\prime}} R_{a} R_{b^{\prime \prime}} \cdots R_{a}$. Hence we see by induction on $r$ that any product $b \cdot b_{1} \cdot a_{1} \cdots b_{k} \cdot a_{k}$ in which $a_{k}=a_{k-r}, r \geqq 1$, is contained in $\mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2}$. This result and the fact that $\mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 3}$ is an ideal implies that if $a_{i}=a_{j}$ for $i<j<k$ then the product is in $\mathfrak{B}^{3}$. Hence we have established the claim made at the outset. Now let $\left(s_{1}, s_{2}, \cdots, s_{m}\right)$ be a basis for $\mathfrak{S} / \Phi$. Then it is clear from the definition of the $\mathfrak{B}_{k}$ that any element of $\mathfrak{B}_{m+1}$ is a linear combination of products of the form $b . b_{1} . s_{i_{1}} . b_{2} . s_{i_{2}} . \ldots . b_{m+1} . s_{i_{m+1}}$ where $b, b_{j} \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $i_{i} \in\{1,2, \cdots, m\}$. Since two of the $s$ 's are equal the result established shows that the product indicated is in $\mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2}$. Hence $\mathfrak{B}_{m+1} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2}$.

We can now prove the following useful result.
Theorem 1. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be an ideal in the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ of finite codimension $m$ in J. Define

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
\mathfrak{B}^{[0]}=\mathfrak{B}, & \mathfrak{B}^{[k]}=\mathfrak{B}^{[k-1]} \cdot \mathfrak{B}+\mathfrak{B}^{[k-1]} \cdot \mathfrak{B} \cdot \mathfrak{J}, & k \geqq 1, & \\
\mathfrak{B}^{(0)}=\mathfrak{B}, & \mathfrak{B}^{(k)}=\mathfrak{B}^{(k-1)} \cdot \mathfrak{B}^{(k-1)}+\mathfrak{B}^{(k-1)} \cdot \mathfrak{B}^{(k-1)} \cdot \mathfrak{J}, & k \geqq 1 . \tag{2}
\end{array}
$$

Then $\mathfrak{B}^{[k]}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}$ are ideals in $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{[m+1]}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{(m+1)}$ are contained in $\mathfrak{B}^{.2}$.
Proof. The fact that $\mathfrak{B}^{[k]}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}$ are ideals follows from Lemma 1 (1). Since $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B}=m$ we can write $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{B}+\mathfrak{S}$ where $\mathfrak{S}$ is a subspace such that $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{S}=m$. Then one proves, by induction on $k$, that if $\mathfrak{B}_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ is defined as in Lemma 2 then $\mathfrak{B}^{[k]} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}_{k}+\mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2}$. It follows from Lemma 2 that $\mathfrak{B}^{[m+1]} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2}$. Also, by induction, we have $\mathfrak{B}^{(k)} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}^{[k]}$. Hence $\mathfrak{B}^{(m+1)} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}^{.2}$.
2. Solvable ideals. We define the powers $\mathfrak{J}^{2^{k}}$ of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ by $\mathfrak{J}^{\cdot 2^{0}}=\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J}^{\cdot 2^{k}}=\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\cdot 2^{k-1}}\right)^{\cdot 2}$. Clearly $\mathfrak{J}^{\cdot 2}$ is an ideal and all the $\mathfrak{J}^{\cdot 2^{k}}$ are subalgebras. However, the $\mathfrak{J}^{\cdot 2^{k}}$ with $k>1$ need not be ideals. We shall call $\mathfrak{J}$ solvable if there exists an integer $N$ such that $\mathfrak{J}^{2^{N}}=0$. It is clear that any subalgebra and any homomorphic image of a solvable algebra is solvable. Moreover, we have the following

Lemma 1. (1) If $\mathfrak{J}$ contains a solvable ideal $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B}$ is solvable then $\mathfrak{J}$ is solvable. (2) If $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ are solvable ideals then $\mathfrak{B}_{1}+\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ is a solvable ideal.

Proof. (1) Assume $(\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B})^{\cdot^{2^{N}}}=0$. It is clear from the definition of the powers that this implies that $\mathfrak{J}^{2^{N}} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$. Also $\mathfrak{J}^{2^{N+M}} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}^{2^{M}}$. Since $\mathfrak{B}$ is solvable this proves that $\mathfrak{J}$ is solvable. (2) We know that $\mathfrak{B}_{1}+\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ is an ideal and $\left(\mathfrak{B}_{1}+\mathfrak{B}_{2}\right) / \mathfrak{B}_{2} \cong \mathfrak{B}_{1} /\left(\mathfrak{B}_{1} \cap \mathfrak{B}_{2}\right)$. Since the right-hand side is a homomorphic image of $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ it is solvable. Hence $\left(\mathfrak{B}_{1}+\mathfrak{B}_{2}\right) / \mathfrak{B}_{2}$ and $\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ are solvable. Then $\mathfrak{B}_{1}+\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ is solvable by (1).

It is clear from Lemma 1 (2) that if $\mathfrak{J}$ satisfies the maximum condition for ideals then $\mathfrak{J}$ contains a solvable ideal $\Re$ such that $\Re$ contains every solvable ideal of $\mathfrak{J}$. In particular, this holds for finite-dimensional $\mathfrak{J}$. In this case we call $\Re$ the radical of $\mathfrak{J}$ (or $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ ). This is analogous to the definition of the radical of a finite-dimensional associative algebra as the maximal nilpotent ideal. If $\Re=0$, or, equivalently, $\mathfrak{J}$ has no nonzero solvable ideals then we shall call $\mathfrak{J}$ semisimple. If $\Re$ is the radical of $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\overline{\mathfrak{S}}$ is the radical of $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\mathfrak{J} / \Re$ then $\overline{\mathfrak{S}}=\mathfrak{S} / \Re$ where $\mathfrak{S}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $\mathfrak{S} / \Re$ and $\Re$ are solvable $\mathfrak{S}$ is solvable. Hence $\mathfrak{S} \subseteq \Re$ and $\overline{\mathfrak{S}}=0$. Thus $\mathfrak{J} / \Re$ is semisimple if $\Re$ is the radical of $\mathfrak{J}$.

The main result we shall obtain in this section is that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is finite-dimensional and $\mathfrak{J}$ is considered as imbedded in its universal multiplication envelope $U(\mathfrak{J})$ in the usual way (§2.9) then the radical $\Re$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ is contained in the radical $\mathfrak{N}$ of $U(\mathfrak{I})$. The proof will be based on several lemmas.

Lemma 2 (Penico). Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{B}$ a solvable ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$ and define $\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}$ by $\mathfrak{B}^{(0)}=\mathfrak{B}, \quad \mathfrak{B}^{(k)}=\mathfrak{B}^{(k-1)} \cdot \mathfrak{B}^{(k-1)}$
$+\mathfrak{B}^{(k-1)} \cdot \mathfrak{B}^{(k-1)} \cdot \mathfrak{I}$. Then the $\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}$ are ideals, $\mathfrak{B}^{(k)} \supseteq \mathfrak{B}^{(k+1)},\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}\right)^{2} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}^{(k+1)}$ and there exists an integer $M$ such that $\mathfrak{B}^{(M)}=0$.

Proof. Everything except the last statement is clear by Lemma 1 of §1. Also, by Theorem 1, if $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{I}=n$ then $\mathfrak{B}^{(n+1)} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}^{.2}$. We claim that for $r=1,2, \cdots$, we have $\mathfrak{B}^{(r(n+1))} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}^{2^{r}}$. Thus assume this holds for $r$. Then $\mathfrak{B}^{(r+1)(n+1))} =\mathfrak{B}^{(r(n+1)+n+1)}=\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(r(n+1))}\right)^{(n+1)}$ since the definition of the $\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}$ gives $\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}\right)^{(j)}=\mathfrak{B}^{(k+j)}$. Hence $\mathfrak{B}^{(r+1)(n+1))}=\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(r(n+1))}\right)^{(n+1)} \subseteq\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(r(n+1))}\right)^{\cdot 2} \subseteq\left(\mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2^{r}}\right)^{\cdot 2} =\mathfrak{B}^{2^{r+1}}$. Hence $\mathfrak{B}^{(r(n+1))} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}^{2^{r}}$ for all $r=1,2, \cdots$. Since $\mathfrak{B}$ is solvable this implies that there exists an integer $M$ such that $\mathcal{B}^{(M)}=0$.
If $\mathfrak{B} \neq 0$ is solvable then $\mathfrak{B}^{(0)} \neq 0$ in the sequence of $\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}$. Let $M$ be minimal such that $\mathfrak{B}^{(M)}=0$. Then $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{B}^{(0)} \supset \mathfrak{B}^{(1)} \supset \cdots \supset \mathfrak{B}^{(M)}=0$ since $\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}=\mathfrak{B}^{(k+1)}$ implies that $\mathfrak{B}^{(k+1)}=\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}\right)^{(1)}=\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(k+1)}\right)^{(1)}=\mathfrak{B}^{(k+2)}$. Then $\mathbb{C}=\mathfrak{B}^{(1)}$ is an ideal properly contained in $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $\mathfrak{B}^{2} \subseteq \mathfrak{C}$. Also $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{B}^{(M-1)}$ is a nonzero ideal such that $\mathfrak{D}^{2}=0$.

Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a solvable ideal in the finite-dimensional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ and let $U(\mathfrak{J})$ be the universal multiplication envelope of $\mathfrak{J}$. We assume that $\mathfrak{J} \subseteq U(\mathfrak{J})$. Then we shall show that $\mathfrak{B}$ generates a nilpotent ideal in $U(\mathfrak{J})$. We shall prove this by induction on $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}$ and we may assume $\mathfrak{B} \neq 0$. Then we have an ideal $\mathfrak{C}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $\mathfrak{B} \supset \mathfrak{C}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{\mathbf{2}} \subseteq \mathfrak{C}$. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be the ideal in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by $\mathfrak{C}$. Then the induction hypothesis implies that $\mathfrak{B}$ is nilpotent. Also we know that $U(\mathfrak{J}) / \mathfrak{B}$ and the mapping $a+\mathfrak{C} \rightarrow a+\mathfrak{B}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, constitute a universal multiplication envelope for $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{C}$ (Theorem 2.11). The ideal $\overline{\mathfrak{B}}=\mathfrak{B} / \mathfrak{C}$ in $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$ satisfies $\overline{\mathfrak{B}}^{2}=0$. Suppose we know that $\overline{\mathfrak{B}}$ generates a nilpotent ideal in the universal multiplication envelope $U(\overline{\mathfrak{I}})$ of $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$. Then the set of cosets $b+\mathfrak{B}, b \in \mathfrak{B}$, generates a nilpotent ideal in $U(\mathfrak{J}) / \mathfrak{B}$. This ideal has the form $\mathfrak{B} / \mathfrak{B}$ where $\mathfrak{B}$ is the ideal in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by $\mathfrak{B}$. Since $\mathfrak{B} / \mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ are nilpotent it follows that $\mathfrak{B}$ is nilpotent. Thus the ideal in $U(\mathfrak{I})$ generated by $\mathfrak{B}$ is nilpotent. The argument therefore shows that it is enough to prove the result for the case in which $\mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2}=0$. This will be achieved in the following two lemmas.

Lemma 3. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra such that $\mathfrak{J}^{\cdot 2}=0$. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ generates a nilpotent ideal in $U(\mathfrak{J})$.

Proof. We note that $\mathfrak{J}$ is associative and we prove first that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finitedimensional associative Jordan algebra then $U(\mathfrak{J})$ contains a nilpotent ideal $\Re$ such that $U(\mathfrak{J}) / \mathfrak{N}$ is commutative. We have the relation $[[c a] b]=[a, b, c]$ in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ for $a, b, c \in \mathfrak{J}$ (eq. (47), p. 96). Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is associative this implies that every commutator $[c a], c, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, is in the center of $U(\mathfrak{J})$. Next we consider the relation $2 a b a+a^{.2} . b=b a^{.2}+2 a(a . b)$ (eq. (46'), p. 96). Taking commutators with $b$ and using the fact that this operation is a derivation, we obtain $2[a, b] b a+2 a b[a, b]+\left[a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b, b\right]=b\left[a^{\cdot 2}, b\right]+2[a, b](a . b)+2 a[a . b, b]$. Since commutators of elements of $\mathfrak{J}$ are in the center, commutation again with $b$ gives
$4[a, b]^{2} b=4[a, b][a . b, b]$. Then commutation with $a$ gives $4[a, b]^{3}=0$ and $[a, b]^{3}=0$. Since $U(\mathfrak{I})$ is finite-dimensional associative it follows that the commutators generate a nilpotent ideal $\mathfrak{N}$ in $U(\mathfrak{J})$. Clearly $U(\mathfrak{J}) / \mathfrak{N}$ is commutative. Next we note that $\mathfrak{J}^{2}=0$ and $2 a b a+a^{2} . b=b a^{2}+2 a(a . b)$ imply that $a^{3}=0$. Hence the cosets $a+\mathfrak{N}$ generate a nilpotent ideal in $U(\mathfrak{J}) / \mathfrak{N}$ and the elements $a$ generate a nilpotent ideal in $U(\mathfrak{I})$.

Lemma 4. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{B}$ a nonzero ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $\mathfrak{B}^{2}=0$. Let $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ be a basis for $\mathfrak{J}$ such that ( $u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{m}$ ) is a basis for $\mathfrak{B}$. Then any monomial $u_{j_{1}} u_{j_{2}} \cdots u_{j_{1}}$ in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ in which $k+m$ of the $u_{j} \in \mathfrak{B}$ is a linear combination of monomials in the $u_{i}$ in which the first $k$ of the $u$ 's $\in \mathfrak{B}$.

Proof. This is clear if $l=k+m$; hence we may use induction on the formal degree $l$ of the monomial $M=u_{j_{1}} u_{j_{2}} \cdots u_{j_{1}}$. Now suppose the first $h u$ 's in $M$ are in $\mathfrak{B}$ but $u_{j_{h+1}} \notin \mathfrak{B}$. Then there is nothing to prove if $h \geqq k$ so for a given $l$ we may use a downward induction on $h$ and we may assume $h<k$. Then there are at least $m+1 u_{j_{q}}{ }^{\prime} s \in \mathfrak{B}$ with $q>h+1$ and hence $M$ has the form

$$
\begin{equation*}
\cdots u \cdots u \cdots \tag{3}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $u=u_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ and the first displayed $u$ in (3) occurs after the ( $h+1$ )-th place. Let $\mathfrak{C}$ denote the subspace of monomials $u_{i_{1}} u_{i_{2}} \cdots u_{i_{k}} \cdots$ where the $u_{i_{p}}, 1 \leqq p \leqq k$, are in $\mathfrak{B}$. Suppose first that the two displayed $u$ 's in (3) are consecutive and let $v$ denote the $u_{j_{q}}$ in (3) preceding the first $u$. If we use the relation $a b c=-c b a-a . c . b +a(b . c)+b(a . c)+c(a . b)$ (eq. (47), p. 96) in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ for $a=v, b=c=u$ we obtain $v u^{2}=-u^{2} v+2 u(u . v)$. Since $u . v \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $u . v=0$ if $v \in \mathfrak{B}$, a succession of replacements of the type indicated shows that $M \equiv \pm M^{\prime}(\bmod \mathfrak{C})$ where $M^{\prime}$ is a monomial in the $u$ 's having $h+2 u_{i}$ 's $\in \mathfrak{B}$ at the beginning and containing $m+k u_{i}{ }^{\prime} s \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then the downward induction on $h$ implies that $M^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{C}$; hence $M \in \mathfrak{C}$. Next assume the two displayed $u$ 's in (3) are separated by a single $v=u_{j_{q}}$. Then we can use the relation $2 u v u+u^{\cdot 2} \cdot v=2 u(u \cdot v)+v\left(u^{\cdot 2}\right)$, which gives $u v u=u(u . v)$, to express $M$ as a linear combination of monomials of formal degree $<l$ all of which have $k+m$ factors $u_{j} \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then induction on $l$ implies that $M \in \mathbb{C}$. Finally, supposed the displayed $u$ 's in (3) are separated by at least two $u_{i} \neq u$. Then we can use the relation $v w u=-u w v-v . u . w+u(v . w) +v(u . w)+w(u . v)$ to show that $M \equiv-M^{\prime}(\bmod \mathfrak{C})$ where $M^{\prime}$ is obtained from $M$ by moving the second $u$ in (3) two places to the left. A succession of moves of this type gives a reduction to one of the first two cases. Hence $M \in \mathfrak{B}$ in all cases.

We can now complete the proof of
Theorem 2. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{B}$ a solvable ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\mathfrak{B}$ generates a nilpotent ideal in $U(\mathfrak{J})$.

Proof. We have reduced the proof to the case $\mathfrak{B}^{.2}=0$. Now it follows from Lemma 3 that there exists an integer $k$ such that the product of any $k$ elements of $\mathfrak{B}$ is 0 . Let $\left(u_{1}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ be a basis for $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $\left(u_{1}, \cdots, u_{m}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{B}$. Then Lemma 4 implies that any monomial $u_{j_{1}} \cdots u_{j_{1}}$ in which $k+m$ of the $u$ 's are in $\mathfrak{B}$ is 0 . This implies that if $\mathfrak{B}$ is ideal generated by $\mathfrak{B}$ then $\mathfrak{B}^{k+m}=0$.

Since the radical of a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra is the maximal solvable ideal and since the radical of a finite-dimensional associative algebra is the maximal nilpotent ideal it is clear that Theorem 2 can be stated in an equivalent form that the radical $\Re$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ is contained in the radical $\mathfrak{N}$ of $U(\mathfrak{J})$.

A nonassociative algebra is called nilpotent if there exists an integer $N$ such that every product (in any association) of $N$ elements of the algebra is 0 . It is evident that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a nilpotent Jordan algebra then $\mathfrak{J}$ is solvable. On the other hand, we have

Corollary 1 (Albert). Any finite-dimensional solvable Jordan algebra J is nilpotent.

Proof. Since we have a homomorphism of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ mapping $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a \rightarrow R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, it follows from Theorem 2 that there exists an integer $N$ such that $R_{a_{1}} R_{a_{2}} \cdots R_{a_{N}}=0$ for any $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$. Now it is immediate by induction on $r$ that a product of $2^{r}$ elements of $\mathfrak{J}$ associated in any way can be written in the form $a R_{a_{1}} R_{a_{2}} \cdots R_{a_{r}}$ for suitable $a, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$. Hence any product of $2^{N}$ elements of $\mathfrak{J}$ is 0 and $\mathfrak{J}$ is nilpotent.

Corollary 2. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ be as in the theorem, $\left(S(\mathfrak{J}), \sigma_{u}\right)$ the special universal envelope of $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\mathfrak{B}^{\sigma_{u}}$ generates a nilpotent ideal in $S(\mathfrak{J})$.

Proof. We have the homomorphism of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $S(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1$, $a \rightarrow \frac{1}{2} a^{\sigma_{u}}$. Since a nilpotent ideal is mapped into a nilpotent ideal under a surjective homomorphism, the result follows from Theorem 2.

In the same way we can obtain the analogous statements to Theorem 2 and Corollary 2 for the unital universal multiplication envelope and the unital special universal envelope for a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with identity element.
3. Finite-dimensional nil algebras. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is a solvable Jordan algebra, say $\mathfrak{J}^{2^{N}}=0$, then $a^{2^{N}}=0$ for every $a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}$ is a nil algebra in the sense that every element of $\mathfrak{J}$ is nilpotent. We shall now prove that for finite-dimensional Jordan algebras one has the converse: nillity implies solvability. For this we need the following

Lemma. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a subalgebra of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}, x$ an element of $\mathfrak{J}, x \notin \mathfrak{B}$, such that $\mathfrak{B} . x \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$. Then there exists a $y \in \mathfrak{J}, y \notin \mathfrak{B}$, such that $\mathfrak{B} . \boldsymbol{y} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{B} . \boldsymbol{y}^{\mathbf{2}} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$.

Proof. Let $b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3} \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then we shall show that

$$
\begin{gather*}
x^{\cdot 2} \cdot\left(b_{1} \cdot b_{2}\right) \in \mathfrak{B}  \tag{4}\\
\left(x^{\cdot 2} \cdot b_{1}\right) \cdot b_{2} \in \mathfrak{B}  \tag{5}\\
\left(x^{\cdot 2} \cdot b_{1}\right) \cdot\left(x^{\cdot 2} \cdot b_{2}\right) \cdot b_{3} \in \mathfrak{B} . \tag{6}
\end{gather*}
$$

For the proofs of these we shall use the associator identity: $[a, b, c]=-[c, b, a]$ which is immediate by commutativity, and ( $B_{1}{ }^{\prime}$ ) on p. 33: $[c . d, a, b]+[b . c, a, d] +[b \cdot d, a, c]=0$. For (4) we have $x^{\cdot 2} \cdot\left(b_{1} \cdot b_{2}\right)=\left[x, x, b_{1} \cdot b_{2}\right]+x \cdot\left(x \cdot\left(b_{1} \cdot b_{2}\right)\right) =\left[b_{1} \cdot x, x, b_{2}\right]+\left[b_{2} \cdot x, x, b_{1}\right]+x \cdot\left(x \cdot\left(b_{1} \cdot b_{2}\right)\right) \in \mathfrak{B}$ since $\mathfrak{B}^{\cdot 2} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$ and $x \cdot \mathfrak{B} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$. For (5) we have $x^{\cdot 2} \cdot b_{1} \cdot b_{2}=\left[x^{\cdot 2}, b_{1}, b_{2}\right]+x^{\cdot 2} \cdot\left(b_{1} \cdot b_{2}\right)=x^{\cdot 2} \cdot\left(b_{1} \cdot b_{2}\right) -2\left[x . b_{2}, b_{1}, x\right] \in \mathfrak{B}$ by the hypotheses and (4). For (6) we have $\left(x^{\cdot 2} \cdot b_{1}\right) \cdot\left(x^{\cdot 2} \cdot b_{2}\right) \cdot b_{3} =\left[x^{\cdot 2}, b_{1}, x^{\cdot 2} \cdot b_{2}\right] \cdot b_{3}+\left(x^{\cdot 2} \cdot\left(b_{1} \cdot\left(x^{\cdot 2} \cdot b_{2}\right)\right)\right) \cdot b_{3}$. Using (5) twice we see that the second term is in $\mathfrak{B}$. The first term equals $-2\left[x, b_{1}, x^{\cdot 2} \cdot b_{2} \cdot x\right] \cdot b_{3} =-2\left[x, b_{1}, b_{2} \cdot x \cdot x^{\cdot 2}\right] \cdot b_{3}$ (by $\left.\left[R_{x} R_{x \cdot 2}\right]=0\right) \in \mathfrak{B}$, by (5). Now if $\mathfrak{B} \cdot x^{\cdot 2} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$ then we take $y=x$. Otherwise, there exists a $b_{1} \in \mathfrak{B}$ such that $y=b_{1} \cdot x^{\cdot 2} \notin \mathfrak{B}$. Then (5) and (6) show that $y . b$ and $y^{2} . b \in \mathfrak{B}$ for all $b \in \mathfrak{B}$, as required.

The condition on $y$ in Lemma 1 can be written in operator form as $\mathfrak{B} R_{y} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{B} R_{\boldsymbol{y} \cdot \mathbf{2}} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$. Since $R_{\boldsymbol{y} \cdot \boldsymbol{k}}$ is a polynomial in $R_{\boldsymbol{y}}$ and $R_{\boldsymbol{y} \cdot \mathbf{2}}$ this implies that $\mathfrak{B} R_{y \cdot k} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}, k=1,2,3, \cdots$. Now let $\mathfrak{Y}$ be the set of polynomials $\beta_{1} y+\beta_{2} y^{\cdot 2} +\beta_{3} y^{\cdot 3}+\cdots, \beta_{i} \in \Phi$. Then it is clear that $\mathbb{C}=\mathfrak{B}+\mathfrak{Y}$ is a subalgebra containing $\mathfrak{B}$ as an ideal. We can now prove

Theorem 3 (Albert). Any finite-dimensional nil algebra is solvable.
Proof. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be finite-dimensional nil and let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a maximal solvable subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$. Consider the subalgebra $\mathfrak{N}$ of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ of linear combinations of elements $R_{b_{1}} R_{b_{2}} \cdots R_{b_{k}}, b_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$. It follows from Theorem 2 that $\mathfrak{N}$ is a nilpotent algebra of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{J}$ mapping $\mathfrak{B}$ into itself. Hence if $\mathfrak{B} \subset \mathfrak{J}$ then there exists an $x \in \mathfrak{J}, \notin \mathfrak{B}$ such that $x R_{b} \in \mathfrak{B}$ for all $b \in \mathfrak{B}$. This is the same as $\boldsymbol{x} . \mathfrak{B} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$. Hence by the Lemma and the remark above we have a subalgebra $\mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{B}+\mathfrak{Y}$ such that $\mathfrak{C} \supset \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{C}$ and $\mathfrak{Y}$ is the set of polynomials $\beta_{1} y+\beta_{2} y^{2}+\cdots$. Since $y$ is nilpotent it is clear that $\mathfrak{Y}$ is solvable. Now $\mathfrak{C} / \mathfrak{B} \cong \mathfrak{Y} /(\mathfrak{Y} \cap \mathfrak{B})$ is solvable and $\mathfrak{B}$ is solvable. Hence $\mathfrak{C}$ is solvable, contrary to the maximality of $\mathfrak{B}$. Thus $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{B}$ is solvable.

An important consequence of Theorem 3 is the
Corollary Any finite-dimensional algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ which is not solvable contains a nonzero idempotent element.

Proof. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is not solvable it contains an element $y$ which is not nilpotent. The subalgebra $\mathfrak{Y}=\left\{\beta_{1} y+\beta_{2} y^{\cdot 2}+\cdots\right\}$ is associative and can be imbedded in an algebra $\Phi[y]$ with 1 . Then, by Lemma 1 on p. 149, $\mathfrak{Y}$ contains a nonzero idempotent element.

## Exercises

1. Show that Lemma 1 of §2 is valid for nil ideals. Use this to prove that any Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ contains a nil ideal $\mathfrak{N}$ which contains every nil ideal of $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{N}$ has no nonzero nil ideals.
2. Give an example of a nil algebra which is not solvable.
3. Reduced Jordan algebras.
