Since $\Delta^{a}$ is a derivation in $\Re$ we have

$$
\begin{align*}
\Delta_{c}^{a}(f+g) & =\Delta_{c}^{a} f+\Delta_{c}^{a} g,  \tag{6}\\
\Delta_{c}^{a}(\gamma f) & =\gamma \Delta_{c}^{a} f,  \tag{7}\\
\Delta_{c}^{a}(f g) & =f(c) \Delta_{c}^{a} g+\left(\Delta_{c}^{a} f\right) g(c),  \tag{8}\\
\Delta_{c}^{a} f^{-1} & =-\left(\Delta_{c}^{a} f\right) f^{-2}(c), \quad \text { if } f(c) \neq 0 \tag{9}
\end{align*}
$$

for $f, g \in \Re$ and $\gamma \in \Phi$. If $b$ is a second element of $\mathfrak{B}$ then we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
\Delta^{b}{ }_{c} \Delta^{a} f=\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} \Delta^{b} f . \tag{10}
\end{equation*}
$$

This follows since the derivations $f \rightarrow \partial f / \partial \xi_{i}$ in $\Phi(\xi)$ commute. Hence the derivations $f \rightarrow \sum \alpha_{i} \partial f / \partial \xi_{i}$ and $f \rightarrow \sum \beta_{i} \partial f / \partial \xi_{i}$ commute if $\alpha_{i}, \beta_{i} \in \Phi$. Since the corresponding derivations in $\Re$ are $\Delta^{a}$ and $\Delta^{b}$ for $a=\sum \alpha_{i} u_{i}, b=\sum \beta_{i} u_{i}$ it is clear that (10) holds.

If $f \in \Re$ we define the logarithmic derivative of $f \neq 0$ in the direction $a$ as

$$
\begin{equation*}
\Delta^{a} \log f=f^{-1} \Delta^{a} f . \tag{11}
\end{equation*}
$$

We have the formulas

$$
\begin{align*}
\Delta^{a} \log f g & =\Delta^{a} \log f+\Delta^{a} \log g  \tag{12}\\
\Delta^{b} \Delta^{a} \log f & =\left[f\left(\Delta^{b} \Delta^{a} f\right)-\Delta^{a} f \Delta^{b} f\right] f^{-2} . \tag{13}
\end{align*}
$$

For a fixed $c$ and $f$ it is clear that the mapping $(a, b) \rightarrow \Delta^{b}{ }_{c} \Delta^{a} f$ is a bilinear form on $\mathfrak{B}$. By (10) this is symmetric. Similarly, the formula (13) shows that $\Delta^{b}{ }_{c} \Delta^{a} \log f =\Delta^{b}{ }_{c}\left(f^{-1} \Delta^{a} f\right)$ for fixed $c$ and $f$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak{B} / \Phi$.

Now let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a second finite-dimensional vector space. Let $f=g h^{-1}$ where $g$ and $h$ are polynomial functions on $\mathfrak{V}$ and let $w \in \mathfrak{W}$. Then $x \rightarrow f(x) w$ is a mapping of the (Zariski) open subset $O_{h}$ defined by $h(x) \neq 0$ into $\mathfrak{W}$. The space generated by such mappings consists of the mappings of the form $x \rightarrow \sum f_{j}(x) w_{j}$ where the $f_{j}$ are rational functions on $\mathfrak{B}$. We shall call these rational mappings
on $\mathfrak{B}$ (more precisely, of an open subset of $\mathfrak{B}$ on which all the $f_{j}$ are defined) in $\mathfrak{B}$ and we denote their totality as $\Re(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B})$. If all the $f_{j}$ in $x \rightarrow \sum f_{j}(x) w_{j}$ are polynomial functions then this mapping is called a polynomial mapping of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ (defined on all of $\mathfrak{B}$ ). The set of these will be denoted as $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{W})$. If $w_{1}, \cdots, w_{r}$ are linearly independent elements of $\mathfrak{B}$ and $\sum_{1}^{r} f_{j}(x) w_{j}=0$ for all $x$ at which the $f_{j}$ are defined then the $f_{j}$ are 0 . This implies that $\Re(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{W})(\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{W}))$ can be identified with $\Re(\mathfrak{B}) \otimes_{\Phi} \mathfrak{W}(\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{B}) \otimes \mathfrak{W})$. If $\left(w_{1}, w_{2}, \cdots, w_{r}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{W} / \Phi$ then it is clear that $\Re(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{W})$ is the set of mappings $x \rightarrow \sum_{1}^{r} f_{j}(x) w_{j}$ where the $f_{j}$ are rational functions. If $F$ is a polynomial or rational mapping on $\mathfrak{V}$ and $F(z)=0$ for all $z$ in a nonvacuous open subset of $\mathfrak{V}$ then $F=0$.

Let $a \in \mathfrak{B}$ and consider the derivation $f \rightarrow \Delta^{a} f$ in $\Re$ corresponding to $a$. Since the space $\mathfrak{R}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{W})$ of rational mappings of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{W}$ is the same as $\mathfrak{R}(\mathfrak{B}) \otimes_{\Phi} \mathfrak{W}$ we can define a linear mapping $F \rightarrow \Delta^{a} F$ in $\Re(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{W})$ by specifying that if $F$ is $x \rightarrow \sum f_{j}(x) w_{j}, f_{j} \in \Re, w_{j} \in \mathfrak{W}$, then $\Delta^{a} F$ is $x \rightarrow \sum\left(\Delta^{a}{ }_{x} f_{j}\right) w_{j}$. As in the special case of rational functions $(\mathfrak{W}=\Phi)$, we denote the value $\Delta^{a} F(c)$ of $\Delta^{a} F$ at $c$ also as $\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} F$. Since $\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} f_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_{i}\left(\partial f_{j} / \partial \xi_{i}\right)_{\xi_{i}=\gamma_{i}}$ if $a=\sum_{1}^{n} \alpha_{i} v_{i}$ and $c=\sum \gamma_{i} v_{i}$ we have $\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} F=\sum_{i, j} \alpha_{i}\left(\partial f_{j} / \partial \xi_{i}\right)_{\xi_{i}=\gamma_{i}} w_{j}$. Since $a \rightarrow \Delta_{c}^{a} f_{j}$ is a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\Phi$, $a \rightarrow \Delta^{a}{ }_{c} F=\Sigma_{j} \Delta^{a}{ }_{c} f_{j} v_{j}$ is a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{W}$. We shall call this mapping the differential $\Delta_{c} F$ of $F$ at $c$. The explicit formula for $\Delta_{c}^{a} F$ shows that if $\left(v_{1}, v_{2}, \cdots, v_{n}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{B}$, as before, and $\left(w_{1}, w_{2}, \cdots, w_{r}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{M}$ then the matrix of $\Delta_{c} F$ relative to this pair of bases is the $n \times r$ Jacobian matrix $\left(\left(\partial f_{j} / \partial \xi_{i}\right)_{\xi_{i}=\gamma_{i}}\right), i=1, \cdots, n, j=1, \cdots, r$. It is immediate from the definition of $\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} F$ and (6)-(8) that if $F, G \in \Re(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{W}), f \in \Re, \gamma \in \Phi$, then

$$
\begin{align*}
\Delta_{c}^{a}(F+G) & =\Delta_{c}^{a} F+\Delta_{c}^{a} G  \tag{14}\\
\Delta_{c}^{a}(\gamma F) & =\gamma \Delta_{c}^{a} F  \tag{15}\\
\Delta_{c}^{a}(f F) & =f(c) \Delta_{c}^{a} F+\left(\Delta_{c}^{a} f\right) F(c) \tag{16}
\end{align*}
$$

Let $F$ be a rational mapping on $\mathfrak{V}$ into $\mathfrak{W}$ and $g$ a rational function on $\mathfrak{W}$. If $\left(v_{1}, \cdots, v_{n}\right)$ and $\left(w_{1}, \cdots, w_{r}\right)$ are bases for $\mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{W}$ then $F$ has the form $\sum_{1}^{n} \alpha_{i} v_{i} \rightarrow \sum_{1}^{r} f_{j}\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right) w_{j}$ and $g$ has the form $\sum_{1}^{r} \beta_{j} w_{j} \rightarrow q\left(\beta_{1}, \cdots, \beta_{r}\right)$ where $f_{1}, \cdots, f_{r}$ are uniquely determined elements of $\Phi\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ and $q$ is a uniquely determined element of $\Phi\left(\sigma_{1}, \cdots, \sigma_{r}\right), \xi_{i}, \sigma_{j}$ indeterminates. We now define the composite function $g \circ F$ on $\mathfrak{V}$ as

$$
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{1}^{n} \alpha_{i} v_{i} \rightarrow q\left(f_{1}\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right), \cdots, f_{r}\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right)\right) . \tag{17}
\end{equation*}
$$

One can check directly that this is independent of the choice of the bases and it is clear that $g \circ F$ is a rational function. Moreover, it is clear that if $c$ is an element of $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $F$ is defined at $c$ and $g$ is defined at $F(c)$, then $g \circ F$ is defined at $c$ and $(g \circ F)(c)=g(F(c))$. (The set of such $c$ 's may be vacuous.) In
this situation the directional derivative $\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} g \circ F$ is defined for any $a$. By (4) and the formula for the directional derivative we obtain

$$
\begin{equation*}
\Delta_{c}^{a} g \circ F=\Delta_{d}^{b} g, \quad b=\Delta_{c}^{a} F, \quad d=F(c) \tag{18}
\end{equation*}
$$

This states that the differential of $g \circ F$ at $c$ is the resultant of the differential of $F$ at $c$ and the differential of $g$ at $F(c)$.

Again let $F: \sum_{1}^{n} \alpha_{i} v_{i} \rightarrow \sum_{1}^{r} f_{j}\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right) w_{j}$ be a rational mapping of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{B}$ and let $G$ be a rational mapping of $\mathfrak{P}$ into the vector space $\mathfrak{S}$ with basis $\left(s_{1}, \cdots, s_{t}\right)$. Assume $G$ has the form $\sum_{1}^{r} \beta_{j} w_{j} \rightarrow \sum_{k=1}^{t} g_{k}\left(\beta_{1}, \cdots, \beta_{r}\right) s_{k}$ where the $g_{k} \in \Phi\left(\sigma_{1}, \cdots, \sigma_{r}\right), \sigma_{i}$ indeterminates. Then we define the composite mapping $G \circ F$ by

$$
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{1}^{n} \alpha_{i} v_{i} \rightarrow \sum_{k=1}^{l} g_{k}\left(f_{1}\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right), \cdots, f_{r}\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right)\right) s_{k} \tag{19}
\end{equation*}
$$

It is clear from the case of composite functions $(\widetilde{S}=\Phi)$ that this is independent of bases and is a rational mapping. Also as in the case $\boldsymbol{S}=\boldsymbol{\Phi}$, if $c$ is an element of $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $F$ is defined at $c$ and $G$ is defined at $F(c)$, then we have the chain rule

$$
\begin{equation*}
\Delta_{c}^{a} G \circ F=\Delta_{d}^{b} G, \quad b=\Delta_{c}^{a} F, \quad d=F(c) . \tag{20}
\end{equation*}
$$

A rational mapping $F$ on $\mathfrak{B}$ is called homogeneous of degree $m=0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \cdots$ if for any $c$ at which $F$ is defined and any $\lambda \neq 0$ in $\Phi, F$ is defined at $\lambda c$ and $F(\lambda c)=\lambda^{m} F(c)$. It is easily seen (ex. 1 below) that if $f$ is a homogeneous rational function on $\mathfrak{V}$ then $f$ has the form $\sum_{1}^{n} \alpha_{i} v_{i} \rightarrow g\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right) h\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right)^{-1}$ where $g$ and $h$ are homogeneous polynomials (in all the $\left.\xi_{i}\right)$ in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$. Let $f$ be a homogeneous rational function on $\mathfrak{B}$ of degree $m$ and let $c$ be an element of $\mathfrak{B}$ at which $f$ is defined. The function $\lambda \rightarrow f(\lambda c)$ on $\Phi$ is a rational function which is the composite $f \circ \lambda c$ where $\lambda c$ is the mapping $\lambda \rightarrow \lambda c$, and the defining equation gives $f \circ \lambda=f(c) \lambda^{m}$. Hence by (18) we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
m f(c)=\Delta_{1}^{1} f \circ \lambda=\Delta_{c}^{c} f \tag{21}
\end{equation*}
$$

which is Euler's differential equation.
If $f \in \Phi\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ satisfies $\partial f / \partial \xi_{1}=0$ then $f \in \Phi\left(\xi_{2}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ if the characteristic is 0 and $f \in \Phi\left(\xi_{1}{ }^{p}, \xi_{2}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ if the characteristic is $p$. It follows that if $f$ is a rational function such that $\Delta^{a} f=0$ for all $a \in \mathfrak{B}$ then $f$ is a constant (function) if the characteristic is 0 and for characteristic $p, f$ has the form $g \circ \tilde{p}$ where $\tilde{p}$ has the form $\sum \alpha_{i} u_{i} \rightarrow \sum \alpha_{i}{ }^{p} u_{i}$ relative to some basis $\left(v_{1}, \cdots, v_{n}\right)$ for $\mathfrak{B}$. The converse is clear also.

If $f$ is a rational function on $\mathfrak{B}$ and $T$ is a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{B}$ into itself then
$f$ is called an invariant (semi-invariant) under $T$ if for any $c$ at which $f$ is defined, $f$ is defined at $c T$ and $f(c T)=f(c)(f(c T)=\gamma f(c)$ for a fixed $\gamma \neq 0$ in $\Phi) . f$ is a Lie invariant (Lie semi-invariant) under $T$ if $\Delta^{c T}{ }_{c} f=0$ ( $\Delta^{c T}{ }_{c} f=\rho f, \rho \in \Phi$ ) for all $c$ at which $f$ is defined. It is clear that the set of invertible $T$ which have a given $f$ as invariant (semi-invariant) form a subgroup of the linear group on $\mathfrak{B}$. On the other hand, the set of $T \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{V})$ having $f$ as Lie invariant (Lie semi-invariant) is a subalgebra of the Lie algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B})^{-}$which is restricted (that is is closed under $p$ th powers) if $\Phi$ is of characteristic $p \neq 0$. To see this we note that if $T \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B})$ then the mapping $g \rightarrow g^{\boldsymbol{D}_{\boldsymbol{T}}}$ where $g^{\boldsymbol{D}_{\boldsymbol{T}}}(x)=\Delta^{\boldsymbol{x} \boldsymbol{T}}{ }_{\boldsymbol{x}} g$ is a derivation in $\Re=\Re(\mathfrak{B})$ over $\Phi$. This is clear from equations (6), (7) and (8). If $l \in \mathfrak{V}^{*}$ then $l^{D_{T}}(x)=\Delta^{x T}{ }_{x} l=l(x T)$ since $\Delta^{a} l=l(a)$ for $l \in \mathfrak{B}^{*}$. Hence $l^{D_{T}}=l T^{*}$ where $T^{*}$ is the transpose of $T\left(l T^{*}(x)=l(x T)\right)$. If $T_{1}, T_{2} \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B})$ and $\alpha \in \Phi$ then $l^{D_{T_{1}}{ }^{+} T_{2}}=l\left(T_{1}+T_{2}\right)^{*}=l\left(T_{1}^{*}+T_{2}^{*}\right)=l T_{1}^{*}+l T_{2}^{*}=l^{D_{T_{1}}}+l^{D_{T_{2}}}=l^{D_{T_{1}}+D_{T_{2}}}$. Hence $l^{D_{T_{1}}{ }^{+} T_{2}}=l^{D_{T_{1}}+D_{T_{2}}}$. Similarly, $\left(\alpha T_{1}\right)^{*}=\alpha T_{1}^{*}$ gives $l^{D_{\alpha T}}=l^{\alpha D_{T}},\left[T_{1} T_{2}\right]^{*} =\left[T_{2}^{*} T_{1}^{*}\right]$ gives $l^{D\left[T_{1} T_{2}\right]}=l^{\left[D_{T_{2}} D_{T_{1}}\right]}$ and $\left(T_{1}^{*}\right)^{p}=\left(T_{1}{ }^{p}\right)^{*}$ gives $l^{\left(D_{T}\right)^{p}}=l^{\left(D_{T}\right)^{p}}$. Since 1 and $\mathfrak{B}^{*}$ generate $\Re / \Phi$ these formulas show that $T \rightarrow D_{T}$ is an antihomomorphism of the Lie algebra (restricted Lie algebra) $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{V}, \mathfrak{V})$ - (if the characteristic is $p$ ) into the Lie algebra (restricted Lie algebra) of derivations of $\Re / \Phi$. It is clear from this that if $f \in \Re$, the elements $T \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B})$ satisfying $f^{\boldsymbol{D}_{\boldsymbol{T}}}=0$ or $f^{\boldsymbol{D}_{\boldsymbol{T}}}=\rho(T) f, \rho(T) \in \Phi$, form a subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{V})^{-}$as Lie algebra (restricted Lie algebra). Since $f^{D_{T}}(c)=\Delta^{c T}{ }_{c} f$ this is just the set of $T$ having $f$ as Lie invariant or Lie semi-invariant.

If $F$ is a rational mapping on $\mathfrak{B}$ to $\mathfrak{P}$ and $F$ is given by $\sum_{1}^{n} \alpha_{i} v_{i} \rightarrow \sum_{1}^{r} f_{j}\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right) w_{j}$ in terms of the basis where the $f_{j} \in \Phi\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ then the same formula can be used to define a rational mapping on $\mathfrak{B}_{\Gamma}$ into $\mathfrak{W}_{\Gamma}$ where $\Gamma$ is an extension field of $\Phi$. It is clear that this is independent of the choices of the bases. We shall call this the extension of $F$ to $\mathfrak{B}_{\Gamma}$ and shall usually denote it as $F$ also. Clearly if $F$ is a polynomial mapping then so is its extension.

Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over $\Phi$ and let $F$ and $G$ be rational mappings on $\mathfrak{B}$ to $\mathfrak{A}$. For bases $\left(v_{1}, \cdots, v_{n}\right),\left(w_{1}, \cdots, w_{r}\right)$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{A}$ respectively these have the form $F: \sum_{1}^{n} \alpha_{i} v_{i} \rightarrow \sum_{1}^{r} f_{g}\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right) w_{j}$ and $G: \sum_{1}^{n} \alpha_{i} v_{i} \rightarrow \sum_{1}^{r} g_{j}\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right) w_{j}$ where $f_{j}, g_{j} \in \Phi\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$. Also we have the multiplication table $w_{j} w_{k}=\sum_{l} \gamma_{j k l} w_{l}, \gamma_{j k l} \in \Phi$, for the basis $\left(w_{j}\right)$. Then $\left(\sum f_{j}(\alpha) w_{j}\right)\left(\sum g_{k}(\alpha) w_{k}\right) =\sum \gamma_{j k l} f_{j}(\alpha) g_{k}(\alpha) w_{l}$ and so the mapping $x \rightarrow F(x) G(x)$ is a rational mapping on $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{A}$. We denote this as $F G$. Evidently, we have $F G: \sum \alpha_{i} v_{i} \rightarrow \sum h_{j}\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right) w_{j}$ where

$$
\begin{equation*}
h_{j}=\sum_{k . l} \gamma_{k l j} f_{k} g_{l}, \quad j, k, l=1, \cdots, r \tag{22}
\end{equation*}
$$

It is immediate from this and (6)-(8) that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\Delta_{c}^{a} F G=F(c) \Delta_{c}^{a} G+\left(\Delta_{c}^{a} F\right) G(c) \tag{23}
\end{equation*}
$$

## Exercises

1. Let $f_{i}, i=1,2$, be a homogeneous rational mapping on $\mathfrak{B}$ of degree $m_{i}$. Show that $f_{1} f_{2}$, and $f_{1} f_{2}^{-1}\left(f_{2} \neq 0\right)$ are homogeneous of degree $m_{1}+m_{2}$ and $m_{1}-m_{2}$ respectively. Use a Vandermonde determinant argument to show that any homogeneous rational mapping on $\mathfrak{B}$ has the form $\sum \alpha_{i} u_{i} \rightarrow g\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right) h\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right)^{-1}$ where $g$ and $h$ are homogeneous polynomials in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$.
2. Let $\Delta^{\xi}{ }_{\xi} f$ for $f \in \Phi\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ be the image of $\Delta^{\eta}{ }_{\xi} f$ under $\eta_{i} \rightarrow \xi_{i}$. Thus $\Delta^{\xi}{ }_{\xi} f=\sum \xi_{i} \partial f / \partial \xi_{i}$. Verify that if $f=\xi_{1}{ }^{m_{1}} \xi_{2}{ }^{m_{2}} \cdots \xi_{n}{ }^{m_{n}}, m_{i} \geqq 0, \sum m_{i}=m$, then $\Delta^{\xi}{ }_{\xi} f=m f$. Use this and ex. 1 to give another proof of Euler's theorem.
3. Let $f$ be a homogeneous polynomial function of degree $m$ on $\mathfrak{B}$. Show that for fixed $a \in \mathfrak{V}, \Delta^{a} f$ is a homogeneous polynomial function of degree $m-1$. Show that if the characteristic is 0 or $p>m$ then $(1 / m!) \Delta^{a_{1}} \Delta^{a_{2}} \cdots \Delta^{a_{m}} f$ is a constant and $f\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{m}\right)=(1 / m!) \Delta^{a_{1}} \Delta^{a_{2}} \cdots \Delta^{a_{m}} f$ is a symmetric multilinear form in $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{m}$ such that $f(x, x, \cdots, x)=f(x)$.
4. Let $f$ and the characteristic be as in 3 . Show that $f$ is a Lie invariant under $T$ if and only if

$$
\begin{aligned}
f\left(a_{1} T, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{m}\right) & +f\left(a_{1}, a_{2} T, a_{3}, \cdots, a_{m}\right) \\
& +\cdots+f\left(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{m-1}, a_{m} T\right)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

3. Generic minimum polynomial of a strictly power associative algebra. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a finite-dimensional power associative algebra with 1 over the field $\Phi$ (which may be finite). We recall that power associativity means $a^{r} a^{s}=a^{r+s}$ if $a^{r}$ is defined by $a^{1}=a, a^{r}=a^{r-1} a$. Equivalently, the condition is that every subalgebra $\Phi[a]$ generated by 1 and a single element $a$ is associative (hence also commutative). Let $\lambda$ be an indeterminate and let $\mu_{a}(\lambda) \in \Phi[\lambda]$ be the minimum polynomial of $a$. As usual, we denote the right multiplication $x \rightarrow x a$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ by $a_{R}$. If $b \in \Phi[a]$ then $b_{R}$ maps $\Phi[a]$ into itself and we let $\overline{b_{R}}$ denote the restriction of $b_{R}$ to $\Phi[a]$. Since $b \rightarrow \overline{b_{R}}$ is a monomorphism of $\Phi[a]$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\Phi[a], \Phi[a])$ the minimum polynomial $\mu_{b}(\lambda)$ of $b$ is the same as the minimum polynomial $\mu_{\overline{b_{R}}}(\lambda)$ of $\overline{b_{R}}$. Also this is a factor of the characteristic polynomial of $\overline{b_{R}}$ which in turn is a factor of the characteristic polynomial $f_{b}(\lambda)$ of $b_{R}$. Hence

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mu_{b}(\lambda) \mid f_{b}(\lambda) \tag{24}
\end{equation*}
$$

We recall also that

$$
\begin{equation*}
f_{b}(\lambda)=\operatorname{det}(\lambda 1-(\beta)) \tag{25}
\end{equation*}
$$

where ( $\beta$ ) is a matrix of $b_{R}$ relative to some basis of $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$. If $b$ is a generator of $\Phi[a]$, that is, $\Phi[b]=\Phi[a]$, then $\operatorname{deg} \mu_{\overline{b_{R}}}(\lambda)=\operatorname{dim} \Phi[a]$ and $\left(1, b, \cdots, b^{m-1}\right)$, where $m=\operatorname{deg} \mu_{b}(\lambda)$, is a basis for $\Phi[a]$. In this case $\operatorname{deg} \mu_{b}(\lambda)$ is the same as the degree of the characteristic polynomial $f_{\bar{b}_{R}}(\lambda)$ of $\overline{b_{R}}$ and since $\mu_{b}(\lambda) \mid f_{\bar{b}_{R}}(\lambda)$ we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mu_{b}(\lambda)=f_{\overrightarrow{b_{R}}}(\lambda) \tag{26}
\end{equation*}
$$

if $b$ is a generator of $\Phi[a]$. In particular, this holds if $b=a$.
If $\Phi$ is infinite then we have the polynomial mappings $p_{r}: a \rightarrow a^{r}, r=1,2, \cdots$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ and the power associativity of $\mathfrak{A}$ is equivalent to the requirement that for every $r, s=1,2, \cdots$ the polynomial mapping $p_{r+s}-p_{r} p_{s}$ is the 0 mapping. Now it is clear that if $\Gamma$ is an extension field of $\Phi$ then the polynomial mapping $p_{r+s}-p_{r} p_{s}$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ is the extension to $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ of the corresponding mapping in $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence the mappings indicated are also 0 in $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ and so $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ is power associative. For $\Phi$ finite it may happen that $\mathfrak{A}$ is power associative but $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ is not power associative for some $\Gamma / \Phi$. We shall now call an algebra strictly power associative if $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ is power associative for every extension field $\Gamma / \Phi$.

We now assume that $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ is finite-dimensional strictly power associative with 1 and ( $u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}$ ) is a basis for $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$. Let $\mathbf{P}=\Phi\left(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ where the $\xi_{i}$ are algebraically independent over $\Phi$ and consider the algebra $\mathfrak{U}_{\mathbf{p}}$. We shall call the element $x=\sum_{1}^{n} \xi_{i} u_{i}$ of $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{P}}$ a generic element of $\mathfrak{A}$. Let $m_{x}(\lambda)$ be the minimum polynomial of $x$ (in $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{P}}$ ) so $m_{x}(\lambda) \in \mathrm{P}[\lambda]$ and has leading coefficient 1. By (24), $m_{x}(\lambda) \mid f_{x}(\lambda)$ the characteristic polynomial of the linear transformation $x_{R}$ in $\mathfrak{U}_{\mathrm{P}}$. Now $\left(u_{i}\right)$ is also a basis for $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}$ and if $u_{i} u_{j}=\sum_{k} \gamma_{i j k} u_{k}$ is the multiplication table for this basis then $u_{i} x=\sum_{j, k} \gamma_{i j k} \xi_{j} u_{k}$ so that the matrix of $x_{R}$ relative to $\left(u_{i}\right)$ is $\left(\xi_{i k}\right)$ where $\xi_{i k}=\sum_{j} \gamma_{i j k} \xi_{j}$. It is clear from this that the characteristic polynomial $f_{x}(\lambda)$ is an element of $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}, \lambda\right]$ which is homogeneous of degree $n$ in $\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}$ and $\lambda$. Also the coefficient of $\lambda^{n}$ in $f_{x}(\lambda)$ is 1 . It follows from Gauss' lemma that $m_{x}(\lambda)$ which is a factor of $f_{x}(\lambda)$ in $\Phi\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)[\lambda]$ has the form

$$
\begin{equation*}
m_{x}(\lambda)=\lambda^{m}-\sigma_{1}(\xi) \lambda^{m-1}+\sigma_{2}(\xi) \lambda^{m-2}-\cdots+(-1)^{m} \sigma_{m}(\xi) \tag{27}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\sigma_{j}(\xi)=\sigma_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) \in \Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$. Moreover, since any factor of a homogeneous polynomial is homogeneous, $m_{x}(\lambda)$ is homogeneous of degree $m$ in $\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}$ and $\lambda$, which implies that $\sigma_{j}(\xi)$ is homogeneous of degree $j$ in the $\xi$ 's.

It is clear by induction on $k$ that if $x^{0}=1$ then

$$
\begin{equation*}
x^{k}=\sum_{i} \rho_{k i}(\xi) u_{i}, \quad k=0,1,2, \cdots \tag{28}
\end{equation*}
$$

( $\rho_{1 i}=\xi_{i}$ ) where $\rho_{k i}(\xi) \in \Phi[\xi]=\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ is homogeneous of degree $k$ in the $\xi$ 's. The relation $m_{x}(x)=0$ is equivalent to the following set of relations in $\Phi[\xi]$ :

$$
\begin{equation*}
\rho_{m i}(\xi)-\sigma_{1}(\xi) \rho_{m-1, i}(\xi)+\cdots+(-1)^{m} \sigma_{m}(\xi) \rho_{0 i}=0 \tag{29}
\end{equation*}
$$

$i=1,2, \cdots, n$. Now let $a=\sum_{1}^{n} \alpha_{i} u_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}$. Then the specialization $\xi_{i}=\alpha_{i}$ in (28) gives $a^{k}=\sum \rho_{k i}(\alpha) u_{i}$ and the same specialization in (29) gives $\rho_{m i}(\alpha)-\sigma_{1}(\alpha) \rho_{m-1, i}(\alpha) +\cdots+(-1)^{m} \sigma_{m}(\alpha) \rho_{0 i}=0$. These relations imply that if we put

$$
\begin{equation*}
m_{a}(\lambda)=\lambda^{m}-\sigma_{1}(a) \lambda^{m-1}+\cdots+(-1)^{m} \sigma_{m}(a) \tag{30}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\sigma_{i}(a)=\sigma_{i}(\alpha)$ then we have $m_{a}(a)=0$ in $\mathfrak{A}$. We shall call the polynomial $m_{a}(\lambda) \in \Phi[\lambda]$ the generic minimum polynomial of $a$ and the elements $\sigma_{1}(a)$ and $\sigma_{m}(a)$ respectively the generic trace and generic norm of $a$. Also we shall call the degree $m$ of all the $m_{a}(\lambda)$ (or of $m_{x}(\lambda)$ in $\lambda$ ) the degree of the algebra $\mathfrak{A}$. We shall see later that this coincides with the degree of a finite dimensional central simple Jordan algebra as defined in the last chapter (§5.7). Since $m_{a}(a)=0$ we have $\mu_{a}(\lambda) \mid m_{a}(\lambda)$ if $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ is the minimum polynomial of $a$.

The generic minimum polynomial has been defined by means of the basis $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ for $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$. We proceed to establish independence of this choice of basis. Accordingly, let $\left(v_{1}, v_{2}, \cdots, v_{n}\right)$ be a second basis for $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ and consider the generic element $y=\sum_{1}^{n} \xi_{i} v_{i}$ associated with the basis. We have $v_{i}=\sum \mu_{i j} u_{j}$ where $\mu_{i j} \in \Phi$ and ( $\mu_{i j}$ ) is nonsingular, and $y=\sum \xi_{i} v_{i}=\sum \xi_{i} \mu_{i j} u_{j}$. The specialization argument used before shows that if $m_{y}(\lambda)$ is the polynomial obtained from $m_{x}(\lambda)$ by replacing $\xi_{j}$ by $\eta_{j}=\sum_{i} \xi_{i} \mu_{i j}$ then $m_{y}(y)=0$. Hence the degree of the minimum polynomial of $y$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}$ is $\leqq m$. By symmetry, it is $m$ and so it is the polynomial $m_{y}(\lambda)$. This implies that for any $a=\sum_{i} \beta_{i} v_{i}=\sum_{i, j} \beta_{i} \mu_{i j} u_{j}$ the generic minimum polynomials of $a$ defined by $x$ and by $y$ are the same.

We note next that $m_{a}(\lambda)$ is unchanged on extension of the base field $\Phi$. By this we mean that if $\Gamma$ is an extension field of $\Phi$ and we identify $\mathfrak{A}$ as usual with a $\Phi$-subalgebra of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ then $m_{a}(\lambda)$ is the same whether calculated in $\mathfrak{A}$ or in $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$. To see this we note that since $\left(u_{i}\right)$ is also a basis for $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ then, assuming, as we may, that the $\xi_{i}$ are algebraically independent over $\Gamma$, we have that $x=\sum \xi_{i} u_{i}$ is a generic element of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$. Moreover, it is clear from properties of the tensor product that the minimum polynomial of an element is unaltered on extension of the base field. Hence $m_{x}(\lambda)$ is also the minimum polynomial of $x$ as element of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma(\xi)}=\Gamma(\xi) \otimes_{\Phi} \mathfrak{A}, \mathrm{P}=\Phi(\xi)$. Clearly this implies that the generic minimum polynomial of $a$ is unchanged on extension of $\Phi$ to $\Gamma$.

The relation $m_{a}(a)=0$ can be written in the form

$$
\begin{equation*}
n(a) 1=a\left[\sigma_{m-1}(a) 1-\sigma_{m-2}(a) a+\cdots+(-1)^{m-1} a^{m-1}\right] \tag{31}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $n(a) \equiv \sigma_{m}(a)$ is the generic norm. We now put

$$
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{adj} a=\sigma_{m-1}(a) 1-\sigma_{m-2}(a) a+\cdots+(-1)^{m-1} a^{m-1} \tag{32}
\end{equation*}
$$

in analogy with the adjoint of a matrix. Then we have the relation

$$
\begin{equation*}
a(\operatorname{adj} a)=n(a) 1=(\operatorname{adj} a) a . \tag{33}
\end{equation*}
$$

We have defined the generic minimum polynomial for $a$ in any finite-dimensional strictly power associative algebra with 1 . In deriving properties of these polynomials and their coefficients we may generally assume the base field is infinite since the generic minimum polynomial is unchanged under extension of the base field. For infinite $\Phi, a \rightarrow \sigma_{i}(a)$ is a homogeneous polynomial function of degree
$i$ on $\mathfrak{A}$. Since the minimum polynomial $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ of $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ is a factor of $m_{a}(\lambda)$ it is clear that the degree of $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$, which is the same as the dimensionality of $\Phi[a]$, does not exceed the degree $m$ of the algebra. We shall call $a$ of maximal degree if $\operatorname{deg} \mu_{a}(\lambda)=m$. This is the case if and only if $\left(1, a, \cdots, a^{m-1}\right)$ is a basis for $\Phi[a] / \Phi$. If $x=\sum \xi_{i} u_{i}$ is generic then the fact that $\left(1, x, \cdots, x^{m-1}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathrm{P}[x], \mathrm{P}=\Phi\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ implies that the $m \times n$ matrix ( $\rho_{i k}$ ) given by (28) is of rank $m$. If $D_{1}(\xi), \cdots, D_{r}(\xi)$ are the nonzero determinants of order $m$ of this matrix then $a=\sum \alpha_{i} u_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}$ is of maximal degree if and only if $D_{i}(a)=\check{D}_{i}(\alpha) \neq 0$ for some $i$. Hence if $\Phi$ is infinite then the set of elements of maximal degree is a nonvacuous Zariski open subset of $\mathfrak{A}$.
We now write $t(a)$ for the generic trace $\sigma_{1}(a)$ and we prove first the following
Theorem 1. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a finite-dimensional strictly power associative algebra with $1, m_{a}(\lambda), t(a), n(a)$ the generic minimum polynomial, trace and norm of $a \in \mathfrak{A}, m$ the degree of $\mathfrak{A}$. Then:
(i) $t(\alpha a)=\alpha t(a), \alpha \in \Phi, t(a+b)=t(a)+t(b)$,
(ii) $n(\alpha a)=\alpha^{m} n(a), \quad n(a b)=n(a) n(b)$
if $a$ and $b$ are in the subalgebra $\Phi[c]$ generated by 1 and a third element $c$.
(iii) $n(\lambda 1-a)=m_{a}(\lambda)$. Here $\lambda 1-a$ is an element of $\mathfrak{U}_{\Phi(\lambda)}, \lambda$ an indeterminate.
(iv) $t(1)=m, n(a)=1$.
(v) Every irreducible factor of $m_{a}(\lambda)$ is a factor of the minimum polynomial $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ of $a$.
(vi) If $\eta$ is an isomorphism or anti-isomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$ then $m_{a^{n}}(\lambda)=m_{a}(\lambda)$.
(vii) If $\Phi$ is infinite then the coefficients of the generic minimum polynomial are Lie invariant under the derivations of $\mathfrak{U}: \Delta^{a d}{ }_{a} \sigma_{i}=0$ if $D$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{A}$.

Proof. (i) and the first part of (ii) are clear since $\sigma_{1}(\xi)$ is homogeneous of degree one in the $\xi$ 's and $\sigma_{m}(\xi)$ is homogeneous of degree $m$ in the $\xi$ 's. For the rest of the proof we assume, as we may without loss of generality, that $\Phi$ is infinite. To prove the second part of (ii) we assume first that $c$ is a fixed element of $\mathfrak{A}$ of maximal degree and consider the subalgebra $\Phi[c]$. Let $a$ be an element of maximal degree in $\Phi[c]$ (and hence in $\mathfrak{A}$ ). Since $b=1$ has the property that $a b$ is of maximal degree in $\Phi[c]$ it is clear that the set of $b$ such that $a b$ is of maximal degree in $\Phi[c]$ is a nonvacuous Zariski open subset of $\Phi[c]$. Hence the set of elements $b \in \Phi[c]$ such that $b$ and $a b$ are of maximal degree in $\Phi[c]$ is open in $\Phi[c]$. Let $b$ be such an element. Then $n(b)=\operatorname{det} \overline{b_{R}}, n(a b)=\operatorname{det}\left(\overline{a b)_{R}}\right.$ as well as $n(a)=\operatorname{det} \overline{a_{R}}$ where $\overline{u_{R}}$ for $u \in \Phi[c]$ is the restriction to $\Phi[c]$ of $u_{R}$. This is clear since for these elements the generic minimum polynomials coincide with the minimum polynomials and with the characteristic polynomials of the
restriction to $\Phi[c]$ of the corresponding right multiplications. We have $\overline{(a b)_{R}}=\overline{a_{R}} \overline{b_{R}}$. Hence $n(a b)=n(a) n(b)$ follows from the multiplicative property of determinants. Since this holds for all $b$ in an open subset of $\Phi[c]$ it holds for all $b$ in $\Phi[c]$. Now $n(a b)=n(a) n(b)$ holds for $a$ in $\Phi[c]$ of maximal degree and $b$ arbitrary in $\Phi[c]$. Hence it holds for all $a, b \in \Phi[c]$. Now let $\alpha_{0}, \alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{m-1}$, $\beta_{0}, \cdots, \beta_{m-1}$ be fixed elements of $\Phi$ and let $c$ be variable in $\mathcal{A}$. Consider the polynomial function $c \rightarrow n(a b)-n(a) n(b)$ where $a=\alpha_{0} 1+\alpha_{1} c+\cdots+\alpha_{m-1} c^{m-1}$, $b=\beta_{0} 1+\beta_{1} c+\cdots+\beta_{m-1} c^{m-1}$. This function has the value 0 for all $c$ in an open subset of $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence it is 0 for all $c \in \mathfrak{A}$. Then $n(a b)=n(a) n(b)$ holds for all $c$ and fixed $\alpha_{i}, \beta_{i}$. Since any pair of elements $a, b \in \Phi[c]$ can be obtained as $a=\sum \alpha_{i} c^{i}, b=\sum \beta_{i} c^{i}$ by a suitable choice of the $\alpha_{i}, \beta_{i}$ in $\Phi$ it is now clear that $n(a b)=n(a) n(b)$ holds for all $a, b \in \Phi[c]$ for any $c$, which proves the second part of (ii). Now let $a$ be of maximal degree and $\lambda$ an indeterminate, so $m_{a}(\lambda)=\operatorname{det}\left(\lambda 1-\overline{a_{R}}\right)$ and $n(a)=\operatorname{det} \overline{a_{R}}$ when $\overline{a_{R}}$ denotes the restriction of $a_{R}$ to $\Phi[a]$. It is easily seen that $\lambda 1-a$ is of maximal degree in $\mathfrak{A}_{\Phi[\lambda]}$, so $n(\lambda 1-a)=\operatorname{det}\left(\overline{\lambda 1-a)_{R}}\right.$ the determinant of the restriction of $(\lambda 1-a)_{R}$ to $\Phi(\lambda)[\lambda 1-a]=\Phi(\lambda)[a]$. Thus

$$
m_{a}(\lambda)=\operatorname{det}\left(\lambda 1-\overline{a_{R}}\right)=\operatorname{det}\left(\overline{\left(\lambda 1-a_{R}\right)}=n(\lambda 1-a) .\right.
$$

Since the set of elements of maximal degree is open we conclude that $m_{a}(\lambda)=n(\lambda 1-a)$ for all $a$, so (iii) holds. We now consider the relation $m_{a}(\lambda)=n(\lambda 1-a)$ for $a=0$. Since $n(\lambda 1)=n(1) \lambda^{m}$ by the first part of (ii) and $m_{a}(\lambda)$ is a polynomial in $\lambda$ with leading coefficient 1 , we see that $n(1)=1$. Also $m_{1}(\lambda)=n(\lambda 1-1)=n((\lambda-1) 1)=(\lambda-1)^{m} n(1)=(\lambda-1)^{m}=\lambda^{m}-m \lambda^{n-1}+\cdots$. Hence $t(1)=m$. Thus (iv) is valid. Next we prove (v). Let $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ and let $\mu_{a}(\lambda) \in \Phi[\lambda]$ be the minimum polynomial. We introduce the commutative associative polynomial ring $\Phi[a][\lambda]$ of polynomials in the indeterminate $\lambda$ with coefficients in $\Phi[a]$. This contains $\Phi[\lambda]$ as subring and it contains the element $\lambda-a$. By the division algorithm in $\Phi[a][\lambda]$ we can write $\mu_{a}(\lambda)=(\lambda-a) Q+R$ where $Q, R \in \Phi[a][\lambda]$ and $R \in \Phi[a]$. We apply to this relation the homomorphism of $\Phi[a][\lambda]$ which is the identity on $\Phi[a]$ and sends $\lambda \rightarrow a$. This gives $0=0+R$ so we have $R=0$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mu_{a}(\lambda)=(\lambda-a) Q, \quad Q \in \Phi[a][\lambda] . \tag{34}
\end{equation*}
$$

Next we consider the algebra $\mathfrak{U}_{\Phi(\lambda)}$ which has the basis $\left(u_{i}\right)$ where this is a basis for $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$, so any element of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Phi(\lambda)}$ has the form $\sum \lambda_{i} u_{i}$ where $\lambda_{i} \in \Phi(\lambda) . \mathfrak{A}_{\Phi(\lambda)}$ contains $\mathfrak{A}$ as $\Phi$-subalgebra and it also contains the $\Phi$-subalgebra $\Phi(\lambda) 1$ of $\Phi(\lambda)$ multiples of $1=\Sigma \gamma_{i} u_{i}$. Clearly $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ commutes with every element of $\Phi(\lambda) 1$. Hence we have a homomorphism $\eta$ of $\Phi[a][\lambda]$ into $\mathfrak{A}_{\Phi(\lambda)}$ such that $\beta(\lambda)^{\eta}=\beta(\lambda) 1$ if $\beta(\lambda) \in \Phi[\lambda]$ and $a^{\eta}=a$. Applying this to (34) we obtain

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mu_{a}(\lambda) 1=(\lambda 1-a) Q^{n} . \tag{35}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since $\lambda^{\eta}=\sum \gamma_{i} \lambda u_{i}$ and $a^{\eta}=\sum \alpha_{i} u_{i}, \alpha_{i} \in \Phi$ it is clear that $Q^{\eta}=\sum \lambda_{i} u_{i}$ where $\lambda_{i} \in \Phi[\lambda]$. Hence $n\left(Q^{\eta}\right) \in \Phi[\lambda]$ since it is obtained by putting $\xi_{i}=\lambda_{i}$ in $n\left(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$. On the other hand, it is clear that $\mu_{a}(\lambda) 1, \lambda 1-a$ and $Q^{\eta} \in \Phi(\lambda)[a]$ the $\Phi(\lambda)$-subalgebra of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Phi(\lambda)}$ generated by 1 and $a$. Hence the second part of (ii) is applicable. Since $n$ is homogeneous of degree $m$ and $n(1)=1$ we obtain from (35) that $\mu_{a}(\lambda)^{m}=n(\lambda 1-a) n\left(Q^{\eta}\right)$. By (iii) this gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mu_{a}(\lambda)^{m}=m_{a}(\lambda) q(\lambda) \tag{36}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $q(\lambda)=n\left(Q^{\eta}\right) \in \Phi[\lambda]$. Clearly (36) implies that every irreducible factor of $m_{a}(\lambda)$ is a factor of $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$. Hence (v) holds. Next let $\eta$ be an isomorphism or antiisomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ onto $\mathfrak{U}^{\prime}$. It is clear that for the minimum polynomials we have $\mu_{a}(\lambda)=\mu_{a^{n}}(\lambda), a \in \mathfrak{A}$. Hence if $a$ has maximal degree then $m_{a}(\lambda)=\mu_{a}(\lambda) =\mu_{a^{n}}(\lambda)$. This implies that $\operatorname{deg} \mathfrak{U}^{\prime} \geqq \operatorname{deg} \mathfrak{U}$. Then, by symmetry, $\operatorname{deg} \mathfrak{U}^{\prime}=\operatorname{deg} \mathfrak{A}$ and $a^{\eta}$ has maximal degree. Then $m_{a}(\lambda)=m_{a^{\eta}}(\lambda)$. Now $a \rightarrow \sigma_{j}\left(a^{\eta}\right)$ is a polynomial function on $\mathfrak{U} / \Phi$ and the result just proved shows that this coincides with $\sigma_{j}(a)$ if $a$ is in the open subset of elements of maximal degree. Hence $\sigma_{j}\left(a^{\eta}\right)=\sigma_{j}(a)$ for all $a \in \mathfrak{U}$ and all $j$. This proves (vi). Let $D$ be a derivation in $\mathfrak{U} / \Phi$. Then applying $D$ to $m_{a}(a)=0$ we obtain

$$
\begin{equation*}
a^{m} D-\sigma_{1}(a)\left(a^{m-1} D\right)+\cdots+(-1)^{m-1} \sigma_{m-1}(a)(a D)=0 . \tag{37}
\end{equation*}
$$

If $f$ is any polynomial mapping of $\mathfrak{U}$ into itself then we have the polynomial mapping $a \rightarrow \Delta^{a D}{ }_{a} f$ of $\mathfrak{A}$. If we apply this to $p_{k}: a \rightarrow a^{k}$ we obtain $\Delta^{a D}{ }_{a} p_{k}=a^{k} D$. This is clear for $k=1$ since $p_{1}$ is the linear mapping $a \rightarrow a$ which implies that $\Delta_{a}^{a D} p_{1}=a D$. Then if $\Delta_{a}^{a D} p_{k-1}=a^{k-1} D$, we have by (23) that $\Delta_{a}^{a D} p_{k}=\Delta_{a}^{a D} p_{k-1} p_{1} =\left(a^{k-1} D\right) a+a^{k-1}(a D)=a^{k} D$. The relation $m_{a}(a)=0$ is equivalent to the functional relation $p_{m}-\sigma_{1} p_{m-1}+\cdots+(-1)^{m} \sigma_{m}=0$. Applying $\Delta_{a}^{a D}$ to this gives

$$
\begin{align*}
& a^{m} D-\sigma_{1}(a) a^{m-1} D-\left(\Delta_{a}^{a D} \sigma_{1}\right) a^{m-1}+\sigma_{2}(a) a^{m-2} D \\
& \quad+\left(\Delta_{a}^{a D} \sigma_{2}\right) a^{m-2}-\cdots=0 \tag{38}
\end{align*}
$$

Subtracting this from (37) gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left(\Delta_{a}^{a D} \sigma_{1}\right) a^{m-1}-\left(\Delta_{a}^{a D} \sigma_{2}\right) a^{m-2}+\cdots=0 . \tag{39}
\end{equation*}
$$

If $a$ is of maximal degree this gives $\Delta_{a}^{a D} \sigma_{j}=0$. This implies that $\Delta_{a}^{a D} \sigma_{j}=0$ for all $a$ and $j$ and proves (vii). $\left(^{1}\right)$

Corollary 1. (1) If $m_{a}(\lambda)$ has distinct roots (in its splitting field) then $m_{a}(\lambda)=\mu_{a}(\lambda)$. (2) An element $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ is nilpotent if and only if $m_{a}(\lambda)=\lambda^{m}$. The generic trace of a nilpotent element is 0 . (3) If $e$ is an idempotent $\neq 0,1$ then $m_{a}(\lambda)=(\lambda-1)^{k} \lambda^{m-k}$ where $0<k<m$ and accordingly $t(e)=k$.

[^16]Proof. The results (1) and (2) are immediate consequences of (v). Now let $e$ be an idempotent $\neq 0,1$. Then the minimum polynomial of $e$ is $\lambda^{2}-\lambda=\lambda(\lambda-1)$. It follows from (v) that $m_{e}(\lambda)=(\lambda-1)^{k} \lambda^{m-k}, 0<k<m$. Then $t(e)=k$.

Corollary 2. An element a has an inverse in $\Phi[a]$ if and only if $n(a) \neq 0$.
Proof. $a$ has an inverse in $\Phi[a]$ if and only if its minimum polynomial $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ has a nonzero constant term. This is equivalent to $\lambda \nmid \mu_{a}(\lambda)$. Hence, by (v), $a$ has an inverse in $\Phi[a]$ if and only if $\lambda \nmid m_{a}(\lambda)$ and this is equivalent to $n(a) \neq 0$.

We shall call a finite-dimensional strictly power associative algebra with 1 a division algebra if every $a \neq 0$ has an inverse in $\Phi[a]$. This is equivalent to our earlier definition for the special case of Jordan algebras. Evidently Corollary 2 implies

Corollary 3. $\mathfrak{A}$ is a division algebra if and only if $n(a) \neq 0$ for every $a \neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{A}$.

By Theorem 1 (i), $a \rightarrow t(a)$ is a linear function on $\mathfrak{A}$. This gives rise to an important bilinear form $(a, b) \rightarrow t(a, b) \equiv t(a b)$ on $\mathfrak{A}$. We shall call this the generic trace (bilinear) form on $\mathfrak{A}$ and we have the following

Corollary 4. The generic trace form of a finite-dimensional associative or Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ with 1 is symmetric and associative, that is,

$$
\begin{equation*}
t(a, b)=t(b, a), \quad t(a b, c)=t(a, b c), \quad a, b, c \in \mathfrak{A} . \tag{40}
\end{equation*}
$$

Proof. We may assume $\Phi$ is infinite and we suppose first that $\mathfrak{A}$ is associative. Then $t(a b, c)-t(a, b c)=t([a, b, c])=0$. Now Theorem 1(vii) and the linearity of the trace imply that $t(a D)=0$ for every derivation $D$. Since $\mathfrak{A}$ is associative $a \rightarrow[a, b]$ is a derivation. Hence we have $t([a, b])=0$ and $t(a, b)=t(b, a)$. Next assume $\mathfrak{A}$ Jordan. Then $t(a, b)=t(b, a)$ is clear from the commutativity of $\mathfrak{A}$. Also in this case we know that $b \rightarrow[a, b, c]$ is a derivation. Hence $t([a, b, c])=0$ which gives the associativity of the generic trace form.

Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a subalgebra containing 1 of the finite-dimensional strictly power asso iative algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ with 1 . Let $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ be a basis for $\mathfrak{A},\left(v_{1}, v_{2}, \cdots, v_{r}\right)$ a basis for $\mathfrak{B}, x=\sum_{1}^{n} \xi_{i} u_{i}, y=\sum_{1}^{r} \xi_{j} v_{j}$ the corresponding generic elements and let $m_{x}(\lambda)$ be the minimum polynomial of $x$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}, \mathbf{P}=\Phi\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right), m_{y \mid \mathfrak{B}}(\lambda)$ the minimum polynomial of $y$ in $\mathfrak{B}_{\mathrm{P}}$. Then $m_{x}(\lambda)$ is the generic minimum polynomial in $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}$ of $x$ and $m_{y \mid \mathfrak{B}}(\lambda)$ is that of $y$ in $\mathfrak{B}_{\mathbf{P}}$. If $v_{j}=\sum \mu_{j i} u_{i}, \mu_{j i} \in \Phi$ then $y=\sum \eta_{i} u_{i}$ where $\eta_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{r} \xi_{j} \mu_{j i}$ and the generic minimum polynomial $m_{y}(\lambda)$ of $y$ as element of $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{P}}$ is obtained by the specialization $\xi_{i} \rightarrow \eta_{i}$ in $m_{x}(\lambda)$. By Theorem $1(\mathrm{v}), m_{y}(\lambda)$ and $m_{y \mid \mathfrak{B}}(\lambda)$ have the same irreducible factors in $\mathrm{P}[\lambda]$. Since these are polynomials in $\lambda$ and $\xi_{1}, \xi_{2}, \cdots, \xi_{r}$ and have leading coefficients of $\lambda=1$ it follows that $m_{y}(\lambda)$ and $m_{y \mid \mathfrak{B}}(\lambda)$ have the same irreducible factors in $\Phi\left[\lambda, \xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right]$. We state this result as

Corollary 5. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a strictly power associative algebra with $1, \mathfrak{B}$ a subalgebra containing $1,\left(u_{1}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ a basis for $\mathfrak{A},\left(v_{1}, \cdots, v_{r}\right)$ a basis for $\mathfrak{B}$, $x=\sum_{1}^{n} \xi_{i} u_{i}, y=\sum_{1}^{r} \xi_{j} v_{j}$ the corresponding generic elements. Let $m_{y}(\lambda)$ be the generic minimum polynomial of $y$ as element of $\mathfrak{U}_{\mathrm{P}}, \mathrm{P}=\Phi\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right), m_{y \mid \mathfrak{B}}(\lambda)$ the generic minumum polynomial of $y$ as element of $\mathfrak{B}_{\mathbf{P}}$. Then $m_{y \mid \mathfrak{B}}(\lambda)$ is a factor of $m_{y}(\lambda)$ in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}, \lambda\right]$ and these have the same irreducible factors in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}, \lambda\right]$.

Let $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ where the $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ are ideals and let $a=a_{1}+a_{2}, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i}$. Then if $f(\lambda)=\lambda^{q}+\alpha_{1} \lambda^{q-1}+\cdots+\alpha_{q} \in \Phi[\lambda], \quad f(a)=f\left(a_{1}\right)+f\left(a_{2}\right) \quad$ where $\quad f\left(a_{i}\right) =a_{i}^{q}+\alpha_{1} a_{i}^{q-1}+\cdots+\alpha_{q} 1_{i}, 1_{i}$ the identity element of $\mathfrak{A}_{i}\left(1=1_{1}+1_{2}\right)$. Since $f(a)=0$ if and only if $f\left(a_{i}\right)=0, i=1,2$, it is clear that the minimum polynomial of $a$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ is the least common multiple of the minimum polynomials of the $a_{i}$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$. Let $\left(u_{1}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ be a basis for $\mathfrak{U} / \Phi$ such that $\left(u_{1}, \cdots, u_{r}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{A}_{1}$ and $\left(u_{r+1}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{A}_{2}$. Then the generic element $x=\sum_{1}^{n} \xi_{i} u_{i}=y+z$ where $y=\sum_{1}^{r} \xi_{j} u_{j}$ and $z=\sum_{r+1}^{n} \xi_{k} u_{k}$ are generic elements of $\mathfrak{A}_{1}, \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ respectively. Let $m^{(1)}{ }_{y}(\lambda)$ and $m^{(2)}{ }_{z}(\lambda)$ be the minimum polynomials of $y$ and $z$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{1 \mathbf{P}}$ and $\mathfrak{A}_{2 \mathbf{P}}$ respectively where $\mathrm{P}=\Phi\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$. Then $m^{(1)}{ }_{y}(\lambda)=\lambda^{m_{1}}- \sigma^{(1)}{ }_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right) \lambda^{m_{1}-1}+\cdots+(-1)^{m_{1}} \sigma^{(1)}{ }_{m_{1}}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right)$ where $\sigma_{l}^{(1)}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right)$ is homogeneous of degree $l$ in $\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}$ and $\sigma_{m_{1}}^{(1)}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right) \neq 0$ (since $\sigma_{m_{1}}^{(1)}\left(1_{1}\right)=1$ ). Similarly, $m^{(2)}{ }_{z}(\lambda)=\lambda^{m_{2}}-\sigma^{(2)}{ }_{1}\left(\xi_{r+1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) \lambda^{m_{2}-1}+\cdots+(-1)^{m_{2}} \sigma^{(2)}{ }_{m_{2}}\left(\xi_{r+1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) \quad$ where $\sigma^{(2)}\left(\xi_{r+1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is homogeneous of degree $q$ in $\xi_{r+1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}$ and $\sigma^{(2)}{ }_{m_{2}}\left(\xi_{r+1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) \neq 0$. We claim that $m^{(1)}{ }_{y}(\lambda)$ and $m^{(2)}{ }_{z}(\lambda)$ are relatively prime in $\mathrm{P}[\lambda]$. Otherwise, these have a common factor of the form $\lambda^{h}+\tau_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) \lambda^{h-1}+\cdots+ \tau_{h}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ in $\Phi\left[\lambda, \xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ where $h \geqq 1$ and $\tau_{i}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is homogeneous of degree $i$ in $\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}$. Putting $\lambda=0$ implies that $\tau_{h}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is a common factor of $\sigma^{(1)}{ }_{m_{1}}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right)$ and $\sigma^{(2)}{ }_{m_{2}}\left(\xi_{r+1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ which is impossible. Hence we see that $m^{(1)}{ }_{y}(\lambda)$ and $m^{(2)}{ }_{z}(\lambda)$ are relatively prime in $\mathrm{P}[\lambda]$ so $m^{(1)}{ }_{y}(\lambda) m^{(2)}{ }_{z}(\lambda)$ is a least common multiple of these polynomials. As we saw before, this is the minimum polynomial of $x$. This result and the definitions clearly imply the first statement in

Theorem 2. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be as in Theorem 1 and suppose $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{2}$ where $\mathfrak{U}_{i}$ is an ideal with identity element $1_{i}$. If $a=a_{1}+a_{2}$ where $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i}$ then the generic minimum polynomial $m_{a}(\lambda)$ of $a$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ is $m^{(1)}{ }_{a_{1}}(\lambda) m^{(2)}{ }_{a_{2}}(\lambda)$ where $m^{(1)}{ }_{a_{i}}(\lambda)$ is the generic minimum polynomial of $a_{i}$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$. Also $n(a)=n^{(1)}\left(a_{1}\right) n^{(2)}\left(a_{2}\right)$ where $n^{(i)}\left(a_{i}\right)$ is the generic norm of $a_{i}$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ and $t\left(a_{i}\right)=t^{(i)}\left(a_{i}\right)$ where $t^{(i)}\left(a_{i}\right)$ is the generic trace of $a_{i}$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$.

Proof. $n(a)=n^{(1)}\left(a_{1}\right) n^{(2)}\left(a_{2}\right)$ and $t(a)=t^{(1)}\left(a_{1}\right)+t^{(2)}\left(a_{2}\right)$ are immediate consequences of the first result. If we take $a_{2}=0$ in the second of these we obtain $t\left(a_{1}\right)=t^{(1)}\left(a_{1}\right)$ and similarly $t\left(a_{2}\right)=t^{(2)}\left(a_{2}\right)$.

The last statement implies also that the trace bilinear form on $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ is the restriction to $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ of the trace bilinear form on $\mathfrak{A}$. It is clear also that Theorem 2 has an
immediate extension to the situation in which $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{1}} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{\mathbf{2}} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{s}$ where the $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ are ideals.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with $1, t$ its generic trace. Define $t(a, b, c)=t(a . b . c)$. Show that $t(a, b, c)$ is symmetric and trilinear. Show that if the characterisic is not three and $\eta$ is a linear mapping in $\mathfrak{J}$ having the first three coefficients $\sigma_{i}$ of the generic minimum polynomial as invariants $\left(\sigma_{i}\left(a^{\eta}\right)=\sigma_{\imath}(a), i=1,2,3\right)$ then $t\left(a^{\eta}, b^{\eta}, c^{\eta}\right)=t(a, b, c)$. Hence show that if $\eta$ is a linear mapping in $\mathfrak{J}$ having $n$ as invariant and sending 1 into 1 and $|\Phi|>m$, the degree of $\mathfrak{J}$ then $t\left(a^{\eta}, b^{\eta}, c^{\eta}\right)=t(a, b, c)$.
2. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ be finite-dimensional Jordan algebras with 1 over an infinite field and let $\eta$ be a 1-1 linear mapping of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ such that $1^{\eta}=1$ and if $c$ is invertible in $\mathfrak{J}$ then $c^{\eta}$ is invertible in $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ and $\left(c^{c^{-1}}\right)^{\eta}=\left(c^{\eta}\right)^{-1}$. Show that $\eta$ is an isomorphism.
3. State an analogue of exercise 2 for derivations.
4. Some important examples. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a finite-dimensional strictly power associative algebra with $1, x=\sum_{1}^{n} \xi_{i} u_{i}$ a generic element of $\mathfrak{A}, m_{x}(\lambda)$ its minimum polynomial. Since $m_{x}(\lambda)=\lambda^{m}-\sigma_{1}(\xi) \lambda^{m-1}+\cdots+(-1)^{m} \sigma_{m}(\xi)$ where $\sigma_{j}(\xi) \in \Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right], \xi_{i}$ indeterminates, it is clear that the discriminant $\delta(x)$ of $m_{x}(\lambda)$ is in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ (Jacobson, Lectures in Abstract Algebra, vol. III, p. 92). We shall call $\mathfrak{A}$ unramified if $\delta(x) \neq 0$. The following lemma gives a criterion for this and is useful for determining the generic minimum polynomials for the algebras we shall consider.

Lemma 1. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a finite-dimensional strictly power associative algebra with $1, m$ the degree of $\mathfrak{U}$. Let $I$ be a set of nonzero orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{A}\left(e_{i}{ }^{2}=e_{i} \neq 0, e_{i} e_{j}=0, i \neq j\right)$. Then the cardinal number $|I| \leqq m$ and $\mathfrak{A}$ is unramified if and only if $\mathfrak{U}_{\Omega}$, where $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of the base field $\Phi$ of $\mathfrak{A}$, contains $m$ nonzero orthogonal idempotents.

Proof We note first that if $e_{1}, e_{2}, \cdots, e_{r}$ are nonzero orthogonal idempotents and $\alpha_{i} \neq \alpha_{j}$ are in $\Phi$ then it is easily seen that $\mu_{a}(\lambda)=\prod_{1}^{r}\left(\lambda-\alpha_{i}\right)$ is the minimum polynomial of $a=\sum \alpha_{i} e_{i}$. Since $\mu_{a}(\lambda) \mid m_{a}(\lambda)$ we have $m \geqq r$. Now if $e_{1}, \cdots, e_{r}$ are given then we can choose distinct $\alpha_{i}$ in an extension field of $\Phi$. Since the degree is unchanged on extension of the base field it is clear that the first statement holds. Now suppose we have $m$ distinct orthogonal idempotents $\neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}$. Then we have an $a \in \mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}$ such that $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ has $m$ distinct roots. Then $m_{a}(\lambda)=\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ by Theorem 1 (v). Hence $m_{a}(\lambda)$ has distinct roots, which implies that the discriminant of $m_{a}(\lambda)$ is not zero. Since $m_{a}(\lambda)$ is obtained by specializing $\xi_{i}=\alpha_{i} \in \Phi$, the discriminant of $m_{a}(\lambda)$ is $\delta(a)$ which is obtained by making the same specialization in $\delta(x)$. Since $\delta(a) \neq 0$ we have $\delta(x) \neq 0$ and $\mathfrak{A}$ is unramified. Conversely, assume
$\mathfrak{A}$ unramified. Then we can choose $a$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}$ so that $\delta(a) \neq 0$. This implies that $m_{a}(\lambda)$ has $m$ distinct roots. Then $\mu_{a}(\lambda)=m_{a}(\lambda)$ by Corollary 1 to Theorem 1 This implies that $\Omega[a]$ contains $m$ nonzero orthogonal idempotents.

We now consider our examples.
A. $\Phi_{n}$, the algebra of $n \times n$ matrices over $\Phi$. If $\left(e_{i j}\right), i, j=1, \cdots, n$, is the usual matrix basis, $\xi_{i j}$ indeterminates, then by the Hamilton-Cayley theorem the generic element $X=\sum \xi_{i j} e_{i j}$ is a root of the characteristic polynomial $f_{X}(\lambda) =\operatorname{det}(\lambda 1-X)$. Hence $m_{X}(\lambda)$, which is a factor of $f_{X}(\lambda)$, has degree $\leqq n$. On the other hand, $\Phi_{n}$ contains the $n$ orthogonal idempotents $e_{i i}, i=1,2, \cdots, n$. Hence $\operatorname{deg} m_{X}(\lambda) \geqq n$. It follows that $\Phi_{n}$ is unramified and $m_{X}(\lambda)=f_{X}(\lambda)$.

We note next that if the characteristic is $\neq 2$ then for the Jordan algebra $\Phi_{n}{ }^{+}$ we also have $m_{X}(\lambda)=f_{X}(\lambda)$ since the Jordan power $X^{\cdot n}=X^{n}$. In both cases $\Phi_{n}$ and $\Phi_{n}{ }^{+}, m_{A}(\lambda)$ is the characteristic polynomial of the matrix $A, t(A)$ is the ordinary trace of $a$ and $n(A)=\operatorname{det} A$.
B. $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ the Jordan algebra of ordinary $n \times n$ symmetric matrices over $\Phi$ (characteristic not two). Since $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ contains the $e_{i i}$ the argument used in A shows that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ is unramified and $m_{A}(\lambda)$ for $A$ in this Jordan algebra is the characteristic polynomial of $A$. Also $t(A)$ is the usual trace and $n(A)=\operatorname{det} A$.
C. $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}\right)$ the Jordan algebra of $2 n \times 2 n$ matrices which are symmetric under the involution $X \rightarrow S^{-1} X^{t} S$ where $S=\operatorname{diag}\{Q, Q, \cdots, Q\}, Q=\left(\begin{array}{rr}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{array}\right)$. The condition $S^{-1} A^{t} S=A$ that $A \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}\right)$ is equivalent to $(S A)^{t}=A^{t} S^{t} =-A^{t} S=-S A$, that is, $S A$ is skew. In order to obtain the generic minimum polynomial for $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}\right)$ we need to consider a factorization property of the Pfaffian of a skew symmetric matrix.

Let $\xi_{i j}, i<j=1, \cdots, 2 n$, be indeterminates and consider the ring $Z\left[\xi_{i j}\right], Z$ the ring of integers. Consider the generic skew symmetric matrix $X=\left(\xi_{i j}\right)$ where $\xi_{i j}=0$ and $\xi_{j i}=-\xi_{i j}$ if $i<j$. Let $X_{i j}$ be the cofactor of $\xi_{j i}$ in $X$. Then $X_{i i}=0$ since the determinant of a skew symmetric matrix of odd order is 0 . Also if $i \neq j$ then $X_{i j}=-X_{j i}$ since $X$ is skew. We shall now prove the following

Lemma 2. $\operatorname{det} X$ is a square in $\mathfrak{X}=Z\left[\xi_{i j}\right]$ and if we let $\operatorname{Pf} X$ denote a square root in $X$ of $\operatorname{det} X$ then $\operatorname{Pf} X \mid X_{k l}$ in $\mathfrak{X}$ for all $k, l$.

Proof. We have the matrix relation $X \operatorname{adj} X=(\operatorname{det} X) 1$ where $\operatorname{adj} X=\left(X_{i j}\right)$. This gives the systems of equations

$$
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{k=1}^{2 n} \xi_{l k} X_{k j}=\delta_{l j}(\operatorname{det} X), \quad l=1,2, \cdots, 2 n \tag{41}
\end{equation*}
$$

for any $j=1,2, \cdots, 2 n$. Let $i$ be an index $\neq j$ and delete the $i$ th equation in this set. If we take into account the fact that $X_{j j}=0$ we obtain $2 n-1$ linear equations
for the $2 n-1$ elements $X_{k j}, k \neq j$. The determinants of the coefficients of these equations is the minor of $\xi_{i j}$ in $X$. This is $(-1)^{i+j}$ cofactor of $\xi_{i j}=(-1)^{i+j} X_{j i} =(-1)^{i+j+1} X_{i j}$. Hence if we solve the equations for $X_{i j}$ by Cramer's rule we obtain

$$
\begin{equation*}
(-1)^{i+j+1} X_{i j}^{2}=(\operatorname{det} X) \Delta_{i j} \tag{42}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\Delta_{i j} \in \mathfrak{X}$. For $i=1, j=2$ this becomes $X_{12}{ }^{2}=(\operatorname{det} X) \Delta_{12}$ and one sees that $\Delta_{12}$ is the determinant of the skew symmetric matrix obtained by deleting the first and second rows and columns from $X$. Assuming this is a square and using unique factorization in $\overline{\mathfrak{X}}$ we see that $\operatorname{det} X$ is a square in $\mathfrak{X}$. This and the fact that if $n=1$ then $X=\left(\begin{array}{cc}0 & \xi_{12} \\ -\xi_{12} & 0\end{array}\right)$, so $\operatorname{det} X=\xi_{12}{ }^{2}$, proves the first statement by induction on $n$. Now put $\operatorname{det} X=(\operatorname{Pf} X)^{2}$. Then (42) becomes $(-1)^{i+j+1} X_{i j}{ }^{2}=(\operatorname{Pf} X)^{2} \Delta_{i j}$ which implies that $\operatorname{Pf} X \mid X_{i j}$ if $i \neq j$. Since $X_{i i}=0$ this proves the second statement.

It is clear that if $S=\operatorname{diag}\left\{\left(\begin{array}{rr}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{array}\right),\left(\begin{array}{rr}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{array}\right), \cdots\right\}$ as before, then $\operatorname{det} S=1$. Hence the specialization of the $\xi_{i j}$ in $Z$ which gives $S$ gives $\operatorname{Pf} S= \pm 1$. We now choose the determination of the sign of $\operatorname{Pf} X$ so that $\operatorname{Pf} S=1$ and from now on call this $\operatorname{Pf} X$. If $A$ is a $2 n \times 2 n$ matrix $A=\left(\alpha_{i j}\right)$ with the $\alpha_{i j}$ in a commutative ring and $\alpha_{i i}=0, \alpha_{j i}=-\alpha_{i j}$ then we can obtain $A$ by the specialization $\xi_{i j} \rightarrow \alpha_{i j}, i<j$ of $X$. Under this the element $\operatorname{Pf} X$ is mapped into an element Pf $A$ which we shall call the Pfaffian of (the skew matrix with diagonal elements 0 ) $A$. Evidently we have $(\operatorname{Pf} A)^{2}=\operatorname{det} A$.

The fact that $\operatorname{Pf} X \mid X_{i j}$ for $X$ generic and $X_{i j}$ the cofactor of $\xi_{j i}$ in $X$ implies that $X_{i j}=Y_{i j}(\operatorname{Pf} X)$ where $Y_{i j} \in \mathfrak{X}$. We can now cancel $\operatorname{Pf} X$ in the relation $X \operatorname{adj} X=(\operatorname{det} X) 1$ and obtain for $Y=\left(Y_{i j}\right)$ that

$$
\begin{equation*}
X Y=\operatorname{Pf}(X) 1 \tag{43}
\end{equation*}
$$

Now let $A \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}\right)$ and let $\lambda$ be an indeterminate. Then $S \lambda-S A$ is skew with entries in $\Phi[\lambda]$. Specialization of (43) now gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
(S \lambda-S A) B(\lambda)=\operatorname{Pf}(S \lambda-S A) 1 \tag{44}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $B(\lambda) \in \Phi[\lambda]_{2 n}$. We can use this relation and the usual proof of the HamiltonCayley theorem (Jacobson, Lectures vol. II, p. 101) to prove that $A$ is a root of the equation $\operatorname{Pf}(S \lambda-S A)=0$. Also this has the leading coefficient $\operatorname{Pf} S=1$. Clearly we have also $\operatorname{Pf}(S \lambda-S X)=0$ for $X$ generic in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}\right)$. Hence $m_{X}(\lambda) \mid \operatorname{Pf}(S \lambda-S X)$ and $\operatorname{deg} m_{X}(\lambda) \leqq n$. On the other hand, it is clear from the fact that $A \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}\right)$ if $S A$ is skew that the elements $e_{1}=e_{11}+e_{22}, e_{2}=e_{33} +e_{44}, \cdots$ are contained in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}\right)$. Clearly we obtain in this way $n$ nonzero orthogonal idempotents. Hence, by Lemma $1, \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}\right)$ is unramified and the generic minimum polynomial of $A \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}\right)$ is

$$
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{Pf}(S \lambda-S A) \tag{45}
\end{equation*}
$$

This implies that the generic norm $n(A)=\operatorname{Pf}(S A)$. Also since $\operatorname{Pf}(S \lambda-S A)^{2} =\operatorname{det}(S \lambda-S A)=\operatorname{det}(\lambda 1-A)$ it is clear that the generic trace $t(A)=\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{tr} A, \operatorname{tr} A$ the usual trace.
D. $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ the Jordan algebra of the symmetric bilinear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{V}$. It is easy to see that if $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}>0$ and $a=\alpha 1+u, \alpha \in \Phi, u \in \mathfrak{B}$, then $m_{a}(\lambda)=\lambda^{2}-2 \alpha \lambda+\left(\alpha^{2}-f(u, u)\right)$. Hence $t(a)=2 \alpha$ and $n(a)=\alpha^{2}-f(u, u)$. It is easy to see also that if $f \neq 0$ then $\mathfrak{J}$ is unramified.
E. $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{O}$ is an algebra of octonions and $\gamma=\operatorname{diag}\left\{\gamma_{1}, \gamma_{2}, \gamma_{3}\right\}$, $\gamma_{i} \neq 0$ in $\Phi$. We consider a generic element of this Jordan algebra. This has the form

$$
X=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\xi_{1} & z & \gamma_{1}^{-1} \gamma_{3} \bar{y}  \tag{46}\\
\gamma_{2}^{-1} \gamma_{1} \bar{z} & \xi_{2} & x \\
y & \gamma_{3}^{-1} \gamma_{2} \bar{x} & \xi_{3}
\end{array}\right)
$$

where the $\xi_{i}$ are indeterminates and $x, y, z$ are generic elements of $\mathfrak{O}$ defined respectively by the indeterminates $\xi_{4}, \cdots, \xi_{11} ; \xi_{12}, \cdots, \xi_{19} ; \xi_{20}, \cdots, \xi_{27}$. We introduce the matrix

$$
\begin{equation*}
X \times X=X^{.2}-\tau(X) X+\frac{1}{2}\left(\tau\left(X^{.2}\right)-\tau(X)^{2}\right) 1 \tag{47}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\tau(X)=\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}+\xi_{3}$. A direct calculation shows that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& X \times X= \\
& \quad\left(\begin{array}{lll}
\xi_{2} \xi_{3}-\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{2} n(x) & \gamma_{1}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{2} \bar{y} \bar{x}-\xi_{3} z & x z-\gamma_{1}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{3} \xi_{3} \bar{y} \\
x y-\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{1} \xi_{3} \bar{z} & \xi_{1} \xi_{3}-\gamma_{1}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{3} n(y) & \gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{3} \bar{z} \bar{y}-\xi_{1} x \\
\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{1} \bar{z} \bar{x}-\xi_{3} y & y z-\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{2} \xi_{1} \bar{x} & \xi_{1} \xi_{2}-\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{1} n(z)
\end{array}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $n(x)$ denotes the given quadratic form on $\mathfrak{O}(x \bar{x}=n(x) 1=\bar{x} x)$. Direct multiplication of (48) by $X$ gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
(X \times X) \cdot X=(\operatorname{det} X) 1 \tag{49}
\end{equation*}
$$

where

$$
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{det} X= & \xi_{1} \xi_{2} \xi_{3}-\gamma_{3}^{-1} \gamma_{2} n(x)-\gamma_{1}^{-1} \gamma_{3} n(y)-\gamma_{2}^{-1} \gamma_{1} n(z)  \tag{50}\\
& +t((z x) y)
\end{align*}
$$

where $t(x) 1=x+\bar{x}$. By (47) and (49) we have the following analogue of the Hamilton-Cayley theorem for $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ which is due to Freudenthal [1]

$$
\begin{equation*}
X^{\cdot 3}-\tau(X) X^{\cdot 2}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\tau(X)^{2}-\tau\left(X^{\cdot 2}\right) X-(\operatorname{det} X) 1=0 .\right. \tag{51}
\end{equation*}
$$

It is clear that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ contains three nonzero orthogonal idempotent elements. Hence $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ is unramified and the generic minimum polynomial of

$$
A=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\alpha_{1} & c & \gamma_{1}^{-1} \gamma_{3} \bar{b}  \tag{52}\\
\gamma_{2}^{-1} \gamma_{1} \bar{c} & \alpha_{2} & a \\
b & \gamma_{3}^{-1} \gamma_{2} \bar{a} & \alpha_{3}
\end{array}\right)
$$

is

$$
\begin{equation*}
m_{A}(\lambda)=\lambda^{3}-t(A) \lambda^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left(t(A)^{2}-t\left(A^{\cdot 2}\right)\right) \lambda-n(A) \tag{53}
\end{equation*}
$$

where the generic trace $t(A)=\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}$ and the generic norm is

$$
\begin{align*}
n(A)=\operatorname{det} A= & \alpha_{1} \alpha_{2} \alpha_{3}-\gamma_{3}^{-1} \gamma_{2} \alpha_{1} n(a)-\gamma_{1}^{-1} \gamma_{3} \alpha_{2} n(b)-\gamma_{2}^{-1} \gamma_{1} \alpha_{3} n(c)  \tag{54}\\
& +t((c a) b)
\end{align*}
$$

We note also that

$$
\begin{equation*}
t\left(A^{\cdot 2}\right)=\alpha_{1}^{2}+\alpha_{2}^{2}+\alpha_{3}^{2}+2\left(\gamma_{3}^{-1} \gamma_{2} n(x)+\gamma_{1}^{-1} \gamma_{3} n(y)+\gamma_{2}^{-1} \gamma_{1} n(z)\right) . \tag{55}
\end{equation*}
$$

The results we have just derived give us the generic minimum polynomials of all finite-dimensional simple Jordan algebras over algebraically closed fields. We have seen in §5.6 that a complete list of these algebras is the following: (1) $\Phi$, (2) the Jordan algebras of nondegenerate symmetric bilinear forms in vector spaces of finite dimensionalities $>1$, (3) the Jordan matrix algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ with $n \geqq 3$ and $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ a composition algebra which is associative if $n>3$. We have seen also that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is the split two-dimensional composition algebra is isomorphic to $\Phi_{n}{ }^{+}$and $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a split quaternion algebra is isomorphic to the algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{2 n}, J_{S}\right)$ which we considered in example C above. Thus it is clear that we have determined the generic minimum polynomials of all the finite dimensional simple Jordan algebras with $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}>1$ over algebraically closed fields. Since the generic minimum polynomial is unchanged under extension of the base field it is clear that, in principle, we have determined the generic minimum polynomials of all finite-dimensional central simple Jordan algebras. If J is a Jordan algebra over $\Phi$ such that $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ where $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of $\Phi,(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a composition algebra, and $n \geqq 3$ then we defined the degree of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\S 5.7$ to be $n$ (p. 209). It is clear from our results that this is the same as the degree of $\mathfrak{J}$ as defined in this chapter.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{O}$ be an algebra of octonions over $\Phi$. Show that $m_{a}(\lambda)=\lambda^{2}-t(a) \lambda+n(a)$ where $a+\bar{a}=t(a) 1, a \bar{a}=n(a) 1$.
2. Prove that in all of the examples $\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}, \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{D}, \mathbf{E}$ above the generic norm $n(x), x=\sum \xi_{i} u_{i}$ a generic element, is irreducible in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \xi_{2}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$.
3. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple Jordan algebra over an algebraically closed field, $n(x)=n\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ the generic norm. Show that the structure of $\mathfrak{J}$ can be deduced from the factorization of $n(x)$ into irreducible factors in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$. By this we mean that if $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{s}$ where the $\mathfrak{J}_{\imath}$ are simple ideals then the $\mathfrak{I}_{i}$ are in 1-1 correspondence with the irreducible factors of $n(x)$ and the isomorphism class of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ is determined by the corresponding irreducible factor.
4. Note that in example $\mathrm{E}, A \times A=\operatorname{adj} A$. Call an element $A$ in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ of rank 1 if $A \neq 0$ and $A \times A=0$. Show that this is equivalent to: either $A$ is nilpotent of index two or $A=\alpha E$ where $\alpha \neq 0$ in $\Phi$ and $E^{\cdot 2}=E, t(E)=1$.
5. Show that the associative algebra of all triangular matrices $\sum_{i \leqq j} \alpha_{i j} e_{i j}$ is unramified and has degree $n$ (the size of the matrices).
6. Multiplicative properties of the generic norm. In this section we shall derive the important multiplicative properties of the generic norm. For these we require the following two lemmas.

Lemma 1. Let $\mathfrak{V}$ be an $n$-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field $\Omega$ with basis $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$. Let $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) \in \Omega\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ be of positive degree and let $Q$ be the polynomial function $a=\sum \alpha_{i} u_{i} \rightarrow Q(a)=Q\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right)$. Suppose $T$ is a linear isomorphism of $\mathfrak{V}$ onto $\mathfrak{V}$ which maps $O_{Q}=\{a \mid Q(a) \neq 0\}$ onto itself. Let $Q_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right), \cdots, Q_{r}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ be the distinct irreducible factors of $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ in $\Omega\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ (determined up to nonzero multipliers in $\Omega$ ). Then there exists a permutation $\pi$ of $1,2, \cdots, r$ and nonzero elements $\rho_{j} \in \Omega$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
Q_{j}(x T)=\rho_{j} Q_{j \pi}(x), \quad x \in \mathfrak{V}, \quad j=1, \cdots, r . \tag{56}
\end{equation*}
$$

Moreover, if $Q_{0}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)=\prod{ }_{1}^{r} Q_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ then

$$
\begin{equation*}
Q_{0}(x T)=\rho Q(x), \quad x \in \mathfrak{B}, \quad \rho=\Pi \rho_{j} . \tag{57}
\end{equation*}
$$

Proof. Let $u_{i} T=\sum \tau_{i k} u_{k}$. Then $a T=\sum \alpha_{i}{ }^{\prime} u_{i}$ where $\alpha_{i}{ }^{\prime}=\sum_{k} \alpha_{k} \tau_{k i}$ if $a=\sum \alpha_{i} u_{i}$. If $f\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) \in \Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ then we define $f^{T}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)=f\left(\xi_{1}{ }^{\prime}, \cdots, \xi_{n}^{\prime}\right)$ where $\xi_{i}{ }^{\prime}=\sum \xi_{k} \tau_{k l}$. Then $f\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) \rightarrow f^{T}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is an automorphism of $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right] / \Phi$ so $f\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is irreducible if and only if $f^{T}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is irreducible. It follows from this that $Q_{j}{ }^{T}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right), j=1, \cdots, r$, are the distinct irreducible factors of $Q^{T}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$. On the other hand, $Q^{T}(a)=Q(a T)$ is clear from our definitions. Hence by the hypothesis of the lemma, $Q^{T}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ and $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ have the same set of zeroes in $\Omega$. Since the base field is algebraically closed we can invoke the Hilbert Nullstellensatz (Jacobson, Lectures, vol. III, p. 254) to conclude that $Q^{T}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ and $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ have the same irreducible factors in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$. Hence there exists a permutation $\pi$ of $\{1, \cdots, r\}$ and $\rho_{j} \neq 0$ in $\Phi$ such that $Q_{j}^{T}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)=\rho_{j} Q_{j \pi}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$. This is equivalent to (56). Evidently (57) follows from this.

Lemma 2 (McCrimmon). Let $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ be of positive degree in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ and let $M_{i}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right), 1 \leqq i \leqq n$, be elements of $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right]$, $\xi$ 's indeterminates, such that $M_{i}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)$ is of total degree one in $\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}$. Assume also that there exists $\gamma_{i}, 1 \leqq i \leqq n$, in $\Phi$ such that $M_{i}\left(\gamma_{1}, \cdots, \gamma_{n}, \xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)=\xi_{n+i}$ and a polynomial $m\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) \in \Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
Q\left(M_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right), \cdots, M_{n}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)\right)=m\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) Q\left(\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right) . \tag{58}
\end{equation*}
$$

Then for each irreducible factor $Q_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ of $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ there exists a polynomial $m_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) \in \Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
Q_{j}\left(M_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right), \cdots, M_{n}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)\right)=m_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) Q_{j}\left(\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right) . \tag{59}
\end{equation*}
$$

Proof. Let $Q_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right), \cdots, Q_{r}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ be the distinct irreducible factors of $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$. Clearly $Q_{j}\left(\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)$ is irreducible in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right]$ and, by (58), this is a factor of $Q\left(M_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right), \cdots, M_{n}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)\right)$ which is a product of a nonzero element of $\Phi$ and the polynomials $Q_{k}\left(M_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right), \cdots, M_{n}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)\right)$. Hence there exists a $j^{\prime}$ and a polynomial $m_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right) \in \Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right]$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
Q_{j^{\prime}}\left(M_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right), \cdots, M_{n}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)\right)=m_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right) Q_{j}\left(\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right) \tag{60}
\end{equation*}
$$

Putting $\xi_{i}=\gamma_{i}, 1 \leqq i \leqq n$, in this gives

$$
Q_{j^{\prime}}\left(\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)=m_{j}\left(\gamma_{1}, \cdots, \gamma_{n}, \xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right) Q_{j}\left(\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)
$$

which implies that $j^{\prime}=j$ in (60). Since the total degree of every $M_{i}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)$ in $\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}$ is one, the total degree in $\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}$ of $Q_{j}\left(M_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right), \cdots\right.$, $\left.M_{n}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)\right)$ does not exceed the total degree $d_{j}$ of $Q_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$. It follows from (60) that the total degree of $m_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right) Q_{j}\left(\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)$ in $\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}$ does not exceed $d_{j}$. This implies that $m_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)$ is of degree 0 in $\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}$. Hence $m_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)=m_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) \in \Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$. Then (59) is valid.

If $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{A}$ is an algebra and $1=\sum_{1}^{n} \gamma_{i} u_{i},\left(u_{i}\right)$ a basis then the polynomial $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) \in \Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ will be called normalized if $Q(1)=Q\left(\gamma_{1}, \cdots, \gamma_{n}\right)=1$. This is the case for the generic norm polynomial $n\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)=n(x)$. If $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is normalized then $Q_{j}(1) \neq 0$ for every irreducible factor $Q_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ of $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$. It follows that any normalized polynomial of positive degree has a unique factorization as a product of normalized irreducible polynomials.

We can now prove
Theorem 3. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a strictly power associative algebra with 1 over the field $\Phi,\left(u_{1}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ a basis for $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi, x=\sum \xi_{i} u_{i}$ a generic element, $n\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) =n(x)$ the generic norm, $m$ the degree of $\mathfrak{A}$. Then:
(i) $Q(a b)=Q(a) Q(b)$ if $a$ and $b$ are in an associative subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ and $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is a product of normalized irreducible factors of $n\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$.
(ii) $Q(\{a b a\})=Q(a)^{2} Q(b)$ if $\mathfrak{A}$ is Jordan and $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is as in (i).
(iii) If $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $q$ such that $Q(1)=1$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
Q(a(\operatorname{adj} a))=Q(a) Q(\operatorname{adj} a) \tag{61}
\end{equation*}
$$

for all $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ and the cardinal number $|\Phi|>m q$ then $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is a product of normalized irreducible factors of the generic norm $n\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$.
(iv) If $\mathfrak{A}$ is Jordan and $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $q$ such that $Q(1)=1$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
Q(\{a(\operatorname{adj} a) a\})=Q(a)^{2} Q(\operatorname{adj} a) \tag{62}
\end{equation*}
$$

for all $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ and $|\Phi|>(m+1) q$, then $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is the product of normalized irreducible factors of the generic norm.

Proof. We may assume $\Phi$ algebraically closed in (i) and (ii). Also we may assume that the associative subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}$ in (i) contains 1 .
(i) Let $\left(v_{1}, \cdots, v_{r}\right)$ be a basis for $\mathfrak{B} / \Phi, v_{k}=\sum_{1}^{n} \beta_{k i} u_{i}$. Then $y=\sum_{1}^{r} \xi_{k} v_{k} =\sum \xi_{k} \beta_{k l} u_{i}$ is a generic element of $\mathfrak{B}$. Then $n(y)=n\left(\sum \xi_{k} \beta_{k 1}, \cdots, \sum \xi_{k} \beta_{k r}\right) \in \Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right]$ and $Q\left(\sum \xi_{k} \beta_{k 1}, \cdots, \sum \xi_{k} \beta_{k r}\right)$ is a product of normalized irreducible factors of $n(y)$ in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right]$. It is enough to prove $n_{j}(a b)=n_{j}(a) n_{j}(b), a, b \in \mathfrak{B}$, for every normalized irreducible factor $n_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right)$ of $n(y)$ in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right]$. Let $\mathfrak{U}=\{a \in \mathfrak{B} \mid n(a) \neq 0\}$. Then $\mathfrak{U}$ is the set of invertible elements of the associative algebra $\mathfrak{B}$ and the linear mapping $x \rightarrow x b$ in $\mathfrak{B}$ for $b \in \mathfrak{U}$ is a linear isomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$ onto $\mathfrak{B}$ mapping $\mathfrak{U}$ onto $\mathfrak{U}$. Hence, by Lemma 1 , if $n_{0}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is the product of the distinct normalized irreducible factors $n_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right)$ of $n\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right)$ then there exists a nonzero $\rho$ in $\Omega$ such that $n_{0}(a b)=\rho n_{0}(a) n_{0}(b), a \in \mathfrak{B}, b \in \mathfrak{U}$. Putting $a=1$ gives $n_{0}(b)=\rho$. Hence we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
n_{0}(a b)=n_{0}(a) n_{0}(b) \tag{63}
\end{equation*}
$$
