for $a \in \mathfrak{B}, b \in \mathfrak{U}$. Since $\mathfrak{U}$ is a Zariski open subset we have (63) for all $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$. Now put $z=\sum_{k=1}^{r} \xi_{r+k} v_{k}, v_{k} v_{l}=\sum \delta_{k l q} v_{q}$. Then $y z=\sum M_{k}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 r}\right) v_{k}$ where $M_{k}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 r}\right) \in \Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 r}\right]$ and is of total degree one in $\xi_{r+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 r}$. Also if $1=\sum \delta_{k} v_{k}$ then $M_{k}\left(\delta_{1}, \cdots, \delta_{r}, \xi_{r+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 r}\right)=\xi_{r+k}$ since $1 z=z$. We have $n_{0}\left(M_{1}\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{2 r}\right), \cdots, M_{r}\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{2 r}\right)\right)=n_{0}\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{r}\right) n_{0}\left(\alpha_{r+1}, \cdots, \alpha_{2 r}\right)$ for all $\alpha_{i} \in \Phi$. Hence $n_{0}\left(M_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 r}\right), \cdots, M_{r}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 r}\right)\right)=n_{0}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right) n_{0}\left(\xi_{r+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 r}\right)$. It follows from Lemma 2 that for each $n_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right)$ there exists a polynomial $m_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right)$ such that

$$
n_{j}\left(M_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 r}\right), \cdots, M_{r}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 r}\right)\right)=m_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{r}\right) n_{j}\left(\xi_{r+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 r}\right) .
$$

This implies that $n_{j}(a b)=m_{j}(a) n_{j}(b)$. Putting $b=1$ gives $n_{j}(a)=m_{j}(a)$. Hence $n_{j}(a b)=n_{j}(a) n_{j}(b)$.
(ii) The proof of this is similar to that of (i). Here we let $n_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right), \cdots$, $n_{s}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ be the distinct normalized irreducible factors of $n\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)=n(x)$
and we put $n_{0}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)=\prod_{1}^{s} n_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$. It is enough to show $n_{j}(\{a b a\}) =n_{j}(a)^{2} n_{j}(b)$ for all $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$ and $j=1,2, \cdots, s$. Let $\mathfrak{U}$ be the set of invertible elements so $\mathfrak{U}=\{b \mid n(b) \neq 0\}$. If $a \in \mathfrak{U}$ then $U_{a}$ is a linear isomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ mapping $\mathfrak{U}$ onto $\mathfrak{U}$. Hence as in the proof of (i) we have, by Lemma 1, that there is a non zero $\rho$ in $\Phi$ such that $n_{0}(\{a b a\})=n_{0}\left(b U_{a}\right)=\rho n_{0}(b)$ for all $b \in \mathfrak{A}$. Putting $b=1$ gives $\rho=n_{0}\left(a^{2}\right)=n_{0}(a)^{2}$, by (i), so $n_{0}(\{a b a\})=n_{0}(b) n_{0}(a)^{2}$ holds for all $b \in \mathfrak{A}$ and all $a \in \mathfrak{U}$. It follows that this holds for all $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$ and this implies that if we take $x=\sum_{1}{ }^{n} \xi_{i} u_{i}, y=\sum_{1}{ }^{n} \xi_{n+i} u_{i}$ then $\{x y x\}=\sum_{i} M_{i}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right) u_{i}$ and $n_{0}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)^{2} n_{0}\left(\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)=n_{0}\left(M_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right), \cdots, M_{n}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)\right)$. Clearly $M_{i}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)$ is of total degree one in $\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}$ and if $1=\sum \gamma_{i} u_{i}$ then $\{1 y 1\}=y$ gives $M_{i}\left(\gamma_{1}, \cdots, \gamma_{n}, \xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)=\xi_{n+i}$. Hence, by Lemma 2 , there exists a polynomial $m_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ such that $n_{j}\left(M_{1}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right), \cdots, M_{n}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)\right) =m_{j}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) n_{j}\left(\xi_{n+1}, \cdots, \xi_{2 n}\right)$. This gives $n_{j}(\{a b a\})=m_{j}(a) n_{j}(b)$. Taking $b=1$ gives $m_{j}(a)=n_{j}\left(a^{2}\right)$. Since $n_{j}\left(a^{2}\right)=n_{j}(a)^{2}$ by (i) this gives $n_{j}(\{a b a\})=n_{j}(a)^{2} n_{j}(b)$ which completes the proof of (ii).
(iii) Since $a(\operatorname{adj} a)=n(a) 1$ and $Q(1)=1$ we have $Q(a) Q(\operatorname{adj} a)=n(a)^{q}$. If $x=\sum \xi_{i} u_{i}$ then it is clear from the definition that $\operatorname{adj} x=\sum M_{i}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) u_{i}$ where $M_{i}\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is homogeneous of degree $m-1$ in the $\xi$ 's. Hence $Q(\operatorname{adj} x)$ is homogeneous of degree $q(m-1)$ in the $\xi$ 's and $F\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)=Q(x) Q(\operatorname{adj} x)-n(x)^{q}$ is homogeneous of degree $q m$ in the $\xi$ 's. Also we see that $F\left(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\right)=0$ for $\alpha_{i} \in \Phi$. Since $|\Phi|>q m$, the usual proof of the theorem on zeros of a polynomial (Jacobson, Lectures, vol. I p. 112) shows that we have $F\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)=0$. Hence $Q(x) Q(\operatorname{adj} x)=n(x)^{q}$ and this implies that $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is a product of irreducible factors of $n\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$. Since $Q(1)=1$ we can take these to be normalized.
(iv) Since $\operatorname{adj} a \in \Phi[a]$ and $a(\operatorname{adj} a)=n(a) 1$ we have $\{a(\operatorname{adj} a) a\}=n(a) a$ and our hypothesis gives $n(a)^{q} Q(a)=Q(a)^{2} Q(\operatorname{adj} a)$. As in (iii) this gives $n(x)^{q} Q(x)=Q(x)^{2} Q(\operatorname{adj} x)$. Since $Q(1)=1, Q(x) \neq 0$ and $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ can be cancelled in this relation. This gives $n(x)^{q}=Q(x) Q(\operatorname{adj} x)$ which implies that $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is a product of irreducible factors of $n\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ and these can be taken to be normalized.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a finite-dimensional strictly power associative algebra with 1 , $\mathfrak{B}$ a subalgebra containing $1,\left(v_{1}, \cdots, v_{r}\right)$ a basis for $\mathfrak{B}, y=\sum \xi_{j} v_{j}$ a generic element of $\mathfrak{B}$. Let $n(y)$ and $n_{\mathfrak{B}}(y)$ denote the generic norms of $y$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ respectively. Show that $n(y)$ and $n_{\mathfrak{B}}(y)$ have the same irreducible factors in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{i}\right]$.
2. Show that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is alternative then $Q(a b)=Q(a) Q(b)$ for $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$ if $Q$ is a normalized irreducible factor of $n(x)=n\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right), x=\sum \xi_{i} u_{i}$ generic.
3. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be alternative with basis $\left(u_{1}, \cdots, u_{n}\right), Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ a nonzero homogeneous polynomial of degree $q$ in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ such that $Q(a b)=Q(a) Q(b)$, $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$. Assume $|\Phi|>q$. Show that $Q\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)$ is a product of normalized
irreducible factors of $n\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)=n(x), x=\sum \xi_{i} u_{i}$. Show that the same conclusion holds if $\mathfrak{A}$ is Jordan, $Q(\{a b a\})=Q(a)^{2} Q(b)$ and $|\Phi|>2 q$.
4. Let $\mathfrak{A}=\Phi_{n}, e_{i j}, i, j=1, \cdots, n$, the usual matrix basis, $\xi_{i j}$ indeterminates and let $Q$ be a nonzero homogeneous polynomial in the $\xi$ 's such that $Q(A B)=Q(A) Q(B) A, B \in \Phi_{n}$. Assume also that $|\Phi|>\operatorname{deg} Q$. Show that $Q$ is a power of $\operatorname{det} X$, $X=\sum \xi_{i j} e_{i j}$.

## 6. Separable algebras.

Definition 1. A finite-dimensional algebra $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ is called separable if $\mathfrak{U}_{\mathbf{P}}$ is a direct sum of simple ideals for every extension field $\mathrm{P} / \Phi$.

We note first that if $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ is a field then $\mathfrak{U} / \Phi$ is separable in the sense of Definition 1 if and only if it is a separable extension field in the usual sense. It is well known that if $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ is a separable extension field then $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}$ is a direct sum of fields (Jacobson, Lectures, vol. III, p. 87). On the other hand, if $\mathfrak{U} / \Phi$ is an inseparable extension field and $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of $\Phi$ then $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}$ contains a nonzero nilpotent element (loc. cit. p. 197). Hence $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}$ is not a direct sum of simple ideals since this structure for a commutative associative algebra implies that the algebra is a direct sum of fields, and this is impossible if the algebra contains a nonzero nilpotent element. Thus if $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ is an inseparable finite-dimensional field extension then $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ is not a separable algebra. We recall also that if an algebra is central simple then $\mathfrak{U}_{\mathbf{P}}$ is simple for any $\mathbf{P}$ (p. 00). Hence any finite-dimensional central simple algebra is separable. It is clear also that a direct sum of a finite number of separable algebras is separable.

Now let $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ be an arbitrary finite-dimensional algebra and let $M(\mathfrak{A})$ and $C(\mathfrak{A})$ be the multiplication algebra and centroid of $\mathfrak{A}$ as defined in §5.7. Thus $M(\mathfrak{A})$ is the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$ generated by 1 and the $a_{L}, a_{R}, a \in \mathfrak{A}$, and $C(\mathfrak{A})$ is the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$ of elements $\gamma$ which commute with every $m \in M(\mathfrak{A})$. Suppose $\mathfrak{A}$ has an identity element 1 and $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{s}$ where $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{A}$. Then $\mathfrak{A}_{i} \mathfrak{A}_{j}=0$ if $i \neq j$ and if $1=\sum_{i=1}^{s} 1_{i}$ where $1_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i}$ then $1_{i}$ is the identity element of $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$. Also $M(\mathfrak{A})$ is the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$ generated by the $a_{L}, a_{R}, a \in \mathfrak{A}$. It follows easily that $\mathfrak{M}=M(\mathfrak{A})=\mathfrak{M}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{s}$ where $\mathfrak{M}_{i}$ is the subalgebra generated by the elements $a_{i L}, a_{i R}, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i}$ and $\mathfrak{M}_{i}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{M}$. Moreover, $\mathfrak{M}_{i}$ annihilates every $\mathfrak{A}_{j}, j \neq i$, and the mapping $m_{i} \rightarrow m_{i} \mid \mathfrak{A}_{i}$, the restriction of $m_{i}$ to $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$, is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{M}_{i}$ onto the multiplication algebra $M\left(\mathfrak{A}_{i}\right)$. Identifying $\mathfrak{M}_{i}$ with $M\left(\mathfrak{A}_{i}\right)$ ( $m_{i}$ with its restriction) we can say that $M(\mathfrak{A})$ is a direct sum of the $M\left(\mathfrak{A}_{i}\right)$. We have $\mathfrak{A}_{i}=\mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{M}_{i}$ and if $\gamma \in C(\mathfrak{A})$ then $\mathfrak{A}_{i} \gamma=\mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{M}_{i} \gamma=(\mathfrak{A} \gamma) \mathfrak{M}_{i} \subseteq \mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{M}_{i}=\mathfrak{A}_{i}$. Thus $\gamma$ maps $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ into itself and the restriction of $y$ to $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ is contained in $C\left(\mathfrak{A}_{i}\right)$. On the other hand, if $\gamma_{i} \in C\left(\mathfrak{A}_{i}\right)$ for $i=1,2, \cdots, s$ and $\gamma$ is the linear mapping in $\mathfrak{A}$ which coincides with $\gamma_{i}$ on $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ then $\gamma \in C\left(\mathfrak{A}_{i}\right)$. It follows that $C(\mathfrak{A})$ is isomorphic to $C\left(\mathfrak{A}_{1}\right) \oplus C\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}\right) \oplus \cdots \oplus C\left(\mathfrak{A}_{s}\right)$.

If $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple then it is known that $C(\mathfrak{A})$ is an extension field of $\Phi$ and $M(\mathfrak{A})$
is the algebra of linear transformations of $\mathfrak{U}$ considered as a vector space over $C(\mathfrak{A})$ (Jacobson, Lie Algebras, p. 293). Thus $M=M(\mathfrak{A})$ is isomorphic to the algebra $\mathfrak{C}_{r}$ of $r \times r$ matrices over $\mathfrak{C}=C(\mathfrak{A})$. Here $r=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{U} / \mathfrak{C}$. We have also that $\mathfrak{C}_{\boldsymbol{r}} \cong \mathfrak{C} \otimes_{\Phi} \Phi_{\boldsymbol{r}}$. Hence $M(\mathfrak{A}) \cong \mathbb{C} \otimes \Phi_{\boldsymbol{r}}$ where $\mathbb{C}$ is the centroid and $r=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A} / \mathbb{C}$. If $\mathfrak{A}$ has an identity element then we know also that $\mathbb{C}$ can be identified with the center of $\mathfrak{A}$.

Now suppose $\mathfrak{A}$ has an identity 1 and $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{s}$ where $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ is a simple ideal. Then our results show that $M(\mathfrak{A})=\mathfrak{M}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{s}$ where $\mathfrak{M}_{\boldsymbol{i}}$ is an ideal isomorphic to $\mathfrak{C}_{\boldsymbol{i}} \otimes \Phi_{\boldsymbol{r}_{\boldsymbol{i}}}$ where $\mathbb{C}_{\boldsymbol{i}}$ is the center of $\mathfrak{A}_{\boldsymbol{i}}$ and $r_{\boldsymbol{i}}=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A}_{\boldsymbol{i}} / \mathbb{C}_{\boldsymbol{i}}$. We can now prove

Theorem 4. Let $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ be a finite-dimensional algebra with 1 . Then the following conditions on $\mathfrak{A}$ are equivalent: (1) $\mathfrak{A}$ is separable. (2) $M(\mathfrak{A})$ is a direct sum of ideals $\mathfrak{M}_{i}$ where $\mathfrak{M}_{i} \cong \Gamma_{i} \otimes \Phi_{r_{i}}$ where $\Gamma_{i} / \Phi$ is a separable field. (3) $\mathfrak{A}$ is a direct sum of simple ideals whose centers are separable fields. (4) $M(\mathfrak{Q})$ is separable.

Proof. Assume $\mathfrak{A}$ is separable. Then $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{s}$ where $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ is a simple ideal. If $\mathfrak{C}_{i}$ is the center of $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ then we have seen that $M(\mathfrak{A})$ is a direct sum of ideals $\mathfrak{M}_{i}, i=1, \cdots, s$, where $\mathfrak{M}_{i} \cong \mathfrak{C}_{i} \otimes \Phi_{r_{i}}$. Now it is easily seen that if P is an extension of the base field $\Phi$ then on identifying the elements $m \in M(\mathfrak{A})$ with their P-linear extensions to $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}, M\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}\right)=M\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}=\mathbf{P} \otimes_{\Phi} M(\mathfrak{A})\right.$. Since $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}$ is a direct sum of simple ideals it follows that $M(\mathfrak{A})_{\mathrm{P}}$ is a direct sum of ideals of the form $\Gamma \otimes \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{r}}$ where $\Gamma / \mathbf{P}$ is a field. This implies that every $\mathfrak{C}_{i \mathbf{P}}$ is a direct sum of fields. If $\mathbf{P}$ is taken to be the algebraic closure $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ of $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ then this implies that $\mathbb{C}_{i} / \Phi$ is separable. Hence we have proved that (1) implies (2) and (3). We note next that it is clear from the results preceding the statement of the theorem that (3) implies (2). Now assume (2) and let $\mathbf{P}$ be an extension field of $\Phi$. Then $\Gamma_{i \mathbf{P}}$ is a direct sum of fields. Hence $M(\mathfrak{A})_{\mathbf{P}}$ is a direct sum of simple algebras. Since $M\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{p}}\right)=M(\mathfrak{A})_{\mathbf{p}}$ we have this structure for $M\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{p}}\right)$. It follows that $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{p}}$ as right module for $M\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{p}}\right)$ is completely reducible. Since the submodules of $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{p}}$ as $M\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{p}}\right)$ module are the ideals of $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}$ this implies that $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}$ is a direct sum of simple ideals. Since $\mathbf{P}$ is arbitrary it follows that $\mathfrak{A}$ is separable. Hence (2) implies (1) and consequently also (3) and so (1), (2) and (3) are equivalent. If we apply the equivalence of (1) and (3) for $M(\mathfrak{A})$ in place of $\mathfrak{A}$ we see also that (4) is equivalent to the other conditions.

We shall now consider finite-dimensional associative or Jordan algebras with 1 and we shall show that such an algebra is separable if and only if its generic trace bilinear form is nondegenerate. We require first the following

Lemma (Dieudonné). Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a finite-dimensional nonassociative algebra satisfying the following conditions: (1) there exists a nondegenerate symmetric
associative bilinear form fon $\mathfrak{A}$, (2) $\mathfrak{A}$ contains no ideal $\mathfrak{N} \neq 0$ such that $\mathfrak{N}^{2}=0$. Then $\mathfrak{A}$ is a direct sum of simple ideals.

Proof. It is immediate from the symmetry and associativity of $f$ that if $\mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{A}$ then the orthogonal complement $\mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ relative to $f$ is an ideal. Then $\mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak{B} \cap \mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ is an ideal. If $z, w \in \mathfrak{N}$ and $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ we have $f(z w, a)=f(z, w a)=0$ since $z \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $w a \in \mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$. Since $f$ is nondegnerate this implies that $z w=0$. Hence $\mathfrak{N}^{2}=0$ and so $\mathfrak{N}=0$. Thus $\mathfrak{B} \cap \mathfrak{B}^{\perp}=0$ and $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$. We have therefore shown that every ideal in $\mathfrak{A}$ has a complementary ideal. This implies, as is well known, that $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{s}$ where the $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ are simple ideals.

We shall now prove the following important criterion.

Theorem 5. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a finite-dimensional algebra with 1 which is either associative or Jordan. Then $\mathfrak{A}$ is separable if and only if its generic trace form $t$ is nondegenerate.

Proof. Assume first that $t$ is nondegenerate. By Corollary 4 to Theorem 1, $t$ is symmetric and associative. Hence the first hypothesis of Dieudonné's lemma is satisfied for the bilinear form $f=t$. Now let $\mathfrak{N}$ be an ideal such that $\mathfrak{N}^{2}=0$. Since nilpotent elements have generic trace 0 (Corollary 1 to Theorem 1) we have $t(a, z)=t(a z)=0$ if $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ and $z \in \mathfrak{N}$. Hence $z=0$ by the nondegeneracy of $t$ and so $\mathfrak{N}=0$. It now follows from Dieudonné's lemma that $\mathfrak{A}$ is a direct sum of simple ideals. Now let $\mathbf{P}$ be an extension field of $\Phi$. Then the generic trace form $t$ on $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}$ is the P-bilinear extension of the generic trace form on $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence this is nondegenerate and so $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{P}}$ is a direct sum of simple ideals. Thus $\mathfrak{A}$ is separable. Conversely, assume $\mathfrak{A}$ is separable and let $\Omega$ be the algebraic closure of $\Phi$. Then $\mathfrak{U}_{\Omega}$ is a direct sum of simple ideals. We have seen in §3 that these ideals are orthogonal and the restriction of the generic trace form of $\mathfrak{A}$ to the ideal is the generic trace form of this ideal. Hence to prove nondegeneracy of $t$ on $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}$ it is sufficient to assume that $\mathfrak{U}_{\Omega}$ is simple. Since $t$ is symmetric and associative $\mathfrak{U}_{\Omega}{ }^{\perp}$ is an ideal. Hence either $t$ is nondegenerate or $t=0$. Hence the nondegeneracy of $t$ on $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}$ will follow if we can show that $t \neq 0$ on $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}$. To verify this we use the structure theory. First, assume $\mathfrak{A}$ is associative. Then $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega} \cong \Omega_{n}$ by the Wedderburn theorem. We have seen in §4 that $t$ is the usual trace of the matrix (in $\Omega_{n}$ ). If $e_{\imath j}$ is the usual matrix unit then we have $t\left(e_{11}\right)=1$. Hence $t$ is nondegenerate in this case. Next assume $\mathfrak{A}$ is Jordan. Then the possibilities for a simple algebra $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}$ are: $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}=\Omega 1$; $\mathfrak{U}_{\Omega}=\Omega 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ the Jordan algebra of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional vector space $\mathfrak{B}$ with $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}>1 ; \Omega_{n}{ }^{+}$with $n \geqq 3 ; \mathfrak{H}\left(\Omega_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ with $n \geqq 3 ; \mathfrak{H}\left(\Omega_{2 n}, J_{S}\right), n \geqq 3 ; \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$. The notations here are those in §4. Now it is clear that $t$ is nondegenerate in the first case: $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}=\Omega 1$. In the second case the degree is two so $t(1,1)=t(1)=2 \neq 0$. In the remaining cases one sees directly from the determination of the generic trace in §4 that $t \neq 0$. Hence we
see that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is separable then the generic trace form on $\mathfrak{U}_{\Omega}$ is nondegenerate. Then the generic trace form on $\mathfrak{A}$ is nondegenerate also.

## 7. Norm similarity of Jordan algebras. The group of norm preserving linear transformations.

Definition 2. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{A}$ ' be finite-dimensional strictly power associative algebras with 1. Then a bijective linear mapping $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$ is called a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{A}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$ if $n^{\prime}\left(a^{\eta}\right)=\rho n(a)$ for all $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ where $n$ and $n^{\prime}$ are the generic norm in $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$ respectively and $\rho$ is a nonzero element of the base field. The element $\rho$ is called the multiplier of $\eta$.

It is clear that the identity mapping is a norm similarity on $\mathfrak{A}$, that if $\eta$ is a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{A}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$ with multiplier $\rho$ and $\zeta$ is norm similarity of $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime \prime}$ with multiplier $\sigma$ then $\eta \zeta$ is a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{A}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime \prime}$ with multiplier $\rho \sigma$ and $\eta^{-1}$ is a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}$ with multiplier $\rho^{-1}$. Hence norm similarity is an equivalence relation and the set of norm similarities of $\mathfrak{A}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}$ is a subgroup $\mathbf{M}(\mathfrak{A})$ of the group of bijective linear transformations of $\mathfrak{A}$. The norm similarities of $\mathfrak{A}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}$ with multiplier 1 form an invariant subgroup $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{A})$ of $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{A})$ called the norm preserving group of $\mathfrak{A}$. Since $n\left(a^{\eta}\right)=n(a)$ for any automorphism or antiautomorphism, $\mathbf{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{A})$ contains the group of automorphisms and antiautomorphisms of $\mathfrak{A}$.

Let $m^{\prime}$ be the degree of $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}, m$ the degree of $\mathfrak{A}$ and let $\eta$ be a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{A}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$. Then $n^{\prime}\left(1^{\eta}\right)=\rho$ and if $\beta \neq 0$ is in $\Phi$ then $n^{\prime}\left((\beta 1)^{\eta}\right)=\rho n(\beta 1)$ gives $\beta^{m^{\prime}}=\beta^{m}$ so $\beta^{\left|m-m^{\prime}\right|}=1$ for all $\beta \neq 0$ in $\Phi$. If $m^{\prime} \neq m$ this implies that $|\Phi| \leqq\left|m-m^{\prime}\right|+1$. We shall usually assume that $|\Phi|$ exceeds the degrees of the algebras under consideration. This will imply that if $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$ are norm similar then they have the same degree. If this degree is $m$ then $n^{\prime}\left(x^{\eta}\right)-\rho n(x)$ for $x=\sum \xi_{i} u_{\imath}$ generic for $\mathfrak{A}$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $\leqq m$ in the $\xi^{\prime} s$. Morever, the norm similarity $n^{\prime}\left(a^{\eta}\right)=\rho n(a), a \in \mathfrak{A}$, and $|\Phi|>m$ implies that $n^{\prime}\left(x^{\eta}\right)=\rho n(x)$. This implies that the linear extension $\eta$ of $\eta$ to $\mathfrak{U}_{\Gamma}$ into $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}^{\prime}, \Gamma$ an extension field of $\Phi$, is a norm similarity.

We shall now study norm similarity for Jordan algebras and we shall see that this notion is closely related to that of isotopy defined in §1.12. We recall that if $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ are Jordan algebras with 1 then an isotopy $\alpha$ is a bijective linear mapping of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ such that $(x . y)^{\alpha}=\left\{x^{\alpha} b y^{\alpha}\right\}$ where $b$ is a fixed invertible element of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ and $x, y \in \mathfrak{J}$. This is just an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto the $b$-isotope $\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}, b\right)$ of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. We recall also that a mapping $\alpha$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is an isotopy if and only if $\alpha$ is bijective and linear and there exists a $\beta \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
U_{c} \alpha=\beta U_{c^{\alpha}} \tag{64}
\end{equation*}
$$

holds for all $c \in \mathfrak{J}$. In this case $1^{\alpha}$ is an invertible element of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ and the element
$b$ in the definition of isotopy is the inverse $\left(1^{\alpha}\right)^{-1}$. Also it is clear from the definition that an isotopy $\alpha$ is an isomorphism if and only if $1^{\alpha}=1$.

We shall show first that an isotopy of a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 onto a second such algebra is necessarily a norm similarity. For this we require the following well-known result.

Lemma. If $\Omega$ is an algebraically closed field of characteristic $\neq 2$ and $\Omega[a]$ is the commutative associative algebra with 1 generated by 1 and an invertible element $a$, then there exists an invertible element $b$ in $\Omega[a]$ such that $b^{2}=a$.

Proof. Let $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ be the minimum polynomial of $a$. Then $\mu_{a}(\lambda)=\prod_{1}^{s}\left(\lambda-\rho_{i}\right)^{\boldsymbol{e}_{i}}$ where the $\rho_{i}$ are distinct and nonzero. Then $\mathfrak{A}=\Omega[a]=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{s}$ where $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ has the identity $1_{i}$ and is generated by this element and the element $a_{i}$ such that $a=a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{s}, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i}$. Moreover, the minimum polynomial of $a_{i}$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ is $\left(\lambda-\rho_{i}\right)^{\boldsymbol{e}_{i}}$. This implies that $a_{i}=\rho_{i} 1_{i}+z_{i}$ where $z_{\imath}{ }^{n_{i}}=0$. By Lemma 4 on p.150, there exists an element $1_{i}+w_{i}$, $w_{i}$ nilpotent in $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$, such that $\left(1_{i}+w_{i}\right)^{2}=1_{i}+\rho_{i}{ }^{-1} z_{i}$. If $\sigma_{i}=\rho_{i}^{\frac{1}{2}}$ a square root of $\rho_{i}$ in $\Omega$ then $\left(\sigma_{i}\left(1+w_{i}\right)\right)^{2} =\rho_{i} 1_{i}+z_{i}$ and $b=\sum_{1}{ }^{r} \sigma_{i}\left(1+w_{i}\right)$ is a square root of $a$ in $\Omega[a]$. Clearly $b$ is invertible.

We can now prove
Throrem 6. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ be finite-dimensional Jordan algebras with 1 and let $\alpha$ be an isotopy of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Then $\alpha$ is a norm similarity.

Proof. We consider first the relation between the generic norm of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ and its isotope $(\mathfrak{J}, a)$ defined by the invertible element $a$. Denoting the generic norm of $b$ in $(\mathfrak{J}, a)$ by $n^{(a)}(b)$ we claim that

$$
\begin{equation*}
n^{(a)}(b)=n(a) n(b) . \tag{65}
\end{equation*}
$$

To prove this we may assume the base field is algebraically closed. Then the lemma implies that there exists a square root $c$ of $a$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ so we have $(\mathfrak{J}, a)=\left(\mathfrak{J}, c^{\cdot^{2}}\right)$. Then $U_{c}$ is an isomorphism of $(\mathfrak{J}, a)$ onto $\mathfrak{J}$ (see p.155). The image of $b$ under this isomorphism is $\{c b c\}$. Hence, by Theorem 1 (vi), $n^{(a)}(b)=n(\{c b c\})$. By Theorem 3, $n(\{c b c\})=n(c)^{2} n(b)=n\left(c^{\cdot 2}\right) n(b)=n(a) n(b)$. Hence $n^{(a)}(b)=n(a) n(b)$ which is (65). Now let $\alpha$ be an isotopy of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Then $\alpha$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto an isotope $\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}, b\right)$ of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. If $n$ and $n^{\prime}$ are the generic norms in $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ respectively then $n(a)=n^{\prime(b)}\left(a^{\alpha}\right)$ where $n^{\prime(b)}$ is the generic norm in $\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}, b\right)$. By (65) applied to $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ we have $n^{\prime(b)}\left(a^{\alpha}\right)=n^{\prime}(b) n^{\prime}\left(a^{\alpha}\right)$. Hence $n(a)=n^{\prime}(b) n^{\prime}\left(a^{\alpha}\right)$ and $n^{\prime}\left(a^{\alpha}\right)=\rho n(a)$ where $\rho=n^{\prime}(b)^{-1}$.

We shall prove next that the converse of Theorem 6 holds provided that the algebras are separable and $\Phi$ has enough elements. For this purpose we shall
derive some important differentiation formulas for the generic norm in any finite dimensional Jordan algebra over an infinite field.

First, let $\mathfrak{V}$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over an infinite field and let $f$ be a polynomial function on $\mathfrak{B}$ defined by an element $f\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right) \in \Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ of degree $m$. Let $a$ be a fixed vector in $\mathfrak{B}$. Then it is clear that there exist uniquely determined polynomial functions $f_{1}, f_{2}, \cdots, f_{m}$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
f(c+\lambda a)=f(c)+f_{1}(c) \lambda+\cdots+f_{m}(c) \lambda^{m} \tag{66}
\end{equation*}
$$

for all $c \in \mathfrak{V}$ and $\lambda \in \Phi$. We indicate (66) more briefly as

$$
\begin{equation*}
f(c+\lambda a) \equiv f(c)+f_{1}(c) \lambda\left(\bmod \lambda^{2}\right) . \tag{$\prime$}
\end{equation*}
$$

It is immediate that $f \rightarrow f_{1}$ is a derivation in the algebra $\mathfrak{P}$ of polynomial functions. Moreover, if $f=l$ is linear then $f_{1}$ is the constant function $c \rightarrow a$. It follows that

$$
\begin{equation*}
f_{1}=\Delta^{a} f \quad \text { and } \quad f_{1}(c)=\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} f . \tag{67}
\end{equation*}
$$

Now let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1 over the infinite field $\Phi, n$ and $t$ the generic norm and trace on $\mathfrak{J}$. These are homogeneous polynomial functions on $\mathfrak{J}$ of degrees $m$ and one, respectively, where the degree of $\mathfrak{J}$ is $m$. As usual, we have the generic trace form $t(a, b)=t(a . b)$. We shall show first that for arbitrary $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ and invertible $c \in \mathfrak{J}$ we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} n=n(c) t\left(c^{-^{-1}}, a\right) . \tag{68}
\end{equation*}
$$

To see this we begin with the formula $n(\lambda 1-a)=m_{a}(\lambda)=\lambda^{m}-t(a) \lambda^{m-1}+\cdots$. We may assume the base field is algebraically closed and then we have a $d \in \mathfrak{J}$ such that $d^{.2}=c$. Then

$$
\begin{align*}
n(c+\lambda a) & =n\left(\left(1+\lambda a U_{d}^{-1}\right) U_{d}\right) \\
& =n(c) n\left(1+\lambda a U_{d}^{-1}\right)  \tag{69}\\
& \equiv n(c)+n(c) t\left(a U_{d}^{-1}\right) \lambda\left(\bmod \lambda^{2}\right),
\end{align*}
$$

since $n(1+\lambda b) \equiv 1+t(b) \lambda\left(\bmod \lambda^{2}\right)$ is an immediate consequence of $n(\lambda 1-a) =\lambda^{m}-t(a) \lambda^{m-1}+\cdots$. Hence by what we showed above, $\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} n=n(c) t\left(a U_{d}{ }^{-1}\right) =n(c) t\left\{d^{\cdot^{-1}} a d^{\cdot^{-1}}\right\}=n(c) t\left(c^{-1}, a\right)$ by the associativity of $t$. Hence (68) holds. Now by the definition of the logarithmic derivative (68) can be written also as

$$
\begin{equation*}
\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} \log n=t\left(c^{\cdot^{-1}}, a\right) . \tag{$\prime$}
\end{equation*}
$$

For later application it is useful to note also that since $c^{c^{-1}}=n(c)^{-1} \operatorname{adj} c$, (68) is also equivalent to

$$
\begin{equation*}
\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} n=t(\operatorname{adj} c, a) \tag{$\prime\prime$}
\end{equation*}
$$

which is valid for all $a$ and $c$.

We now use the customary notation $x$ for the identity mapping $c \rightarrow c$ and $x^{.^{-1}}$ for $c \rightarrow c^{.^{-1}}$ which is a rational mapping on $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{J}$ defined on the open set of invertible elements. Then we claim that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\Delta_{c}^{a} x^{r^{-1}}=-a U_{c}^{-1} . \tag{70}
\end{equation*}
$$

To see this we differentiate the relation

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left\{x x^{-1} x\right\}=x \tag{71}
\end{equation*}
$$

to obtain

$$
a=\left\{c\left(\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} x^{-1}\right) c\right\}+\left\{a c^{-1} c\right\}+\left\{c c^{-1} a\right\} .
$$

Since $\left\{a c^{\cdot^{-1}} c\right\}=\left\{c c^{\cdot^{-1}} a\right\}=a$ this gives $\left(\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} x^{\cdot^{-1}}\right) U_{c}=-a$ which is equivalent to (70).

Next we compute $\Delta^{b}{ }_{c} \Delta^{a} \log n=\Delta^{b}{ }_{c} t\left(x^{\cdot-1}, a\right)$. Since $t$ is bilinear the chain rule and (70) gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
-\Delta^{b}{ }_{c} \Delta^{a} \log n=t\left(b U_{c}^{-1}, a\right) . \tag{72}
\end{equation*}
$$

We can now prove
Theorem 7. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ be finite-dimensional Jordan algebras with 1 such that $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is separable. Assume also that $|\Phi|>\operatorname{deg} m, \operatorname{deg} m^{\prime}$. Then: (1) If $\eta$ is a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ mapping 1 into the identity element $1^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ then $\eta$ is an isomorphism. (2) If $\eta$ is a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ then $\eta$ is an isotopy and $\mathfrak{J}$ is separable.

Proof. The condition on $|\Phi|$ implies that the linear extension of $\eta$ to $\Im_{\Gamma}$ is a norm similarity. Hence we may assume $\Phi$ is infinite and employ the formulas developed above. (1) Let $n^{\prime}, t^{\prime}$ be the generic norm and trace on $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. It is clear that $\eta$ maps the set of invertible elements of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto the set of invertible elements of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Let $a$ be arbitrary in $\mathfrak{J}, c$ invertible in $\mathfrak{J}$. Then, by (68), and the chain rule (20) we obtain

$$
\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} n^{\prime} \circ \eta=n^{\prime}\left(c^{\eta}\right) t^{\prime}\left(\left(c^{\eta}\right)^{-1}, a^{\eta}\right) .
$$

Hence $\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} \log n^{\prime} \circ \eta=t^{\prime}\left(\left(c^{\eta}\right)^{-1}, a^{\eta}\right)$. Similarly, we obtain $\Delta^{a}{ }_{c}\left(x^{\eta}\right)^{-1}=-a^{\eta} U_{c^{\eta}}{ }^{-1}$. Hence

$$
\begin{equation*}
-\Delta^{b}{ }_{c} \Delta^{a} \log n^{\prime} \circ \eta=t^{\prime}\left(b^{\eta} U_{c^{\eta}}{ }^{-1}, a^{\eta}\right) . \tag{73}
\end{equation*}
$$

On the other hand, we are given that $n^{\prime} \circ \eta=\rho n$ where $\rho \neq 0$ is in $\Phi$. Hence $\Delta^{a} \log n^{\prime} \circ \eta=\Delta^{a} \log \rho n=\Delta^{a} \log n$ (by (12)). It follows from (72) and (73) that we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
t\left(b U_{c}^{-1}, a\right)=t^{\prime}\left(b^{\eta} U_{c^{\eta}}{ }^{-1}, a^{\eta}\right) \tag{74}
\end{equation*}
$$

for all $a, b$ and invertible $c$. Also we are given that $1^{\eta}$ is the identity of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Hence, taking $c=1$ in (74), we obtain $t(b, a)=t^{\prime}(b \eta, a \eta)\left(\equiv t^{\prime}\left(b^{\eta}, a^{\eta}\right)\right)$ which permits us to rewrite (74) as

$$
\begin{equation*}
t^{\prime}\left(b U_{c}^{-1} \eta, a \eta\right)=t^{\prime}\left(b \eta U_{c^{\eta}}{ }^{-1}, a \eta\right) . \tag{75}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is separable, $t^{\prime}$ is nondegenerate. Hence (75) implies that $b U_{c}^{-1} \eta=b \eta U_{c^{\eta}}{ }^{-1}$ for all $b$ and invertible $c$. If we put $b=c$ in this we obtain $\left(c^{-1}\right)^{\eta}=\left(c^{\eta}\right)^{-1}$. Hence $b U_{c^{\cdot-1}} \eta=b U_{c}{ }^{-1} \eta=b \eta U_{c^{\eta}}{ }^{-1}=b \eta U_{\left(c^{\eta}\right)^{\cdot-1}}=b \eta U_{\left(c^{\cdot-1}\right) \eta}$. Replacing $c$ by $c^{\cdot^{-1}}$ we obtain $b U_{c} \eta=b \eta U_{c} \eta$. Putting $b=1$ then $\left(c^{\cdot 2}\right)^{\eta}=\left(c^{\eta}\right)^{\cdot 2}$ for invertible $c$. It follows that this holds for all $c$ and hence $\eta$ is an isomorphism. This completes the proof of (1).
(2) Again we have that $c$ is invertible if and only if $c^{\eta}$ is invertible. Hence $1^{\eta}$ is invertible so we can define the isotope $\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime},\left(1^{n}\right)^{-1}\right)$ whose identity element is $1^{\eta}$. If $n^{\prime \prime}$ denotes the generic norm in this algebra then $n^{\prime \prime}\left(a^{\eta}\right)=n^{\prime}\left(\left(1^{\eta}\right)^{-1}\right) n^{\prime}\left(a^{\eta}\right) =\mu n(a), \mu \neq 0$. Hence $\eta$ is a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime},\left(1^{\eta}\right)^{-1}\right)$ and $\eta$ maps 1 into the identity element of the second algebra. Hence, by (1), $\eta$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto an isotope of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. This means that $\eta$ is an isotopy of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. It remains to show that $\mathfrak{J}$ is separable. This will follow by showing that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is separable then any isotope ( $\mathfrak{J}, a$ ) is separable. We have seen in §1.12 that $\mathfrak{J}$ and $(\mathfrak{J}, a)$ have the same ideals. Hence if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a direct sum of simple ideals then $(\mathfrak{J}, a)$ is a direct sum of simple ideals. Thus $\mathfrak{J}$ semisimple implies $(\mathfrak{J}, a)$ semisimple and if $\mathbf{P}$ is any extension of the base field then $\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbf{P}}$ semisimple implies $\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbf{P}}, a\right)=(\mathfrak{J}, a)_{\mathbf{P}}$ is semisimple. Hence $\mathfrak{J}$ separable implies $(\mathfrak{J}, a)$ is separable.
While Theorem 7 requires a restriction on the cardinality of the base field, the following corollary requires no such restriction.
Corollary. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional separable Jordan algebra over an arbitrary field; let $\eta=U_{a_{1}} U_{a_{2}} \cdots U_{a_{r}}, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$, satisfy $1^{\eta}=1$. Then $\eta$ is an automorphism of J.
Proof. We have $1=n(1)=n\left(1^{n}\right)=n\left(1 U_{a_{1}} \cdots U_{a_{r}}\right)=\Pi n\left(a_{i}\right)^{2}$. Hence the $a_{i}$ are invertible and $\eta$ is a bijective linear mapping contained in $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ since $n\left(a^{\eta}\right)=\rho n(a)$ where $\rho=\Pi n\left(a_{i}\right)^{2}$. If $\Phi$ is infinite Theorem 7 implies that $\eta$ is an automorphism. If $\Phi$ is finite we can extend $\Phi$ to an infinite field $\Gamma$ and consider the linear mappings $U_{a_{i}}$ in $\mathfrak{I}_{\Gamma}$. Clearly $\eta=U_{a_{1}} \cdots U_{a_{r}}$ is linear extension of the given $\eta$ to $\mathfrak{I}_{\Gamma}$ and this is an automorphism. Hence the given $\eta$ is an automorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$.

We recall that if $\mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{\prime}$ are finite-dimensional vector spaces equipped with nondegenerate symmetric bilinear forms $f$ and $f^{\prime}$ respectively then for any linear mapping $T$ of $\mathfrak{V}$ into $\mathfrak{B}^{\prime}$ we can define a unique linear mapping $T^{*}$ of $\mathfrak{V}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{V}$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
f^{\prime}\left(x T, y^{\prime}\right)=f\left(x, y^{\prime} T^{*}\right) \tag{76}
\end{equation*}
$$

for all $x \in \mathfrak{B}, y^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{B}^{\prime}$. If $T$ is bijective so is $T^{*}$. If $\mathfrak{B}^{\prime \prime}$ is another finite-dimensional
vector space with nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $f^{\prime \prime}$ and $U \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{\prime}, \mathfrak{B}^{\prime \prime}\right)$ then we have the element $U^{*} \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{\prime \prime}, \mathfrak{B}^{\prime}\right)$ defined by $f^{\prime}$ and $f^{\prime \prime}$ and $(T U)^{*} \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{\prime \prime}, \mathfrak{B}\right)$ defined by $f$ and $f^{\prime \prime}$. The definitions give $(T U)^{*}=U^{*} T^{*}$

Now let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a separable Jordan algebra with generic trace $t$. Since $t$ is associative, $t(x . c, y)=t(x, y . c)$ which shows that $R_{c}{ }^{*}=R_{c}$ (relative to $t$ ). Since $U_{c}=2 R_{c}{ }^{2}-R_{c \cdot 2}$ we have also $U_{c}{ }^{*}=U_{c}$. Now suppose $\eta$ is a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto a second separable Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Then the relation (74) is valid. Since $\eta$ is bijective this gives

$$
t^{\prime}\left(b \eta U_{c^{\eta}}{ }^{-1}, a^{\prime}\right)=t\left(b U_{c}^{-1}, a^{\prime} \eta^{-1}\right)
$$

for all $b \in \mathfrak{J}, a^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. If we put $c=1$ in this we obtain $\eta^{-1}=\left(\eta U_{1} \eta^{-1}\right)^{*}=U_{1} \eta^{-1} \eta^{*}$. Hence

$$
\begin{equation*}
\eta^{*}=U_{1} \eta \eta^{-1} . \tag{77}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since $U_{1} \eta$ and $\eta^{-1}$ are norm similarities this equation shows that $\eta^{*}$ is a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}$. If $n^{\prime}\left(a^{\eta}\right)=\rho n(a)$ then $n^{\prime}\left(1^{\eta}\right)=\rho$ and (77) imply that $n\left(a^{\prime \prime *}\right)=\rho n^{\prime}\left(a^{\prime}\right), a^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. In particular, if $n^{\prime}\left(a^{\eta}\right)=n(a)$ then $n\left(a^{\prime \eta^{*}}\right)=n^{\prime}\left(a^{\prime}\right)$.

We now let $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{J}$ and we consider the group $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ of norm similarities of the separable Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ onto itself. We assume also that $|\Phi|>\operatorname{deg} \mathfrak{J}$. Then Theorem 7 implies that $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ coincides with the structure group $\Gamma(\mathfrak{J})$, that is, the group of isotopies of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}(\S 1.12)$. We recall that $\Gamma(\mathfrak{J})$ contains as invariant subgroup the inner structure group $\Gamma_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ which is defined to be the subgroup generated by the $U_{a}, a$ invertible in $\mathfrak{J}$. We have defined the group $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ of norm preserving linear transformations of $\mathfrak{J}$ as the subgroup of $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ specified by $n\left(a^{\eta}\right)=n(a)$. We shall call the invariant subgroup $\mathbf{M}_{1}^{(1)}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathbf{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cap \Gamma_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ the inner norm preserving group of $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $n\left(a U_{c}\right)=n(a) n(c)^{2}$ it is clear that $\mathbf{M}_{1}^{(1)}(\mathfrak{J})$ is the set of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{J}$ which have the form $U_{c_{1}} U_{c_{2}} \cdots U_{c_{r}}$ where $\prod_{1}^{r} n\left(c_{i}\right)^{2}=1$. The subset $\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)}(\mathfrak{J})$ of the transformations of the form $U_{c_{1}} U_{c_{2}} \cdots U_{c_{r}}$ such that $\prod_{1}^{r} n\left(c_{t}\right)=1$ is a subgroup of $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(1)}(\mathfrak{J})$.

If $\eta$ is an automorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ then $1^{\eta}=1$ and $n\left(a^{\eta}\right)=n(a), a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Hence $\mathbf{M}(\mathfrak{J}) \supseteq \mathbf{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \supseteq$ Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ where Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ is the group of automorphisms of $\mathfrak{J}$. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is separable then it follows from Theorem 7 (1) that Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ is the subgroup of $\mathbf{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ of $\eta$ such that $1^{n}=1$.

We have seen also that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is separable then the adjoint $\eta^{*}$ of $\eta$ relative to the generic trace form (which is nondegenerate) is in $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ for any $\eta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$. The mapping $\eta \rightarrow \hat{\eta}=\left(\eta^{*}\right)^{-1}$ is an automorphism of period two in $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$. By (77), we have $\hat{\eta}=\eta U_{1} \eta^{-1}$. Hence $\hat{\eta}=\eta$ if $\eta$ is an automorphism. On the other hand, if $\hat{\eta}=\eta$ then $U_{1} \eta=1$ which need not imply that $1^{\eta}=1$. For example, if we take $\eta=-1$ then $\eta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $U_{1} \eta=1$ so $\hat{\eta}=\eta$. Hence the set of fixed points of $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ under the automorphism $\eta \rightarrow \hat{\eta}$ is a subgroup which contains properly the group of automorphisms.

If $\mathfrak{J}$ is finite-dimensional semisimple over an algebraically closed field then $\mathfrak{J}$
is separable. If $\eta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ then $1^{\eta}=a$ is invertible so $1^{\eta}=c^{.2}, c$ invertible. Then $U_{c} \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $1 U_{c}=1^{\eta}$. Hence $\alpha=\eta U_{c}{ }^{-1} \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $1^{\alpha}=1$. Then $\alpha$ is an automorphism. Thus in the case of an algebraically closed field we have that any element $\eta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ has the form $\eta=\alpha U_{c}$ where $\alpha$ is an automorphism.

## Exercises

1. Show that $\Delta^{a}{ }_{1} \log n=t(a)$ holds for any finite-dimensional strictly power associative algebra with 1 .
2. Let $\alpha$ be an isotopy of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ with 1 and let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a quadratic ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that $\mathfrak{B}^{\alpha}$ is a quadratic ideal in $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Assume $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ are finite-dimensional separable and let $\eta$ be a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Show that $\mathfrak{B}^{\eta}$ is a quadratic ideal.
3. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a separable Jordan algebra of characteristic $\neq 3$ and define $t(a, b, c)=t(a . b . c)$ on $\mathfrak{J}$ (cf. ex. 1, p. 229). Show that a bijective linear mapping $\eta$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ is an automorphism if and only if $t\left(a^{\eta}, b^{\eta}\right)=t(a, b)$ and $t\left(a^{\eta}, b^{\eta}, c^{\eta}\right) =t(a, b, c), a, b, c \in \mathfrak{J}$. Show also that $D \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ is a derivation if and only if $t(a D, b)+t(a, b D)=0$ and $t(a D, b, c)+t(a, b D, c)+t(a, b, c D)=0$.
4. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be as in exercise 3. Show that if $\eta$ is a bijective linear mapping of $\mathfrak{J}$ having the first three coefficients of the generic minimum polynomial as invariants then $\eta$ is an automorphism.
5. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ the Jordan algebra of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{B}, t$ and $n$ the generic trace and norm on $\mathfrak{J}$. Let $n(a, b) =\frac{1}{2}[n(a+b)-n(a)-n(b)]$ the symmetric bilinear form corresponding to the quadratic form $n$. If $a=\alpha 1+u, \alpha \in \Phi, u \in \mathfrak{B}$ then $t(a)=2 \alpha$ and $n(a)=\alpha^{2}-f(u, u)$ (cf. §4). If $a$ is invertible let $S_{a}$ denote the symmetry in the vector space $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the hyperplane orthogonal to $a$ relative to $n\left(x S_{a}=x-2 n(x, a) i n(a)^{-1} a\right)$. Verify the formula $U_{a}=n(a) S_{1} S_{a}$. Use this result and the theorem of CartanDieudonné on the decomposition of orthogonal transformations as products of symmetries (Artin's Geometric Algebra, p. 129) to show that any rotation in $\Im$ relative to $n$ is a product c ${ }^{\complement}$ mappings $V_{a} \equiv n(a)^{-1} U_{a}$ where $a$ is invertible. Show also that the group $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)}(\mathfrak{J})$ defined to be the set of elements $U_{a_{1}} U_{a_{2}} \cdots U_{a_{r}}$ such that $\Pi n\left(a_{i}\right)=1$ coincides with the reduced orthogonal group (definition in Artin's Geometric Algebra, p. 194).
6. Show that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is as in exercise 5 and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{V}>1$ tien the only elements $a$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $U_{a}=1$ are $a= \pm 1$. Hence show that if $\eta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ satisfies $\hat{\eta}=\eta$ then $\eta$ is either an automorphism or the negative of an automorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$.
7. Determination of $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ special central simple of degree $\geqq 3$. The Jordan algebras described in the title have the form $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is a finite-dimensional central simple associative algebra with involution. Moreover, $\mathfrak{A}$ and the injection mapping constitute a unital special universal envelope of $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}$ generates the associative algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ and every automor-
phism of $\mathfrak{J}$ has a unique extension to an automorphism of $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. We can distinguish three types of ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ):
I. $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{\circ}$ where $\mathfrak{B}$ is central simple over the base field $\Phi$ and $J$ is the involution $(a, b) \rightarrow(b, a), a, b \in \mathfrak{B}$.
II. $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple with center $\mathrm{P} / \Phi$ a quadratic extension field of $\Phi$ and the restriction of $J$ to P is not the identity mapping.
III. $\mathfrak{A}$ is central simple over $\Phi$.

We recall the theorem of Skolem-Noether that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is a finite-dimensional central simple Jordan algebra over $\Phi$ then every automorphism of $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ is inner, that is, it has the form $x \rightarrow c^{-1} x c$. It is clear that if $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{s}$ where $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ is finite dimensional simple then any automorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ which is the identity on the center maps every $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ onto itself and is the identity on the centers of the $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$. Hence, by the Skolem-Noether theorem applied to the $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$, it is an inner automorphism. If ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) is central simple and $x \rightarrow c^{-1} x c$ is an automorphism of ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) then $c^{-1} x^{J} c=c^{J} x^{J}\left(c^{J}\right)^{-1}$. This implies that $c c^{\boldsymbol{J}}$ is in the center of $\mathfrak{A}$. Since $c c^{\boldsymbol{J}} \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ we have $c c^{\boldsymbol{J}}=\gamma 1$ where $\gamma \neq 0$ is in $\Phi$. The converse is clear also: If $c c^{J}=\gamma 1 \neq 0, \gamma$ in $\Phi$, then $x \rightarrow c^{-1} x c$ is an automorphism of $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. We shall call these inner automorphisms of $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. Note that $x \rightarrow c^{-1} x c=\gamma^{-1} c^{J} x c$.

If ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) is of type I or II then the center of $\mathfrak{A}$ is two dimensional. In the first case it is $\Phi \oplus \Phi$ and in the second case it is the field $\mathrm{P} / \Phi$. In both cases the group of auotmorphisms of $\mathrm{P} / \Phi$ has order two. Also in either case there may exist automorphisms of $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ which induce an automorphism $\neq 1$ on the center. However, it is clear that any two such automorphisms have the same effect on the center and therefore they differ by an inner automorphism. Thus the group of inner automorphisms has index one or two in the group Aut $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ of automorphisms of $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$. If $\sigma$ is an outer (noninner) automorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ then $\sigma$ and $J$ have the same effect on the center of $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence $\sigma^{-1} J \sigma J$ is an automorphism which is the identity on the center and so is inner. Hence there exists a $c \in \mathfrak{A}$ such that $x^{\sigma J}=c^{-1} x^{J \sigma} c$ for all $x \in \mathfrak{A}$. Applying $J$ we obtain $x^{\sigma}=c^{J} x^{J \sigma J}\left(c^{J}\right)^{-1}$ and replacing $x$ by $x^{J}$ in the first relation we obtain $x^{J \sigma J}=c^{-1} x^{\sigma} c$. Hence $x^{\sigma}=c^{J} c^{-1} x^{\sigma} c\left(c^{J}\right)^{-1}$ so $c^{\boldsymbol{J}} c^{-1}=\gamma$ is in the center of $\mathfrak{A}$. Then $c^{\boldsymbol{J}}=\gamma c$ and $c=\gamma^{\boldsymbol{J}} c^{\boldsymbol{J}}=\gamma^{\boldsymbol{J}} \gamma c$ so $\gamma^{\boldsymbol{J}} \gamma=1$. If the center is a field $\mathbf{P}$ it follows from Hilbert's Satz 90 (Jacobson, Lectures, vol. III, p. 76) that $\gamma=\delta^{J} \delta^{-1}, \delta \in \mathrm{P}$. If the center is $\Phi \oplus \Phi$ then $J$ has the form $(\alpha, \beta) \rightarrow(\beta, \alpha)$ in $\Phi \oplus \Phi$, so if $\gamma=(\alpha, \beta)$ satisfies $\gamma \gamma^{J}=1$, then $\gamma=\left(\alpha, \alpha^{-1}\right)$ and $\gamma=\delta^{J} \delta^{-1}$ where $\delta=(1, \alpha)$. Clearly we may replace $c$ by $\delta^{-1} c$ and obtain $\left(\delta^{-1} c\right)^{J}=\delta^{-1} c$. Hence we may assume that the element $c$ such that $x^{\sigma J}=c^{-1} x^{J \sigma} c$ satisfies $c^{\boldsymbol{J}}=c$, that is, $c \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$.

We now consider the group $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ of norm similarities of $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) is finite dimensional central simple associative with involution and the degree of $\mathfrak{J}$ is $\geqq 3$. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is separable and Theorem 5 is applicable. Also if $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of $\Phi$, then $\mathcal{J}_{\Omega}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}, J\right)$ and these are the algebras
whose generic minimum polynomials were determined in §4. The results obtained in §4 show that the generic norm of $a \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}, J\right)$ as element of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}$ either equals or is the square of the generic norm of $a$ as element of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}, J\right)$. It follows that this relation holds also for $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and $\mathfrak{A}$. We can use this remark to define certain elements of $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$. First let $a$ be an invertible element of $\mathfrak{A}$ and let $\gamma \neq 0$ be in $\Phi$. Then the mapping

$$
\begin{equation*}
x \rightarrow x^{\eta}=\gamma a^{J} x a \tag{78}
\end{equation*}
$$

in $\mathfrak{A}$ maps $\mathfrak{J}$ onto itself and is clearly a bijective linear mapping of $\mathfrak{J}$. We consider its linear extensions $\eta$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$. Since the norm on $\mathfrak{A}$ is multiplicative it is clear that in $\Im_{\Omega}$ we have $n\left(x^{\eta}\right)= \pm \rho n(x)$ where $\rho=\gamma^{m} n\left(a^{J} a\right)$. Also we have $n\left(1^{\eta}\right)=\rho$ so the set of $u$ such that $n\left(u^{\eta}\right) \neq-\rho n(u)$ is nonvacuous Zariski open subset of $\mathfrak{J}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$. On this set the polynomial function $x \rightarrow n\left(x^{\eta}\right)-\rho n(x)$ is 0 . Hence we have $n\left(x^{\eta}\right)=\rho n(x)$ for all $x \in \mathfrak{J}$ and so $\eta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$. Next let $\sigma$ be an outer automorphism of $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ and let $c=c^{J}$ satisfy $x^{\sigma J}=c^{-1} x^{J} \sigma_{c}$ for all $x \in \mathfrak{A}$. Then $c$ is determined up to a nonzero multiplier in $\Phi$. Let $x \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then $\left(c^{-1} x^{\sigma}\right)^{J}=x^{\sigma J} c^{-1}=c^{-1} x^{J \sigma}=c^{-1} x^{\sigma}$. Hence $c^{-1} x^{\sigma} \in \mathfrak{J}$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
\zeta_{\sigma, c}: x \rightarrow c^{-1} x^{\sigma} \tag{79}
\end{equation*}
$$

is a bijective linear mapping in $\mathfrak{J}$. The argument just used to prove that $\eta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ shows also that $n\left(c^{-1} x^{\sigma}\right)=n(c)^{-1} n(x)$ for all $x \in \mathfrak{J}$. Hence (79) defines an element of $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$. It is clear that the set $\mathrm{M}^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ of elements $\eta$ of the form (78) is a subgroup of $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$. We claim also that no $\zeta_{\sigma, c}$ for $\sigma$ outer is contained in $\mathrm{M}^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$. Otherwise we have an invertible $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ and a $\gamma \neq 0$ in $\Phi$ such that $c^{-1} x^{\sigma}=\gamma a^{J} x a$, $x \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then $x^{\sigma}=b x a$ where $b=\gamma c a^{J}$ and $1^{\sigma}=1$ gives $a=b^{-1}$ Hence $x^{\sigma}=b x b^{-1}$ for all $x$ in $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ generates $\mathfrak{A}$ we have $x^{\sigma}=b x b^{-1}$ for all $x$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ contrary to the assumption that $\sigma$ is outer. Thus the existence of an outer automorphism of $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ implies that $\mathbf{M}(\mathfrak{J}) \supset \mathbf{M}^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$. We can now state the following

Theorem 8. Let J be a finite-dimensional special central simple Jordan algebra of degree $m \geqq 3$ and assume $|\Phi|>m$. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ and the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{J}$ be a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}, J$ the main involution in $\mathfrak{A}$. Then $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and the set $\mathrm{M}^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ of mappings $\eta$ of the form (78), where a is an invertible element of $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\gamma \neq 0$ is in $\Phi$, is a subgroup of index one or two in the group $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ of norm similarities of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto itself. Moreover, the index is two and if and only if there exist outer automorphisms of $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$. In this case if $\sigma$ is such an automorphism then $\zeta_{\sigma, c}$ defined by (79) is a representative of the coset $\neq \mathrm{M}^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ of $\mathrm{M}^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ in $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$.

Proof. The fact that $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is the reflexivitity of $\mathfrak{J}$ which we proved in §5.7. We shall now distinguish the three types of ( $\mathfrak{A}, J)$ listed above.

Type I. Here $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{\circ}$ and $J$ is the mapping $\left(b_{1}, b_{2}\right) \rightarrow\left(b_{2}, b_{1}\right)$. Hence $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is the set of elements of the form $(b, b), b \in \mathfrak{B}$. We have the isomorphism $(b, b) \rightarrow b$ of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ onto $\mathfrak{B}^{+}$. Then the mapping in $\mathfrak{B}^{+}$corresponding to $\eta$ : $(x, x) \rightarrow \gamma(a, b)^{J}(x, x)(a, b)$ is $x \rightarrow \gamma b x a$ and every mapping of the form $x \rightarrow a x b$ in $\mathfrak{B}^{+}$is obtained in this way. We note also that $\mathfrak{A}$ has an outer automorphism if and only if $\mathfrak{B}$ has an antiautomorphism. For, if $\sigma$ is an outer automorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ then $\sigma$ maps $\mathfrak{B}$ onto $\mathfrak{B}^{\circ}$ so we have an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$ onto its opposite algebra $\mathfrak{B}^{\circ}$ and consequently we have an antiautomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$. Conversely, if $\tau$ is an antiautomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$ then $(x, y) \rightarrow\left(y^{\tau}, x^{\tau}\right)$ is an outer automorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$. Finally, it is clear that if $\tau$ is an antiautomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$ then $\tau$ is not of the form $x \rightarrow a x b, a, b \in \mathfrak{B}$. The theorem for Type I algebras will now follow by showing that if $\mathfrak{B}$ has no antiautomorphisms then $\mathrm{M}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{+}\right)$is the set of mappings $x \rightarrow a x b, a$ and $b$ invertible in $\mathfrak{B}$ and if $\mathfrak{B}$ has an antiautomorphism then $\mathrm{M}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{+}\right)$consists of these mappings and the mappings $x \rightarrow a x^{\tau} b$, where $a$ and $b$ are invertible and $\tau$ is a fixed antiautomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$. If $\zeta \in \mathrm{M}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{+}\right)$then $1^{\zeta}$ is invertible in $\mathfrak{B}^{+}$and hence in $\mathfrak{B}$. Then $\eta_{1}: x \rightarrow 1^{\zeta} x$ is in $\mathrm{M}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{+}\right)$and $\alpha=\zeta \eta^{-1} \in \mathrm{M}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{+}\right)$and $1^{\alpha}=1$. Hence, by Theorem 7, $\alpha$ is an automorphism of $\mathfrak{B}^{+}$. By $\S 5.7, \alpha$ is either an automorphism or an antiautomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$. Since $\mathfrak{B}$ is central simple, in the first case $\alpha$ is inner and in the second case $\alpha=\tau \beta$ where $\tau$ is any fixed antiautomorphism and $\beta$ is an inner automorphism. Accordingly, $\zeta=\alpha \eta$ or $\zeta=\tau \beta \eta$ has the form $x \rightarrow a x b$ or the form $x \rightarrow a x^{\tau} b$.

Type II. Here we have $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple with center a quadratic extension field $\mathrm{P} / \Phi$ and the restriction of $J$ to P is not the identity. If $q$ is a skew element $\neq 0$ in P then every element of $\mathfrak{A}$ can be written in one and only one way in the form $x+y q$ where $x, y \in \mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. This implies that as vector spaces we have $\mathfrak{A} \cong \mathbf{P} \otimes_{\Phi} \mathfrak{J}$. Hence $\mathfrak{A}^{+} / \mathbf{P}$ can be identified with $\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbf{P}}$. Now let $\zeta \in \mathbf{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ and let $\zeta$ be its linear extension to $\mathfrak{A}^{+} / \mathbf{P}$. Since $|\Phi|>m, \zeta$ is an element of $\mathbf{M}\left(\mathfrak{A}^{+}\right)$. Hence by the result established for the Type $I$ algebras the mapping $\zeta$ of $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$is either of the form $x \rightarrow a x b, a, b$ invertible elements of $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$or of the form $x \rightarrow a x^{\tau} b$ where $a$ and $b$ are invertible and $\tau$ is any antiautomorphism of $\mathfrak{A} / P$. In the first case, since $\zeta$ maps $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ onto itself we have $b^{J} x a^{J}=a x b$, $x \in \mathfrak{J}$. Since $1 \in \mathfrak{J}$ this implies that $c=a^{-1} b^{J}=b\left(a^{J}\right)^{-1}=c^{J}$. Then $c$ commutes with every $x \in \mathfrak{J}$ and hence also with every $x \in \mathfrak{A}=\mathrm{P} \mathfrak{J}$. Hence $c \in \mathrm{P}$ and since $c^{\boldsymbol{J}}=c, c=\gamma^{-\mathbf{1}} \in \Phi$ and $a=\gamma b^{\boldsymbol{J}}$. Thus the given mapping $\zeta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ has the form $x \rightarrow y b^{J} x b$ so $\zeta \in \mathbf{M}^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ as defined above. Suppose next that the linear extension $\zeta$ of $\zeta$ to $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$has the form $x \rightarrow a x^{\tau} b$ where $\tau$ is an antiautomorphism of $\mathfrak{A} / \mathbf{P}$. We now note that $\tau$ is an antiautomorphism of $\mathfrak{A} / \mathbf{P}$, if and only if $\sigma=J \tau$ is an outer automorphism of $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$. Hence we may assume that $\tau=J \sigma$ where $\sigma$ is any chosen outer automorphism of $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$. If $x \in \mathfrak{J}$ we have $a x^{\tau} b=a x^{J \tau} b=a x^{\sigma} b \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then $\left(b^{J}\right)^{-1} a x^{\sigma}=\left(b^{J}\right)^{-1}\left(a x^{\sigma} b\right) b^{-1} \in \mathfrak{J}$ so $c^{-1} x^{\sigma} \in \mathfrak{J}$ for $c=a^{-1} b^{J}$. Then $c^{-1}=c^{-1} 1^{\sigma} \in \mathfrak{J}$ and $c \in \mathfrak{J}$. We have $x^{\sigma J} c^{-1}=\left(c^{-1} x^{\sigma}\right)^{J}=c^{-1} x^{\sigma}=c^{-1} x^{J \sigma}$,
$x \in \mathfrak{J}$. Hence $x^{\sigma J}=c^{-1} x^{J \sigma} c$ holds for $x \in \mathfrak{J}$ and hence also for all $x \in \mathfrak{A}$. It follows that the mapping $x \rightarrow c^{-1} x^{\sigma}$ is a mapping $\zeta_{\sigma, c}$ defined by the given outer automorphism $\sigma$. Moreover, the given mapping $\zeta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ has the form $x \rightarrow a x^{\sigma} b=b^{J}\left(c^{-1} x^{\sigma}\right) b$ and so it is a product $\zeta_{\sigma, c} \eta$ where $\eta \in \mathbf{M}^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$. This proves the result for Type II algebras.

Type III. Here $\mathfrak{A}$ is central simple over $\Phi$. It is well known that there exists a finite-dimensional separable splitting field $\Gamma / \Phi$ (Jacobson, Structure of Rings, p. 181). Then $\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}, J\right)=\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right)$ and the involution $J$ in $\Gamma_{n}$ has the form $X \rightarrow S^{-1} X^{t} S$ where $S^{t}= \pm S$. If $S^{t}=-S$ then we may assume the entries of $S$ are in the prime field. We can make the same assumption if $S^{t}=S$ provided we adjoin suitable square roots to $\Gamma$. Since the characteristic is $\neq 2$ these adjunctions do not destroy the separability over $\Phi$. Hence we may suppose that $\Gamma$ already has the required property and that, moreover, $\Gamma / \Phi$ is Galois. Let $G=\{1, s, \cdots, u\}$ be the Galois group of $\Gamma / \Phi$. Let $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n^{2}}\right)$ be a basis for $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$, hence, also for $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}=\Gamma_{n}$ over $\Gamma$, and let $\left(e_{i j}\right)$ be a matrix basis for $\Gamma_{n} / \Gamma$. The multiplication constants determined by these two bases are contained in $\Phi$. Hence if $s \in G$ then $A_{s}: \sum \gamma_{k} u_{k} \rightarrow i \sum \gamma_{k}{ }^{s} u_{k}$ and $B_{s}: X=\sum \gamma_{i j} e_{i j} \rightarrow X^{s} \equiv \sum \gamma_{i j}{ }^{s} e_{i j}$ are automorphisms of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ as algebra over $\Phi$ and both are $s$-semilinear transformations of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma} / \Gamma$. Now $A_{s}$ is the identity on $\mathfrak{A}$ so it commutes with $J$ on $\mathfrak{A}$. It follows also that it commutes with $J$ on $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ since $J$ is the $\Gamma$-linear extension of $J$ to $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ and $A_{s}$ is the $s$-semilinear extension of the identity on $\mathfrak{A}$. Also since $X^{J}=S^{-1} X^{t} S$ where the entries of $S$ are in $\Phi$ it is clear that $B_{s} J=J B_{s}$. Hence $A_{s}$ and $B_{s}$ are automorphisms of $\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma} / \Phi, J\right)$. Also it is clear from the definition of $A_{s}$ for $s \in G$ that $A_{s} A_{t}=A_{s t}, s, t \in G$, and that $\mathfrak{A}$, which is the set of $\Phi$-linear combinations of the elements $u_{i}$, is the set of common fixed points $\left(x^{A_{s}}=x\right)$ of the $A_{s}$ for every $s \in G$. Since $A_{s}$ and $B_{s}$ are both $s$-semilinear automorphisms of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}$ it is clear that $C_{s}=B_{s}{ }^{-1} A_{s}$ is an automorphism of $\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma} / \Gamma, J\right)$. Since $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma} / \Gamma$ is central simple this implies that there exist $M_{s} \in \mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma}=\Gamma_{n}$ which are determined up to nonzero multipliers in $\Gamma$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
X^{C_{s}}=M_{s}^{-1} X M_{s}, \quad M_{s}^{j} M_{s}=\mu_{s} 1, \quad \mu_{s} \in \Gamma . \tag{80}
\end{equation*}
$$

Then $X^{A_{s}}=X^{B_{s} C_{s}}=M_{s}{ }^{-1} X^{s} M_{s}$ and since $A_{s} A_{t}=A_{s t}$ we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
M_{s}^{t} M_{t}=\mu_{s, t} M_{s t} \tag{81}
\end{equation*}
$$

for some $\mu_{s, t} \neq 0$ in $\Gamma$. Also since $\mathfrak{A}=\left\{x \in \Gamma_{n} \mid x^{A_{s}}=x, s \in G\right\}$ it is clear that $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)=\left\{x \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right) \mid x^{A_{s}}=x, s \in G\right\}$.

Now let $\zeta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$. Then $1^{\zeta}=D \in \mathfrak{J}$ and so $D \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right)$ and hence $S^{-1} D^{t} S=D$. Now let $X \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right)$ and consider the equation $X^{J} X=D$. This is equivalent to $X^{t} S X=S D$ and $S$ and $S D$ satisfy $S^{t}= \pm S,(S D)^{t}= \pm S D$. Hence in a suitable extension of $\Gamma$ by square roots we can solve our equation for $X$. Since $\zeta$ is fixed in our discussion we may assume that the Galois extension field $\Gamma$ chosen at the
beginning has the property that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right)$ contains a matrix $E$ such that $E^{J} E=D$. We now extend $\zeta$ linearly to $\Gamma_{n}$ and obtain $\zeta$ which is contained in the group of norm similarities $\mathrm{M}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right)\right)$. Also we have $1^{\zeta}=D=E^{J} E$ so if we let $\eta$ be the mapping $X \rightarrow E^{J} X E$ in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right)$ then $\eta \in \mathrm{M}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right)\right)$ and $1^{\eta}=1^{\zeta}$. Hence $\alpha=\zeta \eta^{-1} \in \mathrm{M}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right)\right)$ and satisfies $1^{\alpha}=1$. Hence $\alpha$ is an automorphism of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right)$ and consequently there exists a matrix $F \in \Gamma_{n}$ such that $X^{\alpha}=F^{-1} X F$, $X \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right)$, and $F^{J} F=\rho 1, \rho \in \Gamma$. Also, since by adjunction of a square root we may assume $\rho=1$, we may suppose this, too, holds in $\Gamma$ and then we see that the extension $\zeta$ of $\zeta$ to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right)$ has the form $X \rightarrow C^{J} X C, C \in \Gamma_{n}$. We now apply the automorphism $A_{s}$ of $\left(\Gamma_{n} / \Phi, J\right)$ to both sides of the equation $X^{\zeta}=C^{J} X C, X \in \mathfrak{J}$ to obtain $X^{\zeta}=C^{J A^{s}} X C^{A_{s}}, X \in \mathfrak{J}$. Taking into account the form of $A_{s}$ we have

$$
\left(M_{s}^{-1} C^{s J} M_{s}\right) X\left(M_{s}^{-1} C^{s} M_{s}\right)=X^{\zeta}, \quad X \in \mathfrak{J} .
$$

Since $M_{s}{ }^{J} M_{s}=\mu_{s} 1$ this gives

$$
\left(M_{s}^{-1} C^{s} M_{s}\right)^{J} X\left(M_{s}^{-1} C^{s} M_{s}\right)=X^{\zeta}=C^{J} X C
$$

for all $X \in \mathfrak{J}$. This implies that $M_{s}^{-1} C^{s} M_{s} C^{-1}$ commutes with every $X \in \mathfrak{J}$ and hence with every $X \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right)$. Since the subalgebra of $\Gamma_{n}$ generated by $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Gamma_{n}, J\right)$ is $\Gamma_{n}$ it now follows that we have an element $\rho_{s} \neq 0$ in $\Gamma$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
C^{A_{s}}=M_{s}^{-1} C^{s} M_{s}=\rho_{s} C, \quad s \in G . \tag{82}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since $A_{s}$ is $s$-semilinear and $A_{s} A_{t}=A_{s t}$ this gives E. Noether's equations: $\rho_{s}{ }^{t} \rho_{t}=\rho_{s t}$ so by Noether's lemma (Jacobson, Lectures, vol. III, p. 75) there exists an element $\delta \neq 0$ in $\Gamma$ such that $\rho_{s}=\delta^{s} \delta^{-1}$. Then $\left(\delta^{-1} C\right)^{A_{s}}=\left(\delta^{s}\right)^{-1} \rho_{s} C=\delta^{-1} C$. Since $\mathfrak{A}$ is the set of elements $a \in \Gamma_{n}$ such that $a^{A s}=a, s \in G$, this shows that $a=\delta^{-1} C \in \mathfrak{A}$ and we have $x^{\zeta}=C^{J} x C=\delta^{2} a^{J} x a, x \in \mathfrak{J}$. Applying this to 1 we see that $\gamma=\delta^{2} \in \Phi$ and so $x^{\zeta}=\gamma a^{J} x a$ is contained in $\mathrm{M}^{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. Hence in this case $\mathrm{M}^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ which is what is asserted in the theorem. This completes the proof.

We note that the proof of the theorem shows also that if $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{A}^{+}$where $\mathfrak{A}$ is finite dimensional central simple associative of degree $\geqq 3$ then $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ consists of the mappings $x \rightarrow a x b$ and $x \rightarrow a x^{\sigma} b$ where $n(a) \neq 0, n(b) \neq 0$ and $\sigma$ is a fixed antiautomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$. We have shown also that if $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is finite dimensional central simple with involution and $x \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ then $n\left(\gamma a^{J} x a\right)=\gamma^{m} n\left(a^{J} a\right) n(x)$. Moreover, if $\sigma$ is an outer automorphism of $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ and $c$ is an invertible element of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ such that $x^{\sigma J}=c^{-1} x^{J \sigma} c, x \in \mathfrak{A}$ then $n\left(c^{-1} x^{\sigma}\right)=n(c)^{-1} n(x)$. It follows from Theorem 6 that if the degree of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)=m \geqq 3$ then $\mathrm{M}_{1}(J)$ consists of the mappings

$$
\begin{equation*}
x \rightarrow \gamma a^{J} x a \tag{83}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\gamma^{m} n\left(a^{J} a\right)=1$ and the mappings

$$
\begin{equation*}
x \rightarrow \gamma a^{J} c^{-1} x^{\sigma} a \tag{84}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\sigma$ is an outer automorphism, $c$ is as indicated and $\gamma^{m} n(c)^{-1} n\left(a^{J} a\right)=1$.

## Exercises

1. Show that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is as in Theorem 6 then the only elements $\eta$ of $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $\hat{\eta}=\left(\eta^{*}\right)^{-1}=\eta$ are the automorphisms and negatives of automorphisms of $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence show that if the degree $m$ is odd then the automorphism group is the subgroup of $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ of elements $\eta$ such that $\hat{\eta}=\eta$.
2. Let $\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{\prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ denote the commutator subgroup of $\mathbf{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. Prove that $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{\prime}\left(\Phi_{m}{ }^{+}\right), \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(1)}\left(\Phi_{m}{ }^{+}\right), \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)}\left(\Phi_{m}{ }^{+}\right)$for $m \geqq 3$ consist of the mappings $x \rightarrow a x b$ where $\operatorname{det} a b=1$ and (1) $\operatorname{det} a$ is a square for $\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{\prime}$, (2) $\operatorname{det} a= \pm 1$ for $\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(1)}$, (3) $\operatorname{det} a=1$ for $\mathrm{M}_{1}^{(2)}$.
3. Let $\gamma=\operatorname{diag}\left\{\gamma_{1}, \gamma_{2}, \cdots, \gamma_{m}\right\}, \gamma_{i} \neq 0$ in $\Phi$. Show that any element of $\Phi_{m}$ such that $\operatorname{det} A=1$ is a product of elements of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{m}, J_{\gamma}\right)$. Use this to prove that if $m \geqq 3$ then $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{\prime}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{m}, J_{\gamma}\right)\right)=\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{m}, J_{\gamma}\right)\right)$ and this is the set of mappings $x \rightarrow a^{*} x a$ where $\operatorname{det} a=1$ and $a^{*}=a^{J_{\gamma}}$. Show also that $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(1)}\left(\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{m}, J_{\gamma}\right)\right)$ is the set of mappings $x \rightarrow a^{*} x a$ where $\operatorname{det} a= \pm 1$.
4. The Lie algebras $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J}), \mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ and Der $\mathfrak{J}$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ separable. In this section we shall obtain the Lie algebra analogues of the group theoretic results of the last two sections.

If $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ is an algebra we denote the Lie algebra of derivations in $\mathfrak{A}$ by Der $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence Der $\mathfrak{A}$ is the subalgebra of the Lie algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})^{-}$of elements $D$ such that $(a b) D=(a D) b+a(b D), a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$. Moreover, if $\left(u_{\imath}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ then a $D \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$ is a derivation if and only if $\left(u_{\imath} u_{\kappa}\right) D=\left(u_{\imath} D\right) u_{\kappa}+u_{\imath}\left(u_{\kappa} D\right)$. Thus if $u_{\imath} D=\sum \alpha_{\imath \kappa} u_{\kappa}$, so that $\left(\alpha_{\imath \kappa}\right)$ is the (row-finite) matrix of the linear transformation $D$ relative to the basis $\left(u_{\imath}\right)$, and $u_{\imath} u_{\kappa}=\sum \gamma_{\imath \kappa \lambda} u_{\lambda}, \gamma_{\imath \kappa \lambda} \in \Phi$, then $D$ is a derivation if and only if

$$
\sum_{\lambda} \gamma_{\imath \kappa \lambda} \alpha_{\lambda \mu}=\sum_{\lambda} \alpha_{\imath \lambda} \gamma_{\lambda \kappa \mu}+\sum_{\lambda} \alpha_{\kappa \lambda} \gamma_{\imath \lambda \mu}
$$

for all $\iota, \kappa, \mu$. It is clear from this that if $\mathbf{P}$ is an extension field of the base field $\Phi$ and we identify a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ into itself with its linear extension to $\mathfrak{U}_{\mathbf{P}} / \mathbf{P}$ then every derivation of $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}} / \mathbf{P}$ and every derivation of $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}} / \mathbf{P}$ is a P-linear combination of derivations in $\mathfrak{U} / \Phi$. In this way one can identify Der $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}$ with $(\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{A})_{\mathbf{P}}=\mathbf{P} \otimes_{\Phi}$ Der $\mathfrak{A}$.

We recall that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a Jordan algebra then the mapping $\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right], a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}(\S 1.7)$. The derivations of the form $\sum\left[R_{a_{i}} R_{b_{i}}\right], a_{i}, b_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$, are called inner and these constitute an ideal Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ in the Lie algebra Der $\mathfrak{J}$. It is clear that the inner derivations of $\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbf{P}}$ are P-linear combinations of inner derivations of $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence we have Inder $\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbf{P}}=(\text { Inder } \mathfrak{J})_{\mathbf{P}}$.

We shall now study the derivation algebra of a separable Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$. We have $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{s}$ where $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ is simple with center $\mathfrak{C}_{i}$ a separable extension field of the base field $\Phi$. If $D$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ then $\mathfrak{J}_{i}{ }^{2}=\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ gives $\mathfrak{J}_{i} D \subseteq\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i} D\right) \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{i} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{i}$ so $D$ maps $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ into itself and hence the restriction $D_{i}$ of $D$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ is a derivation in $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Conversely, if $D_{i}, i=1,2, \cdots, s$, is a derivation in $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ then the linear mapping $D$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ which coincides with $D_{i}$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ is a derivation. It follows that $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} \cong \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}_{s}$. Hence the study of Der $\mathfrak{J}$ can be reduced to the case in which $\mathfrak{J}$ is simple with center $\mathfrak{C}$ a separable field. It is immediate from the definition of the center of a nonassociative algebra that any derivation of the algebra maps the center into itself and hence induces a derivation in the center. Let $D$ be a derivation in the simple Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\mathbb{C} D \subseteq \mathbb{C}$. Since $\mathbb{C} / \Phi$ is a separable field we have $\mathbb{C}=\Phi(\theta)$ where the minimum polynomial $f(\lambda)$ of $\theta$ has distinct roots. If we apply $D$ to the relation $f(\theta)=0$ we obtain $f^{\prime}(\theta)(\theta D)=0$ where $f^{\prime}(\lambda)$ is the usual formal derivative of the polynomial $f(\lambda)$. Since $f(\lambda)$ has distinct roots $f^{\prime}(\lambda) \neq 0$ and since its degree is less than that of $f(\lambda), f^{\prime}(\theta) \neq 0$. Hence $f^{\prime}(\theta)^{-1}$ exists in $\mathbb{C}$ and $f^{\prime}(\theta)(\theta D)=0$ gives $\theta D=0$. Hence $\mathscr{C} D=0$ and this implies that if we consider $\mathfrak{J}$ as an algebra over its center $\mathfrak{C}$ then $D$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J} / \mathbb{C}$. Since $\mathfrak{J} / \mathbb{C}$ is central simple we have now reduced the consideration to central simple Jordan algebras.

Accordingly, we now suppose $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional central simple Jordan algebra over $\Phi$. If the degree of $\mathfrak{J}$ is one, then $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1$ and Der $\mathfrak{J}=0$. We shall leave the consideration of the degree two case to the exercises and we shall postpone the study of Der J for J exceptional central simple to Chapter IX. We now consider the remaining possibility: $\mathfrak{J}$ is finite dimensional special central simple of degree $m \geqq 3$. Then $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is a finite-dimensional central simple associative algebra with involution. Moreover, we know that $\mathfrak{A}$ and the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ is a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$ (§5.7). Hence if $D$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ then $D$ has a unique extension to a derivation of ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ), that is, a derivation of $\mathfrak{A}$ which commutes with $J$. We now have

Theorem 9. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional special central simple Jordan algebra of degree $m \geqq 3$, ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) the corresponding finite-dimensional central simple associative algebra with involution, so that $\mathfrak{J}$ can be identified with $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and $\mathfrak{A}$ with the unital special universal envelope of $\mathfrak{J}$.
