Then any derivation of $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ has the form

$$
\begin{equation*}
x \rightarrow[x d] \tag{85}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $d^{\boldsymbol{J}}=-d \in \mathfrak{A}$, and conversely. Moreover, every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ is inner (that is, of the form $\left.\sum\left[R_{a_{i}} R_{b_{i}}\right]\right)$ if and only if either the center of $\mathfrak{A}$ is $\Phi$ or the center is not $\Phi$ and the characteristic is either 0 or a prime $p$ not dividing $m$.

Proof. Let $D$ be a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. Then $D$ is the restriction to $\mathfrak{J}$ of a derivation of $D$ of $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. It is well known that every derivation of a finite-
dimensional separable associative algebra is inner in the sense that it has the form $x \rightarrow[x d]$ for a suitable $d$ in the algebra. $\left({ }^{2}\right)$ Hence there exists a $d \in \mathfrak{A}$ such that $x D=[x d], x \in \mathfrak{J}$. Applying $J$ we obtain also $x D=-\left[x d^{J}\right]$ so $d^{J}+d$ commutes with every $x \in \mathfrak{J}$. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ generates $\mathfrak{A}$ it follows that $d^{J}+d$ is in the center of $\mathfrak{A}$. Since $d^{J}+d \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ we see that $d^{J}+d=\delta 1$ where $\delta \in \Phi$. Then $\left(d-\frac{1}{2} \delta 1\right)^{J}+\left(d-\frac{1}{2} \delta 1\right)=0$ so $d-\frac{1}{2} \delta 1$ is skew. Since we can replace $d$ by this element we may suppose that $d^{J}=-d$. Thus $x D=[x d]$ where $d^{J}=-d$. Let $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ denote the set of skew elements of $\mathfrak{A}$. This is a subalgebra of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{A}^{-}$. Moreover, if $x \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and $d \in \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ then $[x d] \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. Also $[x . y, d]=x .[y d]+[x d] . y$ so $x \rightarrow[x d]$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. This completes the proof of the first statement of the theorem. Now let $x, a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$ and consider $x\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right]=x . a . b-x . b . a$. A direct calculation using $x . a=\frac{1}{2}(x a+a x)$ shows that $4 x\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right]=[x[a b]]$. This and the first part of the theorem implies that every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ is inner if every $d \in \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ has the form $\Sigma\left[a_{i} b_{i}\right]$ where $a_{i}, b_{i} \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. We have $[\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J), \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)] \subseteq \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$, so a sufficient condition that every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ is inner that $[\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J), \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)]=\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. We now suppose the base field $\Phi$ is algebraically closed and later we shall reduce the general case to this one. If $\Phi$ is algebraically closed then $(\mathfrak{A}, J)=\left(\mathfrak{D}_{m}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is an associative composition algebra and $J_{1}$ is the standard involution in $\mathfrak{D}_{m}$. The possibilities for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ are $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi, j$ the identity $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi \oplus \Phi, j$ the involution exchanging the two components; $\mathfrak{D}$, a (split) quaternion algebra, $j$ standard. In the first and third cases the center of $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{D}_{m}$ is $\Phi$ and in the second it is not. Now we have shown that a sufficient condition that $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)=[\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J), \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)]$ for $(\mathfrak{A}, J)=\left(\mathfrak{D}_{m}, J_{1}\right), m \geqq 3$, is that $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)=[\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{D}, j)]+[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)]$ (p. 148). If $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi$ then $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)=0$ so this is clear. If $\mathfrak{D}$ is quaternion and $j$ is standard one checks directly that $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)=[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j), \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)]$. Hence we see that the derivations are inner if the center of $\mathfrak{A}$ is $\Phi$. Now assume that the center is not $\Phi$, which is equivalent to assuming $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi \oplus \Phi, j$ exchanging the two factors. In this case $\mathfrak{J} \cong \Phi_{m}{ }^{+}(m \geqq 3)$. By Corollary 4 to Theorem 3.6 (p. 144), any derivation of $\Phi_{m}{ }^{+}$is a derivation of $\Phi_{m}$. Hence this has the form $x \rightarrow[x d]$. On the other hand, the inner derivations of $\Phi_{m}{ }^{+}$have the form $x \rightarrow[x f]$ where $f=\sum\left[a_{i} b_{i}\right]$. Hence all derivations will be inner if and only if every $d \in \Phi_{m}$ can be written in the form $\delta 1+\sum\left[a_{i} b_{i}\right], \delta \in \Phi, a_{i}, b_{i} \in \Phi_{m}$. If the characteristic is 0 or a prime $p$ not dividing $m$ then $d=(1 / m) t(d) 1+d_{0}$ where $t(d)$ is the trace of the matrix $d$ and $d_{0}=d-(1 / m) t(d) 1$ has trace 0 . Also a direct calculation with matrix units shows that every matrix of trace 0 is a sum of commutators (for any characteristic and any $m$ ). Hence if the characteristic is 0 or a prime not dividing $m$ then any $d \in \Phi_{m}$ has the form $\delta 1+\sum\left[a_{i} b_{i}\right]$ and so every derivation of $\Phi_{m}{ }^{+}$is inner in this case. On the other hand, suppose

[^17]the characteristic is a prime $p \mid m$. Then any element of the form $\delta 1+\sum\left[a_{i} b_{i}\right]$ has trace 0 . Hence if we choose $d$ so that $t(d) \neq 0$ then $x \rightarrow[x d]$ is a derivation of $\Phi_{m}{ }^{+}$which is not inner. This completes the proof of the second statement of the theorem in the algebraically closed case. Now assume $\Phi$ is arbitrary and let $\mathfrak{J}$, ( $\mathfrak{A}, J)$ be as before and let $\Omega$ be the algebraic closure of $\Phi$. Let Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ denote the space of inner derivations of $\mathfrak{J}$. We have $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}=\left(\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}, \operatorname{Inder} \mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}\right. =(\text { Inder } \mathfrak{J})_{\Omega}$. Hence every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ is inner if and only if this is the case for $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$. Next we note that $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{U}_{\Omega}, J\right)$ and the center of $\mathfrak{U}_{\Omega}$ is $\Omega$ if and only if the center of $\mathfrak{A}$ is $\Phi$. It is now clear that the result for $\mathfrak{J}$ follows from that for $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ and the proof is complete.
We now suppose that $\mathfrak{J}$ is an arbitrary finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1 over an infinite field $\Phi$. Let $\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ be the Lie algebras of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{J}$ which have the generic norm $n$ as Lie invariant and Lie semiinvariant respectively (§2). The defining condition that $T \in \mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $T \in \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ are respectively: $\Delta^{a T}{ }_{a} n=0$ and $\Delta^{a T}{ }_{a} n=\rho(T) n(a), \rho(T) \in \Phi$. It is enough to have these conditions for $a=c$ invertible. In this case we have equation (68): $\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} n=n(c) t\left(c^{\cdot^{-1}}, a\right)$ which gives the conditions: $t\left(c T, c^{\cdot^{-1}}\right)=0$ for $T \in \mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $t\left(c T, c^{-1}\right)=\rho(T)$ for $T \in \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$. We have $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J}) \supseteq \mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J}) \supseteq$ Der $\mathfrak{J}$ where the last inclusion is a special case of (vii) of Theorem 1. Let $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ denote the subspace of $\mathfrak{J}$ of elements $a$ such that $t(a)=0$ and let $R(\mathfrak{J})$ and $R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ be the subspaces of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ of elements $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$ and $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$, respectively. We have $t\left(c R_{a}, c^{-1}\right)=t\left(c . a, c^{-1}\right)=t\left(a, c . c^{-1}\right)=t(a, 1)=t(a)$. Hence $R_{a} \in \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $R_{a} \in \mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ if and only if $t(a)=0$. Hence $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{I}) \supseteq R(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{I}) \supseteq R\left(\mathfrak{I}^{\prime}\right)$. If $D$ is a derivation then $1 D=0$. Since $1 R_{a}=a$ we see that Der $\mathfrak{J} \cap R(\mathfrak{J})=0$.
We now assume $\mathfrak{J}$ separable and we prove first
Theorem 10. Let J be a finite-dimensional separable Jordan algebra over an infinite field $\Phi$. Then a $D \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ is a derivation if and only if $D \in \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $1 D=0$.

Proof. We have seen that the conditions are necessary. Now assume $D \in \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $1 D=0$. Since $t\left(c D, c^{-1}\right)=\rho(D)$ for invertible $c$, if we put $c=1$ we obtain $\rho(D)=0$. Hence $D \in \mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$. We have $t\left(c D, c^{-1}\right)=t\left(c D . c^{-1}\right)=0$. As usual, let $x$ denote the identity mapping $a \rightarrow a, x D$ its resultant with $D(=D \circ x)$ and $x^{-1}$ the mapping $c \rightarrow c^{\cdot^{-1}}, c$ invertible. Then we have $\Delta^{a}{ }_{c}\left(x D \cdot x^{-1}\right)=c D \cdot \Delta^{a}{ }_{c} x^{-1}+\left(\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} x D\right) \cdot c^{-1} =-c D \cdot a U_{c}{ }^{-1}+a D \cdot c^{-1}$, by (70). Hence $-t\left(c D, a U_{c}{ }^{-1}\right)+t\left(a D, c^{-1}\right)= t\left(\Delta^{a}{ }_{c}\left(x D . x^{-1}\right)\right)$. Now apply the chain rule to the composite function $t \circ\left(x D . x^{-1}\right)$. This gives $\Delta^{a}{ }_{c}\left(t \circ\left(x D \cdot x^{-1}\right)\right)=\Delta^{b}{ }_{d} t, b=\Delta^{a}{ }_{c}\left(x D \cdot x^{-1}\right), d=c D \cdot c^{-1}$, so $\Delta^{a}{ }_{c}\left(t \circ\left(x D \cdot x^{-1}\right)\right)=t(b)=t\left(\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} x D \cdot x^{-1}\right)$. On the other hand, $t\left(c D \cdot c^{-1}\right)=0$ for all invertible $c$. Hence $t\left(\Delta^{a}{ }_{c} x D . x^{-1}\right)=0$ and so the above relation gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
t\left(a D, c^{-1}\right)=t\left(c D, a U_{c}^{-1}\right) \tag{86}
\end{equation*}
$$

for all $a$ and invertible $c$. Since the generic trace form $t$ is nondegenerate and $U_{c}{ }^{-1}$ is selfadjoint relative to $t$, this implies

$$
\begin{equation*}
c D=c^{\cdot-1} D^{*} U_{c} \tag{87}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $D^{*}$ is the adjoint of $D$ relative to $t$.
Next we calculate

$$
\begin{align*}
\Delta^{1}{ }_{c}\left(U_{x} \circ D^{*} \circ x^{\cdot^{-1}}\right) & =\Delta^{1}{ }_{c}\left\{x\left(x^{\cdot^{-1}} D^{*}\right) x\right\} \\
& =\left\{c\left(\Delta^{1}{ }_{c} x^{-1} D^{*}\right) c\right\}+2\left(c^{-1} D^{*}\right) \cdot c \\
& =-1 U_{c}^{-1} D^{*} U_{c}+2\left(c^{-1} D^{*}\right) \cdot c \tag{70}
\end{align*}
$$

Also $U_{x} \circ D^{*} \circ x^{-1}=x D$ by (87) and $\Delta^{1}{ }_{c}(x D)=1 D=0$. Hence we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
2 c^{-1} D^{*} \cdot c=c^{-.2} D^{*} U_{c} . \tag{88}
\end{equation*}
$$

Now consider

$$
\begin{aligned}
c^{\cdot 2} D-2 c . c D & =c^{\cdot-2} D^{*} U_{c}{ }^{2}-2 c .\left(c^{\cdot-1} D^{*} U_{c}\right) \\
& =\left(c^{\cdot-2} D^{*} U_{c}-2 c . c^{-1} D^{*}\right) U_{c} \\
& =0, \quad \text { by }(88) .
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $c^{2} D=2 c . c D$ and $D$ is a derivation.
We can now prove
Theorem 11. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is finite dimensional separable over an infinite field then $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$.

Proof. Let $T \in \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{I})$. Then $D=T-R_{1 T} \in \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $1 D=0$. Hence $D$ is a derivation, by Theorem 10. Hence $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})=R(\mathfrak{J})+$ Der $\mathfrak{J}$. Also we have seen that $R(\mathfrak{J}) \cap$ Der $\mathfrak{J}=0$. Hence $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus$ Der $\mathfrak{J}$. Next let $T \in \mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$. Then $t\left(c T, c^{\cdot^{-1}}\right)=0$ gives for $c=1$ that $t(1 T)=0$. Hence $1 T \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ and $R_{1 T} \in R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$. As before, $T-R_{1 T}=D$ is a derivation. This implies that $\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})=R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right) \oplus$ Der $\mathfrak{J}$.

If $D$ is a derivation then (87) is valid for any invertible $c$. This gives $c^{\cdot-1} D=c D^{*} U_{c}{ }^{-1}$. On the other hand, since $D$ is a derivation $c^{\cdot-1} D=-c D U_{c}{ }^{-1}$. Hence $D^{*}=-D$ so every derivation is skew relative to the involution $A \rightarrow A^{*}$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ where $A^{*}$ is the adjoint of $A$ relative to $t$. Also since $t$ is an associative form, $R_{a}{ }^{*}=R_{a}$. It follows from Theorem 11 that if $T \in \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})\left(\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})\right)$ then $T^{*} \in \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})\left(\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})\right)$ and $T \in \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ is a derivation if and only if. $T^{*}=-T$. Also if $T \in \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})\left(\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})\right)$ then $T=R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}\left(a \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ if and only if $T^{*}=T$.

We now suppose that $\mathfrak{J}$ is special central simple of degree $m \geqq 3$ and we prove the following analogue (or infinitesimal form) of Theorem 8.

Theorem 12. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional special central simple Jordan algebra of degree $m \geqq 3$ over an infinite field, $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ the corresponding finite-
dimensional central simple associative algebra as in Theorem 9. Then any element of $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ has the form

$$
\begin{equation*}
x \rightarrow a^{J} x+x a \tag{89}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ and conversely. Moreover, the condition that such an element is in $\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ is that $t\left(a+a^{J}\right)=0$.

Proof. We have $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})=R(\mathfrak{J})+$ Der $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence if $T \in \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J}), T=R_{c}+D$ where $c \in \mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and $D \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$. By Theorem 9, there exists a $d \in \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ such that $x D=[x d]$. Hence $x T=\frac{1}{2}(c x+x c)+(x d-d x)=a^{J} x+x a$ where $a=\frac{1}{2} c+d$. The converse is clear since any $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ can be written as $a=\frac{1}{2} c+d$ where $c^{J}=c$ and $d^{J}=-d$. The condition that $T$ of the form indicated is in $\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ is that $t(c)=0$. Since $a=\frac{1}{2} c+d, a+a^{J}=c$, so this is equivalent to $t\left(a+a^{J}\right)=0$.

If $\mathfrak{J}$ is any Jordan algebra then we have the basic identity $\left[\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right] R_{c}\right]=R_{d}$ where $d=[b, c, a]$. Now consider the set $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ of linear transformation of the form $R_{a}+\sum\left[R_{b_{j}} R_{c_{j}}\right]$ where $a, b_{j}, c_{j} \in \mathfrak{J}$. Clearly, this is a subspace of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$. Also, since $\left[R_{a}\left[R_{b} R_{c}\right]\right]=R_{d}$ and $\left[\left[R_{b} R_{c}\right],\left[R_{e} R_{f}\right]\right]=\left[\left[R_{b}\left[R_{e} R_{f}\right]\right] R_{c}\right]+ \left[R_{b}\left[R_{c}\left[R_{e} R_{f}\right]\right]\right]$, by the Jacobi identity, it is clear that the set $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ is a subalgebra of the Lie algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(J, J)^{-}$. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is finite dimensional with 1 then $R_{a} \in \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ and so $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J}) \subseteq \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$. Also $\left[\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right] R_{c}\right]=R_{d}$ where $d=[b, c, a]$ and $t(d)=0$. This and the argument used for $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ shows that the set $\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ of linear transformations of the form $R_{a}+\sum\left[R_{b_{j}} R_{c_{j}}\right]$, where $t(a)=0$, is a subalgebra of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$. An immediate consequence of Theorem 9 and the decompositions $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})=R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right) \oplus \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ for separable $\mathfrak{J}$ is the following

Theorem 13. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional special central simple Jordan algebra of degree $m \geqq 3$ over an infinite field. Then $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ if and only if either the center of $\mathfrak{U}($ the unital special universal envelope of $\mathfrak{J}$ ) is $\Phi$, or the center properly contains $\Phi$ and the characteristic is either 0 or a prime $p$ not dividing $m$.

Show that $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$, $\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ and that every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ is inner.
2. Show that $\mathfrak{M}_{0} \mathfrak{J}$ ) acts irreduciblty on $\mathfrak{J}$ (that is, $\mathfrak{J}$ has no $\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$-invariant subspace $\neq 0, \mathfrak{J}$ ) and that Der $\mathfrak{J}$ acts irreducibly on $\mathfrak{V}$.

## Chapter VII

## REPRESENTATION THEORY FOR SEPARABLE JORDAN ALGEBRAS

The representation theory of a Jordan algebra is concerned with the study of the structure of the bimodules of $\mathfrak{J}$. Since any such bimodule is a right module for the universal multiplication envelope $U(\mathfrak{J})$ one can reduce the problem to the representation theory of the associative algebra $U(\mathfrak{J})$ provided one has enough information on $U(\mathfrak{J})$. Thus a central problem is the determination of the structure of $U(\mathfrak{J})$. In this chapter we consider this for finite-dimensional separable Jordan algebras $\mathfrak{J}$. One of the main results we shall obtain is that $\mathfrak{J}$ is separable if and only if $U(\mathfrak{J})$ is separable. Since a finite-dimensional associative algebra is semisimple if and only if all its right modules are compietely reducible, the separability of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ implies that every bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ is completely reducible. We shall obtain also the simple components of $U(\mathfrak{J})$, which is equivalent to obtaining the irreducible bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}$.

Our proof of the separability of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ separable will rest heavily on the determination of the simple Jordan algebras over an algebraically closed field given in Chapter V. We note first that since $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element we have the decomposition $U(\mathfrak{J})=\Phi z \oplus S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ where $z^{2}=z \neq 0, S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is the special unital universal envelope of $\mathfrak{J}$, and $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is the unital universal multiplication envelope. We can also reduce the discussion to the case $\mathfrak{J}$ simple and ultimately to the case $\mathfrak{J}$ (central) simple over an algebraically closed field. In the latter case we distinguish the cases: the degree, $\operatorname{deg} \mathfrak{J}=1, \operatorname{deg} \mathfrak{J}=2$ and $\operatorname{deg} \mathfrak{J} \geqq 3$ : The first is trivial, since in this case $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}=1$. The case $\operatorname{deg} \mathfrak{J}=2$ amounts to the study of Clifford algebras and meson algebras (§2.3 and §2.13). If $\mathfrak{J}$ is finitedimensional central simple of degree $n \geqq 3$ then $\mathfrak{J} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a composition algebra. If $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \mathfrak{D}_{n}$ since $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ is a perfect algebra with involution. Also one can reduce the study of the bimodules of $\mathfrak{J}$ to that of the bimodules with involution for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. We determine the latter and prove complete reducibility for these. This gives the same information on $\mathfrak{J} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right), n \geqq 3$, and determines the structure of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$.

The pattern of proof just indicated is used also to establish the other two main results of the present chapter: the radical splitting theorem (Albert-Penico-Taft theorem) and the theorem on derivations of separable algebras into bimodules (Jacobson-Harris theorem). The first of these asserts that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional

Jordan algebra with radical ( = maximal solvable ideal) $\Re$ and $\mathfrak{J} / \Re$ is separable, then there exists a subalgebra $\mathfrak{K}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ isomorphic to $\mathfrak{J} / \Re$. A special case of this is a "cohomology" result that any factor set of a separable Jordan algebra in a bimodule splits. The second result is that any derivation of a separable Jordan algebra into a bimodule is inner in a certain sense provided that the simple components have degrees over their centers prime to the characteristic. This result is applicable to proving a uniqueness theorem for the decomposition $\mathfrak{J}=\Re \oplus \Re$ where $\mathfrak{J} / \Re$ is separable and $\Re \cong \mathfrak{J} / \Re$. This result is proved only in the characteristic 0 case.

In the next chapter we shall prove all of the main theorems in the present one in the characteristic 0 case by Lie methods which do not require the detailed structure theory of semisimple Jordan algebras.

1. Structure of Clifford algebras. We recall that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a Jordan algebra with identity element then the universal multiplication envelope $U(\mathfrak{J})$ is isomorphic to the direct sum of a one-dimensional algebra $\Phi z\left(z^{2}=z\right)$, the universal unital multiplication envelope $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$, and the unital special universal envelope $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ (§ 2.11). The problem of determining $U(\mathfrak{J})$ is therefore reduced to that of determining $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. Now let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ the Jordan algebra of the symmetric bilinear form $f$ on the vector space $\mathfrak{B}$. Then we have seen that if $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is the Clifford algebra of $\mathfrak{V}$ relative to $f$ then we can identify $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ with $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ and take the associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ to be given by $(\alpha 1+x)^{\sigma_{u}}=\alpha 1+x+\mathfrak{K}$ where $x \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{K}$ is the ideal in the tensor algebra $T(\mathfrak{B})$ defining $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)(\S 2.3)$. Thus $\mathfrak{K}$ is the ideal generated by all the elements $x \otimes x-f(x, x) 1, \quad x \in \mathfrak{B}$. We recall also that if $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}=n+1<\infty$ then $\operatorname{dim} S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \leqq 2^{n} \quad(\S 2.2)$. Hence if $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=n<\infty$ then $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \leqq 2^{n}$.

If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=n<\infty$ and $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{B} / \Phi$ then $\delta=\operatorname{det}\left(f\left(u_{i}, u_{j}\right)\right)$, the determinant of the matrix $\left(f\left(u_{\imath}, u_{j}\right)\right)$, is called a discriminant of the form $f$. $f$ is nondegenerate if and only if $\delta \neq 0$. A change of basis replaces $\delta$ by $\delta \rho^{2}$ where $\rho$ is a nonzero element of $\Phi$.

We now proceed to determine the structure of the Clifford algebra $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. The key result for the method we shall use is the following

Lemma 1. Let $\mathfrak{N}$ be a $2 r$-dimensional nonisotropic subspace of $\mathfrak{B}$. Then the subalgebra of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ generated by the image of $\mathfrak{N}$ and 1 is isomorphic to $C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$ and $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cong C(\mathfrak{N}, f) \otimes C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},(-1)^{r} \delta f\right)$ where $\delta$ is a discriminant of the restriction of $f$ to $\mathfrak{N}$.

Proof. Let $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{2 r}\right)$ be an orthogonal basis for $\mathfrak{N} / \Phi$ and put $v_{i}=u_{i}^{\sigma_{u}}$. We have $v_{i} v_{j}=-v_{j} v_{i}, i \neq j, v_{i}^{2}=\beta_{i} 1, \beta_{i}=f\left(u_{i}, u_{i}\right) \neq 0$. Hence, if $c=v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{2 r}$ then $v_{i} c=-c v_{i}$ and $c^{2}=(-1)^{r} \delta 1$ where $\delta=\prod_{1}^{2 r} \beta_{i}$ is a discriminant of the restriction of $f$ to $\mathfrak{N}$. Since $\mathfrak{N}$ is finite-dimensional nonisotropic we have $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{N} \oplus \mathfrak{N}^{\perp}$. Let $y \in \mathfrak{N}^{\perp}$ and put $z=y^{\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{u}}$. Then $z v_{i}=-v_{i} z$, so $c z=z c$ and
$(z c)^{2}=(-1)^{r} \delta f(y, y)$. Also $(z c) v_{i}=v_{i}(z c)$. Now consider the Clifford algebras $C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$ and $C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},(-1)^{r} \delta f\right)$ and denote the mappings of $\Phi 1+\mathfrak{N}$ and $\Phi 1+\mathfrak{N}^{\perp}$ into these algebras by $\sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime}$ and $\sigma_{u}{ }^{\prime \prime}$ respectively. We have the homomorphism of $C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$ into $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ sending $(\alpha 1+x)^{\sigma^{\prime}{ }^{\prime \prime}} \rightarrow(\alpha 1+x)^{\sigma_{u}}, x \in \mathfrak{N}$. Also if $y \in \mathfrak{N}^{\perp}$, $z=y^{\sigma_{u}}$, then the relation $(z c)^{2}=(-1)^{r} \delta f(y, y)$ in $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ implies that we have a homomorphism of $C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},(-1)^{r} \delta f\right)$ into $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ sending $(\alpha 1+y)^{\sigma^{\prime \prime}}{ }^{( } \rightarrow \alpha 1+c z$. Since $x^{\sigma_{u}}, x \in \mathfrak{N}$, is a linear combination of the elements $v_{i}$ it is clear that the elements of the image of $C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$ under our homomorphism commute with the elements of the image of $C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},(-1)^{r} \delta f\right)$ under the homomorphism of this algebra. Consequently, we have a homomorphism $\lambda$ of $C(\mathfrak{N}, f) \otimes C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},(-1)^{r} \delta f\right)$ into $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\lambda: x^{\sigma^{\prime} u} \otimes 1+1 \otimes y^{\sigma^{\prime \prime} u} \rightarrow x^{\sigma_{u}}+c y^{\sigma_{u}}, \quad x \in \mathfrak{N}, \quad y \in \mathfrak{N}^{\perp} \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

and $1 \rightarrow 1$. We note next that we have the relations $u_{i}^{\sigma^{\prime}{ }_{u}} u_{j}^{\sigma^{\prime}{ }_{u}}=-u_{j}{ }^{\sigma^{\prime} u_{u}} u_{i}{ }^{\sigma^{\prime}{ }_{u}}$, $i \neq j,\left(u_{i}{ }^{\sigma^{\prime}}{ }^{*}\right)^{2}=\beta_{i} 1$ in $C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$ which imply that $c^{\prime}=u_{1}{ }^{\sigma^{\prime}}{ }^{*} u_{2}{ }^{\sigma^{\prime}} u^{*} \ldots u_{2 r}{ }^{\sigma^{\prime}{ }_{u}}$ satisfies $\left(c^{\prime}\right)^{2}=\left((-1)^{r} \delta\right) 1 \neq 0$. Hence $c^{\prime}$ is invertible in $C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$. Also $c^{\prime} x^{\sigma^{\prime} u}=-x^{\sigma^{\prime} u} c^{\prime}$ if $x \in \mathfrak{N}$. Hence for $x \in \mathfrak{N}, y \in \mathfrak{N}{ }^{\perp}$ we have

$$
\begin{align*}
\left(x^{\left.\sigma_{u} \otimes 1+\left(c^{\prime}\right)^{-1} \otimes y^{\sigma_{u} u}\right)^{2}}\right. & =\left(\left(f(x, x)+(-1)^{r} \delta^{-1}(-1)^{r} \delta f(y, y)\right)\right) 1 \\
& =(f(x, x)+f(y, y)) 1 \tag{2}
\end{align*}
$$

Since $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{N} \oplus \mathfrak{N}^{\perp}$ this and the universal property of $C(\mathfrak{V}, f)$ implies that we have a homomorphism $\mu$ of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into $C(\mathfrak{N}, f) \otimes C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},(-1)^{r} \delta f\right)$ sending $1 \rightarrow 1$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mu:(x+y)^{\sigma_{u}} \rightarrow x^{\sigma_{u}} \otimes 1+\left(c^{\prime}\right)^{-1} \otimes y^{\sigma_{u}} \tag{3}
\end{equation*}
$$

If follows from (1) and (3) and the fact that 1 and the elements $x^{\sigma_{u}}+y^{\sigma_{u}}$ generate $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ while 1 and the elements $x^{\sigma^{\prime} u} \otimes 1+1 \otimes y^{\sigma^{\prime \prime} u}$ generate $C(\mathfrak{N}, f) \otimes C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},(-1)^{r} \delta f\right)$ that $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are inverses, so both are isomorphisms. This implies that the restriction of $\lambda$ to $C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$ is an isomorphism. Hence the the subalgebra of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ generated by 1 and $\mathfrak{N}^{\sigma_{u}}$ is isomorphic to $C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$ and $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cong C(\mathfrak{N}, f) \otimes C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},(-1)^{r} \delta f\right)$.

We can now prove our first main theorem on Clifford algebras.
Theorem 1. The associative specialization $\sigma_{u}$ of $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ in $C(\mathfrak{V}, f)$ is 1-1. (Equivalently, by Theorem 2.3, $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ is a special Jordan algebra.) If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{V}=n<\infty$ then $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{V}, f)=2^{n}$.

Proof. Evidently if $\mathfrak{N}$ is a subspace of $\mathfrak{B}$ then $\mathfrak{K}=\Phi 1+\mathfrak{N}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{K}$ is the Jordan algebra of the restriction of $f$ to $\mathfrak{N}$. Hence the first statement for infinite-dimensional $\mathfrak{B}$ will follow from the result for finitedimensional $\mathfrak{B}$ using Theorem 2.4. Hence we may assume $\mathfrak{V}$ is finite dimensional. We note next that the second statement of the theorem implies the first for finite-
dimensional $\mathfrak{V}$. Let $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ be a basis for $\mathfrak{V}$. Then $\left(1, u_{1}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{J}$ and we have seen in §2.2 that every element of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)=S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is a linear combination of the elements $v_{1}{ }^{\varepsilon_{1}} v_{2}{ }^{\varepsilon_{2}} \cdots v_{n}{ }^{\varepsilon_{n}}$ where $v_{i}=u_{i}^{\sigma_{u}}, \varepsilon_{i}=0,1$ and $v_{i}{ }^{0}=1$. Hence, if $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{B}, f)=2^{n}$, then the $2^{n}$ elements $v_{1}{ }^{\varepsilon_{1}} v_{2}{ }^{\varepsilon_{2}} \cdots v_{n}{ }^{\varepsilon_{n}}$ are linearly independent. À fortiori the elements $1, v_{1}, \cdots, v_{n}$ are linearly independent, which implies that the linear mapping $\sigma_{u}$ is 1-1. As a final preliminary to the proof we obtain a reduction to the case of a nondegenerate $f$. For this, suppose $\mathfrak{V}^{\perp} \neq 0$ and write $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{B}^{\perp} \oplus \mathfrak{N}$. Now form the vector space $\mathfrak{P}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{V}^{\prime}$ where $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}^{\prime} =\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ and extend $f$ to a symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak{P}$ by choosing bases $\left(u_{1}, \cdots, u_{r}\right)$ for $\mathfrak{B}^{\perp},\left(u_{1}{ }^{\prime}, \cdots, u_{r}{ }^{\prime}\right)$ for $\mathfrak{B}^{\prime}$ and requiring that $f\left(u_{i}, u_{j}{ }^{\prime}\right)=\delta_{i j}, f\left(u_{i}{ }^{\prime}, u_{j}{ }^{\prime}\right) =0, f\left(u_{i}{ }^{\prime}, y\right)=0=f\left(y, u_{i}{ }^{\prime}\right)$ if $y \in \mathfrak{N}$. Then $f$ is nondegenerate on $\mathfrak{P}$. Assuming the second statement holds for nondegenerate $f$ we have that $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{P}, f)=2^{n+r}$. It follows that if $\left(u_{1}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{V}$ then $\left(u_{1}, \cdots, u_{n+r}\right)$, where $u_{n+j}=u_{j}{ }^{\prime}$, is a basis for $\mathfrak{P}$ and the $2^{n+r}$ elements $v_{1}{ }^{\varepsilon_{1}} v_{2}{ }^{\varepsilon_{2}} \cdots v_{n+r}{ }^{\varepsilon_{n+r}}, v_{i}=u_{i}^{\sigma_{u}}$, are linearly independent. Hence the elements $v_{1}^{\varepsilon_{1}} \cdots v_{n}^{\varepsilon_{n}}$ are linearly independent. This implies that $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{B}, f)=2^{n}$. We now suppose that $f$ is nondegenerate and that $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=n<\infty$. We treat separately the cases $n=1$ and $n=2$. In the first case, $\mathfrak{B}=\Phi u$ where $f(u, u)=\beta \neq 0$. Then we form the algebra $C^{\prime}$ with basis $(1, v), 1$ the identity element, and $v^{2}=\beta 1$. This is associative. The linear mapping $\sigma$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $C^{\prime}$ such that $u \rightarrow v$ satisfies $\left(x^{\sigma}\right)^{2}=f(x, x) 1$. Hence we have a homomorphism of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ onto $C^{\prime}$. Since $\operatorname{dim} C^{\prime}=2$ we have $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \geqq 2$. Since we know that $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \leqq 2^{\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}}=2$ we have $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{V}, f)=2$. Next suppose $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{V}=2$ and let $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}\right)$ be an orthogonal basis for $\mathfrak{B}$. Let $\beta_{i}=f\left(u_{i}, u_{i}\right) \neq 0$ and let $C^{\prime}$ be the quaternion algebra generated by $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ which satisfy $v_{i}{ }^{2}=\beta_{i} 1, v_{1} v_{2}= -v_{2} v_{1}$. Let $\sigma$ be the linear mapping of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $C^{\prime}$ such that $u_{i} \rightarrow v_{i}, i=1,2$. Then $\left(x^{\sigma}\right)^{2}=f(x, x) 1, x \in \mathfrak{B}$, so we have a homomorphism of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ onto $C^{\prime}$. Then $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \geqq 2^{2}=\operatorname{dim} C^{\prime}$, and this implies that $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{B}, f)=2^{2}$. We now assume $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=n \geqq 3$ and we shall prove that $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{B}, f)=2^{n}$ by induction on $n$. For this we decompose $\mathfrak{V}$ as $\mathfrak{V}=\mathfrak{N} \oplus \mathfrak{N}^{\perp}$ where $\mathfrak{N}$ is a two-dimensional nonisotropic subspace. By the induction assumption we have $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{N}, f)=2^{2}$ and $\operatorname{dim} C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},-\delta f\right)=2^{n-2}$ if $\delta$ is a discriminant of $f$ in $\Re$. By Lemma 1, $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cong C(\mathfrak{N}, f) \otimes C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},-\delta f\right)$. Hence $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{B}, f)=2^{2} \cdot 2^{n-2}=2^{n}$, which completes the proof.

The first part of Theorem 1, that is, the fact that $\sigma_{u}$ is 1-1 permits us to identify $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{B}$ with the corresponding subalgebra of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)^{+}$. We shall do this from now on. In this way the associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is the identity mapping and the main involution $\pi$ in $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is characterized by the condition $x^{\pi}=x, x \in \mathfrak{B}$.

It is easy to see that $\Re=\mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ generates a nil ideal $\mathfrak{N}$ in $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ and that $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) / \mathfrak{N} \cong C(\overline{\mathfrak{B}}, \bar{f})$ where $\overline{\mathfrak{B}}=\mathfrak{B} / \Re$ and $\bar{f}$ is the symmetric bilinear form on $\overline{\mathfrak{B}}$ induced by $f$ on $\mathfrak{B}$. Since $\bar{f}$ is nondegenerate this reduces the study of the structure of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ to the case of a nondegenerate form. We proceed now to determine
the structure of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ for a nondegenerate $f$. For this purpose we shall require a special case of the following well-known

Lemma 2. If $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ are finite-dimensional central simple associative algebras then $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{B}$ is central simple.

Proof. Let $\Omega$ be the algebraic closure of the base field $\Phi$. Since $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ is central simple, $\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{\Omega}$ is simple by Theorem 5.9. Hence, $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega} \cong \Omega_{n}$. Similarly $\mathfrak{B}_{\Omega} \cong \Omega_{m}$. Hence $(\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{B})_{\Omega}=\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega} \otimes \mathfrak{B}_{\Omega} \cong \Omega_{n} \otimes \Omega_{m} \cong \Omega_{m n}$. Since $\Omega_{n m}$ is simple this implies that $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{B}$ is simple. Since the center of $\Omega_{m n}$ is $\Omega 1$ and so is one dimensional over the base field $\Omega$, the center of $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{B}$ is one dimensional over $\Phi$ and so it coincides with $\Phi 1$. Hence $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{B}$ is central.

We can now prove the second main theorem on Clifford algebras.
Theorem 2. Let $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ be the Clifford algebra defined by a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{B}$. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=n=2 v$ is even then $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is central simple and is isomorphic to a tensor product of quaternion algebras. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B} =n=2 v+1$ is odd then $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is isomorphic to a tensor product of a central simple algebra which is a tensor product of quaternion algebras and the center $\mathfrak{C}$ of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Moreover, $\mathfrak{C}$ is a two-dimensional algebra $\mathfrak{C}=\Phi[c]$ where $c^{2}=(-1)^{v} \delta, \delta$ a discriminant of $f$. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}$ is infinite then $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is central simple.

Proof. Assume first that $n=2 v$. If $v=1$ then the proof of Theorem 1 shows that $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is a quaternion algebra. Since any quaternion algebra is central simple we have the result in this case. We now use induction on $v$ and assume $v>1$. Let $\mathfrak{N}$ be a two-dimensional nonisotropic subspace of $\mathfrak{B}$. Then $C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$ is a quaternion algebra and, by Lemma 1, $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cong C(\mathfrak{N}, f) \otimes C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},-\delta f\right)$ where $\delta$ is a discriminant of the restriction of $f$ to $\mathfrak{N}$. By the induction assumption $C\left(\Re^{\perp},-\delta f\right)$ is isomorphic to a tensor product of quaternion algebras. Hence this is true also for $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Since quaternion algebras are central simple, the tensor product of a finite number of such algebras is central simple by Lemma 2. Next let $n=2 v+1$ and let $\mathfrak{N}$ be a $2 v$-dimensional nonisotropic subspace of $\mathfrak{V}$. Clearly $\mathfrak{N}^{\perp}$ is one dimensional, so $\mathfrak{N}^{\perp}=\Phi u$. If $f(u, u)=\beta$ and $\gamma$ is a discriminant of the restriction of $f$ to $\mathfrak{N}$ then $\delta=\beta \gamma$ is a discriminant of $f$. By Lemma $1, C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cong C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$ ⊗ $C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},(-1)^{v} \gamma f\right)$ and, by the case $n=2 v, C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$ is isomorphic to a tensor product of quaternion algebras and is central simple. Now the proof of Theorem 1 shows that the Clifford algebra of $\Re^{\perp}=\Phi u$ relative to the form $(-1)^{\nu} \gamma f$ is isomorphic to an algebra $\Phi[c]$ with basis $(1, c)$ and $c^{2}=(-1)^{\nu} \gamma \beta=(-1)^{\nu} \delta$. On the other hand, since $C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$ is central simple, it is easily seen that the center of $C(\mathfrak{N}, f) \otimes C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},(-1)^{\nu} \gamma f\right)$ is the commutative subalgebra $C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},(-1)^{\nu} \gamma f\right)$ (identified with $1 \otimes C\left(\mathfrak{N}^{\perp},(-1)^{\nu} \gamma f\right)$. This proves the result for $n=2 v+1$. Now assume $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{V}$ is infinite. We note that any finite-dimensional subspace
$\mathfrak{F}$ of $\mathfrak{V}$ can be imbedded in an even-dimensional nonisotropic subspace. We may assume that $\mathfrak{F} \cap \mathfrak{F}^{\perp} \neq 0$ and choose a nonzero $z$ in this intersection. Then there exists a $w \in \mathfrak{V}$ such that $f(z, w) \neq 0$. It is immediate that $(\mathfrak{F}+\Phi w) \cap(\mathfrak{F}+\Phi w)^{\perp} \subset \mathfrak{F} \cap \mathfrak{F}^{\perp}$. A finite number of steps of this type yields a finite-dimensional nonisotropic subspace $\mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak{F}+\Phi w_{1}+\Phi w_{2}+\cdots+\Phi w_{r}$ containing $\mathfrak{F}$. If this is odd dimensional we can adjoin a nonisotropic vector in $\mathfrak{N}^{\perp}$ to obtain an even-dimensional nonisotropic space. If $\mathfrak{N}$ is even dimensional nonisotropic then $C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$ is central simple. Hence the subalgebra of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ generated by 1 and $\mathfrak{N}$, which is a homomorphic image of $C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$, is isomorphic to $C(\mathfrak{N}, f)$ and so is central simple. It is now clear that any finite subset of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ can be imbedded in a central simple subalgebra containing 1 . It is immediate that this implies that $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is central simple.

In the odd-dimensional case the center of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ has the form $\Phi[c]$ where the minimum equation of $c$ is $c^{2}=(-1)^{v} \delta$. If $(-1)^{v} \delta$ is a square of an element in $\Phi$ then $\Phi[c] \cong \Phi \oplus \Phi$ and consequently $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ which is isomorphic to a tensor product of a central simple algebra and $\Phi \oplus \Phi$ is a direct sum of two isomorphic central simple algebras. If $(-1)^{v} \delta$ is not a square then $\Phi[c]$ is a quadratic field over $\Phi$. In this case it is easy to see that $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is simple.

## Exercises

1. Let $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=2 v$ and let $f$ be nondegenerate of maximal Witt index. Then $\mathfrak{B}$ has a basis $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{2 v}\right)$ such that the matrix of $f$ relative to this basis is $\operatorname{diag}\{1,-1,1,-1, \cdots, 1,-1\}$. Show that $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is isomorphic to the tensor product of $\nu$ split quaternion algebras and hence that $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cong \Phi_{2} \nu$.
2. Let $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=2 v+1$ and let $f$ be nondegenerate of maximal Witt index. Show that $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cong \mathrm{P}_{2} v$ where $\mathrm{P}=\Phi[c]$ has a basis $(1, c)$ with $c^{2}=(-1)^{v} \delta, \delta$ a discriminant of $f$.
3. Let $f$ be a symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak{B}$ which has the basis ( $u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{2 v}$ ) such that the matrix of $f$ relative to this basis is diag $\left\{\alpha_{1}, \beta_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \beta_{2}, \cdots, \alpha_{v}, \beta_{v}\right\}$. Let $(\alpha, \beta)$ denote the quaternion algebra with basis $(1, i, j, k)$ such that $i^{2}=\alpha 1$, $j^{2}=\beta 1, \quad i j=-j i$. Show that $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cong\left(\alpha_{1}, \beta_{1}\right) \otimes\left(\gamma_{1} \alpha_{2}, \gamma_{1} \beta_{2}\right) \otimes \cdots \otimes\left(\gamma_{v-1} \alpha_{v}, \gamma_{v-1} \beta_{v}\right)$ where $\gamma_{i}=-\alpha_{i} \beta_{i}$.
4. Let $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=2 v, f$ nondegenerate, $\pi$ the main involution in $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Show that $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{H}(C(\mathfrak{B}, f), \pi)=2^{v-1}\left(2^{v}+1\right)$ if $v \equiv 0,1(\bmod 4)$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{H}(C(\mathfrak{B}, f), \pi) =2^{v-1}\left(2^{v}-1\right)$ if $v \equiv 2,3(\bmod 4)$.
5. Let $\mathfrak{B}, f$ be as in 4. Assume, moreover, that $f$ has maximal Witt index and $v \equiv 0,1(\bmod 4)$. Show that if we identify $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ with $\Phi_{2} v$ using ex. 2 , then $\pi$ can be identified with the involution $X \rightarrow S^{-1} X^{t} S$ where $S=\operatorname{diag}\{1,-1,1,-1$, $\cdots, 1,-1\}$.
6. Structure of meson algebras. The meson algebra $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ defined by the vector space $\mathfrak{B}$ and the symmetric bilinear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{B}$ is $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)=T(\mathfrak{B}) / \mathfrak{L}$
where $T(\mathfrak{B})$ is the tensor algebra based on $\mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{L}$ is the ideal in $T(\mathfrak{B})$ generated by the elements $x \otimes y \otimes x-f(x, y) x, x, y \in \mathfrak{B}$. We have seen in $\S 2.13$ that this can be taken to be the universal unital multiplication envelope $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ for the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi \oplus \mathfrak{B}$ with the multiplication specialization $\rho_{u}$ defined by $(\alpha 1+x)^{\rho_{u}}=\alpha 1+x+\mathcal{L}$. We have seen also that the canonical homomorphism $\xi$ of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ onto the squared special unital universal envelope $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ coincides with the homomorphism of $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \otimes C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ sending $x^{\boldsymbol{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}(x \otimes 1+1 \otimes x), x \in \mathfrak{J}$, ( $\mathfrak{J}$ identified with the corresponding subset of the Clifford algebra). For the sake of simplicity we assume throughout this section that $\mathfrak{B}$ is finite dimensional.

Theorem 3. The canonical homomorphism of the meson algebra $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \otimes C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is a monomorphism. Moreover, $\operatorname{dim} D(\mathfrak{B}, f)=\binom{2 n+1}{n}$
if $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=n$. if $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=n$.

Proof. Let ( $u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}$ ) be an orthogonal basis for $\mathfrak{V} / \Phi$. Then we know that every element of $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)=U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is a linear combination of the elements

$$
\begin{equation*}
v_{k_{1}}^{2} v_{k_{2}}^{2} \cdots v_{k_{r}}^{2} v_{k_{r}+1} v_{k_{r}+2} \cdots v_{k_{s}} \tag{4}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $v_{i} \equiv u_{\imath}^{\rho_{u}}$, the $k_{i}$ are distinct and satisfy $k_{1}<k_{2}<\cdots<k_{r} ; k_{r+1}<k_{r+3}<\cdots$; $k_{r+2}<k_{r+4}<\cdots$ (§2.9, p. 97 and p. 103). The image of the element (4) under the hommorphism of $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \otimes C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is

$$
\begin{equation*}
w_{k_{1}}^{2} w_{k_{2}}^{2} \cdots w_{k_{r}}^{2} w_{k_{r+1}} w_{k_{r+2}} \cdots w_{k_{s}} \tag{5}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $w_{i}=u_{i}^{\prime \prime}=\frac{1}{2}\left(u_{i} \otimes 1+1 \otimes u_{i}\right)$. We have seen also that the number of sets of indices $\left(k_{1}, \cdots, k_{s}\right)$ satisfying the indicated conditions is $\binom{2 n+1}{n}$ (p. 99). It is clear from this that both assertions of the theorem will follow if we can show that the elements given by (5) associated with the set of indices ( $k_{1}, \cdots, k_{s}$ ) satisfying our conditions are linearly independent (and consequently distinct). In $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ we have the relations $u_{i} u_{j}=-u_{j} u_{i}, i \neq j, u_{i}^{2}=\beta_{i} 1, \beta_{i}=f\left(u_{i}, u_{i}\right)$. Also we have seen that the $2^{n}$ elements $u_{i_{1}} u_{i_{2}} \cdots u_{i_{h}}, i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{h}$ form a basis for $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Here we allow $h=0$ and agree that the corresponding element is 1 . It follows that the $2^{2 n}$ elements $u_{i_{1}} u_{i_{2}} \cdots u_{i_{h}} \otimes u_{j_{1}} u_{j_{2}} \cdots u_{j_{k}}, i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{h}$, $j_{1}<j_{2}<\cdots<j_{k}$ form a basis for $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \otimes C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. We now examine the expression of the element (5) in terms of this basis. We note first that if no $k_{j}$ in (5) has the value $i$ then the expression of this element in terms of the basis $\left\{u_{i_{1}} \cdots u_{i_{h}} \otimes u_{j_{1}} \cdots u_{j_{k}}\right\}$ involves only those base elements for which every $i_{p} \neq i$ and every $j_{q} \neq i$. Next suppose $k_{l}=i$ for $r+1 \leqq l \leqq s$. Then since $w_{i}=\frac{1}{2}\left(u_{i} \otimes 1+1 \otimes u_{i}\right)$ it is clear that the element (5) is a linear combination of the base elements $u_{i_{1}} \cdots u_{i_{h}} \otimes u_{j_{1}} \cdots u_{j_{k}}$ for which either one $i_{j}=i$ or one $j_{q}=i$ but not both. Finally, suppose $k_{l}=i, 1 \leqq l \leqq r$. Then since $2 w_{i}{ }^{2}=f\left(u_{i}, u_{i}\right) 1+u_{i} \otimes u_{i}$
it is clear that the expression of (5) in terms of our basis contains only base elements in which an $i_{p}=i$ and a $j_{q}=i$ and base elements in which no $i_{p}=i$ and no $j_{q}=i$. It follows from this that if we have a relation $A_{i}+B_{i}+C_{i}=0$ where $A_{i}$ is a linear combination of elements (5) in which one of the $k_{l}=i$ for $1 \leqq l \leqq r, B_{i}$ a linear combination of elements (5) in which one of the $k_{l}=i$ for $r+1 \leqq l \leqq s$ and $C_{i}$ is a linear combination of elements (5) in which no $k_{l}=i$ then $B_{i}=0$ and $A_{i}+C_{i}=0$. If $i=1$ then $A_{1}=w_{1}{ }^{2} A_{1}{ }^{\prime}$ where $A_{1}{ }^{\prime}$ is a linear combination of elements (5) in which no $k_{l}=1$. Then it is clear from the form of $w_{1}{ }^{2}$ that $A_{1}+C_{1}=w_{1}{ }^{2} A_{1}{ }^{\prime}+C_{1}=0$ implies that $A_{1}{ }^{\prime}=0$ and $C_{1}=0$. This implies that if we have a nontrivial linear relation connecting the elements (5) then we have one in which either no term contains $w_{1}$ or every term contains $w_{1}$ but not $w_{1}{ }^{2}$. By induction we see that we have a nontrivial relation in which for every $i, 1 \leqq i \leqq n$, every term occurring in the relation is either of degree 0 or 1 in $w_{i}$. Thus if we have a nontrivial linear relation connecting the elements (5) then we have one of the form $\sum \alpha_{j_{1} \cdots j_{t}} w_{j_{1}} w_{j_{2}} \cdots w_{j_{t}}=0$ where the $j$ 's are a permutation of a subset of $\{1, \cdots, n\}$, which by reordering the basis, we may suppose is $\{1, \cdots, t\}$. Also, of course, we have $j_{1}<j_{3}<\cdots, j_{2}<j_{4}<\cdots$. We may assume also that $t$ is minimal. Now the inequalities on the $j$ 's imply that $w_{1}$ occurs either in the first or second position in the terms $w_{j_{1}} w_{j_{2}} \cdots w_{j_{t}}$ occurring in our relation. The relation $x y x=f(x, y) x$ in $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ and the orthogonality of the $u_{i}$ imply that $w_{i} w_{j} w_{i}=0$, if $i \neq j$, holds in $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \otimes C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Hence if we multiply our relation on the left by $w_{1}$, then after dropping the terms $w_{1} w_{j} w_{1} \cdots=0$ we obtain a relation of the form $w_{1}{ }^{2} A=0$ where $A$ is a linear combination of $w_{j_{2}} w_{j_{3}} \cdots$ where $j_{2}, j_{3}, \cdots$ is a permutation of $2,3, \cdots, t$ and the $j$ 's satisfy the usual inequalities. This implies that $A=0$ which contradicts the minimality of $t$ unless $w_{1}$ occurs in the second position in every term in our relation. Now suppose we already know that $w_{i}, 1 \leqq i \leqq r$, $2 r \leqq l$, occurs in the $2 i$-position in all $w_{j_{1}} \cdots w_{j_{t}}$ having nonzero coefficients in our relation. Consider $w_{r+1}$. Either this occurs in the first or in the $2 r+2$ position in the $w_{j_{1}} \cdots w_{j_{t}}$ in our relation. The latter possibility occurs only if $2 r+2 \leqq t$. Now linearization of the basic relation in $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ gives $x y z+z y x=f(x, y) z+ +f(y, z) x$. This and the orthogonality of the $u_{i}$ imply that $w_{i} w_{j} w_{k}=-w_{k} w_{j} w_{i}$ if $i, j, k$ are distinct. It follows from this and the relation $w_{i} w_{j} w_{i}=0$ that if we multiply $w_{j_{1}} w_{j_{2}} \cdots w_{j_{t}}$ on the left by $w_{j_{2 h}}, 2 h \leqq t$, then we obtain 0 . This permits us to apply the argument used for $w_{1}$ to show that $2 r+2 \leqq t$ and $w_{r+1}$ occurs in the ( $2 r+2$ )-position in every $w_{j_{1}} w_{j_{2}} \cdots w_{j_{u}}$ in our relation. Since $t$ is finite this argument leads to a contradiction. Hence we have proved the linear independence of the elements (5), which proves the theorem.

We shall determine next the structure of $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ for $\mathfrak{V}$ finite dimensional and $f$ nondegenerate, and we begin with the case $n=2 v$ is even. Then $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is central simple and hence also $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \otimes C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is central simple. Now we have the homomorphism of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into $\mathfrak{E}=\operatorname{Hom}(C(\mathfrak{B}, f), C(\mathfrak{B}, f))$ sending $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $x \rightarrow x_{\boldsymbol{R}}$ for $x \in \mathfrak{B}$. Also, since we have an involution in $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ sending $x \rightarrow x$ we have
a homomorphism of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ sending $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $x \rightarrow x_{L}, x \in \mathfrak{V}$. Since left and right multiplications commute, this gives a homomorphism of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \otimes C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ mapping $1 \rightarrow 1,1 \otimes x \rightarrow x_{R}, x \otimes 1 \rightarrow x_{L}, x \in \mathfrak{B}$. Since $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \otimes C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is simple this is a monomorphism. Consequently, its restriction to $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$, the subalgebra of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \otimes C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ generated by 1 and the elements $\frac{1}{2}(x \otimes 1+1 \otimes x), x \in \mathfrak{B}$, is a monomorphism. Combining this with the monomorphism given in Theorem 3 of $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ onto $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$, we obtain a monomorphism of $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into E such that $1 \rightarrow 1, x^{\rho_{u}} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\left(x_{L}+x_{R}\right), x \in \mathfrak{B}$. Thus to obtain the structure of $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ it is equivalent to obtaining the structure of the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{E}=\operatorname{Hom}(C(\mathfrak{B}, f), C(\mathfrak{B}, f))$ generated by 1 and the elements $\frac{1}{2}\left(x_{L}+x_{R}\right), x \in \mathfrak{V}$. Now it is clear that this algebra of linear transformations is the same as the enveloping algebra of linear transformations of $R_{\mathrm{C}(\mathfrak{B}, f)^{+}}(\mathfrak{J})$, the set of multiplications $R_{a}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a_{L}+a_{R}\right), a \in \mathfrak{J}$, acting in the Jordan algebra $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)^{+}$. We shall now obtain the structure of this algebra of linear transformations, hence of $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$, by determining certain subspaces of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)^{+}$which are invariant under the $R_{x}, x \in \mathfrak{J}$.

For the moment we drop the assumptions that $n$ is even and that $f$ is nondegenerate. Let $x_{i} \in \mathfrak{V}$. Then we define $\left[x_{1}, \cdots, x_{r}\right]$ inductively by

$$
\begin{align*}
{\left[x_{1}\right] } & =x_{1}, \\
{\left[x_{1}, \cdots, x_{2 k}\right] } & =\left[\left[x_{1}, \cdots, x_{2 k-1}\right], x_{2 k}\right],  \tag{6}\\
{\left[x_{1}, \cdots, x_{2 k+1}\right] } & =2\left[x_{1}, \cdots, x_{2 k}\right] \cdot x_{2 k+1} .
\end{align*}
$$

We now put $\mathfrak{B}^{[0]}=\Phi 1, \mathfrak{B}^{[r]}$, for $r>0$, the space spanned by all the elements $\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{r}\right], x_{i} \in \mathfrak{V}$.

Lemma 1. $\left[x_{1}, \cdots, x_{r}\right]$ is an alternating multilinear function of its arguments.
Proof. The multilinear character is clear, and this and the fact that the characteristic is not two imply that the alternating property is equivalent to: $\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{r}\right]=0$ if $x_{i}=x_{j}, i \neq j$. For $r=2$ this is clear since $[x x]=x x-x x=0$. Now assume the result for $r$. To prove it for $r+1$ it is enough, in view of the alternating character of $\left[x_{1}, \cdots, x_{r-1}\right]$, to prove that $\left[x_{1}, \cdots, x_{r-1}, x, x\right]=0$. We put $\left[x_{1}, \cdots, x_{r-1}\right]=a$. Then we have the following two cases:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2[a \cdot x, x] & =(a x+x a) x-x(a x+x a) \\
& =a x^{2}-x^{2} a=f(x, x) a-f(x, x) a=0, \\
2[a, x] \cdot x & =(a x-x a) x+x(a x-x a) \\
& =a x^{2}-x^{2} a=0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

This proves the alternating character of $\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{r+1}\right]$.

Lemma 2. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{V}=n$ then $C(\mathfrak{V}, f)=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V} \oplus \mathfrak{V}^{[2]} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{V}^{[n]}$, $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}^{[i]}=\binom{n}{i}$ and if $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ is an orthogonal basis for $\mathfrak{B}$ then the set $\left\{\left[u_{i_{1}}, u_{i_{2}}, \cdots, u_{i_{r}}\right] \mid i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{r}\right\}$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{B}^{[r]}$.

Proof. Since $\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{r}\right]$ is multilinear and alternating it is clear that every element of $\mathfrak{B}^{[r]}$ is a linear combination of the elements $\left[u_{i_{1}}, u_{i_{2}}, \cdots, u_{i_{r}}\right]$, $i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{r}$. It follows directly from the definition and induction on $r$ that $\left[u_{i_{1}}, u_{i_{2}}, \cdots, u_{i_{r}}\right]=2^{r-1} u_{i_{1}} u_{i_{2}} \cdots u_{i_{r}}, i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{r}$. Since the set $\left\{u_{i_{1}} \cdots u_{i_{r}} \mid i_{1}<i_{2}<\right. \left.\cdots<i_{v}, r=0,1, \cdots, n\right\}$ is a basis for $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ all the statements of the lemma are clear.

Lemma 3. If $y \in \mathfrak{B}^{[2 k-1]}$ and $x \in \mathfrak{B}$ then $y . x \in \mathfrak{B}^{[2 k-2]}, k=1,2, \cdots$.
Proof. We have the following identity in any associative algebra:

$$
x_{1} \cdots x_{2 k-1} \cdot x=\sum_{h=0}^{2 k-2}(-1)^{h} x_{1} \cdots x_{2 k-h-2}\left(x_{2 k-h-1} \cdot x\right) x_{2 k-h} \cdots x_{2 k-1} .
$$

Since $u_{i} . x=f\left(u_{i}, x\right) 1$ and the set of elements $\left\{u_{i_{1}} \cdots u_{i_{r}} \mid i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{r}\right\}$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{B}^{[r]}$, this relation shows that $\mathfrak{B}^{[2 k-1]} \cdot \mathfrak{B} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}^{[2 k-2]}$.

Lemma 4. If $n=2 v$ is even then

$$
\begin{equation*}
\binom{2 n+1}{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{\nu}\binom{n+1}{k}^{2}=\sum_{k=0}^{\nu}\binom{n+1}{2 k+1}^{2} . \tag{7}
\end{equation*}
$$

Proof. For any $n$ the relation $(1+x)^{2 n+1}=(1+x)^{n}(1+x)^{n+1}$ gives the identity

$$
\begin{equation*}
\binom{2 n+1}{n}=\sum_{0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}\binom{n+1}{n-j+1} \tag{8}
\end{equation*}
$$

on comparing coefficients of $x^{n+1}$. Then if $n=2 v$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}\binom{n+1}{n-j+1} & =1+\sum_{1}^{v}\binom{n+1}{n-j+1}\left(\binom{n}{j}+\binom{n}{n+1-j}\right) \\
& =1+\sum_{1}^{v}\binom{n+1}{j}\left(\binom{n}{j}+\binom{n}{j-1}\right) \\
& =1+\sum_{1}^{v}\binom{n+1}{j}^{2}=\sum_{0}^{v}\binom{n+1}{j}^{2} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\binom{n+1}{2 h}=\binom{n+1}{2(v-h)+1}$ this and (8) give

$$
\binom{2 n+1}{n}=\binom{n+1}{1}^{2}+\binom{n+1}{3}^{2}+\cdots+\binom{n+1}{n+1}^{2}
$$

as required.

We are now ready to prove the following
Theorem 4. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=n=2 v$ and $f$ is nondegenerate then the meson algebra $D(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cong \Sigma_{k=0}^{\nu} \oplus \Phi_{\binom{n+1}{(2 k+1)} \text {. }}$

Proof. We have seen that $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is isomorphic to the algebra $\mathfrak{D}$ of linear transformations in $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)^{+}$generated by the elements $R_{a}, \quad a \in \mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$. By Lemma 2, $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V} \oplus \mathfrak{V}^{[2]} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{V}^{[n]}$. By the definition (6) of $\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{2 k+1}\right]$, the subspace $\mathfrak{B}^{[2 k]}$ is mapped into $\mathfrak{B}^{[2 k+1]}$ by $R_{x}, x \in \mathfrak{B}$, if $k<v$. By Lemma 1, $\mathfrak{B}^{[2 v]} R_{x}=0$. By Lemma 3, $\mathfrak{V}^{[2 k-1]}$ is mapped into $\mathfrak{V}^{[2 k-2]}$ if $x \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $k=1,2, \cdots$. It is clear from this that the subspaces $\Phi 1+\mathfrak{B}$, $\mathfrak{B}^{[2]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[3]}, \cdots, \mathfrak{B}^{[2 v-2]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[2 v-1]}, \mathfrak{B}^{[2 v]}$ are invariant under the $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. The dimensionalities of these spaces are respectively $\binom{n+1}{1},\binom{n}{2}+\binom{n}{3}=\binom{n+1}{3}$, $\binom{n+1}{5}, \cdots,\binom{n+1}{2 v+1}$. The dimensionality of the algebras of linear transformations in these spaces are therefore $\binom{n+1}{1}^{2},\binom{n+1}{3}^{2}, \cdots,\binom{n+1}{2 v+1}^{2}$. Hence we obtain the bound $\binom{n+1}{1}^{2}+\binom{n+1}{3}^{2}+\cdots+\binom{n+1}{2 v+1}^{2}$ for $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}$. By Lemma 4 this is $\binom{2 n+1}{n}$. On the other hand, by Theorem 3, $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}=\operatorname{dim} D(\mathfrak{B}, f) =\binom{2 n+1}{n}$. Thus the bound is achieved. Clearly this implies that given any sequence ( $A_{0}, A_{1}, \cdots, A_{v}$ ) where $A_{i}$ is a linear transformation in the $i$ th space in the sequence $\Phi 1+\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B}^{[2]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[3]}, \cdots, \mathfrak{V}^{[2 \text { v }]}$, then there exists a $D \in \mathfrak{D}$ such that the restrictions of $D$ to the $i$ th subspace is $A_{i}$. This implies that $\mathfrak{D} \cong \Phi_{\binom{n+1}{1}} \oplus \Phi_{\binom{n+1}{3}} \oplus \cdots \oplus \Phi_{\binom{n+1}{n+1}}$. Hence $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ has the indicated structure.
We now assume $n=2 v-1, v=1,2, \cdots, f$ nondegenerate. In this case $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ has the center $\Phi[c]$ where $c=u_{1} u_{2} \cdots u_{n},\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ an orthogonal basis for $\mathfrak{B}$. Hence $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is not central simple and so we can not identify $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ with the algebra of linear transformations which we used in the foregoing case. To circumvent this difficulty we imbed $\mathfrak{V}$ in an $n+1=2 \nu$ dimensional space $\mathfrak{W}=\mathfrak{V} \oplus \Phi u_{n+1}$ and extend $f$ to $f$ on $\mathfrak{P}$ so that $f\left(u_{i}, u_{n+1}\right)=0=f\left(u_{n+1}, u_{i}\right)$ for $i \leqq n$ and $f\left(u_{n+1}, u_{n+1}\right)=1$. Then the $2^{n+1}$ elements $u_{1}{ }^{\varepsilon_{1}} u_{2}{ }^{\varepsilon_{2}} \cdots u_{n+1}{ }^{\varepsilon_{n+1}}, \varepsilon_{i}=0,1$, form a basis for $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ so it is clear that $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ can be identified with the subalgebra of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ generated by 1 and the $u_{i}, i \leqq n$. Also we have $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)=C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \oplus C(\mathfrak{B}, f) u_{n+1}$. It is clear also that $f$ is nondegenerate on $\mathfrak{B}$ and hence $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is central simple. The argument given in the even-dimensional case now implies that $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is isomorphic to the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(C(\mathfrak{W}, f), C(\mathfrak{W}, f))$ generated by the $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{I}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$, acting in $C(\mathfrak{W}, f)$. Hence we consider the decomposition of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into invariant subspaces relative to the $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$.

If we define the spaces $\mathfrak{W}^{[i]}$ as before (for the $\mathfrak{B}^{[i]}$ ) then the result in the evendimensional case implies that the spaces $\Phi 1+\mathfrak{P}, \mathfrak{W}^{[2]}+\mathfrak{M}^{[3]}, \cdots, \mathfrak{W}^{[2 \text { v }]}$ are invariant under $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. It is clear also that $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is invariant under $R_{a}$. Also $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) u_{n+1}$ is invariant, since if $y \in C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ and $x \in \mathfrak{J}$, then $y u_{n+1} \cdot x=\frac{1}{2}\left(x y u_{n+1}+y u_{n+1} x\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(x y u_{n+1}-y x u_{n+1}\right)$, by the orthogonality of $x$ and $u_{n+1}$. Thus $y u_{n+1} . x \in C(\mathfrak{B}, f) u_{n+1}$. Taking intersections we obtain the invariant subspaces $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cap\left(\mathfrak{W}^{[2 i]}+\mathfrak{W}^{[2 i+1]}\right)$ and $C(\mathfrak{B}, f) u_{n+1} \cap\left(\mathfrak{W}^{[2 i]}+\mathfrak{W}^{[2 i+1]}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{W}^{[0]}=\Phi 1, \mathfrak{W}^{[1]}=\mathfrak{W}$. Since $\left\{u_{i_{1}} u_{i_{2}} \cdots u_{i_{r}} \mid 1 \leqq i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{r} \leqq n+1\right\}$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{W}^{[r]}$ and $\left\{u_{j_{1}} u_{j_{2}} \cdots u_{j_{r}} \mid 1 \leqq j_{1}<j_{2}<\cdots<j_{k} \leqq n, k=1,2, \cdots, n\right\}$ is, a basis for $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ it is clear that

$$
\begin{align*}
C(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cap\left(\mathfrak{W}^{[2 i]}+\mathfrak{W}^{[2 i+1]}\right) & =\mathfrak{B}^{[2 i]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[2 i+1]} \\
C(\mathfrak{B}, f) u_{n+1} \cap\left(\mathfrak{W}^{[2 i]}+\mathfrak{W}^{[2 i+1]}\right) & =\mathfrak{B}^{[2 i-1]} u_{n+1}+\mathfrak{B}^{[2 i]} u_{n+1} \tag{9}
\end{align*}
$$

are invariant under $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Also it is clear that $C(\mathfrak{W}, f)$ is a direct sum of the spaces given in (9).

If $c=u_{1} u_{2} \cdots u_{n}$, as before, then $c$ is an element of the center of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ and so the left multiplication $C=c_{L}$ in $C(\mathfrak{W}, f)$ commutes with the $a_{L}$ acting in $C(\mathfrak{W}, f)$, $a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Clearly $C$ commutes also with $a_{R}$, so $C R_{a}=R_{a} C$ holds in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(C(\mathfrak{W}, f)$, $C(\mathfrak{W}, f))$. Since $n=2 v-1, c^{2}=(-1)^{v-1} \delta 1$ where $\delta$ is a discriminant of $f$. Hence $c$ is invertible and consequently $C$ is invertible. It is clear from the basis for $\mathfrak{B}^{[r]}$ and the multiplication table for the $u_{i}$ that $C$ maps $\mathfrak{B}^{[r]}, 0 \leqq r \leqq n$, onto $\mathfrak{B}^{[n-r]}$. Hence $C$ maps $\mathfrak{B}^{[2 i]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[2 i+1]}$ onto $\mathfrak{B}^{[2(v-i-1)]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[2(v-i-1)+1]}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{[2 i-1]} u_{n+1}+\mathfrak{B}^{[2 i]} u_{n+1}$ onto $\mathfrak{B}^{[2(\nu-i)-1]} u_{n+1}+\mathfrak{B}^{[2(\nu-i]} u_{n+1}$. Since $C$ commutes with the $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, the restriction of $C$ to $\mathfrak{V}^{[2 i]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[2 i+1]}$ and to $\mathfrak{B}^{[2 i-1]} u_{n+1} +\mathfrak{B}^{[2 i]} u_{n+1}$ is a $\mathfrak{J}$-isomorphism (more precisely a $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ module isomorphism). It follows that if $v$ is odd then $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is isomorphic to the associative algebra of linear transformations generated by the restrictions of the $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, to the space $\mathfrak{S}=\Sigma_{i=0}^{v} \mathfrak{B}^{[i]}+\Sigma_{j=0}^{v-1} \mathfrak{B}^{[j]} u_{n+1}$. If $v$ is even we may consider the restrictions of the $R_{a}$ to the space $\mathfrak{S}=\sum_{j=0}^{\nu-1} \mathfrak{B}^{[j]}+\sum_{i=0}^{\nu} \mathfrak{B}^{[i]} u_{n+1}$. If $v$ is odd, $C$ maps $\mathfrak{B}^{[\nu-1]}$ onto $\mathfrak{B}^{[\nu]}$ and if $v$ is even $C$ maps $\mathfrak{B}^{[\nu-1]} u_{n+1}$ onto $\mathfrak{B}^{[\nu]} u_{n+1}$. These spaces have the same dimensionality $\binom{n}{v-1}=\binom{n}{v}=\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}$.

Now suppose that $(-1)^{\nu-1} \delta=\rho^{2}, \rho \in \Phi$. We have $C^{2}=(-1)^{\nu-1} \delta 1=\rho^{2} 1$ and if $v$ is odd (even) then $\mathfrak{B}^{[v-1]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[v]}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{[v-1]} u_{n+1}+\mathfrak{B}^{[v]} u_{n+1}\right)$ is a direct sum of two spaces corresponding to the characteristic roots $\rho$ and $-\rho$ of $C$ and these have the same dimensionality $\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}$. Moreover, these spaces are invariant under the $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Besides these we have the invariant subspaces $\mathfrak{B}^{[0]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[1]}$, $\mathfrak{B}^{[2]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[3]}, \cdots, \mathfrak{B}^{[v-3]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[v-2]}, \mathfrak{B}^{[0]} u_{n+1}, \mathfrak{B}^{[1]} u_{n+1}+\mathfrak{B}^{[2]} u_{n+1}, \cdots, \mathfrak{B}^{[v-2]} u_{n+1} +\mathfrak{B}^{[\nu-1]} u_{n+1} \quad\left(\mathfrak{B}^{[0]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[1]}, \mathfrak{B}^{[2]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[3]}, \cdots, \mathfrak{B}^{[\nu-2]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[\nu-1]}, \quad \mathfrak{B}^{[0]} u_{n+1}\right.$,
$\left.\mathfrak{B}^{[1]} u_{n+1}+\mathfrak{B}^{[2]} u_{n+1}, \cdots, \mathfrak{B}^{[v-3]} u_{n+1}+\mathfrak{B}^{[v-2]} u_{n+1}\right)$ if $v$ is odd (even). The dimensionalities for the invariant subspaces we have listed are $\binom{n+1}{k}$, $k=0,1, \cdots, v-1$, and $\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}$ and $\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}$. In this way we obtain the bound $\sum_{k=0}^{v-1}\binom{n+1}{k}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}^{2}$ for $\operatorname{dim} D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. On the other hand, we know that $\operatorname{dim} D(\mathfrak{B}, f)=\binom{2 n+1}{n}$, and we have the relation $\sum_{k=0}^{v-1}\binom{n+1}{k}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}^{2} =\binom{2 n+1}{n}$. For, by (8),

$$
\begin{aligned}
\binom{2 n+1}{n} & =\sum_{0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}\binom{n+1}{n-j+1} \\
& =1+\sum_{k=1}^{v-1}\binom{n+1}{k}\left(\binom{n}{k}+\binom{n}{k-1}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}\left(\binom{n}{v}+\binom{n}{v}\right) \\
& =1+\sum_{k=1}^{v-1}\binom{n+1}{k}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the bound we obtained for $\operatorname{dim} D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is attained it follows as in the even dimensional case that $D(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cong \sum_{k=0}^{v-1} \oplus \Phi_{\binom{n+1}{k}} \oplus \Phi_{\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}} \oplus \Phi_{\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}}$.

Next assume $(-1)^{\nu-1} \delta$ is not a square in $\Phi$. Then $\mathrm{P}=\Phi[C]$ is a field. If $v$ is odd (even) then $\mathfrak{B}^{[\nu-1]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[\nu]}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{[\nu-1]} u_{n+1}+\mathfrak{B}^{[\nu]} u_{n+1}\right)$, which is mapped into itself by $C$, can be considered as a vector space over P . Since the dimensionality of this space over $\Phi$ is $\binom{n+1}{v}$ its dimensionality over P is $\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}$. Then the dimensionality of the space of linear transformations of this space over P considered as a vector space over P is $\frac{1}{4}\binom{n+1}{v}^{2}$. Hence as a space over $\Phi$ the dimensionality is $\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}^{2}$. Since the $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, commute with $C$ it is clear that the restriction of $R_{a}$ to $\mathfrak{V}^{[\nu-1]}+\mathfrak{B}^{[\nu]}$ or $\mathfrak{B}^{[\nu-1]} u_{n+1}+\mathfrak{B}^{[\nu]} u_{n+1}$ according as $v$ is odd or even is contained in the algebra of linear transformations of this space over $\mathbf{P}$. If we take into account also the other invariant subspaces we obtain the bound $\sum_{-0}^{v-1}\binom{n+1}{k}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}^{2}$ for the $\operatorname{dim} D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Since this is attained we conclude as before that $D(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cong \sum_{0}^{\nu-1} \oplus \Phi_{\binom{n+1}{k}} \oplus \mathrm{P}_{\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{\nu}}$.

The field $\mathbf{P}$ is isomorphic to the center of the Clifford algebra $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ and it can be identified with this center. If $(-1)^{\nu-1} \delta$ is a square then the center P of the Clifford algebra is isomorphic to $\Phi \oplus \Phi$. Then $\Phi_{\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}} \oplus \Phi_{\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}} \cong \mathrm{P}_{\frac{1}{2}(n+1)}$.

Hence we can state the results we have obtained in the following uniform way.
Theorem 5. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=n=2 v-1$ and $f$ is nondegenerate then the meson algebra $D(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cong \Sigma_{k=0}^{v-1} \oplus \Phi_{\binom{n+1}{k}} \oplus \mathbf{P}_{\frac{1}{2}\binom{n+1}{v}}$ where $\mathbf{P}$ is the center of the Clifford algebra.

We remark finally that in the case $n=2 v$ we have $\binom{n+1}{2(v-h)+1}=\binom{n+1}{2 h}$. Hence the structure of $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ in this case as given in Theorem 4 can be described by $D(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cong \sum_{j=0}^{\nu} \oplus \Phi_{\binom{n+1}{j}}$, which is similar to that given in Theorem 5 .

## Exercise

1. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be an arbitrary vector space, $f$ a symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak{B}$ and let $\overline{\mathfrak{B}}=\mathfrak{V} / \mathfrak{V}^{\perp}$. Let $\bar{f}$ denote the form on $\overline{\mathfrak{B}}$ determined by $f\left(\bar{f}\left(x+\mathfrak{V}^{\perp}, y+\mathfrak{V}^{\perp}\right)\right. =f(x, y)$ ). Show that the elements $z^{\rho_{u}}, z \in \mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ generate a nil ideal $\Re$ in $D(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ and $D(\mathfrak{B}, f) / \Re \cong D(\overline{\mathfrak{V}}, \bar{f})$.
2. Universal envelopes for finite-dimensional special central simple Jordan algebras of degree $\geqq 3$. We recall that a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ is finite-dimensional special central simple of degree $m \geqq 3$ if and only if $\mathfrak{J} \cong \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is a finite-dimensional central simple associative algebra with involution such that if $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of the base field then $\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}, J\right) \cong\left(\mathfrak{D}_{m}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a (split) associative composition algebra and $J_{1}$ is the standard involution (§5.7). We know also that if we identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ then $\mathfrak{A}$ and the injection mapping constitute a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $J$ is the main involution. We now consider the other basic universal envelopes $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. For these we have the following

Theorem 6. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional central simple Jordan algebra of degree $m \geqq 4$ then $\mathfrak{J}$ is strongly special, that is, the canonical homomorphism of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ is an isomorphism. Moreover, for any $m \geqq 3, S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ coincides with the subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \otimes S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ of fixed elements under the exchange automorphism.

Proof. It is clear that the hypotheses and conclusions are linear properties in the sense of §2.4. Hence it is enough to prove the assertions for an algebraically closed base field. Then we can take $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{m}, J_{1}\right),(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ an associative composition algebra. If $m \geqq 4, \mathfrak{J}$ is strongly special by §3.6. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}=1$ or 2 then $\mathfrak{D}$ is generated by 1 and a single element. Then $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{V}_{1}$, by Theorem 3.9 (p. 148), if $m \geqq 3$. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}=4$ so that $\mathfrak{D}$ is a quaternion algebra (the only other possibility for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ ) then $\mathfrak{D}$ is generated by two elements. Then again Theorem 3.9 implies $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ if $m \geqq 4$. The only case remaining is $m=3, \mathfrak{D}$ quaternion. In this case Theorem 3.7 (p. 148) is applicable since it is easy to verify that $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)=[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$, $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, j)]$.

We shall now determine the structure of $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$. We distinguish the three cases: I. $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{A}$ is central simple; II. $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{J}, \mathfrak{B}$ an ideal. III. $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{A}$ is simple with center P a quadratic extension of $\Phi, J$ an involution of second kind. In I, the dimensionality of $\mathfrak{A}$ is a square $n^{2}$ and in II and III it has the form $2 n^{2}$. In all cases $n \geqq 3$ and we can identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. Moreover, in II, $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \cong \mathfrak{B}^{+}$so we can also identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with $\mathfrak{B}^{+}$. By Theorem $6, S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{V}_{1}$, the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{A}$ of fixed elements under the exchange automorphism. Hence in I, $\operatorname{dim} S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})=n^{2}\left(n^{2}+1\right) / 2$ and in II and III, $\operatorname{dim} S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})=n^{2}\left(2 n^{2}+1\right)$. We remark also that if the base field is algebraically closed then I and II are the only possibilities. We prove first the following

Theorem 7. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional special central simple Jordan algebra of degree $m \geqq 3, \mathfrak{A}=S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), J$ the main involution in $\mathfrak{A}$. (1) If $\mathfrak{A}$ is central simple, so $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A}=n^{2}$, then $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \Phi_{n(n+1) / 2}$ and $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ (the space of $J$-skew elements) are nonisomorphic irreducible unital bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ under the action $x . h=\frac{1}{2}(x h+h x)$. (2) Let $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{J}$ and assume $\mathfrak{B}$ has an involution $K$. Then $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{n^{2}} \oplus \Phi_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \Phi_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \Phi_{n(n+1) / 2} \oplus \Phi_{n(n+1) / 2}$ and we have the following nonisomorphic irreducible unital bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{B}^{+}$: (i) $\mathfrak{B}$, with the action of $b \in \mathfrak{B}^{+}$given by $x . b=\frac{1}{2}(x b+b x)$, (ii) $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{B}, K)$, with the action of $b \in \mathfrak{B}^{+}$given by $x . b=\frac{1}{2}\left(x b^{K}+b x\right)$, (iii) $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{B}, K)$ with $x . b=\frac{1}{2}\left(x b+b^{K} x\right)$, (iv) $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{B}, K)$ with $x . b=\frac{1}{2}\left(x b^{K}+b x\right)$, (v) $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{B}, K)$ with $x . b=\frac{1}{2}\left(x b+b^{K} x\right)$. (3) Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be simple with center a quadratic field $\mathbf{P}, J$ of second kind and assume $\mathfrak{A} / \mathbf{P}$ has an involution $K$ which commutes with $J$. Then $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{n^{2}} \oplus \mathrm{P}_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \mathrm{P}_{n(n+1) / 2}$ and we have the following nonisomorphic irreducible unital bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J):(\mathrm{i}) \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ with $x . h=\frac{1}{2}(x h+h x),(\mathrm{ii}) \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, K)$ with $x . h=\frac{1}{2}\left(h x+x h^{K}\right)$ (iii) $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, K)$ with $x . h=\frac{1}{2}\left(h x+x h^{K}\right)$.

Proof. (1) In this case $\mathfrak{A}$ is central simple and hence, as in the proofs of Theorem 4 and 5, we can identify $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ with the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak{\Phi}}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$ generated by the $R_{h}, h$ in the subalgebra $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ of $\mathfrak{U}^{+}$. We have $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \oplus \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and these two subspaces are invariant under the $R_{h}$, $h \in \mathfrak{J}$. If $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of $\Phi$ then $\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}, J\right) \cong\left(\Omega_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ or $\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}, J\right) \cong\left(\mathfrak{Q}_{n / 2}, J_{1}\right)$ where $n$ is even and $\mathfrak{Q}$ is a quaternion algebra with standard involution. Accordingly, $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)=n(n+1) / 2$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A}-n(n+1) / 2=n^{2} -n(n+1) / 2=n(n-1) / 2$, or $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)=n(n-1) / 2 \quad$ and $\quad \operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J) =n(n+1) / 2$. In either case we obtain the bound $n^{2}(n+1)^{2} / 4+n^{2}(n-1)^{2} / 4 =n^{2}\left(n^{2}+1\right) / 2$ for $\operatorname{dim} S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$. On the other hand, Theorem 6 shows that $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ and the latter has the dimensionality $n^{2}\left(n^{2}+1\right) / 2$. The fact that the bound is attained implies, as in the proof of Theorem 4, that the algebras of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ generated by the restrictions of the $R_{h}$ to these subspaces are the complete algebras $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{H}, \mathfrak{H})$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{S}, \mathfrak{S})$.

Moreover, we have $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \Phi_{n(n+1) / 2}$. It is clear that $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ are irreducible relative to the $R_{h}, h \in \mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$, and these are not isomorphic.
(2) Now assume that $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{B}^{+}$where $\mathfrak{B}$ is finite-dimensional central simple of dimensionality $n^{2}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ has the involution $K$. We now consider the $2 \times 2$ matrix algebra $\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ with matrix units $e_{i j}, i, j=1,2$. This is central simple and we have the isomorphism $b \rightarrow h=b e_{11}+b^{K} e_{22}$ of $\mathfrak{B}^{+}$into $\mathfrak{B}_{2}{ }^{+}$.
