Hence we can identify $\boldsymbol{S}_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ with the algebra of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ generated by the $R_{h}$, $h=b e_{11}+b^{K} e_{22}$. We now decompose $\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ as $\mathfrak{B}_{2}=\mathfrak{B} e_{11} \oplus \mathfrak{B} e_{22} \oplus \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{B}, K) e_{12} \oplus \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{B}, K) e_{21} \oplus \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{B}, K) e_{12} \oplus \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{B}, K) e_{21}$. One checks that these are invariant under the $R_{h}$ and hence are unital bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}$. Also it is clear that the bimodules $\mathfrak{B} e_{11}$ and $\mathfrak{B} e_{22}$ are isomorphic, so we may drop $\mathfrak{B} e_{22}$ and identify $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ with the subalgebra of the algebra of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{B} e_{11}+\mathfrak{B} e_{12} +\mathfrak{B} e_{21}$ generated by the $R_{h}, h=b e_{11}+b^{K} e_{22}$. Using the five invariant subspaces $\mathfrak{B} e_{11}, \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{B}, K) e_{12}, \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{S}) e_{21}, \mathfrak{S}\left((\mathfrak{B}, K) e_{12}, \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{B}, K) e_{21}\right.$ we obtain the following bound for $\operatorname{dim} S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}): n^{4}+n^{2}(n-1)^{2} / 4+n^{2}(n+1)^{2} / 4+n^{2}(n-1)^{2} / 4 +n^{2}(n+1)^{2} / 4=n^{2}\left(2 n^{2}+1\right)$. Since $\operatorname{dim} S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{V}_{1}=n^{2}\left(2 n^{2}+1\right)$ we can conclude that $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{n^{2}} \oplus \Phi_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \Phi_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \Phi_{n(n+1) / 2} \oplus \Phi_{n(n+1) / 2}$. Also it is clear that the five bimodules $\mathfrak{B} e_{11}, \cdots$ are irreducible. Moreover, no two of these are isomorphic since there exists an element in the algebra of linear transformations generated by the $R_{h}$ which acts as the identity on one of the subspaces and annihilates the other. It is immediate also that the five subspaces are isomorphic respectively to the bimodules $\mathfrak{B}, \cdots$ specified in the statement of the theorem.
(3) Here $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple with center a quadratic field $\mathbf{P}$ and $J$ is an involution of the second kind. Also we are assuming that $\mathfrak{A} / \mathbf{P}$ has an involution $K$ which commutes with $J$. Put $\theta=J K$. Then $\theta$ is an automorphism of period two in $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ whose restriction to $\mathbf{P}$ is also of period two. Let $G=\{1, \theta\}$ and form the crossed product ( $\mathfrak{A}, G, 1$ ). This is the set of elements of the form $a+b u, a$, $b \in \mathfrak{A}$ with the vector space composition as usual and multiplication given by $(a+b u)(c+d u)=\left(a c+b d^{\theta}\right)+\left(a d+b c^{\theta}\right) u$. It is straightforward to check that ( $\mathfrak{A}, G, 1$ ) is a central simple associative algebra containing $\mathfrak{A}$ as a subalgebra. Hence $(\mathfrak{A}, G, 1)^{+}$has the subalgebra $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ can be identified with the subalgebra of the algebra of linear transformations in ( $\mathfrak{A}, G, 1$ ) generated by the $R_{h}, h \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. We now have the decomposition $(\mathfrak{A}, G, 1)=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \oplus \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \oplus \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, K) u \oplus \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, K) u$. Clearly the first two are invariant under the $R_{h}, h \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. Also if $\xi$ is a $J$-skew element of P then $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \xi$ and $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is isomorphic as $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule to $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. If $x \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, K)$ and $h \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ then $x u . h=\frac{1}{2}\left(h x+x h^{\theta}\right) u =\frac{1}{2}\left(h x+x h^{K}\right) u \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, K) u$. Hence $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, K) u$ is invariant under the $R_{h}$ and it is clear that this is $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule isomorphic to $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, K)$ with $x . h=\frac{1}{2}\left(h x+x h^{K}\right)$. Similarly $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, K) u$ is invariant under the $R_{h}$ and is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, K)$ under the action indicated. It is clear also that if $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)+\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, K) u+\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, K) u$
then $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ can be identified with the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ generated by the restrictions of the $R_{h}, h \in \mathfrak{J}$, to $\mathfrak{M}$. We note also that the spaces $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, K) u$, $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, K) u$ are P -spaces and the action of the $R_{h}$ in these commutes with that of the $\rho \in \mathrm{P}$. It follows that we obtain the bound $n^{4}+2\left(\frac{1}{2} n(n-1)\right)^{2}+2\left(\frac{1}{2} n(n+1)\right)^{2} =n^{2}\left(2 n^{2}+1\right)$ for $\operatorname{dim} S_{1}^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$. Since this is attained, we see as before that $S_{1}^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{n^{2}} \oplus \mathbf{P}_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \mathbf{P}_{n(n+1) / 2}$. The other assertion is clear also. This completes the proof.

We shall obtain next the structure of the algebra $S_{1}$ "(J) without imposing the supplementary conditions of Theorem 7. For this purpose we recall some wellknown results on simple associative algebras. First, we note that if $\mathfrak{U}$ is finitedimensional simple over $\Phi$ then the center $\mathbf{P}$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ is a field and if $\operatorname{dim} \mathbf{P} / \Phi=r$ then $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A} / \Phi=n^{2} r$. If P is separable and $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of $\Phi$ then $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}$ is isomorphic to a direct sum of $r$ matrix algebras $\Omega_{n}$ (see, for example, Jacobson Theory of Rings, p. 115). It is an easy consequence of this and Theorem 6.4 that if $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ are finite-dimensional separable associative algebras then $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{B}$ is separable. Now assume that $\mathfrak{A}$ is finite-dimensional simple with center a Galois extension field $\mathbf{P} / \Phi$ such that $\operatorname{dim} \mathbf{P} / \Phi=r$. It is known that $\mathbf{P} \otimes \mathbf{P}=\mathbf{P}^{(1)} \oplus \mathbf{P}^{(2)} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathrm{P}^{(r)}$ where $\mathrm{P}^{(i)} \cong \mathrm{P}$ (Jacobson, Theory of Rings, p. 97). Since $\mathrm{P} \otimes \mathrm{P}$ is the center of $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{A}$ is separable it is clear that $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}^{(1)} \oplus \mathfrak{A}^{(2)} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{A}^{(\boldsymbol{r})}$ where the center of $\mathfrak{A}^{(i)}$ is isomorphic to P . Then $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A}^{(i)}=n_{i}{ }^{2} r$ and $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}{ }^{(i)}$ is isomorphic to a direct sum of $r$ matrix algebras $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{n_{i}}$. On the other hand, $(\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{A})_{\Omega} \cong \mathfrak{A}_{\Omega} \otimes \mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}$ is isomorphic to a direct sum of $r^{2}$ complete matrix algebras $\Omega_{n^{2}} \cong \Omega_{n} \otimes \Omega_{n}$. Since the decomposition of an algebra as a direct sum of simple ideals is unique we see that $n_{i}=n^{2}$. Thus $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{A}$ is isomorphic to a direct sum of $r$ simple algebras having centers isomorphic to P and dimensionalities $n^{4} r$. We shall require also the following

Lemma 1. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a central simple associative algebra of dimensionality $n^{2} \geqq 9$ and let $\mathfrak{B}$ be the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{A}$ of fixed points under the exchange automorphism. Then $\mathfrak{B}$ is a direct sum of two central simple algebras of dimensionalities $n^{2}(n-1)^{2} / 4$ and $n^{2}(n+1)^{2} / 4$ respectively.

Proof. Assume first that $\Phi$ is algebraically closed. Then $\mathfrak{A}=\Phi_{n}, n \geqq 3$, and we have the involution $X \rightarrow X^{t}$ in $\mathfrak{A}$. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is the Jordan algebra of symmetric elements under this involution then $\mathfrak{A}$ is a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence the first part of Theorem 7 shows that $\mathfrak{B} \cong \Phi_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \Phi_{n(n+1) / 2}$. Now let $\Phi$ be arbitrary and let $\Omega$ be its algebraic closure. Then $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega} \cong \Omega_{n}$ and the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{A}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}} \otimes \mathfrak{A}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ of fixed points under the exchange automorphism is isomorphic to $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{n(n+1) / 2}$. Hence $\mathfrak{B}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ has this structure and consequently $\mathfrak{B}$ is separable. Now $\mathfrak{B}$ is not simple since this would imply that $\mathfrak{B}_{\Omega}$ is a direct sum of ideals of the same dimensionality. Since $\mathfrak{B}_{\Omega} \cong \Omega_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \Omega_{n(n+1) / 2}$ it now follows that $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{B}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{B}_{2}$ where $\mathfrak{B}_{i}$ is an ideal, and $\mathfrak{B}_{1 \Omega} \cong \Omega_{n(n-1) / 2}$ and $\mathfrak{B}_{2 \Omega} \cong \Omega_{n(n+1) / 2}$.

Then $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ is central simple of dimensionality $n^{2}(n-1)^{2} / 4$ and $\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ is central simple of dimensionality $n^{2}(n+1)^{2} / 4$.
Lemma 2. Let $\eta$ be an automorphism of period two in a finite-dimensional simple associative algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ with center P and let $\mathfrak{B}$ be the subalgebra of $\eta$ fixed points. If $\mathrm{P}_{0} \equiv \mathfrak{B} \cap \mathrm{P} \subset \mathrm{P}$ then $\mathfrak{B}$ is simple with center $\mathrm{P}_{0}$. If $\mathrm{P}_{0}=\mathrm{P}$ then either $\mathfrak{B}$ is simple with center a quadratic extension field of $\mathbf{P}$, or (assuming the characteristic is not two) $\mathfrak{B}$ is a direct sum of two simple ideals with centers isomorphic to $\mathbf{P}$.
Proof. Assume first that $\mathrm{P}_{0} \subset \mathrm{P}$. Since $\eta$ maps P into itself and $\mathrm{P}_{0}$ is the subfield of P of $\eta$-fixed points it follows by Galois theory that P is a separable quadratic extension of $\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{0}}$. Since we may consider $\mathfrak{A}$ as an algebra over $\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{0}}$ we may assume for the sake of simplicity of notation that $\mathrm{P}_{0}=\Phi$ the base field. Let $\Omega$ be the algebraic closure of $\Phi$. Then $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega} \cong \Omega_{n} \oplus \Omega_{n}$ and the linear extension of $\eta$ is an automorphism of period two in $\mathfrak{A}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$. It follows that $\eta$ permutes the two simple components and consequently the algebra of $\eta$-fixed points of $\mathfrak{U}_{\Omega}$ is isomorphic to $\Omega_{n}$. Then $\mathfrak{B}_{\Omega} \cong \Omega_{n}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ is central simple over $\Phi=\mathrm{P}_{0}$. Next suppose $\mathrm{P}_{0}=\mathrm{P}$. Then we may as well assume that $\mathrm{P}=\Phi 1$. By the Skolem-Noether theorem $\eta$ is an inner automorphism so we have an element $c \in \mathfrak{A}$ such that $x^{\eta}=c^{-1} x c$, $x \in \mathfrak{A}$. Since $\eta^{2}=1, c^{2}=\gamma \in \Phi 1$. Clearly $\mathfrak{B}$ is the centralizer of $c$ in $\mathfrak{A}$. If $\gamma$ is not a square in $\Phi$ then $\Phi[c]$ is a field and $\mathfrak{B}$ is simple with center $\Phi[c]$ (see, for example, Jacobson's Theory of Rings, p. 104). If $c$ is a square then $\Phi[c]=\Phi[e]$ where $e$ is an idempotent. We have the two sided Peirce decomposition $\mathfrak{A}=e \mathfrak{A} e \oplus e \mathfrak{A}(1-e) \oplus(1-e) \mathfrak{A} e \oplus(1-e) \mathfrak{A}(1-e)$. It is easy to see that $\mathfrak{B}=e \mathfrak{A} e \oplus(1-e) \mathfrak{A}(1-e), e \mathfrak{A} e$ and $(1-e) \mathfrak{A}(1-e)$ are ideals in $\mathfrak{B}$. It is easy to see fom the Wedderburn theorem that these are central simple over $\Phi=P$.

We are now ready to prove
Theorem 8. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional special central simple Jordan algebra of degree $m \geqq 3, \mathfrak{A}=S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), J$ the main involution in $\mathfrak{A}$. Then we have the following possibilities for the structure of $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ :
(1) If $\mathfrak{A}$ is central simple, so $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A}=n^{2}$, then $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \Phi_{n(n+1) / 2}$.
(2) If $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{J}$ where $\mathfrak{B}$ is central simple and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=n^{2}$, then $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ is a direct sum of five central simple ideals, such that one of these is isomorphic to $\Phi_{n^{2}}$, two are anti-isomorphic and have dimensionality $n^{2}(n-1)^{2} / 4$ and two are anti-isomorphic and have dimensionality $n^{2}(n+1)^{2} / 4$.
(3) If $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple with center a quadratic field $\mathrm{P} / \Phi, \operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A}=2 n^{2}$, and $J$ is of second kind, then $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ is a direct sum of three simple ideals such that one of these is isomorphic to $\Phi_{n^{2}}$ and the other two have centers isomorphic to $\mathbf{P}$ and dimensionalities $n^{2}(n-1)^{2} / 2$ and $n^{2} /(n+1)^{2} / 2$ respectively.

Proof. (1) This case has been settled in Theorem 7.
(2) We know that $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ coincides with the subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ of $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{A}$ of fixed points under the exhange automorphism $\varepsilon$. We have $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{J}$ where $\mathfrak{B}$ is central simple and $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{A}=(\mathfrak{B} \otimes \mathfrak{B}) \oplus\left(\mathfrak{B} \otimes \mathfrak{B}^{J}\right) \oplus\left(\mathfrak{B}^{J} \otimes \mathfrak{B}\right) \oplus\left(\mathfrak{B}^{J} \otimes \mathfrak{B}^{J}\right)$. The exchange automorphism $\varepsilon$ maps the ideals $\mathfrak{B} \otimes \mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{J} \otimes \mathfrak{B}^{J}$ into themselves and interchanges the ideals $\mathfrak{B} \otimes \mathfrak{B}^{\boldsymbol{J}}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{\boldsymbol{J}} \otimes \mathfrak{B}$. It follows that $\mathfrak{V}_{1}$ is a direct sum of the two ideals consisting of the fixed points under the exchange automorphism in $\mathfrak{B} \otimes \mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{J} \otimes \mathfrak{B}^{J}$ respectively and an ideal isomorphic to $\mathfrak{B} \otimes \mathfrak{B}^{\text {J }}$. By Lemma 1, the first of these is a direct sum of two ideals which are central simple algebras of dimensionalities $n^{2}(n-1)^{2} / 4$ and $n^{2}(n+1)^{2} / 4$ respectively. The same is true of the ideals obtained from $\mathfrak{B}^{J} \otimes \mathfrak{B}^{J}$. Moreover, since $\mathfrak{B}^{\boldsymbol{J}} \otimes \mathfrak{B}^{\boldsymbol{J}}$ is anti-isomorphic to $\mathfrak{B} \otimes \mathfrak{B}$ it is clear that we have the anti-isomorphism of the components asserted in the theorem. The last ideal, isomorphic to $\mathfrak{B} \otimes \mathfrak{B}^{J}$, is isomorphic to $\Phi_{n^{2}}$ since $\mathfrak{B} \otimes \mathfrak{B}^{0} \cong \Phi_{n^{2}}$, by the theory of the Brauer group.
(3)Again $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{V}_{1}$. If $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of $\Phi$ then $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})_{\Omega} \cong S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}\right)$, and since $\Im_{\Omega}$ is as in (2), $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\Im)_{\Omega} \cong \Omega_{n^{2}} \oplus \Omega_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \Omega_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \Omega_{n(n+1) / 2} \oplus \Omega_{n(n+1) / 2}$. Since $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple with center the (separable) quadratic field $\mathbf{P}$ we have $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ where $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ is simple with center $\mathbf{P}_{i}$ isomorphic to $\mathbf{P}$. If $\varepsilon$ exchanges the two components $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ then $\mathfrak{V}_{1} \cong \mathfrak{A}_{1} \cong \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ and $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})_{\Omega} \cong \mathfrak{V}_{1 \Omega}$ is a direct sum of two simple ideals. This contradicts the fact that $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{I})_{\Omega}$ is a direct sum of five simple ideals. Hence $\varepsilon$ maps each $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ into itself and consequently it maps the center $\mathrm{P}_{i}$ of $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ into itself. Clearly $\mathfrak{B}_{1}=\mathfrak{B}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{B}_{2}$ where $\mathfrak{B}_{i}$ is the set of $\varepsilon$-fixed points of $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$. If the restriction $\varepsilon_{i}$ of $\varepsilon$ to $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ is the identity on $\mathbf{P}_{i}$ then either $\varepsilon_{i}=1$ so $\mathfrak{B}_{\boldsymbol{i}}=\mathfrak{A}_{\boldsymbol{i}}$ or $\varepsilon_{\boldsymbol{i}}$ is of period two. In the latter case, by Lemma 2, either $\mathfrak{B}_{\boldsymbol{i}}$ is simple with center a quadratic extension of $\mathrm{P}_{i}$ or $\mathfrak{B}_{i}$ is a direct sum of two simple ideals with centers isomorphic to $\mathrm{P}_{i}$. These three possibilities for $\mathfrak{B}_{i}$ give rise to the following respective possibilities for $\mathfrak{B}_{i \Omega}$ : (i) $\mathfrak{B}_{i \Omega}$ is a direct sum of two simple ideals of the same dimensionality, (ii) $\mathfrak{B}_{i \Omega}$ is a direct sum of four simple ideals of the same dimensionality, (iii) $\mathfrak{B}_{i \Omega}$ is a direct sum of four simple ideals having the same dimensionality by pairs. Next suppose $\varepsilon_{i}$ is not the identity on $\mathbf{P}_{\boldsymbol{i}}$. Then, by Lemma $2, \mathfrak{B}_{i}$ is central simple and we have (iv): $\mathfrak{B}_{i \Omega}$ is simple. If we take into account the possibilities (i)-(iv) and the fact that $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})_{\Omega} \cong \mathfrak{B}_{1 \Omega} \oplus \mathfrak{B}_{2 \Omega} \cong \Omega_{n^{2}} \oplus \Omega_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \Omega_{n(n-1) / 2} \oplus \Omega_{n(n+1) / 2} \oplus \Omega_{n(n+1) / 2}$ we see that one of the ideals, say $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$, is a direct sum of two simple ideals with centers isomorphic to P while $\mathfrak{B}_{2}$ is central simple. It is clear also that these ideals have dimensionalities $n^{2}(n-1)^{2} / 2$ and $n^{2}(n+1)^{2} / 2$. It remains to see that $\mathfrak{B}_{2} \cong \Phi_{n^{2}}$. Now $\mathfrak{J}$ is special. Hence we have the canonical homomorphism of $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ onto the multiplication algebra $M(\mathfrak{J})$ sending $\frac{1}{2}(a \otimes 1+1 \otimes a) \rightarrow R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Also since $\mathfrak{J}$ is central simple of dimensionality $n^{2}, M(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{n^{2}}$. Hence $\Phi_{n^{2}}$ is a homomorphic image of $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$. This implies that one of the simple components of $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ is isomorphic to $\Phi_{n^{2}}$. Clearly this must be $\mathfrak{B}_{2}$.
4. Bimodules for composition algebras and reduced Jordan Algebras. It is well
known that all modules for a finite-dimensional associative algebra are completely reducible if and only if the algebra is semisimple, that is, is a direct sum of simple ideals. Moreover, if $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{s}$ where the $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ are simple, then there are exactly $s$ isomorphism classes of irreducible $\mathfrak{A}$-modules. If $\mathfrak{I}_{j}$ is a minimal right ideal of $\mathfrak{A}_{j}$ then $\left\{\mathfrak{I}_{1}, \mathfrak{I}_{2}, \cdots, \mathfrak{I}_{s}\right\}$ is a set of representatives of these isomorphism classes. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra then we know that the bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}$ are just the right modules for the universal envelope $U(\mathfrak{J})$. The results of §§1-3 on the structure of $U(\mathfrak{J})=S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus U_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus \Phi z$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ finitedimensional central simple show that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is not of degree three then $U(\mathfrak{J})$ is semisimple. Hence the associative theory shows that the bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}$ are completely reducible and gives a determination of the (representatives of the isomorphism classes of) irreducible bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}$. The gap in the degree three case is due to the fact that for some $\mathfrak{J}$ of this type (e.g. $\mathfrak{J}$ exceptional), $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ are not isomorphic. We shall now give another method for dealing with unital bimodules for reduced simple Jordan algebras of degree $\geqq 3$ which will permit us to fill the gap we have indicated. This is based on the category isomorphism established in §3.5 of the category of unital bimodules for Jordan algebras of order $\geqq 3$ and that of certain bimodules for the coefficient algebra with involution. For reduced simple Jordan algebras of degree $\geqq 3$ this leads to the consideration of alternative bimodules with involution for composition algebras. We consider these first and we shall determine their structure by an inductive method which is due to McCrimmon in [4].

We recall that if $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a composition algebra with involution $j$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}>1$ then $\mathfrak{D}$ contains a composition subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}$ with $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}$ (p. 163). Moreover, $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ where $\mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ is the orthogonal complement of $\mathfrak{B}$ relative to the symmetric bilinear form associated with the quadratic form $Q$ such that $Q(x) 1=x \bar{x}=\bar{x} x$ (p. 163). We recall that $\mathfrak{D}$ is alternative and $\mathfrak{B}$ is associative and $\bar{v}=-v$, if $v \in \mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$. If $q$ is any element of $\mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ such that $Q(q)=\mu 1 \neq 0$ then $\mathfrak{B}^{\perp}=\mathfrak{B} q$ and we have the multiplication formula

$$
\begin{equation*}
(a+b q)(c+d q)=(a c+\mu \bar{d} b)+(d a+b \bar{c}) q \tag{10}
\end{equation*}
$$

for $a, b, c, d \in \mathfrak{B}$. We note also that the construction of an algebra of octonions from a quaternion algebra (p. 16) can be duplicated for any associative composition algebra ( $\mathfrak{B}, j$ ). As in the special case, let $\mu$ be any nonzero element of $\Phi$ and let $\mathfrak{D}$ be the vector space $\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}$ of pairs $(a, b), a, b \in \mathfrak{B}$ with multiplication defined, as in (10), by $(a, b)(c, d)=(a c+\mu \bar{d} b, d a+b \bar{c})$. Also, define $(a, b)^{j} =(\bar{a},-b)$. Then $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a composition algebra containing $\mathfrak{B}$ as the subalgebra of elements $(a, 0)$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{\perp}=\{(0, a)\}$.

If $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is any composition algebra then the vector space $\mathfrak{D}$ considered in the usual way as a bimodule for $\mathfrak{D}$ together with the involution $j$ constitute a unital alternative bimodule with involution for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. We shall call this the regular bimodule with involution for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ and denote it as reg $\mathfrak{D}$.

Next assume $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}>1$ and let $(\mathfrak{B}, j)$ be a composition subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ such that $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}$. Then it is clear that if we restrict the operators to $\mathfrak{B}$ then reg $\mathfrak{D}$ can be considered as a bimodule with involution for $(\mathfrak{B}, j)$. We have the decomposition $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ and the space $\mathfrak{B}$ is is a sub-bimodule for $(\mathfrak{B}, j)$. Moreover, $\mathfrak{B}^{\perp}=\mathfrak{B} q$ where $q \in \mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ and $Q(q) \neq 0$. By (10), we have $a(b q)=(b a) q$, $(b q) a=(b \bar{a}) q$ for $a, b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Also $\overline{b q}=-b q$. Hence $\mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ is also a sub-bimodule of reg $\mathfrak{D}$ considered as a bimodule for $(\mathfrak{B}, j)$. It is clear that the $(\mathfrak{B}, j)$-bimodule structure of $\mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ is independent of the containing algebra. In fact, we can give a direct description of this bimodule as follows.

It is convenient to give this construction for an arbitrary composition algebra $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be the underlying vector space and make $\mathfrak{D}$ into a bimodule with involution for ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ) by defining the bimodule compositions $x \circ d, d \circ x, x \in \mathfrak{D}$, $d \in(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ and $\bar{x}$ by

$$
\begin{equation*}
x \circ d=x \bar{d}, \quad d \circ x=x d, \quad \bar{x}=-x \tag{11}
\end{equation*}
$$

We shall call this bimodule with involution the Cayley bimodule with involution, cay $\mathfrak{D}$, for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. If $(\mathfrak{B}, j)$ is an associative composition algebra then we can imbed $(\mathfrak{B}, j)$ in a composition algebra $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ with $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}=2 \operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}$. If $q \in \mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ satisfies $Q(q) \neq 0$ then we have seen that $\mathfrak{B}^{\perp}=\mathfrak{B} q$. It is immediate that $x \rightarrow x q$ is an isomorphism of cay $\mathfrak{B}$ onto the sub- $(\mathfrak{B}, j)$-bimodule $\mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ of reg $\mathfrak{D}$ considered as a bimodule with involution for $(\mathfrak{B}, j)$. This implies that cay $\mathfrak{B}$ is unital and alternative if ( $\mathfrak{B}, j$ ) is an associative composition algebra. On the other hand, suppose ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ) is not associative and let $a, b, c \in \mathfrak{D}$ satisfy $[a, b, c] \neq 0$. Consider the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus$ cay $\mathfrak{D}$ as algebra with involution. We write the elements of $\mathfrak{E}$ as $(a, x), a \in \mathfrak{D}, x \in \operatorname{cay} \mathfrak{D}$. Then $\overline{(a, x)}+(a, x)=(a+\bar{a}, 0)=\alpha(1,0)$ where $\alpha \in \Phi$. Hence if $u=(a, x)$ then $u+\bar{u}$ is in the nucleus of $\mathfrak{E}$ so the associator $[u, u, v]=0$ if and only if $[\bar{u}, u, v]=0$. Now put $u=(\bar{c},-a), v=(\bar{b}, 0)$. Then a direct calculation shows that $[\bar{u}, u, v]=(0,-[a, b, c]) \neq 0$. Hence cay $\mathfrak{D}$ is not alternative. Thus cay $\mathfrak{D}$ is alternative if and only if $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative.

Let ( $\mathfrak{M}, j$ ) be a bimodule (with involution) for the algebra with involution ( $\mathfrak{A}, j$ ) and put $j^{*}=-j$ where $j$ is the operator in $\mathfrak{M}$. Then $x^{j^{*}}=-\bar{x}$. If $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ we have $(a x)^{j^{*}}=-\bar{x} \bar{a}=x^{j^{*}} \bar{a},(x a)^{j^{*}}=-\bar{a} \bar{x}=\bar{a} x^{j^{*}}$. Hence $\left(\mathfrak{M}, j^{*}\right)$ is a bimodule with involution for ( $\mathfrak{A}, j$ ). We shall call this the negative, $-\mathfrak{M}$, of $(\mathfrak{M}, j)$. In particular, we can apply this to reg $\mathfrak{D}$ and cay $\mathfrak{D}$ for the composition algebra $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ to obtain the bimodules - reg $\mathfrak{D}$ and - cay $\mathfrak{D}$.

If $(\mathfrak{M}, j)$ is a bimodule for $(\mathfrak{A}, j)$ then we shall say that $(\mathfrak{M}, j)$ is left free cyclic if ( $\mathfrak{M}, j$ ) contains an element $u$ which is either symmetric or skew such that the mapping $a \rightarrow a u$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ is a linear isomorphism onto $\mathfrak{M}$. It is clear that if $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a composition algebra then the four bimodules reg $\mathfrak{D},-\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D}$, cay $\mathfrak{D}$ and - cay $\mathfrak{D}$ are left free cyclic. In all of these we can take $u=1$. For reg $\mathfrak{D}$ and - cay $\mathfrak{D}$ this is symmetric and for - reg $\mathfrak{D}$, cay $\mathfrak{D}$ it is skew. We consider next
the homomorphisms of the bimodules reg $\mathfrak{D},-\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D}$, cay $\mathfrak{D},-\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D}$. For this we require the following

Lemma 1. Let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a unital alternative bimodule for $\mathfrak{D},(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ a composition algebra. (1) Let $a \in \mathfrak{D}$ satisfy $a^{2}=\alpha 1 \neq 0$ in $\Phi 1$ and let $u \in \mathfrak{M}$ satisfy $a u=u a$. Then $[a, u, b]=0$ for all $b \in \mathfrak{D}$. (2) Let $a \in \mathfrak{D}, v \in \mathfrak{M}$ satisfy $a v=v \bar{a}$. Then $a(v b)=v(\bar{a} b),(b v) a=(b \bar{a}) v$ for all $b \in \mathfrak{D}$.

Proof. (1) We have $\alpha[a, u, b]=\alpha(a u) b-\alpha a(u b)=\alpha(u a) b-a\left(u\left(a^{2} b\right)\right) =\alpha(u a) b-a(u(a(a b)))=\alpha(u a) b-(a u a)(a b)$ (by one of Moufang's identities applied to the split null extension by $\mathfrak{M})=\alpha(u a) b-\left(a^{2} u\right)(a b)=\alpha(u a) b-\alpha u(a b) =\alpha[u, a, b]=-\alpha[a, u, b]$. Hence $\alpha[a, u, b]=0$ and $[a, u, b]=0$. (2) We have $a(v b)-v(\bar{a} b)=a(v b)+v(a b)-v(a b)-v(\bar{a} b)=a(v b)+v(a b)-v(\alpha b)$ where $a+\bar{a}=\alpha 1, \alpha$ in $\Phi$. Hence $a(v b)-v(\bar{a} b)=a(v b)+v(a b)-(\alpha v) b$. Since $[a, v, b] +[v, a, b]=0$ we have $a(v b)+v(a b)=(a v) b+(v a) b$. Hence $a(v b)-v(\tilde{a} b) =(a v) b+(v a) b-((a+\bar{a}) v) b=(v a-\bar{a} v) b=0$. In a similar fashion one proves the second relation: $(b v) a=(b \bar{a}) v$.

Lemma 2. Let ( $\mathfrak{M}, j$ ) be a unital alternative bimodule for the composition algebra $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. (1) Assume $u$ is an element of $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $a u=u a, a \in \mathfrak{D}$ and $\bar{u}=u(\bar{u}=-u)$. Then the mapping $a \rightarrow a u$ is a homomorphism of $\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D}(-\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D})$ into $\mathfrak{M}$. (2) Assume $v$ is an element of $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $a v=v \bar{a}, a \in \mathfrak{D}$ and $\bar{v}=v (\bar{v}=-v)$. Then $a \rightarrow a v$ is a homomorphism of - cay $\mathfrak{D}$ (cay $\mathfrak{D}$ ) into $\mathfrak{M}$.

Proof. (1) Since $\mathfrak{D}$ has a basis of elements $a$ satisfying $a^{2}=\alpha 1 \neq 0, \alpha \in \Phi$, Lemma 1 (1) implies that $[a, u, b]$ for all $a, b \in \mathfrak{D}$. Hence $u$ is in the nucleus and consequently in the center of the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$. Now the mapping $a \rightarrow a u$ of reg $\mathfrak{D}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ sends $a b \rightarrow(a b) u=a(b u)$ and $b a \rightarrow(b a) u=b(a u)=b(u a) =(b u) a$. Hence this is a bimodule homomorphism. If $\bar{u}= \pm u$ then $( \pm \bar{a}) u=\bar{a} \bar{u} =\overline{u a}=\overline{a u}$. This shows that the homomorphism is one of the bimodule with involution reg $\mathfrak{D}$ or $-\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D}$ according as $\bar{u}=u$ or $\bar{u}=-u$. (2) The mapping $a \rightarrow a v$ of cay $\mathfrak{D}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ sends $b \circ a=a b, b \in \mathfrak{D}, a \in$ cay $\mathfrak{D}$ into $(a b) \bar{u}=v(\bar{b} \bar{a}) =b(v \bar{a})=b(a v)$, by Lemma 1 (2). Also $a \circ b=a \bar{b} \rightarrow(a \tilde{b}) v=(a v) b$. Hence the mapping is a bimodule homomorphism. The result about the involutions follows as in (1).

It is clear that the sub-bimodules with involution of reg $\mathfrak{D}$ are the ideals of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. Since $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is simple, reg $\mathfrak{D}$ is an irreducible bimodule with involution. Evidently the same is true of $-\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D}$. The definition (11) and the fact that $j=-1$ for cay $\mathfrak{D}$ shows that the sub-bimodules of cay $\mathfrak{D}$ and - cay $\mathfrak{D}$ are the right ideals of $\mathfrak{D}$. Since we have to consider these bimodules only in the case $\mathfrak{D}$ associative and in these cases $\mathfrak{D}$ is a direct sum of irreducible right ideals, it is clear that all four of the bimodules with involution we are considering are direct sums of irreducible ones. Clearly this holds also for their homomorphic images.

We now suppose $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}>1$ and $(\mathfrak{B}, j)$ is a composition subalgebra with $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}$. As before, we let $q$ be an element of $\mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ such that $Q(q) \neq 0$. Then $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B} q$. We now prove

Lemma 3. Let ( $a_{i}$ ) be an orthogonal basis for $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $a_{1}=1$. Then $\bar{a}_{i}=-a_{i}, i>1, Q\left(a_{i}\right)=\lambda_{i} \neq 0$ and $Q\left(a_{i} q\right) \neq 0$. Let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a unital alternative bimodule for $\mathfrak{D}$. (1) If $u \in \mathfrak{M}$ satisfies $b u=u b, b \in \mathfrak{B}$, then $v=q u$ satisfies $b v=v \bar{b}, b \in \mathfrak{B}$. (2) Let $v \in \mathfrak{M}$ satisfy $b v=v \bar{b}, b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then the elements $v_{i}=\left(a_{i} q\right) v+v\left(a_{i} q\right)$ satisfy $d v_{i}=v_{i} d, d \in \mathfrak{D}$, and the element $w=v+ \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i} Q\left(a_{i} q\right)^{-1}\left(a_{i} q\right) v_{i}$ satisfies $d w=w \bar{d}, d \in \mathfrak{D}$.

Proof. The first statement is clear since $a_{i}, i>1$, is orthogonal to 1 , and $\Phi 1^{\perp}$ is the space of skew elements. Since $Q$ is nondegenerate, we have $Q\left(a_{i}\right) \neq 0$ and $Q\left(a_{i} q\right)=Q\left(a_{i}\right) Q(q) \neq 0$. (1) If $u \in \mathfrak{M}$ satisfies $u b=b u, b \in \mathfrak{B}$, then by Lemma 1 (1), $[b, u, q]=0$. Then $b v=b(q u)=(b q) u=(q \bar{b}) u=q(\bar{b} u)=q(u \bar{b})=(q u) \bar{b}=v \bar{b}$. (2) Let $v \in \mathfrak{M}$ satisfy $b v=v \bar{b}, b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Put $c_{i}=a_{i} q$ and $v_{i}=c_{i} v+v c_{i}$. The set $\left\{a_{i}, c_{j}\right\}$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{D}$. Hence to prove the assertion in (2) on $d \in \mathfrak{D}$, it is enough to prove these for $d=a_{j}$ and $d=c_{j}$. We consider first $d=a_{j}$. We have $a_{j} v_{i}=a_{j}\left(c_{i} v+v c_{i}\right)=a_{j}\left(c_{i} v\right)+a_{j}\left(v c_{i}\right)=a_{j}\left(c_{i} v\right)+v\left(\bar{a}_{j} c_{i}\right)$ (by Lemma 1 (2)) $=a_{j}\left(c_{i} v\right)+v\left(c_{i} a_{j}\right)$. Similarly, we can show that $v_{i} a_{j}=\left(a_{j} c_{i}\right) v+\left(v c_{i}\right) a_{j}$. It follows by alternativity that $v_{i} a_{j}=a_{j} v_{i}$ and hence $v_{i} b=b v_{i}, b \in \mathfrak{B}$. We note next that the elements $c_{\boldsymbol{i}} \in \mathfrak{B}^{\perp}$ and $Q\left(c_{\boldsymbol{i}}\right) \neq 0$. Hence $\mathfrak{B}^{\perp}=\mathfrak{B} c_{\boldsymbol{i}}$ and consequently there exists elements $b_{j i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ such that $c_{j}=b_{j i} c_{i}$. Then $\left[c_{j}, v_{i}\right]=\left[b_{j i} c_{i}, v_{i}\right]=\left(b_{j i} c_{i}\right) v_{i} -v_{i}\left(b_{j i} c_{i}\right)=b_{j i}\left[c_{i}, v_{i}\right]$ by Lemma 1 (1) and the result just proved. Now $\left[c_{i}, v_{i}\right] =c_{i}\left(c_{i} v+v c_{i}\right)=-\left(c_{i} v+v c_{i}\right) c_{i}=\left(c_{i}^{2} v-v c_{i}^{2}\right)=0$ since $c_{i}^{2} \in \Phi 1$. Hence $\left[c_{j}, v_{i}\right]=0$, which completes the proof of the first statement in (2). Let $w=v+\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i} Q\left(c_{i}\right)^{-1} c_{i} v_{\imath}$. Since $a_{j} v_{i}=v_{i} a_{j}$, by Lemma 1 (1), we have $a_{j}\left(c_{i} v_{i}\right)=\left(a_{j} c_{i}\right) v_{i}=\left(c_{i} \bar{a}_{j}\right) v_{i}=c_{i}\left(\bar{a}_{j} v_{i}\right) =c_{i}\left(v_{i} \bar{a}_{j}\right)=\left(c_{i} v_{i}\right) \bar{a}_{j}$. Also by hypothesis, $a_{j} v=v a_{j}$. Hence $a_{j} w=w \bar{a}_{j}$. Again, by Lemma 1 (1), we have $c_{j}\left(c_{i} v_{i}\right)-\left(c_{i} v_{i}\right) \bar{c}_{j}=\left(c_{j} c_{i}-c_{i} \bar{c}_{j}\right) v_{i}$. Since $c_{j}=a_{j} q$ we have $c_{j} c_{i}=c_{i} \bar{c}_{j}$ if $i \neq j$ and $c_{i}^{2}-c_{i} \bar{c}_{i}=2 c_{\imath}^{2}=-2 Q\left(c_{i}\right) 1$. Hence $c_{j}\left(c_{i} v_{i}\right)-\left(c_{i} v_{i}\right) \bar{c}_{j} =-2 Q\left(c_{i}\right) \delta_{i j} v_{i}$ and $c_{j}\left(\sum_{i} c_{i} v_{i}\right)-\left(\sum_{i} c_{i} v_{i}\right) \bar{c}_{j}=-2 Q\left(c_{j}\right) v_{j}$. Also $c_{j} v-v \bar{c}_{j}=c_{j} v+v c_{j}=v_{j}$. Hence $c_{j} w=w \bar{c}_{j}$.

We can now prove the following
Theorem 9. (1) Any unital alternative bimodule with involution for a composition algebra $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a sum of homomorphic images of one of the four bimodules reg $\mathfrak{D},-\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D}$, cay $\mathfrak{D},-$ cay $\mathfrak{D}$, where the last two can be dropped if $\mathfrak{D}$ is not associative. (2) Any unital alternative bimodule with involution for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is completely reducible and any irreducible one is isomorphic to an irreducible component of reg $\mathfrak{D},-\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D}$, cay $\mathfrak{D}$ or $-\operatorname{cay} \mathfrak{D}$ if $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative and to an irreducible component of reg $\mathfrak{D}$ or-reg $\mathfrak{D}$ if $\mathfrak{D}$ is not associative (hence an algebra of octonions).

Proof. Since the four bimodules with involution, reg $\mathfrak{D}$, $-\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D}$, cay $\mathfrak{D}$, - cay $\mathfrak{D}$ are completely reducible, the complete reducibility of unital alternative
bimodules with involution will follow from (1). We note also that if $\mathfrak{D}$ is an algebra of octonions then, as is easily verified, the only right ideals in $\mathfrak{D}$ are $\mathfrak{D}$ and 0 (ex. 5, p. 170). Hence cay $\mathfrak{D}$ and - cay $\mathfrak{D}$ are irreducible. Since these are not alternative it is clear that we can drop these if $\mathfrak{D}$ is not associative. Hence everything will follow if we can show that if $(\mathfrak{M}, j)$ is a unital alternative bimodule for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ then $\mathfrak{M}$ is a sum of homomorphic images of $\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D}$, - reg $\mathfrak{D}$, cay $\mathfrak{D}$ or - cay $\mathfrak{D}$. We shall prove this by induction on $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}$. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}=1, \mathfrak{D}=\Phi 1$ and $(\mathfrak{M}, j)$ is just a vector space with a linear transformation $j$ of period two. Then $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{-1}$ where $\mathfrak{M}_{i}=\left\{x \mid x^{j}=i x\right\}$. Hence the result is clear in this case. Now assume $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}>1$ and let $(\mathfrak{B}, j)$ be a composition subalgebra such that $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}$. Then we may assume that ( $\mathfrak{M}, j$ ) as bimodule with involution for ( $\mathfrak{B}, j$ ) is a sum of homomorphic images of reg $\mathfrak{B}$, - reg $\mathfrak{B}$, cay $\mathfrak{B}$, - cay $\mathfrak{B}$. If $u$ is the image of 1 under a homomorphism of one of these bimodules with involution into $\mathfrak{M}$ then $u$ is a generator of the image and $u^{j}= \pm u$, and either $b u=u b, b \in \mathfrak{B}$, or $b u=u \bar{b}, b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Our result will follow if we can show that any such $u$ is contained in a homomorphic image of one of the basic bimodules reg $\mathfrak{D}$, -reg $\mathfrak{D}$, cay $\mathfrak{D}$, - cay $\mathfrak{D}$. Suppose first that $u=v$ satisfies $b v=v \bar{b}, b \in \mathfrak{B}, \bar{v}= \pm v$. Let $v_{i}$ and $w$ be the elements given in (2) of Lemma 3. Then $d v_{i}=v_{i} d$ and $d w=w \bar{d}$, $d \in \mathfrak{D}$. Also $v_{i}=\left(a_{i} q\right) v+v\left(a_{i} q\right)$ and $w=v+\frac{1}{2} \sum Q\left(a_{i} q\right)^{-1}\left(a_{i} q\right) v_{i}$. Hence $\overline{v_{i}}= \pm v\left(\overline{\left.a_{i} q\right)} \pm\left(\overline{a_{i} q}\right) \bar{v}=\mp v\left(a_{i} q\right) \mp\left(a_{i} q\right) v=\mp v_{i}\right.$ and $\bar{w}= \pm v \pm \frac{1}{2} \sum Q\left(a_{i} q\right)^{-1} v_{i}\left(a_{i} q\right) = \pm v \pm \frac{1}{2} \sum Q\left(a_{i} q\right)^{-1}\left(a_{i} q\right) v_{i}$. Hence, by Lemma 2, there is a homomorphism of one of our basic $\mathfrak{D}$-bimodules into $\mathfrak{M}$ mapping 1 into any $v_{i}$ or into $w$. Moreover, it is clear from the definition of $w$ that $v$ is contained in the sum of these homomorphic images. Next assume $u b=b u, b \in \mathfrak{B}, \bar{u}= \pm u$. By Lemma 3 (1), $v=q u$ satisfies $v b=\bar{b} v, b \in \mathfrak{B}$. The same condition holds for the elements $v+\bar{v}$ and $v-\bar{v}$ which are respectively symmetric and skew. The result we have established shows that these elements are contained in a sum of homomorphic images of our four basic bimodules. Hence the same is true of $u=q^{-1} v=\frac{1}{2} q^{-1}(v+\bar{v}) +\frac{1}{2} q^{-1}(v-\bar{v})$. This completes the proof.

We shall now determine representatives of the isomorphism classes of irreducible unital bimodules for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. Since the category isomorphism for bimodules of a Jordan matrix algebra is one with associative bimodules of the associative coefficient algebra if the order $n \geqq 4$ and with Jordan admissible bimodules if $n=3$, we shall need to sort out these bimodules from our list of representatives. We shall distinguish the following cases for the structure of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ :
I. $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi 1, j=1$. Here $\operatorname{cay} \mathfrak{D}=\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D}$ is one dimensional and hence irreducible. Hence we have two nonisomorphic irreducible $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$-bimodules: reg $\mathfrak{D}$ and -reg $\mathfrak{D}$.
$\mathrm{II}_{\mathrm{a}} . \quad \mathfrak{D}=\Phi e_{1} \oplus \Phi e_{2}$ where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents such that $e_{1}+e_{2}=1, \bar{e}_{1}=e_{2}, \bar{e}_{2}=e_{1}$. We have seen that reg $\mathfrak{D}$ is irreducible as bimodule with involution. A direct verification shows that the linear mapping in $\mathfrak{D}$ which interchanges $e_{1}+e_{2}$ and $e_{1}-e_{2}$ is an isomorphism of reg $\mathfrak{D}$ onto -reg $\mathfrak{D}$. Hence
we drop - reg $\mathfrak{D}$. For cay $\mathfrak{D}$ we have $j=-1$ so $\Phi e_{1}$ and $\Phi e_{2}$ are sub-bimodules. These are also sub-bimodules of - cay $\mathfrak{D}$. Clearly they are irreducible. Also it is immediate that no two of these are isomorphic. Hence we have five isomorphism classes of irreducible $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$-bimodules. Since $\mathfrak{D}$ has a single generator $a=e_{1}-e_{2}$ it is clear that all bimodules for $\mathfrak{D}$ are associative.
$\mathrm{II}_{\mathrm{b}} . \quad \mathfrak{D}$ is a quadratic field $\Phi[l], l^{2}=\lambda 1, \bar{l}=-l$. reg $\mathfrak{D}$ is irreducible and isomorphic to $-\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D}$ under the mapping $x \rightarrow l x$. cay $\mathfrak{D}$ is irreducible. We have three nonisomorphic $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$-bimodules: reg $\mathfrak{D}$, cay $\mathfrak{D}$, - cay $\mathfrak{D}$. All are associative.
$\mathrm{III}_{\mathrm{a}} . \mathfrak{D}$ is a split quaternion algebra, $j$ the standard involution. reg $\mathfrak{D}$ and -reg $\mathfrak{D}$ are irreducible, associative and not isomorphic. The last assertion can be seen by comparing dimensionalities of the symmetric elements of the two bimodules with involution. cay $\mathfrak{D}$ is a direct sum of two isomorphic irreducible bimodules. To see this let $e_{i j}, i, j=1,2$ be a matrix basis for $\mathfrak{D} \cong \Phi_{2}$. Then $\mathfrak{D}=e_{11} \mathfrak{D} \oplus e_{22} \mathfrak{D}$ and the $e_{i i} \mathfrak{D}$ are minimal right ideals; hence irreducible subbimodules of cay $\mathfrak{D}$ ( $j=-1$ for this). The mapping $x \rightarrow e_{21} x$ is an isomorphism of $e_{11} \mathfrak{D}$ onto $e_{22} \mathfrak{D}$. We now obtain the nonisomorphic irreducible bimodules $e_{11} \mathfrak{D}$ and $-e_{11} \mathfrak{D}$. It is easily seen that cay $\mathfrak{D}$ ( - cay $\mathfrak{D}$ ) is not associative. This implies that $e_{11} \mathfrak{D}\left(-e_{11} \mathfrak{D}\right)$ is not associative. The first of these is Jordan admissible, the second not. Hence we have two irreducible associative bimodules and altogether we have three alternative Jordan admissible ones.
$\mathrm{III}_{\mathrm{b}}$. $\mathfrak{D}$, a quaternion division algebra, standard involution. As in $\mathrm{III}_{\mathrm{a}}$ we obtain two irreducible associative bimodules reg $\mathfrak{D}$, -reg $\mathfrak{D}$ and two irreducible alternative not-associative bimodules cay $\mathfrak{D}$, - cay $\mathfrak{D}$. The first is Jordan admissible, the second is not.
IV. $\mathfrak{D}$, an algebra of octonions, standard involution. We have two irreducible unital alternative bimodules: reg $\mathfrak{D}$ and - reg $\mathfrak{D}$. The rirst is Jordan admissible but not the second.

Now let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a reduced simple Jordan algebra of degree $n \geqq 3$. Then $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{\boldsymbol{r}}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a composition algebra. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is central simple and if $n \geqq 4$, the results of the last section (Theorems 6 and 8) show that $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong S_{1}^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ and give the structure of this algebra. On the other hand, the category isomorphism between the category of unital Jordan bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}$ and the category of unital associative bimodules for the (associative) composition algebra and Theorem 9 imply that every unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ is completely reducible. This implies that $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is semisimple. Also the determination of the unital irreducible associative bimodules for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ can be used to give a determination of the irreducible unital Jordan bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}$. This will give the structure of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. This method can be used to recover the results of §3. We leave the details to the reader and proceed to use the present method to investigate $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$, $\Im$ central simple of degree three, which we were unable to determine by the methods of §3.

Theorem 10. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a reduced simple Jordan algebra of degree three, so $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a composition algebra. Then we have the following possibilities for the structure of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ :
I $\quad U_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{3} \oplus \Phi_{6} \quad$ if $\quad \mathfrak{D}=\Phi$.
$\mathrm{II}_{\mathrm{a}} \quad U_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{9} \oplus \Phi_{3} \oplus \Phi_{3} \oplus \Phi_{6} \oplus \Phi_{6} \quad$ if $\mathfrak{D} \cong \Phi \oplus \Phi$.
$\mathrm{II}_{\mathrm{b}} \quad U_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{9} \oplus \mathfrak{D}_{3} \oplus \mathfrak{D}_{6}$ if $\mathfrak{D} / \Phi$ is a quadratic field.
$\mathrm{III}_{\mathrm{a}} \quad U_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{15} \oplus \Phi_{21} \oplus \Phi_{6} \quad$ if $\quad \mathfrak{D}$ is a split quaternion algebra.
$\mathrm{III}_{\mathbf{b}} \quad U_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{15} \oplus \Phi_{21} \oplus \mathfrak{D}_{3}$ if $\mathfrak{D}$ is a quaternion division algebra.
IV $\quad U_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{27}$ if $\mathfrak{D}$ is an algebra of octonions.
Proof. Since the bimodules with involution for the coefficient algebra $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ are completely reducible the same is true, by §3.5, of the Jordan bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is semisimple and the simple components of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ are in $1-1$ correspondence with the isomorphism classes of irreducible unital bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}$. The latter are the bimodules associated with the unital irreducible bimodules for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ which are alternative Jordan admissible. We recall also that by the associative theory, if $\mathfrak{M}$ is a unital irreducible right module for $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ ( $=$ unital irreducible bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ ) and $\Delta$ is the centralizer of $\mathfrak{M}$, that is, the algebra of linear transformations which commute with the mappings in $\mathfrak{M}$ corresponding to $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ then $\Delta$ is a division algebra and the simple component of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ corresponding to $\mathfrak{M}$ is isomorphic to the matrix algebra $\Delta^{\circ}{ }_{r}$ where $r$ is the dimensionality of $\mathfrak{M}$ considered as vector space over $\Delta^{\circ}$. If we apply these results we can easily obtain the list stated in the theorem. We consider IV first. Here we have just one irreducible Jordan admissible unital alternative bimodule for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ and hence one irreducible unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$. To find this it is unnecessary to go through the procedure indicated since $\mathfrak{J}$ itself as regular bimodule is unital irreducible by the simplicity of $\mathfrak{J}$. Also the centralizer is $\Phi$ since $\mathfrak{J}$ is central simple. Since $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi=27$ we have $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{27}$. Next we consider $\mathrm{III}_{\mathrm{b}}: \mathfrak{D}$ a quaternion division algebra. The results show that there are three unital irreducible bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}$ associated with reg $\mathfrak{D},-\operatorname{reg} \mathfrak{D}$ and cay $\mathfrak{D}$ respectively. Since the first two are associative the corresponding split extensions are associative and the split extension by the associated bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}$ are special. Hence these are irreducible right modules for $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ and are therefore the ones we obtained in Theorem 7. These give the simple components $\Phi_{15}$ and $\Phi_{21}$ of $S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ and of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. The remaining irreducible bimodule cay $\mathfrak{D}$ is not associative and the associated bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ is not special. Since $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{H}\left((\text { cay } \mathfrak{D})_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and $j=-1$ it is immediate that $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M} / \Phi=12$. Since the actions of the algebra $\mathfrak{D}$ on cay $\mathfrak{D}$ consist of right multiplications and since $\mathfrak{D}$ is associative it is clear that the centralizer of cay $\mathfrak{D}$ is the algebra of left multiplications by elements of $\mathfrak{D}$. By the category isomorphism the same is true of $\mathfrak{M}$. Hence the simple component of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ corresponding to $\mathfrak{M}$ is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{D}_{r}$ where $r$ is the dimensionality of $\mathfrak{M} / \Delta$. Since $\mathfrak{M} / \Phi=12$ and $\Delta / \Phi=4$ we have $r=3$ which completes the proof in this case.

The consideration of $\mathrm{III}_{\mathrm{a}}$ is almost identical with this and the remaining cases are easier, particularly, if we take into account our earlier results. We shall therefore omit the remaining details.

A comparison of Theorem 8 with Theorem 10 shows that the only reduced simple Jordan algebras of degree $\geqq 3$ which are not strongly special are the algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{D}$ is either a quaternion algebra or an algebra of octonions. It follows that all central simple Jordan algebras of degree $\geqq 3$ are strongly special with the exception of the exceptional Jordan algebras (which become $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right), \mathfrak{D}$ a split octonion algebra if the base field is extended to its algebraic closure $\Omega$ ) and the algebras of degree three which are of symplectic type in the sense that $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right), \mathfrak{D}$ a split quaternion algebra. The results of the last section give the structure of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}(\mathfrak{J})$ for the strongly special central simple algebras of degree $\geqq 3$. We remark also that our study of meson algebras shows that the central simple Jordan algebras of degree two are also strongly special (Theorem 3) and gives the structure of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ for these $\mathfrak{J}$. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is of degree 1 then $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi$ and everything is trivial. We now treat the missing case in the following

Theorem 11. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is a central simple Jordan algebra of degree three and symplectic type then $\mathfrak{J}$ is reduced; hence the structure of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is given in Theorem 10 (cases $\mathrm{III}_{\mathrm{a}}$ and $\mathrm{III}_{\mathrm{b}}$ ). If $\mathfrak{J}$ is an exceptional central simple Jordan algebra (finite-dimensional) then $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi_{27}$.

Proof. For the first part we note that $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is a central simple associative algebra with involution such that $\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}, J\right) \cong\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a quaternion composition algebra. We have $\mathfrak{U} \cong \Delta_{r}$ where $\Delta$ is a central division algebra which has an involution. Also $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A} / \Phi=36=r^{2} s$ where $s=\operatorname{dim} \Delta / \Phi$. Since $\mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{A} \cong \mathfrak{A} \otimes \mathfrak{A}^{\circ} \cong \Phi_{36}$ it follows from the theory of the Brauer group (see, for example, Jacobson, Theory of Rings, p. 109) that $s$ is a power of two. Hence the only possibilities for $\Delta$ are $\Delta=\Phi$ or $\Delta$ is a quaternion algebra. In the first case, $\mathfrak{A} \cong \Phi_{6}$ and since $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)=15,(\mathfrak{A}, J) \cong\left(\Phi_{6}, K\right)$ where $K$ has the form $X \rightarrow S^{-1} X^{t} S, S=\operatorname{diag}\left\{\left(\begin{array}{rl}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{array}\right),\left(\begin{array}{rr}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{array}\right),\left(\begin{array}{rr}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{array}\right)\right\}$. Thus $(\mathfrak{A}, J) \cong\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a split quaternion algebra with canonical involution. If $\Delta$ is a quaternion division algebra, then $(\mathfrak{A}, J) \cong\left(\Delta_{3}, K\right)$ where $K$ has the form $X \rightarrow a^{-1} \bar{X}^{t} a$ where $x \rightarrow \bar{x}$ is the canonical involution in $\Delta$ and $a=\operatorname{diag}\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\right\}$ where either $\bar{a}_{i}=a_{i}$ or $\bar{a}_{i}=-a_{i}$ for all $i$. In the first case $a_{i}=\gamma_{i} 1, \gamma_{i} \in \Phi$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{H}\left(\Delta_{3}, K\right)=15$. In the second case, it is immediate that $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{H}\left(\Delta_{3}, K\right)=21$. Since $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)=15$ the second case is ruled out, so $K$ is a canonical involution and $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is reduced. Now suppose $\mathfrak{J}$ is finitedimensional central simple and exceptional. Then $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is an algebra of octonions. It follows from Theorem 10 that $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})_{\Omega} \cong U_{1}(\mathfrak{J} \Omega) \cong \Omega_{27}$.

Hence $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is simple. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is central simple, $M(\mathfrak{J})=\Phi_{27}$ and since this is a homomorphic image of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ we have $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=\Phi_{27}$.
5. Separability of $\mathfrak{J}$ and $U(\mathfrak{J})$. We devote this section to the proof of the following fundamental theorem.

Theorem 12. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1. Then the following three conditions on $\mathfrak{J}$ are equivalent: (i) $\mathfrak{J}$ is separable, (ii) $U(\mathfrak{J})$ is separable, (iii) $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is separable. Moreover, these conditions imply that $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is separable and the converse holds if $\mathfrak{J}$ is special.

Proof. Since a finite-dimensional Jordan (associative) algebra with 1 is separable if and only if the algebra obtained by extending the base field to its algebraic closure is semisimple we may assume the base field is algebraically closed and replace "separable" by "semisimple" in the statement of the theorem. Suppose first that $\mathfrak{J}$ is not semisimple so $\mathfrak{J}$ contains a nonzero solvable ideal $\Re$. Then, by Theorem 5.2, the images of $\Re$ under the canonical homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $U(\mathfrak{J}), U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ generates a nil ideal in these algebras. Moreover, the images in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ and $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ are not zero and the same is true of the image in $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ if $\mathfrak{J}$ is special. Hence $U(\mathfrak{J})$ and $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ are not semisimple and $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is not semisimple if $\mathfrak{J}$ is special. Now assume $\mathfrak{J}$ is semisimple. We shall prove that $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ are semisimple, using induction on $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}$. This will imply that $U(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi z \oplus S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is semisimple. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}=1$ then $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=\Phi 1$ and $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=\Phi 1$ so the result is clear. Now suppose $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2}$ where the $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ are nonzero ideals. By Theorem 2.5, $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right) \oplus S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ and, by Theorem 2.16, $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right) \oplus U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right) \oplus S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right) \otimes S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ and since $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}_{i}<\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}$ we may assume that $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{I}_{1}\right), S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{I}_{2}\right), U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{I}_{1}\right)$ and $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ are semisimple. Then $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right) \otimes S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ is semisimple and hence $S_{1}(\mathfrak{I})$ and $U_{1}(\mathfrak{I})$ are semisimple. Hence we may assume $\mathfrak{I}$ is simple and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}>1$. Then the degree $\operatorname{deg} \mathfrak{J} \geqq 2$ and if $\operatorname{deg} \mathfrak{J}=2, S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ are semisimple by the results on Clifford and meson algebras in §§1,2. If $\operatorname{deg} \mathfrak{J} \geqq 3, S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=0$ if $\mathfrak{J}$ is exceptional, and if $\mathfrak{J}$ is special then $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is semisimple by Martindale's theorem (cf. §5.7). Also $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is semisimple by the results of the §§3, 4 . This completes the proof.

Remark. The foregoing proof of the second half of the theorem rests heavily on the structure theory and the results on the representation theory of §§1-4. In the next chapter we shall give a general proof of the result in the characteristic zero case which does not require these detailed results. This will be based on the theory of Lie algebras.
Theorem 12 has the following immediate consequence.
Corollary. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional separable Jordan algebra then every bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ is completely reducible.
6. The Theorem of Albert-Penico-Taft. In this section we consider the finite-
dimensional Jordan algebra extensions of separable Jordan algebras $\mathfrak{J}$. In §2.8 we defined a (Jordan) extension of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ by a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{M}$ as a short exact sequence $0 \rightarrow \mathfrak{M}_{\alpha} \underset{\beta}{\mathfrak{B}} \mathfrak{J} \rightarrow 0$ where $\mathfrak{E}$ is Jordan. We now assume $\mathfrak{J}$, $\mathfrak{E}$ and $\mathfrak{M}$ are finite dimensional and $\mathfrak{J}$ is separable. Without loss of generality we may assume that $\mathfrak{M}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{E}$ and $\alpha$ is the injection mapping. Then $\mathfrak{J} \cong \mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$. We shall show that any extension of the type indicated splits. This is equivalent to showing that if $\mathfrak{E}$ is a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{M}$ an ideal in $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$ is separable then there exists a subalgebra $\mathfrak{K}$ of $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{K} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ (cf. §2.8). This theorem for solvable $\mathfrak{M}$ was first proved by Albert for special Jordan algebras of characteristic 0, by Penico for arbitrary Jordan algebras of characteristic 0, and by Taft in the general case. We shall therefore call the splitting theorem for solvable $\mathfrak{M}$ the Albert-Penico-Taft theorem.
We shall now make a number of reductions of the general theorem to some special cases. For these it will be convenient to collect the following simple consequences of the structure theory of finite-dimensional Jordan algebras.

Lemma 1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with radical (= maximal solvable ideal) $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$. (1) If $\mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$ then $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{B}=\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J} \cap \mathfrak{B}$. Hence $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$. (2) If $\mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal such that $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B}$ is semisimple then the radicals of $\mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{J}$ coincide. (3) If $\mathfrak{B}$ is a semisimple ideal and $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B}$ is semisimple then $\mathfrak{J}$ is semisimple and $\mathfrak{B}$ is a direct summand of $\mathfrak{J}$. (4) If $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{J}$ is the Jordan algebra obtained by adjoining an identity element 1 to $\mathfrak{J}$ then $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ and $\mathfrak{J}$ have the same radical. (5) If $e$ is an idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}$ then $\operatorname{rad}\left(\mathfrak{J} U_{e}\right) =(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}) U_{\boldsymbol{e}}$.

Proof. (1) Clearly $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J} \cap \mathfrak{B} \subseteq \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{B}$ since $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J} \cap \mathfrak{B}$ is a solvable ideal in $\mathfrak{B}$. Also $\mathfrak{B} /(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J} \cap \mathfrak{B}) \cong(\mathfrak{B}+\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}) / \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ which is an ideal in the semisimple algebra $\mathfrak{J} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J}$. Since any ideal in a semisimple Jordan algebra is a direct summand and hence is semisimple, it follows that $\mathfrak{B} /(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J} \cap \mathfrak{B})$ is semisimple. This and $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J} \cap \mathfrak{B} \subseteq \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{B}$ imply that $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{B}=\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J} \cap \mathfrak{B}$. (2) Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be an ideal such that $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B}$ is semisimple. Since $(\mathfrak{B}+\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}) / \mathfrak{B} \cong \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J} /(\mathfrak{B} \cap \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J})$ this is a solvable ideal in $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B}$. Hence it is 0 . Thus $\mathfrak{B}+\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{B} \supseteq \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$. (3) Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a semisimple ideal and assume $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B}$ is semisimple. Then, by (2), $\mathfrak{B} \supseteq \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$. Since $\mathfrak{B}$ is semisimple this implies that $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}=0$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}$ is semisimple. (4) Let $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{J}$ the algebra obtained by adjoining the identity 1 to $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ so rad $\mathfrak{J}$ is a solvable ideal in $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Since $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J} \cong \Phi 1 \oplus(\mathfrak{J} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{J} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ and $(\Phi 1 \oplus(\mathfrak{J} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J}) /(\mathfrak{J} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J}) \cong \Phi 1$ are semisimple, $\Phi 1 \oplus(\mathfrak{J} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J})$ is semisimple, by (3). Hence $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ is semisimple and $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}=\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. (5) Let $e$ be an idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}$. Then clearly $(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}) U_{e} \subseteq \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J} \cap \mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ and if $z \in \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J} \cap \mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ then $z=z U_{e} \in(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}) U_{e}$. Hence $(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}) U_{e} =\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J} \cap \mathfrak{J} U_{\boldsymbol{e}}$ is a solvable ideal in $\mathfrak{J} U_{\boldsymbol{e}}$. To prove that this is the radical we have to show that $\mathfrak{J} U_{e} /(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}) U_{e}$ is semisimple. Since $\mathfrak{J} U_{e} /(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}) U_{e} \cong(\mathfrak{J} / \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}) U_{e^{\prime}}$ where
$e^{\prime}=e+\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ it suffices to show that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is semisimple then $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ is semisimple. By Corollary 1 to Theorem 5.7, $\mathfrak{J}$ is semisimple if and only if it has no absolute zero divisor $\neq 0$. Also we know that any absolute zero divisor of $\mathfrak{J} U_{e}$ is an absolute zero divisor of $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence the result is clear.

Reduction I. To the Albert-Penico-Taft theorem. Let E be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{M}$ an ideal in $\mathfrak{C}$ such that $\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$ is separable. If $\Re$ is the radical of $\mathfrak{M}$ then, by Lemma 1 (2), $\Re$ is the radical of $\mathfrak{E}$ and $\mathfrak{E} / \Re$ is semisimple. Now $\mathfrak{M} / \Re$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{E} / \Re$. Hence $\mathfrak{E} / \Re=(\mathfrak{M} / \Re) \oplus(\mathfrak{F} / \Re)$ where $\mathfrak{F} / \Re$ is an ideal isomorphic to $(\mathfrak{E} / \Re) /(\mathfrak{M} / \Re) \cong \mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$. Hence $\mathfrak{F} / \Re$ is separable and $\Re$ is solvable. Then if we assume the Albert-Penico-Taft theorem we obtain the existence of a subalgebra $\mathfrak{K}$ of $\mathfrak{F}$ such that $\mathfrak{F}=\mathfrak{K} \oplus \Re$. Then $\mathfrak{K} \cong \mathfrak{F} / \Re \cong \mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$. Moreover, $\mathfrak{K} \cap \mathfrak{M} \subseteq \mathfrak{F} \cap \mathfrak{M} \subseteq \Re$ since $\mathfrak{M} / \Re \cap \mathfrak{F} / \Re=0$. Hence $\mathfrak{\Lambda} \cap \mathfrak{M} \subseteq \mathfrak{K} \cap \Re=0$. This and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{K}=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$ imply that $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{K} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$.

Reduction II. To null ( $=$ singular) extensions. We now assume E contains a solvable ideal $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $\mathfrak{C} / \mathfrak{M}$ is separable. Suppose $\mathfrak{M}^{\cdot 2} \neq 0$. By Penico's lemma (Lemma 2 on p. 192) there exists a (solvable) ideal $\mathfrak{N}$ in $\mathfrak{E}$ such that 0 $\subset \mathfrak{N} \subset \mathfrak{M}$. Then $\mathfrak{C}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{N}$ has the solvable ideal $\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{M} / \mathfrak{N}$ and $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime} / \mathfrak{M}^{\prime} \cong \mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$ is separable Also $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{E}^{\prime}<\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{E}$. Since the theorem we wish to prove is clear for one-dimensional algebras we may use induction on dimensionality to conclude that there exists a subalgebra $\mathfrak{F}^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{F}^{\prime}$ such that $\mathfrak{F}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{F}^{\prime} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$. Now $\mathfrak{F}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{F} / \mathfrak{N}$ where $\mathfrak{F}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{E}$ containing $\mathfrak{N}$ and $\mathfrak{F} / \mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak{F}^{\prime} \cong \mathfrak{F}^{\prime} / \mathfrak{M}^{\prime} \cong \mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$ is separable. Also $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{F}=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}+\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{N}<\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}+\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M}=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{E}$. Hence, again, by induction on dimensionality, there exists a subalgebra $\Re$ of $\mathfrak{F}$ such that $\mathfrak{K} \cong \mathfrak{F} / \mathfrak{N} \cong \mathfrak{C} / \mathfrak{M}$. Since $\mathfrak{K}$ is semisimple and $\mathfrak{M}$ is solvable this implies that $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{M} \oplus \mathfrak{K}$. This proves the result in the case $\mathfrak{M}^{2^{2}} \neq 0$ so it remains to consider the case $\mathfrak{M}^{\cdot 2}=0$.

Reduction III. To algebras $\mathfrak{E}$ with 1 . Let $\mathfrak{E}$ contain an ideal $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $\mathfrak{M}^{\cdot 2}=0$ and $\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$ is separable. Let $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{E}$ the Jordan algebra obtained by adjoining the identity element 1 to $\mathfrak{C}$. Then $\mathfrak{M}$ is a solvable ideal in $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime}$ and $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime} / \mathfrak{M} \cong \Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$ is separable. Hence, assuming the theorem for algebras with 1 (and $\mathfrak{M}^{\cdot 2}=0$ ) we obtain the existence of a subalgebra $\mathfrak{K}^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{C}^{\prime}$ such that $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{K}^{\prime} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$. Since $\mathfrak{E} \supseteq \mathfrak{M}$ this gives $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{E}^{\prime} \cap \mathfrak{E}=\left(\mathfrak{E} \cap \mathfrak{K}^{\prime}\right) \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ and $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{C} \cap \mathfrak{K}^{\prime}$ is a subalgebra.

Reduction IV. To algebraically closed base fields. In §2.8 we associated with an extension $0 \rightarrow \mathfrak{M} \rightarrow_{\alpha} \mathfrak{E} \rightarrow_{\beta} \mathfrak{J} \rightarrow 0$, where $\mathfrak{M}$ is an ideal such that $\mathfrak{M}^{\cdot 2}=0$ and $\alpha$ is the injection mapping, an equivalence class of (Jordan) factor sets for $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{M}$. Here $\mathfrak{M}$ is a Jordan bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ and a factor set for $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{M}$ is a bilinear mapping $h((a, b) \rightarrow h(a, b))$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ satisfying the two conditions:

$$
\begin{align*}
h(a, b) & =h(b, a) \\
h(a, a) \cdot b \cdot a & +h\left(a^{\cdot 2}, b\right) \cdot a+h\left(a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b, a\right)  \tag{12}\\
& =h(a, b) \cdot a^{\cdot 2}+h(a, a)(a \cdot b)+h\left(a^{\cdot 2}, a \cdot b\right)
\end{align*}
$$

Given the extension as above we determine a linear mapping $\delta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta \beta=1_{\mathfrak{I}}$. Then we have $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{M} \oplus \mathfrak{I}^{\delta}$ and $h(a, b)=a^{\delta} b^{\delta}-(a b)^{\delta} \in \mathfrak{M}$. A change of $\delta$ to another linear mapping $\delta^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta^{\prime} \beta=1_{\mathfrak{J}}$ replaces the factor set $h$ by the equivalent one $h^{\prime}$. Here equivalence is defined by the existence of a linear mapping $\mu^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $h^{\prime}(a, b)=h(a, b)-(a . b)^{\mu} +a^{\mu} \cdot b+b^{\mu} \cdot a$. Conversely, if $h^{\prime}$ is any factor set for $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{M}$ equivalent to $h$ this $h^{\prime}$ can be obtained by choosing a suitable $\delta$. It is clear from the definition $h(a, b)=a^{\delta} b^{\delta}-(a b)^{\delta}$ that $\mathfrak{J}^{\delta}$ is a subalgebra if and only if $h=0$. It is now clear that $0 \rightarrow \mathfrak{M} \rightarrow_{\alpha} \mathfrak{E} \rightarrow_{\beta} \mathfrak{J} \rightarrow 0$ splits if and only if given any factor set $h$ defined by this extension then there exists a linear mapping $\mu$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
h(a, b)=(a \cdot b)^{\mu}-a^{\mu} \cdot b-b^{\mu} \cdot a, \quad a, b \in \mathfrak{J} . \tag{13}
\end{equation*}
$$

Now let $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ be a basis for $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi,\left(v_{1}, \cdots, v_{r}\right)$ a basis for $\mathfrak{M} / \Phi$. Clearly (13) will hold for a linear mapping $\mu$ if and only if it holds for all $a=u_{i}, b=u_{j}$ in the basis for $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$. Put $u_{i}^{\mu}=\Sigma_{p} \mu_{i p} v_{p}, h\left(u_{i}, u_{j}\right)=\sum_{q} \eta_{i j q} v_{q}, u_{i} . u_{j}=\sum_{k} \gamma_{i j k} u_{k}$, $v_{p} \cdot u_{i}=\sum_{q} \delta_{p i q} v_{q}$. Then (13) for $a=u_{i}, b=u_{j}$ is equivalent to the set of linear equations

$$
\begin{equation*}
\eta_{i j q}=\sum_{k} \gamma_{i j k} \mu_{k q}-\sum_{p} \mu_{i p} \delta_{p j q}-\sum_{p} \mu_{j p} \delta_{p i q} \tag{14}
\end{equation*}
$$

for the $\mu$ 's in $\Phi$. Here the coefficients $\eta_{i j q}, \delta_{p j q}, \gamma_{i j k}$ are elements of $\Phi$ determined by $h$, the multiplication table in $\mathfrak{J}$ and the multiplication table $v_{p} \cdot u_{i}=\sum \delta_{p i q} v_{q}$ for $\mathfrak{M}$ as $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule. The solvability of (14) for the $\mu$ 's in $\Phi$ is a necessary and sufficient condition that the extension splits.
Let $\Omega$ be the algebraic closure of $\Phi$. Then the exact sequence $0 \rightarrow \mathfrak{M} \rightarrow_{\alpha} \mathfrak{E} \rightarrow_{\beta} \mathfrak{J} \rightarrow 0$ gives rise to the Jordan algebra exact sequence $0 \rightarrow \mathfrak{M}_{\Omega} \rightarrow_{\alpha} \mathfrak{E}_{\Omega} \rightarrow_{\beta} \mathfrak{J}_{\Omega} \rightarrow 0$ where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the linear extensions of the given $\alpha$ and $\beta$. We have $\mathfrak{M}_{\Omega}{ }^{\cdot 2}=0$ so the new extension is a null extension. Also $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ is separable (equivalent to semisimple since the base field is algbraically closed). If $h$ is a factor set determined by the extension $0 \rightarrow \mathfrak{M} \rightarrow \mathfrak{E} \rightarrow \mathfrak{J} \rightarrow 0$ then the linear extension of $h$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ into $\mathfrak{M}_{\Omega}$ is a factor set for $0 \rightarrow \mathfrak{M}_{\Omega} \rightarrow \mathfrak{E}_{\Omega} \rightarrow \mathfrak{J}_{\Omega} \rightarrow 0$. The bases $\left(u_{i}\right),\left(v_{p}\right)$ are bases for $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega} / \Omega$ and $\mathfrak{M}_{\Omega} / \Omega$ and we have the same coefficients $\eta_{i j q}, \delta_{p j q}, \gamma_{i j k}$ as before. Now assume the theorem holds in the algebraically closed case. Then the equations (14) have a solution $\left(\mu_{i p}\right), \mu_{i p} \in \Omega$. Since these are linear equations with coefficients in $\Phi$ it follows that they have a solution also in $\Phi$. Then the given extension splits. Hence it suffices to prove the theorem for algebraically closed base fields. We may assume also that $\mathscr{E}$ has an identity element and $\mathfrak{M}^{\cdot 2}=0$.

Reduction V. To $\mathfrak{J}$ simple. Suppose $\mathfrak{J}$ is not simple. Then $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{s}$ where $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ is a simple ideal and $s>1$. Then $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{E}_{1}{ }^{\prime} \oplus \mathfrak{E}_{2}{ }^{\prime} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{E}_{s}{ }^{\prime}$ where $\mathfrak{E}_{i}{ }^{\prime} \cong \mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Let $1_{i}{ }^{\prime}$ be the identity of $\mathfrak{E}_{i}{ }^{\prime}$. Then the elements $1_{i}{ }^{\prime}, 1 \leqq i \leqq s$, are orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{E}^{\prime}$ such that $\Sigma 1_{i}{ }^{\prime}=1^{\prime}=1+\mathfrak{M}$. By Lemma 3 of
§3.7(p. 149) there exist orthogonal idempotents $e_{i}, 1 \leqq i \leqq s$, in Esuch that $\sum e_{i}=1$ and $1_{i}{ }^{\prime}=e_{i}+\mathfrak{M}$. Let $\mathfrak{E}=\sum_{i \leqq j} \mathfrak{E}_{i j}$ be the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{E}$ relative to the $e_{i}$. Then $\mathfrak{E}_{i i}=\mathfrak{E} U_{e_{i}}$ contains the ideal $\mathfrak{M} U_{e_{i}}=\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{E} U_{e_{i}}$ and $\mathfrak{E}_{i i} / \mathfrak{M} U_{e_{i}} \cong \mathfrak{E}^{\prime} U_{1^{\prime}}=\mathfrak{E}_{i}{ }^{\prime} \cong \mathfrak{J}_{i}{ }^{\prime}$. Since $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}_{i}<\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}, \operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{E}_{i i}<\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{E}$. Also $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ is separable and $\left(\mathfrak{M} U_{e_{i}}\right)^{\cdot 2}=0$. Hence, using induction on dimensionality, we conclude the existence of a subalgebra $\Re_{i}$ of $\mathfrak{C}_{i i}$ such that $\Re_{i} \cong \mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Since $\mathfrak{E}_{i i} \cdot \mathfrak{E}_{j j}=0$ if $i \neq j$ we have $\boldsymbol{K}_{i}, \boldsymbol{K}_{j}=0$. Hence $\mathfrak{K} \equiv \boldsymbol{K}_{1}+\boldsymbol{K}_{2}+\cdots+\boldsymbol{K}_{s}$ is a subalgcbra of $\mathfrak{E}$ isomorphic to $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{s}$. Consequently, $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{K} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$.

We have now reduced the proof to the case: $\Phi$ algebraically closed, $\mathbb{E}$ has 1 , $\mathfrak{M}^{2}=0, \mathfrak{J}$ is simple. We now distinguish the possible structures for $\mathfrak{J}:$ I. $\mathfrak{J} \cong \Phi$. II. $\mathfrak{J}$ is the Jordan algebra of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on a vector space $\mathfrak{B}$ with $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}>1$. III. $\mathfrak{J} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ where $n \geqq 3$ and $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a (split) composition algebra which is associative if $n \geqq 4$. The case I is trivial since $\mathfrak{E}$ has an identity element. To settle case II we prove

Lemma 2. Let $\mathfrak{E}$ be a Jordan algebra with 1 containing an ideal $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $\mathfrak{M}^{\cdot 2}=0$. Assume $\mathbb{E}$ contains elements $v_{1}, v_{2}, \cdots, v_{r}$ such that $v_{i}^{\cdot 2}=1$, $v_{i} \cdot v_{j}=0$ if $i \neq j$ and an element $u$ such that $u^{\cdot 2} \equiv 1(\bmod \mathfrak{M}), v_{i} \cdot u \equiv 0(\bmod \mathfrak{M})$, $i=1, \cdots, r$. Then there exists an element $v$ in $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $v \equiv u(\bmod \mathfrak{M})$, $v . v_{i}=0$ and $v^{2}=1$.
Proof. Since $v_{i}{ }^{.2}=1 R_{v_{i}}{ }^{3}=R_{v_{i}}$. Since $v_{i} \cdot v_{j}=0$ if $i \neq j, R_{v_{i}}{ }^{2} R_{v_{j}}+R_{v_{j}} R_{v_{i}}{ }^{2} +R_{v_{i} \cdot v_{j} \cdot v_{i}}=2 R_{v_{i}} R_{v_{i} \cdot v_{j}}+R_{v_{j}} R_{v_{i} \cdot 2}$ gives $\left(1-R_{v_{i}}{ }^{2}\right) R_{v_{j}}=R_{v_{j}} R_{v_{i}}{ }^{2}$. This and $\left(1-R_{v_{i}}{ }^{2}\right) R_{v_{i}}=0$ imply that if $W=\left(1-R_{v_{1}}{ }^{2}\right)\left(1-R_{v_{2}}{ }^{2}\right) \cdots\left(1-R_{v_{r}}{ }^{2}\right)$ then $W R_{v_{i}}=0, i=1,2, \cdots ; r$. Put $w=u W$. Then $w \equiv u(\bmod \mathfrak{M})$ since $u . v_{i} \equiv 0 (\bmod \mathfrak{M})$. Also $w \cdot v_{i}=0$ since $W R_{v_{i}}=0$. Since $2 R_{w}{ }^{3}+R_{w^{\cdot 3}}=3 R_{w} R_{w^{\cdot 2}}$ we have $w^{\cdot 3} \cdot v_{i}=0$. Now put $v=\frac{1}{2}\left(3 w-w^{\cdot 3}\right)$. Then $v \cdot v_{i}=0$. Also $w^{\cdot 2} \equiv u^{\cdot 2} \equiv 1(\bmod \mathfrak{M})$ so $w^{\cdot 3} \equiv w(\bmod \mathfrak{M})$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}\left(3 w-w^{\cdot 3}\right) \equiv w \equiv u(\bmod \mathfrak{M})$. Since $u^{\cdot 2} \equiv 1 (\bmod \mathfrak{M}), w^{\cdot 2} \equiv 1(\bmod \mathfrak{M})$. Then $w^{\cdot 2}=1+z$ where $z^{\cdot 2}=0$ and $\left(w^{\cdot 2}-1\right)^{\cdot 2} =w^{\cdot 4}-2 w^{\cdot 2}+1=0$. Hence $v^{\cdot 2}=\frac{1}{4}\left(9 w^{\cdot 2}-6 w^{\cdot 4}+w^{\cdot 6}\right)=1$. Hence $v$ satisfies the required conditions.
