If $\mathfrak{J}$ is the Jordan algebra of the nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $f$ on a vector space over an algebraically closed field, then $\mathfrak{J}$ has a basis $\left(1, v_{1}, \cdots, v_{n}\right)$ such that $v_{i}{ }^{2}=1, v_{i} \cdot v_{j}=0$ if $i \neq j$. Clearly this and Lemma 2 imply that if $\mathfrak{E}$ and $\mathfrak{M}$ are as in Lemma 2 and $\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M} \cong \mathfrak{J}$ then $\mathfrak{E}$ contains a subalgebra isomorphic to $\mathfrak{J}$. Thus the splitting theorem holds in case II. To settle the remaining case we require the following result on alternative algebras with involution.
Lemma 3. Let $(\mathfrak{F}, j)$ be an alternative algebra with 1 and involution over an algebraically closed field, $\mathfrak{N}$ an ideal in ( $\mathfrak{F}, j$ ) such that $\mathfrak{N}^{2}=0$ and ( $\mathfrak{F} / \mathfrak{N}, j$ ) is isomorphic to a composition algebra $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. Then $(\mathfrak{F}, j)$ contains a subalgebra ( $\mathfrak{L}, j$ ) isomorphic to ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ).

Proof. Let $(\mathfrak{H}, j)$ be a composition subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{F}, j)$. Since $(\mathfrak{H}, j)$ is simple
the canonical homomorphism of $(\mathfrak{F}, j)$ onto $(\mathfrak{F} / \mathfrak{N}, j)$ maps $(\mathfrak{H}, j)$ isomorphically onto the subalgebra $((\mathfrak{H}+\mathfrak{N}) / \mathfrak{N}, j)$ of $(\mathfrak{F} / \mathfrak{N}, j)$. Assume $\mathfrak{H}+\mathfrak{N} \subset \mathfrak{F}$. Then if we recall the inductive construction of composition algebras given in the proof of Theorem 4.5, we see that there exists an element $u \in \mathfrak{F}$ such that $\bar{u} \equiv-u(\bmod \mathfrak{N})$ (where $\left.\bar{a}=a^{j}\right), u h \equiv \bar{h} u(\bmod \mathfrak{N})$ for every $h \in \mathfrak{H}$ and $u^{2} \equiv 1(\bmod \mathfrak{N})$. Since we may replace $u$ by $\frac{1}{2}(u-\bar{u})$ we may assume $\bar{u}=-u$. Moreover, we can choose a basis $\left(1, v_{1}, \cdots, v_{r}\right)$ for $\mathfrak{H}$ such that $\bar{v}_{i}=-v_{i}, v_{i}^{2}=1$ and $v_{i} v_{j}=-v_{j} v_{i}$, if $i \neq j$. We now consider the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{F}^{+}$which contains the ideal $\mathfrak{N}$ such that $\Re^{\cdot 2}=0$. Also we have $v_{i}^{\cdot 2}=1, v_{i} \cdot v_{j}=\frac{1}{2}\left(v_{i} v_{j}+v_{j} v_{i}\right)=0, i \neq j$, and $u \cdot v_{i}= \frac{1}{2}\left(u v_{i}+v_{i} u\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(u v_{i}-\bar{v}_{i} u\right) \equiv 0(\bmod \mathfrak{N}), u^{\cdot 2} \equiv 1(\bmod \mathfrak{N})$. We can now apply Lemma 2 and its proof to $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{F}^{+}, \mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{N}$. Accordingly, we obtain the element $w=u\left(1-R_{v_{1}}{ }^{2}\right) \cdots\left(1-R_{v_{r}}{ }^{2}\right)$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}\left(3 w-w^{\cdot 2}\right)$ and we have $v \equiv u(\bmod \mathfrak{N})$, $v . v_{i}=0$ and $v^{\cdot 2}=1$. Then $v v_{i}=-v_{i} v$ and consequently $v h=\bar{h} v$ for all $h \in \mathfrak{H}$. Also $v^{2}=1$. Since $\bar{u}=-u$ and $\bar{v}_{i}=-v_{i}, u R_{v_{i}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(u v_{i}+v_{i} u\right)$ is symmetric and $u R_{v_{i}}{ }^{2}$ is skew. It follows that $\bar{w}=-w$ and $\bar{v}=-v$. Now consider the subspace $\mathfrak{H}+\mathfrak{H} v$. We claim that this is a composition subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{F}, j)$. If $h, k \in \mathfrak{H}$ then $(h v)(k v)=(v \bar{h})(k v)=v(h k) v$ (by one of Moufang's identities) $=((\bar{k} h) v) v=(\bar{k} h) v^{2} =\bar{k} h$. Also $k(h v)=((k v) v)(h v)=((v \bar{k}) v)(h v)=(v \bar{k} v)(h v)=v(\bar{k}(v(h v))$ (by one of Moufang's identities $)=v(\bar{k} h)=(h k) v$. Finally, $(\overline{h v) k}=\bar{k}(\overline{h v})=-\bar{k}(v \bar{h}) =-\bar{k}(h v)=-(h \bar{k}) v$ so $(h v) k=v(k \bar{h})=(h \bar{k}) v$. Since $(\mathfrak{H}, j)$ is isomorphic to a proper subalgebra of a composition algebra it is associative. It follows from the proof of Theorem 4.5 and the multiplication formulas just derived that $\mathfrak{H}+\mathfrak{H} v$ is a homomorphic image of a composition algebra whose dimensionality is $2 \operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{H}$. Hence $\mathfrak{H}+\mathfrak{H} v$ is a subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{F}, j)$ isomorphic to a composition algebra of dimensionality $2 \operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{H}$. Since we can begin our process with $\mathfrak{H}=\Phi 1$ this leads to a composition subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{F}, j)$ isomorphic to $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$.

We can now prove
Lemma 4. Let E be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1 over an algebraically closed field containing an ideal $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $\mathfrak{M}^{\cdot 2}=0$ and $\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ where $n \geqq 3$ and $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a composition algebra. Then $\mathfrak{E}$ contains a subalgebra $\mathfrak{K}$ isomorphic to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$.

Proof. We have seen in Theorem 3.10 that the hypotheses of the present lemma imply that $\mathfrak{E} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ where the ideal corresponding to $\mathfrak{M}$ has the form $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{N}_{n}, J_{1}\right), \mathfrak{N}$ an ideal in $(\mathfrak{F}, j)$ such that $(\mathfrak{F}, j) / \mathfrak{N} \cong(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. Since $\mathfrak{M}^{\cdot 2}=0$, $\Re^{\cdot 2}=0$ (Theorem 3.10). It is sufficient to show that there exists a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ isomorphic to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$. By Lemma 3, there exists a subalgebra $(\mathfrak{L}, j)$ of $(\mathfrak{F}, j)$ isomorphic to $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. This gives a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ isomorphic to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$.

Since Lemma 4 settles the case III of the structure of the simple algebra $\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$ we have completed the proof of the following

Theorem 13. Let $\mathfrak{E}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{M}$ an ideal in $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$ is separable. Then there exists a subalgebra $\mathfrak{R}$ of $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{K} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ (as vector spaces).

As we have seen above and in $\S 2.8$, if $\mathfrak{M}^{\cdot 2}=0$, this result is equivalent to the following one.

Corollary. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional separable Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{M}$ a finite-dimensional bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}, h$ a factor set of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{M}$, that is, a bilinear mapping of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{M}$ satisfying (12). Then there exists a linear mapping $\mu$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $h(a, b)=(a . b)^{\mu}-a^{\mu} . b-b^{\mu} . a$.
7. Derivations into bimodules. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is an algebra and $\mathfrak{M}$ is a bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ then a derivation $D$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ is a linear mapping $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $(a b) D=a(b D)+(a D) b$ for all $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$. If $\mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ is the split null extension of $\mathfrak{A}$ by $\mathfrak{M}$ then we extend $D$ linearly to $\mathfrak{E}$ so that $\mathfrak{M} D=0$. Then it is immediate that the extension $D$ is derivation in the algebra $\mathfrak{C}$ mapping $\mathfrak{U}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ and $\mathfrak{M}$ into 0 . It is clear from this that the set Der $(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{M})$ of derivations of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ coincides with the set of restrictions to $\mathfrak{A}$ of Der $\mathfrak{E} \cap \mathfrak{A}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{M})$ where Der $\mathfrak{E}$ is the Lie algebra of derivations of $\mathfrak{E}$ and $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{M})$ is the subspace of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{E}, \mathfrak{E})$ of mappings sending $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}$ into 0 . Hence $\operatorname{Der}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{M})$ is a subspace of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{M})$. Also it is clear that if $D \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{C} \cap \mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{M})$ and the restriction $D \mid \mathfrak{A}$ of $D$ to $\mathfrak{A}$ is 0 then $D=0$. Hence the linear mapping $D \rightarrow D \mid \mathfrak{A}$ of $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{E} \cap \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{M})$ onto $\operatorname{Der}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{M})$ is an isomorphism of vector spaces. In this way we can identify $\operatorname{Der}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{M})$ with $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{E} \cap \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{M})$.

Now let $\mathfrak{J}$ be Jordan and $\mathfrak{M}$ a (Jordan) bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ so that $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ is a Jordan algebra. Then we shall call the derivation $D$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ inner if the corresponding element of $\operatorname{Der~} \mathfrak{E}$ (the linear extension such that $\mathfrak{M D}=0$ ) is an inner derivation in $\mathfrak{E}$. Thus the condition is that there exist $v_{i}, w_{i} \in \mathfrak{E}$ such that $D=\Sigma_{i}\left[R_{v_{i}} R_{w_{i}}\right]$ or, equivalently, $D$ is the mapping $x \rightarrow \Sigma_{i}\left[v_{i}, x, w_{i}\right]$. If we write $v_{i}=y_{i}+b_{i}, w_{i}=z_{i}+c_{i}$ where $y_{i}, z_{i} \in \mathfrak{M}, b_{i}, c_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$, then $\left[R_{v_{i}} R_{w_{i}}\right]=\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right] +\left[R_{y_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right]-\left[R_{z_{i}} R_{b_{i}}\right]$ since $\left[R_{y_{i}} R_{z_{i}}\right]=0$ follows from $\mathfrak{M} . \mathfrak{E} \subseteq \mathfrak{M}$ and $\mathfrak{M}^{\cdot 2}=0$. Hence $D=\sum\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right]+\sum\left[R_{y_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right]-\sum\left[R_{z_{i}} R_{b_{i}}\right]$ and if $x \in \mathfrak{J}$ then the condition $x D \in \mathfrak{M}$ implies that $x \sum\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right]=0$. Also $y D=0$ for $y \in \mathfrak{M}$ implies $y \sum\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right]=0$. Hence $\sum\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right]=0$ and $D$ has the form $\sum\left[R_{y_{i}} R_{b_{i}}\right]$ where the $y_{i} \in \mathfrak{M}$ and the $b_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$. Conversely, it is clear that any derivation $D=\sum\left[R_{y_{i}} R_{b_{i}}\right], y_{i} \in \mathfrak{M}, b_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{E}$ maps $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ and $\mathfrak{M}$ into 0 so its restriction to $\mathfrak{J}$ is an inner derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$. It is clear from the definition that the set Inder $(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{M})$ of inner derivations is a subspace of $\operatorname{Der}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{M})$. In fact, the identification of $\operatorname{Der}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{M})$ with $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{E} \cap \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{M})$ identifies Inder $(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{M})$ with Inder $\mathfrak{E} \cap \mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{M})$.

In this section we shall prove the following theorem on derivations of finitedimensional separable Jordan algebras into bimodules.

Theorem 14 (Harris). Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional separable Jordan algebra such that the degrees of the simple components of $\mathfrak{J}$ over their centers are not divisible by the characteristic of the base field $\Phi$ and let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a finitedimensional bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$. Then every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ is inner.

We shall show also that if $\mathfrak{J}$ has a special simple component whose degree over its center is divisible by the characteristic then there exists a finite-dimensional bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ with a noninner derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$. In Chapter IX we shall show that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is separable and is simple and exceptional then the derivations of $\mathfrak{J}$ into finite-dimensional bimodules are inner for all characteristics. In sum, we shall have that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is finite-dimensional separable then all derivations of $\mathfrak{J}$ into finite-dimensional bimodules are inner if and only if the degrees of the special simple components over their centers are not divisible by the characteristic. This sharper form of Theorem 14 is due also to Harris [2]. We remark also that the special case of this result for characteristic 0 was proved earlier by Jacobson in [9]. For this case we shall give a proof based on Lie algebras in the next chapter. On the other hand, the proof we shall give here of Harris' theorem will make use of the determination of the finite-dimensional simple algebras over an algebraically closed field, and some of the results on bimodules for these algebras which have been obtained in this chapter.

We shall show first that it suffices to prove Theorem 14 for algebraically closed base fields. The reduction of the general case to this one will be based on some well-known results on tensor products of algebras which we shall now derive. First, let $\mathfrak{A}$ be an arbitrary algebra over a field $\Gamma$ which is an extension field of $\Phi$ and let $\mathrm{P} / \Phi$ be another field extension of $\Phi$. Let $\sigma$ be an isomorphism of $\Gamma / \Phi$ into $\mathbf{P} / \Phi$. Then $\mathbf{P}$ is a right module for $\Gamma$ relative to the composition $\rho \gamma=\rho \gamma^{\sigma}=\gamma^{\sigma} \rho$ for $\gamma \in \Gamma, \rho \in \mathrm{P}$. Hence we may form the tensor product $\mathrm{P} \otimes_{\Gamma} \mathfrak{A}$ considering $\mathfrak{A}$ as left $\Gamma$-module and P as right $\Gamma$-module in the manner just indicated. It is immediate that this tensor product is an algebra over $\mathbf{P}$ with the compositions $\rho\left(\sum \rho_{i} \otimes a_{i}\right)=\sum \rho \rho_{i} \otimes a_{i},\left(\sum \rho_{i} \otimes a_{i}\right)\left(\sum \tau_{j} \otimes b_{j}\right)=\sum \rho_{i} \tau_{j} \otimes a_{i} b_{j}$, $\rho, \rho_{i}, \tau_{j} \in \mathrm{P}, a_{i}, b_{j} \in \mathfrak{A}$. We denote this algebra $\mathfrak{A}_{\boldsymbol{P}}^{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}$. The special case in which $\mathbf{P} \supseteq \Gamma$ and $\sigma$ is the injection is the usual algebra $\mathfrak{A}_{\boldsymbol{P}}$ obtained by extending the base field $\Gamma$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ to P . If $\left(u_{\boldsymbol{v}}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{A} / \Gamma$ with multiplication table $u_{\boldsymbol{\imath}} u_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}} =\sum \gamma_{ι κ \lambda} u_{\lambda}, \gamma_{ι κ \lambda} \in \Gamma$, then the elements $u_{\imath}\left(=1 \otimes u_{\imath}\right)$ constitute a basis for $\mathfrak{A}^{\sigma}{ }_{\mathrm{P}}$ over P and these have the multiplication table $u_{\imath} u_{\kappa}=\sum \gamma_{\imath \kappa \lambda}^{\sigma} u_{\lambda}$.

We now assume that $\Gamma$ is finite-dimensional separable over $\Phi$ and $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of $\Phi$. Then there are $n$ distinct isomorphisms, $\sigma_{1}, \cdots, \sigma_{n}$, of $\Gamma / \Phi$ into $\Omega / \Phi$ where $n=\operatorname{dim} \Gamma / \Phi$. We can now state the following result.

Lemma 1. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be an algebra over a field $\Gamma, \Phi$ a subfield of $\Gamma$ such that $\Gamma / \Phi$ is finite-dimensional separable and let $\Omega$ be the algebraic closure of $\Phi$, $\sigma_{1}, \cdots, \sigma_{n}$ the different isomorphisms of $\Gamma / \Phi$ into $\Omega / \Phi$. Then $(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega}=\mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2}$
$\oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{n}$ where $\mathfrak{U}_{i}$ is an ideal and is isomorphic as algebra over $\Omega$ to $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}^{\sigma_{i}}$.

Proof. We recall that $\Gamma_{\Omega}=\Omega_{1} \oplus \Omega_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \Omega_{n}$ where $\Omega_{i}$ is an ideal which is one dimensional over $\Omega: \Omega_{i}=\Omega \varepsilon_{i}, \varepsilon_{i}{ }^{2}=\varepsilon_{i} \neq 0, \sum \varepsilon_{i}=1$ (Jacobson, Theory of Rings, p. 97). We identify $\Gamma$ with the $\Phi$-subalgebra of $\Gamma_{\Omega}$ of elements $\gamma \equiv 1 \otimes \gamma$, $\gamma \in \Phi$, as usual. If $\gamma \in \Gamma, \gamma \varepsilon_{i}=\varepsilon_{i} \gamma=\gamma^{\sigma_{i}} \varepsilon_{i}$ where $\sigma_{1}, \sigma_{2}, \cdots, \sigma_{n}$ are the distinct isomorphisms of $\Gamma / \Phi$ into $\Omega / \Phi$. Now consider $(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega}$. This is an algebra over $\Omega$ and a left $\Gamma$-module such that $\gamma(\omega \otimes a)=\omega \otimes \gamma a, \gamma \in \Gamma, \omega \in \Omega, a \in \mathfrak{A}$. Since this action commutes with the multiplications by elements of $\Omega,(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega}$ is a left $\Gamma_{\Omega}$-module such that $\left(\gamma \otimes \omega^{\prime}\right)(\omega \otimes a)=\omega^{\prime} \omega \otimes \gamma a, \omega^{\prime} \in \Omega$. It is immediate that relative to this composition $(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega}$ is an algebra over the commutative ring $\Gamma_{\Omega}$. Since $\quad \Gamma_{\Omega}=\Omega \varepsilon_{1} \oplus \Omega \varepsilon_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \Omega \varepsilon_{n}, \quad(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega}=\varepsilon_{1}(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega} \oplus \cdots \oplus \varepsilon_{n}(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega}$ and $\varepsilon_{i}(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega}$ is an ideal in $(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega}$. We have $\varepsilon_{i}\left(\omega \gamma^{\sigma_{i}} \otimes a\right)=\gamma^{\sigma^{\delta_{i}}} \varepsilon_{i}(\omega \otimes a)=\gamma \varepsilon_{i}(\omega \otimes a) =\varepsilon_{i}(\omega \otimes \gamma a)$. Hence we have the (algebra) homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}{ }^{\sigma_{i}}$ onto $\varepsilon_{i}(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega}$ sending $\omega \otimes a \rightarrow \varepsilon_{i}(\omega \otimes a)$. We claim that this is an isomorphism. For this let $\left(u_{\imath}\right)$ be a basis for $\mathfrak{A} / \Gamma,\left(\lambda_{1}, \cdots, \lambda_{n}\right)$ a basis for $\Gamma / \Phi$. Then $\left(\lambda_{j} u_{\imath}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi$ and for $(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega}$ over $\Omega$ and $\left(\lambda_{j}\right)$ is a basis for $\Gamma_{\Omega} / \Omega$. Since $\lambda_{j} u_{\imath}=\lambda_{j}\left(1 \otimes u_{\imath}\right)$ the elements $\lambda_{j}\left(1 \otimes u_{\imath}\right)$ constitute a basis for $(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega}$ over $\Omega$. Since $\left(\lambda_{1}, \cdots, \lambda_{n}\right)$ and $\left(\varepsilon_{1}, \cdots, \varepsilon_{n}\right)$ are bases for $\Gamma_{\Omega} / \Omega$ it follows that the elements $\varepsilon_{j}\left(1 \otimes u_{\imath}\right)$ constitute a basis for $(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega}$ over $\Omega$ and for fixed $j$ a basis for $\varepsilon_{j}(\mathfrak{A} / \Phi)_{\Omega}$ over $\Omega$. It follows that the canonical homomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}{ }^{\sigma_{i}}$ onto $\varepsilon_{i}(\mathfrak{U} / \Phi)_{\Omega}$ is an isomorphism. Thus $(\mathfrak{U} / \Phi)_{\Omega} \cong \mathfrak{U}_{\Omega}{ }^{\sigma_{1}} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{U}_{\Omega}{ }^{\sigma_{n}}$.
If $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}{ }^{\sigma_{i}}$ and $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}{ }^{\sigma_{j}}$ are as in the lemma then $\sigma_{i}{ }^{-1} \sigma_{j}$ is an isomorphism of the subfield $\Gamma^{\sigma_{i}}$ of $\Omega / \Phi$ onto $\Gamma^{\sigma_{j}}$. Since $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of $\Phi$ this can be extended to an automorphism $\tau$ in $\Omega / \Phi$. If $\left(u_{\imath}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{A} / \Gamma$ then the corresponding elements, which we write again as $u_{t}$, constitute bases for $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}{ }^{\sigma_{i}}$ and $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}{ }^{\sigma_{j}}$ and we have the multiplication tables $u_{\imath} u_{\kappa}=\sum \gamma_{\imath \kappa \lambda}{ }^{\sigma_{i}} u_{\lambda}$ and $u_{\imath} u_{\kappa}=\sum \gamma_{\imath \kappa \lambda}{ }^{\sigma_{j}} u_{\lambda}$ in these algebras. Let $\eta$ be the mapping $\sum \omega_{\imath} u_{\imath} \rightarrow \sum \omega_{\imath}{ }^{\tau} u_{\imath}, \omega_{\imath} \in \Omega$, of $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}{ }^{\sigma_{i}}$ into $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}{ }^{\sigma_{j}}$. It is clear that this is $\tau$-semilinear and bijective. Moreover, $(a b)^{\eta}=a^{\eta} b^{\eta}$. We shall call such a mapping a $\tau$-semilinear isomorphism of the algebras. This, of course, can be defined in a similar manner for any two algebras over possibly different fields. If $\Omega \supseteq \Gamma$ is the algebraic closure of $\Gamma$ then it is immediate also that the usual extension $(\mathfrak{A} / \Gamma)_{\Omega}$ is semilinearly isomorphic to $\mathfrak{A}^{\sigma_{i}} \Omega$. It is clear also that the semilinear isomorph of a central simple algebra is central simple. Hence if $\mathfrak{A} / \Gamma$ is central simple then the algebras $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}{ }^{\sigma_{i}}$ are simpler over $\Omega$. We remark that the same reasoning shows also that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is finite-dimensional strictly power associative then the same is true of the algebras $\mathfrak{U}_{\Omega}{ }^{\sigma_{i}}$ and their degrees are the same as the degree of $\mathfrak{A} / \Gamma$.
We can now give the reduction of Theorem 14 to the algebraically closed case. We note first that since $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{E}_{\Omega}=\left(\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{E}_{\Omega}\right.$ for $\Omega$ an extension field of the base field of the algebra $\mathfrak{E}$ (p.253), if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a Jordan algebra and $\mathfrak{M}$ is a bimodule then
$\operatorname{Der}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}, \mathfrak{M}_{\Omega}\right)=\operatorname{Der}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{M})_{\Omega}$. Also Inder $\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}, \mathfrak{M}_{\Omega}\right)=(\operatorname{Inder}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{M}))_{\Omega}$. Hence it is clear that all the derivations of $\mathfrak{I}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ are inner, that is, $\operatorname{Der}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{M})=\operatorname{Inder}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{M})$, if and only if all the derivations of $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ into $\mathfrak{M}_{\Omega}$ are inner. Now let $\mathfrak{J}$ satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem 14 and let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a finite-dimensional bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{s}$ be the decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ into simple components. Let $\Gamma_{i}$ be the center of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Then $\Gamma_{i}$ is separable and Lemma 1 and the remarks following it show that $\mathfrak{J}_{i \Omega}$ is a direct sum of simple ideals whose degrees over $\Omega$ are the same as the degree of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ over $\Gamma_{i}$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}=\mathfrak{J}_{1 \Omega} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2 \Omega} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{\Omega \Omega}$ satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 14 so it is clearly sufficient to prove the theorem for an algebraically closed base field. Accordingly, we assume from now on that $\Phi$ is algebraically closed.
Now suppose that $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{k}$ where the $\mathfrak{M}_{j}$ are sub-bimodules. If $E_{j}$ is the projection on $\mathfrak{M}_{j}$ determined by this decomposition and $D$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ then $D_{j}=D E_{j}$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}_{j}$. It is immediate from the definitions that $D$ is inner if and only if every $D_{j}$ is inner. Since every $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule is a direct sum of irreducible bimodules it is clear that it suffices to prove the theorem for irreducible bimudules. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element 1 we have the decomposition $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{\frac{1}{2}} \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{1}$ where $\mathfrak{M}_{i}=\left\{x_{i} \mid x_{i} .1=i x_{i}\right\}$ and the $\mathfrak{M}_{i}$ are sub-bimodules. This is an immediate consequences of the Peirce decomposition $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{E}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{E}_{\frac{1}{2}} \oplus \mathfrak{E}_{1}$ of the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ relative to the idempotent 1 in $\mathfrak{E}$ and the obvious relation $\mathfrak{M}_{i}=\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{E}_{i}$ for the ideal $\mathfrak{M}$ in $\mathfrak{E}$. Since $\mathfrak{J} \subseteq \mathfrak{E}_{1}$ we have $\mathfrak{M}_{0} \cdot \mathfrak{J}=0$ so $\mathfrak{M}_{0}$ is a trivial bimodule in the sense that $x_{0} \cdot a=0, x_{0} \in \mathfrak{M}_{0}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. If $D$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}_{0}$ then $a D=(a \cdot 1) D=a D \cdot 1+1 D \cdot a=0$. Hence $D$ is inner. If $D$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ then $a D=(1 \cdot a) D=1 D \cdot a+a D \cdot 1=1 D \cdot a+\frac{1}{2} a D$ so $a D=2(1 D) \cdot a =4[1, a, 1 D]$. Hence $D$ is inner. It now follows that it is enough to prove the theorem for $\mathfrak{M}$ unital and irreducible. We show next that we may assume $\mathfrak{J}$ simple. Thus, suppose $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2}$ where the $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ are ideals. Then the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ shows that $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M}_{11} \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{12} \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{22}$ where $\mathfrak{M}_{i i}=\left\{x_{i} \mid x_{i} \cdot 1_{i}\right. \left.=x_{i}\right\}, 1_{i}$ the identity of $\mathfrak{I}_{i}$ and $\mathfrak{M}_{12}=\left\{x_{12} \left\lvert\, x_{12} .1_{1}=\frac{1}{2} x_{12}=x_{12} .1_{2}\right.\right\}$. Also $\mathfrak{M}_{i j} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{i} \subseteq \mathfrak{M}_{i j}$ and $\mathfrak{M}_{i i} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{j}=0$ if $i \neq j$. Hence the $\mathfrak{M}_{i j}$ are sub-bimodules so if $\mathfrak{M}$ is irreducible then either $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M}_{11}, \mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M}_{22}$ or $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M}_{12}$. In the first case, $\mathfrak{M}$ is annihilated by $\mathfrak{I}_{2}$ and is a unital irreducible bimodule for $\mathfrak{I}_{1}$. It is clear that if a derivation $D$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ is inner as a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ then it is inner as derivation for $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence in this case, it is enough to prove $D$ is inner as derivation of $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$. Similarly, if $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M}_{22}$ then it is enough to show that $D$ is an inner derivation of $\mathfrak{J}_{2}$. If $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M}_{12}$ then, as above, $a_{i} D=4\left[1_{i}, a_{i}, 1_{i} D\right]$ for $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Also $1_{1} \cdot 1_{2}=0$ gives $0=1_{1} D \cdot 1_{2}+1_{2} D \cdot 1_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1_{1} D\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left(1_{2} D\right)$. Hence $1_{1} D=-1_{2} D$ and $a_{i} D=2\left[1_{i}, a_{i},\left(1_{i}-1_{j}\right) D\right], i \neq j$. Since $\mathfrak{M}$ is unital $[1, a, x]=0$ for all $a \in \mathfrak{J}$, $x \in \mathfrak{M}$. Hence $\left[1_{i}, a, x\right]=-\left[1_{j}, a, x\right]$ if $i \neq j$ and

$$
2\left[1_{i}, a_{i},\left(1_{i}-1_{j}\right) D\right]=\left[1_{i}-1_{j}, a_{i},\left(1_{i}-1_{j}\right) D\right]
$$

Thus $a D=\left[1_{i}-1_{j}, a,\left(1_{i}-1_{j}\right) D\right]$ for all $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ and so $D$ is inner. It is now clear that we may assume $\mathfrak{J}$ simple.

We have now reduced the proof to the following situation: $\Phi$ is algebraically closed, $\mathfrak{M}$ is unital irreducible, $\mathfrak{J}$ is simple. The case $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1$ is trivial so we may assume also that the degree of $\mathfrak{J}$ is $>1$. The results on the determination of the unital irreducible bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\S \S 2,3,4$ shows that unless $\mathfrak{J}$ is either exceptional or $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a (split) quaternion algebra with involution then every unital irreducible bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ is special, that is, there exists a monomorphism $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{M}$ into a bimodule $\mathfrak{N}$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ such that for $y \in \mathfrak{N}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$ we have $y . a=\frac{1}{2} y\left(a^{\sigma_{1}}+a^{\sigma_{2}}\right)$ where $\sigma_{1}$ and $\sigma_{2}$ are commuting unital associative specializations of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{N})$. More precisely, we have the following results. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is of degree two, so $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{B}$ the Jordan algebra of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{V}$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{V}$ is even, then every irreducible unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ is isomorphic to a sub-bimodule of $\mathfrak{N}=C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ considered as a bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ so that $y . a=\frac{1}{2}(y a+a y)$ for $y \in C(\mathfrak{B}, f), a \in \mathfrak{J}$, where $y a$ and $a y$ are the associative products. Since $a \rightarrow a_{R}$ and $a \rightarrow a_{L}$ acting in $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ are unital associative specializations of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(C(\mathfrak{B}, f), C(\mathfrak{B}, f))$ the result indicated is valid in this case. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}$ is odd the same result holds with $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ replaced by $C(\mathfrak{M}, f)$ where $\mathfrak{M}=\Phi u \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ and $f$ is extended to $\mathfrak{W}$ so that $f(u, u)=1$ and $f(u, v)=0=f(v, u), v \in \mathfrak{V}$. Next assume that $\mathfrak{J}$ has degree $n \geqq 3$, so $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a composition algebra over the algebraically closed field $\Phi$. The results of $\oint \S 3,4$ show that if $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}=1$ or 4 , so $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ is central simple, and $n>3$ where $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}=4$, then every unital irreducible bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ is isomorphic to a sub-bimodule of $\mathfrak{N} \equiv \mathfrak{D}_{n}$ considered $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule with the action y. $a=\frac{1}{2}(y a+a y)$ for $y \in \mathfrak{D}_{n}, a \in \mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$. If $n=3$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}=4$ then the irreducible components of $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ as $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule give all the unital irreducible bimodules for $\mathfrak{J}$ except one, namely, the one obtained from an irreducible component of the Cayley bimodule for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}=2$ then $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right) \cong \Phi_{n}{ }^{+}$and every unital irreducible $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule is isomorphic to a sub-bimodule of $\mathfrak{N} \equiv \Phi_{2 n}$ regarded as a bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi_{n}{ }^{+}$so that for $y \in \Phi_{2 n}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$ we have

$$
2 y \cdot a=y\left(\begin{array}{cc}
a & 0  \tag{15}\\
0 & a^{t}
\end{array}\right)+\left(\begin{array}{cc}
a & 0 \\
0 & a^{t}
\end{array}\right) y,
$$

$a^{t}$ the transpose of $a$. If $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is an octonion algebra then the regular bimodule reg $\mathfrak{J}$ is the only irreducible unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ (p. 283). It is now clear that Theorem 14 will follow if we can show that if the degree of $\mathfrak{J}$ is not divisible by the characteristic then the derivations of $\mathfrak{J}$ into the corresponding bimodules $\mathfrak{N}$ just defined are inner and, moreover, the same holds for $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right), \mathfrak{D}$ quaternion with $\mathfrak{M}$ the bimodule obtained from an irreducible component of cay $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$, and $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right), \mathfrak{D}$ octonion with $\mathfrak{M}=$ reg $\mathfrak{J}$.

We shall consider the cases of the special bimodules first and for this we shall
now develop some results which are of general interest. We suppose now that $\mathfrak{I}$ is any special Jordan algebra with 1 and $\mathfrak{N}$ is a unital special bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $y . a=\frac{1}{2}\left(y a^{\sigma_{1}}+a^{\sigma_{2}}\right)$ where $\sigma_{1}$ and $\sigma_{2}$ are commuting unital associative specializations of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{N})$. Let $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ be the unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}, \pi$ the main involution in $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is special we can identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with the corresponding subspace of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is a subalgebra of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})^{+}$ and $\pi$ is characterized by $a^{\pi}=a, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. The $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule $\mathfrak{N}$ can be regarded as an associative bimodule for $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ so that $a y=y a^{\sigma_{1}}, y a=y a^{\sigma_{2}}, y \in \mathfrak{N}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ generates $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ this determines uniquely the actions of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ on $\mathfrak{N}$. Let $\mathfrak{F}=S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus \mathfrak{N}$ the split null extension of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ by $\mathfrak{N}$, so $\mathfrak{F}$ is an associative algebra with 1 . Let $D$ be a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$. Then $\sigma: a \rightarrow a+a D$ is a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{F}$. If $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $(a+a D) \cdot(b+b D)=a \cdot b+a \cdot b D+a D \cdot b =a . b+(a . b) D$. Also $1 D=0$ so $1^{\sigma}=1$. Hence $\sigma$ is a unital associative specialization of $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{F}$ and so there exists a homomorphism of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{F}$ which extends $\sigma$. It is clear that this has the form $x \rightarrow x+z, x \in S_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), z \in \mathfrak{N}$. Then we have the mapping $D_{u}: x \rightarrow z$ which is clearly linear. Since $x \rightarrow x+x D_{u}$ is a homomorphism of associative algebras, $\left(x+x D_{u}\right)\left(y+y D_{u}\right)=x y+(x y) D_{u}$. Since $\Re^{2}=0$ this gives $(x y) D_{u}=x\left(y D_{u}\right)+\left(x D_{u}\right) y$, so $D_{u}$ is a derivation of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ into its bimodule $\mathfrak{N}$. It is clear also that $D_{u}$ is an extension of the given derivation $D$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$.

We recall that a derivation of an associative algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ into a bimodule $\mathfrak{N}$ is called inner if it has the form $x \rightarrow[x, d]=x d-d x$ for some $d \in \mathfrak{N}$. We have the following

Lemma 2. Let $\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{N}, S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ be as above. Then every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$ is inner if and only if : (1) every derivation of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{N}$ is inner and (2) $\mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak{Z}+[\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{J}]$ where $\mathfrak{Z}=\{z \in \mathfrak{N} \mid[a, z]=0, a \in \mathfrak{J}\}$ and $[\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{I}]$ is the subspace of $\mathfrak{N}$ spanned by the elements $[y, a], y \in \mathfrak{N}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$.

Proof. Suppose first that (1) and (2) hold. Let $D$ be a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$, $D_{u}$ the extension $D_{u}$ of $D$ to a derivation of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{N}$ as above. Then $D_{u}$ is an inner derivation of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$, so there exists a $d \in \mathfrak{N}$ such that $x D_{u}=[x, d], x \in S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. Hence for all $a \in \mathfrak{J}, a D=[a, d]$. By (2), $d=z+\sum\left[y_{i}, b_{i}\right]$ where $z \in \mathcal{Z}, y_{i} \in \mathfrak{N}$, $b_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then $a D=\Sigma_{i}\left[a,\left[y_{i}, b_{i}\right]\right]$. Now in $\mathfrak{F}^{+}$we have $[y, a, b]=y . a . b-y .(a . b) =\frac{1}{4}[a,[y, b]]$. Hence $a D=4 \Sigma\left[y_{i}, a, b_{i}\right]$ so $D$ is an inner derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$. Conversely, suppose every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$ is inner. Let $D$ be a derivation of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\mathfrak{N}$. Then the restriction of $D$ to $\mathfrak{J}$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$. Hence there exists elements $y_{i} \in \mathfrak{N}, b_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$ such that $a D=4 \Sigma\left[y_{i}, a, b_{i}\right], a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then $a D=[a, d]$ where $d=\Sigma\left[y_{i}, b_{i}\right] \in \mathfrak{N}$. Since J generates $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ it follows that $D$ coincides with the inner derivation $x \rightarrow[x, d]$ of $S_{1}(\mathfrak{I})$ into $\mathfrak{N}$. Next let $d$ be any element of $\mathfrak{N}$. Then the mapping $a \rightarrow[a, d]$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$ so there exist $y_{i} \in N, b_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$ such that $[a, d]=4 \sum\left[y_{i}, a, b_{i}\right]$. This implies that $z=d -\Sigma\left[y_{i}, b_{i}\right]$ satisfies $[a, z]=0, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Thus, $z \in \mathcal{Z}$ and $d=z+\Sigma\left[y_{i} b_{i}\right]$. Hence $\mathfrak{N}=3+[\mathfrak{N}, \mathfrak{I}]$.

We shall now apply this to the simple $\mathfrak{J}$ over an algebraically closed field of degree $\geqq 2$ and the $\mathfrak{N}$ 's which we indicated before. We note first that in all cases $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is separable. It is well known that every derivation of a separable associative algebra into a finite-dimensional bimodule is inner (Cartan and Eilenberg, Homological Algebra, p. 179). Since $S_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is separable for finite-dimensional separable $\mathfrak{J}$ by Theorem 12, it follows that the first condition of Lemma 2 is satisfied in all cases. It remains to consider the validity of the second condition. Here we have to treat the various cases separately.

Case I. $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ the Jordan algebra of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $f$ on the even-dimensional space $\mathfrak{V}$. Here $\mathfrak{N}=C(\mathfrak{V}, f)$ and $3=\Phi 1$ since $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is central simple and $\mathfrak{J}$ generates $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Let ( $u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{2 m}$ ) be an orthogonal basis for $\mathfrak{B}$. Then $u_{i} u_{j}=-u_{j} u_{i}$ if $i \neq j$ and 1 and the elements $u_{i_{1}} u_{i_{2}} \cdots u_{i_{k}}, i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{k}$, constitute a basis for $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Since for $k$ even and $\geqq 2$ and distinct $j_{i}$,

$$
\begin{align*}
{\left[u_{j_{1}}, u_{j_{1}} u_{j_{2}} \cdots u_{j_{k}}\right] } & =2 f\left(u_{j_{1}}, u_{j_{1}}\right) u_{j_{2}} \cdots u_{j_{k}},  \tag{16}\\
{\left[u_{j_{1}}, u_{j_{2}} \cdots u_{j_{k}}\right] } & =2 u_{j_{1}} \cdots u_{j_{k}}
\end{align*}
$$

it is clear that $3+[\mathfrak{J}, C(\mathfrak{B}, f)]=C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$.
Case II. $\mathfrak{J}$ as in Case I but with $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}$ odd. Then $\mathfrak{N}=C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ where $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \Phi u_{2 m}$. This has an orthogonal basis $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{2 m}\right)$ where ( $u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{2 m-1}$ ) is an orthogonal basis for $\mathfrak{V}$. If we take $j_{1} \neq 2 m$ in (16) we see that $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)=\Phi 1+\Phi u_{1} u_{2} \cdots u_{2 m-1}+[\mathfrak{J}, C(\mathfrak{W}, f)]$. Since 1 and $u_{1} u_{2} \cdots u_{2 m-1} \in 3$ we again have $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)=3+[\mathfrak{J}, C(\mathfrak{W}, f)]$.

Case III. $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right), n \geqq 3,(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ a one or four-dimensional composition algebra. Then $\mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ and $\mathfrak{Z}=\Phi 1$ since $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ is central simple and $\mathfrak{J}$ generates $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$. We shall show that $\mathfrak{D}_{n}=3+\left[\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{D}_{n}\right]$ if and only if the characteristic $p$ of $\Phi$ is not a divisor of $n$. We have $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ and $\mathfrak{D}_{n}=\mathfrak{H} \oplus \mathfrak{S}$ where $\mathfrak{S} \equiv \mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ is the space of $J_{1}$-skew elements. We have seen that $[\mathfrak{H}, \mathfrak{H}]=\mathfrak{S}$ (p. 131). Hence $\left[\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{D}_{n}\right]=[\mathfrak{H}, \mathfrak{H}]+[\mathfrak{H}, \mathfrak{S}]=\mathfrak{S}+[\mathfrak{H},[\mathfrak{H}, \mathfrak{H}]]$. Since $[\mathfrak{H},[\mathfrak{H}, \mathfrak{H}]]$ is the subspace $\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{H}$ spanned by the associators $\left[a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\right], a_{i} \in \mathfrak{H}$, we have $\left[\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{D}_{n}\right]=\mathfrak{S}+\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$ and $\mathfrak{Z}+\left[\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{D}_{n}\right]=\mathfrak{S}+\Phi 1+\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$. Hence $\mathfrak{D}_{n}=3+\left[\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{D}_{n}\right]$ if and only if $\mathfrak{H}=\Phi 1+\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$. We now put $e_{i}=\frac{1}{2}[i i]$ where $d[i j]=d e_{i j}+d e_{j i}$, $d \in \mathfrak{D}, e_{i j}$ the usual matrix units. Then $E=\left\{e_{i}\right\}$ is a reducing set of primitive idempotents for $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}$ and these define the $E$-trace $t_{E}(a)=\Sigma \alpha_{i}$ if $a=\sum \alpha_{i} e_{i}+\sum_{i<j} d_{i j}[i j]$. Then we have seen that $t_{E}$ is associative (p. 199) so $\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$ is contained in the subspace of elements $a$ such that $t_{E}(a)=0$. Clearly the dimensionality of the latter space is $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{H}-1$. If $i \neq j, d[i j]=4\left[d[i j], e_{i}, e_{j}\right]$ and if $k \neq 1$ then $2\left[1[1 k], 1[1 k], e_{1}=e_{1}-e_{k}\right.$. It follows that $\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$ coincides with the space of elements of $E$-trace 0 so $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{H}^{\prime}=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{H}-1$. Since $t_{E}(1)=n$ it is clear that $1 \in \mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$ if and only if $p \mid n$. Thus $\mathfrak{H}=\Phi 1+\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$ if and only if $p \nmid n$ and so $\mathfrak{D}_{n}=3+\left[\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{D}_{n}\right]$ if and only if $p \nmid n$.

Case IV. $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi_{n}{ }^{+}, n \geqq 3$. Here $\mathfrak{N}=\Phi_{2 n}$ and the action of $\Phi_{n}{ }^{+}$on $\Phi_{2 n}$ is given by (15). We identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with the subset of matrices $a^{\sigma} \equiv \operatorname{diag}\left\{a, a^{t}\right\}$. Then $y \cdot a=y \cdot a^{\sigma}$. Since $\left[a^{\sigma}, b^{\sigma}\right]=\operatorname{diag}\left\{[a, b],-[b, a]^{t}\right\}$ it is clear that $[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ is the set of matrices $\operatorname{diag}\left\{a,-a^{t}\right\}$ with trace $\operatorname{tr} a=0$. It is immediate from this that the subalgebra of $\Phi_{2 n}$ generated by $\mathfrak{J}$ is the set of matrices $\operatorname{diag}\{a, b\}, a, b \in \Phi_{n}$. Hence 3 which is the subset of $\Phi_{2 n}$ of matrices commuting with all $a^{\sigma}$ is the set of matrices $\operatorname{diag}\{\alpha 1, \beta 1\}, \alpha, \beta \in \Phi, 1$ the identity of $\Phi_{n}$. Now $\left[\mathcal{J}, \Phi_{2 n}\right]$ contains all the matrices

$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc}
{[p, a]} & q a^{t}-a q  \tag{17}\\
r a-a^{t} r & {\left[s, a^{t}\right]}
\end{array}\right)=\left[\left(\begin{array}{cc}
p & q \\
r & s
\end{array}\right),\left(\begin{array}{cc}
a & 0 \\
0 & a^{t}
\end{array}\right)\right] .
$$

It is easily seen from this that $\left[\mathfrak{J}, \Phi_{2 n}\right]$ is the set of matrices $\left(\begin{array}{ll}p & q \\ r & s\end{array}\right)$ with $\operatorname{tr} p=0=\operatorname{tr} s$. Since $\operatorname{tr} 1=n$ for the identity 1 of $\Phi_{2 n}$ it is clear that $\mathfrak{Z}+\left[\mathfrak{J}, \Phi_{2 n}\right]=\Phi_{2 n}$ if and only if $p \nmid n$.

The results just obtained and Lemma 2 imply that if $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{N}$ are as listed in the foregoing cases then all derivations of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$ are inner if and only if the degree of $\mathfrak{J}$ is not divisible by the characteristic. We have seen that this reduces the proof of Theorem 14 to the following two cases for $\Phi$ algebraically closed of characteristic $\neq 2,3$.

Case V. If $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is quaternion and $\mathfrak{M}$ is an irreducible $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule associated with an irreducible factor of cay $\mathfrak{D}$ then every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ is inner.

Case VI. If $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is octonion and $\mathfrak{M}=$ reg $\mathfrak{D}$ then every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ is inner. It is clear also that we may replace the irreducible bimodule $\mathfrak{M}$ in Case V by cay $\mathfrak{D}$ itself. We shall give a proof which is applicable simultaneously to both cases. This will be based on a reduction to the consideration of bimodules for the coefficient algebra $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. For this we shall need some basic results on derivations of alternative algebras (cf. Schafer's An Introduction to Nonassociative Algebras, pp. 77-80).

Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be an alternative algebra and denote the left and right multiplications on $\mathfrak{A}$ by the element $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ as $a_{L}$ and $a_{R}$ respectively. It is an immediate consequence of the alternating character of the associator $[a, b, c]$ that we have the operator identities

$$
\begin{align*}
{\left[a_{L}, b_{L}\right] } & =-[a, b]_{L}-2\left[a_{L}, b_{R}\right] \\
{\left[a_{R}, b_{R}\right] } & =[a, b]_{R}-2\left[a_{L}, b_{R}\right] \tag{18}
\end{align*}
$$

in $\mathfrak{A}$. If the characteristic is $\neq 2$ then $\mathfrak{A}$ defines the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$with product $a . b=\frac{1}{2}(a b+b a)$ and multiplication $R_{a}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a_{L}+a_{R}\right)(\S 1.5)$. We have seen also that the mappings $a \rightarrow a_{R}$ and $a \rightarrow a_{L}$ are associative specializations
of $\mathfrak{U}^{+}$into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$ (eg. (19') on p.15). It follows that $a \rightarrow \frac{1}{2} a_{L}, a \rightarrow \frac{1}{2} a_{R}$ are multiplication specializations and, consequently, we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
4[a, b, c]_{L}^{+}=\left[\left[c_{L} a_{L}\right] b_{L}\right], \quad 4[a, b, c]_{R}^{+}=\left[\left[c_{R} a_{R}\right] b_{R}\right] \tag{19}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $[a, b, c]^{+}=(a . b) . c-a .(b . c)$, the associator in $\mathfrak{A}^{+}($cf. (47) on p. 96). We recall also that

$$
\begin{equation*}
4[a, b, c]+=-2[a, b, c]+[b[a c]] \tag{20}
\end{equation*}
$$

((33) on p. 19). Hence

$$
\begin{align*}
& {\left[\left[c_{L} a_{L}\right] b_{L}\right]=-2[a, b, c]_{L}+[b[a c]]_{L}}  \tag{21}\\
& {\left[\left[c_{R} a_{R}\right] b_{R}\right]=-2[a, b, c]_{R}+[b[a c]]_{R}}
\end{align*}
$$

The first equation in (18) implies that $\left[a_{L}, b_{R}-b_{L}\right]=[a b]_{L}+3\left[a_{L}, b_{R}\right]$. If we put $D=b_{R}-b_{L}$ then $a D=[a b]$ and so our relation reads $\left[a_{L}, D\right]=(a D)_{L}+3\left[a_{L}, b_{R}\right]$. Since a linear mapping $D$ in an algebra is a derivation if and only if $\left.\left[a_{L}, D\right]=(a D]\right)_{L}$ or if and only if $\left[a_{R}, D\right]=(a D)_{R}$ for all $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ we see that $D=b_{R}-b_{L}$ is a derivation in $\mathfrak{A}$ if and only if $3\left[a_{L}, b_{R}\right]=0$. Since $c\left[a_{L}, b_{R}\right]=[a, c, b]$ this is the case if and only if $3 b$ is in the nucleus. Hence we see that if $b=g \in N(\mathfrak{A})$ the nucleus of $\mathfrak{A}$ then $D=g_{R}-g_{L}$ is a derivation and if the characteristic is not three then, conversely, if $D=g_{R}-g_{L}$ is a derivation in $\mathfrak{A}$ then $g$ is in the nucleus. We shall show next that for any $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$ of characteristic $\neq 2$, the operator

$$
\begin{equation*}
D_{a, b} \equiv[a, b]_{R}-[a, b]_{L}-3\left[a_{L}, b_{R}\right] \tag{22}
\end{equation*}
$$

is a derivation in $\mathfrak{A}$. We have

$$
\begin{align*}
2\left[c_{R}, D_{a, b}\right] & =2\left[c_{R},[a, b]_{R}-[a, b]_{L}-3\left[a_{L}, b_{R}\right]\right] \\
& =3\left[c_{R},[a b]_{R}-2\left[a_{L} b_{R}\right]\right]-\left[c_{R},[a b]_{R}\right]-2\left[c_{R},[a b]_{L}\right] \\
& =3\left[c_{R},\left[a_{R} b_{R}\right]\right]-[c[a b]]_{R} \quad(\text { by }(18))  \tag{18}\\
& =-6[a, c, b]_{R}+2[c[a b]]_{R} \quad(\text { by }(21))  \tag{21}\\
& =2\left(c D_{a, b}\right)_{R}
\end{align*}
$$

Hence $\left[c_{R}, D_{a, b}\right]=\left(c D_{a, b}\right)_{R}$ and $D_{a, b}$ is a derivation. It follows that for arbitrary $a_{i}, b_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}$ (characteristic $\neq 2$ ) the mapping $\sum D_{a_{i}, b_{i}}$ is a derivation in $\mathfrak{A}$. Following Schafer we shall call any derivation of the form

$$
\begin{equation*}
\sum D_{a_{i}, b_{i}}+g_{R}-g_{L}, \quad g \in N(\mathfrak{A}) \tag{23}
\end{equation*}
$$

an inner derivation of $\mathfrak{A}$. It is useful to obtain two other formulas for the inner derivation $D_{a, b}$. First, direct substitution of (18) gives

$$
\begin{align*}
{\left[a_{L}, b_{L}\right]+\left[a_{R}, b_{R}\right]+\left[a_{L} b_{R}\right]=} & {[a, b]_{R}-[a, b]_{L} }  \tag{24}\\
& -3\left[a_{L} b_{R}\right]=D_{a, b}
\end{align*}
$$

Also we have $4\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right]=\left[a_{L} b_{L}\right]+\left[a_{R} b_{R}\right]+\left[a_{L} b_{R}\right]+\left[a_{R} b_{L}\right]=D_{a, b}+\left[a_{R} b_{L}\right]$. Since $\left[a_{R} b_{L}\right]=\left[a_{L} b_{R}\right]$ by the alternative law we have $4\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right]=D_{a, b}+\left[a_{L} b_{R}\right]$. If the characteristic is not three then (22) gives $-\left[a_{L} b_{R}\right]=\frac{1}{3}\left(D_{a, b}-[a, b]_{R}+[a, b]_{L}\right)$. Hence

$$
\begin{equation*}
4\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right]=(2 / 3) D_{a, b}+(1 / 3)[a b]_{R}-(1 / 3)[a b]_{L} \tag{25}
\end{equation*}
$$

if the characteristic of $\mathfrak{A}$ is $\neq 2,3$.
If $D$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{A}$ then clearly $D$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$. We have the following

Lemma 3. Let $\mathfrak{U}$ be an alternative algebra of characteristic $\neq 2,3, D$ a derivation in $\mathfrak{A}$. Assume that $D$ is an inner derivation of $\mathfrak{U}^{+}$. Then $D$ is an inner derivation of $\mathfrak{A}$.

Proof. We are given that there exist elements $a_{i}, b_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}$ such that $D=4 \sum\left[R_{a_{i}} R_{b_{i}}\right]$. Then, by (25), $D=(2 / 3) \sum D_{a_{i}, b_{i}}+g_{R}-g_{L}$ where $g=(1 / 3) \sum\left[a_{i} b_{i}\right]$. Since $\sum D_{a_{i}, b_{i}}$ is a derivation, $g_{R}-g_{L}$ is a derivation and so $g \in N(\mathfrak{A})$. Then $D=(2 / 3) \sum D_{a_{i}, b_{i}}+g_{R}-g_{L}$ is an inner derivation of $\mathfrak{A}$.

Let $\mathfrak{N}$ be an alternative bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{F}=\mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{N}$ the corresponding split null extension. We shall call a derivation $D$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$ inner if its linear extension to $\mathfrak{F}$ such that $\mathfrak{N D}=0$ is an inner derivation of $\mathfrak{F}$. It is easily seen, as in the Jordan case, that $D$ is inner if and only if there exist elements $b_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}$, $y_{i} \in \mathfrak{N}, z \in \mathfrak{N} \cap N(\mathfrak{F})$, such that $D=\sum D_{b_{i}, y_{i}}+z_{R}-z_{L}$. We shall call $\mathfrak{N} \cap N(\mathfrak{F})$ the nucleus of the bimodule $\mathfrak{N}$. Clearly this is the set of elements $z \in \mathfrak{N}$ such that $[z, a, b]=0, a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$.

If $\mathfrak{N}$ is an alternative bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ then $\mathfrak{N}$ is a Jordan bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}+$ relative to the composition $x . a=\frac{1}{2}(x a+a x), x \in \mathfrak{N}, a \in \mathfrak{A}$. It is clear that any derivation of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{A}+$ into $\mathfrak{N}$. Evidently, Lemma 3 implies that if $D$ is an inner derivation of $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$into $\mathfrak{N}$ then $D$ is an inner derivation of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$.

We shall now apply these results to the alternative algebras and bimodules which are needed to treat the remaining Cases V and VI described above. Here we consider a composition algebra $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ over a field of characteristic $\neq 2,3$ which is either quaternion or octonion. Let ( $\mathfrak{N}, j$ ) be a bimodule with involution for $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ which in the quaternion case is cay $\mathfrak{D}$ and in the octonion case is reg $\mathfrak{D}$. By a derivation $D$ of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ into $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$ we shall mean a derivation of $\mathfrak{D}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$ such that $\bar{a} D=\overline{a D}, a \in \mathfrak{D}$. Then we have

Lemma 4. Let $D$ be a derivation of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ into $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$. Then there exist elements $b_{i} \in \mathfrak{D}, y_{i} \in \mathfrak{N}, i=1,2, \cdots, r$, such that $\bar{b}_{i}=-b_{i}, \bar{y}_{i}=-y_{i}, \sum_{1}^{r}\left[y_{i}, b_{i}\right]=0$ and $a D=\sum_{1}^{r}\left[y_{i}, a, b_{i}\right]^{+}, a \in \mathfrak{D}$.

Proof. Since $\mathfrak{D}^{+}$is the Jordan algebra of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear
form and $D$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{D}+$ into $\mathfrak{N}$ the result proved in Cases I and II shows that there exist elements $b_{i} \in \mathfrak{D}, y_{i} \in \mathfrak{N}$ such that $a D=\Sigma_{1}^{r}\left[y_{i}, a, b_{i}\right]^{+}, a \in \mathfrak{D}$. We can write $b_{i}=\beta_{i} 1+c_{i}$ where $\bar{c}_{i}=-c_{i}$. Since $\mathfrak{N}$ is a unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{D}^{+}$we have $\left[y_{i}, a, \beta_{i} 1\right]^{+}=0, a \in \mathfrak{D}$. Hence we may assume $\bar{b}_{i}=-b_{i}$. In the quaternion case $\bar{y}=-y$ for all $y \in \mathfrak{N}$ so $\overline{y_{i}}=-y_{i}$. In the octonion case we have $\mathfrak{N}=N(\mathfrak{N}) \oplus \mathfrak{N}_{0}$ where $N(\mathfrak{N})$ and $\mathfrak{N}_{0}$ are the images of $\Phi 1$ and the set of skew elements of $\mathfrak{D}$ under an isomorphism of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ onto $(\Re, j)$. It follows that $y_{i}=u_{i}+z_{i}$ where $u_{i} \in N(\mathfrak{N})$ and $\bar{z}_{i}=-z_{i}$. Then $u_{i}$ is in the center of the split null extension $\mathfrak{F}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus \mathfrak{N}$ so $\left[u_{i}, a, b_{i}\right]^{+}=0$. Hence we may assume $\overline{y_{i}}=-y_{i}$. Since $a D=\Sigma\left[y_{i}, a, b_{i}\right]^{+}=a \sum\left[R_{y_{i}} R_{b_{i}}\right]$, (25) gives $a D=\frac{1}{6} \sum D_{y_{i}, b_{i}}+a\left(g_{R}-g_{L}\right)$ where $g=\frac{1}{12} \sum\left[y_{i} b_{i}\right]$. Since $\sum D_{y_{i}, b_{i}}$ and $D$ are derivations of $\mathfrak{F}, g_{R}-g_{L}$ is a derivation in $\mathfrak{F}$. Hence $g$ is in the nucleus of $\mathfrak{N}$. On the other hand, $\bar{y}_{i}=-y_{i}$, $\tilde{b}_{i}=-b_{i}$ imply that $\bar{g}=-g$. Since the elements of the nucleus of $\mathfrak{N}$ are symmetric we see that $g=0$. Hence $\Sigma\left[y_{i} b_{i}\right]=0$ as required.

Now let $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{M}$ be as in V and VI and let $D$ be a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$. We have $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is either quaternion or octonion. The restriction of $D$ to the subalgebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ as bimodule for this algebra. Since the characteristic is not three the result proved in Case III above implies that the restriction of $D$ to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ is inner. Hence there exist $x_{i} \in \mathfrak{M}, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ so that $a D=\sum\left[x_{i}, a, a_{i}\right]$ for all $a \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{1}\right)$. Thus if we subtract the inner derivation $x \rightarrow \sum\left[x_{i}, x, a_{i}\right]$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ from $D$ we obtain a derivation annihilating $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{1}\right)$. Hence to prove that every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ is inner it is enough to do this for the derivations $D$ such that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{1}\right) D=0$. Let $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ the split null extension of $\mathfrak{J}$ by $\mathfrak{M}$. Then, as in §3.5, we may identify $\mathfrak{E}$ with the Jordan matrix algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{F}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus \mathfrak{N}$ is the split null extension of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ by the unital bimodule $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$. Moreover, by hypotheses, ( $\mathfrak{N}, j$ ) is cay $\mathfrak{D}$ if $\mathfrak{D}$ is quaternion and ( $\mathfrak{N}, j$ ) is reg $\mathfrak{D}$ if $\mathfrak{D}$ is octonion. Also $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{3}, J_{1}\right) \cap \mathfrak{N}_{3}$ and we extend $D$ to $\mathfrak{F}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{F}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ so that $\mathfrak{M} D=0$. Since $1[i i] D=0$ it is clear that the Peirce component $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the orthogonal idempotents $e_{i}=\frac{1}{2}[i i]$ is mapped by $D$ into the Peirce space $\mathfrak{E}_{i j}$ of $\mathfrak{E}$ relative to the $e_{i}$. Hence for $x \in \mathfrak{D}, i \neq j, x[i j] D=x^{d_{i j}}[i j]$ where $x^{d_{i j}} \in \mathfrak{N}$. This defines a linear mapping $d_{i j}: x \rightarrow x^{d_{i j}}$ of $\mathfrak{D}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$. Since $2 x[i j] .1[j k]=x[i k]$ for distinct $i, j, k$ and $1[j k] D=0$ we see that $2 x^{d_{i j}}[i j] .1[j k]=x^{d_{i k}}[i k]$. Hence $d_{i j}=d_{i k}$ and, similarly, $d_{i j}=d_{k j}$. Hence $d_{i j}=d_{k l}$ if $i \neq j$ and $k \neq l$. Then the relation $2 x[i j] . y[j k]=x y[i k]$ implies that $d \equiv d_{i}$, is a derivation of $\mathfrak{D}$ into $\mathfrak{N}$. Since $x[j i]=\bar{x}[i j], x^{d}[j i]=x[j i] D=\bar{x}[i j] D =\bar{x}^{d}[i j]=\overline{\bar{x}^{d}}[j i]$. Hence $\bar{x}^{d}=\overline{x^{d}}$ so $d$ is a derivation of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ into $(\mathfrak{N}, j)$. Hence, by Lemma 4, there exist elements $y_{i} \in \mathfrak{N}, b_{i} \in \mathfrak{D}$ such that $\bar{y}_{i}=-y_{i}, \bar{b}_{i}=-b_{i}$, $\Sigma\left[y_{i} b_{i}\right]=0$ and $x^{d}=\Sigma\left[y_{i}, x, b_{i}\right]^{+}$for all $x \in \mathfrak{D}$. Now let $E$ be the inner derivation $a \rightarrow \Sigma_{i}\left[y_{i}[21], a, b_{i}[12]\right]$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$. We proceed to show that $E=D$ which will prove that $D$ is inner. It is immediate from the multiplication formulas in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ that this algebra is generated by the elements $x[12], x \in \mathfrak{D}$ and 1 [23].

Hence it is sufficient to show that $x[12] D=x[12] E$ and $1[23] E=0$. Now, it is clear that $4[y[21], x[12], b[12]]=z[12]$ and direct calculation gives

$$
z=(x y+\bar{y} \bar{x}) b+b(y x+\bar{x} \bar{y})-(b \bar{x}+x \bar{b}) \bar{y}-\bar{y}(\bar{x} b+\bar{b} x) .
$$

If $\bar{y}=-y, \bar{b}=-b$ and $x=\xi 1+w$ where $\xi \in \Phi$ and $\bar{w}=-w$ then this becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
z & =(w y+y w) b+b(y w+w y)-(b w+w b) y-y(w b+b w) \\
& =4[y, w, b]^{+}=4[y, x, b]^{+}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $[y[21], x[12]]=[y, x, b]^{+}[12]$ and $x[12] E=\sum\left[y_{i}[21], x[12], b_{i}[12]\right] =\Sigma\left[y_{i}, x, b\right]^{+}[12]=x^{d}[12]=x[12] D$. Also $4[y[21], 1[23], b[12]]=[b, y][23]$. Hence $1[23] E=\Sigma\left[y_{i}[21], 1[23], ; b_{i}[12]\right]=0$. This completes the proof of Theorem 14.

We note also that the consideration of Cases III and IV above show that if a finite-dimensional separable Jordan algebra has a special simple component whose degree over its center is divisible by the characteristic then not all derivations of $\mathfrak{J}$ into finite-dimensional bimodules are inner.

If $\mathfrak{J}$ is a subalgebra of the Jordan algebra and $D$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\Omega$ in the sense that $D$ is linear from $\mathfrak{J}$ to $\mathfrak{K}$ and $(a . b) D=a D . b+a . b D, a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $D$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\Re$ considered as $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule with the composition $x . a, x \in \Re, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, as the product in $\mathfrak{K}$. If $D$ is an inner derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into the $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule $\mathfrak{K}$ then there exist $y_{i} \in \mathfrak{K}, b_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$ such that $a D=\Sigma\left[y_{i}, a, b_{i}\right], a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Evidently this implies the following

Corollary to Theorem 14. Let J be a separable Jordan algebra satisfying the condition of Theorem 14. Then every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{K}$ containing $\mathfrak{J}$ as subalgebra can be extended to an inner derivation of $\Re$.
8. Uniqueness of the Albert-Penico-Taft decomposition. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finitedimensional Jordan algebra, $\Re=\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ and assume $\mathfrak{J} / \Re$ is separable so we have an Albert-Penico-Taft decomposition $\mathfrak{J}=\Re \oplus \Re$ where $\mathfrak{K}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$. We shall now call such a $\mathfrak{K}$ an A.P.T. factor of $\mathfrak{J}$. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ and let $b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then $b=b^{\eta}+b D$ where $b^{\eta} \in \Re$ and $b D \in \Re$ and $\eta$ and $D$ are linear mappings of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{J}$ (or into $\mathfrak{K}$ and $\Re$ respectively). If $b_{1}, b_{2} \in \mathfrak{B}$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}
b_{1} \cdot b_{2} & =\left(b_{1} \cdot b_{2}\right)^{\eta}+\left(b_{1} \cdot b_{2}\right) D \\
& =\left(b_{1}^{\eta}+b_{1} D\right) \cdot\left(b_{2}^{\eta}+b_{2} D\right) \\
& =b_{1}^{\eta} \cdot b_{2}^{\eta}+\left(b_{1} D\right) \cdot b_{2}^{\eta}+b_{1}^{\eta} \cdot b_{2} D+b_{1} D \cdot b_{2} D
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathcal{K}$ is a subalgebra and $\Re$ is an ideal we have

$$
\begin{align*}
& \left(b_{1} \cdot b_{2}\right)^{\eta}=b_{1}^{\eta} \cdot b_{2}^{\eta}  \tag{26}\\
& \left(b_{1} \cdot b_{2}\right) D=b_{1} D \cdot b_{2}^{\eta}+b_{1}^{\eta} \cdot b_{2} D+b_{1} D \cdot b_{2} D
\end{align*}
$$

Hence $\eta$ is a homomorphism and consequently $\mathfrak{K}$ and $\Re$ are bimodules for $\mathfrak{B}$ relative to the composition $x * b=x . b^{\eta}, b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Assume first that $\Re^{\cdot 2}=0$ (so $\mathfrak{J}$ is the split null extension of $\Re$ by $\Re$ as a $\mathfrak{K}$-bimodule). Then we have $\left(b_{1} . b_{2}\right) D =b_{1} D \cdot b_{2}{ }^{\eta}+b_{1}{ }^{\eta} \cdot b_{2} D=b_{1} D * b_{2}+b_{1} * b_{2} D$. Hence $D$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\Re$ as $\mathfrak{B}$-bimodule with the $*$ composition. Now assume that $\mathfrak{B}$ is separable and satisfies the condition of Harris' theorem (Theorem 14). Then $D$ is an inner derivation of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\Re$, which means that there exist elements $y_{i} \in \Re, d_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ such that $b D=\sum_{i}\left(y_{i} * b * d_{i}-y_{i} *\left(b . d_{i}\right)\right)$. We have $y_{i} * b_{i} * d_{i}=y_{i} . b^{\eta} . d_{i}^{\eta}$ and $y_{i} *\left(b . d_{i}\right)=y_{i} .\left(b^{\eta} . d_{i}^{\eta}\right)$. Hence $y_{i} * b * d_{i}-y_{i} *\left(b . d_{i}\right)=b^{\eta}\left[R_{y_{i}}, R_{d_{i}{ }^{\eta}}\right]$ and $b D= b^{\eta} \sum\left[R_{y_{i}} R_{d_{i} \eta}{ }^{\eta}\right]$. Now the mapping $E=\sum\left[R_{y_{i}} R_{d_{i}{ }^{\eta}}\right]$ is an inner derivation in $\mathfrak{J}$ and since the $y_{i} \in \Re, \mathfrak{J} E \subseteq \Re$ and $\Re E=0$ so $E^{2}=0$. These conditions imply that $\zeta=1+E$ is an automorphism with inverse $\zeta^{-1}=1-E$. Moreover, if $b \in \mathfrak{B}$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}
b^{\zeta^{-1}} & =b-b E=b^{\eta}+b D-\left(b^{\eta}+b D\right) E \\
& =b^{\eta}+b D-b^{\eta} E \\
& =b^{\eta} \in \Omega
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $\zeta^{-1}$ is an automorphism mapping $\mathfrak{B}$ into the subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}^{\eta}$ of $\mathfrak{K}$. We therefore have the following theorem.

Theorem 15. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra such that $\Re^{\cdot 2}=0$ for $\Re=\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J} / \Re$ is separable, and let $\mathfrak{J}=\Re \oplus \Re$ where $\mathfrak{K}$ is a subalgebra. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a separable subalgebra such that the degrees over their centers of the simple components of $\mathfrak{B}$ are not divisible by the characteristic. Then there exists an automorphism $\zeta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ of the form $\zeta=1+E$ where $E$ is an inner derivation such that $\mathfrak{J} E \subseteq \Re$ and $\Re E=0$, such that $\mathfrak{B}^{\zeta^{-1}} \subseteq \Re$.

We shall now extend this theorem to the case in which $\Re$ is arbitrary. For this we shall need to assume that the characteristic is 0 . In this case it is well known (and easy to verify using Leibniz' rule) that if $D$ is a nilpotent derivation in an algebra then $\exp D \equiv 1+D+D^{2} / 2!+\cdots+D^{m} / m!$, where $D^{m+1}=0$, is an automorphism of the algebra. We recall that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra then $\Re=\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ generates a nilpotent ideal in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ (Theorem 5.2). It follows that any inner derivation of the form $\sum\left[R_{z_{i}} R_{a_{i}}\right], z_{i} \in \Re, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$, is nilpotent, and in the characteristic 0 case $\exp \left(\sum\left[R_{z_{i}} R_{a_{i}}\right]\right)$ is an automorphism. Let H denote the subgroup of the group of automorphisms generated by these automorphisms. Then we have the following

Theorem 16. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra over a field of characteristic $0, \mathfrak{K}$ a subalgebra such that $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{K} \oplus \Re, \Re=\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ and let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a semisimple subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$. Then there exists an automorphism $\eta \in \mathrm{H}$ such that $\mathfrak{B}^{\eta} \subseteq \mathfrak{R}$.

Proof. The result is trivial if $\Re=0$ so we may use induction on $\operatorname{dim} \Re$ and we may assume $\Re \neq 0$. Then $\Re$ contains an ideal $\mathfrak{S}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $\mathfrak{S} \neq 0$ and $\mathfrak{S}^{\cdot 2}=0$. We consider the algebra $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{S}$ whose radical is $\bar{\Re}=\Re / \mathfrak{S}$. We have the decomposition $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\overline{\mathfrak{K}} \oplus \bar{\Re}$ where $\overline{\mathfrak{K}}$ is the subalgebra $(\mathfrak{K}+\mathfrak{S}) / \mathfrak{S}$. Also $\overline{\mathfrak{B}}=(\mathfrak{B}+\mathfrak{S}) / \mathfrak{S}$ is a semisimple subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $\operatorname{dim} \bar{\Re}<\operatorname{dim} \Re$ we can use the induction hypothesis to conclude that there is an automorphism $\bar{\eta}$ in the group $\overline{\mathrm{H}}$ defined for $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$ such that $\overline{\mathfrak{B}}^{\bar{\eta}} \subseteq \overline{\mathfrak{K}}$. Now $\bar{\eta}$ is a product of automorphisms of the form $\exp \left(\sum\left[R_{\bar{z}_{i}}, R_{\bar{a}_{i}}\right]\right), \bar{z}_{i}=z_{i}+\mathfrak{S}, \bar{a}_{i}=a_{i}+\mathfrak{S}$ where $z_{i} \in \Re, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$. Let $\eta$ be the corresponding product of the automorphisms $\exp \left(\sum\left[R_{z_{i}} R_{a_{i}}\right]\right)$ in $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\eta \in \mathrm{H}$ and it is clear that $\mathfrak{B}^{\eta} \subseteq \mathfrak{K} \oplus \mathfrak{S}$. Now $\mathfrak{K} \oplus \mathfrak{S}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ whose radical is $\mathfrak{S}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{n}$ is a semisimple subalgebra of $\mathfrak{R}+\mathfrak{S}$. Since $\mathfrak{S}^{\cdot 2}=0$ the proof of Theorem 15 shows that there exists an automorphism $\zeta^{-1}=1-E$ where $E=\Sigma\left[R_{y_{i}} R_{b_{i}}\right], y_{i} \in \mathfrak{S}, b_{i} \in \mathfrak{K}+\mathfrak{S}$ such that $\mathfrak{B}^{n \zeta^{-1}} \subseteq \mathfrak{K}$. Also $E^{2}=0$ so $\zeta^{-1}=\exp (-E)$. Hence $\zeta^{-1} \in \mathrm{H}$ and $\eta \zeta^{-1} \in \mathrm{H}$ and maps $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{K}$.

It is clear that any two A.P.T. factors of $\mathfrak{J}$ have the same dimensionality. Moreover, since $\Re$ is mapped into itself by every automorphism it is clear that the image of a A.P.T. factor under an automorphism is an A.P.T. factor. It is now clear that the following corollary is an immediate consequence of Theorem 16.

Corollary. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra over a field of characteristic 0 . Then if $\mathfrak{K}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{K}_{2}$ are A.P.T. factors of $\mathfrak{J}$ there exists an automorphism $\eta \in \mathrm{H}$ such that $\mathfrak{R}_{1}{ }^{\eta}=\mathfrak{R}_{2}$. Also any semisimple subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ is contained in an A.P.T. factor.

## Exercises

1. Let $\Phi[a]$ be the Jordan algebra with 1 generated by a single algebraic element $a$ with minimum polynomial $\mu(\lambda)$ and let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a unital bimodule for $\Phi[a], \mathfrak{E}$ the split null extension. If $f(\lambda) \in \Phi[\lambda]$ we let $f$ be the polynomial mapping $x \rightarrow f(x)$ in $\mathfrak{E}$. Show that there exists a derivation of $\Phi[a]$ in $\mathfrak{M}$ sending $a$ into $z \in \mathfrak{M}$ if and only if the directional derivative $\Delta^{z}{ }_{a} \mu$ of $\mu(\lambda)$ in the direction $z$ at $a$ is 0 .
2. Let $\mathfrak{H}$ be the Jordan algebra of $n \times n$ symmetric matrices over $\Phi, \mathfrak{S}$ the space of $n \times n$ skew matrices, and consider $\mathfrak{S}$ as unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{S}$ relative to $s . h=\frac{1}{2}(s h+h s), h \in \mathfrak{H}, s \in \mathfrak{S}$. Show that for fixed $k \in \mathfrak{H}$ the mapping $x \rightarrow[x, k]=x k-k x, x \in \mathfrak{H}$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{H}$ into $\mathfrak{S}$. Show that if the minimum polynomial $\mu(\lambda)$ of the element $h \in \mathfrak{H}$ has degree $n$ and $s$ is any element of $\mathfrak{S}$ then there exists a derivation of the form indicated mapping $h$ into $s$. Hence
show that $\Delta^{s}{ }_{h^{\mu}}=0$ and that any derivation of $\Phi[\dot{h}]$ into $\mathbb{S}$ can be extended to a derivation of $\mathfrak{H}$ into $\mathfrak{S}$. Does the last result hold without the hypothesis that $\operatorname{deg} \mu(\lambda)=n$ ?
3. Let $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{H} \oplus \mathfrak{S}$ the split null extension of $\mathfrak{H}$ by $\mathfrak{S}$ defined in 2 . Let $a \in \mathfrak{E}$ have minimum polynomial of degree $n$ and satisfy $\Phi[a] \cap \mathfrak{S}=0$. If $b \in \Phi[a]$ write $b=k+t$ where $k \in \mathfrak{H}$ and $t \in \mathfrak{S}$. Show that $b \rightarrow k$ is a monomorphism of $\Phi[a]$ into $\mathfrak{H}$ and that $k \rightarrow t$ is a derivation of $\Phi[h]$ into the bimodule $\mathfrak{S}$. Use this and exercise 2 to show that there exists an automorphism of $\mathfrak{E}$ sending $a$ into $h$ where $a=h+s, h \in \mathfrak{H}, s \in \mathfrak{S}$.
4. Let $\mathfrak{H}, \mathfrak{S}$ be as in 2 . Show that there exist elements $h \in \mathfrak{H}$ and derivations of $\Phi[h]$ into $\mathfrak{S}$ which are not inner.

## Chapter VIII

## CONNECTIONS WITH LIE ALGEBRAS

With a given Jordan algebra J one can associate a number of important Lie algebras. We have already encountered some of these before in special cases, for example, the Lie algebra Der $\mathfrak{J}$ and the Lie algebra of linear transformations having the generic norm as Lie invariant (§6.9). In this chapter we shall study several Lie algebras associated to a Jordan algebra. One of these is the Lie algebra of linear transformations generated by the multiplications $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, and related Lie algebras defined by the universal envelopes $U(\mathfrak{J}), U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ etc. Another important Lie algebra construction we shall consider is one which has been introduced by Tits in [4] and studied further by Koecher in [9]. The constructions we have indicated are interesting from the point of view of Lie theory since they provide realizations of some important classes of Lie algebras. However, our primary interest in these constructions in this chapter stems from the fact that they provide tools for establishing some of the main results of the last chapter in the characteristic 0 case without invoking a detailed knowledge of the classification of simple Jordan algebras and irreducible bimodules. Since this approach is based on results in Lie algebras which are known to be false in the characteristic $p \neq 0$ case it seems unlikely that the Lie algebra techniques developed here can be adapted in a simple manner to the characteristic $p$ case.

It is well known that a fundamental concept in the theory of Lie algebras is that of a Cartan subalgebra of a Lie algebra. In this chapter we shall define an analogous concept for finite-dimensional Jordan algebras. We shall show that the main facts on Cartan subalgebras in the Lie case carry over and we shall apply the theory to obtain a general proof of the generic trace criterion for separability of Jordan algebras (Theorem 6.5). The notion of a Cartan subalgebra is based on the associator structure of a Jordan algebra. As we shall see in §1, this is a special case of a Lie triple system structure, which has a simple axiomatic characterization. Moreover, Lie triple systems give rise to universal enveloping Lie algebras. These Lie algebras defined by the associator structure of a Jordan algebra are interesting too, and are closely related to some of the Lie algebras we have indicated before.

1. Associator structure of a Jordan algebra. Abstract Lie triple systems. We recall that in any Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ we have the basic identity

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[\left[R_{c} R_{a}\right] R_{b}\right]=R_{[a, b, c]} \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $[a, b, c]$ is the associator $[a, b, c]=a . b . c-a .(b . c)$ (e.g. (54) p. 34). As we noted before, this shows that the subspace $R(\mathfrak{J})$ of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ consisting of the linear transformations $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, is a Lie triple system of linear transformations of $\mathfrak{J}$, that is, a subspace of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ closed under the composition $[[A B] C]$. We shall now denote the iterated Lie product $[[C A] B]$ by $[A B C]$ and call this the Lie triple product of the linear transformations $A, B, C$. With this notation we can rewrite (1) as

$$
\begin{equation*}
R_{[a, b, c]}=\left[R_{a} R_{b} R_{c}\right] . \tag{$\prime$}
\end{equation*}
$$

It is clear that the Lie triple product is trilinear and we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
[A B A]=0, \tag{2}
\end{equation*}
$$

which for characteristic not two is equivalent to

$$
\begin{equation*}
[A B C]+[C B A]=0 . \tag{3}
\end{equation*}
$$

Also, we have the Jacobi identity

$$
\begin{equation*}
[A B C]+[B C A]+[C A B]=0 . \tag{3}
\end{equation*}
$$

Moreover, since $[A B C]=[[C A] B],[D[A B C] E]=[[E D],[[C A] B]]$. We now write for the moment $[[E D], X]=X^{\prime}$. Applying the Jacobi identity twice we obtain

$$
\begin{equation*}
[[C A] B]^{\prime}=\left[\left[C^{\prime} A\right] B\right]+\left[\left[C A^{\prime}\right] B\right]+\left[[C A] B^{\prime}\right] . \tag{4}
\end{equation*}
$$

Hence we have following Lie triple product identity

$$
\begin{equation*}
[D[A B C] E]=[[D A E] B C]+[A[D B E] C]+[A B[D C E]] . \tag{4́}
\end{equation*}
$$

In a similar fashion it is clear that if $\mathfrak{L}$ is any Lie algebra with product composition [ab] then

$$
\begin{equation*}
[a b c]=[[c a] b] \tag{5}
\end{equation*}
$$

defines a trilinear composition on $\mathfrak{L}$ satisfying:

$$
\begin{align*}
{[a b a] } & =0,  \tag{i}\\
{[a b c]+[b c a]+[c a b] } & =0,  \tag{ii}\\
{[d[a b c] e] } & =[[d a e] b c]+[a[d b e] c]+[a b[d c e]] . \tag{iii}
\end{align*}
$$

These observations lead us to introduce the following definitions.
Definition 1. A vector space $\mathfrak{T} / \Phi$ with a trilinear composition $(a, b, c) \rightarrow[a, b, c]$ satisfying (i), (ii) and (iii) is called an (abstract) Lie triple system. A linear mapping $D$ in $\mathfrak{T} / \Phi$ is called a derivation if

$$
\begin{equation*}
[a b c] D=[(a D) b c]+[a(b D) c]+[a b(c D)] . \tag{6}
\end{equation*}
$$

It is clear that (iii) states that the linear mapping $I_{d, e}: x \rightarrow[d x e]$ is a derivation in $\mathfrak{T}$. We shall call any derivation of the form $\sum I_{d_{i}, e_{i}}$ an inner derivation in $\mathfrak{T}$. Clearly the set Inder $\mathfrak{T}$ of inner derivations is closed under addition. Moreover, since

$$
\begin{equation*}
\alpha I_{d, e}=I_{\alpha d, e}=I_{d, \alpha e} \tag{7}
\end{equation*}
$$

Inder $\mathfrak{T}$ is a subspace of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{T}, \mathfrak{T})$. It is trivial to verify that the set Der $\mathfrak{T}$ of derivations of $\mathfrak{T}$ is a subalgebra of the Lie algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{T}, \mathfrak{T})^{-}$. If $D$ is any derivation then (6) gives $[a b c] D-[a(b D) c]=[(a D) b c]+[a b(c D)]$ which in operator form is

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[I_{a, c} D\right]=I_{a D, c}+I_{a, c D} \tag{8}
\end{equation*}
$$

Hence it is clear that Inder $\mathfrak{T}$ is an ideal in Der $\mathfrak{T}$.
We now form the vector space

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{T})=\mathfrak{T} \oplus \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{T} . \tag{9}
\end{equation*}
$$

and we introduce the composition $[x y]$ in $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{T})$ by

$$
\begin{equation*}
[a+D, b+E]=(a E-b D)+\left(I_{a, b}+[D, E]\right) . \tag{10}
\end{equation*}
$$

It is clear that this is a bilinear composition, so we have an algebra. Also since $I_{a, a}=0$ by (i) and $[D D]=0$ we have $[a+D, a+D]=0$. Moreover, we have the Jacobi identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}
{[[a} & +D, b+E], c+F]+[[b+E, c+F], a+D] \\
& +[[c+F, a+D], b+E]= \\
a E F & -b D F-[a b c]-c[D E] \\
& +I_{a E-b D, c}+\left[I_{a, b} F\right]+[[D E] F]+ \\
b F D & -c E D-[b a c]-a[E F] \\
& +I_{b F-c E, a}+\left[I_{b, c}, D\right]+[[E F] D]+ \\
c D E & -a F E-[c b a]-b[F D] \\
& +I_{c D-a F, b}+\left[I_{c, a}, E\right]+[[F D] E]=0,
\end{aligned}
$$

since the Jacobi identity holds in Der $\mathfrak{T}$ and (iii) and (8) are valid. Thus $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{T})$ is a Lie algebra. We shall call $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{T})$ the holomorph of the Lie triple system $\mathfrak{T}$. If $a, b \in \mathfrak{T}$ then in $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{T})$ we have, by (8), $[a b]=I_{a, b},\left[a I_{b, c}\right]=a I_{b, c}=[b a c] \in \mathfrak{T}$ and $\left[I_{a, b} I_{c, d}\right]=I_{[c a d], b}+I_{a,[c b d]}$. Hence $[\mathfrak{T T}]=\operatorname{Inder} \mathfrak{T}$ and $\operatorname{SL}(\mathfrak{T}) \equiv \mathfrak{T}+[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$ is the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{T})$ generated by $\mathfrak{T}$. Evidently $S L(\mathfrak{T})=\mathfrak{T} \oplus[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$.

We have noted that if $\mathfrak{L}$ is a Lie algebra then the vector space $\mathfrak{L}$ is a Lie triple system relative to the composition $[a b c]=[[c a] b]$. We denote this Lie triple system as $\mathfrak{L}^{(2)}$. Let $\mathfrak{I}$ be a subsystem of $\mathfrak{L}^{(2)}$ (= subspace closed under $[a b c])$. Then we claim that $[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$ and $\mathfrak{T}+[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$ are subalgebras of $\mathfrak{L}$. Thus let $a, b c, d \in \mathfrak{T}$. Then $[a b] \in[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}],[[c a] b]=[a b c] \in \mathfrak{T}$ and $[[a b],[c d]]= [[[a b] c] d]+[c[[a b] d]]$ (by the Jacobi identity) $=[[b c a] d]+[c[b d a]] \in[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$. Clearly $\mathfrak{T}+[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$ is the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{L}$ generated by $\mathfrak{T}$.

If $\mathfrak{T}$ is a Lie triple system and $\mathfrak{L}$ is a Lie algebra then we shall call a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{T}$ into $\mathfrak{L}^{(2)}$ a Lie specialization of $\mathfrak{T}$ in $\mathfrak{L}$. An important instance of this is the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{T}$ into $S L(\mathfrak{T})=\mathfrak{T} \oplus[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$.
