We shall call this the standard Lie specialization and call $S L(\mathfrak{T})$ the standard Lie envelope of $\mathfrak{T}$. We can easily construct a universal Lie envelope ( $U L(\mathfrak{T}), \sigma_{u}$ ) for any $\mathfrak{T}$, defined to be a Lie algebra $U L(\mathfrak{T})$ and a Lie specialization $\sigma_{u}$ of $\mathfrak{T}$ in $U L(\mathfrak{T})$ such that if $\sigma$ is any Lie specialization of $\mathfrak{T}$ in a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ then there exists a unique homomorphism $\eta$ of $U L(\mathfrak{T})$ into $\mathfrak{L}$ such that $\sigma=\sigma_{u} \eta$. To construct this we begin with the Lie algebra $F L(\mathfrak{T})$ which is defined to be the subalgebra of the Lie algebra $T(\mathfrak{T})^{-}$generated by $\mathfrak{T}$. Here, as usual, $T(\mathfrak{T})$ denotes the tensor algebra based on $\mathfrak{T}$. It is a well known and easy consequence of the Birkhoff-Witt theorem that the linear mapping $\sigma$ of $\mathfrak{T}$ into $\mathfrak{L}$ has a unique extension to a homomorphism $\eta^{\prime}$ of $F L(\mathfrak{T})$ into $\mathfrak{L}$ (Jacobson, Lie Algebras, p. 168). It is clear that the elements $[a b c]-(c \otimes a-a \otimes c) \otimes b+b \otimes(c \otimes a-a \otimes c)$ are in ker $\eta^{\prime}$. Now let $\Omega$ be the ideal in $F L(\mathfrak{T})$ generated by the elements just indicated $(a, b, c \in \mathfrak{T})$ and put $U L(\mathfrak{T})=F L(\mathfrak{T}) / \mathfrak{K}, a^{\sigma{ }}=a+\mathfrak{K}, a \in \mathfrak{T}$. Then it is immediate that $\left(U L(\mathfrak{T}), \sigma_{u}\right)$ is a universal Lie envelope for $\mathfrak{T}$ (cf. p. 68). We have the usual properties of this universal object such as given in Theorem 2.1 (p. 65). Moreover, we have the following result.

THEOREM 1. The homomorphism $\sigma_{u}$ is a monomorphism and UL(T) $=\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \oplus\left[\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}, \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right]$. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{T}=n<\infty$ then $\operatorname{dim} U L(\mathfrak{T}) \leqq n(n+1) / 2$.

Proof. As in Theorem 2.1, $U L(\mathfrak{T})$ is generated by $\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}$. Since $\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}$ is a subsystem of the Lie triple system $U L(\mathfrak{T})^{(2)}$ we have $U L(\mathfrak{T})=\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}+\left[\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right]$. Now consider the standard envelope $S L(\mathfrak{T})=\mathfrak{T} \oplus[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$. We have the homomorphism $\eta$ of $U L(\mathfrak{T})$ onto $S L(\mathfrak{T})$ sending $a^{\sigma_{u}}$ into $a, a \in \mathfrak{T}$. This implies that $\sigma_{u}$ is a monomorphism and $\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \cap\left[\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right]=0$. Hence $U L(\mathfrak{T})=\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \oplus\left[\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right]$. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{T} =n<\infty$ then $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}=n$. Moreover, since $\left[a^{\sigma_{u}} b^{\sigma_{u}}\right]=-\left[b^{\sigma_{u}} a^{\sigma_{u}}\right]$ we have a linear mapping of the space of skew symmetric tensors of degree two onto $\left[\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma, \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}}\right]$. Hence $\operatorname{dim}\left[\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma, \mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}}\right] \leqq n(n-1) / 2$. Then $\operatorname{dim} U L(\mathfrak{T}) \leqq n+n(n-1) / 2 =n(n+1) / 2$

The result noted above shows that if $\mathfrak{T}$ is a subsystem of $\mathfrak{L}^{(2)}, \mathfrak{L}$ a Lie algebra then $[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{L}$. We shall call the subalgebra $[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]\left(\left[\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right]\right)$ of $S L(\mathfrak{T})(U L(\mathfrak{T}))$ the complementary subalgebra of $\mathfrak{T}$ in $S L(\mathfrak{T})(U L(\mathfrak{T}))$.

Example. Let $\mathfrak{T}$ be the trivial Lie triple system consisting of a vector space with the ternary composition $[a b c]=0, a, b, c \in \mathfrak{T}$. Then Inder $\mathfrak{T}=0$ and $S L(\mathfrak{T})=\mathfrak{T}$ considered as Lie algebra with the trivial composition $[a b]=0$. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be the vector space of skew symmetric tensors of degree two based on $\mathfrak{T}$. Thus $\mathfrak{B}$ is the subspace of $\mathfrak{T} \otimes_{\Phi} \mathfrak{T}$ spanned by the vectors $[x y]=x \otimes y-y \otimes x$, $x, y \in \mathfrak{T}$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{V}=n(n-1) / 2$ if $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{T}=n$. Let $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{T} \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ and define

$$
\left[x_{1}+v_{1}, x_{2}+v_{2}\right]=\left[x_{1} x_{2}\right]=x_{1} \otimes x_{2}-x_{2} \otimes x_{1}
$$

for $x_{i} \in \mathfrak{T}, v_{i} \in \mathfrak{V}$. Then it is immediate that this is a Lie algebra which together with the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{T}$ constitute a universal Lie envelope for $\mathfrak{T}$. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{T}=n$ then $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{L}=n(n+1) / 2$.

If $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{C}$ are subspaces of a Lie triple system $\mathfrak{T}$ then we denote the subspace spanned by all the products $[a b c], a \in \mathfrak{A}, b \in \mathfrak{B}, c \in \mathfrak{C}$, by $[\mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{C}]$. It is clear from $[a b c]==-[c b a]$ that $[\mathfrak{A B C}]=[\mathfrak{C B A}]$. Also, by the Jacobi identity (ii) $[\mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{C}] \subseteq[\mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{C} \mathfrak{A}]+[\mathfrak{C} \mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{B}]$. A subspace $\mathfrak{B}$ of $\mathfrak{T}$ is called an ideal if $[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{B}] \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$ or, equivalently, $\left[a_{1} a_{2} b\right] \in \mathfrak{B}$ if $b \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{T}$. If $\mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal then also $[\mathfrak{B T I}] =[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{B}] \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$ and $[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{T}] \subseteq[\mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]+[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{B}] \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$. An ideal $\mathfrak{B}$ determines the difference Lie triple system $\mathfrak{T} / \mathfrak{B}$ which is the vector space $\mathfrak{T} / \mathfrak{B}$ with the composition $\left[a_{1}+\mathfrak{B} a_{2}+\mathfrak{B} a_{3}+\mathfrak{B}\right]=\left[a_{1} a_{2} a_{3}\right]+\mathfrak{B}$. We have the canonical homomorphism $a \rightarrow a+\mathfrak{B}$ onto $\mathfrak{T} / \mathfrak{B}$. The verification is immediate and implies that $\mathfrak{T} / \mathfrak{B}$ is indeed a Lie triple system. The subspace $\mathfrak{T}^{\prime}=[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$ is evidently an ideal. We shall call this the derived Lie triple system of $\mathfrak{T}$.

We consider again a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ and we now note that $\mathfrak{J}$ together with the associator composition $[a b c] \equiv a . b . c-a .(b . c)$ is a Lie triple system, that is, the composition is trilinear and the axioms (i), (ii) and (iii) are fulfilled. Since any Jordan algebra can be imbedded in a Jordan algebra with 1, it is enough to prove our assertion for $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 . Now, by (1), the linear mapping $a \rightarrow R_{a}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto the Lie triple system of linear transformations $R(\mathfrak{J})$ is a homomorphism of the associator structure on $\mathfrak{J}$ (vector space $\mathfrak{J}$ with the associator composition). Since $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element $a \rightarrow R_{a}$ is an isomorphism. Hence it is clear that $[a b c]$ is trilinear and satisfies the axioms for a Lie triple system. We shall call J, as Lie triple system relative to the associator composition, the associator Lie triple system J. As in the general case, we denote the associator ideal [JJI] by $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ (cf. p. 190).

## Exercises

1. Prove the following identities in Lie triple systems:

$$
\begin{gather*}
{[d e[b c a]]+[c e[a d b]]+[a e[c d b]]+[b e[d a c]]=0}  \tag{11}\\
{[f g[d e[b c a]]]+[e g[d f[a e b]]]+[f g[c e[a d b]]]+[c g[c f[b d a]]]}  \tag{12}\\
+Q+R=0
\end{gather*}
$$

where $Q$ and $R$ are obtained from the displayed terms by cyclic permutation of the pairs, $(a, b),(c, d),(e, f)$.
2. Let $\varepsilon$ be an automorphism of period two in a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ and let $\mathfrak{T}=\left\{a \mid a^{\varepsilon}=-a\right\}$. Show that $\mathfrak{T}$ is a Lie triple system (subsystem of $\mathfrak{L}^{(2)}$ ). Conversely, show that if $\mathfrak{T}$ is any Lie triple system then there exists an automorphism $\varepsilon$ in $S L(\mathfrak{T})(U L(\mathfrak{T}))$ such that $\mathfrak{T}\left(\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right)$ is the characteristic space of the root -1 of $\varepsilon$ in the Lie algebra $\operatorname{SL}(\mathfrak{T})(U L(\mathfrak{T}))$.
3. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ the Jordan algebra of a symmetric bilinear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{V}$. Show that $\mathfrak{V}$ is a subsystem of the associator Lie triple system $\mathfrak{J}$ and that if $1 \leqq \operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}<\infty$ and $f$ is nondegenerate then the Lie algebra $R(\mathfrak{B})+[R(\mathfrak{B}), R(\mathfrak{B})]$ and the mapping $a \rightarrow R_{a}$ is a universal Lie envelope for $\mathfrak{B}$.
4. Let $\mathfrak{T}$ be a Lie triple system over a field $\Phi$ and let $\alpha$ be a nonzero element of $\Phi$. Define the product $[a b c]^{\alpha} \equiv \alpha[a b c]$. Show that the vector space $\mathfrak{T}$ with this composition is a Lie triple system $(\mathfrak{T}, \alpha)$. Show that $(\mathfrak{T}, \alpha) \cong(\mathfrak{T}, \beta)$ if $\beta=\rho^{2} \alpha, \rho$ in $\Phi$. Give an example such that $(\mathfrak{T}, \alpha) \nsucceq \mathfrak{T}$.
5. (Yamaguti). Let $\mathfrak{T}$ be a two-dimensional L.t.s. ( $=$ Lie triple system) with basis $(u, v)$. Note that the multiplication in $\mathfrak{T}$ is determined by the formulas:

$$
\begin{align*}
& {[u u v]=\alpha u+\beta v,}  \tag{13}\\
& {[v v u]=\gamma u+\delta v,}
\end{align*}
$$

$\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta \in \Phi$. Show that $\alpha=\delta$. Use this to prove that any two-dimensional L.t.s. over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $\neq 2$ is isomorphic to one of the three L.t.s. with basis $(u, v)$ and multiplication table (13) where the possibilities for $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ are:
I. $\alpha=\beta=\gamma=\delta=0$, II. $\alpha=\gamma=\delta=0, \beta=1$, III. $\alpha=\delta=2, \beta=\gamma=0$.
6. Determine $\operatorname{SL}(\mathfrak{T})$ and $\operatorname{UL}(\mathfrak{T})$ for the L.t.s. I, II and III of exercise 5.
7. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be an ideal in the L.t.s. $\mathfrak{T}$ which is a subsystem of $\mathfrak{L}^{(2)}$. Show that $\mathfrak{B}+[\mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{T}]$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{T}+[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$ and $\mathfrak{B}+[\mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{B}]$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{B}+[\mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{T}]$.
2. Some results on completely reducible Lie algebras of linear transformations with applications to Jordan algebras. In this section we shall recall some wellknown results on completely reducible Lie algebras of linear transformations in a finite-dimensional vector space over a field of characteristic 0 and we shall apply these to obtain: (1) a proof of the semisimplicity of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ a finite-dimensional semisimple Jordan algebra of characteristic 0 , which is independent of the structure theory (cf. §7.5), and (2) a new criterion for semisimplicity in the characteristic 0 case. In this section, except in the exercises, we assume throughout that all vector spaces and algebras are finite dimensional over fields of characteristic 0 . We remark first that under these circumstances semisimplicity and separability are equivalent notions for Jordan and associative algebras (cf. Theorem 6.4, p. 239).

We recall that a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ is called semisimple if it contains no nonzero
abelian ideals. Any such algebra is a direct sum of simple ideals, and more generally, any representation of such an algebra is completely reducible (Jacobson, Lie Algebras, p. 71 and 79). A Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ of linear transformations is completely reducible if and only if $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{C} \oplus[\mathfrak{L} \mathfrak{L}]$ where $\mathfrak{C}$ is the center, $[\mathfrak{L} \mathfrak{L}]$ is semisimple and every element of $\mathbb{C}$ is semisimple, that is, has minimum polynomial without multiple factors (loc. cit. p. 81). The last condition can be improved slightly to: the center has a basis ( $C_{1}, C_{2}, \cdots, C_{m}$ ) of semisimple linear transformations. To see this we have to show that if $C_{1}, C_{2}, \cdots, C_{m}$ commute and are semisimple then any $C=\sum \alpha_{i} C_{i}, \alpha_{i} \in \Phi$, is semisimple. It is sufficient to show this for algebraically closed base fields. Then semisimplicity is equivalent to diagonalizability (of the corresponding matrices) so the result follows from the well-known fact that diagonalizability of the $C_{i}$ and commutativity implies simultaneous diagonalizability. A set of linear transformations is completely reducible if and only if its enveloping associative algebra ( = associative algebra generated by 1 and the given set) is completely reducible. Also an associative algebra of linear transformations is completely reducible if and only if it is semisimple. It is immediate from these results and the fact that any finite-dimensional associative algebra is isomorphic to an algebra of linear transformations that we have the following

Criterion 1. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a finite-dimensional associative algebra with 1 over a field of characteristic $0, \mathfrak{L}$ a subalgebra of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{A}^{-}$which together with 1 generates $\mathfrak{A}$. Then $\mathfrak{A}$ is semisimple if and only if $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{C} \oplus[\mathfrak{L} \mathfrak{L}]$ where $\mathfrak{C}$ is the center of $\mathfrak{L},[\mathfrak{L} \mathfrak{L}]$ is semisimple and $\mathfrak{C}$ has a basis of semisimple elements.

We shall now apply this result to the associative algebra $U(\mathfrak{J}), \mathfrak{J}$ a semisimple Jordan algebra. For this we require the

Theorem 2. Let $\mathfrak{L}$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra over a field of characteristic $0, \mathfrak{T}$ a subsystem of the L.t.s. $\mathfrak{L}^{(2)}$ such that $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{T} \oplus[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$. Then $\mathfrak{L}$ and the injection mapping is a universal Lie envelope for $\mathfrak{T}$.

Proof. Let $\left(U L(\mathfrak{T}), \sigma_{u}\right)$ be a universal Lie envelope of $\mathfrak{T}$. Then we have the homomorphism $\eta$ of $U L(\mathfrak{T})$ onto $\mathfrak{L}$ such that $\sigma_{u} \eta$ is the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{T}$ into $\mathfrak{L}$. We claim that ker $\eta$ is the center $\mathfrak{C}$ of $U L(\mathfrak{T})$. First, let $c \in \mathfrak{C}$. Since $U L(\mathfrak{T}) =\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \oplus\left[\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right], c=a^{\sigma_{u}}+\sum\left[b_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} c_{\imath}^{\sigma_{u}}\right]$ where $a, b_{i}, c_{i} \in \mathfrak{T}$. Applying $\eta$ we see that $a+\sum\left[b_{i} c_{i}\right]$ is in the center of $\mathfrak{L}$. Since $\mathfrak{L}$ is semisimple, $a+\sum\left[b_{i} c_{i}\right]=0$. Hence $c=a^{\sigma_{u}}+\sum\left[b_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} c_{i}^{\sigma_{u}}\right] \in \operatorname{ker} \eta$. Conversely, let $c=a^{\sigma_{u}}+\sum\left[b_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} c_{i}^{\sigma_{u}}\right] \in \operatorname{ker} \eta$. Then $a+\Sigma\left[b_{i} c_{i}\right]=0$. Since $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{T} \oplus[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$ this gives $a=0$ and $\Sigma\left[b_{i} c_{i}\right]=0$. Then $\sum\left[c_{i} x b_{i}\right]=\sum\left[\left[b_{i} c_{i}\right] x\right]=0$ for all $x \in \mathfrak{T}$. Hence $a^{\sigma_{u}}=0$ and $\sum\left[c_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} x^{\sigma_{u}} b_{i}^{\sigma_{u}}\right]=\sum\left[\left[b_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} c_{i}^{\sigma_{u}}\right] x^{\sigma_{u}}\right]=0$ for all $x \in \mathfrak{T}$. Since $\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}$ generates $U L(\mathfrak{T})$ this implies that $c=a^{\sigma_{u}}+\sum\left[b_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} c_{i}^{\sigma_{u}}\right]=\sum\left[b_{i}^{\sigma_{u}} c_{i}^{\sigma_{u}}\right] \in \mathfrak{C}$. Since $\mathfrak{L} \cong U L(\mathfrak{T}) / \operatorname{ker} \eta =U L(\mathfrak{T}) / \mathfrak{C}$ it is clear that the center $\mathfrak{C}$ is the radical ( = maximal solvable ideal) of $U L(\mathfrak{T})$. By the Levi decomposition theorem, $U L(\mathfrak{T})=\mathbb{C} \oplus \mathbb{S}$, where $\mathfrak{S}$ is a
subalgebra isomorphic to $U L(\mathfrak{T}) / \mathbb{C}$ and hence to $\mathfrak{L}$ (loc. cit. p. 91). Since $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{T} \oplus[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$ is semisimple, $[\mathfrak{L} \mathfrak{L}]=\mathfrak{L}$ (loc. cit. p. 72). Hence $[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]+[[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}] \mathfrak{T}] +[[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}][\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]]=\mathfrak{T} \oplus[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$. Since $[[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}] \mathfrak{T}]=[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$ this implies that $\mathfrak{T} =[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$. Then $\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}=\left[\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right]=\left[\left[\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right] \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right]$ and $U L(\mathfrak{T})=\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}+\left[\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right] =\left[\left[\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right] \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right]+\left[\mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}} \mathfrak{T}^{\sigma_{u}}\right]=[U L(\mathfrak{T}), U L(\mathfrak{T})]$. Since $U L(\mathfrak{T})=\mathbb{C} \oplus \mathbb{S},[U L(\mathfrak{T})$, $U L(\mathfrak{T})]=[\mathfrak{S} \mathfrak{S}] \subseteq \mathfrak{S}$. This implies that $\mathfrak{C}=0$ so ker $\eta=0$ and $\eta$ is an isomorphism. Accordingly, $\mathfrak{L}$ and the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{T}$ is a universal Lie envelope for $\mathfrak{T}$.

We can now prove the following result on the associator structure of a semisimple Jordan algebra.

Theorem 3. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple Jordan algebra of characteristic 0 . Then $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{C} \oplus \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ where $\mathfrak{C}$ is the center and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}=[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ is the derived associator ideal. Moreover, the universal Lie envelope of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is semisimple.

Proof. We consider first the Lie triple system of linear transformations $R(\mathfrak{J})$. The Lie algebra of linear transformations generated by $R(\mathfrak{I})$ is $\mathfrak{L}=R(\mathfrak{J}) +[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ has a $1, R(\mathfrak{J}) \cap[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]=0$; for, if $a, b_{i}, c_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $1 R_{a}=a$ and $1 \sum\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right]=0$. Hence if $R_{a}=\sum\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right]$ then $a=0, R_{a}=0$ and $\Sigma\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right]=0$. Thus $\mathfrak{L}=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$. We note next that since $\mathfrak{J}$ is a direct sum of simple ideals and since the invariant subspace of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to $R(\mathfrak{J})$ and to $\mathfrak{L}$ are the ideals, $\mathfrak{L}$ is a completely reducible Lie algebra of linear transformations. Hence $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{S} \oplus[\mathfrak{L} \mathfrak{L}]$ where $\mathfrak{S}$ is the center of $\mathfrak{L}$. It is clear that $\mathfrak{S}$ is contained in the centroid of $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ has 1 , the centroid is $R(\mathbb{C})$, the set of multiplications $R_{c}, c$ in the center $\mathfrak{C}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence $\mathfrak{S}=R(\mathfrak{C})$ and $\mathfrak{L}=R(\mathfrak{C}) \oplus[\mathfrak{L} \mathfrak{L}]$. Since $\mathfrak{L}=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})],[\mathfrak{L} \mathfrak{L}]=[R(\mathfrak{J}) R(\mathfrak{J}) R(\mathfrak{J})] \oplus[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$. Since we have the Lie triple system homomorphism $a \rightarrow R_{a}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $R(\mathfrak{J})$ (cf. (1)), $[R(\mathfrak{J}) R(\mathfrak{J}) R(\mathfrak{J})]=R(\mathfrak{J})^{\prime}=R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$. Hence $[\mathfrak{L} \mathfrak{L}]=R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right) \oplus[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$. Then $\mathfrak{L}=R(\mathfrak{C}) \oplus[\mathfrak{L} \mathfrak{L}]=R(\mathfrak{C}) \oplus R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right) \oplus[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$. Hence $R(\mathfrak{J})=R(\mathfrak{C}) \oplus R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ has a $1, a \rightarrow R_{a}$ is a monomorphism. Hence $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{C} \oplus \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. The Lie algebra generated by $R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ is $R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right) \oplus\left[R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right), R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)\right]=R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right) \oplus[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]=[\mathfrak{L} \mathfrak{L}]$ and this is semisimple. Hence, by Theorem 2, [LLI] and the mapping $a \rightarrow R_{a}$ is a universal Lie envelope for $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. This shows that the universal Lie envelope of the Lie triple system $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$, is semisimple.

We can now give a proof of Theorem 7.12 in the characteristic 0 case which is independent of the structure theory. The result in this case is the following

Theorem 4. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple Jordan algebra of characteristic 0 . Then $U(\mathfrak{J})$ is semisimple.

Proof. We consider $\mathfrak{J}$ as imbedded in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ so $U(\mathfrak{J})$ is generated by $\mathfrak{J}$ and 1 . We have the relation $[a, b, c] \equiv a . b . c-a .(b . c)=[[c a] b]$ in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ (eq. (47) on p. 96). This shows that $\mathfrak{J}$ is a subsystem of the Lie triple system $\left(U(\mathfrak{J})^{-}\right)^{(2)}$ and the composition given in $\mathfrak{J}$ as subsystem coincides with the associator com-
position in $\mathfrak{J}$. We show next that the elements of $\mathfrak{C}$ are semisimple. To see this we may suppose the base field is algebraically closed. Then, if $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{s}, \mathfrak{J}_{i}$ a simple ideal, $\mathfrak{C}$ has the basis $\left(e_{1}, \cdots, e_{s}\right)$ where $e_{i}=1_{i}$, the identity of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Then the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents. Hence $e_{i}\left(2 e_{1}-1\right)\left(e_{i}-1\right)=0$ and $e_{i} e_{j} =e_{j} e_{i}$ in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ (p. 104). Hence the $e_{i}$ are commuting semisimple elements. This implies that every $c \in \mathbb{C}$ is semisimple. It follows that the linear mapping $x \rightarrow[x c]$ in $U(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$is semisimple and its restriction to $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$, the subalgebra of $U(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$generated by $\mathfrak{J}$, is semisimple. On the other hand, $[[x c] c]=[c c x]=0$, $x \in \mathfrak{J}$. Hence $C: x \rightarrow[x c]$ is nilpotent in $\mathfrak{L}\left(C^{3}=0\right)$. Hence $[x c]=0, x \in \mathfrak{J}, c \in \mathfrak{C}$ and $\mathfrak{C}$ is contained in the center of $U(\mathfrak{J})$. Now, by Theorem 3, $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{C} \oplus \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Hence, since $\left[\mathfrak{C} \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right]=0, \mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]=\mathfrak{C}+\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}+\left[\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right]$. By Theorem 3, $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}+\left[\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right]$ is a homomorphic image of a semisimple Lie algebra and hence is semisimple. Then $\mathfrak{C} \cap\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}+\left[\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right]\right)=0$ and $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{C} \oplus\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}+\left[\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right]\right)$. Moreover, we have seen that the elements of $\mathfrak{C}$ are semisimple. Since 1 and $\mathfrak{L}$ generate $U(\mathfrak{J})$ it follows from the above Criterion 1 that $U(\mathfrak{J})$ is semisimple.

We consider next another important criterion for complete reducibility of a Lie algebra of linear transformations or, equivalently, as in Criterion 1, for semisimplicity of an associative algebra. For this we need to recall some definitions in the theory of Lie algebras. We recall first that a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ is split three-dimensional simple or an $A_{1}$-Lie algebra, if it has a basis $(e, f, h)$ with the multiplication table

$$
\begin{equation*}
[e h]=2 e, \quad[f h]=-2 f, \quad[e f]=h \tag{14}
\end{equation*}
$$

We shall call $(e, f, h)$ a canonical basis for the $A_{1}$-Lie algebra. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is a finitedimensional associative algebra with 1 and $\mathfrak{L}$ is an $A_{1}$-Lie subalgebra of $\mathfrak{A}^{-}$ then it is easily seen that the elements $e$ and $f$ in the canonical basis are nilpotent in $\mathfrak{A}$. If $\mathfrak{L}$ is any subalgebra of $\mathfrak{U}^{-}$then we shall say that $\mathfrak{L}$ has the imbedding property for nilpotent elements if every nonzero element of $\mathfrak{L}$ which is nilpotent (in $\mathfrak{A}$ ) can be imbedded in a canonical basis ( $e, f, h$ ) of an $A_{1}$-Lie subalgebra of $\mathfrak{L}$. If $\mathfrak{T}$ is a subsystem of the Lie triple system $\left(\mathfrak{A}^{-}\right)^{(2)}$ then we say that $\mathfrak{T}$ has the imbedding property for nilpotent elements if every nonzero nilpotent $f \in \mathfrak{T}$ can be imbedded in a canonical basis ( $e, f, h$ ) of an $A_{1}$-Lie subalgebra of $\mathfrak{A}^{-}$such the $e \in \mathfrak{T}$. This is equivalent to the existence of an element $e \in \mathfrak{T}$ such that $[e e f]=2 e$, $[f f e]=2 f$.

It is well known that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is a finite-dimensional associative algebra with 1 over a field of characteristic 0 then any $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ can be written in one and only one way as $a=s+n$ where $s$ and $n$ are polynomials in $\mathfrak{A}$ and $s$ is semisimple and $n$ is nilpotent. The elements $s$ and $n$ are called the semisimple and nilpotent components of $a$. A subalgebra $\mathfrak{L}$ of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{U}^{-}$is called almost algebraic if $\mathfrak{L}$ contains the semisimple and nilpotent part of every $a \in \mathfrak{L}$ (loc. cit. p. 98).

We can now state the following criterion which is stated and proved in the
author's Lie Algebras, p. 100, in a slightly different but equivalent form (referring to completely reducible algebras of linear transformations):

Criterion 2. Let $\mathfrak{U}$ be a finite-dimensional associative algebra with 1 over a field of characteristic $0, \mathcal{L}$ a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{A}^{-}$such that $\mathfrak{A}$ is generated by 1 and $\mathfrak{L}$. Then if $\mathfrak{U}$ is semisimple, $\mathfrak{L}$ is almost algebraic and $\mathfrak{L}$ has the imbedding property for nilpotent elements. Conversely, assume $\mathfrak{L}$ has this imbedding property and the center of $\mathfrak{L}$ is almost algebraic. Then $\mathfrak{A}$ is semisimple.

We need to recall also the following result which is a key step in the proof of the foregoing criterion.

Morozov's Lemma. Let $\mathfrak{L}$ be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra of characteristic 0 , and suppose $\mathfrak{L}$ contains elements $f, h$ such that $[f h]=-2 f$ and $h \in[\mathfrak{L} f]$. Then $f$ and $h$ can be imbedded in a canonical basis ( $e, f, h$ ) of an $A_{1}$-Lie subalgebra of $\mathfrak{L}$ (loc. cit. p. 98).

This lemma has the following consequences.
Theorem 5. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be an associative algebra with 1 over a field of characteristic $0, \mathfrak{L}$ a finite-dimensional subalgebra of $\mathfrak{A}^{-}$having the imbedding property for nilpotent elements. Then: (1) Any subalgebra $\mathfrak{K}$ of $\mathfrak{L}$ which has a $\mathfrak{K}$-invariant complement $\mathfrak{M}$ in $\mathfrak{L}$, that is, a subspace $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{K} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ and $[\mathfrak{M} \mathfrak{M}] \subseteq \mathfrak{M}$, has the imbedding property for nilpotent elements. (2) Let $\mathfrak{T}$ be a subsystem of the Lie triple system $\mathfrak{L}^{(2)}$ such that there exists a subalgebra $\mathfrak{K}$ of $\mathfrak{L}$ satisfying $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{T} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{R}] \subseteq \mathfrak{T}, \quad[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}] \subseteq \mathfrak{K} . \tag{15}
\end{equation*}
$$

Then $\mathfrak{T}$ has the imbedding property for nilpotent elements.
Proof. The proofs of the two statements are very similar and since (1) is proved in the author's Lie Algebras, p. 99, we shall just give the proof of (2). Accordingly, let $f$ be a nilpotent element of $\mathfrak{T}$. By hypothesis there exist elements $e, h$ in $\mathfrak{L}$ such that ( $e, f, h$ ) satisfies the multiplication table (14). Write $e=e_{1}+e_{2}, h=h_{1}+h_{2}$ where $e_{1}, h_{1} \in \mathfrak{T}, e_{2}, h_{2} \in \Re$. Then $-2 f=[f, h]=\left[f h_{1}\right] +\left[f h_{2}\right]$ and the conditions on $\mathfrak{T}$ and $\mathfrak{K}$ imply that $\left[f h_{2}\right]=-2 f$. Also the conditions on $\mathfrak{T}$ and $\mathfrak{K}$ and $h_{1}+h_{2}=h=[e f]=\left[e_{1} f\right]+\left[e_{2} f\right]$ imply that $h_{2}=\left[e_{1} f\right] \in[\mathfrak{L} f]$. Hence, by Morozov's Lemma, we may assume that $h=h_{2} \in \mathfrak{R}$. Then $\left[e_{1} f\right]=h$ and $2 e_{1}+2 e_{2}=2 e=[e h]=\left[e_{1} h\right]+\left[e_{2} h\right]$ give $\left[e_{1} h\right]=2 e_{1}$. Hence ( $e_{1}, f, h$ ) gives the required imbedding of $f$ in a canonical basis such that $\boldsymbol{e}_{1} \in \mathfrak{T}$.

It is well known that for any positive integer $n$ then there exists a unique (up to similarity) irreducible representation of degree $n$ ( $=$ dimensionality of the vector space) of the split Lie algebra $A_{1}$ with canonical basis ( $e, f, h$ ). If we denote the linear transformations representing $e, f, h$ in this representation by $E_{n}, F_{n}, H_{n}$
respectively then there exists a basis ( $u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}$ ) for the underlying vector space $\mathfrak{B}_{n}$ such that

$$
\begin{align*}
& u_{1} E_{n}=0, \quad u_{i+1} E_{n}=i(i-n) u_{i}, \quad 1 \leqq i \leqq n-1, \\
& u_{i} F_{n}=u_{i+1}, \quad 1 \leqq i \leqq n-1, \quad u_{n} F_{n}=0,  \tag{16}\\
& \left.u_{i} H_{n}=(n+1-2 i) u_{i} \quad \text { (loc. cit. p. } 85\right) .
\end{align*}
$$

We now introduce the bilinear form $\phi_{n}$ on $\mathfrak{V}_{n} / \Phi$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\phi_{n}\left(u_{i}, u_{n-j+1}\right)=\delta_{i j} . \tag{17}
\end{equation*}
$$

In other words, the matrix of $\phi_{n}$ relative to the given basis is

$$
M_{n}=\left(\begin{array}{lll}
0 & & 1  \tag{18}\\
& . & \\
1 & & 0
\end{array}\right) .
$$

Since $M_{n}$ is symmetric and nonsingular, $\phi_{n}$ is a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form. Since $\mathfrak{W} \equiv \sum_{1}^{v} \Phi u_{i}$, where $v=[n / 2]$, is a totally isotropic subspace, $\phi_{n}$ has maximal Witt index. It is easily seen that any nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of maximal Witt index on an $n$-dimensional vector space is equivalent in the usual sense to a multiple of $\phi_{n}$. Hence the Jordan algebras of selfadjoint linear transformations relative to any two such forms are isomorphic. Now let $\mathfrak{H}^{(n)}$ denote this Jordan algebra corresponding to the form $\phi_{n}$. Thus $\mathfrak{H}^{(n)} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{n}, J_{M_{n}}\right)$ the Jordan algebra of matrices which are symmetric under the involution $X \rightarrow M_{n} X^{t} M_{n}{ }^{-1}$.

By (16) and (17), $\phi_{n}\left(u_{i} E_{n}, u_{n-j+1}\right)=\phi_{n}\left(u_{i}, u_{n-j+1} E_{n}\right)$ and $\phi_{n}\left(u_{i} F_{n}, u_{n-j+1}\right) =\phi_{n}\left(u_{i}, u_{n-j+1} F_{n}\right)$. Hence $E_{n}, F_{n} \in \mathfrak{H}^{(n)}$. We now prove

Lemma 1. If $n>1$ the linear transformations 1 and $E_{n}$ and $F_{n}$ defined in (16) generate the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}^{(n)}$.

Proof. Let $H_{i j}$ be the linear transformation such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
u_{i} H_{i j}=u_{j}, \quad u_{n+1-j} H_{i j}=u_{n+1-i}, \quad u_{l} H_{i j}=0, \quad l \neq i, n+1-j . \tag{19}
\end{equation*}
$$

Then the $H_{i j} \in \mathfrak{H}^{(n)}$ and the set $\left\{H_{i j} \mid i+j \leqq n+1\right\}$ is linearly independent. Since the number of elements in this set is $n(n+1) / 2$ the set is a basis for $\mathfrak{H}^{(n)}$. By Cohn's Theorem (p. 8) $K=H_{n}{ }^{2}=\left[E_{n} F_{n}\right]^{2}$ is in the subalgebra $\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{H}^{(n)}$ generated by $E_{n}$ and $F_{n}$. Now $u_{i} K=(n+1-2 i)^{2} u_{i}$ so $K=\sum_{1}{ }^{v} \beta_{i} H_{i i}$ where $v=[(n+1) / 2]$ and $\beta_{i}=(n+1-2 i)^{2}$. Since the $\beta_{i}$ are distinct and the $H_{i i}$ are orthogonal idempotent elements it follows that every $H_{i i}$ is a polynomial in $K$ and so belongs to $\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$. Then $\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$ contains $H_{i i} F_{n}{ }^{n+1-2 i} H_{i i}=H_{i, n+1-i}$ if $2 i<n+1$ and $H_{i i} F_{n}{ }^{k-i} H_{k k}+H_{k k} F_{n}{ }^{k-i} H_{i i}=H_{i k}$ if $k>i$ and $k \neq n+1-i$. Similarly, $H_{i i} E_{n}{ }^{n+1-2 i} H_{i i}$ is a nonzero multiple of $H_{n+1-i . i}$ for $2 i<n+1$ and $H_{k k} E_{n}{ }^{i-k} H_{i i}$
$+H_{i i} E_{i i}{ }^{i-k} H_{k k}$ is a nonzero multiple of $H_{i k}$ for $k<i$ and $i \neq n+1-k$. Hence $\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}$ contains the basis $\left\{H_{i j} \mid i+j \leqq n+1\right\}$ for $\mathfrak{H}^{(n)}$, so $\mathfrak{H}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{H}^{(n)}$.

It is immediate from the Lie algebra Criterion 2 that if $\mathfrak{L}$ is a finite-dimensional Lie algebra of characteristic 0 then $\mathfrak{L}$ is semisimple if and only if every element $f \neq 0$ such that ad $f$ is nilpotent in $\mathscr{L}$ can be imbedded in an $A_{1}$-Lie subalgebra of $\mathscr{L}$. We shall now derive an analogous result for Jordan algebras. For this we require the following

Definition 2. Two elements $u, v$ of a Jordan algebra will be called associates if they satisfy the associator relations

$$
\begin{equation*}
[u, u, v]=2 u, \quad[v, v, u]=2 v \tag{20}
\end{equation*}
$$

A Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}$ will be called an elementary semisimple Jordan algebra if $\mathfrak{H} \cong \mathfrak{H}^{\left(n_{1}\right)} \oplus \mathfrak{H}^{\left(n_{2}\right)} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{H}^{\left(n_{s}\right)}$ where the $\mathfrak{H}^{(k)}$ are defined as above, $1 \leqq n_{1}<n_{2} <\cdots<n_{s}$. The integer $m=n_{s}$ will be called the index of $\mathfrak{H}$.

The defining conditions for associates are equivalent to $[u u v]=2 u,[v v u]=2 v$ in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ and these are the same as $[u v]=w,[u w]=2 u,[v w]=-2 v$. Hence the condition is that the elements $(u, v,[u v])$ form a canonical basis for an $A_{1}$-Lie subalgebra of $U(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$. It follows that the elements $u$ and $v$ are nilpotent in $U(\mathfrak{J})$ and hence in J.

We now prove the following
Theorem 6. Let $\mathfrak{H}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra over a field of characteristic 0 generated by 1 and two associates $u$ and $v$ with $v \neq 0$. Then $u$ and $v$ are nilpotent of the same index $m$ and $\mathfrak{H}$ is an elementary semisimple Jordan algebra of index $m$.

Proof. By Shirshov-Cohn's Theorem, $\mathfrak{H}$ is special, so we can identify $\mathfrak{H}$ with a subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B})^{+}$for a suitable finite-dimensional vector space $\mathfrak{B} / \Phi$, Since $\frac{1}{2} \sigma$ is a multiplication specialization if $\sigma$ is an associative specialization we have the homomorphism of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B})$ mapping $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $a \rightarrow \frac{1}{2} a$. Since we have the relations $[u v]=w,[u w]=2 u,[v w]=-2 v$ in $U(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$the elements $e=\frac{1}{2} u$ and $f=\frac{1}{2} v, h=[e f]$ form a canonical basis for an $A_{1}$-subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B})^{-}$and, of course, $e$ and $f$ generate $\mathfrak{H}$ as subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B})^{+}$. Since the representations of the Lie algebra $A_{1}$ are completely reducible we can write $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{B}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{B}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{V}_{s}$ where the $\mathfrak{B}_{i}$ are irreducible invariant subspaces of $\mathfrak{B}$ relative to $A_{1}=\Phi e+\Phi f+\Phi h$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}_{i}=n_{i}$. Since the induced representations in any two $\mathfrak{B}_{i}$ of the same dimensionality are similar we may, by dropping duplicates, assume that $n_{1}<n_{2}<\cdots<n_{s}$. Also since the representation of $A_{1}$ in a one-dimensional space is 0 and $f \neq 0$, we may assume $n_{1}>1$. Since the linear transformations $E_{n}$ and $F_{n}$ are nilpotent of index $n$ it is clear that $e$ and $f$ and, hence, $u$ and $v$ are nilpotent of index $m \equiv n_{s}$. Let $\eta_{k}$ be the restriction homomor-
phism of $\mathfrak{H}$ into the Jordan algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{k}, \mathfrak{B}_{k}\right)^{+}$. By Lemma 1, the image of $\mathfrak{H}$ under $\eta_{k}$ is the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}^{\left(n_{k}\right)}$. If $\mathfrak{B}_{k}=\operatorname{ker} \eta_{k}$ then clearly $\bigcap_{1}^{s} \mathfrak{B}_{k}=0$, and $\mathfrak{B}_{k}$ is a maximal ideal in $\mathfrak{H}$, since $\mathfrak{H}^{\left(n_{k}\right)}$ is simple. If $\bigcap_{j \neq k} \mathfrak{B}_{j}=0$ then we have an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{H}$ into the Jordan algebra of restriction of the elements of $\mathfrak{H}$ to $\Sigma_{j \neq k} \mathfrak{B}_{j}$. Hence we may assume that $\bigcap_{j \neq k} \mathfrak{B}_{j} \neq 0$ for $k=1,2, \cdots, s$. Then $\mathfrak{B}_{k}+\bigcap_{j \neq k} \mathfrak{B}_{j}=\mathfrak{H}$ for all $k$. This implies that the homomorphism $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{H}$ into $\mathfrak{H}^{\left(n_{1}\right)} \oplus \mathfrak{H}^{\left(n_{2}\right)} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{H}^{\left(n_{s}\right)}$ defined as $a \rightarrow\left(a^{\left(\eta_{1}\right)}, a^{\left(\eta_{2}\right)}, \cdots, a^{\left(\eta_{s}\right)}\right)$ is an isomorphism.

We can now establish the following criterion for semisimplicity.
Theorem 7. A finite-dimensional Jordan algebra J over a field of characteristic 0 is semisimple if and only if every nonzero nilpotent element $v$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ can be imbedded in an elementary semisimple subalgebra.

Proof. Sufficiency. Assume $\mathfrak{J}$ has the property stated and let $\Re=$ rad $\mathfrak{J}$. If $\Re \neq 0$ let $v \neq 0$ be in $\Re$. Then $v$ is nilpotent since $\Re$ is solvable. Hence there exists an elementary semisimple subalgebra $\mathfrak{H}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ containing v . Since $\Re$ is a solvable ideal, $\mathfrak{H} \cap \Re=0$ contrary to $v \in \mathfrak{H}$ and $v \in \Re$. Hence $\Re=0$ and $\mathfrak{J}$ is semisimple.

Necessity. Assume $\mathfrak{J}$ is semisimple. Then $U(\mathfrak{J})$ is semisimple, by Theorem 4. Hence, by Criterion 2, the subalgebra $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ of $U(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$has the imbedding property for nilpotent elements. Since $R(\mathfrak{J}) \cap[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]=0$ and we have the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{L}$ on $R(\mathfrak{J})+[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$ which is 1-1 on $\mathfrak{J}$ we have $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$. Thus $\mathfrak{T}=\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{K}=[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ and $\mathfrak{L}$ satisfy the hypotheses of (2) of Theorem 5. Hence the Lie triple system $\mathfrak{J}$ has the imbedding property for nilpotent elements, by the conclusion of Theorem 5 (2). Hence if $v$ is a nilpotent element of $\mathfrak{J}$ then $v$ is a nilpotent element of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ and hence there exists a $u \in \mathfrak{J}$ such that $[u u v]=2 u$ and $[v v u]=2 v$. Then we have the associator relations $[u, u, v]=2 u,[v, v, u]=2 v$ in $\mathfrak{J}$, that is, $u$ and $v$ are associates. Hence by Theorem 6, the subalgebra $\mathfrak{H}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ generated by $u$ and $v$ is an elementary semisimple Jordan algebra and we have an imbedding of $v$ in such a subalgebra.

## Exercises

1. (Schafer). Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be finite-dimensional central simple of degree $r$ over an arbitrary field. Show that $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{C} \oplus \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ if the characteristic of $\mathfrak{J}$ does not divide $r$.
2. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a special simple Jordan algebra satisfying the axioms of §4.2. Use the structure theorem for such algebras given in §4.5 to show that if $u$ is a nilpotent element of such an algebra then there exists a nilpotent element $v$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ such that the subalgebra generated by $1, u$ and $v$ is elementary.
3. Let $\mathfrak{T}$ be a Lie triple system of linear transformations of a finite dimensional vector space $\mathfrak{B}$ into itself. Let $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{T} \cap[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$. Show that $\mathfrak{W}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{T}$ and in the Lie algebra $[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$ and that $\mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{P}$ is a subspace of $\mathfrak{B}$ invariant under $\mathfrak{T}$. Assume every element of $\mathfrak{B}$ is nilpotent and $\mathfrak{B}$ is $\mathfrak{T}$-irreducible. Use Engel's theorem (Jacobson, Lie Algebras, p. 36) to show that $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{T} \cap[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]=0$.
4. Let $E$ and $F$ be nonzero linear transformations of a finite-dimensional vector space $\mathfrak{B}$ over a field of characteristic 0 such that $[E E F]=2 E,[F F E]=2 F$. Show that $E \pm F$ are not nilpotent.
5. Use ex. 3 and 4 and Theorem 5 (2) to prove the following analogue of Engel's theorem for Lie triple systems: If $\mathfrak{T}$ is a Lie triple system of nilpotent linear transformations in a finite-dimensional vector space $\mathfrak{B}$ over a field of characteristic 0 then the associative algebra $\mathfrak{T}^{*}$ generated by $\mathfrak{T}$ (without 1 ) is nilpotent.
6. Operator commutativity. We shall say that the elements $a, b$ of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ operator commute (or $o$-commute) in $\mathfrak{J}$ if $\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right]=0$. This notion was first introduced by Jordan, von Neumann and Wigner in [1]. It is easy to give examples in which $a$ and $b$, contained in a subalgebra $\mathfrak{K}$ of $\mathfrak{J}, o$-commute in $\mathfrak{K}$ but not in $\mathfrak{J}$ (ex. 2 below). If $\mathfrak{A}$ is a subset of $\mathfrak{J}$ then we denote the set of elements of $\mathfrak{J}$ which $o$-commute in $\mathfrak{J}$ with every $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ by $C_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{A})$. It is clear that $C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{A})$ is a subspace of $\mathfrak{J}$ containing the center. Moreover, if $c_{1}, c_{2}, c_{3} \in C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{A})$ and $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ then $\left[R_{a}, R_{\left[c_{1}, c_{2}, c_{3}\right]}\right]=\left[R_{a}\left[R_{c_{1}} R_{c_{2}} R_{c_{3}}\right]\right]=\left[R_{a},\left[\left[R_{c_{3}} R_{c_{1}}\right], R_{c_{2}}\right]\right]=0$. Hence $\left[c_{1}, c_{2}, c_{3}\right] \in C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{A})$, so $C_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{A})$ is a subsystem of the associator Lie triple system $\mathfrak{J}$. However, this may not be a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ (ex. 2). It is immediate that if $\mathbf{P}$ is an extension of the base field $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{A}$ is a subset of $\mathfrak{J}$ then $C_{\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbf{P}}}(\mathfrak{A})=\mathrm{P} C_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{A})$, the P -subspace of $\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbf{P}}$ spanned by $C_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{A})$.

We shall now show that if $\mathfrak{B}$ is a finite-dimensional separable subalgebra of an arbitrary Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ then $C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ and if $\mathfrak{K}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ containing $\mathfrak{B}$ then $C_{\boldsymbol{\mathcal { M }}}(\mathfrak{B})=C_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B}) \cap \mathfrak{K}$. The last equation is equivalent to: If $a \in \mathfrak{K} o$-commutes in $\mathfrak{K}$ with every $b \in \mathfrak{B}$, then $a o$-commutes in $\mathfrak{J}$ with every $b \in \mathfrak{B}$.

Lemma 1. If $e$ is an idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}$ then $C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\{e\})=\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)+\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ where $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e) \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{1}(e) \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$ is the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to e. Hence $C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\{e\})$ is a subalgebra.

Proof. We have the relation $\left[R_{a} R_{e \cdot 2}\right]+2\left[R_{e} R_{a . e}\right]=0$. If we take $a$ in $\Im_{0}(e)$ or in $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ this gives $\left[R_{a} R_{e}\right]=0$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)+\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e) \subseteq C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\{e\})$. Now let $a \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$. Then $e R_{e} R_{a}=\frac{1}{2} a$ and $e R_{a} R_{e}=\frac{1}{4} a$. Hence $\left[R_{e} R_{a}\right]=0$ implies $a=0$. It follows that $C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\{e\})=\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)+\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$. Since $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ are subalgebras and $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e) \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{1}(e) =0$ it is clear that $C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\{e\})$ is a subalgebra.

Lemma 2. If $\mathfrak{B}$ is a finite-dimensional semisimple Jordan algebra over an algebraically closed field then $\mathfrak{B}$ has a basis consisting of idempotent elements.

Proof. Suppose first that $\mathfrak{B}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{B}$ the Jordan algebra of a symmetric bilinear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{B}$. Since $\mathfrak{B}$ is semisimple, $f$ is nondegenerate and $\mathfrak{J}$ has a basis $\left(1, u_{1}, \cdots, u_{m}\right)$ such that $u_{i} \cdot u_{j}=\delta_{i j} 1$. Then $u_{i}{ }^{\cdot 2}=1$ implies that $e_{i}=\left(1+u_{i}\right) / 2$ is idempotent. Hence $\left(1, e_{1}, \cdots, e_{n}\right)$ is a basis of idempotents for $\mathfrak{B}$. Suppose next that the base field is of characteristic 0 . Then if $a \in \mathfrak{B}, a=\sum \alpha_{i} e_{i}+v$ where the $e_{i}$
are orthogonal idempotents, $\alpha_{i} \in \Phi$ and $v$ is nilpotent. Hence it is enough to show that every nilpotent element of $\mathfrak{B}$ is a linear combination of idempotents. By Theorem 7, such an element is contained in an elementary semisimple subalgebra $\mathfrak{H}$. Hence it is enough to show that a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}^{(m)}, m \geqq 2$, has a basis of idempotents. Since $\mathfrak{H}^{(m)} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{m}, J_{1}\right)$ it is clear (using a Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{m}, J_{1}\right)$ ) that $\mathfrak{H}^{(m)}$ is a vector space sum of Jordan algebras of nondegenerate symmetric bilinear forms. Since we have shown that these have a basis consisting of idempotents it is clear that $\mathfrak{H}^{(m)}$ has such a basis. Finally, suppose the characteristic is $p \neq 0$. In this case we have to use the classification of simple algebras over an algebraically closed field. Using this it is clear that any simple algebra over an algebraically closed field is either one dimensional or is a vector space sum of Jordan algebras of nondegenerate symmetric bilinear forms. It follows that any simple and hence any semisimple Jordan algebra over $\Phi$ has a basis of idempotents.

We can now prove
Theorem 8. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be an arbitrary Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{B}$ a finite-dimensional separable subalgebra. Then $C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ is a subalgebra and if $\mathfrak{K}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ containing $\mathfrak{B}$ then $C_{\mathfrak{A}}(\mathfrak{B})=C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B}) \cap \mathfrak{K}$.

Proof. It is easy to see that by an extension field argument we can reduce the proof to the case of an algebraically closed base field. Then $\mathfrak{B}$ has a basis $\left(e_{1}, e_{2}, \cdots, e_{n}\right)$ where the $e_{i}$ are idempotents. Then

$$
C_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})=\bigcap_{1}^{n} C_{\mathfrak{J}}\left(\left\{e_{i}\right\}\right)=\bigcap_{1}^{n}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{0}\left(e_{i}\right)+\mathfrak{J}_{1}\left(e_{i}\right)\right)
$$

which is a subalgebra. Also $C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}(\mathfrak{B})=\bigcap_{1}^{n}\left(\Re_{0}\left(e_{i}\right)+\Re_{1}\left(e_{i}\right)\right)$. It is clear that $\left(\mathfrak{J}_{0}\left(e_{i}\right)+\mathfrak{J}_{1}\left(e_{i}\right)\right) \cap \mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{K}_{0}\left(e_{i}\right)+\mathfrak{K}_{1}\left(e_{i}\right)$. Hence $C_{\mathfrak{A}}(\mathfrak{B})=C_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B}) \cap \mathfrak{K}$.

Lemma 3. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with $1, \mathfrak{L}$ the Lie algebra of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{J}$ generated by the Lie triple system $R(\mathfrak{J})$. Then $\mathfrak{L}=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is a subset of $\mathfrak{J}$ we write $R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{A})=\left\{R_{a} \mid a \in \mathfrak{A}\right\}$ where $R_{a}$ acts in $\mathfrak{J}$. Then if $\mathfrak{B}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{K}=R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})+\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B}), R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})\right]$ is the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{L}$ generated by $R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ and the centralizer $\mathfrak{M}$ of $\mathfrak{K}$ in $\mathfrak{L}$ has the form

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{M}=R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{C}) \oplus \mathfrak{N} \tag{21}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\mathfrak{C}=C_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})$ and $\mathfrak{N}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{C}), \mathfrak{N}\right] \subseteq R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{C})$ and $\left[R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{C}), R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{C})\right] \subseteq \mathfrak{N}$.

Proof. The first statement is clear. Since $\mathfrak{B}$ is a subalgebra $R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ is a subsystem of the Lie triple system $R(\mathfrak{J})$. Hence the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{L}$ generated by $R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ is $\mathfrak{M}=R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})+\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B}), R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})\right]$. It is clear also that the centralizer $\mathfrak{M}$ of $\mathfrak{K}$ in $\mathfrak{L}$ is the set of linear transformations $M \in \mathfrak{L}$ such that $\left[M R_{b}\right]=0, b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Now $M=R_{c}+D \quad$ where $c \in \mathfrak{J}$ and $D \in[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$. Then $0=\left[M R_{b}\right]=\left[R_{c} R_{b}\right]$
$+\left[D R_{b}\right]$ and $\left[D R_{b}\right] \in R(\mathfrak{J})$. Hence $\left[R_{c} R_{b}\right]=0$ and $\left[D R_{b}\right]=0$ for all $b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Thus $c \in \mathfrak{C}=C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ and $D \in \mathfrak{N} \equiv \mathfrak{M} \cap[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$, which is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{L}$ since $\mathfrak{M}$ and $[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$ are subalgebras. Now it is clear that (21) holds where $\mathfrak{C}=C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ and $\mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak{M} \cap[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{L}$. If $c \in C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ and $D \in \mathfrak{N}$ then $\left[R_{c} D\right] \in[R(\mathfrak{J}),[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]] \subseteq R(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\left[R_{c} D\right] \in \mathfrak{M}$. Hence $\left[R_{c} D\right] =R_{c^{\prime}}$ where $c^{\prime} \in \mathbb{C}$. Thus $\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathbb{C}), \mathfrak{N}\right] \subseteq R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathbb{C})$. The inclusion $\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathbb{C}), R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathbb{C})\right] \subseteq \mathfrak{N}$ is clear.

We prove next
Theorem 9. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple Jordan algebra over a field of characteristic $0, \mathfrak{B}$ a semisimple subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ is a semisimple subalgebra of J.

Proof. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is semisimple, the Lie algebra of linear transformations $\mathfrak{L} =R(\mathfrak{J})+[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$ is completely reducible. We consider next the Lie algebra of linear transformations $\mathfrak{K}=R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})+\left[R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B}), R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})\right]$ in $\mathfrak{J}$. Now $U(\mathfrak{B})$ is semisimple by Theorem 4 and we have a homomorphism of $U(\mathfrak{B})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ sending $1 \rightarrow 1$ and $b \rightarrow R_{b}, b \in \mathfrak{B}$. The image under this homomorphism is a semisimple associative algebra and is generated by 1 and $\Omega$. Hence $\Omega$ is a completely reducible Lie algebra of linear transformations and, consequently, the centralizer $\mathfrak{M}$ of $\mathfrak{K}$ in $\mathfrak{L}$ is completely reducible (Jacobson, Lie Algebras, p. 102). By Criterion 2, $\mathfrak{M}$ has the imbedding property for nilpotent elements. By Lemma 3, $\mathfrak{M}=R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{C}) \oplus \mathfrak{N}$ where $\mathfrak{C}=C_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ and $\mathfrak{N}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{C}), \mathfrak{N}\right] \subseteq R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{C})$ and $\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{C}), R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{C})\right] \subseteq \mathfrak{N}$. By Theorem 8, $\mathfrak{C}$ is a subalgebra, so $R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{C})$ is a Lie triple system of linear transformations. Thus $\mathfrak{T}=R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{C})$ satisfies the conditions in (2) of Theorem 5. Hence $R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{C})$ has the imbedding property for nilpotent elements. Now let $v$ be a nilpotent element $\neq 0$ of the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{C}=C_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})$. Then $R_{v}$ is a nonzero nilpotent of $R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{C})$. Hence there exists a $u \in \mathfrak{C}$ such that $\left[R_{u} R_{u} R_{v}\right]=2 R_{u},\left[R_{v} R_{v} R_{u}\right]=2 R_{v}$. Then $[u, u, v]=2 u$ and $[v, v, u]=2 v$ so $u$ and $v$ are associates in the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{C}$. Hence the subalgebra $\mathfrak{H}$ generated by $1, u$ and $v$ is an elementary semisimple Jordan algebra and $\mathfrak{C}$ is semisimple by Theorem 7.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a special Jordan algebra and identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with the corresponding subspace of the special universal envelope $S(\mathfrak{J})$. Show that $a, b \in \mathfrak{J} o$-commute in $\mathfrak{J}$ if and only if $[a b]$ is contained in the center of $S(\mathfrak{J})$.
2. Let $Q$ be the field of rational numbers and let $\mathfrak{J}$ be the subalgebra of $Q_{6^{+}}$ generated by 1 and the matrices $a=e_{14}+e_{25}+2 e_{46}, b=e_{42}+e_{53}+e_{65}$. Verify that $[[a b] a]=0$ and $[[a b] b]=0$. Hence show that $a$ and $b o$-commute in $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that $a$ and $b^{\cdot 2}$ do not $o$-commute in $\mathfrak{C}$ and that $a$ and $b$ do not $o$-commute in $Q_{6}{ }^{+}$.
3. Derivations of semisimple Jordan algebras of characteristic 0 into bimodules. In this section we shall prove by a Lie algebra method that every derivation of a finite-dimensional semisimple Jordan algebra of characteristic 0 into a finitedimensional bimodule is inner. We recall that a more general result was given in Theorem 7.14 (Harris' theorem). The proof of the more general result required the determination of the finite-dimensional simple Jordan algebras over an algebraically closed field and their irreducible bimodules.

We note first that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is an arbitrary Jordan algebra, $U(\mathfrak{J})$ its universal multiplication envelope (containing $\mathfrak{J}$ ), then the subalgebra of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$ generated by $\mathfrak{J}$ is $\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ and $\mathfrak{J} \cap[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]=0$. The first statement is clear since $\mathfrak{J}$ is a subsystem of the Lie triple system $\left(U(\mathfrak{J})^{-}\right)^{(2)}$. The second follows if $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element by observing that in this case the mapping $a \rightarrow R_{a}$ is 1-1. Moreover, we have the Lie algebra homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ onto $R(\mathfrak{J})+[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$ induced by the homomorphism of $U(\mathfrak{J})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, a \rightarrow R_{a}$. Since $R(\mathfrak{J}) \cap[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]=0$ and $a \rightarrow R_{a}$ is $1-1$, we have $\mathfrak{J} \cap[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]=0$. If $\mathfrak{J}$ does not have an identity element then we can adjoin one and argue in the same way with the mapping $a \rightarrow R_{a}$ where $R_{a}$ is the multiplication by $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ in the larger algebra. We can now give a Lie algebra proof of the following

Theorem 10. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple Jordan algebra over a field of characteristic $0, \mathfrak{M}$ a finite-dimensional bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$. Then every derivation $D$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ is inner, that is, has the form $x \rightarrow \Sigma\left[b_{i}, x, z_{i}\right]$ where $b_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}, z_{i} \in \mathfrak{M}$.

Proof. As in the proof of Theorem 7.14, we may assume the base field is algebraically closed. We form the split null extension $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ and extend $D$ linearly to $\mathfrak{E}$ so that $\mathfrak{M} D=0$. Then the extended $D$ is a derivation in $\mathfrak{E}$ mapping $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}$ into 0 . Let $U(\mathfrak{E})$ be the universal multiplication envelope of $\mathfrak{E}$ Then $D$ has a unique extension to a derivation $D$ in $U(\mathfrak{E})$ (Theorem 2.13 (ii), p.97). Clearly $D$ is a derivation of the Lie algebra $U(\mathscr{E})^{-}$and this maps the subalgebra $\mathscr{E}+[\mathscr{E} \mathfrak{E}]$ of $U(\mathfrak{E})^{-}$into itself. Let $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ be the associator ideal of $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}+\left[\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right]$ is a semisimple Lie algebra, by Theorem 3, and the restriction $D$ of $D$ to $\mathfrak{L}$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{L}$ into the finite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak{E}+[\mathfrak{E} \mathfrak{E}]$ containing $\mathfrak{L}$ as a subalgebra. It follows that this can be extended to an inner derivation of $\mathfrak{N}$ (Jacobson, Lie Algebras, p. 80). Thus there exists an element $f \in \mathfrak{N}$ such that $x D=[x f]$ for all $x \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. We have seen that $\mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak{E} \oplus[\mathfrak{E} \mathfrak{E}]$, and since $[\mathfrak{E}[\mathfrak{E} \mathfrak{E}]] \subseteq \mathfrak{E}$ and $x D \in \mathfrak{M} \subseteq \mathfrak{E}$ for all $x \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ we may assume that $f \in[\mathfrak{E} \mathfrak{E}]=[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{M}] +[\mathfrak{M M}]$. If $z, w \in \mathfrak{M}, x \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ then $[x[z w]]=[[w z] x]=[z x w]=0$ since $\mathfrak{M}^{\cdot 2}=0$ in $\mathfrak{E}$. Hence we may assume $f \in[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{M}]$. Also since $\left[\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]\right] \subseteq \mathfrak{J}^{\prime},\left[\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{M}]\right] \subseteq \mathfrak{M}$ and $x D \in \mathfrak{M}$ if $x \in \mathfrak{J}$, we may assume $f \in[\mathfrak{I} \mathfrak{M}]$. Thus we have $f=\Sigma\left[b_{i} z_{i}\right]$, $b_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}, z_{i} \in \mathfrak{M}$ and $x D=[x f]=\Sigma\left[x\left[b_{i} z_{i}\right]\right]=-\Sigma\left[b_{i} x z_{i}\right], x \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Hence if we sub-
tract the inner derivation $x \rightarrow-\sum\left[b_{i} x z_{i}\right]$ from $D$ we obtain a derivation $E$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} E=0$. It remains to prove $E$ is inner. We now write $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{s}$ where the $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ are the simple components which we assume are ordered so that $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}_{i}>1$ if $1 \leqq i \leqq t$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}_{j}=1$ if $j>t$. Then $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{K} \oplus \mathfrak{A}$ where $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{I}_{1}+\cdots+\mathfrak{J}_{t}$ and $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{J}_{t+1}+\cdots+\mathfrak{J}_{s}$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{K}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{J}_{1}{ }^{\prime}+\cdots +\mathfrak{J}_{t}{ }^{\prime}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{i}=\Phi 1_{i} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{i}{ }^{\prime}$, where $1_{i}$ is the identity of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ (Theorem 3). Evidently, $\mathfrak{J}_{i}{ }^{\prime} \neq 0$ if $i \leqq t$ and the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ generated by $\mathfrak{J}_{i}{ }^{\prime}$ is an ideal. Hence the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ generated by $\mathfrak{J}_{i}{ }^{\prime}$ is $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ and so the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ generated by $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is $\mathfrak{K}$. Since $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} E=0$ we have $\mathfrak{K} E=0$. Let $\left(e_{1}, \cdots, e_{s-t}\right)$ be a basis of $\mathfrak{U}$ consisting of orthogonal idempotent elements (the identities of the $\mathfrak{J}_{j}$ ) and suppose we have $e_{1} E=\cdots=e_{r} E=0$ for some $r<s-t$. The relation $e_{r+1} \cdot{ }^{2}=e_{r+1}$ gives $2 e_{r+1} E \cdot e_{r+1}=e_{r+1} E \quad$ and $\quad 4 e_{r+1} E \cdot e_{r+1} \cdot e_{r+1}=2 e_{r+1} E \cdot e_{r+1}=e_{r+1} E$. Hence $e_{r+1} E=e_{r+1} F$ where $F$ is the inner derivation $\left[R_{4 e_{r+1}} R_{e_{r+1} E}\right]$ and $e_{r+1} E \in \mathfrak{M}$. If $x \in \mathfrak{R}+\sum_{1}^{r} \Phi e_{i}$ then $x . e_{r+1}=0$ and $x E=0$ give $x . e_{r+1} E=0$. Hence $x F=0$ so $G=E-F$ is a derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $\Re G=0$ and $e_{j} G=0$ for $j \leqq r+1$. It follows by induction on $r$ that $G$ and hence $D$ is inner.

As we have seen in §7.7, Theorem 10 implies immediately that if $\Omega$ is a finitedimensional Jordan algebra over a field of characteristic 0 and $\mathfrak{J}$ is a semisimple subalgebra of $\mathfrak{K}$ then every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{K}$ can be extended to an inner derivation of $\Omega$ (Corollary on p. 303). In particular, every derivation of a finitedimensional semisimple Jordan algebra of characteristic 0 is inner. We shall use this fact to prove the following

Theorem 11. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional semisimple Jordan algebra over a field of characteristic 0 then the Lie algebra Der $\mathfrak{J}$ of derivations in $\mathfrak{J}$ is completely reducible.

Proof. It is well known that the Lie algebra of derivations of any finitedimensional algebra is almost algebraic (Jacobson's, Lie Algebras, ex. 8 on p. 54). Hen ceDer $\mathfrak{J}$ is almost algebraic. Now $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}=[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$, by the result noted, and $\mathfrak{L}=R(\mathfrak{J})+\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$ is the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})^{-}$generated by $R(\mathfrak{J})$. Since $\mathfrak{L}$ is completely reducible it has the imbedding property for nilpotent elements. Since $\mathfrak{L}=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$ and $[R(\mathfrak{J})$, Der $\mathfrak{J}] \subseteq R(\mathfrak{J})$ the subalgebra Der $\mathfrak{J}$ has the imbedding property for nilpotent elements by Theorem 5 (1). Hence Der $\mathfrak{J}$ is completely reducible by Criterion 2.
5. The Tits-Koecher construction of a Lie algebra from a Jordan algebra. In this section we shall give a construction of a Lie algebra from an arbitrary Jordan algebra with 1 , which has been given by Koecher in [9], and somewhat earlier and in a more general form by Tits ([4], cf. ex. 2, below). We begin the construction with the Lie algebra of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{J}$ generated by the multiplications $R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Since $R(\mathfrak{J})$ is a Lie triple system, this is

$$
\mathcal{L}=\left\{R_{a}+\sum\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right] \mid a, b_{i} c_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}\right\} .
$$

The set $\left\{\sum\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right]\right\}$ is the Lie algebra Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ of inner derivations. Hence $\mathfrak{L}=R(\mathfrak{J})+$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $1 R_{a}=a$ and $1 D=0$ for any derivation $D$ it is clear that $R(\mathfrak{J}) \cap$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}=0$. Hence $\mathfrak{L}=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ and so we have the linear mapping $\varepsilon: R_{a}+D \rightarrow \overline{R_{a}+D}=-R_{a}+D, a \in \mathfrak{J}, D \in$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$, in $\mathfrak{L}$, which is of period two. Since

$$
\begin{aligned}
{\left[-R_{a}+D,-R_{b}+E\right] } & =\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right]-R_{a E}+R_{b D}+[D E], \\
{\left[R_{a}+D, R_{b}+E\right] } & =\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right]+R_{a E}-R_{b D}+[D E]
\end{aligned}
$$

for $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}, D, E \in$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ it is clear that $\varepsilon$ is an automorphism of period two in $\mathfrak{L}$.
If $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$ we define

$$
\begin{equation*}
a \triangle b=R_{a}^{(b)}=R_{a . b}-\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right] . \tag{22}
\end{equation*}
$$

Hence $R_{a}{ }^{(b)}$ is the multiplication by $a$ in the $b$-homotope $(\mathfrak{J}, b)$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ (cf. p. 58 ). For $c \in \mathfrak{J}$, we have $c(a \triangle b)=c .(a . b)-c . a . b+c . b . a=\{a b c\}$. Since $\{a b c\} =\{c b a\}$ this gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
c(a \triangle b)=a(c \triangle b) . \tag{23}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since $\overline{a \triangle b}=-R_{b . a}-\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right]=-R_{b}{ }^{(a)}$ we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
\overline{a \triangle b}=-(b \triangle a) \quad \text { and } \quad c \overline{(a \triangle b)}=b \overline{(a \triangle c)} \tag{24}
\end{equation*}
$$

If $D \in$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ then $\left[R_{a} D\right]=R_{a D}$. Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
{[a \triangle b, D] } & =\left[R_{a . b}-\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right], D\right] \\
& =R_{a D . b}+R_{a . b D}-\left[R_{a D} R_{b}\right]-\left[R_{a} R_{b D}\right] \\
& =a \triangle b D+a D \triangle b .
\end{aligned}
$$

Also

$$
\begin{aligned}
{[a} & \left.\Delta b, R_{c}\right]-a R_{c} \Delta b+a \Delta b R_{c} \\
= & {\left[R_{a . b}, R_{c}\right]-\left[\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right] R_{c}\right]-R_{a . c . b}+\left[R_{a . c} R_{b}\right] } \\
& +R_{a .(b . c)}-\left[R_{a} R_{b . c}\right] \\
= & R_{[b, c, a]}-\left[R_{b} R_{c} R_{a}\right]=0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
[a \triangle b, L]=a L \triangle b+a \triangle b \bar{L} \tag{25}
\end{equation*}
$$

for $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}, L \in \mathfrak{L}$.
We now form the vector space $\mathfrak{R}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \overline{\mathfrak{J}} \oplus \mathfrak{L}$, where $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$ is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{J}$ under a linear mapping $a \rightarrow \bar{a}$, and we define

$$
\begin{align*}
{\left[a_{1}+\bar{b}_{1}+L_{1}, a_{2}+\bar{b}_{2}+L_{2}\right]=} & a_{1} L_{2}-a_{2} L_{1}+\overline{b_{1} \bar{L}_{2}}-\overline{b_{2} \bar{L}_{1}} \\
& +a_{1} \triangle b_{2}-a_{2} \triangle b_{1}+\left[L_{1} L_{2}\right] \tag{26}
\end{align*}
$$

It is clear that this is skew symmetric and bilinear. Also we have

$$
\left[\left[a_{1}+\bar{b}_{1}+L_{1}, a_{2}+\bar{b}_{2}+L_{2}\right], a_{3}+\bar{b}_{3}+L_{3}\right]=a_{123}+\bar{b}_{123}+L_{123}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{123}= & a_{1} L_{2} L_{3}-a_{2} L_{1} L_{3}-a_{3}\left(a_{1} \triangle b_{2}\right)+a_{3}\left(a_{2} \triangle b_{1}\right)-a_{3}\left[L_{1} L_{2}\right] \\
b_{123}= & b_{1} \bar{L}_{2} \bar{L}_{3}-b_{2} \bar{L}_{1} \bar{L}_{3}-b_{3}\left(\overline{a_{1} \triangle b_{2}}\right)+b_{3}\left(\overline{a_{2} \triangle b_{1}}\right)-b_{3}\left[\bar{L}_{1} \bar{L}_{2}\right] \\
L_{123}= & \left(a_{1} L_{2}-a_{2} L_{1}\right) \triangle b_{3}-a_{3} \triangle\left(b_{1} \bar{L}_{2}-b_{2} \bar{L}_{1}\right) \\
& +\left[a_{1} \triangle b_{2}-a_{2} \triangle b_{1}, L_{3}\right]+\left[\left[L_{1} L_{2}\right] L_{3}\right] .
\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{123}+a_{231}+a_{312}= & -a_{3}\left(a_{1} \Delta b_{2}\right)+a_{3}\left(a_{2} \Delta b_{1}\right)-a_{1}\left(a_{2} \Delta b_{3}\right) \\
& +a_{1}\left(a_{3} \Delta b_{2}\right)-a_{2}\left(a_{3} \Delta b_{1}\right)+a_{2}\left(a_{1} \Delta b_{3}\right)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

by (23). Similarly, (24) implies that $b_{123}+b_{231}+b_{312}=0$. Also, by (25), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
L_{123}= & \left(a_{1} L_{2} \triangle b_{3}+a_{1} L_{3} \triangle b_{2}-a_{2} L_{1} \triangle b_{3}-a_{2} L_{3} \triangle b_{1}\right) \\
& +\left(a_{3} \triangle b_{2} \bar{L}_{1}+a_{1} \triangle b_{2} \bar{L}_{3}-a_{3} \triangle b_{1} \bar{L}_{2}-a_{2} \triangle b_{1} \bar{L}_{3}\right) \\
& +\left[\left[L_{1} L_{2}\right] L_{3}\right] .
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence by the Jacobi identity in $\mathfrak{L}$, we have $L_{123}+L_{231}+L_{312}=\Sigma_{\sigma} a_{1 \sigma} L_{2 \sigma} \triangle b_{3 \sigma} -\sum_{\sigma} a_{1 \sigma} L_{2 \sigma} \Delta b_{3 \sigma}+\sum_{\sigma} a_{1 \sigma} \Delta b_{2 \sigma} \bar{L}_{3 \sigma}-\sum_{\sigma} a_{1 \sigma} \Delta b_{2 \sigma} \bar{L}_{3 \sigma}$, where $\sigma$ ranges over all the permutations of $1,2,3$. Hence $L_{123}+L_{231}+L_{312}=0$. Thus the Jacobi identity holds in $\Re$ and $\Re$ is a Lie algebra.

It is clear from the multiplication formula (26) that

$$
\begin{equation*}
[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]=0, \quad[\overline{\mathfrak{J}} \overline{\mathfrak{J}}]=0 . \tag{27}
\end{equation*}
$$

Also, we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
[a, L]=a L, \quad[\bar{a}, L]=\overline{a \bar{L}} \tag{28}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since $1=R_{1} \in \mathfrak{L}$ and $1^{\varepsilon}=-1$, it is clear that

$$
\begin{equation*}
[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{L}]=\mathfrak{J}, \quad[\overline{\mathfrak{J}} \mathfrak{L}]=\overline{\mathfrak{J}} \tag{29}
\end{equation*}
$$

Next we note that

$$
\begin{equation*}
[a, \tilde{b}]=a \triangle b . \tag{30}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since the space spanned by the $a \triangle b, a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$ includes every $R_{b}=1 \triangle b$ and every $\left[R_{b} R_{a}\right]=a \triangle b-R_{a . b}$ it is clear that

$$
\begin{equation*}
[\mathfrak{J} \overline{\mathfrak{I}}]=\mathfrak{L} . \tag{31}
\end{equation*}
$$

Let $\varepsilon$ be the extension to $\mathfrak{K}$ of the automorphism $\varepsilon$ on $\mathfrak{L}$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
a+\bar{b}+L \rightarrow \overline{a+\bar{b}+L}=b+\bar{a}+\bar{L} \tag{32}
\end{equation*}
$$

Clearly this is linear and of period two. By (30) and (24), $\overline{[a, \bar{b}]}=-b \triangle a= -[b, \bar{a}]=[\bar{a}, b]$. Also $\overline{[a, L]}=\overline{a L}=[\bar{a}, \bar{L}]$ and $\overline{[\bar{a}, L]}=a \bar{L}=[a, \bar{L}]$. It is clear from this and (27) that $\varepsilon$ is an automorphism of $\Re$. The subalgebra of $\Re$ of $\varepsilon$-fixed points is $\mathfrak{F}=\{a+\bar{a}+D \mid a \in \mathfrak{J}, D \in$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}\}$ and the Lie triple system (subsystem of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{(2)}$ ) of elements $x \in \boldsymbol{\Omega}$ such that $\bar{x}=-x$ is

$$
\mathfrak{T}=\left\{a-\tilde{a}+R_{b} \mid a, b \in \mathfrak{J}\right\} .
$$

We have the multiplication formulas

$$
\begin{equation*}
[a+\bar{a}, D]=a D+\overline{a D}, \quad[a+\bar{a}, b+\bar{b}]=-2\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right] \tag{33}
\end{equation*}
$$

in $\mathfrak{F}$ and the Lie triple system formula:

$$
\begin{align*}
& {\left[a_{1}-\bar{a}_{1}+R_{b_{1}}, a_{2}-\bar{a}_{2}+R_{b_{2}}, a_{3}-\bar{a}_{3}+R_{b_{3}}\right]} \\
& \quad=\left[\left[a_{3}-\bar{a}_{3}+R_{b_{3}}, a_{1}-\bar{a}_{1}+R_{b_{1}}\right], a_{2}-\bar{a}_{2}+R_{b_{2}}\right]  \tag{34}\\
& \quad=a-\bar{a}+R_{b}
\end{align*}
$$

where

$$
\begin{align*}
& a=a_{3} \cdot b_{1} \cdot b_{2}-a_{1} \cdot b_{3} \cdot b_{2}+2\left[a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\right]+\left[b_{1}, a_{2}, b_{3}\right] \\
& b=\left[b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}\right]+2\left[a_{1}, b_{2}, a_{3}\right]-2 a_{3} \cdot b_{1} \cdot a_{2}+2 a_{1} \cdot b_{3} \cdot a_{2} . \tag{35}
\end{align*}
$$

Now put

$$
\begin{equation*}
e=1, \quad f=2(\overline{1}), \quad h=2 R_{1} \tag{36}
\end{equation*}
$$

where 1 is the identity element of $\mathfrak{J}$ and the elements indicated are in $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{J} +\overline{\mathfrak{J}}+\mathcal{L}$. Then (28) and (30) show that $[e f]=h,[e h]=2 e,[f h]=-2 f$. Hence if we define an $A_{1}$-Lie algebra and canonical basis for arbitrary characteristic $\neq 2$ as on p.315, then $(e, f, h)$ is a canonical basis for the $A_{1}$-subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}=\Phi e +\Phi f+\Phi h$ of $\Re$. If $D \in$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$, then $1 D=0$ and $\left[R_{1}, D\right]=0$. Hence $[e, D] =[f, D]=[h, D]=0$. Consequently, the subalgebra Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ centralizes $\mathfrak{A}$. If $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ we put $\mathfrak{M}_{a}=\Phi a+\Phi \bar{a}+\Phi R_{a}$. Then (28) and (30) show that $\left[\mathfrak{M}_{a} \mathfrak{A}\right] \subseteq \mathfrak{M}_{a}$ and $\mathfrak{M}_{a}$ as $\mathfrak{A}$-module is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{A}$. Clearly, $\mathfrak{K}=\operatorname{Inder} \mathfrak{J}+\Sigma_{a \in \mathfrak{I}} \mathfrak{M}_{a}$. Hence $\mathfrak{K}$ as $\mathfrak{A}$-module (with respect to the module product for $x \in \mathfrak{K}, b \in \mathfrak{A}$ as $[x, b]$ ) is a sum of the submodule Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ and three-dimensional submodules isomorphic to $\mathfrak{A}$. It follows that the centralizer of $\mathfrak{A}$ in $\mathfrak{K}$ is Inder $\mathfrak{J}$.

Let $c$ be an invertible element of $\mathfrak{J}$ and consider the isotope $\mathfrak{J}^{(c)} \equiv(\mathfrak{J}, c)$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ and the Lie algebras $\mathfrak{L}^{(c)}=R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{(c)}\right)+$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}^{(c)}$ and $\mathfrak{K}^{(c)}=\mathfrak{J}^{(c)} \oplus \overline{\mathfrak{J}^{(c)}} \oplus \mathfrak{L}^{(c)}$ defined by $\mathfrak{J}^{(c)}$. We write $R_{a}^{(c)}$ for the multiplication by $a$ in $\mathfrak{J}^{(c)}, \Delta^{(c)}$ for the multiplication $\triangle$ on $\mathfrak{J}^{(c)}$ and $\varepsilon^{(c)}$ for the automorphism $R_{a}{ }^{(c)}+\sum\left[R_{b_{i}}{ }^{(c)} R_{c_{i}}{ }^{(c)}\right]$
$\rightarrow-R_{a}^{(c)}+\Sigma\left[R_{b_{i}}{ }^{(c)} R_{c_{i}}{ }^{(c)}\right]$. We have $R_{a}^{(c)}=R_{a . c}-\left[R_{a} R_{c}\right] \in \mathfrak{L}$. Hence $\mathfrak{L}^{(c)} \subseteq \mathfrak{L}$. Since isotopy is a symmetric relation we have $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{L}^{(c)}$. Also, by definition $a \Delta^{(c)} b=R_{a}^{(c, b)}$, the multiplication by $a$ in the $b$-homotope of $\mathfrak{J}^{(c)}$. We have seen that the $b$-homotope of the $c$-homotope of $\mathfrak{J}$ is the $\{c b c\}$-homotope of $\mathfrak{J}$ (p.57). Hence we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
a \triangle^{(c)} b=a \triangle\{c b c\}=a \triangle b U_{c} . \tag{37}
\end{equation*}
$$

We obtain next the relation between the automorphism $\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon^{(c)}$ in $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{L}^{(c)}$. We have $(a \triangle c)^{\varepsilon(c)}=\left(R_{a}{ }^{(c)}\right)^{\varepsilon(c)}=-R_{a}{ }^{(c)}=-a \triangle c$. By (24), $(a \triangle c)^{\varepsilon}=-(c \triangle a)$. Now it is immediate that the identity $\{c\{b c a\} c\}=\{\{c b c\} a c\}$ is valid for special Jordan algebras. Hence, by Macdonald's Theorem it holds for arbitrary Jordan algebras. In operator form the identity reads $(a \triangle c) U_{c}=U_{c}(c \triangle a)$. Hence the foregoing equations show that

$$
\begin{equation*}
L^{\left(e^{c}\right)}=U_{c} L^{\varepsilon} U_{c}^{-1} \tag{38}
\end{equation*}
$$

holds for every $L=a \triangle c$. Since $\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon^{(c)}$ are automorphisms and the elements $a \Delta c=R_{a}{ }^{(c)}$ generate $\mathfrak{L}^{(c)}=\mathfrak{L}$ it is clear that (38) holds for all $L \in \mathfrak{L}$.
We can now prove
Theorem 12 (Koecher). The mapping $a+\bar{b}+L \rightarrow a+\bar{b} \bar{U}_{c}+L$ is an isomorphism of $\Re^{(c)}$ onto $\Re$.

Proof. Since $U_{c}$ is linear and bijective in $\mathfrak{J}$ it is clear that the indicated mapping is linear and bijective. In view of the multiplication formulas (27), (28) and (30) and the fact that $\mathfrak{L}^{(c)}=\mathfrak{L}$, it is enough to verify that $a \triangle^{(c)} b=a \triangle b U_{c}$ and $b L^{\varepsilon^{(c)}} U_{c}=b U_{c} L^{\varepsilon}$ for $b \in \mathfrak{J}, L \in \mathfrak{L}$. These hold by (37) and (38) so the proof is complete.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be a subalgebra of Der $\mathfrak{J}$ containing Inder $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that $R(\mathfrak{J})+\mathfrak{D}$ is a subalgebra of the Lie algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})^{-}$and $R_{a}+D \rightarrow \overline{R_{a}+D}=-R_{a}+D$ is an automorphism in this algebra. Consider the vector space $\mathfrak{J} \oplus \mathfrak{J} \oplus(R(\mathfrak{J})+\mathfrak{D})$ and define $\left[a_{1}+\bar{b}_{1}+L_{1}, a_{2}+\bar{b}_{2}+L_{2}\right], a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}, \bar{b}_{i} \in \overline{\mathfrak{J}}, L_{i} \in R(\mathfrak{J})+\mathfrak{D}$ as in (26). Show that this is a Lie algebra and show that the foregoing results on $\Re$ with the exception of Theorem 12 carry over to this Lie algebra.
2. (Tits) Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a three-dimensional simple Lie algebra, $\mathfrak{J}$ a Jordan algebra and $\mathfrak{D}$ a subalgebra of Der $\mathfrak{J}$ containing Inder $\mathfrak{J}$. If $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$ put $(a, b)= \frac{1}{2} \operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad} a)(\operatorname{ad} b)$ (half the Killing form). Let $\mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus(\mathfrak{J} \otimes \mathfrak{A})$ and define for $D_{i} \in \mathfrak{D}, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}, u_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}$,

$$
\begin{align*}
{\left[D_{1}+a_{1} \otimes u_{1}, D_{2}+a_{2} \otimes u_{2}\right] } & =\left[D_{1}, D_{2}\right]+\left(u_{1}, u_{2}\right)\left[R_{a_{1}} R_{a_{2}}\right] \\
& +a_{1} D_{2} \otimes u_{1}-a_{2} D_{1} \otimes u_{2}+a_{1} \cdot a_{2} \otimes\left[u_{1}, u_{2}\right] . \tag{39}
\end{align*}
$$

Show that this defines a Lie algebra structure on $\mathfrak{N}$. Prove that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is split and $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity 1 then $\mathfrak{N}$ is isomorphic to the Lie algebra defined in ex.1.
3. Show that the center of $\Omega$ is 0 .
4. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with $1, \Re=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \overline{\mathfrak{J}} \oplus \mathfrak{L}$ the Lie algebra defined by $\mathfrak{J}$ as in the text. Verify that $(\operatorname{ad} a)^{3}=0$ in $\Re$ for every $a \in \mathfrak{J}$.
5. Let $\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{K}, \mathfrak{L}$ be as in 4 . and assume the characteristic is $p \neq 0$. Show that $\mathfrak{L}=R(\mathfrak{J})+$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ is a restricted Lie algebra of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that a $p$-mapping $x \rightarrow x^{[p]}$ can be introduced in $\Omega$ in one and only one way so that: (1) $\Re$ with this mapping is a restricted Lie algebra, (2) $\mathfrak{L}$ with $L^{[p]}=L^{p}$ is a subalgebra of $\Re$ as restricted Lie algebra. Show that for the $p$ mapping satisfying these conditions we have $a^{[p]}=0$ for all $a \in \mathfrak{J}$.
6. Let $D$ be a derivation in $\mathfrak{J}$ ( $\mathfrak{J}$ arbitrary with 1 ). Show that the mapping $a+\bar{b}+L \rightarrow a D+\overline{b D}+[L, D]$ is a derivation in $\Omega$.
