7. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be an arbitrary Jordan algebra and let $\mathfrak{T}=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \overline{\mathfrak{J}}$ where $\varepsilon: a \rightarrow \bar{a}$ is a linear isomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$. Define

$$
\left[a_{1}+\tilde{b}_{1}, a_{2}+\tilde{b}_{2}, a_{3}+\bar{a}_{3}\right]=a+\bar{b}
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are given by the formulas (35). Prove that $\mathfrak{T}$ with this composition is a Lie triple system.
6. Subalgebras and ideals of $\Re=\Re(\mathfrak{J})$. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be an arbitrary Jordan algebra with 1 . We now denote the Lie algebra of linear transformations $R(\mathfrak{J})+$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ by $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ and the extension $\mathfrak{J} \oplus \overline{\mathfrak{J}} \oplus \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ constructed in the last section by $\Re(\mathfrak{J})$. We have the subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}=\Phi e+\Phi f+\Phi h$ where $e=1, f=2(\overline{1}), h=2 R_{1}$ and the automorphism of period two $\varepsilon: a+\bar{b}+L \rightarrow \overline{a+\bar{b}+L}=b+\bar{a}+\bar{L}$, where $\bar{R}_{a}=-R_{a}$. We shall consider first the subalgebras of $(\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon)$ containing $\mathfrak{A}$, where by a subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon)$ we mean a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ which is invariant under $\varepsilon$.
First, let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ containing 1 and let $l_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ be the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by the subspace $R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B}) \equiv\left\{R_{b} \mid b \in \mathfrak{J}\right\}$, ( $R_{b}$ acting in $\mathfrak{J}$ ). If $b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3} \in \mathfrak{B}$ then $\left[R_{b_{1}} R_{b_{2}} R_{b_{3}}\right]=R_{\left[b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}\right]}$ and since $\left[b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}\right] \in \mathfrak{B}$, it is clear that $R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ is a Lie triple system of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence $l_{1}(\mathfrak{B}) =R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})+\left[R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B}), R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})\right]$. If we restrict $R_{b}$ to $\mathfrak{B}$ we obtain the multiplication by $b$ in $\mathfrak{B}$ and it is clear that we have the restriction homomorphism of $l_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ onto $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{B})$ sending $R_{b}$ into its restriction $R_{b} \mid \mathfrak{B}$. Since $1 \in \mathfrak{B}$ it is clear that if $b \neq 0$ then $R_{b}$ is not contained in the kernel of the restriction homomorphism. It follows that the kernel is the set of elements $\Sigma\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right], b_{i}, c_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$, such that $x\left(\sum\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right]\right)=0$ for all $x \in \mathfrak{B}$. If $b, c \in \mathfrak{B}$ then $b \triangle c=R_{b . c}-\left[R_{b} R_{c}\right] \in l_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$. Since $1 \in \mathfrak{B}$ the argument used for $\mathfrak{J}$ shows that every element of $l_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ is a sum of elements $b \triangle c, b, c \in \mathfrak{B}$.

Let $L_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ be the subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{A}(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon)$ generated by the subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}$ with 1 of $\mathfrak{J}$ considered as a subspace of $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{J}+\overline{\mathfrak{J}}+\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$. Then $L_{1}(\mathfrak{B}) \supseteq \mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+[\mathfrak{B} \overline{\mathfrak{B}}]$
and since $[\mathfrak{B} \overline{\mathfrak{B}}]$ is the space spanned by the elements $b \triangle c=[b, \bar{c}], b, c \in \mathfrak{B}$, it is clear that $[\mathfrak{B} \overline{\mathfrak{B}}]=l_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ and $\mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+[\mathfrak{B} \overline{\mathfrak{B}}]=\mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+l_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$. Also, if $b, c, d \in \mathfrak{B}$ then $[d, b \triangle c]=d(b \triangle c) \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $[\bar{d}, b \triangle c]=d \overline{(b \triangle c)}=-d \overline{(c \triangle b)} \in \mathfrak{B}$. Hence it is clear that $\mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+l_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ and this is invariant under $\varepsilon$. Consequently, $L_{1}(\mathfrak{B})=\mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+l_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$. Since $1 \in \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{A}=\Phi e +\Phi f+\Phi h \subseteq L_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$.

We shall define next a larger subalgebra than $L_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ determined by $\mathfrak{B}$. For this we let

$$
\begin{equation*}
d(\mathfrak{B})=\{D \in \operatorname{Inder} \mathfrak{J} \mid \mathfrak{B} D \subseteq \mathfrak{B}\} . \tag{40}
\end{equation*}
$$

Then $d(\mathfrak{B})$ is a subalgebra of Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ containing $\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B}), R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})\right]$. Since $\left[R_{b} D\right] =R_{b D}$ for a derivation $D$ it is clear that $\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B}), R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})\right]$ is an ideal in $d(\mathfrak{B})$ and that $l_{2}(\mathfrak{B}) \equiv R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})+d(\mathfrak{B})$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ containing $l_{1}(\mathfrak{B})=R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B}) +[R(\mathfrak{B}), R(\mathfrak{B})]$ as ideal. Also since $b L \in \mathfrak{B}$ if $b \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $L \in l_{2}(\mathfrak{B})$ and $l_{2}(\mathfrak{B})^{\varepsilon} =l_{2}(\mathfrak{B})$ it is clear that $L_{2}(\mathfrak{B}) \equiv \mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+l_{2}(\mathfrak{B})$ is a subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon)$ containing $L_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ as ideal. Finally, we note that any subalgebra of $L_{2}(\mathfrak{B})$ containing $L_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ has the form $\mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})+\mathfrak{M}$ where $\mathfrak{M}$ is a subalgebra of $d(\mathfrak{B})$ containing $\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B}), R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})\right]$ and hence is invariant under $\varepsilon$.

Conversely, let $\mathfrak{M}$ be any subalgebra of ( $\mathfrak{K}, \varepsilon$ ) containing $\mathfrak{A}$. Let $a+\bar{b}+L \in \mathfrak{M}$.
Then

$$
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{2}[a+\bar{b}+L, h] & =\left[a+\bar{b}+L, R_{1}\right] \\
& =a-\bar{b} \in \mathfrak{M} . \tag{41}
\end{align*}
$$

Then $\frac{1}{2}[a-\bar{b}, h]=a+\bar{b} \in \mathfrak{M}$ and consequently $a, \bar{b}$ and $L \in \mathfrak{M}$. Thus

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{M}=(\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{J})+(\mathfrak{M} \cap \overline{\mathfrak{J}})+(\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})) . \tag{42}
\end{equation*}
$$

Put $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{J}$. Then $\overline{\mathfrak{M}}=\mathfrak{M}$ implies that $\mathfrak{M} \cap \overline{\mathfrak{J}}=\overline{\mathfrak{B}}$ and $\overline{\mathfrak{M}} \cap \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ is a subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon)$. We have $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+(\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J}))$. Let $b, c \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then $\bar{c} \in \overline{\mathfrak{B}}$ and $[b, \bar{c}]=b \triangle c=R_{b . c}-\left[R_{b} R_{c}\right] \in \mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$. Then $[1, b \triangle c] =1(b \triangle c)=b . c \in \mathfrak{B}$. Hence $\mathfrak{B}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ containing 1. Since $[\mathfrak{B}, \overline{\mathfrak{B}}]=l_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ we see that $\mathfrak{M} \supseteq L_{1}(\mathfrak{B})=\mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+l_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$. Since $\mathfrak{M}=\overline{\mathfrak{M}}$ and $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{J}$ it is immediate that $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+\left(R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})+\mathfrak{N}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{N}$ is a subalgebra of Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ containing $\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B}), R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})\right]$. If $D \in \mathfrak{N}$ and $b \in \mathfrak{B}$ then $b D=[b, D] \in \mathfrak{B}$. Hence $\mathfrak{N} \subseteq d(\mathfrak{B})$ defined by (40). Thus $\mathfrak{M} \subseteq L_{2}(\mathfrak{B})$ and we have proved the following

Theorem 13. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ containing 1. Then $L_{1}(\mathfrak{B})=\mathfrak{B} +\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+l_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ where $l_{1}(\mathfrak{B})=R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})+\left[R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B}), R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})\right]$ and $L_{2}(\mathfrak{B})=\mathfrak{B}+\mathfrak{B}+l_{2}(\mathfrak{B})$ where $l_{2}(\mathfrak{B})=R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})+d(\mathfrak{B})$ (as in (40)) are subalgebras of ( $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$, $\varepsilon$ ) containing $\mathfrak{U}=\Phi e+\Phi f+\Phi h$. Also $L_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ is an ideal in $L_{2}(\mathfrak{B})$ and any subalgebra of $L_{2}(\mathfrak{B})$ containing $L_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ is a subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{I}), \varepsilon)$. Conversely, if $\mathfrak{M}$ is any
subalgebra of ( $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon$ ) containing $\mathfrak{A}$ then $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{J}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ containing 1 and $L_{1}(\mathfrak{B}) \subseteq \mathfrak{M} \subseteq L_{2}(\mathfrak{B})$.

Next let $\mathfrak{B}$ be an ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$. Then the ideal in $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by $R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ is $i_{1}(\mathfrak{B}) \equiv R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})+\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B}), R(\mathfrak{J})\right]$. Let $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ be the ideal in $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{I})$ generated by the subspace $\mathfrak{B}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ contains every $R_{b}, b \in \mathfrak{B}$, since $R_{b}=b \triangle 1=[b, \overline{1}]$. Hence $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ contains $i_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$. Also $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ contains $\overline{\mathfrak{B}}$ since it contains $\bar{b}=\overline{1 R_{b}}=\left[R_{b}, \overline{1}\right], b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Hence $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B}) \supseteq \mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+i_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$. Since it is clear that the right-hand side is an ideal, we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})=\mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+i_{1}(\mathfrak{B}), \quad i_{1}(\mathfrak{B})=R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})+\left[R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B}), R(\mathfrak{J})\right] . \tag{43}
\end{equation*}
$$

Next consider the Lie algebras $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B})$ and $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B})$ determined by the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B}$. It is clear that we have the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B})$ such that $R_{a} \rightarrow R_{a+\mathfrak{B}}$. An element $D$ in $\operatorname{Inder} \mathfrak{J}$ is in the kernel of this homomorphism, if and only if $\mathfrak{J} D \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$. Hence if we put

$$
\begin{equation*}
p(\mathfrak{B})=\{D \in \operatorname{Inder} \mathfrak{J} \mid \mathfrak{J} D \subseteq \mathfrak{B}\} \tag{44}
\end{equation*}
$$

then $p(\mathfrak{B})$ is an ideal in Inder $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B}) =R(\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B}) \oplus$ Inder $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B}$ it is clear that the kernel of the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B})$ is $R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})+p(\mathfrak{B})$. The homomorphism of $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ has a unique extension to a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{I})$ onto $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B})$ such that $a \rightarrow a+\mathfrak{B}, \tilde{a} \rightarrow \overline{a+\mathfrak{B}}$, $a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Since $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \overline{\mathfrak{J}} \oplus \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B})=\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B} \oplus \overline{\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B}} \oplus \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B})$ it is clear that the kernel of the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ is

$$
\begin{equation*}
I_{2}(\mathfrak{B})=\mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+i_{2}(\mathfrak{B}), \quad i_{2}(\mathfrak{B})=R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})+p(\mathfrak{B}) . \tag{45}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since $\mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal it is clear that $\mathfrak{J}\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B}), R(\mathfrak{J})\right] \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$. Hence $p(\mathfrak{B}) \supseteq\left[R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B}), R(\mathfrak{J})\right]$, $i_{2}(\mathfrak{B}) \supseteq i_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ and $I_{2}(\mathfrak{B}) \supseteq I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$. Also we have $[p(\mathfrak{B}), R(\mathfrak{J})] \subseteq R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})$ which implies that $\left[i_{2}(\mathfrak{B}), \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})\right] \subseteq i_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ and $\left[I_{2}(\mathfrak{B}), \mathfrak{A}(\mathfrak{J})\right] \subseteq I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$.

Now let $\mathfrak{M}$ be any ideal in $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$. Then (41) holds. Hence we have the decomposition (42). Let $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{J}$ and $b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then $R_{b}=[b, \overline{1}] \in \mathfrak{M}$ and $\bar{b}=\left[R_{b}, \overline{1}\right] \in \mathfrak{M} \cap \overline{\mathfrak{J}}$. Similarly, if $\bar{b} \in \mathfrak{M} \cap \overline{\mathfrak{J}}$ then $b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Hence $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+(\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J}))$ and $\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ is an ideal of $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ containing $R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})$ and hence containing $R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})+\left[R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B}), R(\mathfrak{J})\right]$. If $b \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $a . b=\left[b, R_{a}\right] \in \mathfrak{B}$. Hence $\mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{M} \supseteq I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})=\mathfrak{B}+\bar{B}+i_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$. Let $L=R_{c}+D \in \mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ where $D \in$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $[1, L]=1 L=c \in \mathfrak{B}$ so $R_{c} \in R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B}) \subseteq \mathfrak{M}$. Then $D \in \mathfrak{M}$ and $a D=[a, D] \in \mathfrak{B}$ for every $a \in \mathfrak{J}$, Thus $D \in p(\mathfrak{B})$ and $\mathfrak{M} \subseteq I_{2}(\mathfrak{B})$. We note also that since $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+R_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{B})+(\mathfrak{M} \cap$ Inder $\mathfrak{J})$ it is clear that $\overline{\mathfrak{M}}=\mathfrak{M}$, that is, $\mathfrak{M}$ is an ideal of $(\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon)$.

We summarize our results in the following
Theorem 14. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be an ideal in the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 . Then $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ given in (43) is the ideal in $\mathfrak{R}(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by the subspace $\mathfrak{B}$ of $\mathfrak{R}(\mathfrak{I})(\subseteq \mathfrak{J})$
and $I_{2}(\mathfrak{B})$ defined by (45) and (44) is the kernel of the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $\mathfrak{R}(\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{B})$ such that $a \rightarrow a+\mathfrak{B}, \bar{a} \rightarrow \overline{a+\mathfrak{B}}, R_{a} \rightarrow R_{a+\mathfrak{B}}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$. We have

$$
\begin{equation*}
I_{2}(\mathfrak{B}) \supseteq I_{1}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{1}\right), \quad\left[I_{2}(\mathfrak{B}), \Re(\mathfrak{J})\right] \subseteq I_{1}(\mathfrak{B}) . \tag{46}
\end{equation*}
$$

If $\mathfrak{M}$ is any ideal in $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ then $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{J}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$ and $I_{2}(\mathfrak{B}) \supseteq \mathfrak{M} \supseteq I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$. Moreover, $\mathfrak{M}$ is an ideal of $(\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon)$.

The definitions give $I_{2}(0)=0$ and $I_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=\Re(\mathfrak{J})$. Hence we have the following
Corollary. $\mathfrak{J}$ is simple if and only if $\mathfrak{R}(\mathfrak{J})$ is simple.
Theorems 13 and 14 give a mapping $\mathfrak{M} \rightarrow \mathfrak{J} \cap \mathfrak{M}$ of the set of subalgebras of ( $\Re(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon$ ) containing $\mathfrak{A}$ and the set of ideals of $\Re(\mathfrak{J})$ onto the set of subalgebras of $\mathfrak{J}$ containing 1 and the set of ideals of $\mathfrak{J}$ respectively. If $\mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$ we have the sequence of ideals $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{B}^{(0)} \supseteq \mathfrak{B}^{(1)} \supseteq \cdots$ where

$$
\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}=\mathfrak{B}^{(k-1)} \cdot \mathfrak{B}^{(k-1)}+\mathfrak{B}^{(k-1)} \cdot \mathfrak{B}^{(k-1)} \cdot \mathfrak{J}
$$

(cf. §5.2). We shall now call this the Penico sequence for $\mathfrak{B}$ and we shall say that $\mathfrak{B}$ is Penico solvable if there exists an integer $s \geqq 1$ such that $\mathfrak{B}^{\text {(s) }}=0$. We now have the following result (Koecher [9]).

Theorem 15. Let $\mathfrak{M}$ be an ideal in $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}), \mathfrak{B}$ the corresponding ideal $\mathfrak{B}= \mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\mathfrak{M}$ is solvable if and only if $\mathfrak{B}$ is Penico solvable.

Proof. If $\mathfrak{M}$ is an ideal in a Lie algebra we define the derived series $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M}^{(0)} \supseteq \mathfrak{M}^{(1)} \supseteq \cdots$ inductively by $\mathfrak{M}^{(k)}=\left[\mathfrak{M}^{(k-1)}, \mathfrak{M}^{(k-1)}\right]$. These are ideals of the algebra and solvability means that there exists an $s$ such that $\mathfrak{M}^{(\mathbf{s})}=0$. Now let $\mathfrak{M}$ be an ideal in $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}), \mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{M} \cap \mathfrak{J}$. Then $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B}) \subseteq \mathfrak{M} \subseteq I_{2}(\mathfrak{B})$, so, by (46), $[\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{A}(\mathfrak{I})] \subseteq I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$. Hence $\mathfrak{M}^{(1)}=[\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}] \subseteq I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ and so, by induction, $\mathfrak{M}^{(k+1)} \subseteq I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})^{(k)}$. This shows that $\mathfrak{M}$ is solvable if and only if $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ is solvable. For, if $\mathfrak{M}$ is solvable then $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ is solvable since any subalgebra of a solvable Lie algebra is solvable. Conversely, if $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ is solvable then $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})^{(s)}=0$ for a suitable $s$; hence $\mathfrak{M}^{(s+1)}=0$. Next we note that $\left(I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})\right)^{(1)} \cap \mathfrak{J} =\mathfrak{B}^{(1)}$ since $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})=\mathfrak{B}+\overline{\mathfrak{B}}+R_{\mathfrak{Z}}(\mathfrak{B})+\left[R_{\mathfrak{y}}(\mathfrak{B}), R(\mathfrak{J})\right]$ which gives $\left(I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})\right)^{(1)} \cap \mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{B}\left(R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B})+\left[R_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{B}), R(\mathfrak{J})\right]\right)=\mathfrak{B} \cdot \mathfrak{B}+\mathfrak{B} \cdot \mathfrak{B} \cdot \mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{B}^{(1)}$. Now $\left(I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})\right)^{(1)} \cap \mathfrak{J} =\mathfrak{B}^{(1)}$ implies that $I_{1}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(1)}\right) \subseteq\left(I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})\right)^{(1)} \subseteq I_{2}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(1)}\right)$. By induction, we have $I_{1}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}\right) \subseteq\left(I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})\right)^{(k)}$. Also $\left(I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})\right)^{(1)} \subseteq I_{2}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(1)}\right)$ implies that $\left(I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})\right)^{(2)}=\left[\left(I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})\right)^{(1)}\right.$, $\left.\left(I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})\right)^{(1)}\right] \subseteq\left[I_{2}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(1)}\right), I_{2}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(1)}\right)\right] \subseteq\left[I_{2}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(1)}\right), \Re(\mathfrak{J})\right] \subseteq I_{1}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(1)}\right)$. One can now establish by induction that

$$
\left(I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})\right)^{(2 k-1)} \subseteq I_{2}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}\right), \quad\left(I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})\right)^{(2 k)} \subseteq I_{1}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}\right) .
$$

Now suppose $\mathfrak{B}$ is Penico solvable. Then there exists an $s$ such that $\mathfrak{B}^{(s)}=0$. Then $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})^{(2 s-1)}=0$ and $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ is a solvable Lie algebra. Then $\mathfrak{M}$ is solvable.

Conversely, assume $\mathfrak{M}$ is solvable. Then $I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})$ is solvable so $I_{1}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{(k)}\right) \subseteq I_{1}(\mathfrak{B})^{(k)}$ implies that $\mathfrak{B}$ is Penico solvable.
It is clear that if an ideal $\mathfrak{B}$ in a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ is Penico solvable then it is solvable. The converse holds if $\mathfrak{J}$ is finite dimensional (p. 192). We recall that the radical of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}, \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{L}$, is defined to be the maximal solvable ideal. $\mathfrak{L}$ is semisimple if and only if $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{L}=0$. We can now state the following corollary to Theorem 15.

Corollary. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1. Then $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})=I_{2}(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{J}$ is semisimple if and only if $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ is semisimple.

Proof. Since $I_{2}(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}) \cap \mathfrak{J}=\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ is solvable, $I_{2}(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J})$ is a solvable ideal in $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ so $I_{2}(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}) \subseteq \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$. On the other hand, $\mathfrak{B}=\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}) \cap \mathfrak{J}$ is a solvable ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}) \subseteq I_{2}(\mathfrak{B}) \subseteq I_{2}(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J})$. Hence $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})=I_{2}(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J})$. Clearly this implies that $\mathfrak{J}$ is semisimple if and only if $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ is semisimple.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{M}_{i}, i=1,2$, be ideals in $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}), \mathfrak{B}_{i}=\mathfrak{M}_{i} \cap \mathfrak{J}$. Show that $\mathfrak{B}_{1} i_{2}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{2}\right) +\mathfrak{B}_{2} i_{2}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{1}\right)$, where $i_{2}(\mathfrak{B})=\{L \in \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J}) \mid \mathfrak{J} L \subseteq \mathfrak{B}\}$, is an ideal in $\mathfrak{J}$ and

$$
\mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2}+\mathfrak{B}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{B}_{2} \cdot \mathfrak{J} \subseteq\left[\mathfrak{M}_{1}, \mathfrak{M}_{2}\right] \cap \mathfrak{J} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}_{1} i_{2}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{2}\right)+\mathfrak{B}_{2} i_{2}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{1}\right) .
$$

Define $\mathfrak{B}^{\langle 0\rangle}=\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B}^{\langle k\rangle}=\mathfrak{B}^{\langle k-1\rangle} i_{2}\left(\mathfrak{B}^{\langle k-1\rangle}\right)$ and prove that an ideal $\mathfrak{B}$ is Penico solvable if and only if there exists an $s$ such that $\mathfrak{B}^{\langle s\rangle}=0$.
2. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be finite-dimensional semisimple, $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{s}$ the decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ into simple ideals $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Show that $\mathfrak{K}_{i} \equiv I_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right)=I_{2}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right)$ and $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}) =\Re_{1} \oplus \Re_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \Re_{s}$ is the decomposition of $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ into simple ideals.
3. Let $\eta$ be an automorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that $L \rightarrow \eta^{-1} L \eta$ is an automorphism of $(\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon)$ and $\zeta: a+\bar{b}+L \rightarrow a \eta+\overline{b \eta}+\eta^{-1} L \eta$ is an automorphism of ( $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon$ ) leaving fixed the elements of the subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}=\Phi 1+\Phi \overline{1}+\Phi R_{1}$. Show that the converse holds: if $\zeta$ is an automorphism of ( $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon$ ) leaving the elements of $\mathfrak{A}$ fixed then $\zeta$ is obtained from an automorphism $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ in the manner indicated.
4. Prove the analogue of exercise 3 for derivations.
7. Application to a proof of the Albert-Penico Theorem. Let J be a finitedimensional Jordan algebra with 1 over a field of characteristic 0 . We shall now apply the ideal and subalgebra correspondences of the last section and a theorem on Lie algebras to prove the Albert-Penico theorem on $\mathfrak{J}$. We recall that this asserts that there exists a subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}$ containing 1 such that $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$. This will be proved by proving an extension due to Taft ([4]) of the Levi decomposition theorem for Lie algebras. We have seen that the radical rad $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ of $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ is $I_{2}(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J})$. By Taft's theorem, we shall have the existence of a subalgebra $\mathfrak{S}$ of $(\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon)$ containing $\mathfrak{A}=\Phi 1+\Phi \overline{1}+\Phi R_{1}$ such that $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{S} \oplus \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$.

Since $\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{R}(\mathfrak{J})=\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}+\overline{\operatorname{rad}} \overline{\mathfrak{J}}+(\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{I}) \cap \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J}))$ and $\mathfrak{S}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \bar{B} \oplus(\mathfrak{S} \cap \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J}))$ where $\mathfrak{B}$ is a subalgebra with 1 , and $\mathfrak{I}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \overline{\mathfrak{J}} \oplus \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$, this will give $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{B}$ ⊕ $\operatorname{rad}$ J.
We proceed to derive Taft's theorem. Let $G$ be a group. Then we shall call an algebra $\mathfrak{E} / \Phi$ a $G$-algebra if $\mathscr{E}$ is a $G$-module such that for each $\sigma \in G$ the mapping $x \rightarrow x^{\sigma}$ is either an automorphism or antiautomorphism of $\mathfrak{E}$. We recall that the $G$-module property is that $x \rightarrow x^{\sigma}$ is a linear transformation in $\mathfrak{E}, x^{1}=x$ if 1 is the identity of $G$ and $x^{\sigma \tau}=\left(x^{\sigma}\right)^{\tau}, \sigma, \tau \in G$. The notions of $G$-subalgebra, homomorphism for $G$-algebras, etc. are clear. As for ordinary algebras, we shall call an exact sequence of $G$-algebras $0 \rightarrow \mathfrak{M} \underset{\alpha}{\rightarrow} \mathfrak{E} \rightarrow \underset{\beta}{\mathfrak{B}} \rightarrow 0$ an extension of $\mathfrak{B}$ by $\mathfrak{M}$.
We may assume that $\mathfrak{M} \subseteq \mathfrak{E}$ and $\alpha$ is the injection mapping.
We now assume that $\mathfrak{M}^{2}=0$ and that the extension splits both as $G$-module and as algebra extension (without the $G$ ). The first condition is that there exists a $G$-module homomorphism $\delta$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta \beta=1_{\mathfrak{B}}$. Then $\mathfrak{B}^{\delta}$ is a $G$ submodule of $\mathfrak{E}$ and $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{M} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{\delta}$. The second is that there exists an algebra homomorphism $\delta^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta^{\prime} \beta=\frac{1}{2}$. Then $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{M} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{\delta^{\prime}}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{\delta^{\prime}}$ is a subalgebra. We shall now fix $\delta$ and we consider all the $\delta^{\prime}$ satisfying $\delta^{\prime} \beta=1_{\mathfrak{B}}$. As in §2.8, we put $h(a, b)=a^{\delta} b^{\delta}-(a b)^{\delta}, a, b \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then $h(a, b) \in \mathfrak{M}$ and $(a, b) \rightarrow h(a, b)$ is a bilinear mapping of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$. Also, if $\mu=\delta^{\prime}-\delta$-then $\mu$ is a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$. Moreover, since $(a b)^{\delta^{\prime}}=a^{\delta^{\prime}} b^{\delta^{\prime}}$ and $\mathfrak{M}^{2}=0$ we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
h(a, b)=(a b)^{\mu}-a^{\delta} b^{\mu}-a^{\mu} b^{\delta} \tag{47}
\end{equation*}
$$

Conversely, if $\mu \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{M})$ satisfies (47) then $\delta^{\prime}=\delta+\mu$ is an algebra homomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta^{\prime} \beta=1_{\mathfrak{B}}$. Also $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{M} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{\delta^{\prime}}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{\delta^{\prime}}$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{E}$. Let $\mathfrak{H}$ be the subset of $\mu \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{M})$ satisfying (47). Then if $\mu_{1}, \mu_{2} \in \mathfrak{H}, v=\mu_{1}-\mu_{2}$ satisfies $(a b)^{v}=a^{v} b^{\delta}+a^{\delta} b^{v}, a, b \in \mathfrak{B}$. The set $\mathfrak{D}$ of the mappings $v$ is a subspace of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{M})$ and $\mathfrak{H}$ is a coset $\mu+\mathfrak{D}$ where $\mu \in \mathfrak{H}$.
We can make $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{M})$ into a $G$-module by defining $L^{\sigma}$ for $L \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{M})$ and $\sigma \in G$ by $L^{\sigma}=\sigma_{\mathfrak{B}}{ }^{-1} L \sigma_{\mathfrak{M}}$ where $\sigma_{\mathfrak{B}}\left(\sigma_{\mathfrak{M}}\right.$, etc.) is the mapping $x \rightarrow x^{\sigma}$ in $\mathfrak{B}(\mathfrak{M}$, etc.). Let $\mu \in \mathfrak{H}=\mu+\mathfrak{D}$. Then $\delta^{\prime}=\delta+\mu$ is an algebra homomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ and $\sigma_{\mathfrak{B}}{ }^{-1} \delta^{\prime} \sigma_{\mathfrak{G}}$ is also an algebra homomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$. Hence $\sigma_{\mathfrak{B}}{ }^{-1} \delta^{\prime} \sigma_{\mathfrak{G}}-\delta \in \mathfrak{H}$. Since $\delta$ is a $G$-homomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$, $\delta=\sigma_{\mathfrak{B}}{ }^{-1} \delta \sigma_{\mathfrak{G}}$. Hence $\sigma_{\mathfrak{B}}{ }^{-1} \delta^{\prime} \sigma_{\mathfrak{G}}-\delta=\sigma_{\mathfrak{B}}{ }^{-1}\left(\delta^{\prime}-\delta\right) \sigma_{\mathfrak{G}}=\sigma_{\mathfrak{B}}{ }^{-1}\left(\delta^{\prime}-\delta\right) \sigma_{\mathfrak{M}} \in \mathfrak{H}$. Thus $\mu^{\sigma} \in \mathfrak{H}$. Hence $\mathfrak{H}^{\sigma} \subseteq \mathfrak{H}$ and consequently $\mathfrak{D}^{\sigma} \subseteq \mathfrak{D}$. The argument shows also that $\delta^{\prime}=\delta+\mu$ is a $G$-algebra homomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ if and only if $\mu^{\sigma}=\mu$ for all $\sigma \in G$.
Let $\mathfrak{T}_{\mu}$ be the subspace of $\mathfrak{D}$ spanned by the elements $\mu^{\sigma}-\mu^{\tau}, \sigma, \tau \in G$. Then $\mathfrak{T}_{\mu}{ }^{\sigma} \subseteq \mathfrak{T}_{\mu}$ and $\left(\mathfrak{T}_{\mu}+\mu\right)^{\sigma}=\mathfrak{T}_{\mu}+\mu, \sigma \in G$. Then we have the following criterion.

Lemma. Suppose there exists a $G$-submodule $\mathfrak{C}$ of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{M})$ such that $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{M})=\mathfrak{T}_{\mu} \oplus \mathfrak{C}$. Then there exists a G-algebra homomorphism $\delta^{\prime \prime}$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that the restriction $\delta^{\prime \prime}\left|\mathfrak{A}=\delta^{\prime}\right| \mathfrak{A}\left(\delta^{\prime}=\delta+\mu\right)$ for every G-subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $\delta^{\prime} \mid \mathfrak{A}$ is a G-algebra homomorphism.

Proof. Since $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{M})=\mathfrak{T}_{\mu} \oplus \mathbb{C}$ it is clear that $\left(\mathfrak{T}_{\mu}+\mu\right) \cap \mathfrak{C}=\left\{\mu^{\prime}\right\}$. Since $\left(\mathfrak{T}_{\mu}+\mu\right)^{\sigma} \subseteq \mathfrak{T}_{\mu}+\mu$ and $\mathfrak{C}^{\sigma} \subseteq \mathfrak{C}$ we have $\mu^{\prime \sigma}=\mu^{\prime}, \sigma \in G$. Since $\mu^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{T}_{\mu} +\mu \subseteq \mathfrak{D}+\mu$ it is clear that $\mu^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{H}$ and $\delta^{\prime \prime} \equiv \delta+\mu^{\prime}$ is a $G$-algebra homomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$. Now let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a $G$-subalgebra of $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $\delta^{\prime} \mid \mathfrak{A}$ is a $G$-algebra homomorphism. We have $\delta^{\prime \prime}-\delta^{\prime}=\mu^{\prime}-\mu=\sum \alpha_{i j}\left(\mu^{\sigma_{i}}-\mu^{\sigma_{j}}\right), \sigma_{i}, \sigma_{j} \in G, \alpha_{i j} \in \Phi$. Since $\delta^{\prime} \mid \mathfrak{A}$ is a $G$-homomorphism, $\mu \mid \mathfrak{A}$ is a $G$-homomorphism. It follows that $\mu^{\sigma}|\mathfrak{A}=\mu| \mathfrak{A}, \sigma \in G$. Then $\mu^{\sigma_{i}}\left|\mathfrak{A}=\mu^{\sigma_{j}}\right| \mathfrak{A}$ and consequently $\delta^{\prime \prime}\left|\mathfrak{A}=\delta^{\prime}\right| \mathfrak{A}$.

The hypothesis of the lemma is satisfied if $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{M})$ is completely reducible as $G$-module. Now we recall that if $G$ is finite and the order $(G: 1)$ of $G$ is not divisible by the characteristic then every $G$-module is completely reducible. We shall use this to prove

Theorem 16. Let $G$ be a finite group whose order is not divisible by the characteristic and let $0 \rightarrow \mathfrak{M}_{\underset{\alpha}{\rightarrow}} \mathfrak{E} \underset{\beta}{\rightarrow} \mathfrak{B} \rightarrow 0$ be an exact sequence of G-algebras such that $\mathfrak{M} \subseteq \mathfrak{E}, \alpha$ is the injection mapping and $\mathfrak{M}^{2}=0$. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a $G$-subalgebra of $\mathfrak{B}$. Assume there exists an algebra homomorphism $\delta^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta^{\prime} \beta=1_{\mathfrak{B}}$ and the restriction $\delta^{\prime} \mid \mathfrak{A}$ is a $G$-homomorphism. Then there exists a G-algebra homomorphism $\delta^{\prime \prime}$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta^{\prime \prime} \beta=1_{\mathfrak{B}}$ and $\delta^{\prime \prime}\left|\mathfrak{A}=\delta^{\prime}\right| \mathfrak{A}$.

Proof. We have $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{M} \oplus \mathfrak{B}_{1}$ where $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ is a $G$-submodule of $\mathfrak{E}$. It is clear that the restriction $\beta \mid \mathfrak{B}_{1}$ is a $G$-isomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ onto $\mathfrak{B}$. Let $\delta$ be its inverse. Then $\delta$ is a $G$-homomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta \beta=1_{\mathfrak{B}}$. We apply the foregoing considerations to this $\delta$ and to $\mu=\delta^{\prime}-\delta$. Since $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{M})$ is completely reducible as $G$-module, the lemma gives a $G$-algebra homomorphism $\delta^{\prime \prime}$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta^{\prime \prime}\left|\mathfrak{A}=\delta^{\prime}\right| \mathfrak{A}$.

For our immediate purposes it is useful to have the following alternative formulation of Theorem 16.

Corollary. Let $G$ be a finite group whose order is not divisible by the characteristic, $\mathfrak{E}$ aG-algebra, $\mathfrak{M}$ a G-ideal in $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\mathfrak{M}^{2}=0$. Assume there exists a subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}$ of $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ and let $\mathfrak{U}$ be a $G$-subalgebra of $\mathfrak{B}$. Then there exists a G-subalgebra $\mathfrak{C}$ of $\mathfrak{E}$ containing $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $\mathfrak{E}=\mathfrak{C} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$.

Proof. We have the exact sequence of $G$-algebra $0 \rightarrow \mathfrak{M}_{\underset{\alpha}{\rightarrow}}^{\mathfrak{E}} \underset{\beta}{\rightarrow} \mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M} \rightarrow 0$ where $\alpha$ is the injection and $\beta$ is the canonical homomorphism of $\mathfrak{E}$ onto $\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$. If $x=b+u, b \in \mathfrak{B}, u \in \mathfrak{M}$ then $x+\mathfrak{M} \rightarrow b$ is an algebra homomorphism $\delta^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta^{\prime} \beta=1_{\mathfrak{B}}$. The restriction of $\delta^{\prime}$ to the $G$-subalgebra $(\mathfrak{A}+\mathfrak{M}) / \mathfrak{M}$ is the mapping $a+\mathfrak{M} \rightarrow a, a \in \mathfrak{A}$, and this is a $G$-homomorphism. Hence, by Theorem 16, there exists a $G$-algebra homomorphism $\delta^{\prime \prime}$ of $\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}$ into $\mathfrak{E}$ such that $\delta^{\prime \prime} \beta=1_{\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M}}$ and $\delta^{\prime \prime}\left|(\mathfrak{A}+\mathfrak{M}) / \mathfrak{M}=\delta^{\prime}\right|(\mathfrak{A}+\mathfrak{M}) / \mathfrak{M}$. Then $\mathfrak{E}= \mathfrak{M} \oplus(\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M})^{\delta^{\prime \prime}}$ where $(\mathfrak{E} / \mathfrak{M})$ is a $G$-subalgebra of $\mathfrak{E}$ containing $((\mathfrak{A}+\mathfrak{M}) / \mathfrak{M})^{\delta^{\prime \prime}} =((\mathfrak{A}+\mathfrak{M}) / \mathfrak{M})^{\delta^{\prime}}=\mathfrak{A}$.

We shall now apply this to obtain a generalization of the Levi decomposition theorem for Lie algebras. Let $G$ be an arbitrary finite group, $\mathfrak{L}$ a finite-dimensional $G$-Lie algebra of characteristic $0, \mathfrak{A}$ a semisimple $G$-subalgebra of $\mathfrak{L}$. The maximal solvable ideal $\mathfrak{M}$ of $\mathfrak{L}$ is clearly a $G$-ideal in $\mathfrak{L}$. We now have the following

Theorem 17 (Taft). Let $G$ be a finite group, $\mathfrak{L}$ a finite-dimensional G-Lie algebra of characteristic $0, \mathfrak{M}$ the maximal solvable ideal of $\mathfrak{L}, \mathfrak{A}$ a semisimple G-subalgebra of $\mathfrak{L}$. Then there exists a G-subalgebra $\mathfrak{C}$ of $\mathfrak{L}$ containing $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{C} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$.

Proof. If $[\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}] \neq 0$ the inductive argument on dimensionality given in Reduction II of the proof of the Albert-Penico-Taft theorem (p. 288) is applicable. Hence we may assume $[\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}]=0$. By the Levi-Malcev-Harish-Chandra theorems (Jacobson, Lie Algebras, pp. 91-92) there exists a subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}$ of $\mathfrak{L}$ containing $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$. Then the above corollary gives a $G$-subalgebra $\mathfrak{C}$ of $\mathfrak{L}$ such that $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{C} \oplus \mathfrak{M}$ and $\mathfrak{C} \supseteq \mathfrak{A}$.

We now apply this to $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ considered as a G-Lie algebra for the cyclic group of order two where the action of the element $\neq 1$ is the automorphism $\varepsilon$. If $\mathfrak{A}=\Phi 1 +\Phi \overline{1}+\Phi R_{1}$ then $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple and $\mathfrak{U}^{\varepsilon}=\mathfrak{A}$. Hence the foregoing theorem gives a subalgebra $\mathfrak{S}$ of $(\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}), \varepsilon$ ) containing $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{M} \oplus \mathfrak{S}$. As we saw before, this implies the Albert-Penico theorem.

## Exercises

1. Let $G$ be a finite group of order not divisible by the characteristic, $\mathfrak{J}$ a finitedimensional $G$-Jordan algebra. Prove that there exist a $G$-subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$.
2. Assume that $G$ and $\mathfrak{J}$ are as in 1 . and the characteristic is 0 . Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be semisimple $G$-subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$. Prove that the $\mathfrak{B}$ in 1 . can be chosen so that $\mathfrak{B} \supseteq \mathfrak{U}$.
3. Associative bilinear forms. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be an arbitrary Jordan algebra with $1, f$ an associative symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak{J}$. Thus $f(a, b)=f(b, a), f(a . b, c) =f(a, b . c), a, b, c \in \mathfrak{J}$. We shall now show how $f$ can be transferred to invariant forms on Inder $\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ (cf. Braun and Koecher [1]). The associativity condition is equivalent to

$$
\begin{equation*}
f\left(a R_{b}, c\right)=f\left(a, c R_{b}\right) . \tag{48}
\end{equation*}
$$

This implies

$$
\begin{equation*}
f\left(a\left[R_{b} R_{d}\right], c\right)=f\left(a, c\left[R_{d} R_{b}\right]\right) . \tag{49}
\end{equation*}
$$

Also we have

$$
f(c, d \cdot a \cdot b)=f(c \cdot b, d \cdot a)=f(c \cdot b \cdot d, a),
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
f\left(c, d\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right]\right)=f(c . b, d . a)-f(c . a, d . b)=f\left(a, b\left[R_{c} R_{d}\right]\right) . \tag{50}
\end{equation*}
$$

Let $D=\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\left[R_{a_{i}} R_{b_{i}}\right], E=\sum_{j}\left[R_{c_{j}} R_{d_{j}}\right]$. Then (50) implies that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{j} f\left(c_{j}, d_{j} D\right)=\sum_{i} f\left(a_{i}, b_{i} E\right)=\sum_{i, j} f\left(c_{j} . b_{i}, d_{j} . a_{i}\right)-\sum_{i, j} f\left(c_{j} . a_{i}, d_{j} . b_{i}\right) . \tag{51}
\end{equation*}
$$

The first of these formulas shows that the element in $\Phi$ which is given is independent of the particular representation of $D$ as $\sum\left[R_{a_{i}} R_{b_{i}}\right]$ and the second shows that it is independent of the expression of $E=\sum\left[R_{c_{j}} R_{a_{j}}\right]$. Hence

$$
\begin{equation*}
f_{d}(D, E)=\sum_{j} f\left(c_{j} d_{j} D\right)=\sum_{i} f\left(a_{i}, b_{i} E\right) \tag{52}
\end{equation*}
$$

defines a single valued function from Inder $\mathfrak{J} \times$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\Phi$. It is clear also that this is bilinear. The last expression in (51) (or (52)) shows that $f_{d}$ is symmetric:

$$
\begin{equation*}
f_{d}(D, E)=f_{d}(E, D) \tag{53}
\end{equation*}
$$

Let $F \in$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f_{d}\left(\left[\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right], F\right],\left[R_{c} R_{d}\right]\right)+f_{a}\left(\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right],\left[\left[R_{c} R_{d}\right], F\right]\right) \\
&= f_{d}\left(\left[R_{a F} R_{b}\right]+\left[R_{a} R_{b F}\right],\left[R_{c} R_{d}\right]\right)+f_{d}\left(\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right],\left[R_{c F} R_{d}\right]+\left[R_{c} R_{d F}\right]\right) \\
&= f(c \cdot b, d \cdot a F)-f(c \cdot a F, d \cdot b)+f(c \cdot b F, d \cdot a)-f(c \cdot a, d \cdot b F) \\
&+f(c F \cdot b, d \cdot a)-f(c F \cdot a, d \cdot b)+f(c \cdot b, d F \cdot a)-f(c \cdot a, d F \cdot b) \\
&= f(c \cdot b,(d \cdot a) F)+f((c \cdot b) F, d \cdot a)-f((c \cdot a) F, d \cdot b) \\
&-f(c \cdot a,(d \cdot b) F)
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $F$ has the form $F=\sum\left[R_{g_{k}} R_{h_{k}}\right]$ this is 0 by (49). It follows that

$$
\begin{equation*}
f_{d}([D F], E)=f_{d}(D,[F, E]) \tag{54}
\end{equation*}
$$

for $D, E, F \in$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$, that is, $f_{d}$ is an associative form on the Lie algebra Inder $\mathfrak{J}$.
We consider next the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ and we extend $f_{d}$ to a symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ by defining

$$
\begin{equation*}
f_{l}\left(R_{a}+D, R_{b}+E\right)=f(a, b)+f_{d}(D, E) \tag{55}
\end{equation*}
$$

for $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}, D, E \in$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{l}\left(\left[R_{a}+\right.\right. & \left.\left.D, R_{c}+F\right], R_{b}+E\right)+f_{l}\left(R_{a}+D,\left[R_{b}+E, R_{c}+F\right]\right) \\
= & f_{l}\left(\left[R_{a} R_{c}\right]+R_{a F}-R_{c D}+[D F], R_{b}+E\right) \\
& +f_{l}\left(R_{a}+D,\left[R_{b} R_{c}\right]+R_{b F}-R_{c E}+[E F]\right) \\
= & f_{d}\left(\left[R_{a} R_{c}\right]+[D F], E\right)+f(a F-c D, b) \\
& +f_{d}\left(D,\left[R_{b} R_{c}\right]+[E F]\right)+f(a, b F-c E) \\
= & f_{d}\left(\left[R_{a} R_{c}\right], E\right)+f(a F-c D, b)+f_{d}\left(D,\left[R_{b} R_{c}\right]\right)+f(a, b F-c E) \\
= & f(a, c E)+f(a F, b)-f(c D, b)+f(b, c D)+f(a, b F)-f(a, c E)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

by (49). Hence $f_{l}$ is a symmetric associative bilinear form on $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$. It is clear from the definition (55) that $R(\mathfrak{J})$ and Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ are orthogonal subspaces relative to $f_{l}$ and $f_{l}$ coincides with $f_{d}$ on Inder $\mathfrak{J}$. We have $f_{l}\left(a \triangle b, R_{c}\right)=f_{l}\left(R_{a . b}-\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right], R_{c}\right) =f(a . b, c)=f(a . c, b)=f\left(a R_{c}, b\right)$. Then $f_{l}\left(a \triangle b,\left[R_{c} R_{d}\right]\right)=-f_{l}\left(\left[(a \triangle b), R_{d}\right], R_{c}\right) =-f_{l}\left(a . d \Delta b, R_{c}\right)+f_{l}\left(a \Delta b . d, R_{c}\right) \quad($ by $\quad(25))=-f(a . d . c, b)+f(a . c, b . d) =f\left(a\left[R_{c} R_{a}\right], b\right)$. Hence we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
f_{l}(a \triangle b, L)=f(a L, b) \tag{56}
\end{equation*}
$$

for $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}, L \in \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$.
We consider finally the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{R}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \overline{\mathfrak{J}} \oplus \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$. We define for $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}, b_{i} \in \overline{\mathfrak{J}}, L_{i} \in \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$,

$$
\begin{equation*}
f_{k}\left(a_{1}+\bar{b}_{1}+L_{1}, a_{2}+\bar{b}_{2}+L_{2}\right)=f\left(a_{1}, b_{2}\right)+f\left(a_{2}, b_{1}\right)-f_{l}\left(L_{1}, L_{2}\right) . \tag{57}
\end{equation*}
$$

This is a symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ whose restriction to the subalgebra $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ coincides with $-f_{l}$. It is clear also that $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$ are totally isotropic and $\mathfrak{J}+\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$ is orthogonal to $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ relative to this form. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{k}( & {\left.\left[a_{1}+\bar{b}_{1}+L_{1}, a_{2}+\bar{b}_{2}+L_{2}\right], a_{3}+\bar{b}_{3}+L_{3}\right) } \\
= & f\left(a_{1} L_{2}-a_{2} L_{1}, b_{3}\right) \\
& +f\left(a_{3}, b_{1} \bar{L}_{2}-b_{2} \bar{L}_{1}\right)-f_{l}\left(a_{1} \Delta b_{2}, L_{3}\right)+f_{l}\left(a_{2} \Delta b_{1}, L_{3}\right) \\
& -f_{l}\left(\left[L_{1} L_{2}\right], L_{3}\right) \\
= & f\left(a_{1} L_{2}, b_{3}\right)-f\left(a_{2} L_{1}, b_{3}\right)-f\left(a_{3} L_{2}, b_{1}\right) \\
& +f\left(a_{3} L_{1}, b_{2}\right)-f\left(a_{1} L_{3}, b_{2}\right)+f\left(a_{2} L_{3}, b_{1}\right)-f_{l}\left(\left[L_{1} L_{2}\right], L_{3}\right),
\end{aligned}
$$

by (48), (49) and (56). Since $f_{l}$ is associative $f_{l}\left(\left[L_{1} L_{2}\right], L_{3}\right)=f_{l}\left(\left[L_{2} L_{3}\right], L_{1}\right)$. It follows that the right-hand side of the foregoing formula is invariant under cyclic permutation of $1,2,3$. Hence the left-hand side is invariant under cyclic permutation of $1,2,3$ and this is equivalent to the associativity of $f_{k}$ on $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$.

Now suppose the form $f$ is nondegenerate and let $L \in \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})^{\perp}$, the radical of the form $f_{l}$ on $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$. Then (56) implies that $f(a L, b)=0$ for all $a, b$. Hence $L=0$, which shows that $f_{l}$ is nondegenerate on $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$. Since $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ and $R(\mathfrak{J})$ and Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ are orthogonal relative to $f_{l}$ it is clear that Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ is a nonisotropic subspace of $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$. Since $f_{l}=f_{d}$ on Inder $\mathfrak{J}, f_{d}$ is nondegenerate. We note finally that $f_{k}$ is nondegenerate since the definition shows that $\mathfrak{J}+\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$ is not isotropic. Moreover, $\mathfrak{J}+\overline{\mathfrak{J}}$ is orthogonal to $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ and this space is not isotropic.

If $\mathfrak{J}$ is simple then we have seen that $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ is simple. Also if P is an extension of the base field then $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})_{\mathbf{P}} \cong \mathfrak{M}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbf{P}}\right)$. It follows that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is central simple then $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ is central simple. If, in addition, the dimensionality is finite and the characteristic is 0 then the Killing form of $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ is nondegenerate and every invariant symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ is a multiple of the Killing form (cf. Jacobson,

Lie Algebras, ex. 9, p. 104). It follows that in this case $f_{k}$ is a nonzero multiple of the Killing form on $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$.
9. Examples. Functorial constructions. We assume first that $\mathfrak{J}$ is finitedimensional special central simple of degree $m \geqq 3$. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ can be identified with an algebra $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where ( $\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is a finite-dimensional central simple associative algebra with involution which is perfect (§5.7). Thus $\mathfrak{U}$ and the injection mapping of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ into $\mathfrak{A}$ is a unital special universal envelope for $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and $J$ is the main involution. We have shown in §6.9 that Der $\mathfrak{J}$ consists of the set of mappings $x \rightarrow[x d], d \in \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$, the set of $J$-skew elements of $\mathfrak{A}$. We showed also that the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{J}$ having the generic norm as Lie semi-invariant coincides with Der $\mathfrak{J}+R(\mathfrak{J})$ and this is the set of mappings

$$
\begin{equation*}
S_{a}: x \rightarrow a^{J} x+x a, \quad x \in \mathfrak{J}, \quad a \in \mathfrak{A} . \tag{58}
\end{equation*}
$$

If we are not in the exceptional case in which the center of $\mathfrak{U}$ is two dimensional and the characteristic is a prime $p$ dividing $m$ then Der $\mathfrak{J}=$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J}) =\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})=R(\mathfrak{J})+[R(\mathfrak{J}), R(\mathfrak{J})]$. If $h \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $S_{h}=R_{2 h}$. Hence if $h, k \in \mathfrak{J}$ then

$$
\begin{equation*}
h \Delta k=R_{h . k}-\left[R_{h} R_{k}\right]=S_{\frac{1}{2} k h} . \tag{59}
\end{equation*}
$$

We now consider the algebra $\mathfrak{U}_{2}$ of $2 \times 2$ matrices with entries in $\mathfrak{A}$ and the involution $J_{Q}$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{2}: X \rightarrow Q^{-1} X^{J t} Q$ where $Q=\left(\begin{array}{rr}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{array}\right)$ and $X^{J}=\left(x_{i j}{ }^{J}\right)$ for $X=\left(x_{i j}\right)$. A direct calculation shows that the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)$ of $J_{Q}$-skew elements of $\mathfrak{U}_{2}$ is the set of matrices of the form

$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc}
a & k  \tag{60}\\
h & -a^{J}
\end{array}\right), \quad a \in \mathfrak{A}, \quad h, k \in \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J) .
$$

Clearly the subset of $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)$ of diagonal elements $\operatorname{diag}\left\{a,-a^{J}\right\}$ is a subalgebra isomorphic to $\mathfrak{A}^{-}$and we have the homomorphism $\operatorname{diag}\left\{a,-a^{J}\right\} \rightarrow S_{a}$ of this subalgebra onto $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{I})$. Also we have $\left[h e_{12}, k e_{21}\right]=h k e_{11}-k h e_{22} =\operatorname{diag}\left\{h k,-(h k)^{J}\right\},\left[h e_{12}, a e_{11}-a^{J} e_{22}\right]=-\left(h a^{J}+a h\right) e_{12}$ and $\left[k e_{21}, a e_{11}-a^{J} e_{22}\right] =\left(k a+a^{J} k\right) e_{21}$. It is easily seen from these formulas that we have a homomorphism of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)$ onto the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{J}+\overline{\mathfrak{J}}+R(\mathfrak{J})+$ Der $\mathfrak{J}$ defined in exercise 1 p. 328. We proceed now to define a homomorphism of a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)$ into $\mathfrak{R}(\mathfrak{J})$.
Let $\mathfrak{A}^{*}=\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$. Since $[[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}] \mathfrak{J}] \subseteq \mathfrak{J}$ in $\mathfrak{A}^{-}, \mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{A}^{-}$and this is the Lie subalgebra generated by $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $1 \in \mathfrak{J}$ and $h k=h . k +\frac{1}{2}[h, k]$ it is clear that $\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]=\mathfrak{J}^{2}$ the space spanned by the products $h k, h, k \in \mathfrak{J}$. Let $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)^{*}$ denote the subset of $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)$ of matrices of the form (60) with $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ *. One checks directly that $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)^{*}$ is a subalgebra. If $a \in \mathfrak{A}$ *
then $a=\Sigma h_{i} k_{i}, h_{i}, k_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$. Hence (59) shows that $S_{a} \in \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$. The foregoing formulas show that the mapping

$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc}
a & -\frac{1}{2} k  \tag{61}\\
h & -a^{J}
\end{array}\right) \rightarrow h+\bar{k}+S_{a}
$$

is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)^{*}$ onto $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$.
We can now determine the structure of the Lie algebras Der $\mathfrak{J}$, Inder $\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$, $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$. We have the homomorphism $d \rightarrow S_{d}(x \rightarrow[x d])$ of $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ onto Der $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ generates $\mathfrak{A}$ the kernel of this homomorphism is $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \cap \mathfrak{C}$ where $\mathfrak{C}$ is the center of $\mathfrak{A}$. If $\mathfrak{C}=\Phi$ so $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple and $J$ is of first kind, then $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \cap \mathfrak{C}=0$ and Der $\mathfrak{J} \cong \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$. Also in this case Der $\mathfrak{J}=$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ and if $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of the base field then $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{m}, J_{1}\right)$ where either $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi$ or $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a split quaternion algebra with involution. Then $(\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J})_{\Omega} =(\text { Inder } \mathfrak{J})_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}} \cong \mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{m}, J_{1}\right)$ is a simple Lie algebra of type $B$ if $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi$ and $m$ is odd, of type $D$ if $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi$ and $m$ is even and of type $C$ if $\mathfrak{D}$ is quaternion (Jacobson, Lie Algebras, pp. 298-302 and Seligman, Modular Lie Algebras, Chapter III). If $\mathfrak{A}$ is not simple then $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{J}$ where $\mathfrak{B}$ is a central simple ideal and $\mathfrak{J} \cong \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \cong \mathfrak{B} .^{+}$Then Der $\mathfrak{J} \cong \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J) /(\mathfrak{C} \cap \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)) \cong \mathfrak{B}^{-} / \Phi$. Thus in this case Der $\mathfrak{J}$ is a Lie algebra of type $\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{I}}$. We have Der $\mathfrak{J}=$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ unless $p \mid m$. In the latter case it is easily seen that Inder $\mathfrak{I} \cong\left[\mathfrak{B}^{-}, \mathfrak{B}^{-}\right] / \Phi$. The last case we have to consider is that in which $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple but not central simple, that is, $J$ is an involution of second kind. Then the center $\mathrm{P}=\Phi(i), i^{2}=\alpha \in \Phi$ and $i^{J}=-i$ and Der $\mathfrak{J} \cong \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J) / \Phi i$. Unless the characteristic is a prime $p$ dividing $m$, Der $\mathfrak{J}=$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$. If $p \mid m$ then Inder $\mathfrak{J} \cong[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J), \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)] / \Phi i$. The Lie algebras $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J) / \Phi i$ are of type $\mathrm{A}_{\text {II }}$. It is well known that the Lie algebras of types $A, B, C, D$ which we obtained here for Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ are simple except for the case in which $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\Omega_{4}, J_{1}\right)$ (loc. cit. above).

We consider next the Lie algebras $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$. We have the homomorphism $a \rightarrow S_{a}$ of $\mathfrak{A}^{-}$onto $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$. Since $S_{a}=0$ implies $1 S_{a}=a^{J}+a=0$, the kernel of the homomorphism is $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \cap \mathfrak{C}$. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is central simple ( $J$ of first kind) then $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \cap \mathfrak{C}=0$ and $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{I}) \cong \mathfrak{A}-$. If $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{J}$ where $\mathfrak{B}$ is an ideal then $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \cap \mathfrak{C}=\Phi(1,-1)$ so $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \mathfrak{A}^{-} / \Phi(1,-1)$. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple and $\mathfrak{C}$ is a quadratic extension field $\Phi(i)$ with $i^{J}=-i$ then $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \mathfrak{A}-/ \Phi i$. We have $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J}) =\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{I})$ unless $\mathfrak{C} \supset \Phi$ and the characteristic is a prime $p$ dividing $m$. It is easy to see that in this case $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong\left(\left[\mathfrak{B}^{-}, \mathfrak{B}^{-}\right] \oplus\left[\left(\mathfrak{B}^{J}\right)^{-},\left(\mathfrak{B}^{J}\right)^{-}\right] / \Phi(1,-1)\right.$ if $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{J}$ and $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong\left[\mathfrak{U}^{-}, \mathfrak{A}^{-}\right] / \Phi i$ if $\mathfrak{U}$ is simple and $J$ is of second kind.

We now consider the algebras $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ and we obtain first an improved description of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)^{*}$. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is central simple (equivalently, $J$ is of first kind) then the proof of Theorem 6.9 shows that $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)=[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{I}]$. Since $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{J} +\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ we have $\mathfrak{A}^{*}=\mathfrak{A}$. Hence in this case

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)^{*}=\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right) \tag{62}
\end{equation*}
$$

We shall show next that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is not central simple then

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)^{*}=\left[\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right), \mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)\right] . \tag{63}
\end{equation*}
$$

We note first that if $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{A}, h_{i}, k_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$ then

$$
\left[\left(\begin{array}{cc}
a_{1} & k_{1}  \tag{64}\\
h_{1} & -a_{1}{ }^{J}
\end{array}\right),\left(\begin{array}{cc}
a_{2} & k_{2} \\
h_{2} & -a_{2}{ }^{J}
\end{array}\right)\right]=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
a & k \\
h & -a^{J}
\end{array}\right)
$$

where

$$
\begin{align*}
& a=\left[a_{1} a_{2}\right]+k_{1} h_{2}-k_{2} h_{1}, \\
& h=h_{1} a_{2}+a_{2}^{J} h_{1}-h_{2} a_{1}-a_{1}^{J} h_{2},  \tag{65}\\
& k=a_{1} k_{2}+k_{2} a_{1}^{J}-a_{2} k_{1}-k_{1} a_{2}^{J} .
\end{align*}
$$

These formulas show that $\left[\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right), \mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)\right]$ is the set of matrices of the form (60) in which $h, k \in \mathfrak{J}$ and $a \in[\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A}]+\mathfrak{A}^{*}, \mathfrak{A}^{*}=\mathfrak{J}^{2}=\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$. Hence $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)^{*} \subseteq\left[\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right), \mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)\right]$ and equality holds if and only if $[\mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{A}] \subseteq \mathfrak{A}^{*}$. Since $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ and $[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J), \mathfrak{J}] \subseteq \mathfrak{J},[\mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{A}] \subseteq \mathfrak{A}$ * if and only if $[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J), \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)] \subseteq[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$. Now this holds if $\mathfrak{A}$ is not central simple. It is enough to prove this for $\Phi$ algebraically closed. Then $\mathfrak{A}=\Phi_{m} \oplus \Phi_{m}$ and $J$ can be taken to the involution $\left(b_{1}, b_{2}{ }^{t}\right) \rightarrow\left(b_{2}, b_{1}{ }^{t}\right), b_{i} \in \Phi_{m}$. We have

$$
\left[\left(b, b^{t}\right),\left(c, c^{t}\right)\right]=\left[\left(b,-b^{t}\right),\left(c,-c^{t}\right)\right] .
$$

Hence $[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J), \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)]=[\mathfrak{I} \mathfrak{J}]$ and so (63) holds.
The kernel of the homomorphism (61) of $\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)^{*}$ onto $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ is the set of matrices $\delta 1=\operatorname{diag}\{\delta, \delta\}$ where $\delta \in \mathfrak{A}^{*} \cap \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \cap \mathfrak{C}, \mathfrak{C}$ the center of $\mathfrak{A}$. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is central simple the kernel is 0 and $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong \mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)$, by (62). If $\mathfrak{A}$ is not central simple, then $\mathfrak{A} * \cap \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)=(\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]) \cap \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)=[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]=[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J), \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)]$. Hence the kernel of (61) in this case is $[\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J), \mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)] \cap \mathfrak{C}$. As in the proof of Theorem 6.9, one sees that this is 0 unless $p \mid m$ in which case the intersection is one dimensional. Accordingly, we have $\mathfrak{R}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong\left[\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right), \mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)\right]$ if $p \nmid m$ and $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong\left[\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right), \mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)\right] / \Phi(1,-1)$ if $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{B}^{J}$ and $p \mid m$ and $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong\left[\mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right), \mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)\right] / \Phi i$ if $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple, $J$ of second kind, $\mathfrak{C}=\Phi(i)$, $i^{J}=-i$ and $p \mid m$. We remark that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is not simple then the isomorphism indicated can be replaced by $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong\left[\mathfrak{B}^{-}, \mathfrak{B}^{-}\right]$or $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J}) \cong\left[\mathfrak{B}^{-}, \mathfrak{B}^{-}\right] / \Phi 1$ according as $p \nmid m$ or $p \mid m$. We remark also that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is central simple and $J$ is of orthogonal (symplectic) type in the sense that $\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}, J\right) \cong\left(\Omega_{m}, J_{1}\right)\left(\cong\left(\mathfrak{Q}_{m}, J_{1}\right), \mathfrak{Q}\right.$ quaternion with standard involution) then the involution $J_{Q}$ in $\mathfrak{A}_{2}$ is of symplectic (orthogonal) type. This is easily seen, for example, by calculating $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{S}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{2}, J_{Q}\right)$.

We close our discussion of the Lie algebras Inder $\mathfrak{J}$, Der $\mathfrak{J}$ etc. by noting that the mappings $\mathfrak{J} \rightarrow$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ etc. are not satisfactory from the category point of
view since a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ into $\mathfrak{J}_{2}$ does not always give rise to one between Inder $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ into Inder $\mathfrak{J}_{2}$ etc. This is the case if the homomorphism is surjective but may not be so otherwise. We shall now indicate some modifications of the Lie algebra constructions which are free of this defect. We restrict the considerations to Jordan algebras with 1. Let $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ be the unital universal multiplication algebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ and consider $\mathfrak{J}$ as imbedded in $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ in the usual way. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is subsystem of the Lie triple system $\left(U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})^{-}\right)^{(2)}$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]=\mathfrak{J} \oplus[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ is the subalgebra of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$generated by $\mathfrak{J}$. Also we have the subalgebra [JJ]. We have the canonical homomorphism of $[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ onto Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $\Sigma\left[a_{i} b_{i}\right] \rightarrow \Sigma\left[R_{a_{i}} R_{b_{i}}\right]$ and of $\mathfrak{J} \oplus[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ onto $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $a \rightarrow R_{a}$. We can replace the Lie algebras Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ by $[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ and $\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ respectively. It is clear that a homomorphism of the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ into the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}_{2}$ sending $1 \rightarrow 1$ gives rise to a unique homomorphism of $\left[\mathfrak{J}_{1} \mathfrak{J}_{1}\right]$ into $\left[\mathfrak{J}_{2} \mathfrak{J}_{2}\right]$ and of $\mathfrak{J}_{1}+\left[\mathfrak{J}_{1} \mathfrak{J}_{1}\right]$ into $\mathfrak{J}_{2}+\left[\mathfrak{J}_{2} \mathfrak{J}_{2}\right]$. We obtain in this way functors from the category of Jordan algebras with 1, where the morphisms are homomorphisms preserving 1, into the category of Lie algebras.

We can also make a similar modification of the construction of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$. Here we let $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{2}$ be vector spaces isomorphic to $\mathfrak{J}$ under the mappings $a \rightarrow a_{l}, \quad i=1,2$. We consider the space $\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2} \oplus(\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}])$, where $\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ is the subspace of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ defined in the last paragraph, and make this into an algebra with composition [ , ] such that

$$
\begin{align*}
{\left[a_{1}+b_{2}+l, c_{1}+d_{2}+m\right]=} & (a M)_{1}-(c L)_{1}+\left(b M^{\varepsilon}\right)_{2}-\left(d L^{\varepsilon}\right)_{2}  \tag{66}\\
& +(a \cdot d-[a d]-b \cdot c+[b c]+[l m])
\end{align*}
$$

where $a, b, c, d \in \mathfrak{J}, l, m \in \mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ and $l \rightarrow L, m \rightarrow M$ in the canonical homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ onto $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$. If we have a homomorphism $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into a second Jordan algebra mapping $1 \rightarrow 1$ then $a_{1}+b_{2}+l \rightarrow a_{1}{ }_{1}+b^{\eta}{ }_{2}+l^{\eta}$, where $l \rightarrow l^{\eta}$ is the homomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ such that $a \rightarrow a^{\eta}$, is a Lie algebra homomorphism. In this way we obtain another functor from the category of Jordan algebras with 1 into the category of Lie algebras.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ the Jordan algebra of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{B}$ with $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}>1$. Let $\mathfrak{Y}$ be a three-dimensional vector space with bilinear form $g$ such that the matrix of $g$ relative to a basis $(u, v, w)$ is

$$
\left[\begin{array}{rrr}
0 & 1 & 0 \\
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & -1
\end{array}\right]
$$

Let $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{B} \oplus \mathfrak{Y}$ and define a symmetric bilinear form $h$ on $\mathfrak{W}$ so that $\mathfrak{V} \perp \mathfrak{V}$ and $h=f$ on $\mathfrak{V}$ and $h=g$ on $\mathfrak{Y}$. Show that $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ is isomorphic to the Lie algebra of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{W}$ which are skew relative to $h$. Use this to prove that the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{S}\left(\Phi_{n}, J_{1}\right)$ is central simple if $n \geqq 5$.
2. Use the results on $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ in the text to prove that the symplectic Lie algebra $\mathfrak{S}\left(\Phi_{2 m}, J_{S}\right)$ where $J_{S}$ is the involution $X \rightarrow S^{-1} X^{t} S, S=\operatorname{diag}\{Q, Q, \cdots, Q\}$, $Q=\left(\begin{array}{rr}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{array}\right)$ is simple if $m \geqq 3$.
3. Use the same method to show that $\left[\Phi_{m}^{-}, \Phi_{m}^{-}\right]$is simple if $m \geqq 3$ and $m$ is not divisible by the characteristic and that $\left[\Phi_{m}^{-}, \Phi_{m}^{-}\right] / \Phi 1$ is simple if $m \geqq 3$ and is divisible by the characteristic $p$ of $\Phi$.
10. Associator nilpotent Jordan algebras. If $\mathfrak{L}$ is a Lie algebra we shall write

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[a_{1} a_{2} \cdots a_{N}\right]^{\prime}=\left[\left[\cdots\left[\left[a_{1} a_{2}\right] a_{3}\right] \cdots\right] a_{N}\right], \quad a_{i} \in \mathfrak{L} . \tag{67}
\end{equation*}
$$

We recall that $\mathfrak{L}$ is called nilpotent if there exists a positive integer $N$ such that every $\left[a_{1} a_{2} \cdots a_{N}\right]^{\prime}=0, a_{i} \in \mathfrak{L}$. The minimum $N$ with this property is called the index of nilpotency. We have, for $1<k+1<N$,

$$
\begin{align*}
{\left[\left[a_{1} \cdots a_{k}\right]^{\prime},\left[a_{k+1} \cdots a_{N}\right]^{\prime}\right]=} & {\left[\left[a_{1} \cdots a_{k}\right]^{\prime},\left[\left[a_{k+1} \cdots a_{N-1}\right]^{\prime} a_{N}\right]\right] } \\
= & {\left[\left[\left[a_{1} \cdots a_{k}\right]^{\prime},\left[a_{k+1} \cdots a_{N-1}\right]^{\prime}\right] a_{N}\right] }  \tag{68}\\
& -\left[\left[a_{1} \cdots a_{k} a_{N}\right]^{\prime},\left[a_{k+1} \cdots a_{N-1}\right]^{\prime}\right] .
\end{align*}
$$

This implies that any product of $N a_{i} \in \mathfrak{L}$ in any association is a linear combination of the normalized products $\left[a_{1} \cdots a_{N}\right]^{\prime}$. Hence any such product is 0 if $\mathfrak{L}$ is nilpotent of index $N$. If $S$ is a set of generators for a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ then (68) implies also that every element of $\mathfrak{L}$ is a linear combination of normalized products $\left[s_{1} \cdots s_{r}\right]^{\prime}, s_{i} \in S$. Hence it is clear (again using (68)) that $\mathfrak{L}$ is nilpotent if there exists an integer $N$ such that every $\left[s_{1} s_{2} \cdots s_{N}\right]^{\prime}=0, s_{i} \in S$.

We shall call a Lie triple system $\mathfrak{T}$ nilpotent if there exists a positive odd integer $M$ such that every product

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left[\left[\cdots\left[\left[a_{1} a_{2} a_{3}\right] a_{4} a_{5}\right] \cdots\right] a_{M-1} a_{M}\right], \quad a_{i} \in \mathfrak{T} \tag{69}
\end{equation*}
$$

is 0 . The minimal $M$ for this is the index of nilpotency. If $\mathfrak{L}$ is a Lie algebra then $\mathcal{L}$ is Lie triple system $\mathfrak{L}^{(2)}$ relative to the composition $[a b c]=[[c a] b]=[c a b]^{\prime}$. It follows that (69) is a normalized product $\left[a_{i_{1}} \cdots a_{i_{M}}\right]^{\prime}$ for some permutation ( $i_{1} \cdots i_{M}$ ) of ( $1, \cdots, M$ ) and conversely any such normalized product can be expressed in the form (69). Hence it is clear that $\mathfrak{L}$ is nilpotent if and only if $\mathfrak{L}^{(2)}$ is nilpotent. It is clear also that if $\mathfrak{T}$ is a subsystem of $\mathfrak{L}^{(2)}$ which generates $\mathfrak{L}$, so that $\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{T}+[\mathfrak{T} \mathfrak{T}]$, then $\mathfrak{L}$ is nilpotent if and only if $\mathfrak{T}$ is nilpotent.

We now define a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ to be associator nilpotent if the associator

Lie triple system $\mathfrak{J}$ (with $[a b c]=[a, b, c]$ ) is nilpotent. In $\mathfrak{J}$ we have $[x, a, b] =x\left(R_{a} R_{b}-R_{a, b}\right)$ and we define

$$
\begin{equation*}
R_{a, b}=R_{a} R_{b}-R_{a, b} . \tag{70}
\end{equation*}
$$

Then it is clear that the definition of associator nilpotency of $\mathfrak{J}$ is equivalent to the existence of a positive integer $k$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
R_{a_{1}, b_{1}} R_{a_{2}, b_{2}} \cdots R_{a_{k} b_{k}}=0 \tag{71}
\end{equation*}
$$

for all $a_{i}, b_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$.
It is clear that any subalgebra and any homomorphic image of an associator nilpotent Lie algebra is associator nilpotent. Also since the condition for associator nilpotency is multilinear, $\mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent if and only if $\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbf{P}}$ is associator nilpotent for any extension field P of the base field of $\mathfrak{J}$. If $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element and $\Gamma$ is a subfield of the center of $\mathfrak{J}$ containing 1 then $\mathfrak{J}$ can be regarded as an algebra over $\Gamma$. It is clear also that $\mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent if and only if $\mathfrak{J} / \Gamma$ is associator nilpotent. We shall now determine the structure of finite-dimensional associator nilpotent Jordan algebras with 1. For this purpose we shall say that a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 is purely inseparable if $\mathfrak{J}$ contains a nil ideal $\mathfrak{N}$ such that $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{N}$ is an (associative) purely inseparable (algebraic) field over $\Phi$. If the base field $\Phi$ is perfect (for example, if the characteristic is 0 ) then the condition is that $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{N} \cong \Phi$, which is equivalent to: $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1+\mathfrak{N}$. We recall that a finite-dimensional nil algebra is nilpotent. Hence in this case the word "nil" in the definition of a purely inseparable Jordan algebra can be replaced by "nilpotent." We now prove the following

Lemma 1. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional purely inseparable Jordan algebra with 1 and $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of the base field $\Phi$ then $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}=\Omega 1+\mathfrak{P}$ where $\mathfrak{P}$ is a nil (nilpotent) ideal.

Proof. We note first that if $\mathrm{P} / \Phi$ is a purely inseparable field then $\mathrm{P}_{\Omega}=\Omega 1+\mathfrak{M}$ where $\mathfrak{M}$ is the nil radical (= ideal of nilpotent elements) of the commutative associative algebra $\mathrm{P}_{\Omega}$. This is trivial if the characteristic is 0 . If the characteristic is $p \neq 0$ and $a \in \mathrm{P}$ then $a^{p^{e}}=\alpha 1, \alpha \in \Phi$, for some positive integer $e$. Now there exists a $\beta \in \Omega$ such that $\beta^{p^{e}}=\alpha$. Then in $\mathrm{P}_{\Omega}$ we have $a=\beta 1+z$ where $z=a-\beta 1$ satisfies $z^{p^{e}}=a^{p^{e}}-\beta^{p^{e}} 1=0$. It follows that every element of $\mathrm{P}_{\Omega}$ has the form $\gamma 1+w, \gamma \in \Omega, w$ nilpotent. This means that $\mathrm{P}_{\Omega}=\Omega 1+\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M}$ the nil radical. Now suppose $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1 which is purely inseparable over $\Phi$. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ has a nil ideal $\mathfrak{N}$ such that $\mathbf{P} \equiv \mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{N}$ is a purely inseparable field. Then $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega} / \mathfrak{N}_{\Omega}$, which can be identified with $\mathrm{P}_{\Omega}$, has the form $\Omega 1+\mathfrak{M}$ where $\mathfrak{M}$ is the nil radical. Then we have an ideal $\mathfrak{P}$ in $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ such that $\mathfrak{P} / \mathfrak{N}_{\Omega}=\mathfrak{M}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega} / \mathfrak{P} \cong \Omega$. Since $\mathfrak{N}$ is nilpotent $\mathfrak{N}_{\Omega}$ is nilpotent and hence nil and consequently $\mathfrak{P}$ is a nil ideal in $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$. Then $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}=\Omega 1+\mathfrak{P}$.

We shall call an element $a$ of a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1 separable if the subalgebra $\Phi[a]$ generated by $a$ and 1 is separable. We remark that if $e$ is an idempotent then $e$ is separable and if $a$ is separable then $\Phi[a]_{\Omega} =\Omega e_{1} \oplus \Omega e_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \Omega e_{r}$ where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents such that $\sum e_{\imath}=1$.

Lemma 2. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional associator nilpotent Jordan algebra with 1 then every separable element of $\mathfrak{J}$ and in particular every idempotent is contained in the center.

Proof. Since $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ is associator nilpotent and the center of $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ is $\mathfrak{C}_{\Omega}$, C the center of $\mathfrak{J}$, it is sufficient to prove that idempotents are central ( $=$ contained in the center). Hence let $e$ be an idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}$ and let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)+\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)+\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ be the Peirce decomposition relative to $e$. Put $f=1-e$. If $a \in \mathfrak{I}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ then $4[a, e, f]=a$. Iteration of this $k$ times gives

$$
2^{2 k}[\cdots[[a, e, f], e, f] \cdots e, f]=a .
$$

Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent $a=0$. Thus $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}=0$ and $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{1}$. This implies that $e \in \mathfrak{C}$.

We can now establish the following criterion.
Theorem 18. A necessary and sufficient condition that a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 is associator nilpotent is that $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{s}$ where $\mathfrak{I}_{i}$ is an ideal which contains a separable subfield $\Gamma_{i}$ of its center containing the identity $1_{i}$ of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ such that $\mathfrak{J}_{i} / \Gamma_{i}$ is purely inseparable.

Proof. To prove the sufficiency it is enough to show that any finite-dimensional purely inseparable Jordan algebra (with 1) is associator nilpotent. By Lemma 1, we have $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}=\Omega 1+\mathfrak{P}, \Omega$ the algebraic closure of $\Phi, \mathfrak{P}$ a nil ideal. Then any higher associator of the form (69) with $a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ equals an associator of the same form in elements $z_{i} \in \mathfrak{P}$. Since $\mathfrak{P}$ is finite-dimensional nil it is nilpotent. Hence for a suitable integer $M$ all the associators in which the $a_{i}=z_{i} \in \mathfrak{P}$ are 0 . Thus $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ and hence $\mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent. Conversely, assume $\mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent and write $1=\Sigma_{1}^{s} e_{i}$ where the $e_{i}$ are primitive idempotents. By Lemma 2, the $e_{i}$ are central so if $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{i \leqq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ is the Peirce decomposition relative to the $e_{i}$ then the $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}=0$ for $i \neq j$. Then $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{1}^{s} \mathfrak{J}_{i}$ where $\mathfrak{J}_{i}=\mathfrak{J}_{i i}$ is an ideal. It suffices to show that the $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ have the property stated in the theorem. We may therefore simplify the notation and assume 1 is primitive. Since we can lift idempotents from $\mathfrak{J} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ to $\mathfrak{J}$ (Lemma 2 of §3.7) it is clear that the identity is a primitive idempotent in $\mathfrak{S}=\mathfrak{J} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J}$. Since $\mathfrak{S}$ is semisimple and 1 is primitive in this algebra it follows from Theorem 4.3 that $\mathfrak{S}$ (which contains no absolute zero divisors by Theorem 5.7) is a division algebra. Now let $\Gamma$ be the set of separable elements of $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\Gamma$ is contained in the center of $\mathfrak{J}$. If $\gamma \in \Gamma$ then $\Phi[\gamma]$ is a separable associative
commutative algebra with only one nonzero idempotent. Hence $\Phi[\gamma]$ is a field. If $\gamma_{1}, \gamma_{2} \in \Gamma$ then the subalgebra $\Phi\left[\gamma_{1}, \gamma_{2}\right]$ generated by $\gamma_{1}$ and $\gamma_{2}$ is a homomorphic image of $\Phi\left[\gamma_{1}\right] \otimes \Phi\left[\gamma_{2}\right]$ which is a direct sum of fields. Since 1 is primitive in $\Phi\left[\gamma_{1}, \gamma_{2}\right]$ this is a field. Hence $\Gamma$ is a separable subfield of the center containing 1 and we may regard $\mathfrak{J}$ as an algebra over $\Gamma$. Then $\mathfrak{J} / \Gamma$ has the same properties as $\mathfrak{J}$ and in addition every element of $\mathfrak{J} / \Gamma$ which is separable (over $\Gamma$, hence over $\Phi$ ) is contained in $\Gamma$. To simplify the notation we assume that $\Gamma=\Phi$. Now let P be the center of $\mathfrak{S}=\mathfrak{J} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ and consider $\mathfrak{S}$ as an algebra over P. Then $(\mathfrak{S} / \mathrm{P})_{\Omega}$, for $\Omega$ the algebraic closure of P , is simple. Since this algebra is also associator nilpotent the result established shows that this is a division algebra. Since $\Omega$ is algebraically closed we must have $(\mathfrak{S} / \mathrm{P})_{\Omega}=\Omega 1$. Hence $\mathfrak{S} / \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{P}$, so $\mathfrak{J} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ is a field. We claim that this is purely inseparable.
