Otherwise, we have an $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ such that the minimum polynomial $\phi(\lambda)$ of $a+\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ is separable of degree $>1$. Then the minimum polynomial of $a$ is of the form $\phi(\lambda)^{r}$. It follows that $\Phi[a]$ contains an element $b$ whose minimum polynomial is $\phi(\lambda)$ (Jacobson, Lie Algebras, p. 96, where the proof given for characteristic 0 is valid for $\phi(\lambda)$ separable). This contradicts the fact that all the separable elements of $\mathfrak{J}$ are contained in $\Phi$ and completes the proof of the theorem.

If $\Phi$ is a perfect field then the condition established reduces to the following
Corollary 1. If $\Phi$ is perfect then a necessary and sufficient condition that a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ with 1 is associator nilpotent is that $\mathfrak{J}$ is a direct sum of ideals $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ which have the form $\mathfrak{J}_{i}=\Gamma_{i} \oplus \mathfrak{N}_{i}$ where $\Gamma_{i}$ is a subfield of the center and $\mathfrak{N}_{i}$ is a nil ideal.

We shall also state explicitly the following useful
Corollary 2. If $\Phi$ is algebraically closed then a necessary and sufficient condition that a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ with 1 is associator nilpotent is that $\mathfrak{J}$ is a direct sum of ideals $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ of the form $\mathfrak{J}_{i}=\Phi 1_{i}+\mathfrak{N}_{i}$, where $1_{i}$ is the identity of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ and $\mathfrak{N}_{i}$ is a nil ideal.

We shall derive next an analogue of Engel's theorem in the theory of Lie algebras. We recall that for (abstract) finite-dimensional Lie algebras this asserts that $\mathfrak{L}$ is nilpotent if and only if ad $a$ is nilpotent for every $a \in \mathfrak{L}$. We now note that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent then, by (71), $R_{a, b}$ is nilpotent for every $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$. In particular $R_{a, a}$ is nilpotent for every $a$. We shall now call an element $a$ of a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ associator nilpotent in $\mathfrak{J}$ if $J_{a} \equiv R_{a, a}$ is a nilpotent linear transformation in $\mathfrak{J}$. Thus $a$ is associator nilpotent in $\mathfrak{J}$ if and only if there exists an integer $N$ such that $[[\cdots[[x, a, a], a, a] \cdots], a, a]=0$ for all $x \in \mathfrak{J}$, where the number of $a$ 's displayed in our expression is $2 N$. We prove first the following

Lemma 3 (Schafer). If $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent then every linear transformation $R_{a^{\cdot i}, a^{\cdot j}}, i, j=0,1,2, \cdots$ is nilpotent.

Proof. Since we are defining $a^{\cdot 0}=1$ and $R_{a^{\cdot i}, a^{\cdot j}}=R_{a^{\cdot i}} R_{a^{\cdot j}}-R_{a^{\cdot i+j}}$ the result is clear if $i$ or $j=0$. Hence assume $i, j>0$. Since the operators $R_{a^{\cdot i}, a^{\cdot j}}$ are contained in the commutative algebra of linear transformations $\mathfrak{A}$ generated by $\mathbf{1}, \boldsymbol{R}_{\boldsymbol{a}}, \boldsymbol{R}_{\boldsymbol{a} \cdot \mathbf{2}}$ our result will follow by showing that every $R_{a^{\cdot i}, a^{\cdot j},} i, j>0$, has the form $T_{i j} J_{a}$ where $T_{i j} \in \mathfrak{A}$. We prove this by induction on $h=i+j$. For this we note that the basic Jordan identity $R_{c} R_{a . b}-R_{c} R_{b} R_{a}+R_{b} R_{a . c}-R_{a . c . b}+R_{a} R_{b . c}-R_{a} R_{b} R_{c} =0$ can be written in terms of the operators $R_{u, v}$ as $R_{b, a, c}=R_{c} R_{b, a}+R_{a} R_{b, c}$. Since $R_{a^{\cdot i}, a^{\cdot j}}=R_{a^{\cdot j}, a^{\cdot i}}$ and $R_{a, a}=J_{a}$ it is enough to show that $R_{a^{\cdot i}, a^{\cdot j+1}}=T_{i, j+1} J_{a}$ assuming $R_{a^{\cdot k}, a^{\cdot l}}=T_{k, l} J_{a}$ for all $k, l>0$ such that $k, l>0$ and $k+l \leqq i+j$. Since we have $R_{a^{\cdot i}, a^{\cdot j+1}}=R_{a^{\cdot j}} R_{a^{\cdot i}, a}+R_{a} R_{a^{\cdot i}, a^{\cdot j}}$ the result is clear.

We can now prove the following analogue of Engel's theorem in the theory of Lie algebras.

Theorem 19. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent if and only if every element of $\mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent.

Proof. The necessity of the condition has been noted above. Conversely, assume every element of $\mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent. We show first that this implies the key result, Lemma 2, used in the proof of Theorem 18, namely, that every separable element $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ is in the center. Let $\Omega$ be the algebraic closure of $\Phi$. Then, by Schafer's lemma, $R_{a^{\cdot i}, a^{\cdot j}}$ is nilpotent in $\mathfrak{J}$ for all $i, j=0,1,2, \cdots$. Hence every $R_{a^{\cdot i}, a^{\cdot j}}$ is nilpotent in $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$. In $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ we have the orthogonal idempotents $e_{k} \in \Omega[a]$ such that $a=\sum \alpha_{i} e_{i}, \alpha_{i} \in \Omega$, and $\sum e_{k}=1$. Then $R_{e_{k}, e_{l}}$ is a linear combination of the operators $R_{a^{\cdot i}, a^{\cdot j}}$. Since these are nilpotent and commute, $R_{e_{k}, e_{i}}$ is nilpotent. Let $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}=\Sigma_{k \leqq l} \mathfrak{J}_{k l}$ be the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ relative to the $e_{k}$. If $k \neq l$, $\mathfrak{J}_{k l}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{k}, e_{l}}=\mathfrak{J} R_{e_{k}} R_{e_{l}}=\mathfrak{J} R_{e_{k}, e_{l}}$ since $R_{e_{k}, e_{l}}=R_{e_{k}} R_{e_{l}}$. Since $R_{e_{k}, e_{l}}$ is nilpotent we have $\mathfrak{J}_{k l}=0$. Then the $e_{k}$ are in the center of $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ and $a$ is in the center of $\mathfrak{J}$. We note next that if $n=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}$ and $\Phi$ is infinite then the hypothesis states that the polynomial mapping $a \rightarrow J_{a}{ }^{n}=R_{a, a}{ }^{n}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ is 0 . It follows that the polynomial mapping $a \rightarrow J_{a}{ }^{n}$ of $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ is 0 . This shows that for infinite base fields the hypothesis carries over to $\mathfrak{J}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$. This and the result noted permits us to carrỳ over word for word the necessity part of the proof of Theorem 18 to show that $\mathfrak{J}$ has the structure given in Theorem 18. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent by this theorem. Now assume $\Phi$ finite. Then the necessity proof of Theorem 18 carries over to show that it is sufficient to prove the result with the added conditions that $\mathfrak{J} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ is a division algebra and every element of $\mathfrak{J}$ which is separable is contained in $\Phi 1$. We claim that in this case $\mathfrak{J} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J} \cong \Phi$. Otherwise, let $\bar{a}=a+\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J} \notin \Phi 1$. Then the minimum polynomial $\mu(\lambda)$ of $\bar{a}$ is of degree $\geqq 1$ and this is irreducible. Moreover, since $\Phi$ is perfect $\mu(\lambda)$ is separable. Then the lifting property noted in the last part of the proof of Theorem 18 shows that we may assume that $\mu(a)=0$. Then $a$ is a separable element of $\mathfrak{J}$ and so this is contained in $\Phi 1$. This contradicts the assumption that $\bar{a} \notin \Phi 1$. Hence $\mathfrak{J} / \mathrm{rad} \mathfrak{J} \cong \Phi$ and $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1+\operatorname{rad} \mathfrak{J}$ so this is associator nilpotent by the sufficiency part of Theorem 18.

We now consider the unital universal multiplication envelope $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ a Jordan algebra with 1 and we imbed $\mathfrak{J}$ as a subspace of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ as usual. We shall be interested in the Lie algebra $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$, its subalgebra $\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ generated by $\mathfrak{J}$ and the subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}(\mathfrak{J})$ of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$generated by the elements $a b-a . b$, $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$. Since $[a, b]=(a b-a . b)-(b a-b . a)$ it is clear that $\mathfrak{A}(\mathfrak{J}) \supseteq[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ which is also a subalgebra of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$. Since $[a, b, c]=[a b c]=[[c a] b]$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ it is clear that the Lie triple system structure of $\mathfrak{J}$ given by the associator composition coincides with that given as a subsystem of $\left(U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})^{-}\right)^{(2)}$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent if and only if $\mathfrak{J}$ as subsystem of $\left(U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})^{-}\right)^{(2)}$ is a nilpotent Lie triple system and this is the case if and only if the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ is nilpotent. Hence we have the equivalence of the first two conditions in the following theorem.

Theorem 20. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with $1, U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ the unital universal multiplication envelope of $\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{A}(\mathfrak{J})$ the subalgebra of the Lie algebra $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$generated $b y$ the elements $a b-a . b, a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then the following conditions are equivalent: (1) $\mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent. (2) $\mathfrak{J}+[\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{J}]$ is a nilpotent Lie algebra. (3) $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$is nilpotent. These imply: (4) $\mathfrak{A}(\mathfrak{J})$ is nilpotent.

Proof. Since we have noted the equivalence of (1) and (2) and since a subalgebra of a nilpotent Lie algebra is nilpotent everything will follow if we can show that (1) implies (3). Also we may assume the base field $\Phi$ is algebraically closed. Then by Corollary 2 to Theorem 18, $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{s}$ where the $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ are ideals and $\mathfrak{J}_{i}=\Phi 1_{i}+\mathfrak{N}_{i}$ where $1_{i}$ is the identity of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ and $\mathfrak{N}_{i}$ is a nil ideal. By the extension of Theorem 2.16 from two to $s$ components (which is immediate), $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is a direct sum of ideals which are isomorphic to the algebras $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right)$ and the algebras $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right) \otimes S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{j}\right)$ where $i \neq j$ and $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right)$ is the special unital universal envelope of $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$. By Theorem 5.2 and the remarks following it, $\mathfrak{N}_{i}$ generates a nilpotent ideal $\Re_{i}$ in $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right)$ and the image of $\mathfrak{N}_{i}$ in $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right)$ generates a nilpotent ideal $\mathfrak{S}_{i}$ in $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right)$. By Theorem 2.1 (5) and 2.11 (4), $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right) / \Re_{i} \cong U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i} / \Re_{i}\right) \cong U_{1}\left(\Phi 1_{i}\right) \cong \Phi$ and $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right) / \mathfrak{S}_{i} \cong S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i} / \mathfrak{N}_{i}\right) \cong S_{1}\left(\Phi 1_{i}\right) \cong \Phi$. Hence $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right)=\Phi 1 +\Re_{i}$ and $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right)=\Phi 1+\mathfrak{S}_{i}$ where $\Re_{i}$ and $\mathfrak{S}_{i}$ are nilpotent ideals. Then $S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{i}\right) \otimes S_{1}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{j}\right)=\Phi 1+\mathfrak{S}_{1 j}$ where $\mathfrak{S}_{i j}$ is a nilpotent ideal. Now it is clear that if $\mathfrak{E}$ is an associative algebra with 1 such that $\mathfrak{E}=\Phi 1+\mathfrak{M}$ where $\mathfrak{M}$ is a nilpotent ideal, then $\mathfrak{E}^{-}$is nilpotent Lie algebra. Since we have shown that $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is a direct sum of ideals having this structure it is clear that $U_{1}(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$is nilpotent.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be finite-dimensional associator nilpotent with 1 . Show that $U(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$ is nilpotent.
2. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be finite-dimensional Jordan with 1. Suppose the subalgebra of
$U(\mathfrak{J})^{-}$generated by the elements $a b-a, b$ is nilpotent. Does this imply that $\mathfrak{J}$ is associator nilpotent?
3. Cartan subalgebras of Jordan algebras. Associator regular elements. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with $1, \mathcal{K}$ an associator nilpotent subalgebra containing 1 . The mapping $a \rightarrow R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{K}, R_{a} \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$, is a unital multiplication specialization. Hence we have the homomorphism of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{K})$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ mapping $a \rightarrow R_{a}, a \in \mathfrak{K}$. This induces a homomorphism of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{K})^{-}$ and of the subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}(\mathfrak{K})$ of $U_{1}(\mathfrak{K})^{-}$generated by the elements $a b-a . b$, $a, b \in \mathfrak{K}$. We denote the image of $\mathfrak{A}(\mathfrak{K})$ under this homomorphism by $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{K})$. Clearly this is the subalgebra of the Lie algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})^{-}$generated by the elements $R_{a, b}=R_{a} R_{b}-R_{a, b}, a, b \in \mathfrak{K}$. Since $\mathfrak{K}$ is associator nilpotent, $\mathfrak{A}(\mathfrak{K})$ is a nilpotent Lie algebra by Theorem 20. Hence its homomorphic image $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{K})$ is a nilpotent Lie algebra of linear transformations in the vector space $\mathfrak{J}$.

We recall that if $\mathfrak{L}$ is a nilpotent Lie algebra of linear transformations in the finite-dimensional vector space $\mathfrak{M}$ then we have the Fitting decomposition of $\mathfrak{M}$ relative to $\mathfrak{L}: \mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{1}$, where $\mathfrak{M}_{0}=\left\{z \in \mathfrak{M} \mid z L^{n}=0, L \in \mathfrak{L}\right\}, n=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M}$, and $\mathfrak{M}_{1}=\bigcap_{i} \mathfrak{M}\left(\mathfrak{L}^{*}\right)^{i}$ where $\mathfrak{L}^{*}$ is the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{M}, \mathfrak{M})$ generated by $\mathfrak{L}$ (without 1) (Jacobson, Lie Algebras, p. 39). These are invariant subspaces relative to $\mathfrak{L}$ and $\mathfrak{M}_{0}\left(\mathfrak{L}^{*}\right)^{n}=0$. We remark that $\mathfrak{M}_{1}$ is the only complementary space of $\mathfrak{M}_{0}$ in $\mathfrak{M}$ which is invariant relative to $\mathfrak{L}$. For, if $\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}$ is any such space then $\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}$ has the Fitting decomposition $\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}{ }_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{M}^{\prime}{ }_{1}$, where $\mathfrak{M}_{0}{ }^{\prime}=\left\{z \in \mathfrak{M}^{\prime} \mid z L^{n^{\prime}}=0, L \in \mathfrak{L}\right\}$, $\left.n^{\prime}=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{M}^{\prime}, \mathfrak{M}_{1}{ }^{\prime}=\bigcap_{i} \mathfrak{M}^{\prime} \mathfrak{L}^{*}\right)^{i}$. Then $\mathfrak{M}_{0}{ }^{\prime} \subseteq \mathfrak{M}_{0}$ so $\mathfrak{M}_{0}{ }^{\prime}=0$ so $\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{M}_{1}{ }^{\prime} \subseteq \mathfrak{M}_{1}$. Hence $\mathfrak{M}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{M}_{1}$. Let P be an extension field of the base field and consider the extension space $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathbf{P}}$. If $A \in \mathfrak{L}$ then $A$ has a unique extension to a linear transformation in $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathbf{P}}$ and the set $\mathrm{P} \mathfrak{L}$ of P -linear combinations of these linear transformations is a Lie algebra which can be identified with $\mathfrak{L}_{\mathbf{P}}$. If $\mathfrak{L}$ is nilpotent then so is $\mathfrak{L}_{\mathbf{P}}$. It is clear also that the Fitting decomposition $\mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{1}$ of $\mathfrak{M}$ relative to $\mathfrak{L}$ gives rise to the Fitting decomposition $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathbf{P}}=\mathfrak{M}_{\mathbf{O P}} \oplus \mathfrak{M}_{\mathbf{1 P}}$, that is, $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathbf{i P}}=\left(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathbf{P}}\right)_{\boldsymbol{i}}$.

We now consider the Fitting decomposition of the vector space $\mathfrak{J}$ of a finitedimensional Jordan algebra with 1 relative to the Lie algebra of linear transformations $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K})$ where $\mathfrak{K}$ is an associator nilpotent subalgebra containing 1. If $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ then we define

$$
\begin{equation*}
\boldsymbol{3}_{a}=\left\{z \in \mathfrak{J} \mid z J_{a}{ }^{n}=0\right\} \tag{72}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $n=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}$. Thus $a$ is associator nilpotent in $\mathfrak{J}$ if and only if $\mathfrak{Z}_{a}=\mathfrak{J}$. We remark also that $\Phi[a] \subseteq \mathfrak{Z}_{a}$. Moreover, the proof of Schafer's lemma shows that for any $i, j=12, \cdots, R_{a^{i}, a^{\cdot j}}=T_{i j} J_{a}=J_{a} T_{i j}$ where $T_{i j}$ is in the algebra of operators generated by $1, R_{a}$ and $R_{a \cdot 2}$. Hence it is clear that $z\left(R_{a \cdot i, a^{\cdot j}}\right)^{n}=0$ for all $z \in \mathcal{B}_{a}$ and $i, j=0,1,2, \cdots$. We now have the following

Theorem 21. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with $1, \Omega$ an
associator nilpotent subalgebra containing $1, \mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K})$ the nilpotent Lie algebra of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{J}$ generated by the transformations $R_{a, b}=R_{a} R_{b} -R_{a . b}, a, b \in \mathfrak{K}$. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{1}$ be the Fitting decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K})$. Then $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ is a subalgebra and $\mathfrak{J}_{0} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{1} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{1}$. Moreover, if the base field is algebraically closed then $\mathfrak{J}_{0}=\bigcap_{b \in \mathfrak{R}} \mathfrak{Z}_{b}$ where $\mathfrak{Z}_{a}$ is defined by (72).

Proof. It is sufficient to prove the result for algebraically closed base fields. In this case, by Corollary 2 to Theorem 18, $\Re=\Re_{1} \oplus \Re_{2} \oplus \cdots \oplus \Re_{s}$ where $\Re_{i}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{K}$ which has the form $\mathfrak{K}_{i}=\Phi e_{i}+\mathfrak{N}_{i}, e_{i}$ the identity of $\Re_{i}$ and $\Re_{i}$ a nil ideal. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{i \leqq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ be the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the $e_{i}$. We shall now show that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{J}_{0}=\sum_{1}^{s} \mathfrak{J}_{i i}, \quad \mathfrak{J}_{1}=\sum_{i<j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j} . \tag{73}
\end{equation*}
$$

Let $a, b \in \Re, x \in \mathfrak{J}_{i i}$. Then $a=\sum\left(\alpha_{j} e_{j}+z_{j}\right), b=\sum\left(\beta_{j} e_{j}+w_{j}\right)$ where $\alpha_{j}, \beta_{j} \in \Phi$, $z_{j}, w_{j} \in \mathfrak{N}_{j}$. Hence $x R_{a, b}=\left[x, \alpha_{i} e_{i}+z_{i}, \beta_{i} e_{i}+w_{i}\right]=\left[x, z_{i}, w_{i}\right]=x R_{z_{i}, w_{i}}$. Since $\mathfrak{N}_{i}$ is a nilpotent Jordan algebra the associative algebra $\mathfrak{N}_{i}{ }^{*}$ of linear transformations generated by the $R_{u_{i}}, u_{i} \in \mathfrak{N}$, is nilpotent (p. 194). The foregoing equation shows that if $x \in \mathfrak{I}_{i i}$ and $a, b \in \mathfrak{K}$ then $x R_{a, b}=x V$ where $V \in \Re_{i}{ }^{*}$. It follows that if $L \in \mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{K})$ then $x L=x W$ where $W \in \mathfrak{N}_{i}{ }^{*}$. Then $x L^{n}=0$ and so $\mathfrak{J}_{i i} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{0}$. Hence $\sum \mathfrak{J}_{i i} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{0}$. It is clear also from the definition of $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{J}_{0} \subseteq \bigcap_{b \in \Re} 3_{b} \tag{74}
\end{equation*}
$$

We note next that it is clear from the properties of the Peirce decomposition that $\mathfrak{J}_{i j} R_{b} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ if $b \in \mathfrak{K} \subseteq \sum \mathfrak{J}_{i i}$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}_{i j} \mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K}) \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. Let $b=\sum \beta_{i} e_{i}$ where the $\beta_{i}$ are distinct elements of $\Phi$. If $x \in \mathcal{Z}_{b}$ then $x\left(R_{b \cdot k, b \cdot 1}\right)^{n}=0$ for $k, l=01,2, \cdots$. Hence $x\left(R_{e_{i}, e_{j}}\right)^{n}=0$ for $i, j=1,2, \cdots, s$. This and $\mathfrak{I}_{i j} \mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K}) \subseteq \mathfrak{I}_{i j}$ imply that $3_{b} \cap \mathfrak{I}_{i j}=0$ if $i \neq j$ and that $\bigcap_{b \in \Omega} \mathfrak{O}_{b} \subseteq \sum \mathfrak{I}_{i i}$. Hence, by (74), $\sum \mathfrak{I}_{i i}=\mathfrak{J}_{0} =\bigcap_{b \in \mathbb{R}} 3_{b}$. Since $\sum_{i<j} \Im_{i j}$ is invariant under $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{K})$ and is a complement of $\Sigma \mathfrak{J}_{i i}$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ we have $\mathfrak{J}_{1}=\Sigma_{i<j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. The fact that $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ is a subalgebra and $\mathfrak{J}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{0} \subseteq \mathfrak{I}_{1}$ are clear from the properties of the Peirce decomposition.
If $\Re$ is an associator nilpotent subalgebra containing 1 of the finite-dimensional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with 1 then there exists a $k$ such that $x R_{a_{1}, b_{1}} R_{a_{2}, b_{2}} \cdots R_{a_{k}, b_{k}}=0$ for $x, a_{i}, b_{i} \in \Re$. It follows that $\Re \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{0}$ the Fitting null component of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K})$. We shall now define a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak{K}$ of a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1 as a subalgebra containing 1 such that $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{J}_{0}$. This is equivalent to: $\Re$ is an associator nilpotent subalgebra containing 1 such that if $x \in \mathfrak{J}$ satisfies $x R_{a, b} \in \mathfrak{K}$ for all $a, b \in \mathfrak{K}$ then $x \in \mathfrak{K}$. (*). If $x$ satisfies the condition $x R_{a, b} \in \Re$ for all $a, b \in \Re$ then $x R_{a_{1}, b_{1}} \cdots R_{a_{k}, b_{k}}=0$ for all $a_{v}, b_{i} \in \Re$. It follows that $x \in \mathfrak{J}_{0}$, so if $\Re$ is a Cartan subalgebra then $x \in \Re$. On the other hand, suppose $\Re$

[^18]is associator nilpotent with 1 and $\mathfrak{K}$ is not a Cartan subalgebra. Then $\mathfrak{J}_{0} \supset \mathfrak{K}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{0}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{0}(\mathfrak{K})^{*}\right)^{n}=0$ where $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K})^{*}$ is the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ generated by $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K})$ and $n=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}$. Since $\mathfrak{K}$ is an invariant subspace under $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{I}}(\mathfrak{K})^{*}$ there exists a vector $x \in \mathfrak{J}_{0}, \notin \mathfrak{K}$ such that $x \mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K})^{*} \subseteq \mathfrak{R}$. Then $x R_{a, \dot{b}} \in \mathfrak{K}$ for all $a, b \in \mathfrak{K}$ but $x \notin \Re$. Hence $\Re$ does not satisfy the given condition.
If $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ then $\Phi[a]$ is associative and hence is associator nilpotent. It is clear from the remarks following (72) that the subspace $3_{a}$ defined by (72) coincides with the Fitting null component of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}(\Phi[a])$. Let ( $u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}$ ) be a basis for $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ and let $M(a)$ be the matrix of $J_{a}{ }^{n}$ relative to this basis. Then it is clear that $\operatorname{dim} \mathcal{Z}_{a}=n-\operatorname{rank} M(a)$. The element $a$ will be called associator regular if $\operatorname{dim} 3_{a}$ is minimal. As before, let $x=\sum \xi_{i} u_{i}, \xi_{i}$ indeterminates, be a generic element and define $3_{x}$ and $M(x)$ as for $a$. Then the entries of $M(x)$ are in $\Phi\left[\xi_{1}, \xi_{2}, \cdots, \xi_{i n}\right]$. If $r$ is the rank of this matrix then $l=n-r=\operatorname{dim} 3_{x}$. It is clear that rank $M(a) \leqq r$ and $a$ is associator regular if $\operatorname{rank} M(a)=r$. Let $\left\{N_{j}(x)\right\}$ be the set of nonzero $r$-rowed minors in the matrix $M(x)$. Then for infinite $\Phi$ there exist $a=\sum \alpha_{i} u_{l}, \alpha_{i} \in \Phi$, such that $N_{j}(a) \neq 0$ for some $j$. Any such element is associator regular in $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence it is clear that for infinite $\Phi$ the set of associator regular elements is a Zariski open subset of $\mathfrak{J}$.

We now prove the following analogue of the theorem of existence of Cartan subalgebras of Lie algebras.

Theorem 22. If $a$ is an associator regular element of a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1 over an infinite field $\Phi$ then $3_{a}$ is a Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ containing $a$.

Proof. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{1}$ be the Fitting decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the abelian, hence, nilpotent, Lie algebra $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{I}}(\Phi[a])$. Then we have noted that $\mathfrak{J}_{0}=\mathfrak{Z}_{a}$. Let ( $u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{i n}$ ) be a basis for $\mathfrak{J}$ such that ( $u_{1}, \cdots, u_{l}$ ) is a basis for $3_{a}$ and $\left(u_{l+1}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{I}_{1}$. Since $\mathfrak{Z}_{a} \cdot \mathfrak{Z}_{a} \subseteq \mathfrak{Z}_{a}$ and $\mathfrak{I}_{1} \cdot \mathfrak{Z}_{a} \subseteq \mathfrak{I}_{1}$ the matrix $M(b), b \in Z_{a}$, of $J_{b}{ }^{n}$ relative to the basis ( $u_{1}, \cdots, u_{n}$ ) has the form

$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc}
N(b) & 0  \tag{75}\\
0 & P(b)
\end{array}\right)
$$

where $N(b)$ and $P(b)$ are the matrices of the restrictions to $\mathfrak{Z}_{a}$ and $\mathfrak{I}_{1}$ respectively. We shall now show that $N(b)=0$ for all $b \in \mathfrak{Z}_{a}$. Otherwise, let $b \in \mathfrak{Z}_{a}$ have a nonzero entry $\rho$ in one of the matrices $N(b)$. The matrix $N(a)=0$. On the other hand, $a$ is associator regular. Hence $\operatorname{det} P(a) \neq 0$. Let $\xi, \eta$ be indeterminates and consider the element $\xi a+\eta b \in \mathfrak{J}_{\Phi(\xi, \eta)}$. This is contained in $\left(3_{a}\right)_{\Phi(\xi \eta)}$ and it is clear that the determinant of the $r+1$ rowed submatrix of $M(\xi a+\eta b)$ which is formed from the one-rowed matrix in the position of $\rho$ and the $r$-rowed matrix $\xi P(a) +\eta P(b)$ has the form $f(\xi, \eta)=f_{1}(\xi, \eta) f_{2}(\xi, \eta)$ where $f_{1}(1,0)=\operatorname{det} P(a), f_{2}(0,1)=\rho$. Hence $f(\xi, \eta) \neq 0$ and since $\Phi$ is infinite we can choose $\xi=\alpha, \eta=\beta$ in $\Phi$ such that $f(\alpha, \beta) \neq 0$. Then $c=\alpha a+\beta b \in \mathfrak{J}$ and has the property that the rank of
$M(c)$ is $r+1$. This contradicts the associator regularity of $a$. Hence we can conclude that $N(b)=0, b \in \mathfrak{Z}_{a}$. This implies that every element of the subalgebra $\mathfrak{Z}_{a}$ is an associator nilpotent in $\mathfrak{Z}_{a}$. Then, by Theorem 19, $\mathfrak{Z}_{a}$ is an associator nilpotent subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{Z}_{a}$ contains 1 . Since $\mathfrak{Z}_{a}$ is associator nilpotent the Fitting null component of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{a}\right)$ contains $\mathfrak{O}_{a}$. Since $\mathfrak{Z}_{a}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ are invariant under $\mathfrak{U}_{\mathfrak{J}}\left(\mathfrak{Z}_{a}\right)$ the null component of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to $\mathfrak{U}_{\mathfrak{I}}\left(\mathfrak{Z}_{a}\right)$ is $\mathfrak{Z}_{a}+$ the Fitting null component of $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ relative to $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}\left(\mathfrak{Z}_{a}\right)$. Since $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ is the Fitting one component of $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}(\Phi[a])$ it is contained in the Fitting one component of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{I}}\left(\mathfrak{Z}_{a}\right)$. Hence the Fitting null component of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}\left(\mathfrak{Z}_{a}\right)$ is $\mathfrak{Z}_{a}$ and $\mathfrak{Z}_{a}$ is a Cartan subalgebra.

We remark also that the decomposition $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{1}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into Fitting components relative to $\mathfrak{U}_{\mathfrak{I}}(\Phi[a])$ is also the decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ into Fitting components relative to $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{I}}\left(\mathfrak{Z}_{a}\right)$. This implies that an associator regular element cannot be contained in two distinct Cartan subalgebras.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional central simple Jordan algebra, $a$ an element of $\mathfrak{J}$ whose minimum polynomial has $m$ distinct roots where $m=\operatorname{deg} \mathfrak{J}$. Show that $\Phi[a]$ is a Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that the dimensionality of any Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ is $m$.
2. Determine a Cartan subalgebra of the Jordan algebra of triangular matrices.
3. Application to generic traces. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1 . We have called an element $a$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ of maximum degree if the minimum polynomial of $a$ coincides with its generic minimum polynomial. Moreover, we have seen that if the base field is infinite the set of elements of maximum degree is a Zariski open subset of $\mathfrak{J}$ (p. 224). We have seen in the last section that the set of associator regular elements is Zariski open. Hence the set of associator regular elements of maximum degree is Zariski open. By Theorem 22, if $\Phi$ is infinite there exist Cartan subalgebras of $\mathfrak{J}$ containing associator regular elements of maximum degree. We use these to obtain formulas for the generic trace and degree of $\mathfrak{J}$.

Theorem 23. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1 over an algebraically closed field, $\Omega$ a Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ containing an associator regular element of maximum degree. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{K} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{1}$ be the Fitting decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K}), \mathfrak{K}=\Sigma_{1}^{s} \oplus \mathfrak{K}_{i}$ where $\mathfrak{K}_{i}$ is an ideal in $\mathfrak{K}$ and $\mathfrak{K}_{i}=\Phi e_{i} \oplus \mathfrak{N}_{i}, e_{i}$ the identity of $\mathfrak{K}_{i}, \mathfrak{N}_{i}$ a nil ideal and let $n_{i}$ be the maximum index of nilpotency of the elements of $\mathfrak{N}_{i}$. Then if $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ and $a=\sum_{1}^{s}\left(\alpha_{i} e_{i}+z_{1}\right) +a_{1}, \alpha_{i} \in \Phi, z_{i} \in \mathfrak{N}_{i}, a_{1} \in \mathfrak{I}_{1}$, then we have the formula

$$
\begin{equation*}
t(a)=\sum n_{i} \alpha_{i} \tag{76}
\end{equation*}
$$

for the generic trace and $\sum_{1}^{s} n_{i}$ is the degree of $\mathfrak{J}$.

Proof. If $b \in \Re$ then the generic minimum polynomial $m_{b, \boldsymbol{\Omega}}(\lambda)$ of $b$ relative to $\Re$ is a factor of the generic minimum polynomial $m_{b}(\lambda)$ of $b$ in $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $\mathfrak{K}$ contains an element of maximum degree it follows that $m_{b, \boldsymbol{\Omega}}(\lambda)=m_{b}(\lambda)$. If $b=\sum\left(\beta_{i} e_{i}+w_{i}\right)$ where $\beta_{i} \in \Phi$ and $w_{i} \in \Re_{i}$ then the minimum polynomial $\mu_{b}(\lambda)$ of $b$ in $\Re$ (and in $\mathfrak{J}$ ) is the least common multiple L.C.M. $\left(\lambda-\beta_{i}\right)^{m_{i}}$ where $m_{i}$ is the index of nilpotency of $w_{i}$. It follows from this and the definition of the generic minimum polynomial that $m_{b}(\lambda)=m_{b \boldsymbol{\Omega}}(\lambda)=\prod_{1}^{s}\left(\lambda-\beta_{i}\right)^{n_{i}}$ where $n_{i}$ is the maximum index of nilpotency of the elements of $\mathfrak{N}_{i}$. Then it is clear that the degree of $\mathfrak{J} =\operatorname{deg} m_{b}(\lambda)=\Sigma_{1}^{s} n_{i}$ and the generic trace, $t(b)=\Sigma_{1}^{s} n_{i} \beta_{i}$ for $b \in \mathfrak{K}$. We have seen in the proof of Theorem 21 that if $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{1 \leqq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ is the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the $e_{i}$, then $\mathfrak{J}_{1}=\sum_{i<j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ and $\mathfrak{K}_{i}=\mathfrak{J}_{i i}$. Hence if $a=\sum\left(\alpha_{i} e_{i}+z_{i}\right) +a_{1}, \alpha_{i} \in \Phi, z_{i} \in \mathfrak{N}_{i}, a_{1} \in \mathfrak{I}_{1}$ then $a_{1}=\sum_{i<j} a_{i j}$ where $a_{i j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. Then $t(a) =t\left(\sum\left(\alpha_{i} e_{i}+z_{i}\right)\right)+\sum_{i<j} t\left(a_{i j}\right)$. Since $\sum\left(\alpha_{i} e_{\imath}+z_{i}\right) \in \mathfrak{R}$ we have $t\left(\sum\left(\alpha_{i} e_{i}+z_{i}\right)\right) =\sum n_{i} \alpha_{i}$. Since $a_{i j}=4\left[a_{i j}, e_{i}, e_{j}\right]$ if $i<j, t\left(a_{i j}\right)=0$ since $t$ is associative. Hence we have $t\left(a_{1}\right)=0$ and $t(a)=\sum_{1}^{\mathrm{s}} n_{i} \alpha_{i}$.

We can use the formula (76) for the generic trace to give a proof of the following result which is independent of the determination of the simple algebras over an algebraically closed field.

Theorem 24. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is finite-dimensional separable then the generic trace form $t(a, b)=t(a . b)$ is nondegenerate (cf. p. 240).

Proof. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is separable it has an identity element and $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ for $\Omega$ the algebraic closure is a direct sum of simple ideals $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$. Then the $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ are orthogonal relative to the generic trace form and the restriction of this form to $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ is the generic trace form in $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ (p.228). Hence it suffices to prove the nondegeneracy of the generic trace form of a simple Jordan algebra over an algebraically closed field. Then we may choose $\mathfrak{K}$ as in Theorem 23 and we have the formula (76). On the other hand, we have the reduced trace $t_{E}$ such that $t_{E}(a)=\sum_{1}^{s} \alpha_{i}$ relative to the set of idempotents $E=\left\{e_{1}, e_{2}, \cdots, e_{s}\right\}$. Evidently $t_{E}\left(e_{i}\right)=t_{E}\left(e_{i}, e_{i}\right) \neq 0$ so $t_{E} \neq 0$. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is simple and $t_{E}$ is associative, it follows that $t_{E}$ is nondegenerate. Since $\mathfrak{N}_{i}$ defined in Theorem 23 is clearly in the radical of $t_{E}$ we have $\mathfrak{N}_{i}=0$, $i=1,2, \cdots, s$. Then (76) gives $t(a)=\sum \alpha_{i}=t_{E}(a)$. Hence the reduced trace $t_{E}$ coincides with the generic trace and consequently the generic trace form $t$ is nondegenerate.

We remark that the converse of the preceding theorem was proved before (Theorem 6.5) and the proof of this did not require the determination of the simple algebras.
13. Conjugacy of Cartan subalgebras. Throughout this section we assume the base field is of characteristic 0 and we shall make use of some important concepts and results from the theory of algebraic groups of linear transformations. All of these can be found in Chevalley's two books, Théorie des Groupes de Lie, Tome II
and III. We recall first that if $\mathfrak{L}$ is a Lie algebra of linear transformations in a finite-dimensional vector space $\mathfrak{M}$ then the Lie algebra $\overline{\mathcal{L}}$ of the intersection $G$ of all the algebraic groups of linear transformations whose Lie algebras contain $\mathfrak{L}$ contains $\mathfrak{L}$ (Chevalley, Tome II, pp. 158-169 or Hochschild [2]). $\overline{\mathcal{L}}$ is called the algebraic hull of $\mathfrak{L}$. The group $G$ is an irreducible algebraic group. We now apply this to the Lie algebra Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ where $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra and we denote the corresponding group $G$ as $I$. Since the group of automorphisms of $\mathfrak{J}$ is an algebraic group whose Lie algebra is Der $\mathfrak{J}$ (Chevalley, Tome II, p. 179) it is clear that $I$ is contained in the group of automorphisms. We shall now prove the following analogue of the classical conjugacy theorem for Cartan subalgebras of a Lie algebra.

Theorem 25. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1 over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0 . Let $\Omega_{1}$ and $\Omega_{2}$ be Cartan subalgebras of $\mathfrak{J}$. Then there exists an automorphism $s \in I$ such that $\mathfrak{K}_{1}^{s}=\mathfrak{K}_{2}$.

Proof. We pattern our proof after Chevalley's proof of the corresponding Lie algebra result (Chevalley, Tome III, pp. 215-219). Let $\Omega_{1}$ be the orbit of $\Omega_{1}$ under $I$. Then we wish to show that $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{1}}$ contains a Zariski open subset of $\mathfrak{J}$. We note first that since $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{1}$ and $I$ are irreducible, $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{1}$ is épais, that is, it is irreducible and contains a nonvacuous open subset of its Zariski closure (Prop. 3, p. 193 of Chevalley, Tome III). Then the desired result that $\Omega_{1}$ contains an open subset will follow if we can show that the dimensionality of the irreducible set $\Omega_{1}$ is $n=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}$. Let $a \in \Omega_{1}$ and let $T$ be the tangent space to $\Omega_{1}$ at $a$. Then it is known that $T$ contains $\Omega_{1}+a($ Inder $\mathfrak{J})$ where $a($ Inder $\mathfrak{J})=\{a D \mid D \in$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}\}($ Chevalley, Tome III, p. 192). Since the base field is algebraically closed there exists a set of primitive idempotents $e_{i}$ such that $\sum_{1}^{s} e_{i}=1$ and $\mathfrak{K}_{i}=\sum \mathfrak{J}_{\imath \iota}$ where $\mathfrak{J}=\sum_{i \leqq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ is the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the $e_{i}$. Also $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}=\Phi e_{i}+\mathfrak{N}_{i}$ where $\mathfrak{N}_{i}$ is a nil ideal in $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}$. Let $O_{1}$ denote the open subset of $\mathfrak{K}_{1}$ consisting of the elements $\sum\left(\alpha_{i} e_{i}+z_{i}\right), \alpha_{i} \in \Phi, z_{i} \in \mathfrak{N}_{i}$ satisfying $\prod_{i<j}\left(\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{j}\right) \neq 0$. Let $a \in O_{1}$ and consider $a\left[R_{e_{i}} R_{a_{i j}}\right]$ where $i \neq j$ and $a_{i j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. We have

$$
\begin{align*}
a\left[R_{e_{i}} R_{a_{i j}}\right] & =\left(\sum_{k}\left(\alpha_{k} e_{k}+z_{k}\right)\right)\left[R_{e_{i}} R_{a_{i j}}\right] \\
& =\left(\alpha_{i} e_{i}+z_{i}\right)\left[R_{e_{i}} R_{a_{i j}}\right]+\left(\alpha_{j} e_{j}+z_{j}\right)\left[R_{e_{i}} R_{a_{i j}}\right]  \tag{77}\\
& =\frac{1}{4}\left(\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{j}\right) a_{i j}+\frac{1}{2}\left(z_{i}-z_{j}\right) \cdot a_{i j} \\
& =a_{i j} S_{i j}
\end{align*}
$$

where $S_{i j}=\frac{1}{4} R_{\left(\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{j}\right) 1}+\frac{1}{2} R_{z_{i}-z_{j}}$. Since $\alpha_{i} \neq \alpha_{j}$ and $R_{z_{i}-z_{j}}$, is nilpotent it is clear that $S_{i j}$ is invertible. Since it maps $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ into itself we have $\mathfrak{J}_{i j} S_{i j}=\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. Hence (77) shows that $a$ (Inder $\mathfrak{I}$ ) contains $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ for every $i \neq j$. It follows that the tangent
space to $\Omega_{1}$ at $a$ contains $\Omega_{1}$ and every $\mathfrak{I}_{i j}, i \neq j$. Hence this coincides with $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $O_{1}$ is open in $\Re_{1}$ and $\Omega_{1}$ is the orbit of $\Re_{1}$ under $I$ it is clear that $O_{1}$ contains a simple point of $\Omega_{1}$. Hence $\operatorname{dim} \Omega_{1}=n$ and consequetly $\Omega_{1}$ contains an open subset of $\mathfrak{J}$. Similarly, the orbit $\Omega_{2}$ of $\Omega_{2}$ under $I$ contains an open subset of $\mathfrak{J}$. Since the set of associator regular elements of $\mathfrak{J}$ is Zariski open we now see that there exists an associator regular element $b$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ and automorphisms $s_{1}, s_{2} \in I$ such that $b \in \mathfrak{K}_{i}{ }^{s_{i}}$. Now $\mathfrak{Z}_{b}$ and $\mathfrak{K}_{i}{ }^{s_{i}}$ are Cartan subalgebras. Hence $\mathfrak{Z}_{b}=\mathfrak{K}_{i}^{s_{i}}$. Then $\Re_{1}{ }^{s_{1}}=\Re_{2}{ }^{s_{2}}$ and $\Re_{2}=\Re_{1}{ }^{s}$ where $s=s_{1} s_{2}{ }^{-1} \in I$.

## Chapter IX

## EXCEPTIONAL JORDAN ALGEBRAS

This chapter is devoted to the study of the Jordan algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ of $3 \times 3$ hermitian matrices with entries taken from an octonion algebra $\mathfrak{D}$, and the algebras which become these on extension of the base field. As we have seen in Chapter IV and $V$, these algebras have a number of important characterizations. First, we recall that the algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ are precisely the Jordan algebras which are reduced, simple and exceptional (that is, not special, see §5.6). Also the algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and the Jordan division algebras which become these on extension of the base field are just the finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebras (§5.7). Thus the algebras we are concerned with can be separated into two classes: the reduced ones and the division algebras. It is useful also to separate into two subclasses the reduced ones: namely, the ones which are split in the sense that the octonion algebra $\mathfrak{O}$ is split and the nonsplit ones.

After some preliminary results on identities the first main task we address ourselves to is that of determining conditions for the isomorphism of two reduced algebras $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$. These are given in two theorems, the first of which is due to Albert and Jacobson [1] and the second to Springer [4]. For the proofs of both (given in §2 and §4 respectively) the set $\Pi$ of elements of rank one in $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ plays an important role. These are the elements $a$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ which are nonzero but have the property that adj $a=0$ where adj $a$ is defined by the generic minimum polynomial as in §6.3. For the proof of Springer's theorem we shall use also some results on groups of automorphisms and norm equivalences of $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$. These are given in §3 and have important applications also in other parts of the chapter.

In §5 we collect a number of other important results on Aut $\mathfrak{J}$, mostly, for their own sake. The groups Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ are simple algebraic groups of type $F_{4}$ so the results we obtain, particularly, the determination of the involutions of the groups and their centralizers are of interest for the study of this important type of algebraic (or finite) group.

In §6 we consider split algebras and we prove an analogue of the classical invariant factor theorem for these algebras.

In §§7-10 we are concerned with reduced algebras $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ which are not split, so $\mathfrak{O}$ is an octonion division algebra. With any such algebra we can associate a projective plane $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ which is defined by means of the elements of rank one of $\mathfrak{J}$. The plane $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ depends only on the octonion coefficient algebra and these are equivalent to some planes which were constructed first by Moufang [1]. We
study the main properties of these planes and their projective mappings and relate these to the Jordan algebras.

In §11 we consider some of the main connections between the exceptional Jordan algebras $\mathfrak{J}$ and Lie algebras. We study the Jordan algebras Der $\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ and the Tits-Koecher algebras $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$. The dimensionalities of these are respectively 52,78 and 133 and except for $\mathscr{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ in characteristic three the Lie algebras are all simple.

In the last section of this chapter we give a new construction, due to Tits, of exceptional Jordạn division algebras. This construction, which is extremely simple, leads to substantially simpler proofs of Albert's main results on Jordan division algebras ([25] and [32]).

1. Preliminaries on identities and subalgebras. We recall that a Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ is called reduced if $\mathfrak{J}$ has an identity element $1=\sum_{1}^{n} e_{i}$ where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents which are absolutely primitive in the sense that every element of the Peirce space $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{i}}$ has the form $\alpha e_{i}+z$ where $\alpha \in \Phi$ and $z$ is nilpotent (§5.4). A set of $e_{i}$ satisfying these conditions is called a reducing set of idempotents for $\mathfrak{J}$. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is reduced and simple then $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}=\Phi e_{i}$ for every $e_{i}$ in the reducing set $\left\{e_{i}\right\}$. Moreover, if $\mathfrak{J}=\sum_{i \leqq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ is the Peirce decomposition relative to the $e_{i}$ and $a_{i j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i j}, i \neq j$, then $a_{i j}{ }^{2}=\alpha\left(e_{i}+e_{j}\right)$ where $\alpha \in \Phi$ (see $\S 5.6$ for this and other results on reduced simple Jordan algebras). There exist $a_{i j}$ such that $a_{i j}{ }^{2} \neq 0$. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is reduced and simple and $\{1\}$ is a reducing set of idempotents then clearly $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1$ and if $\mathfrak{J}$ has a reducing set of two idempotents then $\mathfrak{J}$ is the Jordan algebra of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form. If $\mathfrak{J}$ has a reducing set of $n \geqq 3$ idempotents then we can choose for $j=2, \cdots, n$ an element $u_{1 j} \in \mathfrak{I}_{1 j}$ such that $u_{1 j}{ }^{2}=\gamma_{j}{ }^{-1}\left(e_{1}+e_{j}\right), \gamma_{j} \in \Phi$. Then there exists an isomorphism $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{n}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a composition algebra and $J_{\gamma}$ is the canonical involution determined by the diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}\left\{1, \gamma_{2}, \cdots, \gamma_{n}\right\}$. Moreover, we have $e_{i}{ }^{\eta}=e_{i i}$ and $u_{1 j}{ }^{\eta}=1[i j]$, where, in general, $a[i j]=a e_{i j}+\gamma_{j}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{i} \bar{a} e_{j i}, a \in \mathfrak{D}$ (see §3.2). We shall now call $\eta$ a coordinatization of $\mathfrak{J}$ and we shall say that this is adapted to the elements $e_{i}$ and $u_{1 j}$ if the foregoing conditions hold. Any reduced simple Jordan algebra which is not the Jordan algebra of a symmetric bilinear form is finite dimensional. The only exceptional algebras in this class are the algebras isomorphic to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{O}, j)$ is an octonion algebra.

We recall that if $A \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$, say,

$$
A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
\alpha_{1} & c & \gamma_{1}^{-1} \gamma_{3} \bar{b}  \tag{1}\\
\gamma_{2}^{-1} \gamma_{1} \bar{c} & \alpha_{2} & a \\
b & \gamma_{3}^{-1} \gamma_{2} \bar{a} & \alpha_{3}
\end{array}\right]
$$

or, $A=\sum_{1}^{3} \alpha_{i} e_{i i}+a[23]+b[31]+c[12]$, and

$$
\begin{equation*}
A \times A=A^{.2}-t(A) A+\frac{1}{2}\left(t(A)^{2}-t\left(A^{.2}\right)\right) 1 \tag{2}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $t(A)=\sum_{1}^{3} \alpha_{i}$ then

$$
\begin{equation*}
A \cdot(A \times A)=n(A) 1 \tag{3}
\end{equation*}
$$

where

$$
\begin{equation*}
n(A)=\alpha_{1} \alpha_{2} \alpha_{3}-\alpha_{1} \gamma_{3}^{-1} \gamma_{2} n(a)-\alpha_{2} \gamma_{1}^{-1} \gamma_{3} n(b)-\alpha_{3} \gamma_{2}^{-1} \gamma_{1} n(c)+t((c a) b) \tag{4}
\end{equation*}
$$

(see §6.4). Here the $n$ and $t$ on the right-hand side are the generic norm and trace in the octonion algebra $\mathfrak{D}: t(a) 1=a+\bar{a}, n(a) 1=a \bar{a}=\bar{a} a$. We remark that if the coordinates $a, b, c$ in $A$ are contained in a commutative subalgebra then $n(A)=\operatorname{det} A$ the usual determinant of the matrix $A$. We have seen in §6.4 that $t(A)=\sum_{1}^{3} \alpha_{i}$ and $n(A)$ are the generic trace and norm respectively of $A \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$. The generic minimum polynomial is

$$
\begin{equation*}
m_{A}(\lambda)=\lambda^{3}-t(A) \lambda^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left[t(A)^{2}-t\left(A^{\cdot 2}\right)\right] \lambda-n(A) . \tag{5}
\end{equation*}
$$

We recall also that direct calculation gives $A \times A=$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{lll}
\alpha_{2} \alpha_{3}-\gamma_{3}^{-1} \gamma_{2} n(a) & \gamma_{1}^{-1} \gamma_{2} \bar{b} \bar{a}-\alpha_{3} c & c a-\gamma_{1}^{-1} \gamma_{3} \alpha_{2} \bar{b}  \tag{6}\\
a b-\gamma_{2}^{-1} \gamma_{1} \alpha_{3} \bar{c} & \alpha_{1} \alpha_{3}-\gamma_{1}^{-1} \gamma_{3} n(b) & \gamma_{2}^{-1} \gamma_{3} \bar{c} \bar{b}-\alpha_{1} a \\
\gamma_{3}^{-1} \gamma_{1} \bar{a} \bar{c}-\alpha_{2} b & b c-\gamma_{3}^{-1} \gamma_{2} \alpha_{1} \bar{a} & \alpha_{1} \alpha_{2}-\gamma_{2}^{-1} \gamma_{1} n(c)
\end{array}\right] .
$$

Now let $\mathfrak{J}$ be an arbitrary finite-dimensional exceptional central simple Jordan algebra and let $\Omega$ be the algebraic closure of the base field. Since the property of a Jordan algebra of being special is linear (Theorem 2.8) it is clear that $\mathcal{J}_{\Omega}$ is an exceptional simple Jordan algebra. Also $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ is reduced (Theorem 5.4). Hence our results apply to this algebra and these can be transferred to $\mathfrak{J}$ itself. In particular, we see that the degree of $\mathfrak{J}$ is three and its dimensionality is 27 since this is clearly the dimensionality of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$. Also, for $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
a \cdot(a \times a)=n(a) 1 \tag{3'}
\end{equation*}
$$

where

$$
\begin{equation*}
a \times a=a^{.2}-t(a) a+\frac{1}{2}\left[t(a)^{2}-t\left(a^{.2}\right)\right] 1 \tag{2'}
\end{equation*}
$$

and $t(a)$ and $n(a)$ are the generic trace and norm of $a$. Thus $a \times a=\operatorname{adj} a$ as defined in §6.3 and the generic minimum polynomial of $a$ is

$$
\begin{equation*}
m_{a}(\lambda)=\lambda^{3}-t(a) \lambda^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left[t(a)^{2}-t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)\right] \lambda-n(a) . \tag{$\prime$}
\end{equation*}
$$

We remark also that $\mathfrak{J}$ is separable since it is central simple. Hence the generic trace form $t(a, b)=t(a . b)$ is nondegenerate. We recall also that any algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ is unramified in the sense that the discriminant $\delta(x)$ of $m_{x}(\lambda)$ for the generic element $x$ is not 0 (p. 232). It follows that any finite-dimensional exceptional central simple Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ is unramified. An element $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ satisfies $\delta(a) \neq 0$
if and only if $m_{a}(\lambda)$ has distinct roots. Since the minimum polynomial $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ is a factor of $m_{a}(\lambda)$ and has the same roots except for multiplicities as $m_{a}(\lambda)$, it is clear that $\delta(a) \neq 0$ if and only if $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ has three distinct roots. For infinite base fields the set of elements satisfying this condition is Zariski open in $\mathfrak{J}$.

Since the degree of $\mathfrak{J}$ is three it is clear that the cardinality of any set $E$ of nonzero orthogonal idempotents does not exceed three and if $E=\left\{e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}\right\}$ then $e_{1}+e_{2}+e_{3}=1$ and the $e_{i}$ are primitive. Moreover, the $e_{i}$ are primitive in $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{i \leqq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ be the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the $\boldsymbol{e}_{\boldsymbol{i}}$. Then the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ is $\Sigma \mathfrak{J}_{i j \Omega}$ and since $e_{i}$ is primitive in $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ we have $\mathfrak{J}_{i i \Omega} =\Omega e_{i}$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}=\Phi e_{i}$. Thus $\mathfrak{J}$ is reduced and $E$ is a reducing set of idempotents for $\mathfrak{J}$. If we use coordinatization $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ adapted to the $e_{i}$ and elements $u_{1 j}$, $j=2,3$ in $\mathfrak{J}_{1 j}$ such that $u_{1 j}{ }^{\cdot 2} \neq 0$ then the generic trace $t\left(e_{i}\right)=t\left(e_{i}^{\eta}\right)=t\left(e_{i i}\right)=1$.

Since $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional simple Jordan algebra, $1=\sum_{1}^{r} e_{i}$ where the $e_{i}$ are completely primitive orthogonal idempotents, that is, the Peirce space $\mathfrak{J}_{i i}=\mathfrak{J} U_{e_{i}}$ are Jordan division algebras (Theorem 4.3 and Corollary 1 to Theorem 5.7). Moreover, the $e_{i}$ are connected (by the proof of the Second Structure Theorem, p. 179). We have just seen that $r \leqq 3$ and if $r=3$ then $\mathfrak{J}$ is reduced. If $r=1$ then 1 is completely primitive and hence $\mathfrak{J}$ is a division algebra. Now suppose $r=2$ and let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{11} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{12} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{22}$ be the Peirce decomposition relative to $e_{1}, e_{2}$, so $\mathfrak{J}_{12}=\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\left(e_{i}\right)$. Let $a \in \mathfrak{J}_{12}$. Then $4\left[a, e_{1}, e_{2}\right]=a$ so $t(a)=0$. Also since $\mathfrak{J}_{12}{ }^{.2} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{11} +\mathfrak{J}_{22}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{i j} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{j j}=\mathfrak{J}_{i j}=\mathfrak{J}_{i j} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{i i}$ we have $a^{\cdot 3} \in \mathfrak{J}_{12}$. The equation $m_{a}(a)=0$ reduces to $a^{\cdot 3}=\frac{1}{2} t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right) a+n(a) 1$ since $m_{a}(\lambda)$ is given by $\left(5^{\prime}\right)$ and $t(a)=0$. Since $a^{\cdot 3}, a \in \mathfrak{I}_{12}$ and $1 \in \mathfrak{I}_{11}+\mathfrak{I}_{22}$ this gives $a^{\cdot 3}=\frac{1}{2} t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right) a$ and $n(a)=0$. The latter condition implies that $a$ is not invertible so we have shown that there exist no invertible elements in $\mathfrak{J}_{12}$. This contradicts the connectedness of $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ so the case $r=2$ is ruled out. Thus we see that any finite dimensional exceptional central simple Jordan algebra is either reduced or it is a division algebra.

Now let $e$ be any idempotent of $\mathfrak{J}$ different from 0 and 1 . (The existence of such an idempotent implies $\mathfrak{J}$ is reduced.) The proof of Theorem 4.3 shows that $e$ and $1-e$ can be written as sums of completely primitive orthogonal idempotents. It follows that one and only one of the idempotents is completely primitive and the other is not. We may as well assume it is $e=e_{1}$. Then $1-e=e_{2}+e_{3}$ where the $e_{i}$ are completely primitive. Hence the $e_{i}$ are absolutely primitive and $t\left(e_{i}\right)=1$. Thus we see that if $e$ is an idempotent $\neq 0,1$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ then either $t(e)=1$ or $t(e)=2$ and the first alternative holds if and only if $e$ is primitive (completely primitive, absolutely primitive).

We remark finally that every reduced exceptional simple Jordan algebra is central simple and finite dimensional. Hence the two classes of Jordan algebras described by the modifiers: "reduced exceptional simple" and "finite dimensional exceptional central simple nondivision algebra" coincide.

We shall develop next some basic identities on adj $a=a \times a$, t(a) and $n(a)$. Since these are unchanged under extension of the base field we may assume this is
infinite and, if we wish, that it is algebraically closed. Then we can apply the concepts and results on polynomial mappings of §6.2.

We wish to linearize the mappings adj and $n$. Since the characteristic is $\neq 2$ but may be three we introduce

$$
\begin{equation*}
a \times b=\frac{1}{2} \Delta^{b}{ }_{a} \mathrm{adj} \tag{7}
\end{equation*}
$$

and

$$
\begin{equation*}
(a, b, c)=\frac{1}{2} \Delta_{a}^{c} \Delta^{b} n . \tag{8}
\end{equation*}
$$

If the characteristic is not three then it is perferable to replace ( $a, b, c$ ) by

$$
\begin{equation*}
n(a, b, c) \equiv \frac{1}{3}(a, b, c)=\frac{1}{3}!\Delta_{a}^{c} \Delta^{b} n . \tag{9}
\end{equation*}
$$

By Euler's equation (p. 219), $\Delta^{a}{ }_{a} \mathrm{adj}=2$ adj $a$ so $a \times a$ as defined by (7) agrees with the original $a \times a$. Since $\Delta^{c}{ }_{a} \Delta^{b}$ adj is symmetric and bilinear in $c$ and $b$ it is clear that $a \times b$ is symmetric and bilinear in $a$ and $b$. It follows that

$$
\begin{equation*}
a \times b=\frac{1}{2}[(a+b) \times(a+b)-a \times a-b \times b] \tag{10}
\end{equation*}
$$

so by the definition (2') of $a \times a^{\prime}$ (or by differentiation) we have

$$
\begin{align*}
a \times b= & a . b-\frac{1}{2} t(a) b-\frac{1}{2} t(b) a \\
& +\frac{1}{2}[t(a) t(b)-t(a . b)] 1 \tag{11}
\end{align*}
$$

In a similar manner one sees that ( $a, b, c$ ) is symmetric and trilinear and ( $a, a, a$ ) $=3 n(a)$, so if the characteristic is not three, then $n(a, a, a)=n(a)$. This gives directly:

$$
\begin{align*}
n(a, b, c)=\frac{1}{3}![n(a+b+c)-n(a+b)-n(b & +c)-n(a+c) \\
& +n(a)+n(b)+n(c)] \tag{12}
\end{align*}
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\begin{align*}
(a, b, c)=\frac{1}{2}[n(a+b+c)-n(a+b)-n & (b+c)-n(a+c) \\
& +n(a)+n(b)+n(c)] . \tag{12'}
\end{align*}
$$

We shall now show that this form of (12) is valid also in the characteristic three case. Let $F(a, b, c)$ denote the right-hand side of (12'). We claim first that, since $n$ is a homogeneous polynomial function of degree three, $F(a, b, c)$ is symmetric and trilinear in $a, b, c$. This is equivalent to showing that if $f(\xi) \equiv f\left(\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi\right)$ is a homogeneous cubic polynomial in indeterminates $\xi_{i}$, and $\eta_{i}, \zeta_{i}$ are other indeterminates then $E f \equiv f(\xi+\eta+\xi)-f(\xi+\eta)-f(\xi+\zeta)-f(\eta+\zeta)+f(\xi) +f(\eta)+f(\zeta)$ is homogeneous of first degree in each of the sets of indeterminates $\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n} ; \eta_{1}, \cdots, \eta_{n} ; \zeta_{1}, \cdots, \zeta_{n}$. It is enough to verify this for monomials since $E$ is a linear mapping of the polynomial algebra. For monomials one can either
carry through a direct verification or establish the result in the ring $Z\left[\xi_{1}, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right]$ by using the corresponding functional result on vector spaces over the rationals. We show next that $\Delta^{b}{ }_{a} n=(a, a, b)$. For this we fix $a$ and consider $(a, a, b)-\Delta^{b}{ }_{a} n$ as function of $a$. This is homogeneous of degree two or 0 , and applying $\frac{1}{2} \Delta^{c}$ gives $\frac{1}{2} \Delta^{c}{ }_{a}(a, a, b)-\frac{1}{2} \Delta^{c}{ }_{a} \Delta^{b} n=(a, c, b)-(a, c, b)=0$. Since $(a, a, b)-\Delta^{b}{ }_{a}$ is homogeneous of degree two or is 0 this implies that $(a, a, b)=\Delta^{b}{ }_{a} n$. We can now use this result and the chain rule for differentiation to evaluate $\Delta^{d} F$ for $F(a, b, c)$ given by the right-hand side regarded as a function of $a$. A simple calculation which we suppress gives $\Delta^{d} F=(d, b, c)$. On the other hand, since $F(a, b, c)$ is linear in $a$ we have $\Delta^{d} F=F(d, b, c)$. Hence $F(a, b, c)=(a, b, c)$ and (12') holds.

As a special case of formula $\left(68^{\prime \prime}\right)$ of Chapter VI (p. 243) we have $\Delta_{a}^{b} n=t(\operatorname{adj} a, b)$. Then, by (7) and (8) we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
(a, b, c)=t(a \times b, c) \tag{13}
\end{equation*}
$$

which implies that the right-hand side is symmetric in $a, b$ and $c$. Substituting (11) in this we obtain

$$
\begin{align*}
(a, b, c)= & t(a . b . c)-\frac{1}{2} t(a) t(b . c)-\frac{1}{2} t(b) t(a . c) \\
& -\frac{1}{2} t(c) t(a . b)+\frac{1}{2} t(a) t(b) t(c) \tag{14}
\end{align*}
$$

For characteristic $\neq 3$ this gives formulas for $n(a, b, c)$ and for $n(a)$ in terms of the trace functions.

We have demonstrated here and elsewhere the efficacy of the differential calculus in establishing identities. We shall now develop another method for verifying identities. For this we shall need some additional consequences of the structure theory. Suppose the base field is algebraically closed and $E=\left\{e_{i}\right\}$ is a reducing set of idempotents in the reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$. Let $u_{12}$ and $u_{13}$ be elements of the corresponding Peirce spaces $\mathfrak{I}_{12}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{13}$ such that $u_{12}{ }^{\cdot 2}=\mu^{2}\left(e_{1}+e_{2}\right), u_{13}^{\cdot 2}=v^{2}\left(e_{1}+e_{3}\right)$ where $\mu v \neq 0$. Then $\left(\mu^{-1} u_{12}\right)^{\cdot 2}=e_{1}+e_{2}$, $\left(v^{-1} u_{13}\right)^{\cdot 2}=e_{1}+e_{3}$. Let $\eta$ be a coordinatization of $\mathfrak{J}$ adapted to the $e_{i}$ and $\mu^{-1} u_{12}, v^{-1} u_{13}$. Then $\mathfrak{J}^{\eta}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ where $J_{1}$ is the standard involution. Moreover, $e_{i}{ }^{\eta}=e_{i i}, u_{12}{ }^{\eta}=\mu[12]=\mu[21], u_{13}{ }^{\eta}=v[13]=v[31]$. Let $F=\left\{f_{i}\right\}$ be a second reducing set of idempotents for $\mathfrak{J}, v_{12}, v_{13}$ elements of the corresponding Peirce $(1,2)$ and $(1,3)$ spaces such that $v_{12} \cdot{ }^{2} \neq 0, v_{13} \cdot{ }^{2} \neq 0$. Then there is an isomorphism $\zeta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto an algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}{ }^{\prime}, J_{1}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{O}^{\prime}$ (like $\mathfrak{D}$ ) is octonion such that $f_{i}{ }^{\zeta}=e_{t i}, v_{12}{ }^{\zeta}=\mu^{\prime}[12], v_{13}{ }^{\zeta}=v^{\prime}[13]$ (in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}{ }^{\prime}, J_{1}\right)$ ) where $\mu^{\prime}, v^{\prime} \in \Phi$. Since the base field is algebraically closed the octonion algebras $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ and $\left(\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}, j\right)$ are split and hence are isomorphic (Theorem 4.7, p. 169). Hence there exists an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}{ }^{\prime}, J_{1}\right)$ sending $1[i j] \rightarrow 1[i j]$ for all $i, j$. It follows that there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $e_{i}=f_{i}, i=1,2,3$ and $u_{12}{ }^{\sigma}=\alpha v_{12}, u_{13}{ }^{\sigma}=\beta v_{13}, \alpha, \beta \in \Phi$.

Let $\mathfrak{J}^{(r)}$ be a vector space direct sum of $r$ copies of $\mathfrak{J}$ and let $f$ be a polynomial
function on $\mathfrak{J}^{(r)}$. We denote the elements of $\mathfrak{J}^{(r)}$ as $r$-tuples $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{r}\right), a_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$, and let $f\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{r}\right)$ be the value of $f$ at $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{r}\right)$. We can now prove the following

Lemma 1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional exceptional simple Jordan algebra over an algebraically closed field and let $f$ be a polynomial function on $\mathfrak{J}^{(r)}$. Assume that if $f\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{r}\right)=0$ then $f\left(a_{1}{ }^{\sigma}, a_{2}{ }^{\sigma}, \cdots, a_{r}{ }^{\sigma}\right)=0$ for every automorphism $\sigma$ of $\mathfrak{J}$. Assume also that if $\eta$ is a particular coordinatization of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ then $f\left(b_{1}{ }^{\eta^{-1}}, b_{2}{ }^{\eta^{-1}}, a_{3}, \cdots, a_{r}\right)=0$ for all $b_{1}$ of the form $\sum \alpha_{i} e_{i i}, b_{2}$ of the form $\sum \beta_{i} e_{i i}+u[23]+\mu[12]+v[13]$ and arbitrary $a_{j}, j \geqq 3$, where $\alpha_{i}, \beta_{i}, \mu, v \in \Phi$ and $u \in \mathfrak{D}$. Then $f=0$.

Proof. We note first that since the set of elements $a$ such that the minimum polynomial $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ has three distinct roots is Zariski open it is enough to prove that $f\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{r}\right)=0$ for all $a_{1}$ such that $\mu_{a_{1}}(\lambda)$ has three distinct roots, $a_{j}$ arbitrary in $\mathfrak{J}$ if $j \geqq 2$. Then $a_{1}=\sum_{1}^{3} \alpha_{i} f_{\imath}$ where the $f_{i}$ form a reducing set of idempotents. Then there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $a_{1}{ }^{\sigma}=b_{1}{ }^{\eta-1}$ where $b_{1} =\sum \alpha_{i} e_{i i}$. The first hypothesis implies that if $f\left(b_{1}{ }^{\eta^{-1}}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{r}\right)=0$ for all $b_{1}=\sum \alpha_{i} e_{i i}, a_{j}$ arbitrary for $j \geqq 2$, then $f=0$. Write $a_{2}{ }^{\eta}=\sum \beta_{i} e_{i i}+u[23] +v[12]+w[13], \beta_{i} \in \Phi, u, v, w \in \mathfrak{D}$. Then the subset of $a_{2}$ such that $n(v) n(w) \neq 0$ is Zariski open so if $f\left(b_{1}{ }^{\eta^{-1}}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{r}\right)=0$ for $b_{1}=\sum \alpha_{i} e_{i i}$ and all $a_{2}$ in this subset, $a_{j}$ arbitrary if $j \geqq 3$ then $f=0$. The condition $n(v) n(w) \neq 0$ and the result noted above on automorphism implies that there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $b_{1}{ }^{\eta^{-1} \sigma}=b_{1}{ }^{\eta^{-1}}$ and $a_{2}{ }^{\sigma}=b_{2}{ }^{\eta^{-1}}$ where $b_{2}=\sum \beta_{i} e_{i i}+u^{\prime}[23]+\mu[12] +v[13]$ where $\mu, v \in \Phi$ and $u^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{O}$. It follows that $f=0$ if $f\left(b_{1}{ }^{\eta^{-1}}, b_{2}{ }^{\eta-1}, a_{3}, \cdots, a_{r}\right) =0$ for arbitrary $a_{j} \in \mathfrak{J}$ and $b_{1}$ and $b_{2}$ of the indicated form.

We shall use this lemma to prove the following important identity for $Q(a)=\frac{1}{2} t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)=\frac{1}{2} t(a, a)$ :

$$
\begin{equation*}
4\left[Q\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)-Q(a)^{2}\right]=t(a)\left[2 t\left(a^{\cdot 3}\right)-t(a) t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)+2 n(a)\right] \tag{15}
\end{equation*}
$$

It suffices to prove this for algebraically closed base fields. Since $t\left(a^{\eta}\right)=t(a)$ and $n\left(a^{\eta}\right)=n(a)$ for any isomorphism $\eta$ it is sufficient in view of the lemma to verify (15) for every $a$ of the form $\sum_{1}^{3} \alpha_{i} e_{i i}$ in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$. Then $Q(a)=\frac{1}{2} \sum_{1}^{3} \alpha_{t}{ }^{2}, Q\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right) =\frac{1}{2} \sum \alpha_{i}{ }^{4}, t\left(a^{\cdot k}\right)=\sum \alpha_{i}{ }^{k}, n(a)=\alpha_{1} \alpha_{2} \alpha_{3}$. Then the verification of (15) becomes a schoolboy exercise.

In the sequel we shall be concerned from time to time with subalgebras of a finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebra J generated by two elements. Such subalgebras are special by the Shirshov-Cohn theorem. We shall now establish the following result on dimensionalities of such subalgebras.

Lemma 2. Let J be a finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{B}$ a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ generated by 1 and two elements $a$ and $b$. Then $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B} \leqq 9$.

Proof. We may assume the base field is algebraically closed. We suppose first that the minimum polynomial of $a$ has three distinct roots. Then $\Phi[a]=\Phi e_{1} \oplus \Phi e_{2} \oplus \Phi e_{3}$ where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents $\neq 0$. Using a suitable coordinatization we can identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ in such a way that $e_{i}$ is identified with $e_{i i}$. Then we have $b=\sum \beta_{i} e_{i}+u[23]+v[31]+w[12]$ and $4 b \cdot e_{1} \cdot e_{2} =w[12] \in \mathfrak{B}$. Similarly, $u$ [23] and $v[31] \in \mathfrak{B}$. Evidently $\mathfrak{B}$ is generated by the $e_{i}$ and the elements $u$ [23], $v$ [31], $w[12]$. Since for $c, d \in \mathfrak{O}$ and $i, j, k$ distinct we have the multiplication formula $2 c[i j] . d[j k]=c d[i k]$ we see that $\mathfrak{B}$ contains the elements $u v[21]=v \bar{u}[12], v w[32]$ and $w u[13]$. It is immediate from the formulas $\left(18^{\prime}\right)-\left(22^{\prime}\right)$ of §3.2 that the product of any two of the nine elements $e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}$, $u[23], v[31], w[12], u v[21], v w[32], w u[13]$ is a linear combination of these elements. Hence $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B} \leqq 9$ if $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ has three distinct roots. Now let $F J^{(2)}$ be the free Jordan algebra with 1 generated by two elements $x$ and $y$. If $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$ let $\eta(a, b)$ be the homomorphism of $F J^{(2)}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, x \rightarrow a, y \rightarrow b$. Then if $z_{1}, z_{2}, \cdots, z_{10}$ are fixed elements of $F J^{(2)}$ we can define a mapping of $\mathfrak{J}^{(2)}$ into the exterior algebra $E(\mathfrak{J})$ by $(a, b) \rightarrow z_{1}{ }^{\eta(a, b)} \wedge z_{2}{ }^{\eta(a, b)} \wedge \cdots \wedge z_{10}{ }^{\eta(a b)}$ where $\wedge$ denotes the product in $E(\mathfrak{J})$. This is a polynomial mapping. Moreover, since the subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}$ generated by 1 and $a, b$ such that $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ has three distinct roots has dimensionality $<10$, it is clear that the mapping we have defined is 0 for all $a$ in an open subset and all $b$ in $\mathfrak{J}$. It follows that the mapping is 0 . This implies that if $\mathfrak{B}$ is a subalgebra generated by 1 and any $a$ and $b$ then any ten elements $c_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ are linearly dependent since $c_{1} \wedge \cdots \wedge c_{10}=0$. Hence $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B} \leqq 9$.

The bound given in Lemma 2 is exact. For example, in $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ take $a=\Sigma_{1}^{3} \alpha_{i} e_{i i}$ where the $\alpha_{1}$ are distinct and let $b=1[23]+1[31]+w[12]$ where $w \notin \Phi 1$. Then the subalgebra $\mathfrak{B}$ generated by $1, a$ and $b$ contains every $1[i j]$, $i, j=1,2,3$ and $w[12]$. Hence, by Theorem 3.2, $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{y}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{D}$ is the subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ generated by 1 and $w$. Since $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}=2, \operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=9$.

## Exercises

1. (Seligman). Prove the following identity for $\mathfrak{J}$ ( $\mathfrak{J}$ any finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebra):

$$
4 t(a \times a, b \times(c \times a))=t(b, c) n(a)+t(a, b)(a, a, c) .
$$

2. Let ( $u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{27}$ ) be a basis for $\mathfrak{J}, \xi_{1}, \xi_{2}, \cdots, \xi_{27}, \eta_{1}, \eta_{2}, \cdots, \eta_{27}$ indeterminates $\mathrm{P}=\Phi\left(\xi_{i}, \eta_{j}\right)$. Show that the subalgebra of $\Im_{\mathrm{P}}$ generated by $1, x=\Sigma \xi_{i} u_{i}$, and $y=\sum \eta_{i} u_{i}$ is special central simple of degree three and dimension nine.
3. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be as in 1., $\Phi$ infinite and let $f$ be an element of the free Jordan algebra $F J^{(2)}$ with 1 and two generators $x, y$ which is an identity for $\Phi_{3}{ }^{+}$, that is, $f$ is mapped into 0 by every homomorphism of $F J^{(2)}$ into $\Phi_{3}{ }^{+}$(cf. §1.9). Show that $f$ is an identity for $\mathfrak{J}$.
4. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be as in exercise 1 , and let $p_{k}=\left[x^{. k}, y, y\right]$ in $F J^{(2)}$. Show that

$$
f=\left[\left[p_{3}, p_{1}, p_{1}\right], p_{2}, p_{2}\right] \neq 0
$$

and that $f$ is an identity for $\mathfrak{J}$.
5. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a Jordan algebra with 1 such that there exists a positive integer $n$ such that every element of $\mathfrak{J}$ is algebraic of degree $\leqq n$, Show that there exists an element $f \neq 0$ in $F J^{(2)}$ which is an identity for $\mathfrak{J}$.
6. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ the Jordan algebra of a symmetric bilinear form $f$ on the vector space $\mathfrak{B}$ and let $F J^{(5)}$ be the free Jordan algebra with 1 and generators $x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}, x_{5}$. Show that $\left[\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right]^{\cdot 2}, x_{4}, x_{5}\right]$ defines a nontrivial identity for $\mathfrak{J}$.
2. Elements of rank one. Uniqueness of the coefficient algebra. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebra. An element $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ is said to be of rank one if $a \neq 0$ and $a \times a=0$. Let $\Pi=\Pi(\mathfrak{J})$ be the set of elements of rank one in $\mathfrak{J}$. If $(a, b, c)=\frac{1}{2} \Delta^{c}{ }_{a} \Delta^{b}{ }_{a} n$ as in (8) then we have seen in (13) that $(a, b, c)=t(a \times b, c)$. Since the trace form is nondegenerate it is clear that $a \in \Pi$ if and only if $a \neq 0$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
(a, a, b)=0 \tag{16}
\end{equation*}
$$

for all $b \in \mathfrak{J}$. If $a$ is an element of $\mathfrak{J}$ then $a$ defines a symmetric bilinear form $F_{a}$ on $\mathfrak{J}$ given by $F_{a}(u, v)=(a, u, v)$. The radical $\Re_{a}$ of $F_{a}$ is the set of $z$ such that $(a, z, v) =0$ for all $v$. Hence we see that $a \in \Pi$ if and only if $a \neq 0$ and $a \in \Re_{a}$. We have $a \times a=a^{.2}-t(a) a+\frac{1}{2}\left[t(a)^{2}-t\left(a^{.2}\right)\right] 1$. Hence if $a \times a=0$ and $t(a)=0$ then $a^{\cdot 2}=\frac{1}{2} t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right) 1$ so $t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)=\frac{3}{2} t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)$ and $t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)=0$. Thus $a^{\cdot 2}=0$. If $a \times a=0$ and $t(a)=1$ then $a^{.2}-a=\frac{1}{2}\left[t\left(a^{.2}\right)-1\right] 1$ so $t\left(a^{.2}\right)-1=\frac{3}{2}\left(t\left(a^{.2}\right)-1\right)=0$. Then $a^{.2}=a$. It follows that $a \in \Pi$ if and only if $a \neq 0$ and $a^{.2}=0$ or $a=\alpha e$ where $\alpha \neq 0$ is in $\Phi$ and $e$ is a primitive idempotent. It is clear from this that $\Pi=\varnothing$ or $\Pi \neq \varnothing$ according as $\mathfrak{J}$ is a division algebra or $\mathfrak{J}$ is reduced.

Let $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ be a second finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebra and let $\eta$ be a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$, so $\eta$ is linear and bijective and $n\left(a^{\eta}\right)=\rho n(a)$ for a fixed nonzero $\rho$ in $\Phi$ and all $a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Since $\eta$ is additive it is clear from (12') that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left(a^{\eta}, b^{\eta}, c^{\eta}\right)=\rho(a, b, c), a, b, c \in \mathfrak{J} . \tag{17}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since $(a, b, c)=t(a \times b, c)$ we have $t\left(a^{\eta} \times b^{\eta}, c^{\eta}\right)=\rho t(a \times b, c)$. Let $\eta^{*}$ denote the adjoint of $\eta$ relative to the trace forms in $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}: t\left(a^{\eta}, b^{\prime}\right)=t\left(a, b^{\prime \eta^{*}}\right), a \in \mathfrak{J}$, $b^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Also put $\hat{\eta}=\left(\eta^{*}\right)^{-1}$. Then we have $t\left(\left(a^{\eta} \times b^{\eta}\right)^{\eta^{*}}, c\right)=\rho t(a \times b, c)$ and since $t$ is nondegenerate, $\left(a^{\eta} \times b^{\eta}\right)^{\eta^{*}}=\rho a \times b$, or

$$
\begin{equation*}
a^{\eta} \times b^{\eta}=\rho(a \times b)^{\eta} \tag{18}
\end{equation*}
$$

This evidently implies that if $a \in \Pi(\mathfrak{J})$ then $a^{\eta} \in \Pi\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$. Let $F_{a}$ be the symmetric bilinear form defined above by $a$ : $F_{a}(b, c)=(a, b, c)$. Then it is clear from (17)
that $F_{a} \eta\left(b^{\eta}, c^{\eta}\right)=\rho F_{a}(b, c)$. Hence $\eta$ is a similarity with ratio $\rho$ of $F_{a}$ on $\mathfrak{J}$ with $F_{a}{ }^{\eta}$ on $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$.

It follows from the results of §6.7 that if $|\Phi|>3$ then $\eta$ is a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ if and only if $\eta$ is an isotopy, $\eta$ is an isomorphism if and only if it is a norm similarity and $1^{\eta}=1^{\prime}$ the identity of $\mathfrak{I}^{\prime}$. Also if $\eta$ is a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ then $\eta^{*}$ is a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\hat{\eta}$ is one from $\mathfrak{J}$ to $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. These results can be established also by another argument which is valid also in the extreme case in which $|\Phi|=3$. We shall indicate this method in the exercises. We remark also that any octonion algebra over a finite field is split since any nondegenerate quadratic form on a vector space of dimensionality $>3$ over a finite field has positive Witt index. It follows that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is reduced and has a coordinatization such that the associated octonion algebra is a division algebra then the base field is necessarily infinite. This case will be the one of primary interest in this section.

We recall that the norm similarities of $\mathfrak{J}$ form a group $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ which contains the norm preserving group $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ consisting of the bijective linear mappings $\eta$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $n\left(a^{\eta}\right)=n(a), a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Moreover, $\mathbf{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ contains the subgroups $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(1)}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)}(\mathfrak{J})$ which are defined to be the sets of mappings in $\mathfrak{J}$ of the form $\Pi U_{a_{i}}$ such that $\Pi n\left(a_{i}\right)^{2}=1$ and $\Pi n\left(a_{i}\right)=1$ respectively. We now assume that $\mathfrak{J}$ contains subalgebras $\mathfrak{K}$ which are nine-dimensional reduced simple of degree three and nonsplit. It is immediate from the determination of reduced simple Jordan algebras given in §5.6 that such a subalgebra is isomorphic to an algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $(\mathrm{P}, j)$ is a quadratic field and conversely. It is clear that if $\mathfrak{J}$ has a coordinatization onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{O}$ is a division algebra then $\mathfrak{J}$ satisfies our condition. If $\Re$ is any subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ we let $\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(1)}{ }_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K})$ and $\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)}{ }_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K})$ be the subgroups of $\mathbf{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ of elements of the form $\Pi U_{a_{i}}$ where the $a_{i} \in \Re$ and $\Pi n\left(a_{i}\right)^{2}=1$ and $\Pi n\left(a_{i}\right)=1$ respectively. Also if $\mathfrak{J}$ contains nonsplit nine-dimensional reduced simple subalgebras $\mathfrak{\Omega}$ of degree three then we let $\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ be the subgroup of $\mathbf{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by all the $\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)} \mathfrak{J}(\mathfrak{K})$ for $\mathfrak{K}$ of the type specified.

Let $\Re$ be as indicated. Then $\Re$ contains a reducing set of three idempotents $e_{i}$. We must have $\sum_{1}{ }^{3} e_{i}=1$, the identity of $\mathfrak{J}$ so $\Re$ contains 1 . Also $\Re$ contains an element $u_{1 j}$ in the Peirce space $\mathfrak{K}_{1 j}$ (hence in $\mathfrak{J}_{1 j}$ ), $j=2,3$, such that $u_{1 j}{ }^{2} =\gamma^{-1}\left(e_{1}+e_{j}\right)$. Then we have a coordinatization $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ adapted to the $e_{i}$ and $u_{1 j}$ and it is clear that $\mathfrak{K}^{\eta}$ is a subalgebra of the form $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ of $\mathfrak{J}^{\eta}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where ( $\mathrm{P}, j$ ) is a quadratic subfield of ( $\mathfrak{D}, j$ ). We now consider the group acting in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ corresponding to $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)}{ }_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K})$. This is the set of mappings in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ of the form $U_{A_{1}} U_{A_{2}}^{\prime} \cdots U_{A_{r}}$ where the $A_{i} \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and $\Pi_{1}^{r} n\left(A_{i}\right)=1$, or, since $n\left(A_{i}\right)$ coincides with the usual determinant, $\operatorname{det}\left(A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{r}\right)=1$. Then we have

Lemma 1. Let $(\mathrm{P}, j)$ be a quadratic subfield of the octonion algebra $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. Let $B \in \mathrm{P}_{3}$ and $X \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and put $B^{*}=B^{J \gamma}$. Then $\left(B^{*} X\right) B=B^{*}(X B)$ and $T_{B}: X \rightarrow B^{*} X B \equiv B^{*}(X B)$ is a mapping of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ into itself. Moreover, the
set of $T_{B}$ with $\operatorname{det} B=1$ coincides with the group of mappings of the form $U_{A_{1}} U_{A_{2}} \cdots U_{A_{r}}$ where the $A_{i} \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and $\Pi n\left(A_{i}\right)=1$ and this group is generated by the $T_{Q_{i j}}$ where $Q_{i j}=1+q e_{i j}, q \in \mathrm{P}, i \neq j$. Finally, $T_{B}{ }^{*}$, the adjoint of $T_{B}$ relative to the trace form in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$, coincides with $T_{B^{*}}$. Hence the group of these elements with $\operatorname{det} B=1$ is closed under the adjoint mapping.

Proof. Since $\mathbf{P}$ is a quadratic subfield of $\mathfrak{O}$ we have $\left[\rho_{1}, \rho_{2}, x\right]=\left[\rho_{1}, x, \rho_{2}\right] =\left[x, \rho_{1}, \rho_{2}\right]=0$ if $x \in \mathfrak{O}$ and $\rho_{i} \in \mathrm{P}$ by the alternative identities. It follows that if $X \in \mathfrak{O}_{3}$ and $B_{1}, B_{2} \in \mathrm{P}_{3}$ then $\left[B_{1}, B_{2}, X\right]=\left[B_{1}, X, B_{2}\right]=\left[X, B_{1}, B_{2}\right]=0$. If $B \in \mathrm{P}_{3}$ then $B^{*}=B^{J \gamma} \in \mathrm{P}_{3}$ so $B^{*} X B=B^{*}(X B)=\left(B^{*} X\right) B$.
