It follows that $T_{B}: X \rightarrow B^{*} X B$ maps $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ into itself and $T_{B_{1} B_{2}}=T_{B_{1}} T_{B_{2}}$ if $B_{i} \in \mathrm{P}_{3}$. If $A \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ then the indicated associativities imply that $X U_{A}=2 X . A . A-X . A^{\cdot 2} =A X A$. Hence, if $A_{i} \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ then $X U_{A_{1}} U_{A_{2}} \cdots U_{A_{r}}=A_{r} A_{r-1} \cdots A_{1} X A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{r} =B^{*} X B$ where $B=A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{r} \in \mathrm{P}_{3}$. Thus if $\Pi_{1}^{r} n\left(A_{i}\right)=1$ then $\operatorname{det} B=1$ and $U_{A_{1}} U_{A_{2}} \cdots U_{A_{r}}=T_{B}$. We note next that $T_{B_{1}} T_{B_{2}}=T_{B_{1} B_{2}}$ and the fact that the unimodular group $S L(\mathrm{P}, 3)$ is generated by the elementary matrices $Q_{i j}=1+q e_{i j}$, $q \in \mathrm{P}, i \neq j$, imply that every $T_{B}, \operatorname{det} B=1$, is a product of $T_{Q_{i j}}$. Thus to show that every $T_{B}, \operatorname{det} B=1$, has the form $U_{A_{1}} U_{A_{2}} \cdots U_{A_{r}}$ where the $A_{l} \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and $\Pi n\left(A_{i}\right)=1$ it is enough to show that every $Q_{i j}$ is a product of $A_{l} \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$. Let $k \neq i, j$. Then $\left(1+q e_{i j}\right)\left(\bar{q}^{-1} e_{i j}+q^{-1} e_{j i}+e_{k k}\right)=\bar{q}^{-1} e_{i j}+q^{-1} e_{j i}+e_{i i}+e_{k k}$ and $C_{1}=\bar{q}^{-1} e_{i j}+q^{-1} e_{j i}+e_{k k}$ and $C_{2}=\bar{q}^{-1} e_{i j}+q^{-1} e_{j i}+e_{i i}+\overline{e_{k k}} \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$. Then $A_{l}=C_{l} \gamma \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and $Q_{i j}=A_{2} A_{1}{ }^{-1}$ is a product of elements of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$. We note next that if $A_{i} \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ then $U_{A_{i}}{ }^{*}=U_{A_{i}}$ since $R_{A}$ is selfadjoint for every $A \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ (by the associativity of the trace form). If $B=A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{r}$ then $T_{B}=U_{A_{1}} U_{A_{2}} \cdots U_{A_{r}}$ and $T_{B}{ }^{*}=U_{A_{r}} U_{A_{r-1}} \cdots U_{A_{1}}=T_{A_{r} \ldots A_{1}}=T_{B^{*}}$. This completes the proof.

We have denoted the set of elements of rank one of the reduced exceptional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ by $\Pi$. If $a \in \Pi$ we write $[a]$ for the ray $\Phi^{*} a$ of multiples $\alpha a, \alpha^{\prime \prime} \neq 0$ in $\Phi$. Also let $[\Pi]$ be the collection of these rays. We have seen that the group M (J) maps $\Pi$ into itself. Hence this maps $[\Pi]$ into itself and the same is true of the varioussubgroups of $\mathbf{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ we have defined. We now prove

Lemma 2. Let J be a reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra which has a coordinatization $\eta$ onto an algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ such that $\mathfrak{D}$ is an octonion division algebra. Let $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{I})$ be the subgroup of $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by the elements of the form $\zeta=\Pi U_{a_{i}}$ where the elements $a_{i}$ for a given $\zeta$ are all contained in the same nonsplit nine-dimensional reduced simple subalgebra of degree three, and $\Pi n\left(a_{i}\right)=1$. Then $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ is transitive on $[\Pi]$.

Proof. We may identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$. Since $\mathfrak{O}$ is a division algebra any $q \in \mathfrak{O}$ is contained in a quadratic subfield. Hence it is clear from Lemma 1 that the subgroup of $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by the elements $T_{Q_{i j}}$ where $Q_{i j}=1+q e_{i j}, i \neq j$, $q \in \mathfrak{D}$, is a subgroup of $\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$. Hence it is sufficient to show that this subgroup
is transitive on [ $\Pi$ ]. If $A \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ is given as in (1), so $A=\sum_{1}^{3} \alpha_{i} e_{i i}+a$ [23] $+b[31]+c[12]$, then it is immediate from the formula (6) for $A \times A$ that if $A \times A=0$ and $\alpha_{1}=0$ then $n(b)=n(c)=0$ so $b=c=0$. Also if $b=0$ then either $\alpha_{1}=0$ or $\alpha_{3}=0$. It follows from this and similar considerations on the other entries of $A$ that if $A \in \Pi$ then either $A$ is a multiple of an element of one of the following forms:

$$
\begin{gather*}
e_{11}+\gamma_{2}^{-1} \gamma_{1} n(q) e_{22}+q[12], \quad e_{22}+\gamma_{3}^{-1} \gamma_{2} n(q) e_{33}+q[23], \\
e_{33}+\gamma_{1}^{-1} \gamma_{3} n(q) e_{11}+q[31], \quad q \in \mathfrak{D}, \tag{19}
\end{gather*}
$$

or every entry of the matrix $A$ is nonzero. A direct calculation shows that the effect of $T_{Q_{i j}}$ is given by the following table:

$$
\begin{align*}
e_{i i} T_{Q_{i j}} & =e_{i i}+\gamma_{j}^{-1} \gamma_{i} n(q) e_{j j}+q[i j], e_{j j} T_{Q_{i j}}=e_{j j}, \quad e_{k k} T_{Q_{i j}}=e_{k k}, \\
x[i j] T_{Q_{i j}} & =x[i j]+\gamma_{j}^{-1} \gamma_{i} t(\bar{q} x) e_{j j}, \quad x[j k] T_{Q_{i j}}=x[j k],  \tag{20}\\
x\left[i k T_{Q_{i j}}\right. & =x[i k]+(\bar{q} x)[j k], \quad i, j, k \neq .
\end{align*}
$$

The first of these shows that the orbit of $e_{i i}$ under $\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ contains every element of the form $e_{i i}+\gamma_{j}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{i} n(q) e_{j j}+q[i j], q \in \mathfrak{D}$. We observe next that $\Pi$ contains elements all of whose entries are nonzero. For example, $\left(\sum_{i, j} e_{i j}\right) \gamma$ is such an element. If $A$ is as in (1), then (20) shows that the component in $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ (in the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the $e_{i i}$ ) of the element $A T_{Q_{i j}}$ is $x[i j]+\alpha_{i i} q[i j]$ where $x[i j]$ is the component of $A$ in $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. If $\alpha_{i i} \neq 0, q$ can be chosen so that this is 0 . Hence if $A \in \Pi$ has all of its entries $\neq 0$ then for every $i \neq j$ the orbit of $A$ under $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ contains either an element of the form $\rho\left(e_{j j}+\gamma_{k}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{j} n(q) e_{k k}+q[j k]\right)$ or of the form $\rho\left(e_{i i}+\gamma_{k}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{i} n(q) e_{k k}+q[i k]\right)$ where $\rho \neq 0$ is in $\Phi$. It follows that the orbit of $[A]$ contains $\left[e_{i}\right], i=1,2,3$. Thus the orbit of $\left[e_{i}\right]$ contains every $[A]$ having only nonzero entries. Clearly our results imply that the orbit of $\left[e_{i}\right]$ is $[\Pi]$ so we have the transitivity of $\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ on $[\Pi]$.

We have seen above that if $\eta$ is a norm similarity in $\mathfrak{J}$ then the symmetric bilinear forms $F_{a}$ and $F_{a^{\eta}}$ are similar for any $a \in \mathfrak{J}$. Hence the following is an immediate consequence of Lemma 2.

Lemma 3. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is as in Lemma 2 then the symmetric bilinear forms $F_{a}, F_{b}$ determined by any two elements $a, b \in \Pi$ are similar.

We shall now determine the form of $F_{e}$ for a primitive idempotent $e$. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)+\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)+\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$ be the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative $e$. Also put $f=1-e$ and let $f=e_{2}+e_{3}$ where the $e_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents. Then $E=\left\{e_{1}=e, e_{2}, e_{3}\right\}$ is a reducing set of idempotents for $\mathfrak{J}$. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ be the Peirce decomposition relative to the $e_{i}$. Then $\mathfrak{I}_{1}(e)=\mathfrak{I}_{11}=\Phi e_{1}, \mathfrak{I}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)=\mathfrak{I}_{12}+\mathfrak{I}_{13}$, $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)=\Phi e_{2}+\Phi e_{3}+\mathfrak{J}_{23}$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}=16, \operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)=10$. We have $e \times e=0$
and if $a \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ then $a \times e=a . e-\frac{1}{2} t(a) e-\frac{1}{2} t(e) a+\frac{1}{2}[t(a) t(e)-t(a . e)] 1=0$ since $a . e=\frac{1}{2} a, t(e)=1$ and $t(a)=0$. Since $F_{e}(u, v)=(e, u, v)=t(e \times u, v)$ the radical $\Re_{e}$ of $F_{e}$ is the set of $u$ such that $e \times u=0$ and we see that $\Re_{e} \supseteq \Phi e+\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$. Now let $b \in \mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ so we can write $b=\alpha e_{2}+\beta e_{3}+c$ where $\alpha, \beta \in \Phi$ and $c \in \mathfrak{J}_{23}$. Then we have $e \times b=\frac{1}{2}\left(\beta e_{2}+\alpha e_{3}-c\right)$ and so

$$
\begin{align*}
F_{e}(b, b) & =t(e \times b, b)=\frac{1}{2} t\left(\beta e_{2}+\alpha e_{3}-c, \alpha e_{2}+\beta e_{3}+c\right) \\
& =\alpha \beta-\frac{1}{2} t\left(c^{\cdot 2}\right)=\alpha \beta-Q(c) \tag{21}
\end{align*}
$$

Hence $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ is nonisotropic relative to $F_{e}$ and consequently $\Re_{e}=\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)+\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$ and $\mathfrak{J} / \Re_{e} \cong \mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ where the isomorphism is one of the vector spaces relative to $F_{e}$ and the induced form in $\mathfrak{J} / \Re_{e}$. The restriction of $F_{e}$ to $\Phi e_{2}+\Phi e_{3}$ has positive Witt index so this space is a hyperbolic plane. Since any two hyperbolic planes are isomorphic it follows from Witt's theorem (Jacobson, Lectures, vol. II, p. 162) that the equivalence class of the restriction of $Q$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{23}$ is determined by that of $F_{e}$ on $\mathfrak{J}$. Thus the equivalence class of $Q$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{23}$ is independent of the choice of the orthogonal idempotents $e_{2}$ and $e_{3}$ such that $e_{2}+e_{3}=f=1-e$. Now let $u_{1 j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{1 j}$ so that $u_{1 j}{ }^{2}=\gamma_{j}{ }^{-1}\left(e_{1}+e_{j}\right), j=2,3$, and let $\eta$ be a coordinatization of $\mathfrak{J}$ adapted to the $e_{i}$ and $u_{1 j}$. Let $\mathfrak{J}^{\eta}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and let $a \in \mathfrak{D}$; then $a[23]^{2^{2}} =\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{3} n(a)\left(e_{22}+e_{33}\right)$ and $Q(a[23])=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{3} n(a)$. It follows that we have a similarity with ratio $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{\mathbf{2}}{ }^{\boldsymbol{-} \mathbf{1}} \gamma_{\mathbf{3}}$ of the restriction of $Q$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbf{2 3}}$ with the norm form on $\mathfrak{D}$. We can now prove the following

Lemma 4. Let $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right), \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}^{\prime}, J_{\gamma^{\prime}}\right)$ be exceptional Jordan matrix algebras, $\mathfrak{D}, \mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ octonion algebras. Assume that there exists a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}^{\prime}{ }_{3}, J_{\gamma^{\prime}}\right)$ which maps the element $e_{11}$ of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ onto $e_{11}$ of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}^{\prime}, J_{\gamma^{\prime}}\right)$. Then the norm forms of $\mathfrak{D}$ and $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ are similar.

Proof. The hypothesis implies that there exists a similarity of the forms $Q$ on the Peirce $(2,3)$-spaces of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}{ }^{\prime}, J_{\gamma^{\prime}}\right)$ relative to the diagonal idempotents. Then the result noted just before the statement of the lemma implies the norm similarity of $\mathfrak{O}$ and $\mathfrak{O}^{\prime}$.

We now consider the norm forms of composition algebras and we prove the following

Lemma 5. Let $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{i}, j\right), i=1,2$, be a composition algebra, $\left(\mathfrak{B}_{i}, j\right)$ a composition subalgebra $(=$ nonisotropic subalgebra containing 1). Assume the norm forms of $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{1}, j\right)$ and $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{2}, j\right)$ are similar and that $\sigma$ is an isomorphism of $\left(\mathfrak{B}_{1}, j\right)$ onto $\left(\mathfrak{B}_{2}, j\right)$. Then $\sigma$ can be extended to an isomorphism of $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{1}, j\right)$ onto $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{2}, j\right)$.

Proof. Our first assumption is that there exists a bijective linear mapping $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{D}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{D}_{2}$ such that for a $\rho \neq 0$ in $\Phi$ we have $n_{2}\left(a_{1}^{\eta}\right)=\rho n_{1}\left(a_{1}\right), a_{1} \in \mathfrak{D}_{1}, n_{i}$ the norm form on $\mathfrak{D}_{i}$. Then $n_{2}\left(1^{\eta}\right)=\rho$ if 1 is the identity of $\mathfrak{D}_{1}$. Then $1^{\eta}$ is invertible in $\mathfrak{D}_{2}$. Let $\zeta$ be defined by $a_{1}^{\zeta}=a_{1}^{\eta}\left(1^{\eta}\right)^{-1}$. Then $n_{2}\left(a_{1}^{\zeta}\right)=n_{2}\left(a_{1}^{\eta}\right) n_{2}\left(1^{\eta}\right)^{-1}=n_{1}\left(a_{1}\right)$.

Hence $n_{2}$ and $n_{1}$ are equivalent, that is, we may assume $\rho=1$. Now let $\sigma$ be an isomorphism of ( $\mathfrak{B}_{1}, j$ ) onto ( $\mathfrak{B}_{2}, j$ ). Then $n_{2}\left(b_{1}{ }^{\sigma}\right)=n_{1}\left(b_{1}\right), b_{1} \in \mathfrak{B}_{1}$. Hence by Witt's theorem, there exists a bijective linear mapping $\tau$ of $\mathfrak{B}_{1}{ }^{\perp}$ onto $\mathfrak{B}_{2}{ }^{\perp}$ such that $n_{2}\left(c_{1}{ }^{\tau}\right)=n_{1}\left(c_{1}\right), c_{1} \in \mathfrak{B}_{1}{ }^{\perp}$. This implies that we can choose $q_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}_{i}{ }^{\perp}$ such that $q_{i}{ }^{2}=\mu 1 \neq 0$. The proof of the structure theorem on composition algebras (Theorem 4.5, p. 164) shows that $\mathfrak{C}_{i}=\left(\mathfrak{B}_{i}+\mathfrak{B}_{i} q_{i}, j\right)$ is a composition subalgebra of $\left(\mathfrak{D}_{i}, j\right)$ and $a_{1}+b_{1} q_{1} \rightarrow a_{1}{ }^{\sigma}+b_{1}{ }^{\sigma} q_{2}, a_{1}, b_{1} \in \mathfrak{B}_{1}$, is an isomorphism of $\left(\mathfrak{C}_{1}, j\right)$ onto ( $\mathfrak{C}_{2}, j$ ) which extends $\sigma$. Continuing in this way we obtain the result.
If we apply Lemma 5 to $\mathfrak{B}_{1}=\mathfrak{B}_{2}=\Phi$ we see that if two composition algebras have similar norm forms then the algebras are isomorphic.
We are now ready to prove the uniqueness (up to isomorphism) of the composition algebras specified in the structure theorem for reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebras. The result is the following

Theorem 1 (Albert-Jacobson [1]). Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra, $\eta_{1}$ and $\eta_{2}$ coordinatizations of $\mathfrak{J}$ as $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}, J_{\gamma^{\prime}}\right)$, respectively, where $\mathfrak{D}$ and $\mathfrak{O}^{\prime}$ are octonion algebras. Then $(\mathfrak{O}, j)$ and $\left(\mathfrak{O}^{\prime}, j\right)$ are isomorphic.

Proof. If the algebras $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ and $\left(\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}, j\right)$ are split then they are isomorphic. Hence we may assume that $(\mathfrak{O}, j)$ is a division algebra. Let $e_{j}, j=1,2,3$, be elements of $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $e_{j}{ }^{\eta_{1}}=e_{j j}$ and let $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{j \leqq k} \Im_{j k}$ be the Peirce decomposition relative to the orthogonal idempotents $e_{j}$. Similarly, let $g_{j}, j=1,2,3$ be elements of $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $g_{j}{ }^{\eta_{2}}=e_{j j}$ (in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}^{\prime}, J_{\gamma^{\prime}}\right)$ ), $\mathfrak{J}=\sum \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}{ }_{j k}$ the corresponding Peirce decomposition. Since $\mathfrak{O}$ is a division algebra and $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ contains all scalar multiplications by nonzero elements of $\Phi$ it is clear from Lemma 2 that there exists a norm similarity in $\mathfrak{J}$ mapping $e_{1}$ onto $g_{1}$. Hence there exists a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}{ }_{3}, J_{\gamma^{\prime}}\right)$ mapping $e_{11}$ onto $e_{11}$. By Lemma $4, \mathfrak{O}$ and $\mathfrak{O}^{\prime}$ are norm similar. Hence $(\mathfrak{O}, j)$ and $\left(\mathfrak{O}^{\prime}, j\right)$ are isomorphic by Lemma 5 .

We shall now call the octonion coordinate algebra which is determined up to isomorphism by the reduced exceptional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ the coefficient algebra of $\mathfrak{J} . \mathfrak{J}$ is split if its coefficient algebra is split. We shall now show that the problem of classifying reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebras with respect to isotopy (or equivalently norm similarity) is equivalent to that of classifying octonion algebras.

Theorem 2 (Jacobson [24]). Let $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ be reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebras. Then the following conditions are equivalent: (1) $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ are isotopic, (2) J and J' are norm similar, (3) J and J' have isomorphic coefficient algebras.

Proof. We may assume the base field infinite since for finite fields all the algebras involved are split and hence are isomorphic. Then, as we have noted
before, (1) and (2) are equivalent. Now suppose $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ are norm similar. We wish to show that $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ have isomorphic coefficient algebras, so we may assume that the coefficient algebra of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is a division algebra. Then, by Lemma 2, $\mathbf{M}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ acts transitively on $\Pi$. Hence if we have a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ then we also have one which maps a given primitive idempotent of $\mathfrak{J}$ into a primitive idempotent of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Then the proof of Theorem 1 shows that $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ have isomorphic coefficient algebras. Thus (2) implies (3). Now assume (3). Then $\mathfrak{J} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3} J_{\gamma}\right)$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\delta}\right)$. We have seen that $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\delta}\right)$ are isotopes (p. 60). Hence $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ are isotopic so (3) implies (1).

We shall conclude this section with a useful isomorphism extension theorem for reduced exceptional simple Jordan algebras.

Theorem 3. Let $\Re$ and $\Re^{\prime}$ be reduced simple subalgebras of degree three of a reduced exceptional simple Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}, \sigma$ an isomorphism of $\Re$ onto $\mathfrak{K}^{\prime}$. Then $\sigma$ can be extended to an automorphism in $\mathfrak{J}$.

Proof. Let $e_{i}, i=1,2,3$, be orthogonal idempotents in $\Re, u_{12}, u_{13}$ elements of the Peirce spaces $\Re_{12}, \Re_{13}$ of $\Re$ relative to the $e_{i}$ such that $u_{12} \cdot{ }^{2} \neq 0, u_{13} \cdot{ }^{2} \neq 0$. Let $\eta$ be a coordinatization of $\mathfrak{J}$ adapted to the $e_{l}, u_{12}, u_{13}$, and $\zeta$ a coordinatizaton of $\mathfrak{J}$ adapted to the elements $e_{i}{ }^{\sigma}, u_{12}{ }^{\sigma}, u_{13}{ }^{\sigma}$. Then $\mathfrak{J}^{\eta}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right), \mathfrak{J}^{\zeta}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}{ }^{\prime}, J_{\gamma^{\prime}}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$, $\left(\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}, j\right)$ are isomorphic octonion algebras. By Theorem 3.2, $\mathfrak{K}^{n} =\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right), \mathfrak{K}^{\prime \zeta}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{3}{ }^{\prime}, J_{\gamma^{\prime}}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{\prime}$ are composition subalgebras of $(\mathfrak{O}, j)$ and $\left(\mathfrak{O}^{\prime}, j\right)$ respectively. Now $\eta^{-1} \sigma \zeta \mid \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ onto $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{3}{ }^{\prime}, J_{\gamma^{\prime}}\right)$ such that $1[i j] \rightarrow 1\{i j\}$ (defined in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{3}{ }^{\prime}, J_{\gamma^{\prime}}\right)$ respectively). By Theorem 3.3 this has the form $\sum b_{i j}[i j] \rightarrow \sum b_{i j}{ }^{\beta}\{i j\}$ where $\beta$ is an isomorphism of $(\mathfrak{B}, j)$ onto $\left(\mathfrak{B}^{\prime}, j\right)$. By Lemma $5, \beta$ can be extended to an isomorphism $\beta$ of $(\mathfrak{O}, j)$ onto $\left(\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}, j\right)$. Then $\sum a_{i j}[i j] \rightarrow \sum a_{i j}{ }^{\beta}\{i j\}$ is an isomorphism $\tau$ of $\mathfrak{J}^{\eta}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime \zeta}$ and $\eta \tau \zeta^{-1}$ is an automorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ extending the given isomorphism of $\mathfrak{K}$ onto $\mathfrak{K}^{\prime}$.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ be reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebras $\eta$ a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ such that $1^{n}=1$ (the identity of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ ). Note that $n\left((1+a)^{n}\right) =n(1+a)$ and $n\left((1-a)^{\eta}\right)=n(1-a)$ imply that $t\left(a^{\eta}\right)=t(a)$ and $t\left(\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)^{\eta}\right)=t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)$. Note also that $a \times 1=\frac{1}{2} t(a) 1-\frac{1}{2} a, 1 \times 1=1$. Show that these relations and (18) imply that $\hat{\eta}=\eta$ so $(a \times b)^{\eta}=a^{\eta} \times b^{\eta}$. Hence show that $\eta$ is an isomorphism.
2. Show that a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is a norm similarity if and only if it is an isotopy. Prove that $\eta^{*}$ is a norm similarity.
3. Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$. Let $e$ be a primitive idempotent in a reduced exceptional simple Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ and let Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ denote the subgroup of the group of automorphisms Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ leaving fixed the element $e$. In this section we shall determine Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ and a larger subgroup of $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ which we shall denote as $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J}, e)$ whose
definition is given below. The results we shall give can be formulated best in terms of certain Clifford groups and spin groups. We shall therefore begin our discussion with a survey of the concepts and results on Clifford algebras and groups which will be needed. A full account of these results can be found in Chevalley's The Algebraic Theory of Spinors, Chapter II. The results we shall derive here, particularly, those on $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J}, e)$, will be used in the next section to derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the isomorphism of reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebras.

Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a finite-dimensional vector space equipped with a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $f$. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ be the associated Jordan algebra, $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ the Clifford algebra, which we consider as containing $\mathfrak{J}$ (as a subalgebra of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)^{+}$). We recall the definition of the even (or second) Clifford algebra $C^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ as the subalgebra of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ generated by the elements $u v, u, v \in \mathfrak{B}$. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=n$ then $\operatorname{dim} C(\mathfrak{B}, f)=2^{n}$ and $\operatorname{dim} C^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, f)=2^{n-1}$. We have described the structure of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ in Theorem 7.2. In a similar manner one can determine the structure of $C^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. One can show that if $n$ is odd then this algebra is central simple while if $n$ is even then either $C^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is simple with center a quadratic field, or it is a direct sum of two simple ideals.

We recall that the Clifford group $\Gamma(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is defined to be the subgroup of the group of invertible elements $c \in C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ such that $c^{-1} \mathfrak{J} c \subseteq \mathfrak{J}$. If $c \in \Gamma(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ then the mapping $\chi(c): x \rightarrow c^{-1} x c, x \in \mathfrak{V}$, is contained in the orthogonal group $O(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ of the vector space $\mathfrak{B}$ relative to $f$. This is clear since $x^{2}=f(x) 1(f(x)=f(x, x))$ and $\left(c^{-1} x c\right)^{2}=f(x) 1$. It is clear also that $c \rightarrow \chi(c)$ is a representation of $\Gamma(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ acting in $\mathfrak{B}$. This is called the vector representation $\chi$ of the Clifford group. If $v \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $f(v) \neq 0$ then $v^{\cdot 2}=v^{2}=f(v) 1$ so $v$ is invertible in the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ and in the associative algebra $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. If $x \in \mathfrak{V}$ we have $v . x=\frac{1}{2}(v x+x v)=f(x, v) 1$ so $v^{-1} x v=-x+2 f(x, v) v^{-1}=-x+2 f(x, v) f(v)^{-1} v$. Thus $v \in \Gamma(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
\chi(v)=-S_{v} \tag{22}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $S_{v}$ is the symmetry determined by $v$, that is, the reflection in the hyperplane orthogonal to $v$ :

$$
\begin{equation*}
S_{v}: x \rightarrow x-\frac{2 f(x, v)}{f(v, v)} v \tag{23}
\end{equation*}
$$

It is now clear that $\Gamma(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ contains all the elements $v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{r}$ where $v_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $f\left(v_{i}\right) \neq 0$. We recall also that the operator $U_{v}=2 R_{v}{ }^{2}-R_{v \cdot 2}$ in $\Gamma(\mathfrak{B}, f)^{+}$has the form $y \rightarrow v y v$. Comparison of this with $x \rightarrow v^{-1} x v$ shows that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\chi(v)=f(v)^{-1} \bar{U}_{v} \tag{24}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\bar{U}_{v}=U_{v} \mid \mathfrak{V}$, the restriction of $U_{v}$ to $\mathfrak{V}$. It is clear from (24) that if $f\left(v_{i}\right) \neq 0$ then

$$
\begin{equation*}
\chi\left(v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{r}\right)=\left(\Pi f\left(v_{i}\right)\right)^{-1} \bar{U}_{v_{1}} \bar{U}_{v_{2}} \cdots \bar{U}_{v} . \tag{25}
\end{equation*}
$$

We define the even (or second) Clifford group $\Gamma^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ to be $\Gamma(\mathfrak{B}, f) \cap C^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. It is clear that $\Gamma^{e}=\Gamma^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ contains all the elements $v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{2 r}$ where $v_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $f\left(v_{i}\right) \neq 0$. By (22), $\chi\left(v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{2 r}\right)=S_{v_{1}} S_{v_{2}} \cdots S_{v_{2 r}}$. By the Cartan-Dieudonné Theorem every rotation is a product of an even number of symmetries. Hence the image $\chi\left(\Gamma^{\boldsymbol{e}}\right)$ contains the rotation group. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}$ is even $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is central simple so $\operatorname{ker} \chi=\Phi^{*}$, the set of nonzero elements of $\Phi$. If $v \in \mathfrak{V}$ and $f(v) \neq 0$ then $v \in \Gamma =\Gamma(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ but $v \notin \Gamma^{e}$. Hence $\chi(v) \notin \chi\left(\Gamma^{e}\right)$. Thus in this case $O(\mathfrak{B}, f) \supseteq \chi(\Gamma) \supset \chi\left(\Gamma^{e}\right) \supseteq O^{+}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$, the rotation group. Since $O^{+}$has index two in $O$ it is clear that $O(\mathfrak{B}, f)=\chi(\Gamma)$ and $O^{+}(\mathfrak{B}, f)=\chi\left(\Gamma^{e}\right)$ if $\mathfrak{B}$ is even dimensional. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}$ is odd then $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ has the center $\Phi 1+\Phi w$ where $w=u_{1} u_{2} \cdots u_{n}$ and $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ is an orthogonal basis for $\mathfrak{B}$. Then $w \notin C^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. An automorphism $\eta$ of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is inner if and only if $w^{\eta}=w$. On the other hand if $A \in O(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ then $w A=(\operatorname{det} A) w$, as can be seen directly. Hence if $c \in \Gamma$ then $\chi(c) \in O^{+}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Hence in the odddimensional case $\chi(\Gamma)=\chi\left(\Gamma^{e}\right)=O^{+}$. Thus in both cases $\chi\left(\Gamma^{e}\right)=O^{+}$. Also in both cases $\operatorname{ker} \chi \cap \Gamma^{e}=\Phi^{*}$. It follows that $\Gamma^{e}$ is the set of elements of the form $v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{2 r}$ where $\Pi_{1}^{2 r} f\left(v_{i}\right) \neq 0$.

If $c \in \Gamma$ and $x \in \mathfrak{B}$ then $c^{-1} x c=x \chi(c)$. Applying the main involution $\pi$ we obtain $c^{\pi} x\left(c^{\pi}\right)^{-1}=x \chi(c)$. Hence $c^{\prime} c^{\pi} x=x c c^{\pi}$ and since $\mathfrak{V}$ generates the Clifford algebra, $c c^{\pi}$ is in the center of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. If $c \in \Gamma^{e}$ then $c^{\pi} \in \Gamma^{e}$ and $c c^{\pi}$ is in the intersection of $\Gamma^{e}$ with the center of $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. Hence $c c^{\pi}=\lambda(c) 1$ where $\lambda(c) \in \Phi^{*}$. If $c_{1}, c_{2} \in \Gamma^{e}$ then $\left(c_{1} c_{2}\right)\left(c_{1} c_{2}\right)^{\pi}=c_{1} c_{2} c_{2}{ }^{\pi} c_{1}{ }^{\pi}=\lambda\left(c_{1}\right) \lambda\left(c_{2}\right) 1$. Hence $\lambda\left(c_{1} c_{2}\right) =\lambda\left(c_{1}\right) \lambda\left(c_{2}\right)$. The subgroup of $\Gamma^{\prime}$ of $c$ such that $\lambda(c)=1$ is called the spin group, $\operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$, and its image $\chi(\operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, f))$ in the orthogonal group is called the reduced orthogonal group $O^{\prime}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. If $v \in \mathfrak{B}$ then $v v^{\pi}=v^{2}=f(v) 1$. Hence if $c=v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{2 r}, v_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}, f\left(v_{i}\right) \neq 0$ then $\lambda(c)=\Pi_{1}^{2 r} f\left(v_{i}\right)$. Since we have seen that $\Gamma^{\boldsymbol{e}}$ is the set of elements $v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{2 r}, v_{i} \in \mathfrak{V}, f\left(v_{i}\right) \neq 0$ it is clear that $\operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ is the set of elements $v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{2 r}$ such that $\Pi f\left(v_{i}\right)=1$.
The reduced orthogonal group is a subgroup of the rotation group $O^{+}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ of $\mathfrak{V}$ relative to $f$. If $A$ is any rotation then there exists a $c \in \Gamma^{e}$ which is determined up to a factor in $\Phi^{*}$ such that $\chi(c)=A$. Since $\lambda(\gamma c)=\gamma^{2} \lambda(c)$ if $\gamma \in \Phi^{*}$ it is clear that the coset $\lambda(c)$ modulo squares of elements of $\Phi^{*}$ is determined by $A$ (where $\chi(c)=A)$. Let $\Phi^{* 2}$ denote the subgroup of squares of elements of $\Phi^{*}$. Then we define the spinorial norm $\lambda(A)$ of the rotation $A$ to be $\lambda(A)=\lambda(c) \Phi^{* 2}$ where $\chi(c)=A$. If $A=S_{v_{1}} S_{v_{2}} \cdots S_{v_{2 r}}$ is a representation of $A$ as a product of symmetries then $c=v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{2 r} \in \Gamma^{e}, \chi(c)=A$ and $\lambda(c)=\Pi_{1}^{2 r} f\left(v_{i}\right)$. Hence $\lambda(A)=\Pi_{1}^{2 r} f\left(v_{i}\right) \Phi^{* 2}$. It is clear that $\lambda$ is a homomorphism of $O^{+}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ into $\Phi^{*} / \Phi^{* 2}$. If $\lambda(A)=1$ then we have a $c \in \Gamma^{e}$ such that $\chi(c)=A$ and $\lambda(c)=\gamma^{2}, \gamma \in \Phi^{*}$. If we replace $c$ by $\gamma^{-1} c$ then we get $\chi\left(\gamma^{-1} c\right)=A, \lambda\left(\gamma^{-1} c\right)=1$ so $A \in O^{\prime}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$. The converse is clear. Thus the reduced orthogonal group $O^{\prime}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ is the kernel of the spinorial norm mapping. It is clear also that $O^{\prime}(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ consists of the rotations $S_{v_{1}} S_{v_{2}} \cdots S_{v_{2 r}}$ such that $\Pi_{1}^{2 r} f\left(v_{i}\right)$ is a square.
We shall now apply these notions and results to the study of the group

Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ where $e$ is a primitive idempotent in the reduced exceptional simple Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)+\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)+\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ be the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to $e$. Then $\mathfrak{I}_{1}(e)=\Phi e$. We shall need to derive some formulas for products of elements in the Peirce spaces $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ and for $Q$ on these spaces where $Q(a)=\frac{1}{2} t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)$. If we imbed $e$ in a reducing set of idempotents $e_{1}=e, e_{2}, e_{3}$ and let $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ be the corresponding Peirce decomposition, then $\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)=\Phi e_{1}, \mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)=\Phi e_{2}+\Phi e_{3} +\mathfrak{J}_{23}, \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)=\mathfrak{J}_{12}+\mathfrak{J}_{13}$. Hence, as we saw before, $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}_{0}=10$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}=16$. We can write $\mathfrak{J}_{0}=\Phi f \oplus \mathfrak{V}$ where $f=1-e=e_{2}+e_{3}$ is the identity element of $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ and $\mathfrak{B}=\Phi\left(e_{2}-e_{3}\right)+\mathfrak{J}_{23}$. Thus $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=9$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ is the subspace of $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ of elements of generic trace 0 . If $v=\alpha\left(e_{2}-e_{3}\right)+w, \alpha \in \Phi, w \in \mathfrak{J}_{23}$, then $v^{\cdot 2}=\alpha^{2} f+w^{\cdot 2}$ and $w^{\cdot 2}=\beta f$. Hence $v^{\cdot 2}=\delta f$ where $\delta \in \Phi$. Also $Q\left(v^{\cdot 2}\right)=\frac{1}{2} t\left(v^{\cdot 2}\right) =\delta$ so $v^{\cdot 2}=Q(v) f$. This gives the formula

$$
\begin{equation*}
v_{1} \cdot v_{2}=Q\left(v_{1}, v_{2}\right) f, \quad v_{i} \in \mathfrak{B} \tag{26}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $Q\left(v_{1}, v_{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2} t\left(v_{1}, v_{2}\right)$. Since the restriction of the trace form to the $\mathfrak{I}_{i}$, is nondegenerate it is clear that $Q$ is nondegenerate on $\mathfrak{J}_{23}$ and hence on $\mathfrak{V}$. Next let $y \in \mathfrak{I}_{\frac{1}{2}}$. Then $y^{\cdot 2} \in \mathfrak{I}_{0}+\mathfrak{I}_{1}$ so $y^{\cdot 2}=\xi e+\eta f+v$ where $\xi, \eta \in \Phi$ and $v \in \mathfrak{B}$. Since $e . f=0=e . v, t\left(y^{\cdot 2} . e\right)=t(\xi e)=\xi$. Hence, by associativity of $t, t(y, y . e) =\xi$ and $Q(y)=\frac{1}{2} t(y, y)=t(y, y . e)=\xi$. Also $t\left(y^{\cdot 2} . f\right)=t(\eta f+v)=2 \eta$ which leads in the same way to $\eta=\frac{1}{2} Q(y)$. Hence $y^{\cdot 2}=\frac{1}{2} Q(y)(1+e)+v$. We now define $y \circ y=v$, the component of $y^{2}$ in $\mathfrak{V}$ in the decomposition $\mathfrak{J}_{0}+\mathfrak{J}_{1}=\boldsymbol{\Phi} e \oplus \Phi f \oplus \mathfrak{B}$. Then we have the formula

$$
\begin{equation*}
y \circ y=v=y^{\cdot 2}-\frac{1}{2} Q(y)(1+e) . \tag{27}
\end{equation*}
$$

If we let $y_{1} \circ y_{2}$ be the linearized form of $y \circ y, y_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{\pi}{2}}$, so

$$
y_{1} \circ y_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(y_{1}+y_{2}\right) \circ\left(y_{1}+y_{2}\right)-y_{1} \circ y_{1}-y_{2} \circ y_{2}\right]
$$

then we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
y_{1} \circ y_{2}=y_{1} . y_{2}-\frac{1}{2} Q\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)(1+e) . \tag{28}
\end{equation*}
$$

We have $t(y)=0$ for $y \in \mathfrak{I}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $y^{\cdot 3} \in \mathfrak{I}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ so $t\left(y^{\cdot 3}\right)=0$. Since $y^{\cdot 3}-t(y) y^{\cdot 2} +\frac{1}{2}\left[t(y)^{2}-t\left(y^{\cdot 2}\right)\right] y-n(y) 1=0, y^{\cdot 3}=Q(y) y+n(y) 1$, which implies

$$
\begin{equation*}
y^{\cdot 3}=Q(y) y, n(y)=0, \quad y \in \mathfrak{I}_{\frac{1}{2}} . \tag{29}
\end{equation*}
$$

This and (27) give directly

$$
\begin{equation*}
(y \circ y) \cdot y=\frac{1}{4} Q(y) y . \tag{30}
\end{equation*}
$$

Let $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ be the subspace of elements of trace 0 . We have $\mathfrak{V}+\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. If $a \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ then $a^{\cdot 3}=\frac{1}{2} t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right) a+n(a) 1$. Applying $\Delta^{b}$ to this considered as a functional relation we obtain $2 b \cdot a \cdot a+a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b=\frac{1}{2} t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right) b+t(a \cdot b) a+(a, a, b) 1=\frac{1}{2} t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right) b+t(a, b) a +t(a \times a, b) 1$ (by (13)). Since $a \times a=a^{\cdot 2}-\frac{1}{2} t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right) 1$ this gives for $a, b \in \mathfrak{I}^{\prime}$

$$
\begin{equation*}
2 b \cdot a \cdot a+a^{\cdot 2} \cdot b=Q(a) b+t(a, b) a+t\left(a^{\cdot 2}, b\right) 1 . \tag{31}
\end{equation*}
$$

Put $a=y \in \mathfrak{I}_{\frac{1}{2}}, b=v \in \mathfrak{V}$. Then $t(v, y)=0$ and $2 v . y . y+y^{\cdot 2} . v=Q(y) v+t\left(y^{\cdot 2}, v\right) 1$ By (28) this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
& Q(v . y, y)(1+e)+2(v . y) \circ y+\frac{1}{2} Q(y)(1+e) . v+(y \circ y) . v \\
& \quad=Q(y) v+t\left(y^{2}, v\right) 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Equating components in $\mathfrak{V}$ in the decomposition $\mathfrak{J}=\Phi e \oplus \Phi f \oplus \mathfrak{V} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ we obtain

$$
\begin{equation*}
(v . y) \circ y=\frac{1}{4} Q(y) v, \quad v \in \mathfrak{B}, \quad y \in \mathfrak{I}_{\frac{1}{2}} . \tag{32}
\end{equation*}
$$

Next we note that (15) gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
Q\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)=Q(a)^{2}, \quad a \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime} \tag{33}
\end{equation*}
$$

Applying $\Delta^{b}, b \in \mathfrak{I}^{\prime}$, gives $2 t\left(a^{\cdot 3}, b\right)=t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right) t(a . b)$, or $2 t\left(a^{\cdot 2}, a . b\right)=t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right) t(a . b)$ Applying $\Delta^{b}$ again to the corresponding functions of $a$ gives $4 t(a . b, a . b) +2 t\left(a^{\cdot 2}, b^{\cdot 2}\right)=2 t(a, b)^{2}+t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right) t\left(b^{\cdot 2}\right)$ or

$$
\begin{equation*}
4 Q(a \cdot b)+t\left(a^{\cdot 2}, b^{\cdot 2}\right)=t(a, b)^{2}+2 Q(a) Q(b) \tag{34}
\end{equation*}
$$

$a, b \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. If $b=v \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $a=y \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ then $t(v, y)=0$ so this and (26) and (28) imply

$$
\begin{equation*}
Q(v . y)=\frac{1}{4} Q(v) Q(y), \quad v \in \mathfrak{B}, \quad y \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}} . \tag{35}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since $y \circ y \in \mathfrak{B}$ this and (30) give $\frac{1}{4} Q(y \circ y) Q(y)=\frac{1}{16} Q(y)^{2} Q(y)$. Hence

$$
\begin{equation*}
Q(y \circ y)=\frac{1}{4} Q(y)^{2} \tag{36}
\end{equation*}
$$

holds if $Q(y) \neq 0$. Since this is a polynomial function relation this is valid for all $y \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$.

We are now ready to consider the group Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ and a larger group $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J}, e)$ which we shall define. Let $b \in \mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ and put $\theta(b)=e+b \in \mathfrak{J}_{1}+\mathfrak{J}_{0}$. We consider the mapping $U_{\theta(b)}$ in $\mathfrak{J}$. It is clear that $\mathfrak{I}_{i} U_{\theta(b)} \subseteq \mathfrak{I}_{i}$ and $e U_{\theta(b)}=e$. The restriction of $U_{\theta(b)}$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ coincides with that of $U_{b}$ so if $b=f$ this is the identity mapping. If $v \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $Q(v) \neq 0$ then $f U_{\theta(v)}=v^{\cdot 2}=Q(v) f$ and if $x \in \mathfrak{B}$ then $x U_{\theta(v)}=x U_{v} =-Q(v) x S_{v}$, by (22) and (24), where $S_{r}$ is the reflection in $\mathfrak{B}$ in the hyperplane orthogonal to $v$. Thus

$$
\begin{align*}
f U_{\theta(v)} & =Q(v) f  \tag{37}\\
x U_{\theta(v)} & =-Q(v) x S_{v}, \quad v, x \in \mathfrak{B}, \quad Q(v) \neq 0
\end{align*}
$$

To obtain the restriction of $U_{\theta(b)}$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ we note that $U_{\theta(b)}=U_{e+b}=U_{e}+U_{b} +2\left(R_{e} R_{b}+R_{b} R_{e}-R_{e . b}\right)=U_{e}+U_{b}+2\left(R_{e} R_{b}+R_{b} R_{e}\right)$. Since $y . e=\frac{1}{2} y$ if $y \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $y . b^{\cdot 2}=2 y . b . b$ if $b \in \mathfrak{J}_{0}$ we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
y U_{\theta(b)}=2 y R_{b}=2 y . b, \quad y \in \mathfrak{I}_{\frac{1}{2}}, \quad b \in \mathfrak{I}_{0} . \tag{38}
\end{equation*}
$$

We have $\theta(f)=e+f=1$ so $U_{\theta(f)}=1$. Also if $v \in \mathfrak{B}$ then $y U_{\theta(v)}{ }^{2}=4 y . v . v =2 y \cdot v^{\cdot 2}=2 Q(v) y \cdot f=Q(v) y$. This equation shows that if we let $U_{\theta(v)}^{\prime}, v \in \mathfrak{B}$, denote the restriction of $U_{\theta(v)}$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ then $\left(U_{\theta(v)}{ }^{\prime}\right)^{2}=Q(v) 1$ (in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ ). This implies that we have a representation $\rho$ of the Clifford algebra $C(\mathfrak{B}, f)$ acting in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ such that $1 \rightarrow 1, v \rightarrow U_{\theta(v)}{ }^{\prime}$. By restriction, we obtain representations of $C^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, Q), \Gamma$, $\Gamma^{\boldsymbol{e}}$ and $\operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$. Since $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=9$ and $Q$ is nondegenerate, $C^{\boldsymbol{e}}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ is central simple and $\operatorname{dim} C^{\boldsymbol{e}}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)=2^{8}$. Hence the homomorphism $\rho$ of $C^{\boldsymbol{e}}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}, \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ is a monomorphism. Since $\operatorname{dim}\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}, \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\right)=16^{2}=2^{8}$ it is clear that $\rho$ is an isomorphism and $C^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)^{\rho}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}, \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ so $\rho$ is an irreducible representation of $C^{\boldsymbol{e}}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$. By Chevalley (loc.cit. p. 57), it follows that the space spanned by $\operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)^{\rho}$ is $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}, \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ so the representation $\rho$ of $\operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ is also irreducible.

Now let $c \in \Gamma^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ the even Clifford group. Then $c$ has the form $v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{2 r}$ where the $v_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $Q\left(v_{i}\right) \neq 0$. Then $\lambda(c)=\prod_{1}^{2 r} Q\left(v_{i}\right)$ Put

$$
\begin{equation*}
\eta=U_{\theta\left(v_{1}\right)} U_{\theta v(2)} \cdots U_{\theta\left(v_{2 r}\right)} . \tag{39}
\end{equation*}
$$

Then the foregoing formulas show that

$$
\begin{align*}
& e^{\eta}=e, \quad f^{\eta}=\lambda(c) f, \\
& x^{\eta}=\lambda(c) x c^{\chi}, \quad x \in \mathfrak{B},  \tag{40}\\
& y^{\eta}=y c^{\rho}, \quad y \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}} .
\end{align*}
$$

It is clear from these formulas that $\eta$ is independent of the representation of $c$ as $c=v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{2 r}$. It is clear also that $\eta$ is a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ with multiplier $\lambda(c)^{2}$. We now write $\eta=\eta(c)$ and we have the homomorphism $\eta: c \rightarrow \eta(c)$ of $\Gamma^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$. We denote the subgroup of $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ which is the image $\Gamma^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)^{\eta}$ as $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J}, e)$. Since $\rho$ is a monomorphism of the even Clifford algebra the last equation of (40) shows that $\eta$ is a monomorphism of $\Gamma^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$.

Now let $c \in \operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$. Then $c=v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{2 r}$ where $\lambda(c)=1$. Then (40) shows that $e^{\eta}=e, f^{\eta}=f$ so $1^{\eta}=1$. Hence, by the Corollary to Theorem 6.7 (p. 245), $\eta$ is an automorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$. Since $e^{\eta}=e, \eta \in$ Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$. Hence $\eta$ is a monomorphism of $\operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ into Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ e.

If $A$ is a similarity in a vector space equipped with a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form then we write $\mu(A)$ for the coset $\mu \Phi^{* 2}$ of the multiplier $\mu$ of $A$ in $\Phi^{*} / \Phi^{* 2}$. We shall now prove

Lemma 1. If $B$ is a rotation in $\mathfrak{V}$ relative to $Q$ then there exists a similarity $A$ in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ relative to $Q$ satisfying

$$
\begin{equation*}
(x, y) A=x B \cdot y A, \quad x \in \mathfrak{B}, \quad y \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}} . \tag{41}
\end{equation*}
$$

Moreover, $A$ is determined up to a factor in $\Phi^{*}$ by this condition, $\mu(A)=\lambda(B)$ the spinorial norm of $B$, and

$$
\begin{equation*}
y A \circ y A=\mu(y \circ y) B, \quad y \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}, \tag{42}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\mu$ is the multiplier of $A$.
Proof. Write $B=S_{v_{1}} S_{v_{2}} \cdots S_{v_{2 r}}$ where the $v_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $Q\left(v_{i}\right) \neq 0$. Put $A =2^{2 r} R^{\prime}{ }_{v_{1}} R^{\prime}{ }_{v_{2}} \cdots R^{\prime}{ }_{v_{2 r}}$ where $R^{\prime}{ }_{v_{i}}$ is the restriction of $R_{v_{i}}$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$. If $y \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ then, by (35), $Q\left(y \cdot v_{i}\right)=\frac{1}{4} Q\left(v_{i}\right) Q(y)$. Hence $A$ is a similarity of ratio $\mu=\Pi_{1}^{2 r} Q\left(v_{i}\right)$. Since the spinorial norm of $B$ is $\Pi_{1}^{2 r} Q\left(v_{i}\right) \Phi^{* 2}$, it is clear that $\mu(A)=\lambda(B)$. We claim that (41) and (42) hold. Using a field extension argument it is enough to prove this under the additional assumption that the base field is algebraically closed. Let $v_{1}{ }^{\prime}=\mu^{-\frac{1}{2}} v_{1}$. Then $S_{v_{1}} S_{v_{2}} \cdots S_{v_{2 r}}=B$ and $2^{2 r} R^{\prime}{ }_{v_{1}}, R^{\prime}{ }_{v_{2}} \cdots R^{\prime}{ }_{v_{2 r}}=\mu^{-} A$. Put $\eta=U_{\theta\left(v_{1}{ }^{\prime}\right)} U_{\theta\left(v_{2}\right)} \cdots U_{\theta\left(v_{2 r}\right)}$. Then, since $Q\left(v_{1}{ }^{\prime}\right) Q\left(v_{2}\right) \cdots Q\left(v_{2 r}\right)=1$, the result proved above shows that $\eta$ is an automorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ fixing $e$ and the formulas show that the restrictions of $\eta$ to $\mathfrak{V}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ are $B$ and $\mu^{-\frac{1}{2}} A$ respectively. Then we have $(x . y)\left(\mu^{-\frac{1}{2}} A\right)=x B . y\left(\mu^{-\frac{1}{2}} A\right)$ if $x \in \mathfrak{B}, y \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$. Hence (41) holds. Also we have $y\left(\mu^{-\frac{1}{2}} A\right) \circ y\left(\mu^{-\frac{1}{2}} A\right)=(y \circ y) B$. Hence (42) holds. We note next that if $A=A_{i}, B=B_{i}, i=1,2$, satisfy (41) then so does $A=A_{1} A_{2}, B=B_{1} B_{2}$ and $A=A_{1}{ }^{-1}, B=B_{1}{ }^{-1}$. Hence to prove the uniqueness statement of the lemma it is enough to prove this for $B=1$. Then $(x . y) A=x . y A$ so, by (38) and the definition of the representation $\rho, A$ commutes with every element of $C(\mathfrak{B}, Q)^{\rho}$. Since $C^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)^{\rho}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}, \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ it follows that $A$ commutes with every element of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}, \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$. Hence $A$ is a scalar multiplication.

We can now prove
Theorem 4. Let $c \in \operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ and write $c=v_{1} v_{2} \cdots v_{2 r}$ where the $v_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$, $\Pi Q\left(v_{i}\right)=1$. Put $\eta(c)=U_{\theta\left(v_{1}\right)} U_{\theta\left(v_{2}\right)} \cdots U_{\theta\left(v_{2 r}\right)}$. Then $\eta: c \rightarrow \eta(c)$ is an isomorphism of $\operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ onto Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$.

Proof. We have seen that $\eta$ is a monomorphism of $\operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{V}, Q)$ into Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$. It remains to show that it is an epimorphism. Let $\eta \in \operatorname{Aut} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$. Then $e^{\eta}=e$, $f^{\eta}=f, \mathfrak{B}^{\eta}=\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}{ }^{\eta}=\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and the restrictions $B$ and $A$ of $\eta$ to $\mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ respectively are $Q$-orthogonal. Clearly (41) holds. We now claim that $B$ is a rotation. Since the lemma provides a similarity $A$ in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ satisfying (41) for any given rotation, it is enough to show that no linear mapping $A \neq 0$ exists in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ such that $(x . y) A =(x B) .(y A)$ for $B=-1$. Then $y R_{x} A=-y A R_{x}, y \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}, x \in \mathfrak{B}$, and $A$ commutes with every linear transformation $R_{v_{1}} R_{v_{2}}, v_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$. Since $C^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)^{\rho}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}, \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ it follows that $A$ is a scalar multiplication. Then $y R_{x} A=-y A R_{x}$ implies $A=0$. Hence the restriction $B$ of $\eta$ to $\mathfrak{V}$ is a rotation. Also the restriction $A$ of $\eta$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ is $Q$-orthogonal. Hence, by Lemma 1, $\mu(A)=\lambda(B)$ and since $\mu(A)=1, B \in O^{\prime}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$. Let $c \in \operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ satisfy $c^{\chi}=B$. Then it follows from the definition of $\eta$ that $\eta(c)=\eta$.

Corollary 1. Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ e acts irreducibly in $\mathfrak{V}$ and in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$.
Proof. The proof of the theorem shows that the action of Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ is
the same as that of $\operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)^{\rho}$ and we have noted that this is irreducible. The action of Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ in $\mathfrak{B}$ is the same as that of $\operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)^{\chi}=O^{\prime}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$. Since $O^{\prime}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ contains the commutator subgroup of $O(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ and the latter acts irreducibly in $\mathfrak{B}$ (Chevalley, loc. cit. p. 53 and p. 33), Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ is irreducible in $\mathfrak{B}$.

We recall the definition in §2 of the subgroup $\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ of $\mathbf{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by the elements $\zeta=U_{a_{1}} U_{a_{2}} \cdots U_{a_{r}}$ where for given $\zeta$ the $a_{i}$ are contained in a nonsplit nine-dimensional reduced simple subalgebra of degree three and $\Pi_{1}^{r} n\left(a_{\imath}\right)=1$. Then we have the

Corollary 2. If the coefficient algebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ is a division algebra then Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e \subseteq \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$.

Proof. We may identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{D}$ is an octonion division algebra, and we may assume $e=e_{11}$. Then we have seen that any $\eta \in \operatorname{Aut} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ has the form $\eta=U_{\theta\left(v_{1}\right)} U_{\theta\left(v_{2}\right)} \cdots U_{\theta\left(v_{2}\right)}$ where $v_{i} \in \mathfrak{V}=\Phi\left(e_{22}-e_{33}\right)+\mathfrak{J}_{23}$ and $\Pi_{1}^{2 \mathrm{r}} Q\left(v_{i}\right)=1$. We have $v_{i}=\beta_{i}\left(e_{22}-e_{33}\right)+w_{i}[23]$ where $\beta_{i} \in \Phi, w_{i} \in \mathfrak{D}$. Then $\theta\left(v_{i}\right)$ is contained in a subalgebra $\Omega_{i}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{i 3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $\mathrm{P}_{i}$ is a quadratic subfield of $\mathfrak{D}$. Also $n\left(\theta\left(v_{i}\right)\right)=-Q\left(v_{i}\right)$. If $\delta \in \Phi$ we put $D(\delta)=e_{11}+e_{22}+\delta e_{33}$ so $n(D(\delta))=\delta$. Now put $\delta_{0}=1, \delta_{i}=\Pi_{j=1}^{i}\left(-Q\left(v_{j}\right)\right)^{-1}$ for $1 \leqq i \leqq 2 r$ and

$$
\begin{equation*}
\eta_{i}=U_{D\left(\delta_{i-1}\right)^{-1}} U_{\theta\left(v_{i}\right)} U_{D\left(\delta_{i}\right)}, \quad i=1,2, \cdots, 2 r . \tag{43}
\end{equation*}
$$

Then, since $\delta_{0}=1=\delta_{2 r}, \eta_{1} \eta_{2} \cdots \eta_{2 r}=\eta$. Moreover, $D\left(\delta_{i-1}\right)^{-1}, \theta\left(v_{i}\right), D\left(\delta_{i}\right) \in \mathfrak{R}_{i}$ and $n\left(D\left(\delta_{i-1}\right)^{-1}\right) n\left(\theta\left(v_{i}\right)\right) n\left(D\left(\delta_{i}\right)\right)=1$. Hence $\eta_{i}$ and consequently $\eta \in \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$.

We note next the following
Corollary 3. The center of Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ coincides with the kernel of the restriction homomorphism of Aut J/Фe to Jo ${ }_{0}(e)$ (or to $\mathfrak{B}$ ). This consists of 1 and the element $\zeta_{e}$ such that $\zeta_{e}=1$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ and $\zeta_{e}=-1$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$.

This follows easily from the proof of the theorem. We leave this as an exercise for the reader.

We return to the considerations of Lemma 1 and the group $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J}, e)$ of elements of the form $\eta=U_{\theta\left(v_{1}\right)} U_{\theta\left(v_{2}\right)} \cdots U_{\theta\left(v_{2}\right)}$ where the $v_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $Q\left(v_{i}\right) \neq 0$. It is clear from Lemma 1 that any spinorial norm of a rotation in $\mathfrak{B}$ relative to $Q$ is a coset $\mu(A)=\mu \Phi^{* 2}$ where $A$ is a similarity in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ relative to $Q$. We shall prove that conversely any $\mu(A)$ for a similarity in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ relative to $Q$ is a spinorial norm. For this we require

Lemma 2. Let $y_{1}$ and $y_{2}$ be any two elements of $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ such that $Q\left(y_{1}\right) Q\left(y_{2}\right) \neq 0$. Then there exists a mapping $\eta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J}, e)$ such that $y_{1}{ }^{\eta}=y_{2}$.

Proof. There is no loss in generality in assuming $y_{1}=u_{12}$ where $u_{12} \in \mathfrak{J}_{12}$ and $\sum_{i \leqq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ is the Peirce decompositions of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to orthogonal idempotents $e_{1}=e, e_{2}, e_{3}$. We note that (30) (or (36)) imply that $y_{i} \circ y_{i} \neq 0$. Assume first that
these elements of $\mathfrak{B}$ are linearly dependent so that we have $y_{2} \circ y_{2}=\beta y_{1} \circ y_{1} \neq 0$, $\beta \in \Phi$. Also $y_{1} \circ y_{1}=u_{12} \circ u_{12}=\frac{1}{2} Q\left(y_{1}\right)\left(e_{2}-e_{3}\right)$, by (27). By (30), $\left(e_{2}-e_{3}\right) \cdot y_{2} =\delta\left(y_{2} \circ y_{2}\right) . y_{2}=v y_{2}$. Since $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}=\mathfrak{J}_{12}+\mathfrak{J}_{13}$ is the decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ into its characteristic subspaces of the restriction $R^{\prime}{ }_{e_{2}-e_{3}}$ of $R_{e_{2}-e_{3}}$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and since the corresponding characteristic roots are $\frac{1}{2}$ and $-\frac{1}{2}$ we have $v= \pm \frac{1}{2}$ and $y_{2} \in \mathfrak{J}_{12}$ or $y_{2} \in \mathfrak{J}_{13}$. If $y_{2} \in \mathfrak{J}_{13}$ then it is clear (for example, from the Coordinatization Theorem) that there exists an element $v_{2}=v_{23} \in \mathfrak{J}_{23} \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$ such that $2 y_{1} . v_{2}=y_{2}$. Put $v_{1}=e_{2}-e_{3} \in \mathfrak{B}$. Then $4 y_{1} \cdot v_{1} \cdot v_{2}=y_{2}$. Then if $\eta=U_{\theta\left(v_{1}\right)} U_{\theta\left(v_{2}\right)}, y_{1}{ }^{\eta}=y_{2}$, by (38). If $y_{2} \in \mathfrak{I}_{12}$ then $y_{2}{ }^{\prime}=y_{2} U_{\theta\left(v_{1}\right)} U_{\theta\left(v_{2}\right)} \in \mathfrak{I}_{13}$ if $v_{1}=e_{2}-e_{3}$ and $v_{2}$ is any element of $\mathfrak{I}_{23}$. Also $Q\left(y_{2}{ }^{\prime}\right) \neq 0$ if $Q\left(v_{2}\right) \neq 0$, so we can reduce this case to the preceding one. Now assume that $y_{1} \circ y_{1}$ and $y_{2} \circ y_{2}$ are linearly independent. By (36), $Q\left(y_{2} \circ y_{2}\right)=\beta^{2} Q\left(y_{1} \circ y_{1}\right), \beta \in \Phi$. By Witt's theorem there exists a $B \in O(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ such that $\left(y_{2} \circ y_{2}\right) B=\beta\left(y_{1} \circ y_{1}\right)$. Since $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{V}=9$ and $\beta$ can be replaced by $-\beta$ we may assume that $B$ is a rotation. By Lemma 1 and its proof there exists an $\eta=U_{\theta\left(v_{1}\right)} U_{\theta\left(v_{2}\right)} \cdots U_{\theta\left(v_{2 r}\right)}$ such that $Q\left(v_{i}\right) \neq 0$ and $\left(y_{2} \circ y_{2}\right)^{\eta} =\beta\left(y_{1} \circ y_{1}\right)$. By (42), $y_{2}{ }^{\eta} \circ y_{2}{ }^{\eta}=\delta\left(y_{1} \circ y_{1}\right)$ so if we replace $y_{2}$ by $y_{2}{ }^{\eta}$ we have reduction to the case considered first.

Theorem 5 (Springer). The group of multipliers of similarities of $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ relative to $Q$ coincides with the group of spinorial norms of the rotation group in $\mathfrak{V}$ relative to $Q$.

Proof. Lemma 1 shows that every spinorial norm has the form $\mu(A)$ where $A$ is a similarity in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ relative to $Q$. Now let $C$ be any similarity in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and let $y_{1} \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ satisfy $Q\left(y_{1}\right) \neq 0$. Then $y_{2}=y_{1} C \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $Q\left(y_{2}\right)=\mu Q\left(y_{1}\right)$ where $\mu$ is the multiplier of $C$. By Lemma 2 there exists an $\eta=U_{\theta\left(v_{1}\right)} U_{\theta\left(v_{2}\right)} \cdots U_{\theta\left(v_{2}\right)}, Q\left(v_{i}\right) \neq 0$, such that $y_{1}{ }^{\eta}=y_{2}$. If we let $A$ and $B$ denote the restrictions of $\eta$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ respectively then the proof of Lemma 1 shows that $y_{1} A=y_{2}$ and $\mu(A)=\lambda(B)$. Then $\mu(C)=\mu(A)=\lambda(B)$.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{V}$ be a finite-dimensional vector space equipped with a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form, $v$ a vector in $\mathfrak{V}$ with $f(v, v) \neq 0$. Show that the subgroup of $\operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{V}, f)$ of elements $c$ such that $v c^{\chi}=v$ is isomorphic to $\operatorname{Spin}\left((\Phi v)^{\perp}, f\right)$.
2. Show that Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Sigma_{1}^{3} \Phi e_{i}$ the subgroup of Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ ( $\mathfrak{J}$ as usual) leaving fixed the three orthogonal idempotents $e_{i}$ is isomorphic to $\operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{D}, n)$ where $\mathfrak{D}$ is a coefficient algebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ and $n$ is its norm form.
3. Conditions for isomorphism. In this section we shall prove Springer's theorem that two reduced exceptional simple Jordan algebras $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{2}$ having isomorphic coefficient algebras are isomorphic if and only if the quadratic forms $Q(x)=\frac{1}{2} t\left(x^{\cdot 2}\right)$ defined by the two algebras are equivalent. Taken together with

Theorem 1 this implies that two reduced exceptional simple Jordan algebras $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{2}$ are isomorphic if and only if they have isomorphic coefficient algebras and equivalent forms $Q$. It is clear also that isomorphism of the algebras implies equivalence of the forms. If $e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}$ are othogonal primitive idempotents in $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{i \leq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ the corresponding Peirce decomposition then any $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ has the form $a=\sum \alpha_{i} e_{i}+\sum_{i<j} a_{i j}$ where $\alpha_{i} \in \Phi$ and $a_{i j} \in \Im_{i j}$. Then $Q(a)=\frac{1}{2} \sum \alpha_{i}^{2} +\sum_{i<j} Q\left(a_{i j}\right)$. It follows from Witt's theorem that the restriction of $Q$ to the 24 dimensional space $\mathfrak{J}_{12}+\mathfrak{J}_{13}+\mathfrak{J}_{23}$ is determined by $Q$ on $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence the forms $Q$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{2}$ are equivalent if and only if the corresponding forms on the 24 dimensional spaces are equivalent. We remark also that the theorem we wish to prove is trivial if the coefficient algebras are split since in this case the algebras $\mathfrak{J}_{i}$ are necessarily isomorphic. We shall therefore assume from now on that the coefficient algebras are octonion division algebras.

Let $e$ be a primitive idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}$. As in §2, we consider the symmetric bilinear form $F_{e}$ on $\mathfrak{J}$ defined by $F_{e}(a, b)=(e, a, b)=t(e \times a, b)$. We have seen that if $\Re_{e}$ is the radical of this form then $\mathfrak{J} / \Re_{e}$ with the induced form is an orthogonal direct sum of a hyperbolic plane and a subspace equivalent to $\mathfrak{J}_{23}$ equipped with the form $-Q$, where $\mathfrak{J}_{\mathbf{2 3}}$, as usual, is the Peirce ( 2,3 )-space defined by orthogonal idempotents $e_{1}=e, e_{2}$ and $e_{3}$. If $u_{i j} \in \mathfrak{I}_{i j}, i \neq j$, then we have $u_{i j}{ }^{\cdot 2}=Q\left(u_{i j}\right)\left(e_{i}+e_{j}\right)$. If we choose $u_{12} \in \mathfrak{I}_{12}, u_{13} \in \mathfrak{I}_{13}$ so that $Q\left(u_{12}\right)=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \neq 0$, $Q\left(u_{13}\right)=\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \neq 0$ and choose a coordinatization of $\mathfrak{J}$ adapted to the $e_{i}$ and $u_{12}$, $u_{13}$ then we have $a[12]^{\cdot 2}=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} n(a)\left(e_{11}+e_{22}\right), \quad a[13]^{\cdot 2}=\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} n(a)\left(e_{11}+e_{33}\right)$, $a[23]^{\cdot 2}=\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{2} n(a)\left(e_{22}+e_{33}\right)$, if $a \in \mathfrak{O}\left(\right.$ where $\left.\mathfrak{J}^{n}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)\right)$. Hence $Q$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{23}$ is equivalent to $\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{2} n$ where $n$ here is the norm form on the coefficient algebra $\mathfrak{D}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$.

Now let $\mathrm{N}^{*}=\mathrm{N}^{*}(\mathfrak{D})$ be the set of elements $n(a) \neq 0, a \in \mathfrak{D}$. Then $\mathrm{N}^{*}$ is a subgroup of the multiplicative group $\Phi^{*}$ containing $\Phi^{* 2}$. If $\alpha \neq 0$ then we shall call the coset $\alpha \mathrm{N}^{*}$ in $\Phi^{*} / \mathrm{N}^{*}$ the norm class of $\alpha$. Now let $e$ and everything else be as in the last paragraph. Choose a hyperbolic plane in $\mathfrak{J} / \Re_{e}$ and let $u$ be any nonisotropic vector such that $u+\Re_{e} \in \mathfrak{J} / \Re_{e}$ is orthogonal to the chosen hyperbolic plane. Then the equivalences of forms we have noted imply that the norm class $-(e, u, u) \mathrm{N}^{*}=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{3} \mathrm{~N}^{*}$. Thus it is clear that this norm class is independent of the choice of $u$ and by Witt's theorem, it is also independent of the choice of the hyperbolic plane. Accordingly, we shall call $-(e, u, u) \mathrm{N}^{*}$ the norm class $\kappa(e)$ of the primitive idempotent $e$. We have $\kappa(e)=\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{2} \mathrm{~N}^{*}$. It is clear from the Coordinatization Theorem that this can be determined by choosing primitive orthogonal idempotents $e_{1}=e, e_{2}, e_{3}$ and $u_{23} \in \mathfrak{J}_{23}$, the Peirce ( 2,3 )-space, so that $Q\left(u_{23}\right) \neq 0$. Then $\kappa(e)=Q\left(u_{23}\right) \mathrm{N}^{*}$. It follows that $\kappa\left(e_{2}\right)=Q\left(u_{13}\right) \mathrm{N}^{*}=\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \mathrm{~N}^{*}$ and $\kappa\left(e_{3}\right)=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \mathrm{~N}^{*}$ if the $\gamma^{\prime}$ 's are as before.
Let $\zeta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ and suppose $n\left(a^{\zeta}\right)=\mu n(a)$, so $\mu$ is the multiplier of the similarity $\zeta$. Suppose $f=e^{\zeta}$ is a primitive idempotent. Then $\left(e^{\zeta}, u^{\zeta}, u^{\zeta}\right)=\mu(e, u, u)$ and hence $\kappa(f)=\mu \kappa(e)$. Next let $\zeta \in \mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{I})$, so $n\left(a^{\zeta}\right)=n(a)$ and assume $e^{\zeta}=\mu f$ where $f$ is a
primitive idempotent. Then $e^{\mu-1} \zeta=f$ and the multiplier of $\mu^{-1} \zeta$ is $\mu^{-3}$. Hence $\kappa(f)=\mu^{-3} \kappa(e)=\mu \kappa(e)$.

We can now prove
Lemma 1. Let $e_{i}, i=1,2,3$, be orthogonal primitive idempotents in $\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{T}$ the subspace of $\mathfrak{J}$ orthogonal to the $e_{i}$ (relative to $Q$ ). Then the set of norm classes of primitive idempotents of $\mathfrak{J}$ coincides with the set of norm classes of the elements $Q(u), u \in \mathfrak{T}, Q(u) \neq 0$.

Proof. As before, let $\mathfrak{J}=\sum_{i \leqq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ be the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to the $e_{i}$ so $\mathfrak{T}=\sum_{i<j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ and if $u_{1 j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{1 j}, j=2,3$ satisfies $Q\left(u_{1 j}\right)=\gamma_{j}{ }^{-1}$, then we can identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right), \mathfrak{D}$, the coefficient algebra. Also in our identification $e_{i}=e_{i i}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}=\{a[i j] \mid a \in \mathfrak{O}\}$. If $u=a[12]+b[13]+c[23]$ then $Q(u)=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} n(a)+\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} n(b)+\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{2} n(c)$ and we have seen that $\kappa(e) =\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{3} \mathrm{~N}^{*}$ which is clearly of the form $Q(u) \mathrm{N}^{*}, u \in \mathfrak{I}_{23}$. Since any primitive idempotent can be imbedded in a set of three orthogonal primitive idempotents and since the spaces $\mathfrak{T}$ orthogonal to any two such sets of idempotents are $Q$ equivalent, it is clear that if $e$ is any primitive idempotent then $\kappa(e)=Q(u) \mathrm{N}^{*}$ for some $u$ in the given space $\mathfrak{T}$. We now consider the mapping $T_{Q_{i j}}$ defined, by $q \in Q$ and $i \neq j$ and a similar mapping $T_{S_{i j}}$ defined by $s \in \mathfrak{D}$. Then, by (20), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
g \equiv e_{11} T_{Q_{12}} T_{S_{13}}= & e_{11}+\gamma_{2}^{-1} \gamma_{1} n(q) e_{22}+\gamma_{3}^{-1} \gamma_{1} n(s) e_{33}+q[12] \\
& +s[13]+\tilde{s} q[32] .
\end{aligned}
$$

Then $t(g)=1+\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{1} n(q)+\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{1} n(s)$ and $g \times g=0$. Hence if $t(g) \neq 0$ then $t(g)^{-1} g$ is a primitive idempotent. Since $T_{Q_{12}} T_{S_{13}}, \in \mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ (Lemma 1 of §2) the result noted above shows that $\kappa\left(t(g)^{-1} g\right)=t(g) \kappa\left(e_{11}\right)=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{3}+\gamma_{2}{ }^{-2} \gamma_{3} \gamma_{1} n(q) +\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{1} n(s)$. Since $\gamma_{1}=1$ this implies that if $\beta=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} n(a)+\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} n(b)+\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{2} n(c) \neq 0$ and $n(c) \neq 0$ then $\beta \mathrm{N}^{*}$ is a norm class of a primitive idempotent of $\mathfrak{J}$. We recall that $\kappa\left(e_{22}\right)=\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \mathrm{~N}^{*}$ and $\kappa\left(e_{33}\right)=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \mathrm{~N}^{*}$. Also, by (20), $e_{22} T_{Q_{23}}=e_{22} +\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{2} n(q) e_{33}+q[23]$ and the trace of this element is $1+\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{2} n(q)$ so if this is $\neq 0$ then the argument just used shows that $\left(\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1}+\gamma_{3}{ }^{-2} \gamma_{2} n(q)\right) N^{*}$ is a norm class of a primitive idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}$. Hence if $\beta=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} n(a)+\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} n(b) \neq 0$ and $n(b) \neq 0$ then $\beta \mathrm{N}^{*}$ is a norm class of a primitive idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}$. It is now clear that every $Q(u) \mathrm{N}^{*}, u \in \mathfrak{T}, Q(u) \neq 0$ is a norm class of a primitive idempotent.

The foregoing lemma shows that the norm classes of primitive idempotents of $\mathfrak{J}$ are determined by the form $Q$. We need to consider next the norm classes of primitive idempotents orthogonal to a given primitive idempotent $e$. By Witt's theorem it is clear that the equivalence class of the quadratic form $Q$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$ is determined by $\kappa(e)$ and $Q$ on $\mathfrak{J}$ (or on a subspace $\mathfrak{T}$ as defined in Lemma 1 ). We now have

Lemma 2. If $e$ is a primitive idempotent then the set of norm classes of
primitive idempotents $e^{\prime}$ orthogonal to $e$ coincides with the set of norm classes of the multipliers of similarities of the quadratic form $n(x)+\kappa(e) n(y)$ with the quadratic form $Q$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$.

Proof. First, let $e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}$ be primitive idempotents with $e_{1}=e$ and let the notations be as before. Then we may take $\kappa=\kappa(e)=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{3}$ and $Q$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ is the quadratic form $\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} n(x)+\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} n(y)$. Since $\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1}\left(n(x)+\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{3} n(y)\right)$ is equivalent to $Q$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ it is clear that $\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1}$ is a multiplier of a similarity of $n(x)+\kappa n(y)$ with $Q$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$. Also we have seen that $\kappa\left(e_{2}\right)=\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \mathrm{~N}^{*}$ and since $e_{2}$ can be taken to be any primitive idempotent orthogonal to $e=e_{1}$ we see that the norm class of any primitive idempotent $e^{\prime}$ orthogonal to $e$ is as specified in the lemma. Next let $\mu$ be any multiplier of a similarity of $n(x)+\kappa n(y)$ with $Q$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$. Then $\gamma_{3} \mu$ is the multiplier of a similarity of $Q$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and, by Theorem $5, \gamma_{3} \mu \mathrm{~N}^{*}$ is a spinorial norm of a rotation $B$ in the space $\mathfrak{B}$ of elements of trace 0 in $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ relative to $Q$. By Lemma 1 of §3, we have a similarity $A$ in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$ such that (41) holds and $\mu(A)=\gamma_{3} \mu \mathrm{~N}^{*}$. Let $v=\left(e_{2}-e_{3}\right) B$. Then $v \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $Q(v)=Q\left(e_{2}-e_{3}\right)=1$ so $e_{2}{ }^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2}(f+v)$ and $e_{3}{ }^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2}(f-v)$ are primitive idempotents and $e_{1}, e^{\prime}{ }_{2}, e^{\prime}{ }_{3}$ are orthogonal. We shall now show that $\kappa\left(e_{2}{ }^{\prime}\right)=\mu \mathrm{N}^{*}$ which will complete the proof. Let $u \in \mathfrak{J}_{13}$ satisfy $Q(u) \neq 0$. Then $\kappa\left(e_{2}\right)=\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \mathrm{~N}^{*}=Q(u) \mathrm{N}^{*}$. Also $u \cdot\left(e_{2}-e_{3}\right)=-\frac{1}{2} u$ so, by (42), $(u A) \cdot v=-\frac{1}{2}(u A)$. Since $(u A) \cdot f=\frac{1}{2} u A$ we have $u A \cdot e_{3}=\frac{1}{2} u A$. Also $u A \cdot e_{1}=\frac{1}{2} u A$ so $u A$ is in the Peirce ( 1,3 )-space for the idempotents $e_{1}, e_{2}{ }^{\prime}, e_{3}{ }^{\prime}$. Hence $\kappa\left(e_{2}{ }^{\prime}\right) =Q(u A) \mathrm{N}^{*}=\gamma_{3} \mu Q(u) \mathrm{N}^{*}=\mu \mathrm{N}^{*}$ as required.

We can now prove
Theorem 6 (Springer). Let $\mathfrak{I}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{2}$ be reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebras with isomorphic coefficient algebras and equivalent forms $Q$ (or trace forms). Then $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{2}$ are isomorphic.

Proof. Let $e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}$ be orthogonal primitive idempotents in $\mathfrak{J}_{1}, u_{1 j}$ an element in the Peirce space $\mathfrak{J}_{11 j}$ of $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ relative to these idempotents such that $u_{1 j}{ }^{2} =\gamma_{j}{ }^{-1}\left(e_{1}+e_{j}\right)$. Then $\mathfrak{I}_{1} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{O}$ is the coefficient algebra and $\kappa\left(e_{1}\right)=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{3} \mathrm{~N}^{*}$ and $\kappa\left(e_{2}\right)=\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \mathrm{~N}^{*}$. By Lemmas 1 and 2 there exist orthogonal primitive idempotents $e_{1}{ }^{\prime}, e_{2}{ }^{\prime}$ in $\mathfrak{J}_{2}$ such that $\kappa\left(e_{1}{ }^{\prime}\right)=\gamma_{2}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{3} \mathrm{~N}^{*}$ and $\kappa\left(e_{2}{ }^{\prime}\right) =\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \mathrm{~N}^{*}$. It follows readily that $\mathfrak{J}_{2} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ so $\mathfrak{J}_{1} \cong \mathfrak{J}_{2}$.

The method of proof of this theorem can be applied in the same way to a single algebra to give the following

Corollary. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra. Then two primitive idempotents $e, e^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{J}$ are in the same orbit under Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ if and only if the norm classes $\kappa(e)=\kappa\left(e^{\prime}\right)$.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{T}$ a subspace orthogonal to three primitive orthogonal idempotents. Show that $\mathfrak{J}$ contains nilpotent elements $\neq 0$ if and only if $Q$ has positive Witt index on $\mathfrak{T}$.
2. Assume the coefficient algebra is an octonion division algebra. Show that any element $a$ can be imbedded in a subalgebra of the form $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $(\mathrm{P}, j)$ is a quadratic field.
3. Use exercise 2 to show that if $\mathfrak{J}$ contains a nonzero nilpotent element then $\mathfrak{J}$ has the form $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $\gamma=\operatorname{diag}\{1,-1,1\}$. Hence prove the following three conditions on a reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra are equivalent: (1) $\mathfrak{J}$ has nilpotent element $\neq 0$, (2) the quadratic form $Q$ on a subspace $\mathfrak{T}$ orthogonal to three primitive orthogonal idempotents has positive Witt index, (3) $Q$ in $\mathfrak{T}$ is equivalent to $n(x)-n(y)+n(z)$ where $n$ is the norm form on the coefficient algebra. Show that two J's containing nonzero nilpotents are isomorphic if and only if their coefficient algebras are isomorphic.
4. Show that if $\mathfrak{J}$ (as in ex. 3) contains a nilpotent element $\neq 0$ then $\mathfrak{J}$ contains a nilpotent element of index three.
5. Call a primitive idempotent $e$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ an s-idempotent if $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ contains nonzero nilpotent elements. Show that $e$ is an $s$-idempotent if and only if the norm class $\kappa(e)=(-1) \mathrm{N}^{*}$. Hence show that any two $s$-idempotents are in the same orbit under Aut J.
6. Show that $\mathfrak{J}$ is split if and only if the restriction of $Q$ to the subspace $\mathfrak{T}$ in exercise 1 of maximum Witt index.
7. Let $\Phi$ be an algebraic number field with $t$ real conjugate fields. Use Hasse's theorem to show that there are at most $3^{t}$ nonisomorphic reduced exceptional simple Jordan algebras over $\Phi$ (cf. ex. 7, p. 171). The number $3^{1}$ is actually the exact number of these algebras (Albert-Jacobson [1])).
8. More on Aut $\mathfrak{J}$. As usual, let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra. We prove first

Theorem 7. The only subspaces of $\mathfrak{J}$ invariant under Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ are $\mathfrak{J}, \Phi 1$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$, the subspace of elements of trace 0 .

Proof. We have seen in §3 (Corollary 1 to Theorem 4) that if $e$ is a primitive idempotent then Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ acts irreducibly on $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$ and on $\mathfrak{B}$, the subspace of $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ of elements of trace 0 . It follows that the only invariant subspaces of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ are sums of $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e), \mathfrak{B}$ and subspaces of $\Phi e+\Phi(1-e)$. Now let $e_{i}, i=1,2,3$, be primitive orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{i \leq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ the Peirce decomposition determined by the $e_{i}$. Then the only invariant subspaces of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e_{i}$ are sums of the subspaces: $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}+\mathfrak{J}_{i k}, \mathfrak{J}_{j k}+\Phi\left(e_{j}-e_{k}\right)$, subspaces of $\Phi e_{i}+\Phi\left(e_{j}+e_{k}\right)$ where $i, j, k$ are unequal. Now let $\mathfrak{K}$ be a subspace invariant under Aut $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $\mathfrak{K}$ Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e_{i} \subseteq \mathfrak{K}$ for every $i$, and this implies that either $\Re$ contains every $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ and every $\Phi\left(e_{i}-e_{j}\right), i \neq j$, or $\Re$ is a subspace of $\Phi e_{i}+\Phi\left(e_{j}+e_{k}\right)$ for all unequal $i, j, k$. In the first case, $\Re$ contains $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ and in the second $\Re=\Phi 1$ and these two alternatives imply the theorem.

If $\mathfrak{B}$ is a subalgebra of an algebra $\mathfrak{U}$ then we denote the subgroup of the
automorphism group Aut $\mathfrak{A}$ leaving fixed the elements of $\mathfrak{B}$ as Aut $\mathfrak{A} / \mathfrak{B}$. We now consider Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K}$ whese $\mathfrak{J}$ is a reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra and $\mathfrak{K}$ is a reduced simple subalgebra of degree three. Then, as we have seen, we can identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$, $(\mathfrak{O}, j)$ an algebra of octonions and $\mathfrak{\Omega}$ with the subalgebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a composition subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. The possible dimensionalities for $\mathfrak{D}$ are $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}=1,2,4,8$. In the first case $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{K}=6$. If $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}=2$ so $\mathfrak{D}=\mathrm{P}$ a quadratic subfield of $\mathfrak{O}$ or a direct sum of two copies of $\Phi$, then $\operatorname{dim} \Re=9$. Next we may have $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}=4$ in which case $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a quaternion algebra and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{K}=15$. Finally we have the trivial case $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{D}$ and $\operatorname{dim} \Re=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}=27$.

Suppose first that $D=\Phi$ so $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{K}=6$. Then $\eta \in \operatorname{Aut} \mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K}$ if and only if $\eta$ is an automorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ and $1[i j]^{\eta}=1[i j], i, j=1,2,3$. By Theorem 3.3, these automorphisms have the form $\sum \alpha_{i} e_{i i}+a[12]+b[23]+c[31] \rightarrow \sum \alpha_{i} e_{i i}+a^{\beta}[12]+b^{\beta}[23]+c^{\beta}[31]$ where $\beta$ is an automorphism of $(\mathfrak{O}, j)$. Conversely, any $\beta \in \operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ defines in the manner indicated an automorphism $\eta \in$ Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K}$. Thus we can identify Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K}$ for $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ with $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$.

Now let $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is an arbitrary composition subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{O}, j)$. Then $\mathfrak{D} \supseteq \Phi$. Hence it is clear that Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K}$ is the set of mappings $\sum \alpha_{i} e_{i i} +a[12]+b[23]+c[31] \rightarrow \sum a_{i} e_{i i}+a^{\beta}[12]+b^{\beta}[23]+c^{\beta}[31]$ where $\beta \in \operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak{D}, j) / \mathfrak{D}$ the subgroup of automorphisms of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ leaving fixed the elements of $\mathfrak{D}$. In this way we can identify Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{M}$ with $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak{D}, j) / \mathfrak{D}$.

We proceed to derive some properties of Aut $\mathfrak{O}$ which we shall need. We note first that if $\beta \in$ Aut $\mathfrak{O}$ then $t\left(a^{\beta}\right)=t(a)$ and $n\left(a^{\beta}\right)=n(a)$ for the generic trace and norm in $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ (Theorem 6.1, p. 224). Since $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi 1 \oplus \mathfrak{O}_{0}$ where $\mathfrak{O}_{0}=\Phi 1^{\perp}$ is the set of elements of trace 0 we have $(\Phi 1)^{\beta}=\Phi 1$ and $\mathfrak{O}_{0}^{\beta}=\mathfrak{O}_{0}$ for $\beta \in$ Aut $\mathfrak{O}$. It follows that $\bar{a}^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\overline{a^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}$ so $\beta \in \operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. Thus Aut $\mathfrak{D}=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. Also the condition $n\left(a^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right)=n(a)$ shows that $\beta \in O(\mathfrak{D}, n)$ the orthogonal group in $\mathfrak{D}$ relative to $n$. We now take up the problem of determining Aut $\mathfrak{O} / \mathfrak{D}$ in the following cases: I. $\mathfrak{D}$ a quaternion subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$, II. $\mathfrak{D}=\mathrm{P}$ a quadratic subfield of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$, III. $\mathfrak{D}$ split and $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi u_{1}+\Phi u_{2}$ where the $u_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents $\neq 0$ and $\bar{u}_{1}=u_{2}, \bar{u}_{2}=u_{1}$.
I. $\mathfrak{D}$ quaternion. We can decompose $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{D} \oplus \mathfrak{D}^{\perp}$ (relative to the norm form in $\mathfrak{D}$ ) and if $q \in \mathfrak{D}^{\perp}$ and $n(q) \neq 0$ then $\mathfrak{D}^{\perp}=\mathfrak{D} q$ ( $\$ 4.3$, p. 163). If $\beta \in \operatorname{Aut} \mathfrak{D} / \mathfrak{D}$ then $\mathfrak{D}^{\perp \boldsymbol{\beta}}=\mathfrak{D}$ so $q^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=u q, u \in \mathfrak{D}$. Since $n(q)=n\left(q^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right)=n(u) n(q), n(u)=1$. Conversely, if $u \in \mathfrak{D}$ satisfies $n(u)=1$ then $q^{\prime}=u q$ satisfies $q^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{D}$ and $n\left(q^{\prime}\right)=n(q)$. The formulas of §4.3 giving the multiplication in $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{D}+\mathfrak{D} q=\mathfrak{D}+\mathfrak{D} q^{\prime}$ show that $a+b q \rightarrow a+b q^{\prime}, a, b \in \mathfrak{D}$, is an automorphism $\beta$ in $\mathfrak{D}$. Clearly $\beta \in$ Aut $\mathfrak{O} / \mathfrak{D}$. It is now clear that the mapping $\beta \rightarrow u$ is an isomorphism of Aut $\mathfrak{D} / \mathfrak{D}$ onto the multiplicative group of elements $u$ of norm one in $\mathfrak{D}$.
II. $\mathfrak{D}=\mathrm{P}$ a quadratic subfield of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$.
