If $x \in \mathfrak{D}$ and $\rho_{1}, \rho_{2} \in \mathrm{P}$ then $\left(\rho_{1} \rho_{2}\right) x =\rho_{1}\left(\rho_{2} x\right)$ since P is generated by a single element and $\mathfrak{O}$ is alternative. Hence $\mathfrak{O}$ is a vector space over P relative to $\rho x$. Since the dimensionality of $\mathfrak{O}$ over $\Phi$ is 8
its dimensionality over P is $\operatorname{dim}_{\mathrm{P}} \mathfrak{D}=4$. Let $i \in \mathrm{P}$ satisfy $\bar{i}=-i$ so $\mathrm{P}=\Phi(i)$ and $i^{2}=\alpha 1, \alpha \in \Phi$. If $x, y \in \mathfrak{D}$ we define

$$
\begin{equation*}
h(x, y)=n(x, y)+\alpha^{-1} i n(i x, y) \in \mathrm{P} . \tag{44}
\end{equation*}
$$

Evidently $h$ is additive in $x$ and $y$ and since $n(i y, x)=-n(i x, y)$, by (10) of p.163, $h(y, x)=n(y, x)+\alpha^{-1} i n(i y, x)=n(x, y)-\alpha^{-1} i n(i x, y)=\overline{h(x, y)}$. Also ï $\delta \in \Phi$ then $h(\delta x, y)=\delta h(x, y)$ and $h(i x, y)=n(i x, y)+\alpha^{-1} i n\left(i^{2} x, y\right)=i n(x, y)+n(i x, y) =i h(x, y)$. Hence $h$ is a hermitian form on $\mathfrak{D} / \mathrm{P}$. It is clear that $h(x, y)=0$ implies $n(x, y)=0$ so $h$ is nondegenerate. Moreover, if $\mathfrak{M}$ is a P -subspace of $\mathfrak{O}$ then $\mathfrak{M}^{\perp}$ as defined by $h$ is the same as $\mathfrak{M}^{\perp}$ relative to $n$.

We now define for $x, y, z \in \mathfrak{O}$

$$
\begin{equation*}
h(x, y, z)=h(x, y \wedge z) \in \mathbf{P} \tag{45}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $y \wedge z=\frac{1}{2}[y z]$. Evidently $h(x, y, z)$ is additive in $x, y$ and $z$ and is linear in $x$. We now let $\mathfrak{V}=\mathrm{P}^{\perp}$, so $\operatorname{dim}_{\mathrm{P}} \mathfrak{V}=3$. We consider the restriction of $h(x, y, z)$ to $\mathfrak{V}$. We note first that if $x, y, z \in \mathfrak{O}$, then

$$
\begin{align*}
n(y, z \wedge x) & =\frac{1}{2} n(y, z x-x z)=-\frac{1}{2} n(z y-y z, x) \\
& =n(x, y \wedge z) \tag{46}
\end{align*}
$$

(by (10) p. 163 and $\bar{z}=-z$, since $z \perp 1$ ). If $z \in \mathfrak{V}$ then $i z+z i=0$ which implies that $i_{L} z_{L}+z_{L} i_{L}=0$ and $i_{R} z_{R}+z_{R} i_{R}=0$ since $a \rightarrow a_{L}$ and $a \rightarrow a_{R}$ are associative specializations of $\mathfrak{O}^{+}$. Thus $z(i x)=-i(z x)$ and $(z i) x=-(z x) i$. Hence if $x, y, z \in \mathfrak{V}$ then

$$
\begin{align*}
n(i y, z \wedge x) & =\frac{1}{2} n(i y, z x-x z) \\
& =\frac{1}{2} n(i y, z x)+\frac{1}{2} n(y i, x z)=-\frac{1}{2} n(y, i(z x)+(x z) i) \\
& =\frac{1}{2} n(y, z(i x)+(x i) z)=\frac{1}{2} n(y, z(i x)-(i x) z)  \tag{47}\\
& =-\frac{1}{2} n(z y, i x)+\frac{1}{2} n(y z, i x)=n(i x, y \wedge z)
\end{align*}
$$

Since $h(x, y, z)=h(x, y \wedge z)=n(x, y \wedge z)+\alpha^{-1} i n(i x, y \wedge z)$ it follows from (46) and (47) that $h(y, z, x)=h(x, y, z)$ for $x, y, z \in \mathfrak{V}=\mathrm{P}^{\perp}$. It follows that $h(x, y, z)$ is trilinear and alternating on $\mathfrak{B}$.

It is easily seen from the inductive construction of $\mathfrak{O}$ that there exists a quaternion subalgebra $\mathfrak{Q}$ orthogonal to $i$. Moreover, $\mathfrak{Q}$ has a basis $\left(1, v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3}\right)$ where $\bar{v}_{i}= -v_{i}, n\left(v_{i}\right) \neq 0, v_{1}=v_{2} v_{3}=-v_{3} v_{2}$. Then the $v_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $n\left(v_{1}, v_{2} \wedge v_{3}\right)=n\left(v_{1}, v_{1}\right) \neq 0$. It follows that $h\left(v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3}\right) \neq 0$ and since $h(x, y, z)$ is P -trilinear and alternating on $\mathfrak{B}$, the $v_{i}$ are P -independent and so form a basis for $\mathfrak{V} / \mathrm{P}$. If $\left(w_{1}, w_{2}, w_{3}\right)$ is any basis for $\mathfrak{B} / \mathrm{P}$ then $w_{i}=\sum \rho_{i j} v_{j}, \rho_{i j} \in \mathrm{P}$ and $h\left(w_{1}, w_{2}, w_{3}\right)=\operatorname{det}\left(\rho_{i j}\right) h\left(v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3}\right) \neq 0$.

Now let $\beta \in \mathrm{Aut} \mathfrak{O} / \mathrm{P}$. Since $\beta$ is an orthogonal transformation in $\mathfrak{D}$ relative to $n$ and $\beta$ is P-linear we have $h\left(x^{\beta}, y^{\beta}\right)=n\left(x^{\beta}, y^{\beta}\right)+\alpha^{-1} \operatorname{in}\left(i x^{\beta}, y^{\beta}\right)=n(x, y)$
$+\alpha^{-1} i n\left((i x)^{\beta}, y^{\beta}\right)=n(x, y)+\alpha^{-1} i n(i x, y)=h(x, y), x, y \in \mathfrak{D}$, so $\beta$ is unitary in $\mathfrak{O} / \mathbf{P}$ relative to $h$. Since $\mathbf{P}^{\beta}=\mathbf{P}$ we have $\mathfrak{B}^{\beta}=\mathfrak{V}$. Let $B$ denote the restriction of $\beta$ to $\mathfrak{V}$ and let $\left(w_{1}, w_{2}, w_{3}\right)$ be a basis of $\mathfrak{V} / \mathrm{P}$. Then $w_{i} B \in \mathfrak{V}$ and $h\left(w_{1} B, w_{2} B, w_{3} B\right) =(\operatorname{det} B) h\left(w_{1}, w_{2}, w_{3}\right)$. On the other hand, since $\beta$ is an automorphism, $w_{2}{ }^{\beta} \wedge w_{3}{ }^{\beta}=\left(w_{2} \wedge w_{3}\right)^{\beta}$. Hence $h\left(w_{1} B, w_{2} B, w_{3} B\right)=h\left(w_{1}{ }^{\beta}, w_{2}{ }^{\beta}, w_{3}{ }^{\beta}\right) =h\left(w_{1}{ }^{\beta}, w_{2}{ }^{\beta} \wedge w_{3}{ }^{\beta}\right)=h\left(w_{1}{ }^{\beta},\left(w_{2} \wedge w_{3}\right)^{\beta}\right)=h\left(w_{1}, w_{2} \wedge w_{3}\right)=h\left(w_{1}, w_{2}, w_{3}\right)$. Since $h\left(w_{1}, w_{2}, w_{3}\right) \neq 0$ we see that $\operatorname{det} B=1$. Thus $B \in S U(\mathfrak{B}, h)$ the unimodular unitary group in $\mathfrak{B} / \mathrm{P}$ relative to $h$.
Conversely, let $B \in \operatorname{SU}(\mathfrak{B}, h)$. Extend $B$ to a linear transformation $\beta$ in $\mathfrak{O} / \mathrm{P}$ such that $\rho^{\beta}=\rho, \rho \in \mathbf{P}$. We claim that $\beta \in \mathrm{Aut} \mathfrak{D} / \mathbf{P}$. If $x \in \mathfrak{V}$ and $\rho \in \mathbf{P}$ then $(\rho x)^{\beta}=\rho x^{\beta}$ is clear. Also $x \rho=\bar{\rho} x$ so $(x \rho)^{\beta}=x^{\beta} \rho$ and if $\rho_{1}, \rho_{2} \in \mathrm{P}$ then $\left(\rho_{1} \rho_{2}\right)^{\beta} =\rho_{1}{ }^{\beta} \rho_{2}{ }^{\beta}$. Now let $\left(w_{1}, w_{2}, w_{3}\right)$ be a basis for $\mathfrak{B} / \mathrm{P}$. Then $h\left(w_{1}, w_{2}, w_{3}\right) =h\left(w_{1} B, w_{2} B, w_{3} B\right)=h\left(w_{1} B, w_{2} B \wedge w_{3} B\right) \quad$ and $\quad h\left(w_{1}, w_{2}, w_{3}\right)=h\left(w_{1}, w_{2} \wedge w_{3}\right) =h\left(w_{1}{ }^{\beta},\left(w_{2} \wedge w_{3}\right)^{\beta}\right)$ since $\beta$ is unitary on $\mathfrak{D} / \mathrm{P}$. This implies that $\left(w_{2} \wedge w_{3}\right)^{\beta} =w_{2}{ }^{\beta} \wedge w_{3}{ }^{\beta}$ if $w_{2}, w_{3}$ are P -linearly independent elements of $\mathfrak{B}$. Also $h\left(v_{2}{ }^{\beta}, v_{3}{ }^{\beta}\right) =h\left(v_{2}, v_{3}\right)$ implies $n\left(v_{2}{ }^{\beta}, v_{3}{ }^{\beta}\right)=n\left(v_{2}, v_{3}\right)$ and this implies that $v_{2}{ }^{\beta} v_{3}{ }^{\beta}+v_{3}{ }^{\beta} v_{2}{ }^{\beta} =v_{2} v_{3}+v_{3} v_{2}$. Hence $\left(v_{2} v_{3}\right)^{\beta}=v_{2}{ }^{\beta} v_{3}{ }^{\beta}$ holds for any linearly independent $v_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$. It follows that this holds for all $v_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ and that $\beta$ is an automorphism. Clearly $\beta \in$ Aut $\mathfrak{V} / \mathrm{P}$.
The result we have established is that $\beta \in \mathrm{Aut} \mathfrak{D} / \mathrm{P}$ if and only if $\beta$ is P -linear on $\mathfrak{D}, 1^{\beta}=1$ and the restriction of $\beta$ to $\mathfrak{B}$ is in $\operatorname{SU}(\mathfrak{B}, h)$. Hence we have an isomorphism of Aut $\mathfrak{O} / \mathrm{P}$ with $\operatorname{SU}(\mathfrak{B}, h)$. We remark finally that the hermitian form $h$ is independent of the choice of $i$ in $\mathbf{P}$ since any other element of $\mathbf{P}$ satisfying $\bar{x}=-x$ is of the form $\delta i$ where $\delta \neq 0$ is in $\Phi$. It is clear from (44) that replacement of $i$ by $\delta i$ does not change $h$.
III. $\mathfrak{D}$ split, $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi u_{1}+\Phi u_{2}$, where the $u_{i}$ are nonzero orthogonal idempotents such that $\bar{u}_{1}=u_{2}, \bar{u}_{2}=u_{1}$. Since the maximum number of nonzero orthogonal idempotents in $\mathfrak{O}$ (and in $\mathfrak{O}^{+}$) is two we have $u_{1}+u_{2}=1$. Let $\mathfrak{O}=\mathfrak{O}_{11} \oplus \mathfrak{O}_{12} \oplus \mathfrak{O}_{21} \oplus \mathfrak{O}_{22}$ be the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{D}$ relative to the $u_{i}$ (see p. ). Then $\mathfrak{O}_{i j}=u_{i} \mathfrak{O} u_{j}$. Since the $u_{i}$ are primitive idempotents in $\mathfrak{O}^{+}$which is a Jordan algebra of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak{O}_{0}$ we have $\mathfrak{O}_{i i}=u_{i} \mathfrak{O} u_{i} =\Phi u_{i}$. If $i \neq j$ then $\mathfrak{O}_{i j} \mathfrak{O}_{j i} \subseteq \mathfrak{O}_{i i}=\Phi u_{i}$ and $\mathfrak{O}_{i j}{ }^{2} \subseteq \mathfrak{O}_{j i}$ (loc.cit.). If $a_{i j} \in \mathfrak{O}_{i j}$ then $a_{i j}=u_{i} a\left(1-u_{i}\right), a \in \mathfrak{O}$. Hence $a_{i j}{ }^{2}=0$ and $n\left(a_{i j}\right)=0$. It follows that $\mathfrak{O}_{i j}$ is a totally isotropic subspace of $\mathfrak{O}$ relative to $n$. We have also $t\left(a_{i j}\right)=0$ so $\mathfrak{O}_{i j} \subseteq \mathfrak{O}_{0}$. Since $n(a, b)=\frac{1}{2} t(a \bar{b})$ we have $n\left(u_{i}, a_{i j}\right)=0=n\left(u_{j}, a_{i j}\right)$. Since $n$ is nondegenerate it is now clear that $n$ gives a nondegenerate bilinear pairing of $\mathfrak{O}_{i j}$ and $\mathfrak{O}_{j i}$. Hence $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{O}_{12}=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{O}_{21}=3$. If $a_{12} \in \mathfrak{O}_{12}$ and $a_{21} \in \mathfrak{O}_{21}$ then $a_{12} a_{21} =\alpha_{1} u_{1}$ and $a_{21} a_{12}=\alpha_{2} u_{2}, \alpha_{i} \in \Phi$. Since $u_{i}+\bar{u}_{i}=1, t\left(u_{i}\right)=1$ and so $n\left(a_{12}, a_{21}\right) =\frac{1}{2} t\left(a_{12} \bar{a}_{21}\right)=-\frac{1}{2} t\left(a_{12} a_{21}\right)=-\frac{1}{2} \alpha_{1}$. Thus $\alpha_{1}=-2 n\left(a_{12}, a_{21}\right)$ and, similarly, $\alpha_{2}=-2 n\left(a_{21}, a_{12}\right)=-2 n\left(a_{12}, a_{21}\right)=\alpha_{1}$. Thus

$$
\begin{equation*}
a_{12} a_{21}=-2 n\left(a_{12}, a_{21}\right) u \quad a_{21} a_{12}=-2 n\left(a_{12}, a_{21}\right) u_{2} \tag{48}
\end{equation*}
$$

for $a_{i j} \in \mathfrak{O}_{i j}$. We now put

$$
\begin{equation*}
n(x, y, z)=n(x, y \wedge z) \in \Phi . \tag{49}
\end{equation*}
$$

It follows from (46) that $n(x, y, z)$ is alternating and $\Phi$-trilinear on $\mathfrak{D}_{0}$. It is easy to see as in the preceding case that if $i \neq j$ and $a_{i j}, b_{i j}, c_{i j} \in \mathfrak{D}_{i j}$ then $\left(a_{i j}, b_{i j}, c_{i j}\right)$ is a basis for $\mathfrak{O}_{i j}$ if and only if $n\left(a_{i j}, b_{i j}, c_{i j}\right) \neq 0$.

Now let $\beta \in$ Aut $\mathfrak{D} / \mathfrak{D}, \mathfrak{D}=\Phi u_{1}+\Phi u_{2}$. Then $\mathfrak{D}_{i j}{ }^{\beta}=\mathfrak{D}_{i j}$. Let $B_{i j}$ be the restriction of $\beta$ to $\mathfrak{O}_{i j}$. Then (48) implies that $n\left(a_{12} B_{12}, a_{21} B_{21}\right)=n\left(a_{12}, a_{21}\right)$. Now we recall that if $\mathfrak{V}$ and $\mathfrak{V}^{*}$ is a pair of finite-dimensional vector spaces with a nondegenerate pairing $\left\langle x, y^{*}\right\rangle, x \in \mathfrak{B}, y^{*} \in \mathfrak{B}^{*}$, then any linear transformation $B$ in $\mathfrak{B}$ has a unique adjoint $B^{*}$ in $\mathfrak{B}^{*}$ such that $\left\langle x B, y^{*}\right\rangle=\left\langle x, y^{*} B^{*}\right\rangle$ for all $x, y^{*}$. The relation is a symmetric one. We write $\hat{B}=\left(B^{*}\right)^{-1}=\left(B^{-1}\right)^{*}$ if $B$ is nonsingular. Then it is clear from the above relation that $B_{21}=\hat{B}_{12}$ (relative to the pairing by $n$ ). Also if ( $a_{i j}, b_{i j}, c_{i j}$ ) is a basis for $\mathfrak{O}_{i j}$ then $n\left(a_{i j} B_{i j}, b_{i j} B_{i j}, c_{i j} B_{i j}\right) =n\left(a_{i j}, b_{i j}, c_{i j}\right)$ and this implies that $B_{i j}$ is unimodular. It is easily seen, as in the discussion of the case II, that, conversely, if $B_{12}$ is any unimodular linear transformation in $\mathfrak{O}_{12}$ and we let $B$ be the linear transformation in $\mathfrak{O}$ which is the identity on the $u_{i}, B_{12}$ on $\mathfrak{O}_{12}$ and $\hat{B}_{12}$ on $\mathfrak{O}_{21}$, then $\beta \in \operatorname{Aut} \mathfrak{O} / \mathfrak{D}$. Thus we have an isomorphism of Aut $\mathfrak{O} / \mathfrak{D}$ onto the unimodular group $\operatorname{SL}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{12}\right)$ in $\mathfrak{D}_{12}$.

If we take into account the results on the groups Aut $\mathfrak{O} / \mathfrak{D}$ and the connection between these and the groups Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K}$ we obtain the following theorem.

Theorem 8. Let $\mathfrak{I}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right), \mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is an octonion algebra and $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a composition subalgebra. Assume we have one the following three cases: I. $\mathfrak{D}$ is a quaternion algebra, II. $\mathfrak{D}$ is a quadratic field, III. $\mathfrak{D}$ is split two-dimensional ( $\cong \Phi \oplus \Phi$ ). Then we have the following possibilities for Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Re$ : I. Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Re$ is isomorphic to the multiplicative group of elements of norm 1 in $\mathfrak{D}$, II. Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K}$ is isomorphic to $\operatorname{SU}(\mathfrak{B}, h)$ where $\mathfrak{B}=\mathrm{P}^{\perp}$, $\mathrm{P}=\mathfrak{D}$ in $\mathfrak{D}$ and $h$ is the hermitian form defined by (44), III. Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Re$ is isomorphic to $S L(\Phi, 3)$.

We remark that, as we indicated at the beginning, this gives a description of Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K}$ for any reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ and any reduced simple subalgebra of degree three with $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{K}=9$ or 15 . Also it should be noted that the results we obtained are considerably sharper than we stated in the theorem since they can be used to describe the action of Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K}$ on $\mathfrak{J}$ in all cases.

We consider next the problem of determining the elements of order two in Aut $\mathfrak{D}$ and Aut $\mathfrak{J}$. In group theory such elements are called the involutions belonging to the group. However, we shall avoid this terminology in the present context for an obvious reason. First, let $\beta$ be an automorphism of period two in $\mathfrak{D}$. Since $\beta$ is orthogonal relative to $n$ we have $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{D}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{D}_{-1}$ whese $\mathfrak{D}_{i}=\left\{x_{i} \mid x_{i}{ }^{\beta}=i x_{i}\right\}$. Then the $\mathfrak{O}_{i}$ are nonisotropic subspaces and $\mathfrak{O}_{1} \perp \mathfrak{O}_{-1}$. Also $\mathfrak{O}_{1}$ is a subalgebra.

Choose $q \in \mathfrak{D}_{-1}$ such that $n(q) \neq 0$. Then $q_{R}$ is a nonsingular linear transformation which interchanges $\mathfrak{D}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{D}_{-1}$. Hence $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}_{1}=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}_{-1}=4$ and $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{D}_{1}$ is a quaternion subalgebra. Thus $\beta$ is the reflection in a quaternion subalgebra in the sense that $\beta$ is the identity mapping on the quaternion subalgebra and is -1 on its orthogonal complement. Conversely, it is easy to see from the description of $\mathfrak{D}$ as $\mathfrak{D}+\mathfrak{D} q, q \in \mathfrak{D}^{\perp}$, that if $\mathfrak{D}$ is any quaternion subalgebra of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ then the reflection in $\mathfrak{D}$ is an automorphism of period two in $\mathfrak{D}$.

Next let $\eta$ be an automorphism of period two in $\mathfrak{J}$, where we assume initially also that the base field is algebraically closed. We have $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{-1}$ where $\mathfrak{J}_{i}=\left\{x_{i} \mid x_{i}{ }^{\eta}=i x_{i}\right\}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ is a subalgebra containing 1. Since $\eta$ is orthogonal relative to the trace form, $\mathfrak{K} \equiv \mathfrak{I}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{I}_{-1}$ are orthogonal and nonisotropic. Thus $\mathfrak{J}_{-1}=\mathfrak{K}^{\perp}$. If $\mathfrak{K}=\Phi 1$ then $\mathfrak{K}^{\perp}=\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ the set of elements of trace 0 . Then $a^{\cdot 2}=\alpha 1, \alpha \in \Phi$, for every $a \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. This is impossible. We note next that if $\mathfrak{B}$ is any subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$ which is not isotropic (relative to the generic trace form on $\mathfrak{J}$ ) then $\mathfrak{B}$ contains no nil ideals $\neq 0$ so $\mathfrak{B}$ is semisimple, and since the base field is algebraically closed, either $\mathfrak{B}$ is one dimensional or it contains an idempotent $\neq 0, \neq$ the identity element of $\mathfrak{B}$. In particular, this applies to $\Re$ and since $\Re \neq \Phi 1$ we see that $\Re$ contains an idempotent $e \neq 0,1$. Since either $e$ or $1-e$ is primitive we may assume $e$ primitive. Then $\eta \in \mathrm{Aut} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ as in §3.

Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)+\mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)+\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$ and $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{K}_{0}(e)+\mathfrak{K}_{1}(e)+\mathfrak{K}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$ be the Peirce decompositions of $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\Re$ relative to $e$. Then $\Re_{i}(e)=\Re \cap \mathfrak{J}_{i}(e)$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)=\Phi f \oplus \mathfrak{B}$ where $f=1-e$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ is the subspace of elements of trace 0 in $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$. Also $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ is the Jordan algebra of the nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $Q$ on $\mathfrak{B}$ (cf. §3). Evidently $\mathfrak{K}_{0}(e)$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e)$ which is nonisotropic relative to $t$ (or $Q=\frac{1}{2} t$ ). Hence either $\Re_{0}(e)$ contains an idempotent $e_{2} \neq 0, \neq f$ or $\Re_{0}(e)=\Phi f$. Then $\mathfrak{K}=\Phi e+\Phi f+\mathfrak{K}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$ and $\mathfrak{B} \subseteq \mathfrak{K}^{\perp}$. Then $v^{\eta}=-v$ for all $v$ in the ninedimensional space $\mathfrak{B}$. This contradicts the fact that any element of Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ induces a rotation in $\mathfrak{B}$ relative to $Q$ (§3). Hence this is ruled out and we can conclude that $\Omega$ contains three orthogonal primitive idempotents $e_{i}$. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\Sigma_{i \leqq j} \mathfrak{J}_{i j}, \Re=\Sigma_{i \leqq j} \Re_{i j}$ be the corresponding Peirce decompositions of $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{K}$. Then the $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ are nonisotropic and the $\mathfrak{K}_{i j}$ are nonisotropic or 0 . Moreover, $\mathfrak{J}_{i j}=\mathfrak{K}_{i j} \oplus \mathfrak{K}_{i j}{ }^{\prime}$ whese $\mathfrak{K}_{i j}{ }^{\prime}=\mathfrak{J}_{i j} \cap \mathfrak{K}^{\perp}$. We now distinguish two cases: I. $\mathfrak{K}_{i j}$ and $\Omega_{i k} \neq 0$ for some choice of $i, j, k=1,2,3, i, j, k \neq$. II. $\Omega_{i j}=0=\Omega_{i k}, i, j, k$ as in I. We may assume $(i, j, k)=(1,2,3)$.
I. In this case we can choose $u_{12} \in \Re_{12}, u_{13} \in \Re_{13}$ such that $u_{12}{ }^{2} \neq 0, u_{13}{ }^{2} \neq 0$. Then we have a coordinatization of $\mathfrak{J}$ adapted to the $e_{i}, u_{12}, u_{13}$ and if we identify $\mathfrak{J}$ with the coordinate algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$, we see that the given automorphism $\eta$ fixes every $1[i j]$. Then $\eta$ has the form $\sum a[i j] \rightarrow \sum a^{\beta}[i j]$ where $\beta$ is an automorphism of period two in $\mathfrak{D}$. Then we have seen that $\beta$ is a reflection in the subalgebra $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ (in the sense that $\eta=1$ on $\mathfrak{K}$ and -1 on $\mathfrak{K}^{\perp}$ ). Conversely, it is immediate that any such reflection is an automorphism of period two in $\mathfrak{J}$.
II. Here $\eta=-1$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{12}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{13}$ so $\eta=1$ on $\mathfrak{J}_{23}=\mathfrak{J}_{12} \cdot \mathfrak{J}_{13}$. Then $\eta$ is the element $\zeta_{e} \neq 1$ in the center of Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ (Corollary 3 to Theorem 4, p. 377).

Our results establish the following theorem in the special case of an algebraically closed base field.

Theorem 9. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional exceptional central simple Jordan algebra. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is reduced if and only if Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ contains elements of period two. If the condition holds then any $\eta \in \operatorname{Aut} \mathfrak{J}$ of period two is either: I. a reflection in a sixteen dimensional central simple subalgebra of degree three, or II. the center element $\zeta_{e} \neq 1$ in a subgroup $\operatorname{Aut} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$, e a primitive idempotent.

Proof. Let $\eta$ be an element of order two in Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ and let $\Re$ be the subalgebra of fixed points, $\Omega$ the algebraic closure of the base field $\Phi$. If $\eta$ is the linear extension of $\eta$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ then $\eta \in$ Aut $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}, \eta^{2}=1$, and $\mathfrak{K}_{\Omega}$ is the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega}$ of fixed points under $\eta$. Our determination of $\eta$ in the algebraically closed case shows that either $\mathfrak{K}_{\Omega} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a (split) quaternion algebra or $\mathfrak{K}_{\Omega}=\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega 1}(e) \oplus \Im_{\Omega 0}(e)$ a direct sum of the one dimensional ideal $\Im_{\Omega 1}(e)=\Omega e$ and a ten-dimensional ideal which is an algebra of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on a nine-dimensional vector space. In the first case, $\mathfrak{K}$ is central simple and is isomorphic to an algebra $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ is a central simple associative algebra with involution (§5.7). Since $\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega} \cong \mathfrak{D}_{3} \cong \Omega_{6}$ and $\mathfrak{A}$ has an involution, the dimensionality of its division algebra (in the Wedderburn theorem) is a power of two. It follows that either $\mathfrak{A} \cong \Phi_{6}$ or $\mathfrak{A} \cong \Delta_{3}$ where $\Delta$ is a division algebra. Also if we take into account the dimensionality of $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ we see that $(\mathfrak{A}, J) \cong\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is quaternion with standard involution. Thus $\mathfrak{K} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ in the first case. Evidently this implies that $\mathfrak{J}$ is reduced and $\eta$ is of the type I specified in the statement of the theorem. Next assume that $\Omega_{\Omega}=\mathfrak{J}_{\Omega 1}(e) \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{\Omega 0}(e)$ as indicated. Then it is easily seen that $\Re$ itself has the same kind of structure so again $\mathfrak{J}$ is reduced. Moreover, it is clear that $\eta=\zeta_{e}$ for a primitive idempotent $e$. Conversely, it is clear that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is reduced then it does contain automorphisms of period two of both of the indicated types.

We shall call the elements of order two in Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ of the types indicated automorphism of order two of type I and type II respectively.

## Exercises

1. Show that the centralizer $\widetilde{C}(\eta)$ of an automorphism of period two and type $I$ in Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ is isomorphic to Aut $\mathfrak{D} \times S L(\mathfrak{D})$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a quaternion subalgebra of the coefficient algebra of $\mathfrak{J}$, Aut $\mathfrak{D}$ is its automorphism group and $S L(\mathfrak{D})$ is the subgroup of elements of (generic) norm 1 in $\mathfrak{D}$. (Note: Aut $\mathfrak{D} \cong \mathfrak{D}^{*} / \Phi^{*}$ where $\mathfrak{D}^{*}$ is the multiplicative group of units of $\mathfrak{D}$, by the Skolem-Noether theorem.)
2. Show that the centralizer $\tilde{C}(\eta)$ of $\eta \in \operatorname{Aut} \mathfrak{J}$ of period two and type II is a subgroup Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e \cong \operatorname{Spin}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ (as in §3).
3. Show that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is split and $e_{i}$ and $f_{i}, i=1,2,3$, are primitive orthogonal idempotents then there exists an automorphism $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $e_{i}{ }^{\eta}=f_{i}$.
4. Show that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is split then any two automorphisms of $\mathfrak{J}$ of period two and type II are conjugate in AutJ.
5. Assume $\Phi$ is either finite or algebraically closed. Prove that any two automorphisms of $\mathfrak{J}$ of period two and type I are conjugate in Aut $\mathfrak{J}$.
6. Let $\Phi$ be finite, $|\Phi|=q$ and let $P$ be the set of primitive idempotents in $\mathfrak{J}$. Show that

$$
|P|=q^{8}\left(q^{8}+q^{4}+1\right)
$$

Show that

$$
|\operatorname{Aut} \mathfrak{J}|=q^{24}\left(q^{12}-1\right)\left(q^{8}-1\right)\left(q^{6}-1\right)\left(q^{2}-1\right)
$$

6. Invariant factor theorem for split $\mathfrak{J}$. In this section we shall prove the following analogue of the invariant factor theorem in a matrix algebra $\Phi_{n}$.

Theorem 10. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional split exceptional simple Jordan algebra. Then $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$ are in the same orbit under Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ if and only if $a$ and $b$ have the same minimum polynomials and the same generic minimum polynomials in J.

We note first that the classical invariant factor theorem implies that two matrices $a, b \in \Phi_{3}$ are similar if and only if they have the same minimum polymonials and characteristic polynomials. We recall also that if $\Omega_{1}$ and $\Omega_{2}$ are subalgebras of $\mathfrak{J}$ isomorphic to $\Phi_{3}{ }^{+}$then there exists an $\eta \in$ Aut $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $\Re_{1}{ }^{\eta}=\Re_{2}$ (Theorem 3 p. 370). It is clear from these two results that the sufficiency of the condition given in Theorem 10 will follow if we can show that any element $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ can be imbedded in a subalgebra $\Re \cong \Phi_{3}{ }^{+}$. Since the necessity of the condition in Theorem 10 is trivial the theorem will follow from the following imbedding theorem.

Theorem 11. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be as in Theorem 10. Then any element $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ can be imbedded in a subalgebra $\mathfrak{K} \cong \Phi_{3}{ }^{+}$.

The proof will be based on several lemmas as follow.
Lemma 1. Any element a of a split finite-dimensional exceptional simple Jordan algebra is contained in a subalgebra $\mathfrak{K}$ of the form $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, \mathfrak{J}_{\gamma}\right)$ where P is a subalgebra of a split octonion algebra generated by 1 and a single element $u$.

Proof (McCrimmon). Let $\left\{e_{i}\right\}$ be a reducing set of idempotents for $\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J} =\sum \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$ the corresponding Peirce decomposition and write $a=\sum \alpha_{i} e_{i}+\sum_{i<j} a_{i j}$ where $\alpha_{i} \in \Phi$ and $a_{i j} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i j}$. We have the following possibilities for the $a_{i j}$ : I. At least two $Q\left(a_{i j}\right) \neq 0$, II. Only one $Q\left(a_{i j}\right) \neq 0$, III. All $Q\left(a_{i j}\right)=0$.

In case $I$ we consider the subalgebra $\Re$ generated by the $e_{i}$ and $a$. As in the
proof of Lemma 2 on p. 362, $\Omega$ is generated by the $e_{i}$ and $a_{i j}$. If $Q\left(a_{i j}\right) \neq 0$ then $e_{i}$ and $e_{j}$ are connected idempotents in $\Re$. Since this is the case for two $a_{i j}$ and connectedness for orthogonal idempotents is a transitive relation, all the $e_{i}$ are connected in $\Re$. Hence by the Coordinatization Theorem and the fact that the $e_{i}$ are absolutely primitive in $\mathfrak{J}$ (and hence in $\mathfrak{K}$ ) it follows that $\mathfrak{K} \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ (cf. the proof of Theorem 5.8 on p. 203). Since $\operatorname{dim} \Re \leqq 9$, by Lemma 2 on p. 362 we have $\operatorname{dim} \mathrm{P} \leqq 2$ so the result is clear in this case.

We shall obtain reductions of cases II and III to case I by introducing new reducing sets of idempotents $\left\{e_{i}^{\prime}\right\}$ relative to which the situation is as in I . We note that if $b_{12} \in \mathfrak{J}_{12}$ satisfies $Q\left(b_{12}\right)=1$ so $b_{12}{ }^{.2}=e$ where $e=e_{1}+e_{2}$ then

$$
\begin{equation*}
e_{1}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2}\left(e+b_{12}\right), \quad e_{2}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2}\left(e-b_{12}\right), \quad e_{3}^{\prime}=e_{3} \tag{50}
\end{equation*}
$$

are nonzero orthogonal idempotents and so form a reducing set. If $a=\sum \alpha_{i}^{\prime} e_{i}^{\prime}+\sum_{i<j} a_{i j}^{\prime}$ is the Peirce decomposition of $a$ relative to the $e_{i}^{\prime}$ then we claim that

$$
\begin{align*}
& a_{12}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}\right)\left(e_{1}-e_{2}\right)+\left(a_{12}-Q\left(a_{12}, b_{12}\right) b_{12}\right)  \tag{51}\\
& a_{13}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2} a_{13}+\frac{1}{2} a_{23}+b_{12} \cdot a_{13}-b_{12} \cdot a_{23}  \tag{52}\\
& a_{23}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2} a_{13}+\frac{1}{2} a_{23}-b_{12} \cdot a_{13}-b_{12} \cdot a_{23} \tag{53}
\end{align*}
$$

We have

$$
\begin{align*}
a_{12}^{\prime} & =2\left\{e_{1}^{\prime} a e_{2}^{\prime}\right\}=\frac{1}{2}\left\{e+b_{12}, a, e-b_{12}\right\}=\frac{1}{2}\{e a e\}-\frac{1}{2}\left\{b_{12} a b_{12}\right\} \\
& =\frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha_{1} e_{1}+\alpha_{2} e_{2}+a_{12}\right)-\frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha_{2} e_{1}+\alpha_{1} e_{2}\right)-\frac{1}{2}\left\{b_{12} a_{12} b_{12}\right\} \quad \text { (by }  \tag{byPD10}\\
& =\frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}\right)\left(e_{1}-e_{2}\right)+\left(a_{12}-Q\left(a_{12}, b_{12}\right) b_{12}\right)
\end{align*}
$$

which is (51). Also

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{13}^{\prime} & =2\left\{e_{1}^{\prime} a e_{3}^{\prime}\right\}=\left\{e+b_{12}, a, e_{3}\right\} \\
& =\frac{1}{2} a_{13}+\frac{1}{2} a_{23}+b_{12} \cdot a_{13}+b_{12} \cdot a_{23}
\end{aligned}
$$

which is (52). Similarly, we obtain (53).
Case II is trivial if two of the $a_{i j}=0$ since in this case $a \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where P is generated by 1 and $u$ where $a_{k i}=u[k i]$ and $a_{i j}=a_{j k}=0, i, j, k \neq$. We now assume at least two $a_{i j} \neq 0$. By symmetry, we may suppose $a_{13} \neq 0, Q\left(a_{23}\right) \neq 0$, $Q\left(a_{12}\right)=Q\left(a_{13}\right)=0$. Since $\mathfrak{J}_{12}$ is eight dimensional and the restriction of $Q$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{12}$ is nondegenerate and of maximal Witt index it is easy to see that if $c_{12} \neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{I}_{12}$ and $\alpha$ is any element of $\Phi$ then there exists a $b_{12} \in \mathfrak{J}_{12}$ such that $Q\left(b_{12}\right)=1$ and $Q\left(b_{12}, c_{12}\right)=\alpha$. We note next that since $a_{13} \neq 0$ and $Q\left(a_{23}\right) \neq 0, c_{12}=a_{13} . a_{23} \neq 0$. Hence, since $|\Phi| \geqq 3$, there exsits a $b_{12} \in \mathfrak{J}_{12}$ such that $Q\left(b_{12}\right)=1$ and
$2 Q\left(b_{12}, c_{12}\right) \neq \pm \frac{1}{2} Q\left(a_{23}\right)$. We use this $b_{12}$ to define the reducing set of idempotents $\left\{e_{i}^{\prime}\right\}$ as above. We claim that we now have $Q\left(a_{13}^{\prime}\right) \neq 0, Q\left(a_{23}^{\prime}\right) \neq 0$. Now

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q\left(a_{13}^{\prime}\right) e_{3}^{\prime} & =a_{13}^{\prime} \cdot 2 \cdot e_{3}^{\prime}=a_{13}^{\prime} \cdot 2 \cdot e_{3} \\
& =\left(\frac{1}{2} a_{13}+b_{12} \cdot a_{23}+\frac{1}{2} a_{23}+b_{12} \cdot a_{13}\right)^{\cdot 2} \cdot e_{3} \\
& =\left(\frac{1}{2} a_{13}+b_{12} \cdot a_{23}\right)^{\cdot 2} \cdot e_{3}+\left(\frac{1}{2} a_{23}+b_{12} \cdot a_{13}\right)^{\cdot 2} \cdot e_{3} \\
& =Q\left(\frac{1}{2} a_{13}+b_{12} \cdot a_{23}\right) e_{3}+Q\left(\frac{1}{2} a_{23}+b_{12} \cdot a_{13}\right) e_{3} \\
& =\left[Q\left(a_{13}, b_{12} \cdot a_{23}\right)+Q\left(b_{12} \cdot a_{23}\right)+\frac{1}{2} Q\left(a_{23}\right)+Q\left(a_{23}, b_{12} \cdot a_{13}\right)\right] e_{3} \\
& =\left[2 Q\left(b_{12}, c_{12}\right)+\frac{1}{2} Q\left(a_{23}\right)\right] e_{3} \neq 0
\end{aligned}
$$

(since $Q\left(a_{i j} \cdot a_{j k}\right)=Q\left(a_{i j}\right) Q\left(a_{j k}\right)$ if $i, j, k \neq$ and $Q$ is an associative bilinear form). Hence $Q\left(a_{13}^{\prime}\right) \neq 0$ and similarly $Q\left(a_{23}^{\prime}\right) \neq 0$. Thus we have case I relative to the $e_{i}^{\prime}$.

Case III is trivial if $a_{12}=a_{23}=a_{13}=0$ so we may assume $a_{12} \neq 0, Q\left(a_{12}\right) =Q\left(a_{23}\right)=Q\left(a_{13}\right)=0$. We can choose $b_{12} \in \mathfrak{J}_{12}$ such that $Q\left(b_{12}\right)=1$ and $Q\left(a_{12}, b_{12}\right) \neq \pm \frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}\right)$. We use this to define the $e_{i}^{\prime}$ as before. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q\left(a_{12}^{\prime}\right) e & =a_{12}^{\prime} \cdot 2=\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}\right)\left(e_{1}-e_{2}\right)+\left(a_{12}-Q\left(a_{12}, b_{12}\right) b_{12}\right)\right]^{\cdot 2} \\
& =\frac{1}{4}\left(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}\right)^{2} e+\left(a_{12}-Q\left(a_{12} \cdot b_{12}\right) b_{12}\right)^{\cdot 2} \\
& =\frac{1}{4}\left(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}\right)^{2} e-2 Q\left(a_{12}, b_{12}\right)^{2} e+Q\left(a_{12}, b_{12}\right)^{2} e \\
& =\left[\frac{1}{4}\left(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}\right)^{2}-Q\left(a_{12}, b_{12}\right)^{2}\right] e \neq 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $Q\left(a_{12}^{\prime}\right) \neq 0$ and we have either case I or II relative to the $e_{\imath}^{\prime}$. This completes the proof.

Lemma 2. Any element $u$ of a split octonion algebra can be imbedded in a split quaternion subalgebra.

Proof. We may assume $\bar{u}=-u \neq 0$. If $n(u) 1=u \bar{u} \neq 0$ we choose $v$ so that $\bar{v}=-v, v \perp u$ and $n(v)=-1$. This can be done since the norm form has maximal Witt index. Then $v^{2}=1$ and the subalgebra generated by $1, u, v$ is split quaternion. Next assume $n(u)=0$. Then we can choose $v$ so that $\bar{v}=-v, n(v)=0, n(u, v)=\frac{1}{2}$. Then if we put $w=u+v, z=u-v$ we have $n(w)=1, n(z)=-1, w \perp z$. Hence the subalgebra generated by $1, w, z$ is a split quaternion and this contains the element $u$.

Lemmas 1 and 2 evidently imply that if $a$ is any element of a finite-dimensional split exceptional simple Jordan algebra then $a$ can be imbedded in a subalgebra of the form $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ where $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$ is a split quaternion algebra. Then $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{6}, J_{S}\right)$ where $J_{S}$ is an involution defined by a skew symmetric
matrix. Then $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{6}, J_{S}\right)$ is isomorphic to the Jordan algebra of linear transformations in a six dimensional vector space which are selfadjoint relative to a nondegenerate skew bilinear form $f$. Hence the proof of Theorem 11 can be completed by proving

Lemma 3. Let $f$ be a nondegenerate skew bilinear form on a $2 n$-dimensional vector space $\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{H}$ the Jordan algebra of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{B}$ which are selfadjoint relative to $f$. Then any $A \in \mathfrak{H}$ can be imbedded in a subalgebra $\Omega$ containing 1 such that $\Re \cong \Phi_{n}{ }^{+}$.

Proof. We shall obtain the proof by deriving a "rational" canonical form for $A$. Let $\mu(\lambda)=\lambda^{m}-\alpha_{1} \lambda^{m-1}+\cdots+(-1)^{m} \alpha_{m}$ be the minimum polynomial of $A$ and let $x \in \mathfrak{B}$ have order polynomial $\mu(\lambda)$. Then $\left(x, x A, \cdots, x A^{m-1}\right)$ are linearly independent and $f\left(x A^{i}, x A^{j}\right)=f\left(x A^{i+j}, x\right)=-f\left(x, x A^{i+j}\right)=-f\left(x A^{i}, x A^{j}\right)=0$. Hence the subspace $\sum_{0}^{m-1} \Phi\left(x A^{i}\right)$ is totally isotropic. Since $f$ is nondegenerate there exists a $y \in \mathfrak{B}$ such that $f\left(x A^{m-1}, y\right)=1, f\left(x A^{i}, y\right)=0,0 \leqq i \leqq m-2$. Then $f\left(x A^{m-2}, y A\right)=1, f\left(x A^{i}, y A\right)=0,0 \leqq i \leqq m-3, f\left(x A^{m-3}, y A^{2}\right)=1, f\left(x A^{i}, y A^{2}\right) =0,0 \leqq i \leqq m-4$, etc. It follows that $\left(y, y A, \cdots, y A^{m-1}\right)$ are linearly independent so the order polynomial of $y$ is also $\mu(\lambda)$. Moreover, $\sum_{0}^{m-1} \Phi\left(y A^{i}\right)$ is totally isotropic and $\mathfrak{B}_{1} \equiv \sum \Phi\left(x A^{i}\right)+\sum \Phi\left(y A^{i}\right)$ is not isotropic. Hence $\mathfrak{V}=\mathfrak{V}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{V}_{1}{ }^{\perp}$. Since $A$ is selfadjoint and maps $\mathfrak{B}_{1}$ into itself we have $\mathfrak{B}_{1}{ }^{\perp} A \subseteq \mathfrak{B}_{1}{ }^{\perp}$. We can repeat the process with the restriction of $A$ to $\mathfrak{V}_{1}{ }^{\perp}$. Continuing in this way we obtain a decomposition of $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{X} \oplus \mathfrak{Y}$ where $\mathfrak{X}$ and $\mathfrak{Y}$ are totally isotropic $n$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathfrak{V}$ such that $\mathfrak{X} A \subseteq \mathfrak{X}$ and $\mathfrak{Y} A \subseteq \mathfrak{Y}$. Let $\mathfrak{K}$ be the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{H}$ of linear transformations $B$ such that $\mathfrak{X} B \subseteq \mathfrak{X}, \mathfrak{Y} B \subseteq \mathfrak{Y}$. It is clear that $f$ gives a nondegenerate bilinear pairing of $\mathfrak{X}$ and $\mathfrak{Y}$. Hence if $C$ is a linear transformation in $\mathfrak{X}$ there exists a unique linear transformation $C^{*}$ in $\mathfrak{Y}$ such that $f(x C, y)=f\left(x, y C^{*}\right), x \in \mathfrak{X}, y \in \mathfrak{Y}$. Then the linear mapping $B$ in $\mathfrak{B}$ which coincides with $C$ on $\mathfrak{X}$ and with $C^{*}$ on $\mathfrak{Y}$ is selfadjoint and so $B \in \mathfrak{R}$. It is now clear that $\Omega$ is isomorphic to $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{X}, \mathfrak{X})^{+}$and so to $\Phi_{n}{ }^{+}$. Since $A \in \Omega$ we have our result.

This completes the proof of Theorem 11 and hence also of the invariant factor theorem (Theorem 10).

## Exercises

1. (Taussky-Zassenhaus). Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field $\Phi$ and let $A \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{B})$. Show that there exists a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $A$ is selfadjoint relative to $f$.
2. Let $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right), \mathrm{P}$ a quadratic field. Show that any element $a \in \mathfrak{K}$ can be imbedded in a subalgebra isomorphic to an algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$.
3. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra. Show that any element $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ can be imbedded in a subalgebra $\Omega$ which is isomorphic to an algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and that if $a$ is nilpotent then we may take $\gamma=\operatorname{diag}\{1,-1,1\}$.
4. Prove that any two nilpotent elements of $\mathfrak{J}$ (as in 3 ) of index three nilpotency are in the same orbit under Aut J.
5. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a split exceptional simple Jordan algebra, $\Gamma$ a cubic subfield. Show that every isomorphism of $\Gamma / \Phi$ in $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ can be extended to an automorphism. Show that if $\Phi$ is finite and $|\Phi|=q$ then the number of isomorphisms of $\Gamma$ into $\mathfrak{J}$ is $q^{12}\left(q^{8}-1\right)\left(q^{4}-1\right)$. Use this and exercise 6, p. 389 to prove that the order of the group Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Gamma$ of automorphisms of $\mathfrak{J}$ leaving fixed the elements of $\Gamma$ is

$$
q^{12}\left(q^{8}+q^{4}+1\right)\left(q^{6}-1\right)\left(q^{2}-1\right)
$$

6. Show that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is split then $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is transitive on the set of elements of generic norm 1 in $\mathfrak{J}$.
7. Assume the base field $\Phi$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ is finite, $|\Phi|=q$. Show that if $N_{\alpha}, \alpha \in \Phi$, is the subset of $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ such that $n(a)=\alpha$ then $\left|N_{\alpha}\right|=\left|N_{\beta}\right|$ if $\alpha, \beta \neq 0$. Prove that

$$
\left|N_{0}\right|=(q-1)\left(q^{21}+q^{17}-q^{12}\right)
$$

and

$$
\left|N_{1}\right|=q^{12}\left(q^{9}-1\right)\left(q^{5}-1\right) .
$$

Use this and exercise 6 p. 389 to prove that the order of $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is

$$
q^{36}\left(q^{12}-1\right)\left(q^{9}-1\right)\left(q^{8}-1\right)\left(q^{6}-1\right)\left(q^{5}-1\right)\left(q^{2}-1\right) .
$$

8. Prove that any finite-dimensional simple exceptional Jordan algebra is regular (see p. 179 for definition).
9. Moufang projective planes. In this section we shall associate with a reduced exceptional simple Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with coefficient algebra $\mathfrak{O}$ a division algebra, a projective plane $\mathfrak{P}=\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$. The planes $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{P}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ determined by isotopic Jordan algebras $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ are isomorphic. Since $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ are isotopic if and only if they have isomorphic coefficient algebras we may regard $\mathfrak{P}$ as determined by the coefficient algebra and, accordingly, we shall write also $\mathfrak{P}=\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{D})$. The projective planes $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{D})$ are isomorphic to some which were first defined in an entirely different manner by R. Moufang [1]. The present construction of Moufang planes was first given by P. Jordan in [3] for the case: $\Phi$, the field of reals. This was rediscovered by Freudenthal in [1] and formulated for arbitrary base fields of characteristic $\neq 2,3$ by Springer in [2]. We shall develop the theory here for arbitrary base fields of characteristic $\neq 2$. Our primary interest will be in the "geometric algebra" of Moufang planes, which is concerned with the algebraic formulations of the basic geometric concepts related to these planes.

We suppose first that $\mathfrak{J}$ is an arbitrary reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra. As in §2, we let $\Pi=\Pi(\mathfrak{J})$ be the set of elements of rank one in $\mathfrak{J} (a \neq 0, a \times a=0)$ and we let $[\Pi]$ be the set of rays $[a]=\Phi^{*} a, a \in \Pi$. We can use $[\Pi]$ to define an incidence structure $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$. We recall that such a structure is an ordered triple $(\pi, \lambda, \iota)$ where $\pi$ and $\lambda$ are nonvacuous sets called respectively
the set of points and the set of lines of the structure and $\iota$ is a correspondence of $\pi$ to $\lambda$, that is, $\iota$ is a subset of the product set $\pi \times \lambda$ (cf. Pickert [1, p. 2]). If $P \in \pi$ and $l \in \lambda$ satisfy $(P, l) \in \iota$ then the point $P$ and the line $l$ are said to be incident or $P$ is said to lie on $l$ and $l$ is said to pass through $P$. We now define $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ by putting $\pi=[\Pi], \lambda=[\Pi]$ and defining incidence of $P=[x], l=[u]$ by the condition $t(x, u)=0$, that is, $x \perp u$ relative to the trace form.

If $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} / \Phi^{\prime}$ are finite-dimensional Jordan algebra with 1 (or more generally strictly power associative algebras) over the fields $\Phi$ and $\Phi^{\prime}$ respectively, then a mapping $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is called a norm semisimilarity if $\eta$ is a bijective semilinear mapping and there exists a $\rho \neq 0$ in $\Phi^{\prime}$ such that $n\left(a^{\eta}\right)=\rho n(a)^{\sigma}$ where $\sigma$ is the isomorphism of $\Phi$ onto $\Phi^{\prime}$ associated with $\eta\left((\alpha x)^{\eta}=\alpha^{\sigma} x^{\eta}, \alpha \in \Phi, x \in \mathfrak{J}\right)$. Suppose now that $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ are reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebras. Then we shall show that a norm semisimilarity $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} / \Phi^{\prime}$ determines an isomorphism $[\eta]$ of the incidence structure $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $\mathfrak{P}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$, that is, bijective mappings $P \rightarrow P^{\prime}$, $l \rightarrow l^{\prime}$ of the sets of points and the sets of lines such that for any point $P$ and line $l$, $P$ is incident to $l$ if and only if $P^{\prime}$ is incident to $l^{\prime}$. We note first that if $(a, b, c) =\frac{1}{2} \Delta^{c}{ }_{a} \Delta^{b} n$ in $\mathfrak{J}$ (and similarly in $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ ) then we have the formula (12') for ( $a, b, c$ ): $(a, b, c)=\frac{1}{2}[n(a+b+c)-n(a+b)-n(b+c)-n(a+c)+n(a)+n(b) +n(c)]$. Evidently this implies that $\left(a^{\eta}, b^{\eta}, c^{\eta}\right)=\rho(a, b, c)^{\sigma}$ if $\eta$ is a norm semisimilarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ (with multiplier $\rho$ ). We recall also that ( $a, b, c$ ) $=t(a \times b, c)$, which implies that $a \in \Pi$ if and only if $a \neq 0$ and $(a, a, x)=0$ for all $x \in \mathfrak{J}$. It is now clear that $a \in \Pi(\mathfrak{J})$ if and only if $a^{n} \in \Pi\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ for the norm semisimilarity $\eta$ and that $[a] \rightarrow\left[a^{\eta}\right]$ is a bijection of $[\Pi(\mathfrak{J})]$ onto $\left[\Pi\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)\right]$.

We recall next that every semilinear mapping $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ into $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} / \Phi^{\prime}$ defines a unique mapping $\eta^{*}$ of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ into $\mathfrak{J}$ by the condition that

$$
\begin{equation*}
t\left(a^{\prime}, b^{\eta}\right)=t\left(a^{\prime \eta^{*}}, b\right)^{\sigma} \tag{54}
\end{equation*}
$$

for all $a^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}, b \in \mathfrak{J}$, where the $t$ on the left is the generic trace in $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ that on the right is the generic trace in $\mathfrak{J}$, and $\sigma$ is the isomorphism of $\Phi$ onto $\Phi^{\prime}$ associated with $\eta$. Then $\eta^{*}$ is a semilinear mapping with associated isomorphism $\sigma^{-1}$ of $\Phi^{\prime}$ onto $\Phi$. If $\eta$ is bijective so is $\eta^{*}$ and $\hat{\eta}=\left(\eta^{*}\right)^{-1}$ is a bijective semilinear mapping of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ with associated isomorphism $\sigma$.

Now let $\eta$ be a norm semisimilarity with multiplier $\rho$. Then $t\left(a^{\eta} \times b^{\eta}, c^{\eta}\right) =\left(a^{\eta}, b^{\eta}, c^{\eta}\right)=\rho(a, b, c)^{\sigma}=\rho t(a \times b, c)^{\sigma}$ gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left(a^{\eta} \times b^{\eta}\right)^{\eta^{*}}=\rho^{\sigma-1} a \times b \tag{55}
\end{equation*}
$$

or

$$
\begin{equation*}
a^{\eta} \times b^{\eta}=\rho(a \times b)^{\eta} . \tag{55'}
\end{equation*}
$$

Suppose further that $1^{n}=1$, the identity element of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Then the condition $n\left(a^{\eta}\right)=\rho n(a)^{\sigma}$ for $a=1$ gives $\rho=1$. Also $n\left((1 \pm a)^{\eta}\right)=n(1 \pm a)^{\sigma}$ and the formula $n(\lambda 1-a)=m_{a}(\lambda)=\lambda^{3}-t(a) \lambda^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left[t(a)^{2}-t\left(a^{-2}\right)\right] \lambda-n(a)$ imply $t\left(a^{\eta}\right)=t(a)^{\sigma}$,
$t\left(\left(a^{\eta}\right)^{\cdot 2}\right)=t\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)^{\sigma}$. Also the formula for $a \times b$ gives $a \times 1=\frac{1}{2} t(a) 1-\frac{1}{2} a, 1 \times 1=1$. Then, by (55') with $\rho=1$, we obtain $1^{\hat{\eta}}=(1 \times 1)^{\hat{\eta}}=1^{\eta} \times 1^{\eta}=1$ and $(a \times 1)^{\hat{\eta}} =a^{\eta} \times 1$ so $\frac{1}{2} t(a)^{\sigma} 1^{\hat{\eta}}-\frac{1}{2} a^{\hat{\eta}}=\frac{1}{2} t\left(a^{\eta}\right) 1-\frac{1}{2} a^{\eta}$. Hence $a^{\hat{\eta}}=a^{\eta}$ and $(a \times b)^{\eta}= a^{\eta} \times b^{\eta}$ by (55'). It follows that $\left(a^{\cdot 2}\right)^{\eta}=\left(a^{\eta}\right)^{\cdot 2}$ and $(a . b)^{\eta}=a^{\eta} . b^{\eta}$. Thus $\eta$ is a semilinear isomorphism of $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} / \Phi^{\prime}$, that is, $\eta$ is a bijective semilinear mapping which preserves the product: $(a . b)^{\eta}=a^{\eta} . b^{\eta}$. Conversely, if $\eta$ is a semilinear isomorphism of $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} / \Phi^{\prime}$ then $1^{n}$ is the identity of $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ and the proof of Theorem 6.1 (VI) (p. ) carries over to show that $n\left(a^{n}\right)=n(a)^{\sigma}, a \in \mathfrak{J}$, so $\eta$ is a norm semisimilarity. Also we have $\hat{\eta}=\eta$ as before.

Now assume $\eta$ is an arbitrary norm semisimilarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Then $1^{\eta}$ is invertible in $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ and this element is the identity element of the isotope $\left(\mathfrak{J}, u^{\prime}\right)$ where $u^{\prime}=\left(1^{\eta}\right)^{.-1}$. The formula relating the generic norm of a Jordan algebra and an isotope (p. 242) shows that the identity mapping is a norm similarity of an algebra onto any isotope. Hence $\eta$ is a norm semisimilarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto the isotope $\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}, u^{\prime}\right)$ sending 1 into the identity of the latter algebra. Hence, by the result just proved, $\eta$ is a semilinear isomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}, u^{\prime}\right)$ and the mapping $\eta^{*\left(u^{\prime}\right)}$ defined as in (54) by the generic trace forms in $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}, u^{\prime}\right)$ satisfies $\eta^{*\left(u^{\prime}\right)}=\eta^{-1}$. Now it is clear that $\eta$ as mapping of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is the product of the semilinear isomorphism $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto ( $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}, u^{\prime}$ ) and the identity mapping considered as norm similarity of ( $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}, u^{\prime}$ ) onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. The formula (77) of Chapter VI (p. 246) shows that for the identity mapping $1_{\mathfrak{J}}$, of $\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}, u^{\prime}\right)$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ we have $1_{\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}}{ }^{*^{\prime}}=U_{1}{ }^{n^{\prime \prime}}$, where the ${ }^{* \prime}$ denotes the mapping associated with $1_{\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}}$ in place of $\eta$ in (54) using the generic trace forms of $\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}, u^{\prime}\right)$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$, and $U_{1^{\prime \prime}}{ }^{\left(u^{\prime}\right)}$ is the $U$-operator in $\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}, u^{\prime}\right)$ determined by $1^{\eta}$. Now we have $\eta^{*}=\left(\eta 1_{\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}}\right)^{*}=1_{\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}}{ }^{* \prime} \eta^{*\left(u^{\prime}\right)}=U_{1^{\prime \prime}}{ }^{\left(u^{\prime}\right)} \eta^{*\left(u^{\prime}\right)}=U_{1^{\prime \prime}}{ }^{\left(u^{\prime}\right)} \eta^{-1}$ and $\hat{\eta}=\eta\left(U_{1^{\eta^{\prime}}}{ }^{\left(u^{\prime}\right)}\right)^{-1}$ which shows that $\hat{\eta}$ is a norm semisimilarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$. Consequently, [a] $\rightarrow\left[a^{\eta}\right]$ is a bijection of $[\Pi(\mathfrak{J})]$ onto $\left[\Pi\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)\right]$.

We can now associate with the given norm semisimilarity $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} / \Phi^{\prime}$ a mapping $[\eta]$ of the incidence structure $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $\mathfrak{P}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$. by means of the following formulas:

$$
[\eta]: \quad \begin{array}{ll}
P=[x] \rightarrow P^{\prime}=\left[x^{\eta}\right], & P \in \pi(\mathfrak{J}), \\
l=[u] \rightarrow l^{\prime}=\left[u^{\eta}\right], & l \in \lambda(\mathfrak{J}) . \tag{56}
\end{array}
$$

As we have seen, this is bijective for the points of $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{P}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ and the lines of $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{P}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$. Also we have from (54) that $t\left(a^{\hat{\eta}}, b^{\eta}\right)=t(a, b)^{\sigma}$ for $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}$ which show that $a \perp b$ if and only if $a^{\hat{\eta}} \perp b^{\eta}$. Hence it is clear that $[\eta]$ is an isomorphism of the incidence structures.

A first consequence of this result, is that if $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ have isomorphic coefficient algebras (so $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ are isotopic) then the incidence structures $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ are isomorphic. Thus we see that $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ depends only on the coefficient algebra $\mathfrak{O}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$, and we may write $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{D})$ for $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$.

We shall now assume that $\mathfrak{O}$ is a division algebra and we shall show that in
this case $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{O})$ is a projective plane. We recall that an incidence structure is a projective plane if it satisfies the following axioms.
I. Any two distinct points are incident with one and only one line.
II. Any two distinct lines are incident with one and only one point.
III. There exist four points no three of which are incident with the same line.

We can state these conditions in a more relaxed form that two distinct points determine a unique line (or lie on a unique line) and two distinct lines meet (or intersect) in a unique point. Also there exist four points no three of which are collinear.

We shall now verify these axioms for $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{O}), \mathfrak{O}$ an octonion division algebra.
Lemma 1. Let $A, B \in \Pi(\mathfrak{J})$ where $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$, $\mathfrak{O}$ a division algebra, and assume $A, B$ are linearly independent. Then $A \times B \in \Pi(\mathfrak{J})$.

Proof. Let $A$ be as in (1): $A=\sum_{1}^{3} \alpha_{i} e_{i i}+a[23]+b[31]+c[12], a, b, c \in \mathfrak{D}$. Suppose first that $B=e_{11}$. Then $A \times e_{11}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha_{3} e_{22}+\alpha_{2} e_{33}-a[23]\right)$. If $A \times e_{11} =0$ we have $\alpha_{2}=\alpha_{3}=a=0$. Now we have shown in the proof of Lemma 2 of $\S 2$ that if $A \in \Pi$ then either $A$ is a nonzero multiple of an element of the form given in (19) or all the entries of $A$ are $\neq 0$. Hence $A \times e_{11}=0$ implies $A$ is a multiple of $e_{11}$ contrary to hypothesis. Hence $A \times e_{11} \neq 0$. The conditions that $A \times A=0$ given by (6) include $\alpha_{2} \alpha_{3}=\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{2} n(a)$ which implies that

$$
A \times e_{11}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha_{3} e_{22}+\alpha_{2} e_{33}-a[23]\right)
$$

satisfies $\left(A \times e_{11}\right) \times\left(A \times e_{11}\right)=0$. Hence $A \times e_{11} \in \Pi$. Now let $A$ and $B$ be arbitrary linearly independent elements of $\Pi$. By Lemma 2 of §2, there exists an $\eta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $B^{\eta}=e_{11}$. If $\rho$ is the multiplier of $\eta$ then (56') gives $\rho(A \times B)^{\eta}=A^{\eta} \times e_{11}$ and $A^{\eta}, e_{11}$ are linearly independent elements of $\Pi$. Then $A^{\eta} \times e_{11} \in \Pi$ which implies that $A \times B \in \Pi$.

Lemma 2. Let $A, B, \mathfrak{J}$ be as in Lemma 1. Then $C \in \Pi(\mathfrak{J})$ satisfies $t(A, C) =0=t(B, C)$ if and only if $C$ is a multiple of $A \times B$.

Proof. We have $t(A, A \times B)=(A, B, A)=(A, A, B)=t(A \times A, B)=0$ and similarly $t(B, A \times B)=0$. Hence any multiple of $A \times B$ satisfies the conditions. Next let $C$ satisfy the conditions. Assume first that $C=e_{11}$. Then $t(A, C)=0$ implies that the $(1,1)$ entry of $A$ is 0 . Then (19) shows that $A$ has the form $\alpha_{2} e_{22} +\alpha_{3} e_{33}+a[23]$. Similarly, $B$ has the form $\beta_{2} e_{22}+\beta_{3} e_{33}+b[23]$. Direct calculation shows that $A \times B$ is a multiple of $C=e_{11}$. Now suppose $C$ is any element of $\Pi$ satisfying $t(A, C)=0=t(B, C)$. By Lemma 2 of §2, there exists an $\eta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $C^{\eta}=e_{11}$. Then $t\left(A^{\hat{\eta}}, e_{11}\right)=t(A, C)=0$ and $t\left(B^{\hat{\eta}}, e_{11}\right)=0$. Hence $A^{\hat{\eta}} \times B^{\hat{\eta}}$ is a multiple of $e_{11}$ by the result just proved. By (56') for $\hat{\eta}$ in place of $\eta$ we see that this implies that $(A \times B)^{\eta}$ is a multiple of $e_{11}=C^{\eta}$. Then $A \times B$ is a multiple of $C$.

We can now prove
Theorem 12. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a reduced exceptional simple Jordan algebra whose coefficient algebra $\mathfrak{O}$ is an octonion division algebra. Then the incidence structure $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{D})$ is a projective plane.

Proof. Let $P_{1}=\left[x_{1}\right], P_{2}=\left[x_{2}\right]$ be distinct points in $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ so $x_{1}, x_{2} \in \Pi(\mathfrak{J})$ and these elements are linearly independent. Put $u=x_{1} \times x_{2}$. Then $u \in \Pi$ and $t\left(x_{i}, u\right)=0$. Thus $[u]$ is a line incident with $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$. Now let $[v]$ be any line incident with $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$. Then, by Lemma 2, $[v]=[u]$. Hence $\left[x_{1} \times x_{2}\right]$ is the only line incident to $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$. Thus axiom I holds. In the same way axiom II holds. To see that axiom III holds we take $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and take $P_{i}=\left[e_{i i}\right]$, for $i=1,2,3$ and $P_{4}$ to be any element of $\Pi$ all of whose entries are nonzero. (The proof of Lemma 2 of §2 shows that there exist such elements in $\Pi$.) Now if $P=[x], Q=[y], R=[z]$ where $x, y, z \in \Pi$ then it is clear from Lemma 2 that $P, Q$ and $R$ are collinear if and only if $(x, y, z)=0$. It follows directly that no three of the four points $P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}, P_{4}$ are collinear.

## Exercises

1. Show that $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ is not a projective plane if $\mathfrak{J}$ is split.
2. Verify that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is reduced and not split then $P=[x]$ is collinear with $\left[e_{1}\right]$ and $\left[e_{2}\right]$ where the $e_{i}$ are primitive orthogonal idempotents if and only if $x \in \Phi e_{1}+\Phi e_{2}+\mathfrak{J}_{12}$.
3. Elations. It is customary to call an isomorphism of a projective plane on a second one a projective transformation and an automorphism of a projective plane a collineation. If ( $\pi, \lambda, \iota$ ) is a projective plane then the dual structure ( $\lambda, \pi, \iota^{\prime}$ ) where $\iota^{\prime}$ is the set of pairs $(l, P)$ such that $(P, l) \in \iota$ is a projective plane. An isomorphism of a plane onto its dual is called a correlation. It is clear that the collineations form a group of transformations on $\lambda \cup \pi$ and it is easy to see that this group is determined by its action on $\pi$ or on $\lambda$. It is easy to see also that if a collineation has a line $l$ of fixed points (that is, all points incident with $l$ are fixed) and it has two distinct fixed points not on $l$ then the collineation is the identity. Let $l$ be a line, $P$ a point on $l$. Then we define an elation $\tau$ with center $P$ and axis $l$ to be a collineation $\neq 1$ which leaves fixed every point on $l$ and every line through $P$ :
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-406.jpg?height=259&width=800&top_left_y=1908&top_left_x=474)

It is clear that the center and axis are uniquely determined and if $X$ is any point not on the axis then the image $X^{\tau}$ is on the line $P X$ (incident with $X$ and $P$ ). Also since $\tau^{-1}$ is an elation with center $P$ and axis $l$ it is clear that $X^{\tau} \neq P$. It is easy to see from the definition and the axioms that $\tau$ is determined by specifying its center and axis and the image $X^{\prime}$ of any point $X$ not on the axis. The elations with a fixed center and axis together with the identity mapping form a subgroup of the collineation group. The subgroup of the collineation group generated by all the elations is called the little projective group (or unimodular group) of the projective plane. If $\tau$ is an elation with center $P$ and axis $l$ and $\varepsilon$ is a collineation then $\varepsilon^{-1} \tau \varepsilon$ is an elation with center $P^{\varepsilon}$ and axis $l^{\varepsilon}$. Hence the little projective group is an invariant subgroup of the collineation group.

We now consider the projective plane $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{I})$ defined by the reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with coefficient algebra $\mathfrak{D}$, an octonion division algebra. Let $\mathrm{N}(\mathfrak{J})$ denote the group of norm semisimilarities of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}$. We have seen that every $\eta \in \mathrm{N}(\mathfrak{J})$ determines a collineation $[\eta]$ in $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ as in (57). The mapping $\eta \rightarrow[\eta]$ is a homomorphism of $\mathrm{N}(\mathfrak{J})$ into the collineation group $\Gamma(\mathfrak{P})$ of $\mathfrak{P}$, whose image we denote as $[\mathrm{N}(\mathfrak{J})]$. Similarly, the subgroup $\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ of norm similarities (and its various subgroups $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(1)}(\mathfrak{J}), \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)}(\mathfrak{J}), \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ previously defined) defines a subgroup $[\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})]\left(\left[\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})\right]\right.$ etc. $)$ of $\Gamma(\mathfrak{P})$. We shall now determine the kernel of the homomorphism $\eta \rightarrow[\eta]$ of $\mathrm{N}(\mathfrak{J})$ in the following

Lemma 1. If $\eta \in \mathrm{N}(\mathfrak{J})$ then $[\eta]=1$ if and only if $\eta \in \Phi^{*}$, that is, $\eta$ is a multiplication by a nonzero element of $\Phi$.

Proof. If $v$ is a norm similarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto a second reduced exceptional simple Jordan algebra then $\eta \rightarrow v^{-1} \eta v$ and $[\eta]=[v]^{-1}[\eta][v]$ are isomorphisms of $\mathrm{N}(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $\mathrm{N}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ and of $[\mathrm{N}(\mathfrak{J})]$ onto $\left[\mathrm{N}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)\right]$ respectively. Hence it is enough to prove the lemma for a suitable isotope $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$. We take this to have the form $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$. Consider the four points $\left[e_{i i}\right], i=1,2,3,[A]$ where $A=\sum_{i . j} e_{i j}$. We have $\left(e_{11}, e_{22}, e_{33}\right)=t\left(e_{11} \times e_{22}, e_{33}\right)=t\left(\frac{1}{2} e_{33}, e_{33}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \quad$ and similarly, $\left(e_{i i}, e_{j j}, A\right)=\frac{1}{2}$ if $i \neq j$. Now suppose $\eta$ is a norm semisimilarity of $\mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ such that $[\eta]=1$ and let $\rho$ be the multiplier and $\sigma$ the automorphism in $\Phi$ of $\eta$. If $a, b, c \in \mathfrak{H}$ then we have $\left(a^{\eta}, b^{\eta}, c^{\eta}\right)=\rho(a, b, c)^{\sigma}$. We have $e_{i i}{ }^{\eta}=\lambda_{i} e_{i i}, A^{\eta}=\lambda A$. Since $\left(\frac{1}{2} 1\right)^{\sigma}=\frac{1}{2} 1$ these conditions give $\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2} \lambda_{3}=\rho, \lambda_{\imath} \lambda_{j} \lambda=\rho$ if $i \neq j$. Then $\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=\lambda_{3}=\lambda$ and so replacing $\eta$ by $\lambda^{-1} \eta$ we may assume $e_{i i}{ }^{\eta}=e_{i i}, A^{\eta}=A$. Then $1^{\eta}=1$ so $\eta$ is a semilinear automorphism of $\mathfrak{H}$ (by the results of §7). Since $e_{i i}{ }^{\eta}=e_{i i}$ we have $\mathfrak{H}_{i j}{ }^{\eta} \subseteq \mathfrak{H}_{i j}$ for the the Peirce spaces $\mathfrak{H}_{i j}$ relative to the $e_{i i}$. Now let $i \neq j$ and let $q \in \mathfrak{D}$. Then the element $e_{i i}+n(q) e_{j j}+q[i j] \in \Pi$. Hence $\left(e_{i i}+n(q) e_{j j}+q[i j]\right)^{\eta}=e_{i i}+n(q)^{\sigma} e_{j j}+q[i j]^{\eta}$ is a multiple of $e_{i i}+n(q) e_{j j} +q[i j]$. This gives $q[i j]^{\eta}=q[i j]$. It follows that $\eta$ is the identity mapping, which proves the lemma.

It is clear from this result that the kernel of the homomorphism $\eta \rightarrow[\eta]$ of $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ consists of the multiplications by elements $\omega \in \Phi$ such that $\omega^{3}=1$. Hence
the kernel of $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is either the identity or it has order three. The main result we shall prove in this section is that $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ and the image of this group under the indicated homomorphism is the little projective group of $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$.

Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right), \mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$, where $(\mathrm{P}, j)$ is a quadratic subfield of $(\mathfrak{D}, j)$. As in §2, let $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)} \mathfrak{I}(\mathfrak{K})$ be the subgroup of $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ of elements of the form $U_{A_{1}} U_{A_{2}} \cdots U_{A_{r}}$ whese the $A_{i} \in \Re$ and $\Pi_{1}^{r} n\left(A_{i}\right)=1$. Then we have seen in Lemma 1 of §2 that $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)}{ }_{\mathfrak{F}}(\mathfrak{K})$ coincides with the set of mappings $T_{B}: X \rightarrow B^{*} X B$ where $B \in \mathrm{P}_{3}$. We saw also that this group is generated by the mappings $T_{Q_{i j}}$ where $Q_{i j}=1+q e_{i j}, q \in \mathrm{P}, i \neq j$. Moreover, (20) gives the form of $T_{Q_{i j}}$. According to this we see that every element of the form $\alpha e_{j j}+\beta e_{k k}+a[j k], j \neq k$, is fixed under $T_{Q_{i j}}$. These include all the elements $A \in \Pi$ such that $t\left(e_{i i}, A\right)=0$. Hence [ $T_{Q_{i j}}$ ] leaves fixed every point on the line [ $e_{i i}$ ]. We saw also that $T_{Q_{i j^{*}}}=T_{Q_{i j}}$ and $Q_{i j}{ }^{*}=1+\gamma_{j}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{i} \bar{q} e_{j i}$. Hence $\hat{T}_{Q_{i j}}=T_{R_{j i}}$ where $r=-\gamma_{j}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{i} \bar{q}$ and consequently $\left[T_{Q_{i j}}\right]$ leaves fixed every line through the point $\left[e_{j j}\right]$. Since $t\left(e_{j j}, e_{i i}\right)=0,\left[e_{j j}\right]$ is on the line $\left[e_{i i}\right]$ so $\left[T_{Q_{i j}}\right]$ is an elation with $\left[e_{j j}\right]$ as center and $\left[e_{i i}\right]$ as axis. Since the $T_{Q_{i j}}$ generate $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)} \mathfrak{J}(\mathfrak{K})$ we see that the image $\left[\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)} \mathfrak{J}(\mathfrak{K})\right]$ of $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)}{ }_{\mathfrak{s}}(\mathfrak{K})$ in the collineation group is contained in the little projective group $\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$ of $\mathfrak{P}=\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{I})$. We note also that $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)}{ }_{\mathfrak{F}}(\mathfrak{K})$ contains every $T_{\omega 1}$ where $\omega \in \Phi$ and $\omega^{3}=1$. Since this is the multiplication by $\omega^{2}$ we see that $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)}{ }_{\mathfrak{J}}(\mathfrak{K})$ contains the kernel of the homomorphism of $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ into the collineation group.

We recall that $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ has been defined essentially as the subgroup of $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ generated by all the subgroups $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(2)} \mathfrak{J}(\mathfrak{K})$ where $\mathfrak{K}$ is a reduced simple subalgebra of degree three and nine dimensions. Clearly, $\left[\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})\right] \subseteq \Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$ and $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ contains every mapping $T_{Q_{i j}}$ where $i \neq j$ and $q \in \mathfrak{D}$. By (20), we have $e_{i i} T_{Q_{i j}}=e_{i i} +\gamma_{j}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{i} n(q) e_{j j}+q[i j]$, which shows that there exists a $T_{Q_{i j}}$ such that $\left[T_{Q_{i j}}\right]$ maps the point $\left[e_{i i}\right]$ into any point $\neq\left[e_{j j}\right]$ on the line $\left[e_{k k}\right]$ joining $\left[e_{i i}\right]$ and $\left[e_{j j}\right]$, $k \neq i, j$. This implies that $\left[\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})\right]$ contains every elation with center $\left[e_{j j}\right]$ and axis $\left[e_{i i}\right]$. We note also that $\left[\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})\right]$ is transitive on the set of points of $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$. Since $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ is mapped into itself by the mapping $\eta \rightarrow \hat{\eta}$ (by Lemma 1 of §2) it is clear that $\left[\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})\right]$ is transitive on the set of lines of $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$.

We wish to show that $\left[\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})\right]$ contains every elation of $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$. For this it suffices to show that if $l$ is any line and $P$ is a point on $l$ then there exists an $\varepsilon=[\eta], \eta \in \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$, such that $\left[e_{11}\right]^{\varepsilon}=l,\left[e_{22}\right]^{\varepsilon}=P$ for the line $\left[e_{11}\right]$ and the point $\left[e_{22}\right]$. Since $\left[\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})\right]$ is transitive on the lines we may assume $l=\left[e_{11}\right]$ and $P$ is on $\left[e_{11}\right]$.
We show first that if $[X]$ is any point not on the line $\left[e_{11}\right]$ then there exists a $\zeta \in \mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ such that [ $\zeta$ ] leaves fixed every point on the line [ $e_{11}$ ] and maps [ $X$ ] into the point $\left[e_{11}\right]$. Write $X=\Sigma_{1}^{3} \xi_{i} e_{i i}+x[23]+y[31]+z[12], x, y, z \in \mathfrak{O}$. Since $X$ is not on the line $\left[e_{11}\right], \xi_{1} \neq 0$. We have $e_{22} T_{Q_{12}}=e_{22}, e_{33} T_{Q_{13}}=e_{33}$, by (20). The formulas (20) show also that $q$ can be chosen so that $X T_{Q_{12}}=\xi_{1} e_{11} +\xi_{2}{ }^{\prime} e_{22}+\xi_{3}{ }^{\prime} e_{33}+x^{\prime}[23]+y^{\prime}[31]$. Since $X^{\prime} \in \Pi$ and $\xi_{1} \neq 0, X^{\prime}$ is a multiple of an element of the form $e_{11}+\gamma_{3}{ }^{-1} \gamma_{2} n(r) e_{33}+r[13]$. Then it is clear that we
have an elation with center [ $e_{33}$ ] and axis [ $e_{11}$ ] mapping [ $X^{\prime}$ ] into [ $e_{11}$ ]. Thus we have a product of two elations with axis $\left[e_{11}\right]$ mapping $[X]$ into $\left[e_{11}\right]$, so this mapping has the required properties.

Now let $P=[X]$ be on the line $\left[e_{11}\right]$. We wish to show that there exists an $[\eta], \eta \in \mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$, such that $\left[e_{11}\right]^{[\eta]}=\left[e_{11}\right]$ for the line $\left[e_{11}\right]$ and $[X]^{[\eta]}=\left[e_{22}\right]$ (which is on the line $\left[e_{11}\right]$ ). Assume first that $[X] \neq\left[e_{33}\right]$. Then $[X]$ is not on the line $\left[e_{22}\right]$ so the result just proved (for the line $\left[e_{11}\right]$ and point $\left[e_{11}\right]$ ) shows that there exists a $[\eta], \eta \in \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$, such that $[\eta]$ fixes every point on the line $\left[e_{22}\right]$ and $[X]^{[\eta]}=\left[e_{22}\right]$. Since $[\eta]$ maps $\left[e_{33}\right] \rightarrow\left[e_{33}\right]$ and $[X] \rightarrow\left[e_{22}\right]$ it is clear that [ $\eta$ ] maps the line [ $e_{11}$ ] into itself and the point [ $X$ ] into [ $e_{22}$ ], as required. Suppose next that $[X]=\left[e_{33}\right]$. Then the required result will follow by showing that there exists an $\eta \in \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $\left[e_{22}\right]^{[\eta]}=\left[e_{33}\right]$ and $\left[e_{33}\right]^{[\eta]}=\left[e_{22}\right]$. Put $B=e_{11}+e_{23}-e_{32}$. Then $\eta=T_{B} \in \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ and a simple calculation shows that $\left[e_{22}\right]^{[n]}=\left[e_{33}\right],\left[e_{33}\right]^{[n]}=\left[e_{22}\right]$. We remark also for later use that $\left[e_{11}\right]^{[n]}=\left[e_{11}\right]$.

The result we have established, that given any line $l$ and point $P$ on $l$ there exists an $[\eta], \eta \in \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$, such that $\left[e_{11}\right] \rightarrow l,\left[e_{22}\right] \rightarrow P$, and the facts that $\left[\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})\right] \subseteq \Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$ and contains all elations with center $\left[e_{22}\right]$ and axis $\left[e_{11}\right]$ imply the following

Lemma 2. $\left[\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{I})\right]=\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$.
We shall show next that $\mathbf{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$. Since $\mathbf{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ contains the kernel of the homomorphism $\eta \rightarrow[\eta]$ of $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ into the collineation group this will follow if we can show that $\left[\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})\right] \subseteq \Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$.

An ordered $k$-tuple ( $P_{1}, P_{2}, \cdots, P_{k}$ ) of points of a projective plane will be called independent if no three of the points $P_{i}, P_{j}, P_{k}, i, j, k \neq$, are collinear. We now prove the following important transitivity property:

Lemma 3. The little projective group $\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$ of $\mathfrak{P}=\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ is transitive on independent ordered triples of points.

Proof. It is enough to show that if ( $Q_{1}, Q_{2}, Q_{3}$ ) is an independent ordered triple of points then there exists an element of $\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$ such that $Q_{i} \rightarrow\left[e_{i i}\right], i=1,2,3$. Since we have seen that $\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})=\left[\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})\right]$ is transitive on points we may assume also that $Q_{1}=\left[e_{11}\right]$. Suppose first that $Q_{2}$ is not on the line $\left[e_{22}\right]$. Then, as we saw above, there exists an element of $\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$ leaving fixed every point on the line [ $e_{22}$ ], so in particular the points [ $e_{11}$ ] and [ $e_{33}$ ], and sending $Q_{2}$ into [ $e_{22}$ ]. This reduces the proof to the case $Q_{1}=\left[e_{11}\right], Q_{2}=\left[e_{22}\right]$. Then $Q_{3}$ is not on the line $\left[e_{33}\right]$ so there is an element of $\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$ leaving the line $\left[e_{33}\right]$ pointwise fixed and sending $Q_{3}$ into $\left[e_{33}\right]$. This proves the result if $Q_{2}$ is not on the line $\left[e_{22}\right]$ (and $Q_{1}=\left[e_{11}\right]$ ). Now assume $Q_{2}$ is on the line $\left[e_{22}\right]$. Then $Q_{2}$ is not on the line $\left[e_{33}\right]$ since $Q_{2} \neq\left[e_{11}\right]=Q_{1}$. Then the argument shows that we have an element of $\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$ fixing $\left[e_{11}\right]$ and $\left[e_{22}\right]$ and sending $Q_{2}$ into $\left[e_{33}\right]$. Since we have
seen that we have an element in $\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$ fixing the point $\left[e_{11}\right]$ and interchanging [ $e_{22}$ ] and [ $e_{33}$ ] we have a reduction of this case to the previous one.
We proceed with the proof that $\left[\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})\right]=\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})=\left[\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})\right]$. Since we may replace $\mathfrak{J}$ by an isotope we may assume $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$. Let $\eta \in \mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$. To prove that $\eta \in \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ it is sufficient, in view of Lemma 3, to do this for any $\eta$ such that $e_{i i}{ }^{\eta}=\lambda_{i} e_{i i}, \quad \lambda_{i} \in \Phi^{*}, i=1,2,3$. Put $A=\sum e_{i j}$, so $A \in \Pi(\mathfrak{J})$. Assume first that $A^{\eta} \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{1}\right)$. It follows from (18) (or (56)) and $2 e_{i i} \times e_{j j}=e_{k k}, 2(1 \times A)=A$ that $e_{i i}{ }^{\hat{\eta}}, A^{\hat{\eta}} \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{1}\right)$. Applying this again with the roles of $\hat{\eta}$ and $\eta$ interchanged we see that $\left(e_{i i} \times A\right)^{\eta} \in \mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{1}\right)$. Since $2 e_{i i} \times A=e_{j j}+e_{k k}-e_{j k}-e_{k j}$, $i, j, k \neq$, the six elements $e_{i i}, e_{i i} \times A$ form a basis for $\mathfrak{L}$. Hence $\mathfrak{L}^{\eta}=\mathfrak{L}$ and the restriction of $\eta$ to $\mathfrak{L}$ is in $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{L})$. Then, by Theorem 6.8 (see also p. 249) there exists a matrix $M \in \Phi_{3}$ such that $X^{n}=\rho M^{*} X M$ for all $X \in \mathfrak{L}$ where $\rho^{3} \operatorname{det} M^{2}=1$. Then det $M$ is a cube and replacing $M$ by a suitable multiple permits us to assume $\rho=1$. Then $\operatorname{det} M= \pm 1$ so replacing $M$ by $-M$, if necessary, gives $\operatorname{det} M=1$. Then $T_{M} \in \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ and we have $X^{\eta}=X T_{M}$ for all $X \in \mathfrak{L}$. If we replace $\eta$ by $\zeta =\eta T_{M}{ }^{-1}$ we obtain $\zeta \in \mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J}), e_{i i}{ }^{\zeta}=e_{i i}, A^{\zeta}=A$. Then $1^{\zeta}=1$ and $\zeta$ is an automorphism which fixed every $e_{i i}$. Then $\zeta \in \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ by Corollary 2 to Theorem 4 (p. 377). Hence $\eta \in \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ if $A^{\eta} \in \mathfrak{L}$. We now drop this supplementary condition and note that no three of the points $\left[e_{i i}\right],\left[A^{\eta}\right]$ are collinear since no three of $\left[e_{i i}\right],[A]$ are collinear. We shall therefore have a reduction to the case which we have settled by proving
Lemma 4. Let $C$ be an element of $\Pi(\mathfrak{J}), \mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ such that the point [C] does not lie on any of the lines $\left[e_{i i}\right], i=1,2,3$. Then there exists ar element $\zeta \in M_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $e_{i i}{ }^{\zeta}=\lambda_{i} e_{i i}, \lambda_{i} \in \Phi^{*}$, and $C^{\zeta} \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{1}\right)$.

Proof. The conditions on $C$ imply that $C=\sum \alpha_{i} e_{i i}+a[23]+b[31]+c[12]$ where every $\alpha_{i}, a, b$ and $c$ are nonzero. Put $Q=e_{11}+c^{-1} e_{22}+c e_{33}$. This is in $\Phi[c]_{3}$ and has determinant 1 , so $T_{Q} \in \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$. Then $C T_{Q}$ has the same form as $C$ and for this element $c=1$. Hence we may suppose $C$ has this property. Then the conditions that $C \times C=0$ (see (6)) imply that $a, b, c=1$ are contained in a quadratic subfield P of $\mathfrak{D}$. Put $R=b^{-1} e_{11}+\bar{b} e_{22}+e_{33}=S U$ where $S=b^{-1} e_{11} +\bar{b} e_{22}+b \bar{b}^{-1} e_{33}, \quad U=e_{11}+e_{22}+b \bar{b}^{-1} e_{33}$. Then $\quad C T_{R}=\sum \alpha_{i}{ }^{\prime} e_{i i}+a^{\prime}[23] +1[31]+1[12]$ and $C T_{R}=C T_{S} T_{U}$. Now $\operatorname{det} S=1$ so $T_{S} \in \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ and the mapping $T_{U}$ restricted to $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ is an automorphism since $n\left(b^{-1} \bar{b}\right)=1$ and $U$ is unitary. Also $e_{1} T_{U}=e_{1}$. Hence $T_{U}$ can be extended to an automorphism in $\mathfrak{J}$ leaving $e_{1}$ fixed. By Corollary 2 to Theorem 4, this extension is contained in $\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$. Thus there exists a $\zeta \in \mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $C^{\zeta}=C T_{R}$. Since $C T_{R} \in \Pi$ the conditions imply that $a^{\prime} \in \Phi$. Hence $C^{\zeta}=C T_{R} \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{1}\right)$. It is clear also that $e_{i i}{ }^{\zeta}=e_{i i} T_{R}=\lambda_{i} e_{i i}$.
This result and Lemma 2 complete the proof of the following
Theorem 13 (Jacobson). Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a reduced exceptional simple Jordan algebra whose coefficient algebra is a division algebra. Then $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathrm{M}_{1}{ }^{(3)}(\mathfrak{J})$
and the image of this group under the homomorphism $\eta \rightarrow[\eta]$ into the collineation group of $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ is the little projective group $\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$.

Since the kernel of the indicated homomorphism is $\Phi^{*} \cap \mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ we see that $\Lambda(\mathfrak{P}) \cong \mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J}) /\left(\Phi^{*} \cap \mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})\right)$.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right), \mathfrak{O}$ an octonion division algebra. Show that $\mathrm{M}_{1}(\mathfrak{J})$ is generated by the mappings $T_{Q_{i j}}, Q=1+q e_{i j}, i \neq j, q \in \mathfrak{D}$. (Note that this is analogous to the theorem that the unimodular group of matrices over a field is generated by elementary matrices.)
2. Prove that any two elations in $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ are conjugate in $\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$.
3. Let $\Lambda_{1}$ be an invariant subgroup $\neq 1$ in $\Lambda=\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$ and let $\eta \neq 1$ be in $\Lambda_{1}$.
