Choose $P$ so that $P^{\eta} \neq P$ and let $\tau$ be an elation with center $P^{\eta}$ and axis $P P^{\eta}$. Put $\omega=\eta \tau \eta^{-1} \tau^{-1}$. Show that $\omega \neq 1$ is in $\Lambda_{1}$ and leaves the line $l=P P^{\eta}$ invariant. Show also that if, in addition, $\eta$ leaves $P P^{\eta}$ invariant then $\omega$ leaves fixed every point of $l$. Hence show that $\Lambda_{1}$ contains an element $\eta \neq 1$ which has a line $l$ of fixed points. Show that if this is not an elation then it has a fixed point $F$ not on $l$. Then if $\tau$ is an elation with axis $l, \omega=\eta \tau \eta^{-1} \tau^{-1} \neq 1$ is an elation. Thus show that $\Lambda_{1}$ contains an elation and hence $\Lambda_{1}=\Lambda$ and $\Lambda$ is a simple group.
4. Prove that if $l$ is any line of $\mathfrak{P}, P$ a point on $l$ and $X$ and $X^{\prime}$ points such that $P, X, X^{\prime}$ are distinct and collinear then there exists an elation with center $P$, axis $l$ mapping $X$ into $X^{\prime}$.
5. Harmonicity. A projective plane $\mathfrak{P}$ is said to be harmonic if the harmonic conjugate $P_{4}$ of a point $P_{3}$ relative to the pair of points $P_{1}, P_{2}$ is uniquely determined. Here $P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}$ are distinct points on a line $l_{0}$ and $P_{4}$ is determined by the following construction: Let $l$ be any line through $P_{3}$ distinct from $l_{0}, P, Q$ points on $l$ such that $P, Q, P_{3}$ are distinct. Consider the four lines $P_{1} P, P_{1} Q, P_{2} P, P_{2} Q$ and let $Q_{1}$ be the intersection of $P_{1} P$ and $P_{2} Q, Q_{2}$ the intersection of $P_{2} P$ and $P_{1} Q$. Then $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$ are distinct and $P_{4}$ is the intersection of $Q_{1} Q_{2}$ with $l_{0}$. Thus we have the following figure:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-411.jpg?height=550&width=999&top_left_y=1628&top_left_x=378)

We define an involution of $\mathfrak{P}$ to be a collineation of $\mathfrak{P}$ of period two. The harmonic property is a consequence of the existence of certain involutions and elations in $\mathfrak{P}$. For, suppose there exists an involution $\varepsilon\left(l, P_{1}, P_{2}\right)$ leaving $l$ pointwise fixed and interchanging $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$. Then $P_{1} P$ and $P_{2} P$ are interchanged by $\varepsilon\left(l, P_{1}, P_{2}\right)$ and so are $P_{1} Q$ and $P_{2} Q$. Hence the points $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$ are interchanged and so the line $Q_{1} Q_{2}$ is invariant under $\varepsilon\left(l, P_{1}, P_{2}\right)$. Then $P_{4}$ is fixed under $\varepsilon\left(l, P_{1}, P_{2}\right)$ since the lines $Q_{1} Q_{2}$ and $P_{1} P_{2}=l_{0}$ are invariant and $P_{4}$ is their intersection. Since a collineation which has a line of fixed points and has two distinct fixed points not on this line in necessarily the identity it is clear that $P_{4}$ is the only fixed point of $\varepsilon\left(l, P_{1}, P_{2}\right)$ not on $l$ and so $P_{4}$ is determined by $\varepsilon\left(l, P_{1}, P_{2}\right)$. Now let $l^{\prime}$ be another line through $P_{3}$ distinct from $l_{0}$ and let $\varepsilon\left(l^{\prime}, P_{1}, P_{2}\right)$ be an involution having $l^{\prime}$ as line of fixed points and interchanging $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$. Assume also that we have an elation $\tau$ with axis $l_{0}$ and center $P_{2}$ mapping $l$ into $l^{\prime}$. Then $\varepsilon\left(l^{\prime}, P_{1}, P_{2}\right) =\tau^{-1} \varepsilon\left(l, P_{1}, P_{2}\right) \tau$ and so $P_{4}=P_{4}{ }^{\tau}$ is the fixed point of $\varepsilon\left(l^{\prime}, P_{1}, P_{2}\right)$ which is not on $l^{\prime}$. Hence we see that $P_{4}$ is independent also of the choice of $l$.

Now let $\mathfrak{P}=\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ be the projective plane associated with the reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$ with coefficient algebra $\mathfrak{O}$ a division algebra. Let the notations be as in the last paragraph and let $P^{\prime}$ be the intersection of the line $P_{2} P$ with $l^{\prime}$. Then it follows easily from the results of §8 (see ex.4) that there exists an elation $\tau$ with center $P_{2}$ and axis $l_{0}$ mapping $P$ into $P^{\prime}$. Then $l^{\tau}=l^{\prime}$ as required above. Hence the harmonic property of $\mathfrak{P}$ will be established if we can show that given any line $l$ and distinct points $P_{1}, P_{2}$ not on $l$ then there exists an involution $\varepsilon\left(l, P_{1}, P_{2}\right)$ having $l$ as line of fixed points and interchanging $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$.

Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{\gamma}\right)$ and let $\eta$ be the linear mapping in $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $e_{i i}{ }^{\eta}=e_{i i}$, $a[12]^{\eta}=-a[12], a[13]^{\eta}=-a[13], a[23]^{\eta}=a[23], a \in \mathfrak{D}$. Then it is clear that $\eta$ is an automorphism of period two in $\mathfrak{J}$ so $[\eta]$ is an involution in $\mathfrak{P}=\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$. The points on the line $\left[e_{11}\right]$ have the form $\left[\alpha e_{22}+\beta e_{33}+a[23]\right]$. Hence every point on the line $\left[e_{11}\right]$ is fixed by $[\eta]$. Since $[\eta] \neq 1$ we can choose a point $P_{1}$ such that $P_{2}=P_{1}{ }^{[\eta]} \neq P_{1}$. Then $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are interchanged by the involution $[\eta]$. Hence $[\eta]=\varepsilon\left(\left[e_{11}\right], P_{1}, P_{2}\right)$, the involution having $\left[e_{11}\right]$ as line of fixed points and interchanging the distinct points $P_{1}, P_{2}$. We prove next the following transitivity property of the subgroup $[\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{H})]$ of the collineation group.

Lemma. $[\mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})]$ is transitive on independent ordered quadruples of points.
Proof. There is no loss in generality in assuming $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ and we do this to simplify the calculations. In view of Lemmas 3 and 4 of §8 it is sufficient to prove that if $P_{i}=Q_{i}=\left[e_{i i}\right], i=1,2,3, P_{4}=A=\sum e_{i j}$ and $Q_{4}=B \in \mathfrak{H}\left(\Phi_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ then there exists a $\zeta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $P_{j}{ }^{[\zeta]}=Q_{j}, j=1,2,3,4$. We may assume that the first row of the matrix $B$ is $(1, \alpha, \beta), \alpha, \beta \in \Phi$. Since $B$ is symmetric and has rank one we have

$$
B=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & \alpha & \beta \\
\alpha & \alpha^{2} & \alpha \beta \\
\beta & \alpha \beta & \beta^{2}
\end{array}\right]
$$

Let $D=\operatorname{diag}\{1, \alpha, \beta\}$. Then $D \in \mathfrak{J}$ and we have $A U_{D}=B$. Moreover, $U_{D} \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ since $n\left(X U_{D}\right)=n(D)^{2} n(X)$. Then $\zeta=U_{D}$ has the required properties since we also have $\left[e_{i i}\right]^{[\zeta]}=\left[e_{i i}\right], i=1,2,3$.

Now let $l$ be any line, $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$ distinct points not on $l$. We have seen that there exists an involution having [ $e_{11}$ ] as line of fixed points. Let $P_{1}, P_{2}$ be distinct points interchanged by this involution which we denote as $\varepsilon\left(\left[e_{11}\right], P_{1}, P_{2}\right)$. Let $P_{3}, P_{4}$ be points on $\left[e_{11}\right]$ which are distinct and are distinct from the intersection of [ $e_{11}$ ] and the line $P_{1}, P_{2}$. In a similar manner choose $Q_{3}, Q_{4}$ on the given line $l$. Then ( $P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}, P_{4}$ ) and ( $Q_{1}, Q_{2}, Q_{3}, Q_{4}$ ) satisfy the condition of the Lemma so there exists a $\zeta \in \mathrm{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ such that $P_{j}{ }^{[\zeta]}=Q_{j}, j=1,2,3,4$. Then $[\zeta]^{-1} \varepsilon\left(\left[e_{11}\right], P_{1}, P_{2}\right)[\zeta]$ is an involution having $l$ as line of fixed points and interchanging $Q_{1}, Q_{2}$. As we have seen, the existence of such involutions for any $l$ and points $Q_{1}, Q_{2}$ implies the following

Theorem 14. The plane $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{I})=\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{D})$ is harmonic.
We remark that the harmonic property was the primary one singled out by Moufang for the projective planes which she constructed. It is well known that this property holds in any Desarguesian projective plane. Moreover, the property is equivalent to a weaker form of Desargues' theorem called the little Desargues' theorem (Pickert [1, p. 187] or M. Hall [1, p. 17]).

## Exercises

1. Call an involution $\varepsilon$ of $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ of first kind if it has a line of fixed points. Show that any such involution is contained in the little projective group and any two such involutions are conjugate in the full collineation group but not necessarily in the little projective group.
2. Let $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right), \mathfrak{O}$ an octonion division algebra. Let $\beta$ be a reflection in a quaternion subalgebra $\mathfrak{Q}$ of $\mathfrak{D}: \beta$ is linear and is 1 on $\mathfrak{Q}$ and -1 on $\mathfrak{Q}^{\perp}$. Let $\eta$ be the linear mapping in $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $a[i j] \rightarrow a^{\beta}[i j], i, j=1,2,3$. Show that $[\eta]$ is an involution having the four fixed points $\left[e_{i l}\right]$ and $[A]$ where $A=\sum e_{i j}$. Show that [ $\eta$ ] is not of first kind.
3. An involution $\varepsilon$ of $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ will be called of second kind if there exists a set of four fixed points of $\varepsilon$ no three of which are collinear. Show that every involution of $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ is either of first kind or second kind.
4. (Pickert). Show that $\Lambda(\mathfrak{P})$ for $\mathfrak{P}=\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ has the transitivity property of the above Lemma if and only if $\Phi^{*}=\Phi^{* 3}=\left\{\alpha^{3} \mid \alpha \in \Phi^{*}\right\}$.
5. Fundamental theorem of projective geometry for the planes $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$. Let $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ and $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} / \Phi^{\prime}$ be reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebras whose coefficient al-
gebras $\mathfrak{O} / \Phi$ and $\mathfrak{O}^{\prime} / \Phi^{\prime}$ are octonion division algebras. We have seen at the very beginning of our discussion (§7) that if $\eta$ is a norm semisimilarity of $\mathfrak{J}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ then the mapping [ $\eta$ ] defined by (56) is a projective transformation of the geometry $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $\mathfrak{P}\left(\mathfrak{J}{ }^{\prime}\right)$. We shall now prove the analogue of the classical "fundamental theorem of projective geometry" of Desarguesian geometries (Artin, Geometric Algebra, p. 88), namely, that every projective transformation of $\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ onto $\mathfrak{P}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ has the form [ $\eta$ ] for some norm semisimilarity $\eta$. We shall base the proof on the classical constructions of addition and multiplication of points on a line. Let $l$ be a line in a projective plane $\mathfrak{P}$ and $O, \infty$ distinct points on $l, B, C$ points on a line $l^{\prime}$ through $O$ distinct from $l$ such that $B, C$ and $O$ are distinct. Let $P$ and $Q$ be points on $l$ distinct from $\infty$. Let $E$ be the intersection of the lines $P C$ and $B \infty, F$ the intersection of lines $B Q$ and $C \infty$. Then we define $P+Q$ to be the point of intersection of lines $E F$ and $l$ :
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-414.jpg?height=534&width=976&top_left_y=902&top_left_x=390)

Next let $l, O, \infty$ be as before and let $A, B$ be two points such that no three points in $\{O, \infty, A, B\}$ are collinear. Let $P, Q$ be points of $l$ distinct from $O, \infty$ Let $C$ be the point of intersection of $\infty B$ and $A P, D$ the intersection of $O A$ and $B Q$. Then we define the product $P \circ Q$ to be the point of intersection of $C D$ with $l$ :
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/6adfec5f-bb4b-4aa0-b589-9a3c82757454-414.jpg?height=540&width=968&top_left_y=1628&top_left_x=390)

Now let $\mathfrak{P}=\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{J})$ where $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ and let $l$ be the line $\left[e_{11}\right], O=\left[e_{22}\right]$, $\infty=\left[e_{33}\right], B=\left[e_{11}\right]$ and let $C$ be the point of intersection of $A=\left[\sum e_{i j}\right], \infty$ with $l^{\prime}=O B$. Let $P_{q}=e_{22}+n(q) e_{33}+q[32], P_{r}=e_{22}+n(r) e_{33}+r[32]$ where $p, q \in \mathfrak{D}$. Then a direct calculation which we leave to the reader shows that

$$
\begin{equation*}
P_{p}+P_{q}=P_{p+q} . \tag{57}
\end{equation*}
$$

Similarly, in the second construction if we take $A=\sum e_{i j}, O, \infty$ and $B$ as before then we find that

$$
\begin{equation*}
P_{p} \circ P_{q}=P_{p q} \tag{58}
\end{equation*}
$$

We can now prove the following "fundamental theorem" which was proved first by Springer [2] in a different way:

Theorem 15. Let $\Im_{1} / \Phi_{1}$ and $\Im_{2} / \Phi_{2}$ be reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebras whose coefficient algebras $\mathfrak{O}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{O}_{2}$ are octonion division algebras. Then any projective transformation of the plane $\mathfrak{P}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right)$ onto $\mathfrak{P}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ has the form [ $\eta$ ] where $\eta$ is a norm semisimilarity of $\mathfrak{J}_{1} / \Phi_{1}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}_{2} / \Phi_{2}$.

Proof. Without loss of generality we may assume $\mathfrak{J}_{i}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{i}, J_{1}\right)$. Let $\tau$ be projective transformation of $\mathfrak{P}\left(\mathfrak{I}_{1}\right)$ onto $\mathfrak{P}\left(\mathfrak{I}_{2}\right)$. Consider the points $\left[e_{i i}\right]$, $A=\left[\sum e_{i j}\right]$ in $\mathfrak{P}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{1}\right)$. Since no three of these are collinear the same is true of their images under $\tau$. Then, by the lemma of §9, we can multiply $\tau$ on the right by a collineation of $\mathfrak{P}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$ which is of the form $[\zeta], \zeta \in \mathrm{M}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{2}\right)$, to arrange that $\left[e_{i i}\right] \rightarrow\left[e_{i i}\right], A \rightarrow A$ (as defined in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{2}, J_{1}\right)$. Thus we may assume $\left[e_{i i}\right]^{\tau}=\left[e_{i i}\right]$, $A^{\tau}=A$. Since $\tau$ is projective it follows that if we carry out the constructions of addition and multiplication of points on the line $\left[e_{11}\right]$ in $\mathfrak{P}_{i}$ by using the "base" $\left[e_{11}\right],\left[e_{22}\right],\left[e_{33}\right], A$, then we have $\left(P_{q}+P_{r}\right)^{\tau}=P_{q}{ }^{\tau}+P_{r}{ }^{\tau},\left(P_{q} \circ P_{r}\right)^{\tau}=P_{q}{ }^{\tau} \circ P_{r}{ }^{\tau}$ if $q, r \neq 0$. Now put $P_{q}{ }^{\tau}=P_{q}{ }^{\beta}, q \in \mathfrak{D}$. Then it is clear from (57) and (58) that $\beta$ is a ring isomorphism of $\mathfrak{O}_{1}$ onto $\mathfrak{O}_{2}$. Let $M\left(\mathfrak{O}_{i}\right), C\left(\mathfrak{O}_{i}\right)$ be the multiplication ring and centroid respectively of $\mathfrak{O}_{i}$ (cf. §5.7). The first of these is the ring of endomorphisms in $\mathfrak{O}_{i}$ generated by the left and right multiplications and the second is the centralizer of $M\left(\mathfrak{O}_{i}\right)$ in the complete ring of endomorphisms of ( $\mathfrak{O}_{i},+$ ). It is immediate that a ring isomorphism $\beta$ of $\mathfrak{O}_{1}$ onto $\mathfrak{O}_{2}$ determines ring isomorphisms $A \rightarrow \beta^{-1} A \beta$, $\gamma \rightarrow \beta^{-1} \gamma \beta$ of $M\left(\mathfrak{O}_{1}\right)$ onto $M\left(\mathfrak{O}_{2}\right)$ and of $C\left(\mathfrak{O}_{1}\right)$ onto $C\left(\mathfrak{O}_{2}\right)$. Since $\mathfrak{O}_{i}$ is central simple over $\Phi_{i}$ its centroid consists of the set of multiplications by elements of $\Phi_{i} 1$. Hence the isomorphism $\gamma \rightarrow \beta^{-1} \gamma \beta$ corresponds to an isomorphism $\sigma$ of $\Phi_{1}$ onto $\Phi_{2}$ and since $(x \gamma)^{\beta}=x^{\beta}\left(\beta^{-1} \gamma \beta\right), x \in \mathfrak{O}_{1}$ we have $(\alpha x)^{\beta}=\alpha^{\sigma} x^{\beta}, \alpha \in \Phi_{1}, x \in \mathfrak{O}_{1}$. Thus $\beta$ is a $\sigma$-semilinear isomorphism of $\mathfrak{D}_{1} / \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{1}$, onto $\mathfrak{D}_{2} / \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{2}$. Then we have the $\sigma$-semilinear isomorphism $\eta$ of $\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}_{2}$ such that $q[k l] \rightarrow q^{\beta}[k l], q \in \mathfrak{O}_{1}, k, l =1,2,3$. Then $\eta$ is a norm semisimilarity and we have $\left(e_{22}+n(q) e_{33}+q[32]\right)^{\eta} =e_{22}+n\left(q^{\beta}\right) e_{33}+q^{\beta}[32]$ which implies that $P_{q}{ }^{[\eta]}=P_{q}{ }^{\tau}, q \in \mathfrak{D}_{1}$. Hence the restriction of $\tau$ and [ $\eta$ ] to the points of the line [ $e_{11}$ ] are identical. Also we have
$A^{[\eta]}=A$ and $\left[e_{11}\right]^{[\eta]}=\left[e_{11}\right]^{\tau}$. Since two projective transformations are identical if they have the same effect on all points of a line and on two distinct points not on the line we have $\tau=[\eta]$ as required.
11. Connections with exceptional Lie algebras. In this section we shall specialize the main constructions of Lie algebras from Jordan algebras given in the last chapter to the case of finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebras. We consider first the Lie algebra Der $\mathfrak{J}$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ of this type. If $D \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$ then $1 D=0$ and $D$ is skew relative to the generic trace form (Theorem 6.1 (vii)), p. 224). Hence $D$ is skew relative to the symmetric bilinear form $Q=\frac{1}{2} t$.

Now let $\mathfrak{J}$ be reduced and let $e$ be a primitive idempotent in $\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}_{0}(e) \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e) \oplus \mathfrak{J}_{1}(e)$ the corresponding Peirce decomposition. Let Der $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ be the subalgebra of Der $\mathfrak{J}$ mapping $e$ into 0 . If $D \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ then the condition $x_{i} \cdot e =i x_{i}, x_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}_{i}=\mathfrak{J}_{i}(e)$, gives $\left(x_{i} D\right) . e=i x_{i} D$. Hence $\mathfrak{J}_{i} D \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_{i}$. In particular, the restriction $D_{0}$ of $D$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ is a derivation in this subalgebra of $\mathfrak{J}$. As in §3, we have $\mathfrak{J}_{0}=\Phi f \oplus \mathfrak{B}$ where $f=1-e$ is the identity of $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ is the subspace of elements of generic trace 0 in $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$. We have $v^{\cdot 2}=Q(v) f$, if $v \in \mathfrak{B}$, and $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ is the Jordan algebra of the nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $Q$ on $\mathfrak{B}$. It follows from this that $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}_{0}=$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ coincides with the set of mappings of the form $\sum\left[\bar{R}_{v_{i}} \bar{R}_{w_{i}}\right]$ where $v_{i}, w_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $\bar{R}_{b}$ for $b \in \mathfrak{J}_{0}$ is the multiplication in $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ determined by $b$ (ex.1, p.328). It is immediate also that $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}_{0}$ maps $\mathfrak{B}$ into itself and the set of restrictions of the derivations in $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ to $\mathfrak{B}$ is the complete set of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{B}$ which are skew relative to $Q$. Since $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{B}=9$ this implies that $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}_{0}$, which is evidently isomorphic to the Lie algebra of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{V}$ which are $Q$-skew, is a simple Lie algebra (cf. ex. 1, p. 343).

We can now prove the following key result.
Theorem 16. Let $e$ be a primitive idempotent in the reduced simple exceptional Jordan algebra. Let Der $\mathfrak{J} /$ Đe be the subalgebra of Der $\mathfrak{J}$ mapping $e$ into 0 . Then the restriction mapping $D \rightarrow D_{0}=D \mid \mathfrak{I}_{0}$ is an isomorphism of Der $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ e onto Der $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$. Moreover, the set of restrictions to $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ of the elements of Der $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ is an irreducible set of linear transformations in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$.

Proof. Let $D_{0} \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}_{0}$ so $D_{0}=\Sigma\left[\bar{R}_{v_{i}} \bar{R}_{w_{i}}\right]$ where $v_{i}, w_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ and $\bar{R}$ denotes multiplication in $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$. Put $D=\Sigma\left[R_{v_{i}} R_{w_{i}}\right]$ where $R$ is multiplication in $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $D \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ and the restriction of $D$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$ is $D_{0}$. Hence $D \rightarrow D \mid \mathfrak{J}_{0}$ is surjective on Der $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$. Now suppose $D \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ satisfies $D \mid \mathfrak{J}_{0}=0$. Let $D_{\frac{1}{2}}$ be the restriction of $D$ to $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$. If $y \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $v \in \mathfrak{B}$ then $y . v \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $(y . v) D_{\frac{1}{2}}=\left(y D_{\frac{1}{2}}\right) . v$. Thus $D_{\frac{1}{2}}$ commutes with all the multiplications $R_{v}{ }^{\prime}$ in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ determined by the elements $v \in \mathfrak{B}$. In $\S 3$ we defined a representation $\rho$ of the Clifford algebra $C(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ by linear transformations in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ such that $v \rightarrow U_{\theta(v)}{ }^{\prime}=2 R_{v}{ }^{\prime}$ (cf. (38)). We saw that $C^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)^{\rho}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}, \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ so, a fortiori, $C(\mathfrak{B}, Q)^{\rho}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}, \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$. Since we have just shown that $D_{\frac{1}{2}}$ commutes with every $R_{v}{ }^{\prime}$ we see that $D_{\frac{1}{2}}$ is a multi-
plication by an element of $\Phi$. Since $D_{\frac{1}{2}}$ is skew relative to the symmetric bilinear form $Q$ we have $D_{\frac{1}{2}}=0$. Since $e D=0$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{0} D=0$ by hypothesis we have $D=0$. Thus $D \rightarrow D \mid \mathfrak{J}_{0}$ is an isomorphism of Der $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ onto Der $\mathfrak{J}_{0}$. Since $C^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)$ is generated by the products $v_{1} v_{2}, v_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$ it is clear that $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\Im_{\frac{1}{2}}, \Im_{\frac{1}{2}}\right) C^{e}(\mathfrak{B}, Q)^{\rho}$ is generated by the products $R_{v_{1}}{ }^{\prime} R_{v_{2}}{ }^{\prime}$. Now we have the relation $y .(a . b)= y . a . b+y . b . a$ for $y \in \mathfrak{I}_{\frac{1}{2}}, a, b \in \mathfrak{I}_{0}$ which shows that $2 R^{\prime}{ }_{v_{1}} . R^{\prime}{ }_{v_{2}}=R^{\prime}{ }_{v_{1}} \cdot v_{v_{2}} =Q\left(v_{1}, v_{2}\right) 1$. Since $R_{v_{1}}{ }^{\prime} R_{v_{2}}{ }^{\prime}=R_{v_{1}}{ }^{\prime} \cdot R_{v_{2}}{ }^{\prime}+\frac{1}{2}\left[R_{v_{1}}{ }^{\prime}, R_{v_{2}}{ }^{\prime}\right]$ this implies that $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}\left(\Im_{\frac{1}{2}}, \Im_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ is generated by 1 and the mappings $\left[R_{v_{1}}{ }^{\prime} R_{v_{2}}{ }^{\prime}\right]$. Since $\left[R_{v_{1}}{ }^{\prime} R_{v_{2}}{ }^{\prime}\right]$ is the restriction to $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ of $D=\left[R_{v_{1}} R_{v_{2}}\right] \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ it is clear that the Lie algebra of restrictions to $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ of the linear transformations in Der $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ is irreducible in $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$.

Now let $E$ be any derivation in $\mathfrak{J}$. Then $e^{\cdot 2}=e$ gives $2 e . e E=e E$ so $e E \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}} =\mathfrak{I}_{\frac{1}{2}}(e)$. On the other hand, let $a \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and put $E_{a}=4\left[R_{e} R_{a}\right]$. Then $E_{a}$ is a derivation in $\mathfrak{J}$ and $e E_{a}=4$ (e.e. $\left.a-e . a . e\right)=a$. We now have the linear mapping $\varepsilon: a \rightarrow E_{a}$ of $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ into Der $\mathfrak{J}$ which is clearly a monomorphism. If $E$ is any derivation then $a=e E \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $e E_{a}=a=e E$. Hence $D=E-E_{a} \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$. Thus $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}=\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e+\varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$. Since $e E_{a}=a$ it is clear also that Der $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e \cap \varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)=0$. Hence we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}=\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e \oplus \varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right) . \tag{59}
\end{equation*}
$$

Now let $\mathfrak{D} \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$. Then $\left[E_{a}, D\right]=4\left[\left[R_{e} R_{a}\right], D\right]=4\left[R_{e} R_{a L}\right]=E_{a D}$. Hence $\left[\varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\right.$, Der $\left.\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e\right] \subseteq \varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ and $\varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ as $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ Lie module is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ as $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ Lie module (defined by the representation $D \rightarrow D_{\frac{1}{2}}$ ). Since we have seen that $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ is irreducible relative to Der $\mathfrak{I} / \Phi e$ we see that $\varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ is irreducible relative to the set of mappings $X \rightarrow[X, D], D \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$. The situation we now have is a special case, as we shall see, of the one described in the following

Lemma. Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be a Lie algebra, $\mathfrak{D}_{0}$ a subalgebra such that $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{D}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ where $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ is a subspace of $\mathfrak{D}$ such that $\left[\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}, \mathfrak{D}_{0}\right] \subseteq \mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$. Assume that $\mathfrak{D}_{0}$ and $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ are irreducible and not isomorphic as Lie modules for $\mathfrak{D}_{0}$ (under $[X, D], X \in \mathfrak{D}_{0}$ or $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}, D \in \mathfrak{D}_{0}$ ) and $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ is not a subalgebra. Then $\mathfrak{D}$ is a simple Lie algebra.

Proof. The hypothesis implies that the only $\mathfrak{D}_{0}$-submodules of $\mathfrak{D}$ are $0, \mathfrak{D}_{0}, \mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ and $\mathfrak{D}$. Now let $\mathfrak{B}$ be an ideal $\neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{D}$. Then $\mathfrak{B}$ is a $\mathfrak{D}_{0}$-submodule of $\mathfrak{D}$ so either $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{D}_{0}, \mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ or $\mathfrak{D}$. If $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{D}_{0}$ then $\mathfrak{B} \supseteq\left[\mathfrak{D}_{0}, \mathfrak{D}^{\prime}\right]=\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ (by irreducibility of $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ ). This contradicts $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{D}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$. If $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ then $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ is a subalgebra contrary to hypothesis. Hence $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{D}$ and $\mathfrak{D}$ is simple.
We can now prove the main result on Der J.
Theorem 17. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional exceptional central simple Jordan algebra. Then every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ is inner and Der $\mathfrak{J}$ is a central simple Lie algebra of 52 dimensions. Moreover, the only invariant subspaces of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to Der $\mathfrak{J}$ are $0, \Phi 1, \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ and $\mathfrak{J}$.

Proof. It suffices to prove the statements for $\Phi$ algebraically closed. Then $\mathfrak{J}$
is reduced and our results are applicable. Since $\varepsilon: a \rightarrow E_{a}$ is a monomorphism, $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}=\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e+\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$, by (59). We have seen also that Der $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ is isomorphic to the Lie algebra of linear transformations in the nine-dimensional vector space $\mathfrak{B}$ which are skew relative to $Q$. The dimensionality of the latter algebra is $\frac{1}{2}(9 \times 8)=36$. Since $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}=16$ we have $\operatorname{dim}$ Der $\mathfrak{J}=36+16=52$. It is clear from the definition that $E_{a}$ is an inner derivation. Hence every element of $\varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ is an inner derivation. Also we have seen that the elements of $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ have the form $\Sigma\left[R_{v_{i}} R_{w_{i}}\right], v_{i}, w_{i} \in \mathfrak{B}$. Hence these are inner and (59) shows that $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}=$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$. To prove the simplicity of Der $\mathfrak{J}$ we shall apply the Lemma with $\mathfrak{D}_{0}=\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ and $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}=\varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$. Then we have Der $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{D}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$. Also $\mathfrak{D}_{0}$ is a simple Lie algebra so $\mathfrak{D}_{0}$ is irreducible as $\mathfrak{D}_{0}$-module. Also we have seen that $\varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ is $\mathfrak{D}_{0}$-irreducible. Since $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}_{0}=36$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{D}^{\prime}=16$ these are not isomorphic as $\mathfrak{D}_{0}$-modules. Now let $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
{\left[E_{a} E_{b}\right] } & =16\left[\left[R_{e} R_{a}\right],\left[R_{e} R_{b}\right]\right] \\
& =16\left[\left[\left[R_{e} R_{a}\right] R_{e}\right] R_{b}\right]-16\left[\left[\left[R_{e} R_{a}\right] R_{b}\right] R_{e}\right] \\
& =16\left[R_{[a, e, e]} R_{b}\right]-16\left[R_{[a b, e]} R_{e}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $[a, e, e]=-\frac{1}{4} a$ and $[a, b, e]=a \cdot b \cdot e-\frac{1}{2} a \cdot b=\frac{1}{2} a \cdot b \cdot(e-f) \in \mathfrak{J}_{0}+\mathfrak{J}_{1}$ this gives

$$
\left[E_{a} E_{b}\right]=-4\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right]
$$

Since $e\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right]=\frac{1}{2}(a . b-b . a)=0,\left[E_{a} E_{b}\right] \in \mathfrak{D}_{0}$. Now we can choose $a, b \in \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ so that $\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right] \neq 0$. Thus let $e=e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}$ be orthogonal idempotents and let $a=u_{12} \in \mathfrak{J}_{12}, b=u_{13} \in \mathfrak{J}_{13}$ satisfy $u_{12}{ }^{\cdot 2} \neq 0, u_{13}{ }^{\cdot 2} \neq 0$. Then we can choose a coordinatization so that $u_{12}$ and $u_{13}$ are mapped into 1 [12] and 1[13]. Since $[1[12], 1[23], 1[13]] \neq 0$ we see that $\left[R_{a} R_{b}\right] \neq 0$. We now see that $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}=\varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ is not a subalgebra of $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$. Hence $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$ is simple by the Lemma. To prove the statement on the invariant subspaces we note that the only invariant subspaces of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to Der $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ are sums of the spaces $\mathfrak{V}, \mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ and subspaces of $\Phi e+\Phi f$. This is clear since $\mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}$ are irreducible and not isomorphic relative to Der $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi$ e. Hence the proof of the statement on the invariant subspace of $\mathfrak{J}$ relative to Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \Phi e$ (Theorem 7) carries over to prove the corresponding statement on Der J/Фe.

We have shown in §7.7 that if $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional separable Jordan algebra such that the degrees of the simple components of $\mathfrak{J}$ over their centers is not divisible by the characteristic of the base field then every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into any finite-dimensional bimodule is inner. In particular this applies to $\mathfrak{J}$ exceptional simple of characteristic $\neq 3$. We shall now give another proof of this special case which is valid also in the characteristic three case. The result is the following

Corollary. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional separable simple exceptional Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{M}$ a finite-dimensional bimodule for $\mathfrak{J}$. Then every derivation of $\mathfrak{J}$ into $\mathfrak{M}$ is inner.

Proof. The reductions given in §7.7 show that it suffices to prove this for algebraically closed base field and $\mathfrak{M}$ unital and irreducible. Then $\mathfrak{J}$ is as in Theorem 17 and $\mathfrak{M}$ as $\mathfrak{J}$-bimodule is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{J}$ by §7.4. Hence the result follows from Theorem 17.

If we take into account the results of §7.7 and the present one we see that we can state the theorem on derivations of separable Jordan algebras into bimodules in the following way. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional separable Jordan algebra. Then the derivations of $\mathfrak{J}$ into finite-dimensional bimodules are inner if and only if the degrees over their centers of the special simple components are not divisible by the characteristic. This is Harris' theorem in its sharpest form.

In Theorem 8 we determined Aut $\mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K}$ for $\mathfrak{J}$ reduced simple exceptional and $\mathfrak{K}$ a reduced simple subalgebra of degree three and dimension nine or fifteen. The same method can be used to obtain analogous results for Der J/ K, the subalgebra of the derivation algebra mapping $\mathfrak{K}$ into 0 . We leave it to the reader to work out the details of this.

We consider next the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})=\left\{R_{a}+\sum\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right] \mid a, b_{i}, c_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}\right\}$ where $\mathfrak{J}$ is finite dimensional central simple exceptional. We have $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})=R(\mathfrak{J}) \oplus \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$ since Der $\mathfrak{J}=$ Inder $\mathfrak{J}$ and $a \rightarrow R_{a}$ is a monomorphism. Hence $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})=27 +52=79$. It is clear that $\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ contains the ideal $\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})=R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right) \oplus$ Der $\mathfrak{J}$ and we have the following result on this algebra.

Theorem 18. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebra, $\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ the Lie algebra of linear transformations of the form $R_{a} +\sum\left[R_{b_{i}} R_{c_{i}}\right]$ where $a, b_{i}, c_{i} \in \mathfrak{J}$ and $t(a)=0$. Then $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})=78$ and $\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ is central simple if the characteristic is $\neq 3$ and $\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ contains the ideal $\Phi 1$ and $\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J}) / \Phi 1$ is central simple if the characteristic is three. Moreover, $\mathfrak{J}$ is irreducible under the action of $\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ for any characteristic.

Proof. We may assume the base field is algebraically closed. The fact that $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})=78$ is clear since $\operatorname{dim} R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)=\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{J}^{\prime}=26$ and $\operatorname{dim}$ Der $\mathfrak{J}=52$. If $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ and $D \in \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$ then $\left[R_{a} D\right]=R_{a D}$. Hence the mapping $a \rightarrow R_{a}$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$ and $R(\mathfrak{J})$ regarded as Der $\mathfrak{J}$-modules. Since we have determined the submodules of $\mathfrak{J}$ under Der $\mathfrak{J}$ in Theorem 17, we can deduce from the isomorphism the submodules of $R(\mathfrak{J})$. It is clear from this that if the characteristic is not three then $R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ is an irreducible Der $\mathfrak{J}$-module and if the characteristic is three, so $t(1)=0$, then $R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right) / \Phi 1$ is Der $\mathfrak{J}$-irreducible. It is clear also that $\left[R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right), R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)\right] =\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$ so $R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ is not a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$. Since Der $\mathfrak{J}$ is simple this is an irreducible module for Der J. Hence if the characteristic is not three, we can apply the Lemma to $\mathfrak{D}_{0}=\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{D}^{\prime}=R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ to conclude that $\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})=\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} \oplus R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$ is simple. If the characteristic is three we use the same argument with $\mathfrak{D}_{0}=\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}=R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right) / \Phi 1$ to prove $\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J}) / \Phi 1$ is simple. Now let $\mathfrak{B}$ be a subspace $\neq 0$ invariant under $\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$. Then $\mathfrak{B}$ is invariant under Der $\mathfrak{J}$ so either $\mathfrak{B}=\Phi 1, \mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{J}$
or $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{J}$, by Theorem 17. Now $\mathfrak{B}=\Phi 1$ is ruled out since $\mathfrak{B} R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right) \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$. Also $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is impossible since this and $\mathfrak{B} R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right) \subseteq \mathfrak{B}$ would imply that $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}$ is a subalgebra, which is clearly not so. Hence $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{J}$ is irreducible under $\mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$.

We note that by Theorem 6.11 (p. 257) if the base field is infinite then $\mathscr{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{B}(\mathfrak{J})$ coincide respectively with $\mathfrak{M}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ and $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ the Lie algebras of linear transformations having the generic norm as Lie invariant and Lie semi-invariant.

Finally, we consider the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ defined by the Tits-Koecher construction from the finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{J}$. We have seen that $\mathfrak{J}$ central simple implies that $\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{J})$ is central simple. Also the definition $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})=\mathfrak{J} \oplus \overline{\mathfrak{J}} \oplus \mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{J})$ shows that $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{R}(\mathfrak{J})=27+27+79 =133$. It can be seen that the simple Lie algebras Der $\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{L}_{0}(\mathfrak{J})$ (for characteristic $\neq 3)$ and $\Re(\mathfrak{J})$ are of types $F_{4}, E_{6}$ and $E_{7}$ respectively. This is easily seen, from the Cartan decompositions relative to suitable Cartan subalgebras. We shall indicate this in the exercises.

## Exercises

1. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a reduced, simple exceptional Jordan algebra, $\left\{e_{i}\right\}$ a reducing set of idempotents for $\mathfrak{J} . \mathcal{L}_{i} \operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \sum \Phi e_{i}$ be subalgebra of Der $\mathfrak{J}$ such that $e_{i} D=0$. Show that $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \sum \Phi e_{i}$ is isomorphic to the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{D}, n)$ of linear transformations in the octonion coefficient algebra $\mathfrak{D}$ which are skew relative to the norm form $n$ in $\mathfrak{D}$.
2. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ as in exercise 1 be split and let $\mathfrak{H}$ be a splitting Cartan subalgebra of the subalgebra Der $\mathfrak{J} / \sum \Phi e_{i}$. Show that this is a splitting Cartan subalgebra for Der $\mathfrak{J}$. Determine the corresponding roots and show that $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$ is of type $F_{4}$ (cf. the author's Lie Algebras, pp. 144-145).
3. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ and $\mathfrak{H}$ be as in exercise 2 and let $\tilde{\mathfrak{H}}=\mathfrak{H}+R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} \cap \sum \Phi e_{i}\right)$ where $R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime} \cap \sum \Phi e_{i}\right)$ denotes the set $R_{b}, b \in \mathfrak{J}^{\prime} \cap \sum \Phi e_{i}$. Show that if the characteristic is $\neq 3$ then $\tilde{\mathfrak{H}}$ is a splitting Cartan subalgebra whose corresponding root system is of type $E_{6}$.
4. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be as in exercise 2. Determine a Cartan subalgebra for $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ and show that $\mathfrak{M}(\mathfrak{J})$ is split of type $E_{7}$.
5. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebra, $\Re$ a separable cubic subfield of $\mathfrak{J}$ and let $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K}$ be the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$ mapping $\mathfrak{K}$ into 0 . Show that $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K}$ is a central simple Lie algebra of type $D_{4}$ in the sense that $(\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K})_{\Omega}$ for $\Omega$ the algebraic closure of $\Phi$ is the simple Lie algebra $D_{4}$. Prove that $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J} / \mathfrak{K}$ is not isomorphic to a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{S}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where ( $\mathfrak{A}, J$ ) is a central simple associative algebra with involution.
6. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be as in exercise $1, e$ a primitive idempotent and let $\varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ be defined by $\mathfrak{J}$ and $e$ as in the text. Show that $\varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ is a subsystem of the Lie triple system $(\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J})^{(2)}$. Use Theorem 8.2 (p. 313) to show that Der $\mathfrak{J}$ is the universal Lie envelope for $\varepsilon\left(\mathfrak{J}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ if the characteristic is 0 . Does this hold also for prime characteristic?
7. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be as in exercise 5 and let $\mathfrak{T}=R\left(\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}\right)$. Let $\alpha$ be a nonzero element of $\Phi$
and define the Lie triple system ( $\mathfrak{T}, \alpha$ ) as in exercise 4, (p. 312). Assume the characteristic is 0 and show that the universal Lie envelope of $(\mathfrak{T}, \alpha)$ is a simple Lie algebra of type $E_{6}$.
8. (Tomber). Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be as in exercise 1, $\Phi$ algebraically closed of characteristic 0 . Prove that every automorphism of $\operatorname{Der} \mathfrak{J}$ has the form $D \rightarrow \eta^{-1} D \eta$ where $\eta$ is a uniquely determined automorphism of $\mathfrak{J}$. Use this and "Galois cohomology" (see Chapter X of the author's Lie algebras) to prove that if $\mathfrak{L}$ is a Lie algebra over a field $\Phi$ of characteristic 0 such that $\mathcal{L}_{\Omega}$ for $\Omega$ the algebraic closure of $\Phi$ is isomorphic to Der $\tilde{\mathfrak{J}} / \Omega, \tilde{\mathfrak{J}}$ the reduced exceptional simple Jordan algebra over $\Omega$ then $\mathfrak{L}$ is isomorphic to a Lie algebra Der $\mathfrak{J}$ where $\mathfrak{J}$ is a finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebra.
9. Exceptional Jordan division algebras. The first examples of finite-dimensional exceptional Jordan division algebras were given by Albert in [25]. In this paper Albert studied the finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebras which contain a given cyclic cubic field. This study was continued in [32] which gave a construction also of the finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebras containing a given cubic noncyclic subfield. In both of Albert's constructions the algebras were given as fixed point sets of semilinear automorphisms of an extension algebra. In this section we shall give two constructions of finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebras which have been communicated to the author by Tits and which are considerably simpler than Albert's. The first construction, as we shall see, gives all the finite-dimensional exceptional central simple Jordan algebras containing a given subalgebra of the form $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$where $\mathfrak{A}$ is a nine-dimensional central simple associative algebra. It is easy to give the conditions that such an algebra be a division algebra and to construct division algebras of this type over appropriate base fields.

Tits' second construction gives all the finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebras containing a given subalgebra of the form $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $\mathfrak{A}$ is nine-dimensional simple associative with center a quadratic field and $J$ is an involution of second kind. Since, as is easily seen, every finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebra contains subalgebras of the form $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$ or of the form $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ as indicated, Tits' constructions give all the finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebras. Both of Tits' constructions are rational in the sense that they do not require an extension of the base field for their definition.

In this section we shall study in some detail the algebras obtained from Tits' first construction. Since an algebra of the second type becomes one of the first type if one makes a suitable quadratic field extension, one can use the first construction alone to derive the main results on exceptional Jordan division algebras. Hence the second construction will not be essential for our purposes and so we shall be content to indicate this only in the exercises at the end of the section.

We proceed to give Tits' first construction. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a nine-dimensional central simple associative algebra, $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$the corresponding Jordan algebra. Then $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$are of degree three. If $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$ we define $a \times b=a . b-\frac{1}{2} t(a) b-\frac{1}{2} t(b) a +\frac{1}{2}(t(a) t(b)-t(a . b)) 1$ (as in §1) so $a \times a=\operatorname{adj} a$. Also we define $\bar{a}=a \times 1 =\frac{1}{2} t(a) 1-\frac{1}{2} a$. Let $\mu$ be a nonzero element of $\Phi$ and let $\mathfrak{A}_{0}, \mathfrak{A}_{1}, \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ be three copies of $\mathfrak{A}: \mathfrak{A}_{i}$ is a vector space and we have a linear isomorphism $a \rightarrow a_{i}$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$. We now put $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)=\mathfrak{A}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ and we define a product in ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mu$ ) so that $\mathfrak{A}_{i} \cdot \mathfrak{A}_{j} \subseteq \mathfrak{A}_{i+j}$ where the subscripts are reduced modulo three and where multiplication of $a_{i}, a_{i}{ }^{\prime}, b_{i}, b_{i}{ }^{\prime}, c_{i}, c_{i}{ }^{\prime} \in \mathfrak{A}_{i}$ is given by the following table:

|  | $a^{\prime}{ }_{0}$ | $b^{\prime}{ }_{1}$ | $c^{\prime}{ }_{2}$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| $a_{0}$ | $a \cdot a^{\prime}$ | $\bar{a} b^{\prime}$ | $c^{\prime} \bar{a}$ |
| $b_{1}$ | $\overline{a^{\prime} b}$ | $\mu b \times b^{\prime}$ | $\overline{b c^{\prime}}$ |
| $c_{2}$ | $c \overline{a^{\prime}}$ | $\overline{b^{\prime} c}$ | $\mu^{-1} c \times c^{\prime}$ |

Here the subscripts in the body of the table have been omitted since these can be immediately supplied by using $\mathfrak{A}_{i} \mathfrak{A}_{j} \subseteq \mathfrak{A}_{i+j}$. Thus we have the complete product formula:

$$
\begin{align*}
\left(a_{0}+b_{1}+c_{2}\right) \cdot\left(a_{0}{ }^{\prime}\right. & \left.+b_{1}{ }^{\prime}+c_{2}{ }^{\prime}\right) \\
= & \left(a \cdot a^{\prime}+\overline{b c^{\prime}}+\overline{b^{\prime} c}\right)_{0}+\left(\bar{a} b^{\prime}+\overline{a^{\prime} b}+\mu^{-1} c \times c^{\prime}\right)_{1}  \tag{61}\\
& +\left(c^{\prime} \bar{a}+c \overline{a^{\prime}}+\mu b \times b^{\prime}\right)_{2}
\end{align*}
$$

It is clear that $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$ is a commutative algebra.
We now note that if $u$ is an invertible element in the associative algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ then $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu) \cong(\mathfrak{A}, \mu n(u))$ where $n(u)$ is the generic norm of $u$ as defined in $\mathfrak{A}$. Observe first that if $a$ and $b$ are elements of a finite-dimensional associative algebra with 1 then

$$
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{adj}(a b)=(\operatorname{adj} b)(\operatorname{adj} a) . \tag{62}
\end{equation*}
$$

It is sufficient to prove this for invertible elements and for these we have $(a b) \operatorname{adj}(a b)=n(a b)$ and $(a b)(\operatorname{adj} b)(\operatorname{adj} a)=n(b) n(a)=n(a b)$ so (62) is valid. The formula (62) in $\mathfrak{A}$ gives the following formulas:

$$
\begin{align*}
u^{-1} a \times u^{-1} b & =n(u)^{-1}(a \times b) u  \tag{63}\\
a u \times b u & =n(u) u^{-1}(a \times b)
\end{align*}
$$

for arbitrary $a, b$ and invertible $u$. These and the relation $\overline{u^{-1} a u}=u^{-1} \bar{a} u$ imply that we have the following multiplication table in $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$ :

|  | $\left(u^{-1} a^{\prime} u\right)_{0}$ | $\left(u^{-1} b^{\prime}\right)_{1}$ | $\left(c^{\prime} u\right)_{2}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\left(u^{-1} a u\right)_{0}$ | $u^{-1}\left(a \cdot a^{\prime}\right) u$ | $u^{-1} \bar{a} b^{\prime}$ | $c^{\prime} \bar{a} u$ |
| $\left(u^{-1} b\right)_{1}$ | $u^{-1} \overline{a^{\prime}} b$ | $\mu n(u)^{-1}\left(b \times b^{\prime}\right) u$ | $\overline{u^{-1} b c^{\prime} u}$ |
| $(c u)_{2}$ | $c \overline{a^{\prime}} u$ | $\overline{u^{-1} b^{\prime} c u}$ | $\mu^{-1} n(u) u^{-1}\left(c \times c^{\prime}\right)$ |

It is clear from this table that we have an isomorphism of ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mu$ ) onto ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mu n(u)^{-1}$ ) such that $\left(u^{-1} a u\right)_{0}+\left(u^{-1} b\right)_{1}+(c u)_{2} \rightarrow a_{0}+b_{1}+c_{2}$. In particular, if $\delta$ is any nonzero element of $\Phi$ then ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mu$ ) and ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mu \delta^{-3}$ ) are isomorphic. Hence if $\mu$ is a cube in $\Phi$ then $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu) \cong(\mathfrak{A}, 1)$.

We shall now show that if $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of $\Phi$ then $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)_{\Omega}$ is the split exceptional simple Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$. This will imply that $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$ is a finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebra. We shall do this by beginning at the other end with $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ and showing that if we take $\mathfrak{A}_{0}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathbf{P}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ where $\mathbf{P} \cong \Phi \oplus \Phi$ then we can choose subspaces $\mathfrak{A}_{1}, \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ in $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ such that we have the multiplication table (60) with $\mu=1$ for these subspaces.

We need first a multiplication table for a split octonion algebra which is a little more explicit than the one we encountered in §5. For this purpose we let $(\mathfrak{Q}, j)$ be any quaternion algebra and we make the standard construction of the octonion algebra $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{Q} \oplus \mathfrak{Q} l$ as on $\mathrm{p} . \quad$, where we now suppose that $l^{2}=1$. Then it is clear that $\mathfrak{D}$ is split. Put $u_{1}=\frac{1}{2}(1+l), u_{2}=\frac{1}{2}(1-l)$. Then the $u_{i}$ are orthogonal idempotents, $u_{1}+u_{2}=1, \bar{u}_{1}=u_{2}, \bar{u}_{2}=u_{1}$. Moreover, if $\mathfrak{Q}_{0}$ denotes the set of elements of trace 0 in $\mathfrak{Q}$ then we have

$$
\begin{equation*}
O=\Phi u_{1} \oplus \Phi u_{2} \oplus \mathfrak{Q}_{0} u_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{Q}_{0} u_{2} . \tag{65}
\end{equation*}
$$

If $b \in \mathfrak{Q}_{0}$ then $u_{1} b=\frac{1}{2}(1+l) b=\frac{1}{2} b-\frac{1}{2} b l=\frac{1}{2} b(1-l)=b u_{2}$ and similarly $u_{2} b=b u_{1}$. It follows that $\mathfrak{Q}_{0} u_{1}=u_{2} \mathfrak{D} u_{1}, \mathfrak{Q}_{0} u_{2}=u_{1} \mathfrak{D} u_{2}$ so (64) is the Peirce decomposition of $\mathfrak{O}$ relative to the $u_{i}$. If $b_{i} \in \mathfrak{Q}_{0}$ then the multiplication formulas in O give

$$
\begin{align*}
& \left(b_{1} u_{i}\right)\left(b_{2} u_{i}\right)=\left(b_{1} \wedge b_{2}\right) u_{j}  \tag{66}\\
& \left(b_{1} u_{i}\right)\left(b_{2} u_{j}\right)=-n\left(b_{1}, b_{2}\right) u_{j} \tag{67}
\end{align*}
$$

where $i \neq j$ and $b_{1} \wedge b_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left[b_{1}, b_{2}\right]$ (cf. (48)). Now suppose $\mathfrak{Q}$ is the usual quaternion algebra with the basis $\left(1, x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right)$ where $\bar{x}_{i}=-x_{i}, x_{i}{ }^{2}=-1, x_{i} x_{j}=-x_{j} x_{i} =x_{k},(i, j, k)$ a cyclic permutation of $(1,2,3)$. Then in $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{Q}_{0}$ we have the usual metric $n\left(\sum_{1}^{3} \xi_{i} x_{i}\right)=\sum \xi_{i}{ }^{2}$ and $b_{1} \wedge b_{2}$ is the usual cross product of vectors in three-dimensional (Euclidean) space since $x_{t} \wedge x_{j}=x_{k}$.

We now consider the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$ where $\mathfrak{O}$ is the split octonion algebra so $\mathfrak{D}=\Phi u_{1} \oplus \Phi u_{2} \oplus \mathfrak{B} u_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{V} u_{2}$ where $\mathfrak{V}$ is the three-dimensional space as just indicated. Put $\mathbf{P}=\Phi u_{1} \oplus \Phi u_{2}, \mathfrak{A}_{0}=\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathrm{P}_{3}, J_{1}\right), \mathfrak{A}_{1}=\left(\mathfrak{B} u_{1}\right)[12]+\left(\mathfrak{B} u_{1}\right)[23] +\left(\mathfrak{B} u_{1}\right)[31], \mathfrak{A}_{2}=\left(\mathfrak{B} u_{2}\right)[12]+\left(\mathfrak{B} u_{2}\right)[23]+\left(\mathfrak{B} u_{2}\right)[31]$ where $\left(\mathfrak{B} u_{i}\right)[j k] =\left\{w[j k] \mid w \in \mathfrak{B} u_{i}\right\}$. We now define linear mappings $X=\sum \xi_{i j} e_{i j} \rightarrow X_{i}$ of $\mathfrak{A}=\Phi_{3}$ onto $\mathfrak{U}_{i}$ by the following formulas:

$$
\begin{align*}
X_{0}= & \sum \xi_{i i} e_{i i}+\left(\xi_{12} u_{1}+\xi_{21} u_{2}\right)[12]+\left(\xi_{23} u_{1}+\xi_{32} u_{2}\right)  \tag{23}\\
& +\left(\xi_{31} u_{1}+\xi_{13} u_{2}\right)[31] \\
X_{1}= & -v_{3} u_{1}[12]-v_{1} u_{1}[23]-v_{2} u_{1}[31]
\end{align*}
$$

where $v_{i}=\sum_{j} \xi_{i j} x_{j},\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right)$ the above basis for $\mathfrak{B}$,

$$
X_{2}=-v_{3}^{\prime} u_{2}[12]-v_{1}^{\prime} u_{2}[23]-v_{2}^{\prime} u_{2}[31], \quad v_{i}^{\prime}=\sum_{j} \xi_{j i} x_{j} .
$$

We have seen on p. 127 that $X \rightarrow X_{0}$ is an isomorphism of $\Phi_{3}{ }^{+}$onto $\mathfrak{A}_{0}$. By (66) we have $X_{1}^{\cdot 2}=-\left(v_{1} \wedge v_{2}\right) u_{2}[12]-\left(v_{2} \wedge v_{3}\right) u_{2}[23]-\left[v_{3} \wedge v_{1}\right] u_{2}[31]$. Since $X \times X \equiv \operatorname{adj} X=\sum \eta_{i j} e_{i j}$ where $\eta_{i j}=$ co-factor of $\xi_{j i}$ in $X$ we have $(X \times X)_{2}=X_{1} \cdot{ }^{2}$. Similarly, $(X \times X)_{1}=X_{2} \cdot{ }^{2}$. Now for $i \neq j$ and $a, b \in \mathfrak{D}$, $a[i j] . b[i j]=n(a, b)\left(e_{i i}+e_{j j}\right)$ and $n(a, b)=0$ if $a \in \Phi u_{1}+\Phi u_{2}$ and $b \in \mathfrak{V} u_{i}$. Hence if $A=\sum \alpha_{i j} e_{i j}$ and $B=\sum \beta_{i j} e_{i j}$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 A_{0} \cdot B_{1}= & -\left[\left(\alpha_{11}+\alpha_{22}\right) b_{3}-\alpha_{31} b_{1}-\alpha_{32} b_{2}\right] u[12] \\
& -\left[\left(\alpha_{22}+\alpha_{33}\right) b_{1}-\alpha_{12} b_{2}-\alpha_{13} b_{3}\right] u_{1}[23] \\
& -\left[\left(\alpha_{33}+\alpha_{11}\right) b_{2}-\alpha_{23} b_{3}-\alpha_{21} b_{1}\right] u_{1}[31]
\end{aligned}
$$

where $b_{i}=\sum_{j} \beta_{i j} x_{j}$. On the other hand,

$$
2 \bar{A}=t(A) 1-A=\left(\begin{array}{lll}
\alpha_{22}+\alpha_{33} & -\alpha_{12} & -\alpha_{13} \\
-\alpha_{21} & \alpha_{11}+\alpha_{33} & -\alpha_{23} \\
-\alpha_{31} & -\alpha_{32} & \alpha_{11}+\alpha_{22}
\end{array}\right)
$$

which implies that the row vectors of the matrix $2 \bar{A} B$ are respectively $\left(\alpha_{22}+\alpha_{33}\right) \beta_{1} -\alpha_{13} \beta_{2}-\alpha_{13} \beta_{3},-\alpha_{21} \beta_{1}+\left(\alpha_{11}+\alpha_{33}\right) \beta_{2}-\alpha_{23} \beta_{3},-\alpha_{31} \beta_{1}-\alpha_{32} \beta_{2} +\left(\alpha_{11}+\alpha_{22}\right) \beta_{3}$ where $\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}, \beta_{3}$ are the row vectors of $B$. It follows that $A_{0} . B_{1} =(\bar{A} B)_{1}$. Similarly, we have $A_{0} \cdot B_{2}=(B \bar{A})_{2}$. Next let $a_{i}=\sum_{j} \alpha_{i j} v_{j}, b_{i}{ }^{\prime}=\sum_{j} \beta_{j i} v_{j}$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 A_{1} \cdot B_{2}=2 & \left(a_{3} u_{1}[12]+a_{1} u_{1}[23]+\right. \\
& \left.+a_{2} u_{1}[31]\right) \cdot\left(b_{3}{ }^{\prime} u_{2}[12]\right. \\
= & \left(n\left(a_{3}, b_{3}{ }^{\prime}\right)+n\left(a_{2}, b_{2}{ }^{\prime}\right)\right) e_{11}+\left(n\left(a_{1}, b_{1}{ }^{\prime}\right)+n\left(a_{3}, b_{3}{ }^{\prime}\right)\right) e_{22} \\
& +\left(n\left(a_{2}, b_{2}{ }^{\prime}\right)+n\left(a_{1}, b_{1}{ }^{\prime}\right)\right) e_{33}-\left(n\left(a_{1}, b_{2}{ }^{\prime}\right) u_{2}+n\left(a_{2}, b_{1}{ }^{\prime}\right) u_{1}\right)[21] \\
& -\left(n\left(a_{2}, b_{3}{ }^{\prime}\right) u_{2}+n\left(a_{3}, b_{2}{ }^{\prime}\right) u_{1}\right)[32]-\left(n\left(a_{3}, b_{1}{ }^{\prime}\right) u_{2}+n\left(a_{1}, b_{3}{ }^{\prime}\right) u_{1}\right)[13] .
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $n\left(a_{i}, b_{j}{ }^{\prime}\right)=\sum_{k} \alpha_{i k} \beta_{k j}$ one sees easily that $A_{1} \cdot B_{2}=(\overline{A B})_{0}$. It is clear from the formulas we have just derived and (60) that if $\mathfrak{O}$ is the split octonion algebra then $\mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right) \cong\left(\Phi_{3}, 1\right)$. This implies

Theorem 19. The algebra ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mu$ ) where $\mathfrak{A}$ is a nine-dimensional central simple associative algebra and $\mu \neq 0$ is in $\Phi$ is a finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebra.

Proof. If $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of $\Phi$ then $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)_{\Omega}=\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}, \mu\right) \cong\left(\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}, 1\right) =\left(\Omega_{3}, 1\right) \cong \mathfrak{H}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{3}, J_{1}\right)$. Hence the result is clear.

We determine next the conditions that ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mu$ ) is a division algebra and the structure of ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mu$ ) if this is not a division algebra. The result is the following

Theorem 20. Necessary and sufficient conditions that $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$ is a division algebra are: $\mathfrak{A}$ is a division algebra and $\mu$ is not a (generic) norm of an element of $\mathfrak{A}$. If $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$ is not a division algebra then this algebra is split.

Proof. Suppose first that $\mathfrak{A}$ is a division algebra but $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$ is not. Then $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$ contains an idempotent $e \neq 0,1$ and $e=a_{0}+b_{1}+c_{2}$ where either $b \neq 0$ or $c \neq 0$ since $\mathfrak{A}_{0} \cong \mathfrak{A}^{+}$has no idempotents $\neq 0,1$. By (60), we have $a^{\cdot 2}+2 \overline{b c}=a$, $2 \bar{a} b+\mu^{-1} c \times c=b, 2 c \bar{a}+\mu b \times b=c$. If we multiply the second of these equations on the left by $c$ and the third on the right by $b$ we obtain $2 c \bar{a} b+\mu^{-1} n(c) =c b, 2 c \bar{a} b+\mu n(b)=c b$. Then $\mu n(b)=\mu^{-1} n(c)$. Since $\mathfrak{A}$ is a division algebra $n(b)=0$ implies $b=0$. Hence $n(b) \neq 0$ and $n(c) \neq 0$. Then $\mu^{2}=n(c) n(b)^{-1} =n\left(c b^{-1}\right)$. This implies that $\mu=n\left(\mu b c^{-1}\right)$. Hence if $\mathfrak{A}$ is a division algebra and $\mu$ is not a norm of an element of $\mathfrak{A}$ then $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$ contains no idempotents $\neq 0,1$ and so $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$ is a division algebra. It is clear also that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is not a division algebra then $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$ is not since this contains a subalgebra isomorphic to $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$. Now assume $\mathfrak{A}$ is a division algebra and $\mu=n(c)$ for some $c \in \mathfrak{A}$. Then, as we have seen above, $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu) \cong(\mathfrak{A}, 1)$. Now in ( $\mathfrak{A}, 1$ ) consider the element $f=1_{0}+1_{1}+1_{2}$. Then it is immediate from the multiplication table (60) that $f^{.2}=3 f$. This shows that ( $\mathfrak{A}, 1$ ) and, consequently, ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mu$ ) is not a division algebra. It remains to prove the last statement that if ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mu$ ) is not a division algebra then this Jordan algebra is split. Since a finite-dimensional exceptional central simple Jordan algebra which contains a subalgebra isomorphic to $\Phi_{3}+$ is split we may assume that $\mathfrak{A}$ is a division algebra. Let $\Gamma$ be a cubic subfield of $\mathfrak{A}$. Then $\Gamma$ is a splitting field for $\mathfrak{A}$ : $\mathfrak{A}_{\Gamma} \cong \Gamma_{3}$. Then $\Gamma$ is a splitting field for $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$, that is, $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)_{\Gamma}$ is split. On the other hand, ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mu$ ) is reduced and the condition that such an algebra is split is that the quadratic form $Q=\frac{1}{2} t$ has maximal Witt index on the subspace $\mathfrak{T}$ orthogonal to a reducing set of idempotents (ex. 6, p. 832). Then the extension of $Q$ on $\mathfrak{T}_{\Gamma}$ has maximal Witt index. Since $\Gamma$ is odd dimensional it follows from a theorem due to Springer [3] that $Q$ has maximal Witt index on $\mathfrak{T}$ and so $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$ is split.

To actually construct a division algebra ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mu$ ) we shall make use of the following

Lemma 1. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a finite-dimensional strictly power associative division algebra over $\Phi$ (see p. 227), $\xi$ an indeterminate. Then $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}$ for $\mathbf{P}=\Phi(\xi)$ is a division algebra and $\xi$ is not a (generic) norm in $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}$ if $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A}>1$.

Proof. Let $\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \cdots, u_{n}\right)$ be a basis for $\mathfrak{A} / \Phi, m$ the degree of $\mathfrak{A}$. Any element of $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}=\mathfrak{A}_{\mathbf{P}}$ has the form $\tilde{a}=\sum \rho_{i}(\xi) u_{i}$ where $\rho_{i}(\xi)$ is a rational expression in $\xi$ with coefficients in $\Phi$. If the generic norm $n(\tilde{a})=0$ for $\tilde{a} \neq 0$ we may assume the $\rho_{i}(\xi)$ are polynomials in $\xi$ and not every $\rho_{i}(\xi)$ is divisible by $\xi$. Then $\boldsymbol{a}=\sum \rho_{\boldsymbol{i}}(0) \boldsymbol{u}_{\boldsymbol{i}} \neq 0$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ and $n(a)=0$ contrary to the assumption that $\mathfrak{A}$ is a division algebra. Hence $\tilde{a} \neq 0$ in $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}$ implies $n(\tilde{a}) \neq 0$ so $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}$ is a division algebra. Now assume $\xi=n(\tilde{a}), \tilde{a}=\sum \rho_{i}(\xi) u_{i}$. Let $v(\xi)$ be a least common multiple of the denominators of the $\rho_{i}(\xi)$. Then we have $\xi v(\xi)^{m}=n\left(\sum \sigma_{i}(\xi) u_{i}\right)$ where the $\sigma_{i}(\xi)$ are polynomials in $\xi$. If $\xi$ is a common factor of the $\sigma_{i}(\xi)$ then $n\left(\sum \sigma_{i}(\xi) u_{i}\right)=\xi^{m} n\left(\sum \sigma_{i}{ }^{\prime}(\xi) u_{i}\right)$ where the $\sigma_{i}{ }^{\prime}(\xi)$ are polynomials. If we assume $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A}>1$ then $m>1$ and so the relation $\xi v(\xi)^{m}=\xi^{m} n\left(\sum \sigma_{i}{ }^{\prime}(\xi) u_{i}\right)$ implies that $\xi \mid v(\xi)$. Then $\xi^{m} \mid v(\xi)^{m}$ and we can cancel the $\xi^{m}$. Continuing in this way we may assume that $\xi \nu(\xi)^{m}=n\left(\sum \sigma_{i}(\xi) u_{i}\right)$ where the $\sigma_{i}(\xi)$ are polynomials in $\xi$ and not every $\sigma_{i}(\xi)$ is divisible by $\xi$. Then $a=\sum \sigma_{i}(0) u_{i} \neq 0$ and $n(a)=0$ contrary to the assumption that $\mathfrak{A}$ is a division algebra.

We can now prove the following theorem which is an immediate consequence of Lemma 1 and the criterion given in Theorem 20.

Theorem 21 (Albert). Let $\Phi$ be a field such that there exists a nine-dimensional central associative division algebra over $\Phi$. Then there exist finite-dimensional central exceptional Jordan division algebras over $\mathbf{P}=\Phi(\xi), \xi$ an indeterminate.

Proof. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a nine-dimensional associative central division algebra over $\Phi$. Then the algebra ( $\mathfrak{U}_{\mathbf{P}}, \xi$ ) is an exceptional central Jordan division algebra.

Examples of fields $\Phi$ satisfying the conditions of the theorem are: $\Phi$, the rationals and $\Phi$, any $p$-adic field.

Now let $\mathfrak{J}$ be any finite-dimensional exceptional central simple Jordan algebra. Assume $\mathfrak{J}$ contains a subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}_{0}$ isomorphic to an algebra $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$where $\mathfrak{A}$ is a central simple associative algebra of degree three. We shall show that $\mathfrak{J}$ is isomorphic to an algebra of the form ( $\mathfrak{A}, \mu$ ). For the proof of this we shall need to apply the theory of bimodules for the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$.

We recall that any unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$is a unital right module for the unital universal multiplication envelope $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{A}^{+}\right)$. By Theorems 7.8 and 7.10, $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{A}^{+}\right) \cong S_{1}{ }^{\prime \prime}\left(\mathfrak{A}^{+}\right)$is a direct sum of five central simple ideals of dimensionalilties $9^{2}, 6^{2}, 6^{2}, 3^{2}, 3^{2}$ respectively. Corresponding to these we have five isomorphism classes of irreducible unital bimodules for the Jordan algebra $\mathfrak{U}^{+}$. We recall also that the component of $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{A}^{+}\right)$of dimensionality $9^{2}$ is $\Phi_{9}$ and a representa-
tive of the corresponding isomorphism class of irreducible unital bimodules is the regular bimodule $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$.

We now construct the Jordan algebra $(\mathfrak{A}, 1)=\mathfrak{A}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ as before. It is clear from the multiplication table $\mathfrak{A}_{i} \cdot \mathfrak{A}_{j} \subseteq \mathfrak{A}_{\boldsymbol{i}_{\boldsymbol{+}}}$ that the $\mathfrak{A}_{\boldsymbol{i}}$ are sub-bimodules of $(\mathfrak{A}, 1)$ considered as unital bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}_{0}$ under the usual action. The table (60) shows that these bimodules for $\mathfrak{A}^{+} \cong \mathfrak{A}_{0}$ can be identified as vector spaces with $\mathfrak{A}$ where the actions in the three cases are respectively x.a, $\bar{a} x$ and $x \bar{a}, x$ in the bimodule, $a$ in $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$. In this way we obtain three bimodules, the first of which is the regular bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$. We shall call the second and third the left and right bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$. The sub-bimodules of the left (right) bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$are the left (right) ideals so this bimodule is irreducible or a direct sum of three isomorphic irreducible bimodules according as $\mathfrak{U}$ is a division algebra or $\mathfrak{A} \cong \Phi_{3}$. Since the regular bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$is nine dimensional and remains irreducible on extension of the base field to its algebraic closure while the left and right bimodules decompose as direct sums of three-dimensional submodules on extension of the base field to its algebraic closure, it is clear that the regular bimodule is not isomorphic to an irreducible component of the left or right bimodules for $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$. We note next that the irreducible bimodules provided by the left and right bimodules are not isomorphic. To prove this it is sufficient to show that the left and right bimodules are not isomorphic. Suppose they are. Then we have a bijective linear mapping $S$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $(\bar{a} x) S=(x S) \bar{a}, a, x \in \mathfrak{A}$. Since $a \rightarrow \ddot{a}$ is surjective this gives $(a x) S=(x S) a, a, x \in \mathfrak{A}$. Putting $x=1$ gives $a S=(1 S) a$ or $x S=(1 S) x$. Then $(a x) S=(1 S)(a x)$ and $(x S) a=(1 S)(x a)$, so $(1 S)(a x)=(1 S)(x a)$. Since $x S=(1 S) x$ and $S$ is bijective, $1 S$ is invertible. Hence we have $a x=x a, a, x \in \mathfrak{A}$, which contradicts the fact that $\mathfrak{A}$ is central simple and $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{U}>1$.

It is clear that the subalgebra of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A})$ generated by the mappings $x \rightarrow \bar{a} x(x \rightarrow x \bar{a})$ is the set $\mathfrak{A}_{L}\left(\mathfrak{A}_{R}\right)$ of left (right) multiplications. Since $\mathfrak{A}_{L} \cong \mathfrak{A}_{R}^{0}$ and $\mathfrak{A}_{R} \cong \mathfrak{A}$ it is clear that the simple component of $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{A}^{+}\right)$corresponding to the irreducible bimodules of the left and the right bimodule for $\mathfrak{A}$ are isomorphic to $\mathfrak{A}^{0}$ and $\mathfrak{A}$ respectively. Since $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{A}=3^{2}$ this identifies the components of dimensionality $3^{2}$.

Now suppose that $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$is imbedded as a subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}_{0}$ of a finite-dimensional central simple exceptional Jordan algebra. Then the isomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$and $\mathfrak{A}_{0}$ permits us to regard $\mathfrak{J}$ as unital $\mathfrak{U}^{+}$-bimodule in the obvious way. We claim that this bimodule has the structure $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{A}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ where $\mathfrak{A}_{0}, \mathfrak{A}_{1}, \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ are sub-bimodules isomorphic to the regular, left and right bimodules respectively for $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$. If $\mathfrak{J}$ is split this is clear since in this case $\mathfrak{J} \cong(\mathfrak{A}, 1)=\mathfrak{A}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ and the identity isomorphism on the common subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}_{0}$ can be extended to an isomorphism of ( $\mathfrak{A}, 1$ ) onto $\mathfrak{J}$. This gives an $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$-bimodule isomorphism of $(\mathfrak{A}, 1)=\mathfrak{A}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ onto $\mathfrak{J}$ and establishes our assertion on $\mathfrak{J}$. Also, we see that in the split case the subalgebra $\mathfrak{E}$ of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Phi}(\mathfrak{J}, \mathfrak{J})$ generated by the
mappings corresponding to the elements of $\mathfrak{U}^{+}$is isomorphic to $\Phi_{9} \oplus \mathfrak{U} \oplus \mathfrak{U}^{0}$ Now let $\mathfrak{J}$ be arbitrary and consider the algebra of linear transformations $\mathfrak{E}$ just defined. Since $\mathfrak{E}$ is a homomorphic image of $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{A}^{+}\right), \mathfrak{E}$ is a direct sum of certain of the five simple components of $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{U}^{+}\right)$. On the other hand, if $\Omega$ is the algebraic closure of $\Phi$ then $\mathfrak{F}_{\Omega} \cong \Omega_{9} \oplus \Omega_{3} \oplus \Omega_{3}$. It follows that $\mathfrak{E} \cong \Phi_{9} \oplus \mathfrak{A} \oplus \mathfrak{A}^{0}$. This in turn implies that $\mathfrak{J}$ as $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$-bimodule is a direct sum of irreducible subbimodules isomorphic to the regular, left and right bimodules for $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is split, $\mathfrak{J}$ is split and the desired decomposition holds for $\mathfrak{J}$. If $\mathfrak{A}$ is a division algebra then the left and right bimodules are irreducible so again we have $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{A}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ where these are isomorphic to the regular, left and right bimodules for $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$respectively. We note also that in all cases the subbimodules $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ of $\mathfrak{J}$ are uniquely determined as the homogeneous components of $\mathfrak{J}$ as completely reducible right $U_{1}\left(\mathfrak{U}^{+}\right)$-module (cf. Jacobson, Structure of Rings, p. 63).

The decomposition $\mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{A}_{0} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{1} \oplus \mathfrak{A}_{2}$ gives a linear isomorphism $\eta_{i}, i=0,1,2$, of $\mathfrak{A}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}_{i}$ such that $\eta_{0}$ is an algebra isomorphism of $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$onto $\mathfrak{A}_{0}$ and we have $x^{\eta_{1}} \cdot a^{\eta_{0}}=(\bar{a} x)^{\eta_{1}}, x^{\eta_{2}} \cdot a^{\eta_{0}}=(x \bar{a})^{\eta_{2}}, a, x \in \mathfrak{A}$. This shows that we have the first row and column of the multiplication table (60). We shall now show that we can modify $\eta_{1}$ so that we have the complete table (60) (for the $\eta_{i}$ in place of the mappings $a \rightarrow a_{i}$ ). We now consider the extension algebra $\tilde{\mathfrak{J}} \equiv \tilde{\mathfrak{J}}_{\Omega}=\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}_{0} \oplus \tilde{\mathfrak{A}}_{1} \oplus \tilde{\mathfrak{A}}_{2}$ where $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}_{i}=\mathfrak{A}_{i \Omega}$ and we let $\eta_{i}$ denote the $\Omega$-linear extension of $\eta_{i}$ to $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}=\mathfrak{A}_{\Omega}$ onto $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}_{i}$. Then $\eta_{0}$ is an algebra isomorphism and the foregoing formulas hold for $x, a \in \tilde{\mathfrak{A}}$. Now form the Jordan algebra $(\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}, 1)=\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}_{0} \oplus \tilde{\mathfrak{A}}_{1} \oplus \tilde{\mathfrak{A}}_{2}$ using the mapping $\eta_{i}$ for the mappings $a \rightarrow a_{i}$ given initially and the multiplication table (60). Then $\tilde{\mathfrak{J}} \cong(\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}, 1)$ and so the identity mapping on $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}_{0}$ can be extended to an isomorphism $\lambda$ of ( $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}, 1$ ) onto $\tilde{\mathfrak{J}}$. Since the spaces $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}_{i}$ in the two algebras are the homogeneous components of the algebras as bimodules for $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}^{+}$and these correspond respectively to the regular, left and right bimodules for $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}^{+}$it is clear that $\lambda$ maps $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}_{i}$ onto itself. Put $\zeta_{i}=\eta_{i} \lambda$, so $\zeta_{0}=\eta_{0}$, and $\zeta_{i}$ is a linear isomorphism of $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}$ onto $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}_{i}$. If $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$ we have $a^{\eta_{1}} \cdot b^{\eta_{1}}=(a \times b)^{\eta_{2}}$ in (A,1). Applying $\lambda$ gives $a^{\zeta_{1}} \cdot b^{\zeta_{1}}=(a \times b)^{\zeta_{2}}$ in $\mathcal{J}$. Similarly, we have $a^{\zeta_{2}} \cdot b^{\zeta_{2}}=(a \times b)^{\zeta_{1}}, a^{\zeta_{1}} \cdot b^{\zeta_{2}}=(\overline{a b})^{\zeta_{0}}$.

We now compare the mappings $\eta_{i}, \zeta_{i}$ as mappings into the algebra $\tilde{\mathfrak{J}}$. We have $a^{\eta_{0}} \cdot b^{\eta_{1}}=(\bar{a} b)^{\eta_{1}}, a^{\eta_{0}} \cdot b^{\zeta_{1}}=(\bar{a} b)^{\zeta_{1}}$. Hence $(\bar{a} b)^{\eta_{1} \zeta_{1}-1}=\left(a^{\eta_{0}} \cdot b^{\eta_{1}}\right)^{\zeta_{1}-1} =\left(a^{\eta_{0}} \cdot b^{\eta_{1} \zeta_{1}-{ }^{1} \zeta_{1}}\right)^{\zeta_{1}-1}=\left(\bar{a} b^{\eta_{1} \zeta_{1}-1}\right)$. Since this holds for all $a, b \in \tilde{\mathfrak{A}}$, it follows, as is well known, that there exists an invertible element $u \in \tilde{\mathfrak{A}}$ such that $b^{\eta_{1} \zeta_{1}-1} =b u, b \in \tilde{\mathfrak{A}}$. Then $b^{\eta_{1}}=(b u)^{\zeta_{1}}$ and $b^{\zeta_{1}}=\left(b u^{-1}\right)^{\eta_{1}}$. Similarly, there exists an invertible $v$ in $\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}$ such that $b^{\eta_{2}}=(v b)^{\zeta_{2}}, b^{\zeta_{2}}=\left(v^{-1} b\right)^{\eta_{2}}, b \in \tilde{\mathfrak{A}}$. .

Now let $a, b \in \mathfrak{A}$. Then $a^{\eta_{i}}, b^{\eta_{i}} \in \mathfrak{J}$ so $a^{\eta_{i}} \cdot b^{\eta_{j}} \in \mathfrak{J}$. Then $a^{\eta_{1}} \cdot b^{\eta_{1}}=(a u)^{\zeta_{1}} \cdot(b u)^{\zeta_{1}} =(a u \times b u)^{\zeta_{2}}=\left(n(u) u^{-1}(a \times b)\right)^{\zeta_{2}}=\left(n(u) v^{-1} u^{-1}(a \times b)\right)^{\eta_{2}}$ which implies that $n(u) v^{-1} u^{-1} \in \mathfrak{A}$. Similarly, the formula for $a^{\eta_{2}} \cdot b^{\eta_{2}}$ shows that $n(v)^{-1} v^{-1} u^{-1} \in \mathfrak{A}$ and that for $a^{\eta_{1}} \cdot b^{\eta_{2}}$ shows that $u v \in \mathfrak{A}$. Then $n(u), n(v) \in \Phi$ and $v^{-1} u^{-1} \in \mathfrak{A}$. If $w \in \mathfrak{A}$ the mapping $x \rightarrow x w$ is an automorphism of $\mathfrak{A}$ considered as left $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$-
bimodule. Hence we may replace the mapping $\eta_{1}$ by $\eta_{1}^{\prime}$ given by $x^{\eta_{1} \prime}=(x w)^{\eta_{1}}$. Taking $w=v^{-1} u^{-1}$ we obtain $b^{\eta_{1}{ }^{\prime}}=\left(b v^{-1}\right)^{\zeta_{1}}$. Then the element $u$ in the foregoing calculations is replaced by $v^{-1}$. Hence we obtain $a^{\eta_{1}{ }^{\prime}} . b^{\eta_{1}{ }^{\prime}}=n(v)^{-1}(a \times b)^{\eta_{2}}$, $a^{\eta_{2}} . b^{\eta_{2}}=n(v)(a \times b)^{\eta_{1}{ }^{\prime}}, a^{\eta_{1}{ }^{\prime}} . b^{\eta_{2}{ }^{\prime}}=(\overline{a b})^{\eta_{0}}$. These relations and the others involving $\eta_{0}$ implb that $\mathfrak{A} \cong\left(\mathfrak{A}_{0}, n(v)^{-1}\right)$. We have therefore proved the following

Theorem 22. Let I be a finite-dimensional exceptional central simple Jordan algebra. Assume $\mathfrak{J}$ contains a subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}_{0}$ isomorphic to $\mathfrak{A}^{+}$where $\mathfrak{A}$ is a central simple associative algebra of degree three. Then $\mathfrak{J} \cong(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$ for some $\mu \neq 0$ in $\Phi$.

We shall now seek to clarify the position of the algebras of the form $(\mathfrak{A}, \mu)$ in the general theory of exceptional Jordan division algebras. For the sake of simplicity (to avoid discussing inseparable elements) we assume the characteristic is not three. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional central exceptional Jordan division algebra. If $a \in \mathfrak{J}$ the minimum polynomial $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ of $a$ is irreducible. Hence the generic minimum polynomial $m_{a}(\lambda)$ is a power of $\mu_{a}(\lambda)$. Since the degree of $m_{a}(\lambda)$ is three we see that either $\mu_{a}(\lambda)=\lambda-\alpha$, which is the case if and only if $a=\alpha 1 \in \Phi 1$, or $m_{a}(\lambda)=\mu_{a}(\lambda)$ is of degree three. Thus any $a \notin \Phi 1$ generates a cubic subfield of $\mathfrak{J}$ and this is separable, since the characteristic is not three. We consider next the subalgebra generated by two elements in the following

Lemma 2. Let $\mathfrak{J}$ be a finite-dimensional central exceptional Jordan division algebra over a field of characteristic not three, $a$ and $b$ elements of $\mathfrak{J}$. Then the subalgebra $\mathfrak{K}$ generated by $a$ and $b$ is of one of the following types: (1) $\mathfrak{K}=\Phi 1$, (2) $\mathfrak{K}$ a separable cubic field, (3) $\mathfrak{K} \cong \mathfrak{U}^{+}$where $\mathfrak{U}$ is an associative division algebra of degree three, (4) $\mathfrak{K} \cong \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $\mathfrak{A}$ is an associative division algebra of degree three over its center, which is a quadratic field, and $J$ is an involution of second kind.

Proof. Suppose neither (1) nor (2) holds. Then $a \notin \Phi 1$ and $b \notin \Phi[a]$. Hence $\operatorname{dim} \Re>3$. Clearly $\mathfrak{K}$ is a special Jordan division algebra. We claim that this is central. Otherwise, we have an element $c$ in the center of $\mathfrak{K}$ such that $\Phi[c]$ is a separable cubic field. If $x \in \Re$ then $\left[x, c^{i}, c^{\cdot j}\right]=0$ for $i, j=0,1,2, \cdots$ and in $\Re_{\Omega}$ we have $\Omega[c]=\Omega e_{1}+\Omega e_{2}+\Omega e_{3}$ where the $e_{i}$ are nonzero orthogonal idempotents. Then $\left[x, e_{i}, e_{j}\right]=0$ which implies (via the Peirce decomposition relative to the $e_{i}$ ) that $x \in \Omega[c]$. Then $x \in \Phi[c]$, contrary to $\operatorname{dim} \Re>3$. Hence $\Re$ is central and clearly the degree of $\Re$ is three. We can now apply the classification of special central simple algebras given in §5.7 (cf. ex.1 on p. 211) to conclude that $\Re$ is of one of the types (3) or (4). ${ }^{1}$

[^19]Lemma 3. If $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)$ where $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple with center a quadratic field P and $J$ is an involution of second kind then $\mathfrak{K}_{\mathbf{P}} \cong(\mathfrak{A} / \mathrm{P})^{+}$. If $\mathfrak{K}$ is as in Lemma 2 then $\mathfrak{K}_{\Sigma}$ is a division algebra for any quadratic extension field $\Sigma$ of $\Phi$.

Proof. Let $\mathrm{P}=\Phi(u)$ where $u^{2} \in \Phi$ and $u^{J}=-u$. Then $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J) \oplus \mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J) u$. It follows from this that $\mathfrak{H}(\mathfrak{A}, J)_{\mathbf{P}} \cong(\mathfrak{A} / \mathrm{P})^{+}$. Now let $\mathfrak{K}$ be as in Lemma 2 and let $\Sigma$ be a quadratic field. If $\Omega$ is as in (1) or (2) then it is clear that $\Omega_{\Sigma}$ is a field. If $\mathfrak{R}$ is as in case (3), so $\mathfrak{K}=\mathfrak{U}^{+}$, where $\mathfrak{A}$ is an associative central division algebra of degree three, then $\mathfrak{A}_{\Sigma}$ is either a division algebra or $\mathfrak{A}_{\Sigma} \cong \Sigma_{3}$. The latter possibility is ruled out since the dimensionality of any splitting field for $\mathfrak{A}$ is $\geqq 3$.
